Batch execution sets two pressures against each other. As batch size \(\BatchSize\) grows from 1 to 128, throughput climbs with diminishing returns as fixed overheads are amortized. Batch service time expands steadily, so a latency budget caps how much of the throughput gain a server can take (figure 2).














Figure 2: Batch Size Trade-Off Curves: Dimensionless schematic with batch service time t(B) = 1 + 0.15(B − 1) and throughput B/t(B), each normalized to its batch-1 value. Larger batches amortize fixed work but take longer to complete. These hypothetical curves are not a benchmark, exclude queuing and batch-formation delay, and establish neither a memory-capacity boundary nor an optimal batch size.



Four properties of these curves guide the choice of batch size across candidate operating points. Together they explain why throughput and latency cannot be optimized independently:

Pareto Frontier: An operating point is Pareto efficient when no other candidate provides at least as much throughput and no more latency, with a strict improvement in at least one objective. The frontier is the set of these nondominated points.
Knee of the Curve: A knee marks diminishing throughput gains relative to increasing service time; it does not by itself select the best operating point.
SLO-Constrained Optimum: The best feasible batch size depends on the optimization objective and measured end-to-end latency, including queuing and batch formation. An SLO boundary can constrain that choice without guaranteeing an intersection or a unique optimum.
Diminishing Returns: In the schematic, fixed work becomes a smaller fraction of each batch, so successive batch-size increases yield smaller throughput gains.

The queuing-theoretic framework provides the mathematical foundation for the batching strategies introduced in Batching Strategies at Scale. Where intuition might suggest “larger batches are better for throughput,” stability constraints, latency targets, and diminishing returns create a well-defined optimal operating region that varies by model type and deployment requirements. For autoregressive transformers, any candidate batch inside that queuing-feasible region must also fit its live attention state into accelerator memory.




During a single 2,048-token GPT-3 generation request, the key and value vectors accumulated across all 96 layers consume roughly 9.4 GB of high-bandwidth memory. A batch of 32 concurrent requests therefore exhausts the remaining memory of an eight-GPU A100 node before compute ever saturates. Memory and Decode-Time Management defines the KV cache and the paged allocation that manages it, and Transformer Arithmetic gives its per-token size. Sizing a serving node around those per-token states requires accounting for three coupled effects: how caching trades quadratic recomputation for linear memory growth, how the resulting footprint scales with sequence length and batch size, and why naive contiguous reservation fragments HBM (Kwon et al. 2023).

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
For a standard attention implementation at fixed model width, autoregressive generation without caching requires \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) computation per token because each transformer layer recomputes the full prefix, including attention among its tokens. The KV cache stores previously computed key and value vectors, allowing each new token to attend to the prefix in \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) computation. For serving at scale, this compute saving creates a memory-management challenge, because KV cache memory can exceed model weights for long contexts. The cache size grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size as calculated by equation 4:
\[\KvCacheMemory = 2 \times \LayerCount \times \HiddenDimension\times \SequenceLength\times \BatchSize\times \ElementStorageSize \tag{4}\]
For standard multihead attention, where the aggregate KV width equals the hidden width, \(\LayerCount\) is the number of layers, \(\HiddenDimension\) is the hidden dimension, \(\SequenceLength\) is sequence length, \(\BatchSize\) is batch size, \(\ElementStorageSize\) is storage size per element in bytes. The factor of 2 accounts for both keys and values. Grouped-query or multiquery attention instead uses the aggregate KV-head width in place of \(\HiddenDimension\).
Evaluating equation 4 for a concrete multi-GPU node shows how quickly the KV cache bounds concurrency. For the 175B GPT-3 model (\(\LayerCount =\) 96, \(\HiddenDimension=\) 12,288, FP16 \(\ElementStorageSize =\) 2 bytes) at its training context length \(\SequenceLength=\) 2,048, each request requires:
\[ M_{\text{KV/req}} = 2 \times 96 \times 12288 \times 2048 \times 2 \text{ B} \approx 9.66 \text{ GB/request} \]
Across 8\(\times\) A100 80-GB GPUs (687.2 GB total HBM), storing model weights in FP16 consumes 350 GB, leaving 337.2 GB for activation and KV cache memory. Dividing that residual capacity by the per-request cache gives a capacity-only upper bound of 34 concurrent requests. This bound assumes balanced sharding and reserves no memory for activations, workspaces, runtime state, or allocator losses; an implementable batch must be smaller (device nameplate capacities are converted to decimal GB before subtracting the decimal model footprint). Together with table 1, this capacity ceiling closes the two-layer serving model: queuing dynamics set the minimum batch size needed for stability and latency headroom, while HBM capacity caps the maximum concurrent batch at long context lengths.

title: Inference Foundations
text: Serving performance is bounded by queues and by memory. As utilization \(\ServingUtilization\) approaches 1, queue depth and latency grow without bound, so production systems retain headroom suited to their workload and SLO. Larger batches raise throughput but add batch-accumulation delay, which produces a latency knee rather than monotonic improvement; the best batch size depends on whether the objective is minimum mean latency, maximum SLO-compliant throughput, or cost. Little’s Law, \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\), gives a one-line consistency check on any serving measurement. The KV cache grows with sequence length, batch size, and KV-head width and can exceed the model weights (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)); paging reduces fragmentation and reservation losses without removing the underlying footprint.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Distributed training spends a substantial fraction of execution time synchronizing gradients, redistributing activations, and routing tokens across network fabrics. Rather than cluttering chapter text with step-by-step proofs, this appendix provides the quantitative communication cost models used throughout the book: point-to-point formulations (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) and LogGP), collective execution bounds (AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll), pipeline bubble math, and gradient compression thresholds.


This appendix is designed as a reference when translating a distributed training symptom (“AllReduce is slow,” “pipeline bubbles are killing throughput,” “should we compress gradients?”) into a quantitative diagnosis. Conventions used here follow the book-wide notation. \(\MessageStartupLatency\) denotes per-message startup latency, and \(\LinkBandwidth\) denotes link bandwidth in bytes per second. \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) denotes point-to-point message size, and \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\) denotes the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover point. \(\DeviceCount\) denotes the number of participating GPUs, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) denotes collective payload size in bytes.

When AllReduce is slow: Use section 1.2 to compute the expected time and compare ring vs. tree costs.
When choosing ring vs. tree: Use section 1.3 and the crossover analysis to match algorithm to message size.
When pipeline bubbles dominate: Use section 1.4 to compute bubble fraction and determine the required microbatch count.
When gradient compression is proposed: Use section 1.5 to run the break-even calculation before committing engineering effort.





Systems Perspective 1.1: Why this mattersThe time a gradient synchronization takes across 256 GPUs must be estimated before a cluster topology is chosen. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model plays the role of a roofline for networks, giving a first-order prediction of transfer time from two hardware parameters and the message size.


Every point-to-point transfer on a network follows the same pattern: the sender pays a fixed startup cost to initiate the message, then transmits the payload at a rate determined by the link’s bandwidth. This two-parameter model captures the essential physics of network communication. Specifically, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (equation 1) predicts the time to transfer a point-to-point message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes:
\[ \PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}  \tag{1}\]
Here \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the startup latency (seconds), the fixed cost of initiating a message including software overhead, network interface card (NIC) processing, and routing setup. \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the link bandwidth (bytes/s), the sustained data rate after startup. \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the message size (bytes). The model decomposes every transfer into exactly two costs: a per-message cost (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) paid regardless of size, and a per-byte cost (\(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\)) that scales linearly with the payload. This decomposition drives all the algorithm selection decisions in section 1.3, and the baseline \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) parameters span more than an order of magnitude across intra-node NVLink and PCIe, inter-node InfiniBand and RoCE fabrics, and kernel TCP stacks (table 1).



Table 1: \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) Parameters by Interconnect: Effective startup latency and sustained bandwidth for interconnects used in ML clusters. \(\MessageStartupLatency\) follows the convention of Interconnect Performance Parameters in Collective Communication, the effective per-message launch latency including the communication library’s software stack, which is why it reaches microseconds even on NVLink. The InfiniBand NDR entry is the single anchor that every worked example in this appendix uses, and it lies inside that table’s NDR range. The \(\LinkBandwidth\) column uses one-way or per-direction bandwidth, so the H100 NVLink entry is half of the 900 GB/s bidirectional aggregate specification. NVLink and PCIe operate within a node; InfiniBand and RoCE operate between nodes. TCP latency is dominated by kernel software stack overhead.

Sending a 64-byte control flag over InfiniBand NDR takes nearly the same five microseconds as sending a 64 KB tensor, whereas a 100 MB gradient shard spends almost all of its transfer time streaming bytes at line rate. That contrast separates the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model into two operating regimes: for small messages, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) dominates and the link spends most of its time initiating transfers, whereas for large messages, the bandwidth term \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) dominates and the startup cost becomes negligible. The crossover message size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), defined by equation 2, is the point where both terms contribute equally:
\[ \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth \tag{2}\]
Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is latency dominated: sending more small messages wastes time on repeated startups. Above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is bandwidth dominated: payload transfer dominates; reducing bytes or increasing effective bandwidth can lower its cost.

Napkin Math 1.1: Worked example: Crossover on InfiniBand NDRSetup: InfiniBand NDR has \(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s.
Question: At what message size does the bandwidth term equal the latency term?
Math:
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth=\) 1.5 μs \(\times\) 50 GB/s \(=\) 75 KB
Analysis: Messages smaller than 75 KB are latency dominated on IB NDR. Gradient tensors from a single layer of a large model are typically 10–100 MB, well above this threshold. Control messages, heartbeats, and barrier synchronizations, however, are well below it.
Systems insight: This is why NCCL and Gloo batch small gradient tensors into larger “buckets” before launching AllReduce. Sending each tensor individually would pay the 1.5 μs startup cost hundreds of times per iteration instead of a handful.





The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model assumes a message is a single, atomic transfer. In practice, networks pipeline messages: a sender can inject a new packet before the previous one has been fully received. The LogGP model (Alexandrov et al. 1995) extends LogP with a long-message gap parameter:

Alexandrov, Albert D., Mihai F. Ionescu, Klaus E. Schauser, and Chris J. Scheiman. 1995. “LogGP: Incorporating Long Messages into the LogP Model—One Step Closer Towards a Realistic Model for Parallel Computation.” Proceedings of the Seventh Annual ACM Symposium on Parallel Algorithms and Architectures - SPAA ’95 30: 95–105. https://doi.org/10.1145/215399.215427.

\(\MessageInjectionGap\) (gap): The minimum interval between consecutive message injections at the sender. This models the NIC’s injection rate limit.
\(\SenderOverhead\), \(\ReceiverOverhead\) (overhead): The CPU time consumed by the processor to initiate or complete a message, during which it cannot do useful compute.

For a long message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes, LogGP models transfer time by separating network transit from endpoint processor overhead and per-byte injection gaps: \[\LoggpLongMessageTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx \SenderOverhead + \LogpNetworkLatency + (\PointToPointMessageSize- 1)\LongMessageGapPerByte+ \ReceiverOverhead\]
Here \(\LogpNetworkLatency\) is the network latency, \(\SenderOverhead\) and \(\ReceiverOverhead\) are sender and receiver overheads, \(\LongMessageGapPerByte\) is the gap per byte for long messages, and \(\MessageInjectionGap\) controls the minimum interval between consecutive message injections. Informal alpha-beta-style approximations can be useful for ML profiling, but the standard LogGP model keeps these gap parameters distinct from a simple bandwidth term.
In most ML training scenarios, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model is sufficient because gradient tensors are large enough that pipelining effects are secondary to raw bandwidth. The LogGP model becomes important when analyzing the overhead of many small control messages or when modeling the interaction between communication and computation overlap, situations that arise in fine-grained pipeline parallelism and asynchronous gradient updates. Whereas the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) and LogGP equations describe single point-to-point transfers, collective operations in which all GPUs participate compose multiple point-to-point transfers, and their cost formulas derive directly from the model above.





Systems Perspective 1.2: Why this mattersEvery distributed training step ends with a collective synchronization. The cost of that collective, rather than the cost of the matrix multiplies, often determines whether scaling from 8 GPUs to 256 is feasible. Understanding the exact complexity of each collective reveals which parallelism strategy (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) will dominate wall time at a given scale.


When \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs synchronize gradients, reconstruct sharded weights, or route tokens at the end of a computation phase, the collective primitive coordinates a multi-step schedule of point-to-point transfers across every participating rank. Each collective therefore has a characteristic bandwidth term (how many bytes traverse the bottleneck link) and latency term (how many sequential message steps must complete). The formulas below use the bandwidth-optimal ring algorithm unless otherwise noted; section 1.3 discusses when other algorithms are preferable.


AllReduce is the workhorse of data-parallel training: every GPU starts with a local gradient tensor of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and ends with the globally reduced (summed) result. The ring algorithm decomposes AllReduce into a ReduceScatter phase followed by an AllGather phase. Ring AllReduce time is given by equation 3:
\[ \RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \cdot \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2(\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{3}\]
The factor \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) approaches 2 as \(\DeviceCount\) grows. Each rank sends that factor times \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and receives the same amount. With full-duplex links, sending and receiving overlap; \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the effective bandwidth in one direction, so sent-plus-received bytes must not be divided by that one-direction rate. The latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\), which makes the ring algorithm expensive in latency for large GPU counts.
Tree AllReduce trades that linear latency growth for logarithmic depth. Equation 4 charges both the bandwidth and the latency term once per tree level, \(2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\) times in total:
\[ \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{4}\]
This unsegmented tree algorithm trades bandwidth efficiency for latency efficiency: the latency term grows as \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) instead of \(\DeviceCount\), but the bandwidth term sends the full message \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) at each tree level instead of \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) chunks. Comparing the two formulas shows why large payloads favor ring topologies while small control synchronizations favor trees.

Napkin Math 1.2: Worked example: Ring vs. tree AllReduceSetup: 256 H100 GPUs connected via InfiniBand NDR (\(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs, \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s). The gradient tensor is 1 GB (a 500M-parameter model in FP16).
Question: How long does AllReduce take with ring vs. tree?
Ring AllReduce:
\(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 40.6 ms
Tree AllReduce:
\(\TreeAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 320 ms
Analysis: For this 1 GB message, ring AllReduce takes 40.6 ms, and tree takes 320 ms. The ring is significantly faster because it distributes the bandwidth load across all links. The tree’s logarithmic latency advantage is negligible compared to its bandwidth penalty for large messages.
Systems insight: For the large gradient tensors typical of data-parallel training, ring (or ring-based) algorithms dominate. This unsegmented tree model favors small messages. Production tree variants can pipeline or partition messages and must be evaluated with their own cost models.





AllGather is the complement of ReduceScatter: each GPU starts with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard and ends with the complete \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor. It is the core communication primitive in fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) for reconstructing parameters before each forward pass, and in tensor parallelism for reassembling split activations. Ring AllGather execution time (equation 5) requires half the transfer volume of AllReduce:
\[ \AllGatherCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{5}\]
For this comparison, the full gathered tensor has the same byte size as each rank’s AllReduce input payload. In this model, AllGather takes half the communication time of AllReduce for that matched tensor size and link parameters: it uses one ring pass instead of two. Local reduction work and implementation overheads can change the measured ratio.



ReduceScatter is the dual of AllGather: each GPU starts with a full \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor and ends with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard that contains the globally reduced values for that shard. It is the gradient synchronization primitive in FSDP and ZeRO, replacing the full AllReduce with a cheaper operation when each GPU only needs its own parameter shard’s gradient. Ring ReduceScatter execution time (equation 6) provides the gradient sharding primitive:
\[ \ReduceScatterCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{6}\]
The symmetry with equation 5 is not a coincidence: ring AllReduce decomposes into one ReduceScatter followed by one AllGather, and the costs add up exactly to equation 3. Because each phase traverses the ring once, sharded data-parallel schemes that defer the AllGather until the next forward pass cut immediate post-backward communication in half.



AllToAll is the most general collective: each GPU sends a distinct \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized chunk to every other GPU, and receives a distinct chunk from each. It is the routing primitive for mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, where tokens must be dispatched to the correct expert and the results gathered back. Pairwise-exchange AllToAll execution time (equation 7) trades personalized data chunks across peers:
\[ \AllToAllCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{7}\]
Although the formula matches AllGather and ReduceScatter in form, the communication pattern is structurally different. AllToAll is a personalized exchange in which each GPU sends different data to each peer, which makes it harder to overlap with computation and much more sensitive to network bisection congestion.



Broadcast sends a single \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor from one root GPU to all \(\DeviceCount- 1\) others. It is used for distributing initial model weights, updated learning rates, and configuration changes during training. Tree Broadcast execution time (equation 8) scales logarithmically with the participating GPU count:
\[ \BroadcastCompletionTime= \log_2 \DeviceCount\left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\right)  \tag{8}\]
Broadcast is structurally asymmetric (one sender, many receivers), which makes a tree topology natural. In an unsegmented tree broadcast, the full \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte payload is forwarded at each tree level, so both the latency and bandwidth terms appear along the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\)-level critical path. Segmented or scatter-allgather broadcast variants can reduce the bandwidth term, but they require a different algorithm-specific model.



With the individual formulas in place, table 2 provides a compact reference for comparing the cost structure of each collective operation. Checking the bandwidth and latency columns side by side shows how each collective scales as either payload size or device count grows.

The bandwidth term determines cost for large messages (gradients, parameters); the latency term determines cost for small messages (scalars, barriers). \(\DeviceCount\) = GPU count, \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) = per-rank input payload in bytes, and \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) = full tensor size in bytes for AllGather and ReduceScatter.

Two patterns emerge from this table. First, the ring and pairwise-exchange models contain the \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) factor, which approaches 1 for large \(\DeviceCount\). Per-rank communication therefore approaches a constant multiple of the relevant size: about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) for ring AllReduce, about \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) for ring AllGather or ReduceScatter, and about \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) for pairwise AllToAll. Aggregate traffic still scales with the number of ranks. Second, the latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\) for ring algorithms but logarithmically for tree algorithms, creating the algorithm selection trade-off analyzed next.





Systems Perspective 1.3: Why this mattersNCCL automatically selects a collective algorithm based on message size and GPU topology, but understanding why it chooses ring for large messages and tree for small ones helps diagnose when the auto-selection is suboptimal and how to structure communication to stay in the efficient regime.




Sending a 1 GB gradient tensor across 256 GPUs favors an algorithm that spreads bytes across every link, whereas synchronizing a 4-byte scalar loss flag favors an algorithm that finishes in the fewest hop steps. The ring algorithm minimizes bandwidth usage but pays a latency cost that grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\). The tree algorithm minimizes latency but wastes bandwidth because it sends the full message at each level. Recursive halving-doubling splits the difference: it uses halving (like a tree) for the reduce phase and doubling for the gather phase, achieving near-optimal bandwidth with \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) latency steps.
The decision boundary between ring and tree depends on both message size and participant count. For the power-of-two case modeled by equation 3 and equation 4, equating the two times gives the crossover in equation 9, which table 3 translates into practical selection rules across payload regimes:
\[ \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount) = \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize \times \frac{(\DeviceCount-1)-\log_2 \DeviceCount}{\log_2 \DeviceCount-(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount}, \qquad \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize=\MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth \tag{9}\]

\(\CollectivePayloadSize> \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (large gradients): The ring has the lower modeled cost because its smaller bandwidth coefficient outweighs its additional startup steps.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize< \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (barriers, scalars): The tree has the lower modeled cost because its logarithmic startup term outweighs its additional bandwidth cost.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize\approx \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (medium tensors): The two modeled costs are similar, so benchmark them alongside recursive halving-doubling on the target topology.

Modern clusters have a two-level topology: GPUs within a node are connected by NVLink (450 GB/s), while nodes are connected by InfiniBand (50 GB/s). Hierarchical AllReduce exploits this asymmetry in three phases:

Intra-node reduce (NVLink): Each node reduces its 8 local GPUs to a single result using NVLink’s 450 GB/s bandwidth. This is fast because NVLink’s per-direction rate is 9× that of an InfiniBand NDR port.
Inter-node AllReduce (InfiniBand): An AllReduce combines the per-node results across nodes. Only one representative per 8 local GPUs participates, so the inter-node ring has one-eighth as many participants as a flat GPU-level ring.
Intra-node broadcast (NVLink): Each node broadcasts the global result to its 8 local GPUs.

The hierarchical approach reduces the inter-node ring size from all GPUs to one representative per 8 local GPUs, cutting the latency-step term by about 8\(\times\) while keeping local aggregation on fast intra-node links. The inter-node representative still exchanges the full reduced tensor; the gain is not a universal reduction of payload bytes by the number of local GPUs. NCCL selects among topology-aware algorithms such as Ring, Tree, CollNet variants, NVLS/NVLSTree, and PAT based on the collective, message size, topology, architecture, and version. Hierarchical communication is common on multi-node systems but is not a universal default. The cost structure of collectives lets an engineer reason about data-parallel overhead. Pipeline parallelism, in contrast, introduces a different kind of overhead, idle time caused by the sequential dependency between pipeline stages.





Systems Perspective 1.4: Why this mattersPipeline parallelism splits a model across multiple GPUs so that each GPU holds only a fraction of the layers. The trade-off is bubble time: idle cycles where GPUs wait for activations or gradients from upstream or downstream stages. Quantifying the bubble fraction reveals whether pipeline parallelism is worth the complexity at a given scale.




When a model is split across eight pipeline stages, Stage 8 sits idle while Stages 1 through 7 compute the first microbatch’s forward pass, and Stage 1 sits idle again while the pipeline drains at the end of the step. In a pipeline with \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) stages and \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches, equation 10 defines the bubble fraction as the proportion of total GPU-time spent idle:
\[ \PipelineBubbleFraction = \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount}  \tag{10}\]
For balanced stages with negligible transfer overhead, this formula applies to both GPipe (where all forward passes complete before any backward pass begins) and 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward interleaving). The 1F1B schedule has the same asymptotic bubble fraction but uses less peak memory because it retires microbatches earlier.
The bubble fraction depends on the ratio of stages to microbatches, so adding more microbatches for a fixed number of stages amortizes the pipeline fill and drain across more useful work. As a rule of thumb, keeping bubble overhead at or below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\), while staying strictly below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount> 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\). The practical rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) is a convenient conservative target across typical stage depths and microbatch counts (table 4).

Deeper pipelines require proportionally more microbatches to maintain high accelerator utilization. When activation memory bounds limit the microbatch count, systems must adopt alternative scheduling strategies to mitigate bubble overhead.



When activation memory prevents a team from increasing \(\MicrobatchCount\), splitting each GPU’s layer assignment into smaller nonconsecutive model chunks lets the first microbatch reach the last device after fewer layers per stage. Interleaved scheduling (used in Megatron-LM) assigns \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages to each physical GPU instead of one, so the pipeline has \(\PipelineParallelDegree \times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages while the bubble numerator retains the physical stage count \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), as equation 11 shows:
\[ \InterleavedPipelineBubbleFraction= \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount\times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice}  \tag{11}\]
The microbatch term in the denominator is multiplied by \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) compared to equation 10, so the bubble reduction approaches \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) when \(\MicrobatchCount\) dominates \(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1\). For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) = 8, \(\MicrobatchCount\) = 16, and \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) = 4, the bubble fraction drops from 30.4 percent to 9.9 percent, a 3.1× reduction that comes at the cost of more frequent, smaller communication between stages.
Interleaved scheduling highlights a recurring theme in distributed ML: communication granularity is a tunable knob. Smaller, more frequent transfers improve overlap and reduce idle time, but increase the aggregate latency overhead. The same trade-off governs gradient compression.





Systems Perspective 1.5: Why this mattersGradient compression promises to reduce communication volume by 10–1000\(\times\), making AllReduce nearly free. Compression, however, has overhead (encoding and decoding time), and it only helps if that overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves. A quick break-even analysis prevents wasted effort on compression schemes that will not actually speed up training.




Compressing a 1 GB gradient tensor down to 16 MB cuts network transfer time on a 256-GPU ring from 40 ms to less than 2 ms, but only if the GPU kernels that quantize or sparsify the tensor finish in less than the 38 ms saved. Gradient compression replaces the original \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte gradient with a compressed representation of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio\), where \(\CompressionRatio\) is the compression ratio. Equation 12 expresses the total time with compression:
\[ \CompressedCommunicationTime = \CodecEncodeTime + \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right) + \CodecDecodeTime  \tag{12}\]
Compression is beneficial when \(\CompressedCommunicationTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\) and the reduced precision or sparsity does not slow model convergence. Rearranging this inequality yields the break-even condition in equation 13:
\[ \CodecEncodeTime + \CodecDecodeTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) - \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right)  \tag{13}\]
In the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(\CollectivePayloadSize\gg \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)), the communication time scales linearly with message size, and the right-hand side simplifies to approximately \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) \times (1 - 1/\CompressionRatio)\). For high compression ratios (\(\CompressionRatio \gg 1\)), this approaches \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\), so compression is worthwhile as long as the codec overhead is less than the uncompressed communication time.

Napkin Math 1.3: Worked example: Is compression worth it?Setup: Ring AllReduce of a 1 GB gradient across 256 H100 GPUs on InfiniBand NDR, taking 40.6 ms uncompressed. Assume a collective-compatible compressed representation achieves 64× compression with 2 ms total encode + decode overhead.

Systems insight: Compression saves communication time under the assumed payload ratio, codec cost, and unchanged collective structure. Independent top-k selections do not generally preserve that structure: sparse indices, differing supports, and merge operations must also be modeled. Lossy compression can require more iterations to reach the same accuracy, negating a per-iteration gain.


Break-even codec overhead limits (table 5) scale with compression ratio and uncompressed AllReduce time. Higher compression ratios tolerate larger codec overheads, up to the bandwidth-dependent portion of the uncompressed collective. These break-even limits show that gradient compression delivers the highest net benefit on lower-bandwidth interconnects where transfer times dominate. On high-speed fabrics, the tolerable codec overhead budget is tightly constrained and requires lightweight quantization or sparsification algorithms.

The communication models in this appendix rest on two hardware parameters, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and the bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)). They also rest on two workload parameters, the payload (\(\PointToPointMessageSize\) or \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)) and, for collectives, the participant count \(\DeviceCount\). The crossover size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\) separates latency-dominated from bandwidth-dominated transfers. Ring collectives carry a \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) bandwidth factor and a latency term linear in \(\DeviceCount\), while tree algorithms trade bandwidth for logarithmic latency, so message size relative to the crossover \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) selects the algorithm. Pipeline parallelism adds the bubble fraction \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\), which the rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) keeps below 20 percent. Gradient compression pays only when codec overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves and convergence is unaffected. Measuring \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) for a cluster therefore yields a first-order prediction of its communication overhead.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
This appendix is designed as a reference when translating a distributed training symptom (“AllReduce is slow,” “pipeline bubbles are killing throughput,” “should we compress gradients?”) into a quantitative diagnosis. Conventions used here follow the book-wide notation. \(\MessageStartupLatency\) denotes per-message startup latency, and \(\LinkBandwidth\) denotes link bandwidth in bytes per second. \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) denotes point-to-point message size, and \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\) denotes the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover point. \(\DeviceCount\) denotes the number of participating GPUs, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) denotes collective payload size in bytes.

When AllReduce is slow: Use section 1.2 to compute the expected time and compare ring vs. tree costs.
When choosing ring vs. tree: Use section 1.3 and the crossover analysis to match algorithm to message size.
When pipeline bubbles dominate: Use section 1.4 to compute bubble fraction and determine the required microbatch count.
When gradient compression is proposed: Use section 1.5 to run the break-even calculation before committing engineering effort.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.1: Why this mattersThe time a gradient synchronization takes across 256 GPUs must be estimated before a cluster topology is chosen. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model plays the role of a roofline for networks, giving a first-order prediction of transfer time from two hardware parameters and the message size.


Every point-to-point transfer on a network follows the same pattern: the sender pays a fixed startup cost to initiate the message, then transmits the payload at a rate determined by the link’s bandwidth. This two-parameter model captures the essential physics of network communication. Specifically, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (equation 1) predicts the time to transfer a point-to-point message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes:
\[ \PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}  \tag{1}\]
Here \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the startup latency (seconds), the fixed cost of initiating a message including software overhead, network interface card (NIC) processing, and routing setup. \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the link bandwidth (bytes/s), the sustained data rate after startup. \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the message size (bytes). The model decomposes every transfer into exactly two costs: a per-message cost (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) paid regardless of size, and a per-byte cost (\(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\)) that scales linearly with the payload. This decomposition drives all the algorithm selection decisions in section 1.3, and the baseline \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) parameters span more than an order of magnitude across intra-node NVLink and PCIe, inter-node InfiniBand and RoCE fabrics, and kernel TCP stacks (table 1).



Table 1: \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) Parameters by Interconnect: Effective startup latency and sustained bandwidth for interconnects used in ML clusters. \(\MessageStartupLatency\) follows the convention of Interconnect Performance Parameters in Collective Communication, the effective per-message launch latency including the communication library’s software stack, which is why it reaches microseconds even on NVLink. The InfiniBand NDR entry is the single anchor that every worked example in this appendix uses, and it lies inside that table’s NDR range. The \(\LinkBandwidth\) column uses one-way or per-direction bandwidth, so the H100 NVLink entry is half of the 900 GB/s bidirectional aggregate specification. NVLink and PCIe operate within a node; InfiniBand and RoCE operate between nodes. TCP latency is dominated by kernel software stack overhead.

Sending a 64-byte control flag over InfiniBand NDR takes nearly the same five microseconds as sending a 64 KB tensor, whereas a 100 MB gradient shard spends almost all of its transfer time streaming bytes at line rate. That contrast separates the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model into two operating regimes: for small messages, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) dominates and the link spends most of its time initiating transfers, whereas for large messages, the bandwidth term \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) dominates and the startup cost becomes negligible. The crossover message size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), defined by equation 2, is the point where both terms contribute equally:
\[ \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth \tag{2}\]
Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is latency dominated: sending more small messages wastes time on repeated startups. Above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), communication is bandwidth dominated: payload transfer dominates; reducing bytes or increasing effective bandwidth can lower its cost.

Napkin Math 1.1: Worked example: Crossover on InfiniBand NDRSetup: InfiniBand NDR has \(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s.
Question: At what message size does the bandwidth term equal the latency term?
Math:
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\times \LinkBandwidth=\) 1.5 μs \(\times\) 50 GB/s \(=\) 75 KB
Analysis: Messages smaller than 75 KB are latency dominated on IB NDR. Gradient tensors from a single layer of a large model are typically 10–100 MB, well above this threshold. Control messages, heartbeats, and barrier synchronizations, however, are well below it.
Systems insight: This is why NCCL and Gloo batch small gradient tensors into larger “buckets” before launching AllReduce. Sending each tensor individually would pay the 1.5 μs startup cost hundreds of times per iteration instead of a handful.





The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model assumes a message is a single, atomic transfer. In practice, networks pipeline messages: a sender can inject a new packet before the previous one has been fully received. The LogGP model (Alexandrov et al. 1995) extends LogP with a long-message gap parameter:

Alexandrov, Albert D., Mihai F. Ionescu, Klaus E. Schauser, and Chris J. Scheiman. 1995. “LogGP: Incorporating Long Messages into the LogP Model—One Step Closer Towards a Realistic Model for Parallel Computation.” Proceedings of the Seventh Annual ACM Symposium on Parallel Algorithms and Architectures - SPAA ’95 30: 95–105. https://doi.org/10.1145/215399.215427.

\(\MessageInjectionGap\) (gap): The minimum interval between consecutive message injections at the sender. This models the NIC’s injection rate limit.
\(\SenderOverhead\), \(\ReceiverOverhead\) (overhead): The CPU time consumed by the processor to initiate or complete a message, during which it cannot do useful compute.

For a long message of \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes, LogGP models transfer time by separating network transit from endpoint processor overhead and per-byte injection gaps: \[\LoggpLongMessageTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx \SenderOverhead + \LogpNetworkLatency + (\PointToPointMessageSize- 1)\LongMessageGapPerByte+ \ReceiverOverhead\]
Here \(\LogpNetworkLatency\) is the network latency, \(\SenderOverhead\) and \(\ReceiverOverhead\) are sender and receiver overheads, \(\LongMessageGapPerByte\) is the gap per byte for long messages, and \(\MessageInjectionGap\) controls the minimum interval between consecutive message injections. Informal alpha-beta-style approximations can be useful for ML profiling, but the standard LogGP model keeps these gap parameters distinct from a simple bandwidth term.
In most ML training scenarios, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model is sufficient because gradient tensors are large enough that pipelining effects are secondary to raw bandwidth. The LogGP model becomes important when analyzing the overhead of many small control messages or when modeling the interaction between communication and computation overlap, situations that arise in fine-grained pipeline parallelism and asynchronous gradient updates. Whereas the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) and LogGP equations describe single point-to-point transfers, collective operations in which all GPUs participate compose multiple point-to-point transfers, and their cost formulas derive directly from the model above.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.2: Why this mattersEvery distributed training step ends with a collective synchronization. The cost of that collective, rather than the cost of the matrix multiplies, often determines whether scaling from 8 GPUs to 256 is feasible. Understanding the exact complexity of each collective reveals which parallelism strategy (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) will dominate wall time at a given scale.


When \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs synchronize gradients, reconstruct sharded weights, or route tokens at the end of a computation phase, the collective primitive coordinates a multi-step schedule of point-to-point transfers across every participating rank. Each collective therefore has a characteristic bandwidth term (how many bytes traverse the bottleneck link) and latency term (how many sequential message steps must complete). The formulas below use the bandwidth-optimal ring algorithm unless otherwise noted; section 1.3 discusses when other algorithms are preferable.


AllReduce is the workhorse of data-parallel training: every GPU starts with a local gradient tensor of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and ends with the globally reduced (summed) result. The ring algorithm decomposes AllReduce into a ReduceScatter phase followed by an AllGather phase. Ring AllReduce time is given by equation 3:
\[ \RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \cdot \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2(\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{3}\]
The factor \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) approaches 2 as \(\DeviceCount\) grows. Each rank sends that factor times \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and receives the same amount. With full-duplex links, sending and receiving overlap; \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the effective bandwidth in one direction, so sent-plus-received bytes must not be divided by that one-direction rate. The latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\), which makes the ring algorithm expensive in latency for large GPU counts.
Tree AllReduce trades that linear latency growth for logarithmic depth. Equation 4 charges both the bandwidth and the latency term once per tree level, \(2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\) times in total:
\[ \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime = 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + 2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{4}\]
This unsegmented tree algorithm trades bandwidth efficiency for latency efficiency: the latency term grows as \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) instead of \(\DeviceCount\), but the bandwidth term sends the full message \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) at each tree level instead of \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) chunks. Comparing the two formulas shows why large payloads favor ring topologies while small control synchronizations favor trees.

Napkin Math 1.2: Worked example: Ring vs. tree AllReduceSetup: 256 H100 GPUs connected via InfiniBand NDR (\(\MessageStartupLatency\) = 1.5 μs, \(\LinkBandwidth\) = 50 GB/s). The gradient tensor is 1 GB (a 500M-parameter model in FP16).
Question: How long does AllReduce take with ring vs. tree?
Ring AllReduce:
\(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 40.6 ms
Tree AllReduce:
\(\TreeAllReduceCompletionTime \approx\) 320 ms
Analysis: For this 1 GB message, ring AllReduce takes 40.6 ms, and tree takes 320 ms. The ring is significantly faster because it distributes the bandwidth load across all links. The tree’s logarithmic latency advantage is negligible compared to its bandwidth penalty for large messages.
Systems insight: For the large gradient tensors typical of data-parallel training, ring (or ring-based) algorithms dominate. This unsegmented tree model favors small messages. Production tree variants can pipeline or partition messages and must be evaluated with their own cost models.





AllGather is the complement of ReduceScatter: each GPU starts with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard and ends with the complete \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor. It is the core communication primitive in fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) for reconstructing parameters before each forward pass, and in tensor parallelism for reassembling split activations. Ring AllGather execution time (equation 5) requires half the transfer volume of AllReduce:
\[ \AllGatherCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{5}\]
For this comparison, the full gathered tensor has the same byte size as each rank’s AllReduce input payload. In this model, AllGather takes half the communication time of AllReduce for that matched tensor size and link parameters: it uses one ring pass instead of two. Local reduction work and implementation overheads can change the measured ratio.



ReduceScatter is the dual of AllGather: each GPU starts with a full \(\CollectiveTensorSize\)-byte tensor and ends with a \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized shard that contains the globally reduced values for that shard. It is the gradient synchronization primitive in FSDP and ZeRO, replacing the full AllReduce with a cheaper operation when each GPU only needs its own parameter shard’s gradient. Ring ReduceScatter execution time (equation 6) provides the gradient sharding primitive:
\[ \ReduceScatterCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectiveTensorSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{6}\]
The symmetry with equation 5 is not a coincidence: ring AllReduce decomposes into one ReduceScatter followed by one AllGather, and the costs add up exactly to equation 3. Because each phase traverses the ring once, sharded data-parallel schemes that defer the AllGather until the next forward pass cut immediate post-backward communication in half.



AllToAll is the most general collective: each GPU sends a distinct \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\)-sized chunk to every other GPU, and receives a distinct chunk from each. It is the routing primitive for mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, where tokens must be dispatched to the correct expert and the results gathered back. Pairwise-exchange AllToAll execution time (equation 7) trades personalized data chunks across peers:
\[ \AllToAllCompletionTime= \frac{\DeviceCount- 1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} + (\DeviceCount- 1) \cdot \MessageStartupLatency \tag{7}\]
Although the formula matches AllGather and ReduceScatter in form, the communication pattern is structurally different. AllToAll is a personalized exchange in which each GPU sends different data to each peer, which makes it harder to overlap with computation and much more sensitive to network bisection congestion.



Broadcast sends a single \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor from one root GPU to all \(\DeviceCount- 1\) others. It is used for distributing initial model weights, updated learning rates, and configuration changes during training. Tree Broadcast execution time (equation 8) scales logarithmically with the participating GPU count:
\[ \BroadcastCompletionTime= \log_2 \DeviceCount\left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\right)  \tag{8}\]
Broadcast is structurally asymmetric (one sender, many receivers), which makes a tree topology natural. In an unsegmented tree broadcast, the full \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte payload is forwarded at each tree level, so both the latency and bandwidth terms appear along the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\)-level critical path. Segmented or scatter-allgather broadcast variants can reduce the bandwidth term, but they require a different algorithm-specific model.



With the individual formulas in place, table 2 provides a compact reference for comparing the cost structure of each collective operation. Checking the bandwidth and latency columns side by side shows how each collective scales as either payload size or device count grows.

Two patterns emerge from this table. First, the ring and pairwise-exchange models contain the \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) factor, which approaches 1 for large \(\DeviceCount\). Per-rank communication therefore approaches a constant multiple of the relevant size: about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) for ring AllReduce, about \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) for ring AllGather or ReduceScatter, and about \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) for pairwise AllToAll. Aggregate traffic still scales with the number of ranks. Second, the latency term grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\) for ring algorithms but logarithmically for tree algorithms, creating the algorithm selection trade-off analyzed next.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.3: Why this mattersNCCL automatically selects a collective algorithm based on message size and GPU topology, but understanding why it chooses ring for large messages and tree for small ones helps diagnose when the auto-selection is suboptimal and how to structure communication to stay in the efficient regime.




Sending a 1 GB gradient tensor across 256 GPUs favors an algorithm that spreads bytes across every link, whereas synchronizing a 4-byte scalar loss flag favors an algorithm that finishes in the fewest hop steps. The ring algorithm minimizes bandwidth usage but pays a latency cost that grows linearly with \(\DeviceCount\). The tree algorithm minimizes latency but wastes bandwidth because it sends the full message at each level. Recursive halving-doubling splits the difference: it uses halving (like a tree) for the reduce phase and doubling for the gather phase, achieving near-optimal bandwidth with \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) latency steps.
The decision boundary between ring and tree depends on both message size and participant count. For the power-of-two case modeled by equation 3 and equation 4, equating the two times gives the crossover in equation 9, which table 3 translates into practical selection rules across payload regimes:
\[ \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount) = \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize \times \frac{(\DeviceCount-1)-\log_2 \DeviceCount}{\log_2 \DeviceCount-(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount}, \qquad \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize=\MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth \tag{9}\]

\(\CollectivePayloadSize> \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (large gradients): The ring has the lower modeled cost because its smaller bandwidth coefficient outweighs its additional startup steps.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize< \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (barriers, scalars): The tree has the lower modeled cost because its logarithmic startup term outweighs its additional bandwidth cost.
\(\CollectivePayloadSize\approx \RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) (medium tensors): The two modeled costs are similar, so benchmark them alongside recursive halving-doubling on the target topology.




Table 3: Algorithm Selection Guide: Strengths and weaknesses of ring, tree, and recursive halving-doubling relative to the participant-dependent ring-tree crossover \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) in equation 9.

Modern clusters have a two-level topology: GPUs within a node are connected by NVLink (450 GB/s), while nodes are connected by InfiniBand (50 GB/s). Hierarchical AllReduce exploits this asymmetry in three phases:

Intra-node reduce (NVLink): Each node reduces its 8 local GPUs to a single result using NVLink’s 450 GB/s bandwidth. This is fast because NVLink’s per-direction rate is 9× that of an InfiniBand NDR port.
Inter-node AllReduce (InfiniBand): An AllReduce combines the per-node results across nodes. Only one representative per 8 local GPUs participates, so the inter-node ring has one-eighth as many participants as a flat GPU-level ring.
Intra-node broadcast (NVLink): Each node broadcasts the global result to its 8 local GPUs.

The hierarchical approach reduces the inter-node ring size from all GPUs to one representative per 8 local GPUs, cutting the latency-step term by about 8\(\times\) while keeping local aggregation on fast intra-node links. The inter-node representative still exchanges the full reduced tensor; the gain is not a universal reduction of payload bytes by the number of local GPUs. NCCL selects among topology-aware algorithms such as Ring, Tree, CollNet variants, NVLS/NVLSTree, and PAT based on the collective, message size, topology, architecture, and version. Hierarchical communication is common on multi-node systems but is not a universal default. The cost structure of collectives lets an engineer reason about data-parallel overhead. Pipeline parallelism, in contrast, introduces a different kind of overhead, idle time caused by the sequential dependency between pipeline stages.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.4: Why this mattersPipeline parallelism splits a model across multiple GPUs so that each GPU holds only a fraction of the layers. The trade-off is bubble time: idle cycles where GPUs wait for activations or gradients from upstream or downstream stages. Quantifying the bubble fraction reveals whether pipeline parallelism is worth the complexity at a given scale.




When a model is split across eight pipeline stages, Stage 8 sits idle while Stages 1 through 7 compute the first microbatch’s forward pass, and Stage 1 sits idle again while the pipeline drains at the end of the step. In a pipeline with \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) stages and \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches, equation 10 defines the bubble fraction as the proportion of total GPU-time spent idle:
\[ \PipelineBubbleFraction = \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount}  \tag{10}\]
For balanced stages with negligible transfer overhead, this formula applies to both GPipe (where all forward passes complete before any backward pass begins) and 1F1B (one-forward-one-backward interleaving). The 1F1B schedule has the same asymptotic bubble fraction but uses less peak memory because it retires microbatches earlier.
The bubble fraction depends on the ratio of stages to microbatches, so adding more microbatches for a fixed number of stages amortizes the pipeline fill and drain across more useful work. As a rule of thumb, keeping bubble overhead at or below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\), while staying strictly below 20 percent requires \(\MicrobatchCount> 4(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1)\). The practical rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) is a convenient conservative target across typical stage depths and microbatch counts (table 4).



Table 4: Pipeline Bubble Fraction: Percentage of GPU-time lost to pipeline bubbles for various stage counts and microbatch counts. The conservative choice \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) keeps the modeled fraction below 20 percent.

Deeper pipelines require proportionally more microbatches to maintain high accelerator utilization. When activation memory bounds limit the microbatch count, systems must adopt alternative scheduling strategies to mitigate bubble overhead.



When activation memory prevents a team from increasing \(\MicrobatchCount\), splitting each GPU’s layer assignment into smaller nonconsecutive model chunks lets the first microbatch reach the last device after fewer layers per stage. Interleaved scheduling (used in Megatron-LM) assigns \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages to each physical GPU instead of one, so the pipeline has \(\PipelineParallelDegree \times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) virtual stages while the bubble numerator retains the physical stage count \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), as equation 11 shows:
\[ \InterleavedPipelineBubbleFraction= \frac{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1}{\PipelineParallelDegree - 1 + \MicrobatchCount\times \VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice}  \tag{11}\]
The microbatch term in the denominator is multiplied by \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) compared to equation 10, so the bubble reduction approaches \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) when \(\MicrobatchCount\) dominates \(\PipelineParallelDegree - 1\). For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) = 8, \(\MicrobatchCount\) = 16, and \(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\) = 4, the bubble fraction drops from 30.4 percent to 9.9 percent, a 3.1× reduction that comes at the cost of more frequent, smaller communication between stages.
Interleaved scheduling highlights a recurring theme in distributed ML: communication granularity is a tunable knob. Smaller, more frequent transfers improve overlap and reduce idle time, but increase the aggregate latency overhead. The same trade-off governs gradient compression.

title: Communication Foundations
text:
Systems Perspective 1.5: Why this mattersGradient compression promises to reduce communication volume by 10–1000\(\times\), making AllReduce nearly free. Compression, however, has overhead (encoding and decoding time), and it only helps if that overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves. A quick break-even analysis prevents wasted effort on compression schemes that will not actually speed up training.




Compressing a 1 GB gradient tensor down to 16 MB cuts network transfer time on a 256-GPU ring from 40 ms to less than 2 ms, but only if the GPU kernels that quantize or sparsify the tensor finish in less than the 38 ms saved. Gradient compression replaces the original \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte gradient with a compressed representation of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio\), where \(\CompressionRatio\) is the compression ratio. Equation 12 expresses the total time with compression:
\[ \CompressedCommunicationTime = \CodecEncodeTime + \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right) + \CodecDecodeTime  \tag{12}\]
Compression is beneficial when \(\CompressedCommunicationTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\) and the reduced precision or sparsity does not slow model convergence. Rearranging this inequality yields the break-even condition in equation 13:
\[ \CodecEncodeTime + \CodecDecodeTime < \TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) - \TransferTimeForPayload\!\left(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\CompressionRatio}\right)  \tag{13}\]
In the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(\CollectivePayloadSize\gg \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)), the communication time scales linearly with message size, and the right-hand side simplifies to approximately \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize) \times (1 - 1/\CompressionRatio)\). For high compression ratios (\(\CompressionRatio \gg 1\)), this approaches \(\TransferTimeForPayload(\CollectivePayloadSize)\), so compression is worthwhile as long as the codec overhead is less than the uncompressed communication time.

Napkin Math 1.3: Worked example: Is compression worth it?Setup: Ring AllReduce of a 1 GB gradient across 256 H100 GPUs on InfiniBand NDR, taking 40.6 ms uncompressed. Assume a collective-compatible compressed representation achieves 64× compression with 2 ms total encode + decode overhead.
Question: Does compression reduce the total AllReduce time?
Math:

Uncompressed AllReduce: 40.6 ms
Compressed communication: 1.4 ms
Total with compression: 3.4 ms
Speedup: 12×

Result: Compression shortens communication time by 12×. The 2 ms codec overhead is a small fraction of the 40.6 ms uncompressed baseline.
Systems insight: Compression saves communication time under the assumed payload ratio, codec cost, and unchanged collective structure. Independent top-k selections do not generally preserve that structure: sparse indices, differing supports, and merge operations must also be modeled. Lossy compression can require more iterations to reach the same accuracy, negating a per-iteration gain.


Break-even codec overhead limits (table 5) scale with compression ratio and uncompressed AllReduce time. Higher compression ratios tolerate larger codec overheads, up to the bandwidth-dependent portion of the uncompressed collective. These break-even limits show that gradient compression delivers the highest net benefit on lower-bandwidth interconnects where transfer times dominate. On high-speed fabrics, the tolerable codec overhead budget is tightly constrained and requires lightweight quantization or sparsification algorithms.

title: Communication Foundations
text: The communication models in this appendix rest on two hardware parameters, the startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and the bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) of the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)). They also rest on two workload parameters, the payload (\(\PointToPointMessageSize\) or \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)) and, for collectives, the participant count \(\DeviceCount\). The crossover size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\) separates latency-dominated from bandwidth-dominated transfers. Ring collectives carry a \((\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) bandwidth factor and a latency term linear in \(\DeviceCount\), while tree algorithms trade bandwidth for logarithmic latency, so message size relative to the crossover \(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload(\DeviceCount)\) selects the algorithm. Pipeline parallelism adds the bubble fraction \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\), which the rule \(\MicrobatchCount\geq 4\PipelineParallelDegree\) keeps below 20 percent. Gradient compression pays only when codec overhead is smaller than the communication time it saves and convergence is unaffected. Measuring \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) for a cluster therefore yields a first-order prediction of its communication overhead.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
How to Use This Appendix
This appendix is designed as a symptom-first reference for fleet-scale diagnosis. Start with the observed failure mode, form a hypothesis about which C\(^3\) axis dominates, and select the measurement that confirms or falsifies that hypothesis:

When training throughput is low: Check model FLOPs utilization (MFU), communication fraction, and runtime goodput in the diagnostic summary (section 1.2) and traffic light thresholds (section 1.4.7) to isolate the compute, communication, or coordination axis.
When scaling efficiency drops as GPUs are added: Use the Fleet Law decomposition (section 1.3) and the intersection landscape (section 1.4) to identify which noncompute term grew.
When a production job stalls, restarts, or fires hardware alerts: Match the symptom in the troubleshooting matrix (section 1.6), select a profiler from the tooling map (section 1.7), or trace silicon counters through the telemetry decision tree (section 1.9).
When translating a scaling-law compute budget into cluster capacity: Use the C\(^3\) scorecard (section 1.8) and the effective FLOP/s model (section 1.10) so optimization effort targets the dominant loss term rather than a nonbottleneck.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
From D·A·M to C\(^3\)
Where the single-machine D·A·M framework (The D·A·M Taxonomy) diagnoses bottlenecks within one node (data starvation, algorithmic overhead, or hardware saturation), a distributed job can stall even when every individual node is healthy. The C\(^3\) taxonomy is the diagnostic framework for fleet-scale ML systems engineering. It isolates the dominant cluster-level axis across Compute (whether the accelerators are doing useful math), Communication (whether the network is moving data fast enough), and Coordination (whether the system is spending too much time on synchronization, failure recovery, and scheduling), along with the intersections between them. Rather than replacing D·A·M, C\(^3\) extends each single-machine axis to the new failure modes that appear when a workload spans a fleet (table 1).



Table 1: Mapping D·A·M to C\(^3\): How single-machine diagnostic concerns generalize to fleet-scale challenges.

Single-machine concern

The most important row in table 1 is the last one. On a single machine, the overhead term (\(\Latency\)) in the iron law is typically small, consisting of kernel launch latency, Python dispatch, and synchronization barriers. At fleet scale, coordination becomes an axis in its own right: checkpoint writes, failure detection and recovery, pipeline bubble overhead, scheduler preemptions, and maintenance windows collectively consume a significant fraction of wall time. Coordination is the axis that single-machine diagnosis lacks, and much of this book is devoted to it.

When a distributed training job runs below expected throughput, the symptom appears first as idle tensor cores, exposed collective transfers, or frequent barrier and restart stalls. Matching that symptom to the C\(^3\) axis that constrains the fleet links each physical bottleneck directly to its headline metric and highest-leverage optimization (table 2).

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
The Fleet Law
Under ideal partitioning of fixed work, the same classification can be written as a time budget for each distributed step. The Fleet Law, introduced in The Fleet Law, decomposes every distributed training step into the distributed-step time budget:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \]
This equation is the fleet-scale counterpart of the iron law. Where the iron law decomposes single-machine execution into data movement, compute, and overhead, the Fleet Law decomposes distributed execution into local arithmetic, network data transfer, and synchronization logic. The diagnostic strategy is identical: measure each term, identify which dominates, and direct engineering effort at the dominant term.

Component decomposition
Each Fleet Law term maps to specific measurable activities that can be isolated in a timeline trace or cluster telemetry log. By attributing every millisecond of step duration to one of four terms, engineers can tell whether hardware is doing useful math, moving bytes across wires, or waiting on barriers:

\(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\): Forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer step, all local arithmetic after distribution across \(\DeviceCount\) devices. Governed by MFU and per-GPU kernel efficiency. Improvements come from better kernels, mixed precision, and operator fusion.
\(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\): AllReduce of gradients, AllGather of parameters (in FSDP/ZeRO), activation transfers in tensor/pipeline parallelism. Governed by network bandwidth and collective algorithm choice. Improvements come from gradient compression, hierarchical collectives, and compute-communication overlap.
\(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\): Synchronization barriers, checkpoint writes, failure detection and recovery, pipeline bubble idle time, scheduler preemptions, and maintenance windows. Governed by cluster reliability and orchestration software. Improvements come from asynchronous checkpointing, elastic training, and faster failure detection.
\(\OverlappedTime\): Communication or coordination time hidden behind useful arithmetic. Governed by scheduling and implementation overlap.

Operational events may be amortized into the step budget or accounted for separately in runtime goodput. The same checkpoint or recovery delay must not appear in both. The compute-time fraction follows:
\[ \UsefulComputeFraction = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount}{\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)} \]
When \(\UsefulComputeFraction\) drops below 0.5, the fleet spends more time on communication and coordination than on useful arithmetic. This compute-time fraction is not total fleet efficiency; useful fleet efficiency also depends on MFU, scaling efficiency, and goodput. The C\(^3\) taxonomy identifies which noncompute term is responsible.

title: Rules of Thumb
text:
C\(^3\) Intersections
In a production cluster, a stalled training step rarely comes from a single isolated resource; a slow collective can idle tensor cores while a synchronous checkpoint write blocks both the GPUs and the network fabric. The Venn diagram in figure 1 maps how distributed execution spans the node substrate (\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\)), the networking backbone (\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)), and the orchestration layer (\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)). Because real bottlenecks arise at the pairwise and central boundaries where two or more of these dimensions compound, diagnosing them requires mapping observed symptoms back to the governing intersection and the engineering techniques that address it (table 3).






Figure 1: The C\(^3\) Intersection Landscape: Each circle is one operational dimension (Compute, \(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\), the node substrate; Communication, \(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\), the network backbone; Coordination, \(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\), the orchestration layer), labeled with the Fleet Law term it contributes to step time. Each pairwise overlap names the interaction between two dimensions (hiding network latency behind computation, preserving training progress against failure, and synchronizing collectives). At the center, where all three meet, is fleet ML systems engineering.
