Keyword spotting (KWS) systems are a common target for data-efficient on-device adaptation; Speech Commands provides a dataset for training and evaluating limited-vocabulary KWS models (Warden 2018). A detector must distinguish its target phrase from background speech while meeting latency and false-activation requirements. One design uses a pretrained acoustic encoder, such as a small convolutional or recurrent network, to map audio into embeddings for a lightweight classifier. A shared encoder supplies reusable features, while local examples can support a custom wake word or an underrepresented accent. Whether those examples justify local training depends on their coverage, transfer restrictions, and the improvement over the shared detector.
Few-shot adaptation can train an output classifier or another small parameter subset from utterances collected directly on the device. A user might provide 5–10 recordings of a custom wake word while the acoustic encoder remains frozen. Those positive examples define what to recognize, but the false-activation rate on other speech and background noise is a separate measurement, and the personalized detector should not be accepted until it has been made.
Head-only adaptation is cheap in a way the peak-memory budget of equation 1 makes precise. Because the backward pass stops at the classifier, the encoder’s saved activations leave the activation term, and the encoder outputs for the support set can be computed once and reused across update steps. What remains is running the encoder forward, holding the support examples or their features, and evaluating the adapted classifier. Those costs, not the size of the head, decide whether the update fits a particular phone or microcontroller.
Many on-device scenarios instead call for streaming adaptation, in which the model learns incrementally as data arrives over time rather than from a fixed support set (Hayes et al. 2020). Let \(\{\ModelInput_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}\) represent the observations selected from the stream for admitted updates. In streaming settings, observations arrive continuously, but the runtime admits training only when memory, energy, and foreground-latency budgets permit. The following rule describes one admitted update; it does not require a gradient step on every arrival. The index \(\OptimizerStepIndex\) counts these update steps. The computable loss may come from implicit feedback, pseudo-labels, self-supervised objectives, reconstruction error, or a task-specific proxy rather than explicit human labels. The model update can be written generically as: \[
\ModelParameters_{t+1} = \ModelParameters_t - \LearningRate_t \nabla \LossFunction(\ModelInput_t; \ModelParameters_t)
\] where \(\LearningRate_t\) is the learning rate at time \(\OptimizerStepIndex\). This form of adaptation is sensitive to noise and drift in the input distribution, and thus often incorporates mechanisms such as learning rate decay, meta-learned initialization, or update gating to improve stability.
The same strategies apply beyond keyword spotting. In wearable health devices, a model that classifies physical activities may begin with a generic classifier and adapt to user-specific motion patterns using only a few labeled activity segments. In smart assistants, user voice profiles are fine-tuned over time using ongoing speech input, even when explicit supervision is unavailable. Local corrections, repetitions, or downstream task completion can provide implicit signals, but only after the system defines which event counts as feedback and tests its validity. A user may accept a suggestion because it is convenient rather than correct, abandon a task for reasons unrelated to the model, or correct an error that the model itself induced. Production adaptation should therefore separate observed events from inferred labels, retain a nonadapting control cohort, measure delayed outcomes when available, and gate learning when the proxy-to-outcome relationship drifts. A stream of such updates also raises a stability problem that few-shot and streaming rules do not address on their own.



When a streaming update rule trains only on a user’s newest interactions, gradient steps on recent examples overwrite the weights that recognized earlier classes, causing accuracy on prior tasks to collapse within a few updates. Retaining a small sample of earlier observations on the device directly counters this failure mode.

Definition 11.3: Catastrophic forgetting
Catastrophic forgetting is the phenomenon in which a neural network trained sequentially on new tasks or data distributions rapidly loses performance on previously learned tasks, because gradient updates that optimize the new objective overwrite weight configurations that supported the old ones.


Significance: Without explicit mitigation, fine-tuning a deployed classifier on a new domain can sharply reduce prior-task accuracy, even when the new domain is closely related to the old one (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017). This is the central failure mode of on-device and federated learning. Every device that adapts locally to its user’s recent data risks erasing the general capabilities the centralized training run paid for, and the loss is invisible until inference encounters out-of-recent-context inputs.
Distinction: Unlike overfitting (a generalization failure on a single fixed task) and distribution shift (a deployment-time mismatch between training and inference data), forgetting is a training-time phenomenon caused by the sequential structure of the update stream itself. Updates for new data can interfere with earlier solutions even when a representation capable of supporting both tasks exists.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a small experience-replay buffer is sufficient protection. A small buffer can hold aggregate accuracy on a held-out set while rare classes, which it samples too seldom, continue to degrade. Forgetting must therefore be measured per class or per cohort, and the remedies range from capacity-proportional or prioritized buffers to weight-regularization methods such as elastic weight consolidation, which store no examples (section 11.8.2).





Learning a new task can erode accuracy on an earlier one.

Mnih, Volodymyr, Koray Kavukcuoglu, David Silver, Andrei A. Rusu, Joel Veness, Marc G. Bellemare, Alex Graves, et al. 2015. “Human-Level Control Through Deep Reinforcement Learning.” Nature 518 (7540): 529–33. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14236.
Experience replay addresses forgetting by retaining examples from earlier learning episodes and reusing them during later updates. Replay also appears in reinforcement learning (Mnih et al. 2015); here its role is to keep earlier local observations represented as new data arrives. It is one stability mechanism with an explicit storage cost. Section 11.8.2 returns to the problem with parameter-importance penalties, bounded update footprints, and rollback.
Unlike server-side replay strategies that rely on large datasets and extensive compute, on-device replay must operate with extremely limited capacity, often with tens or hundreds of samples, and must avoid interfering with user experience (Rolnick et al. 2019). Buffers may store only compressed features or distilled summaries, and updates must occur opportunistically (e.g., during idle cycles or charging). These system-level constraints reshape how replay is implemented and evaluated in the context of embedded ML.

Rolnick, David, Arun Ahuja, Jonathan Schwarz, Timothy Lillicrap, and Greg Wayne. 2019. “Experience Replay for Continual Learning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS).
Let \(\ReplayBuffer\) represent a memory buffer that retains a fixed-size subset of training examples. At time step \(\OptimizerStepIndex\), the model receives a new data point \((\ModelInput_t, \ExampleLabel_t)\) and appends it to \(\ReplayBuffer\). A replay-based update then samples a batch \(\{(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i)\}_{i=1}^{\BatchSize}\) of size \(\BatchSize\) from \(\ReplayBuffer\) and applies a gradient step: \[
\ModelParameters_{t+1} = \ModelParameters_t - \LearningRate\nabla_\ModelParameters\left[ \frac{1}{\BatchSize} \sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \LossFunction(\ModelInput_i, \ExampleLabel_i; \ModelParameters_t) \right]
\] This is the streaming update of section 11.5.1 with one change of data source, from the newest observation to a batch drawn from \(\ReplayBuffer\). The systems cost lies in what that change requires, namely buffer storage that competes with model state and forward and backward work on old examples in every admitted window. Over time, this replay mechanism allows the model to reinforce prior knowledge while incorporating new information.
A practical on-device implementation might use a ring buffer to store a small set of compressed feature vectors rather than full input examples. The buffer has a fixed capacity and overwrites its oldest entry once full, so one parameter bounds its memory and sets the balance between retained history and new data (listing 4).



Listing 4: Replay Buffer: Implements a circular storage mechanism for efficient memory management in constrained environments. This approach allows models to efficiently retain and sample from recent data points, balancing the need to use historical information while incorporating new insights.


import random


# Ring buffer for experience replay on memory-constrained devices
# Stores compressed features (not raw inputs) to minimize footprint
class ReplayBuffer:
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.capacity = capacity  # Fixed size, e.g., 1000 examples
        self.buffer = []
        self.index = 0  # Circular write pointer

    def store(self, feature_vec, label):
        if len(self.buffer) < self.capacity:
            self.buffer.append((feature_vec, label))  # Fill phase
        else:
            self.buffer[self.index] = (
                feature_vec,
                label,
            )  # Overwrite oldest
        self.index = (self.index + 1) % self.capacity  # Wrap around

    def sample(self, k):
        # Uniform sampling within the retained buffer; older examples are absent
        return random.sample(self.buffer, min(k, len(self.buffer)))



This implementation maintains a fixed-capacity cyclic buffer, storing compressed representations (e.g., last-layer embeddings) and associated labels. Uniform sampling here covers only the retained recent window; it does not remove the history bias introduced by overwriting old examples. Reservoir sampling is an alternative when the goal is to represent the full stream, though any finite buffer still requires coverage checks.
In TinyML applications, experience replay has been applied to problems such as gesture recognition, where devices must continuously improve predictions while observing a small number of events per day. Instead of training directly on the streaming data, the device stores representative feature vectors from recent gestures and uses them to finetune classification boundaries periodically. Similarly, in on-device keyword spotting, replaying past utterances can improve wake-word detection accuracy without the need to transmit audio data off-device.
Experience replay spends storage and additional update work to preserve earlier behavior. Raw inputs can exceed storage or retention budgets, especially in vision and audio applications. Cached feature vectors reduce that footprint, but an update starting from those vectors trains the downstream model without reconstructing the original encoder computation. If the encoder changes, old features may no longer match its current representation; the system must retain a compatible encoder, refresh the features from retained inputs, or expire incompatible entries. Persistent replay also consumes flash write cycles. Buffer contents, representation versions, and replay frequency therefore belong in the same resource and retention policy.



Experience replay is limited by how many examples fit in the buffer: storing raw \(224{\times}224\) camera frames or uncompressed audio waveforms inside an on-device replay buffer fills a wearable’s or microcontroller’s memory after only a few dozen observations. When raw training inputs are too large, noisy, or redundant to store and process directly, transforming them into lower-dimensional embeddings or compact encodings preserves task-relevant structure while shrinking memory and compute costs. Compressed representations serve two complementary goals. They reduce the footprint of stored data, allowing devices to maintain longer histories or replay buffers under tight memory budgets (Hayes et al. 2020). They also simplify the learning task by projecting raw inputs into more structured feature spaces, often learned via pretraining or meta-learning, in which efficient adaptation is possible with minimal supervision.

Hayes, T. L., K. Kafle, R. Shrestha, M. Acharya, and C. Kanan. 2020. “REMIND Your Neural Network to Prevent Catastrophic Forgetting.” In Computer Vision – ECCV 2020. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-58598-3_28.
One common approach is to encode data points using a pretrained feature extractor and discard the original high-dimensional input. For example, an image \(\ModelInput_i\) might be passed through a CNN to produce an embedding vector \(\StoredEmbedding_i = \FrozenFeatureEncoder(\ModelInput_i)\), where \(\FrozenFeatureEncoder(\cdot)\) is a fixed feature encoder. This embedding captures visual structure (e.g., shape, texture, or spatial layout) in a compact representation, usually ranging from 64 to 512 dimensions, suitable for lightweight downstream adaptation.
Mathematically, training can proceed over compressed samples \((\StoredEmbedding_i, \ExampleLabel_i)\) using a lightweight decoder or projection head. Let \(\ModelParameters\) represent the trainable parameters of this decoder model, which is typically a small neural network that maps from compressed representations to output predictions. As each example is presented, the model parameters are updated using gradient descent: \[
\ModelParameters_{t+1} = \ModelParameters_t - \LearningRate\nabla_\ModelParameters\LossFunction\big(\PredictionHeadFunction(\StoredEmbedding_i; \ModelParameters), \ExampleLabel_i\big)
\] The rule is the same gradient step once more, now applied to stored embeddings \(\StoredEmbedding_i\) and a small head whose prediction is \(\PredictionHeadFunction(\StoredEmbedding_i; \ModelParameters)\), rather than to raw inputs. Only the head’s parameters \(\ModelParameters\) change, so this is the head-only case of equation 1, and the encoder runs once per example when the embedding is stored rather than on every update. This bounds the trainable portion of the model, but feasibility still depends on the head’s activations and optimizer state alongside the replay buffer and runtime reserves.
When replay storage rather than model compute binds, a device can go further and learn a dictionary of recurring sensor-trace patterns, storing each example as a few nonzero coefficients over that dictionary instead of as raw samples. A dataset of traces \(\SensorTraceMatrix\) then factorizes as \(\SensorTraceMatrix\approx \SensorPatternDictionary\DictionaryCoefficientMatrix\), where the columns of \(\SensorPatternDictionary\) are the basis patterns and the block-sparse coefficient matrix \(\DictionaryCoefficientMatrix\) records which patterns are active in each example. The saving is real only if the dictionary plus all stored coefficients is smaller than the raw replay examples. Updating the dictionary changes the representation of every stored example, so reconstruction quality and compatibility become part of the replay policy.
Compressed representations can reduce how long raw inputs remain stored, but an embedding is not anonymized merely because it is lower dimensional. It may preserve identity, attributes, or enough structure for inversion, and it must receive the same access-control, retention, and deletion analysis as the source data unless a separate privacy mechanism establishes a stronger guarantee. Compression can also act as an implicit regularizer, smoothing learning and mitigating overfitting when only a few training examples are available.
In keyword spotting, raw audio can first be transformed into mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs),12 a compact, lossy representation derived from the speech power spectrum. Storing these vectors instead of waveforms reduces the replay payload. The complete adaptation budget must still include feature extraction, model state, and the working memory needed for updates.
12 MFCCs (mel-frequency cepstral coefficients): For a 320-sample audio window (20 ms at 16 kHz), 16-bit samples occupy 640 bytes, while 12–13 coefficients stored at 32 bits each occupy approximately 50 bytes. The roughly 13\(\times\) reduction compares one waveform window with one feature vector; overlapping windows, additional features, and metadata change the storage ratio for a complete recording. Replay capacity depends on that complete representation, and keyword detection quality must be evaluated separately from byte savings.


Each of these three mechanisms spends a different scarce resource: replaying raw observations when memory is the bottleneck overflows device storage, whereas compressing inputs into fixed embeddings when the feature extractor itself needs to adapt freezes the wrong representation. Few-shot adaptation uses a small informative support set, replay spends memory and compute to preserve prior behavior, and compressed representations extend the history that fits on-device. Their limits remain different: weak pretrained features can defeat few-shot adaptation, a replay buffer can omit rare cases, and compression can discard task-relevant information. Combining mechanisms does not escape these on-device learning trade-offs (table 5), because every combination must fit the same memory, energy, and privacy budget.

In practice, these methods are not mutually exclusive. Many real-world systems combine them to achieve robust, efficient adaptation. For example, a keyword spotting system may use compressed audio features (e.g., MFCCs), finetune a few parameters from a small support set, and maintain a replay buffer of past embeddings for continual refinement.
Efficient adaptation and data strategies establish how a single device can learn from its user. Sharing those gains requires another decision: whether local updates contain information useful to a common model and can be combined within communication and privacy constraints. Federated learning supplies that coordination protocol. Personal state can remain local when sharing would not improve the population objective, and privacy controls must separately limit what transmitted updates disclose.

The voice assistant of the chapter’s opening, now deployed to millions of homes whose intermittently available devices contribute updates when local conditions permit, shows what local adaptation alone cannot do. One household pronounces “data” as “DAY-tuh” and another as “DA-tuh”; a third, a technical household, says “machine learning” every day, while a fourth never has. Local adaptation can specialize each model to its own household, but nothing it learns travels. If the fourth household starts using the phrase, its model must learn it from scratch, even though millions of other devices already handle it. Federation offers that transfer when the observations support a common objective. The system must decide which changes improve shared representations and which should remain personal, then evaluate whether aggregation helps the intended users.
Federated learning (definition 11.2) supplies that transfer while each device keeps its raw examples local. The approach turns data locality into one privacy control, not a complete privacy guarantee. A system must still treat gradients, model deltas, participation timing, device identifiers, and aggregate statistics as sensitive outputs because these signals can reveal information about local users (Kairouz and McMahan 2021; Zhu et al. 2019). Of the three architectures in figure 2, only federated learning pools experience across users without moving raw examples, and it buys that position with a protocol.


Before choosing a federated optimization or privacy protocol, an architect must specify who the participants are, because a mobile cohort-sampling protocol applied to ten collaborating hospitals breaks scheduling, weighting, and fault recovery, as does a hospital consortium’s stable round membership expected from millions of intermittently connected phones. The voice assistant is cross-device, with millions of unreliable phones, whereas a group of hospitals that want to train a complication-prediction model without centralizing patient records is cross-silo, with a few reliable institutions that each hold a large dataset. That distinction changes the failure model, scheduling policy, and privacy unit before any optimizer is selected (table 6) (Kairouz and McMahan 2021).

Once the participant population is defined, a federated round must coordinate devices that hold different data distributions, connect over constrained links, and drop out unpredictably. If devices trained on unaligned starting versions and uploaded raw weight tensors whenever they came online, the coordinator would sum incompatible parameter spaces and stall on offline stragglers. Practical distributed coordination protocols must therefore solve three engineering challenges simultaneously. Local training must produce compatible updates despite non-IID data distributions. Aggregation must combine those updates efficiently despite bandwidth constraints. Timing must be coordinated across devices with heterogeneous availability patterns.


Local training turns the device’s adaptation policy into a contribution to a shared model. Every contribution needs a known starting version, a compatible parameter schema, and a declared local update rule. Otherwise, arrays with the same shape may describe changes to different models. A synchronous protocol therefore starts every participating client from the same shared version, trains on local examples under that rule, and returns the difference from the starting parameters, while personal parameters stay outside the aggregate.
The process repeats with a new shared version for each accepted round. Update frequency depends on device availability, local work, and communication cost. A secure transmission channel protects the transfer, but the receiving server can still inspect the update unless the aggregation protocol separately hides individual contributions. Model compatibility and update confidentiality are therefore distinct protocol obligations.



The most widely used rule for combining client updates is federated averaging (FedAvg), which has become a canonical algorithm for federated learning (McMahan et al. 2017). In FedAvg, each device trains its local copy of the model using SGD on its private data. The algorithm is local SGD, which synchronizes only after several local steps to save communication, run with two changes that the data center version never faces. Only a sampled subset of clients participates in each round, and each client’s data is a non-IID shard of the population. The local steps that save communication therefore also pull each client toward its own optimum.

↩︎ Local SGD and the trade-off between synchronization frequency and convergence that it exposes are established in Scaling Efficiency and Convergence.

Formally, let \(\ClientLocalDataset_k\) denote the local dataset on client \(\ClientIndex\), and let \(\ModelParameters_k^\FederatedRoundIndex\) be the parameters of the model on client \(\ClientIndex\) at round \(\FederatedRoundIndex\). Each client performs \(\LocalEpochCount\) epochs of SGD on its local data, yielding an update \(\ModelParameters_k^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1}\). The central server then aggregates these updates as: \[
\ModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{\ParticipatingClientCount} \frac{\ClientSampleCount_k}{\RoundSampleCount} \ModelParameters_k^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1}
\tag{3}\] where \(\ClientSampleCount_k = |\ClientLocalDataset_k|\) is the number of samples on device \(\ClientIndex\), \(\RoundSampleCount= \sum_k \ClientSampleCount_k\) is the total number of samples across participating clients, and \(\ParticipatingClientCount\) is the number of active devices in the current round. Here \(\ParticipatingClientCount\) is a client count, unrelated to the C³ axes, and bare \(\LocalEpochCount\) counts local epochs; the energy quantities of equation 2 always carry a subscript.
This formula optimizes an example-weighted objective, in which a client with ten times as many local examples receives ten times the influence. That choice is appropriate when every example should contribute equally, but it can let prolific users or large institutions dominate the model. A user-weighted objective instead assigns each participating client weight \(1/\ParticipatingClientCount\), optionally capping or normalizing each client’s local contribution before aggregation. Neither choice is universally fair. The system must declare whether its unit of interest is an example, a user, an organization, or a deployment cohort, then evaluate that population rather than inherit \(\ClientSampleCount_k/\RoundSampleCount\) as an implementation default.
A deployed round wraps the averaging rule in policy that the equation leaves unstated (figure 10). Equation 3 fixes how completed models combine, but not which clients are invited, how long the coordinator waits, or how few completions force a round to be abandoned. Those protocol choices decide which contributions enter the sum. A client that misses the deadline contributes nothing, and its examples are absent from \(\RoundSampleCount\) for that round. Over-selection and its population-coverage trade-off are developed in section 11.7.1.






Figure 10: Federated Averaging Protocol: One FedAvg round in four steps. (1) The coordinator selects a cohort, over-selecting to absorb dropouts, and broadcasts the global model \(\ModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex}\). (2) Each client runs \(\LocalEpochCount\) local epochs on its private data. (3) Clients that finish before the round deadline upload \(\ModelParameters_k^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1}\); a straggler that misses the deadline is dropped. (4) The coordinator forms the example-weighted average of equation 3, which becomes the next global model.



This basic structure introduces a number of design choices and trade-offs. The number of local epochs \(\LocalEpochCount\) sets the balance between computation and communication. A larger \(\LocalEpochCount\) reduces communication frequency but risks divergence if local data distributions vary too much. The selection of participating clients affects convergence stability and fairness. In real-world deployments, not all devices are available at all times, and hardware capabilities may differ substantially, requiring robust participation scheduling and failure tolerance.


⇄ Contrast: Federated rounds over intermittent wide-area clients contrast with the synchronous AllReduce collectives on low-latency cluster fabrics established in AllReduce Algorithms and Topologies.



A federated deployment must reach a quality target within its time, energy, and participation budgets. More local training can reduce how often clients communicate, but it also changes their updates and the time each selected cohort takes to finish. The engineering comparison is therefore time to an agreed quality target, not communication rounds alone.


FedAvg exposes the number of participating clients \(\ParticipatingClientCount\), local epochs \(\LocalEpochCount\), and communication rounds \(\FederatedRoundCount\) as controls (McMahan et al. 2017). Their product \(\ParticipatingClientCount \LocalEpochCount \FederatedRoundCount\) counts client-epochs when participation is fixed, which makes it a tally of the work a run performs rather than a measure of its progress. Clients can have different dataset sizes, and equal client-epoch counts can process different examples or produce conflicting updates, so two runs with the same \(\ParticipatingClientCount \LocalEpochCount \FederatedRoundCount\) can end at very different quality. A convergence result is useful only when its assumptions match the optimizer, client sampling, and data distributions.

McMahan, Brendan, Eider Moore, Daniel Ramage, Seth Hampson, and Blaise Agüera y Arcas. 2017. “Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data.” International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 54: 1273–82.



Non-IID data is where federated averaging departs from the data center version of local SGD. Each local step moves a client toward the optimum of its own shard. After many local steps the client models sit near different optima, and their weighted average lands at a point that need not minimize the population objective. This client drift grows with the number of local steps and with how far the client distributions differ, and it degrades federated averaging relative to i.i.d. baselines (Li et al. 2020; Zhao et al. 2018). It therefore eats into the benefit of fewer communications exactly where communication is most expensive. How strongly depends on the partition, update rule, participation policy, and local step size. No universal heterogeneity score predicts a round count across applications, which is why section 11.6.2.3.3 measures the trade-off rather than computing it.
When statistical heterogeneity causes FedAvg to diverge or stall, two foundational algorithmic extensions address the root cause of client drift:

FedProx (Li et al. 2020) adds a proximal penalty proportional to \(\|\ModelParameters - \GlobalModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex}\|^2\) to each client’s local loss function. This penalty constrains local updates to remain in the neighborhood of the current global model \(\GlobalModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex}\), stabilizing convergence under statistical heterogeneity and permitting devices to execute variable numbers of local epochs without destabilizing the server aggregate.
SCAFFOLD (Kairouz and McMahan 2021) corrects the local update direction directly using control variates. By maintaining a server control variate and per-client control variates that estimate the difference between client-local and global gradient directions, SCAFFOLD applies an additive correction to each local SGD step. This correction counters client drift under heterogeneous local data, although it roughly doubles the communication volume per round by transmitting control variates alongside model parameters.




Compare candidate local-epoch settings under the same initialization, data partition, participation policy, and held-out quality target. For each setting \(\LocalEpochCount\), record the first validated round \(\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)\) that reaches the target and the elapsed duration \(\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)\) of each completed round, including client selection, local work, transfer, aggregation, and any waiting. The observed time to target is
\[
\TimeToTarget(\LocalEpochCount) = \sum_{\CompletedRoundIndex=1}^{\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)} \RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount).
\]
Each \(\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)\) is one instance of the round budget sketched at the opening of the chapter. Read through the Fleet Law, it is the local training on the slowest client the round still awaits, plus the upload, plus the wait for enough reports, less whatever overlaps. The communication piece is easy to estimate. Over a constrained mobile uplink of 1–10 Mb/s, the chapter’s reference adapter update of 50 MB takes about 7 minutes to upload at the low end and about 42 seconds at the high end. That cost recurs in every one of the \(\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)\) rounds. A setting of \(\LocalEpochCount\) that halves \(\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)\) therefore removes half of the cumulative upload time. It pays off only if the extra local training it adds to each round, on the slowest awaited client, costs less than the uploads it removes. Client drift keeps that comparison from being settled on paper, because more local steps can also raise \(\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)\), and only measured runs can rank the settings.
A useful experiment log records local epochs, completed clients, rounds to target, elapsed time, transmitted bytes, and device energy. If a run never reaches the quality target within the budget, report that outcome rather than extrapolating an invented convergence curve. Repeated runs and cohort-level validation distinguish a stable improvement from a fortunate sample of participating devices.



Local work \(\LocalEpochCount\) acts on the wall clock through two opposing paths, drawn as a timeline of rounds in figure 11. Increasing local epochs lengthens per-round execution duration \(\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)\) (the width of each round) while reducing synchronization frequency (the number of rounds in a row), which can lower the required rounds \(\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)\) until client drift penalizes convergence. Both paths combine into the cumulative time to target \(\TimeToTarget(\LocalEpochCount)\), where each row ends, which remains admissible only if total consumption fits within client energy and fleet-coverage budgets. A setting that requires fewer rounds can still prolong total wall-clock duration. Selecting \(\LocalEpochCount\) therefore requires comparing measured times to target against physical admission constraints, rather than relying on ungrounded heuristics.






Figure 11: Measuring the Local-Work Trade-Off: The local-work setting \(\LocalEpochCount\) acts through two opposing paths. More local epochs lengthen each round, \(\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)\), while reducing how often clients synchronize, which can lower the rounds to target, \(\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)\), unless client drift raises it. Only their combination, the measured time to target \(\TimeToTarget(\LocalEpochCount)\), ranks candidate settings, and a setting is admissible only if it also fits the client energy and population-coverage budgets.



The operating point depends on the deployment. Larger local updates can amortize transfer overhead, but they also change drift, completion time, and which clients finish. The network alone can move the optimum, as a cost model in relative units shows (figure 12). Its minimum \(\LocalEpochCount^*\) shifts from \(\LocalEpochCount=10\) on the fast-network curve to \(\LocalEpochCount=40\) on the slow-network curve because amortizing expensive transfers justifies more local work. These curves are not measured convergence results. A deployment must establish whether additional local work actually reduces time to target after drift and client completion are counted, and adaptive epoch policies need the same outcome and coverage checks as fixed settings.














Figure 12: Communication-Computation Trade-Off in Federated Learning: As network bandwidth decreases from fast to slow, the time-minimizing number of local epochs shifts rightward because additional local computation amortizes more communication. The curves come from an illustrative cost model in relative units, not measurements; its growing local-work term stands in for the longer rounds and added drift that make excessive local work counterproductive.






Federated convergence results depend on the update rule, objective, sampling policy, and assumptions about client data (Kairouz and McMahan 2021). Heterogeneity, participation, and local sample counts are therefore inputs to a feasibility assessment, not universal pass/fail thresholds. A deployment must demonstrate that its chosen configuration reaches the declared quality target within time and device budgets, with evaluation that represents the intended population.
When a configuration misses that target, the measured failure guides the next experiment. Conflicting local updates motivate testing less local work, adding proximal regularization (FedProx), incorporating control variates (SCAFFOLD), or switching to personalization. Long waits motivate scheduling or asynchronous alternatives, subject to privacy-protocol compatibility. Sparse local evidence motivates bounded adaptation and stronger validation. None of these changes replaces observations from absent cohorts; each must be reevaluated for quality, resource cost, and population coverage.
The aggregation rule specifies how compatible local models produce a shared model. The measured time to target establishes whether a configuration reaches its objective within budget. A controlled lab can hold participant availability and network conditions steady. A phone fleet cannot, so the implementation must define how selection, deadlines, and failures change the set of updates that actually enters each aggregate. These protocol decisions connect learning behavior to fleet orchestration.

A round selects a cohort from the deployment population, but some selected devices overheat, lose Wi-Fi, enter power-saving mode, or power off before returning an update. A fleet of millions of smartphones need not participate in one round for these failures to matter. Turning the FedAvg protocol into a production fleet system requires deciding which clients are eligible and how long to wait, compressing updates to fit constrained uplinks, separating personal state from shared weights, enforcing cryptographic and statistical privacy bounds, and reconciling asynchronous updates across heterogeneous hardware.


The first decision in any round is which devices to invite. Sampling devices uniformly at random without checking their power and network state would interrupt users mid-task, whereas accepting updates only from plugged-in flagship phones on fast Wi-Fi trains a global model skewed toward affluent, overnight-charging cohorts. Because real-world client availability shifts continuously with battery state, charging habits, and network coverage, client scheduling governs both the completion speed and the population coverage of distributed learning.
At a baseline level, federated ML systems define eligibility criteria for participation. A mobile deployment may require devices to be plugged in, connected to Wi-Fi, and idle to limit interference with foreground work and battery use. The chosen criteria determine which subset of the total population is considered “available” for a training round; they are deployment policy rather than requirements of federated learning itself.
Beyond these operational filters, devices also differ in their hardware capabilities, data availability, and network conditions. Some smartphones contain many recent examples relevant to the current task, while others have outdated or irrelevant data. Network bandwidth and upload speed may vary widely depending on geography and carrier infrastructure. As a result, uniform random selection from the eligible pool does not guarantee coverage of the full deployment population; eligibility has already excluded some devices and their data.
Availability-driven selection introduces participation bias, the fleet-level consequence of the admission test in equation 2 (principle \(\ref{pri-participation-selects-population}\)). Clients with favorable conditions, such as frequent charging, high-end hardware, and consistent connectivity, pass admission and participate repeatedly, while others are systematically underrepresented. This can skew the resulting model toward behaviors and preferences of a privileged subset of the population, raising both fairness and generalization concerns.
Participation bias becomes severe when a small eligible cohort supplies most completed updates while other cohorts rarely participate. The skew is measured per cohort as a coverage ratio, the cohort’s share of completed updates divided by its share of the deployed population. A ratio near one means the cohort is represented in proportion to its size, and a ratio well below one means the shared model learns that cohort’s behavior at less than its population weight. Completion logs supply the numerator and the deployment inventory the denominator, so the ratio can be computed without inspecting any update. The admission test and the round deadline both remove constrained devices faster than capable ones. Uniform selection among admitted devices passes the resulting skew through unchanged, so a budget cohort can fall from a fifth of the fleet to a sliver of the completed updates (figure 13). Low coverage also feeds itself, because models become more strongly optimized for users with high-end devices and stable connectivity, potentially degrading performance for resource-constrained users who need adaptation the most. A keyboard prediction model might become biased toward the typing patterns of users with flagship phones who charge overnight, missing important linguistic variations from users with budget devices or irregular charging patterns.

The order of these decisions limits what any remedy can do. Fleet orchestration admits only feasible allocations before a fairness policy divides them (principle \(\ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}\)), and a federated scheduler inherits the same order with a sharper consequence. Its eligibility filter fixes the candidate pool, so a fairness policy can redistribute rounds only among devices the admission test already accepted; a device that never qualifies is invisible to it.
Scheduling must therefore balance completion speed with population coverage. Stratified or quota-based sampling can prioritize underrepresented groups among eligible devices, while cumulative participation records can guide later invitations. Weighting methods require estimates of the population and selection process; they cannot recover observations from a cohort that never participates. Buffered asynchronous aggregation (Nguyen et al. 2021), whose mechanism section 11.7.5.1 describes, staleness-aware methods (Rodio and Neglia 2024), and fairness-oriented weighting (Ma et al. 2024) offer additional controls. Their effectiveness must be checked through completed participation and cohort quality, rather than inferred from the scheduling rule alone. Example weighting in the aggregate (equation 3) also gives large local datasets more influence whether or not they represent the target population any better.

Scheduling must also bound how long a round waits on its slowest participants. Network latency, battery depletion, or background process contention can make some devices (stragglers) take 10\(\times\) longer than the median, and the round cannot aggregate until enough updates arrive.



Enough valid reports let the round close before its slowest clients finish.
To reduce waiting for stragglers, production federated learning (FL) systems employ over-selection. The server selects a candidate pool size \(\CandidateClientCount\) larger than the target number of updates \(\TargetUpdateCount\) (the production system of Bonawitz et al. (2019) selects about 130 percent of the target, \(\CandidateClientCount \approx 1.3 \times \TargetUpdateCount\)). When enough valid reports arrive, the server can form an aggregate from \(\TargetUpdateCount\) completed updates rather than wait for every selected device. Completion then depends on the target-th valid report, but over-selection alone does not guarantee that the target is reached. A round deadline and an explicit acceptance or abandonment rule handle insufficient completion. Secure aggregation adds a participation floor and dropout recovery (section 11.7.4); selecting the fastest reports must remain compatible with that protocol. Accepting the fastest responders can amplify the participation bias just described, so shorter rounds must be evaluated against cohort coverage and wall-clock time to the declared quality target. Because these scheduling decisions set convergence rate, model generalization, energy consumption, and user experience together, poor scheduling produces excessive stragglers, overfitting to narrow client segments, or wasted computation.



Many of the stragglers that miss a round deadline fail on the network transfer rather than on local computation: transmitting full-precision weights or gradients over an asymmetric mobile uplink can exhaust a client’s connectivity window or battery allowance before its update ever reaches the coordinator.13 Update compression therefore begins with a bottleneck diagnosis: when transfer is limiting, the design decision is which information to quantize, sparsify, or keep local. The smaller payload must then be evaluated against encoding cost, update error, and the rounds required to reach the quality target.
13 Wireless upload asymmetry: Federated updates use the uplink, whose available throughput can differ substantially from the downlink and vary with coverage and contention. Transfer time depends on encoded update size and effective uplink goodput; energy also depends on radio state and transfer duration. Low-power links may add duty-cycle constraints. Compression is useful when these costs bind the update budget, but its necessity depends on the payload, link, and permitted synchronization interval.14 Gradient sparsification: Selecting the largest 1–10 percent of gradient elements by magnitude reduces transmitted value count by 10–100\(\times\) before coordinate indices and other metadata are included. Sparsified SGD and deep gradient compression retain untransmitted residuals for later updates rather than assuming that small components can be discarded permanently (Stich et al. 2018; Lin et al. 2018). Wire-byte savings depend on the encoding, while convergence depends on the residual handling, optimizer, and compression schedule; a value-count reduction alone establishes neither.

The compression decision separates into three levers, each changing a different part of the communication bottleneck: model compression reduces bits per update, selective sharing reduces which parameters travel, and architectural partitioning keeps some state local. Model compression methods reduce the wire footprint of transmitted updates through quantization, sparsification, or subsampling. Instead of sending full-precision gradients, a client transmits 8-bit quantized updates or communicates only the top-\(\RetainedGradientElementCount\) gradient elements14 with highest magnitude, the same encodings that cluster training applies to its collective payloads. At the edge they bind in a different place. They act on a slow, asymmetric uplink rather than a fabric, under secure aggregation that must still combine the encoded updates, and inside a per-round communication total (equation 4) that also counts downloads and retries. These transformations are communication mechanisms, not privacy mechanisms; a smaller embedding, sparse update, or low-precision gradient may still expose membership, attributes, or reconstructable features.


↩︎ Gradient quantization, top-\(\Glyph{k}\) sparsification, and error feedback that carries unsent updates forward are established in Gradient Compression Under Bandwidth Scarcity. Convergence depends on the optimizer and compression assumptions.
Selective update sharing further reduces communication by transmitting only subsets of model parameters or updates. In layer-wise selective sharing, clients update only certain layers, typically the final classifier or adapter modules, while keeping the majority of the backbone frozen. This reduces the update payload and limits which shared representations can change, but the trainable subset can still overfit nonrepresentative client data.
Architectural partitioning requires specifying what crosses the boundary. A personal/shared parameter partition keeps local modules private while aggregating selected shared parameters. Split learning instead divides execution between client and server, exchanging intermediate activations and backward gradients at the cut. These designs have different traffic and exposure patterns; neither guarantees a communication reduction or privacy merely by dividing the model.
These approaches can use the FedAvg aggregation protocol (section 11.6.2.2) only when their encoding and shared parameter schema support weighted aggregation. When the server sees cleartext uploads, it can dequantize each client’s tensor with that client’s scale factor and scatter sparse index-value pairs into a dense buffer before summing. Secure aggregation removes that option because the server sums cryptographically masked integer vectors element by element without inspecting individual uploads. Clients that quantize updates must therefore quantize to a shared fixed-point scale so their masked integers represent the same unit at every coordinate, and clients that sparsify updates must project onto a shared coordinate template or sketch rather than uploading client-specific index lists that would fail to align and would reveal which parameters changed. Local-only parameters must stay outside the shared aggregate altogether. Across all of these encodings, the total communication volume for round \(\CompletedRoundIndex\) is
\[
\RoundCommunicationVolume= \RoundDownloadVolume+ \RoundUploadVolume+ \RoundProtocolVolume+ \RoundRetryVolume,
\tag{4}\]
Equation 4 makes download, upload, protocol, and retry traffic explicit. The download distributes model state, the upload carries client updates, protocol traffic covers authentication and cryptographic setup, and retries account for failed or repeated transfers. Optimizing only \(\RoundUploadVolume\) can therefore move rather than remove the bottleneck. Additional local computation amortizes network transfers, and each communication-efficient alternative to it carries its own cost. Compression may degrade gradient fidelity, selective updates can limit model capacity, and split architectures complicate coordination. Summed over a training run, the upload term alone can exceed the raw data that federation was meant to keep local, even when each update is far smaller than that data.

Math: Bandwidth efficiency is the ratio of raw data volume to model update size.

Raw data upload: 200 MB/week.

One-round uplink reduction: 200 MB/2.5 MB = 80×.

Systems insight: For this scenario, one 2.5 MB uplink is 80× smaller than one 200 MB raw-data upload. That ratio is not the end-to-end communication saving of a training run: after roughly 80× uplink rounds, cumulative update uploads alone equal the raw-data volume, before counting global-model downloads, retries, or protocol overhead. The verdict therefore turns on the round schedule. A deployment that runs one round per day uploads seven updates per week of data, far below the break-even count, and saves most of the uplink traffic. One that runs a round every hour uploads 168 updates per week, more than the break-even count, and moves more bytes than shipping the images would. Per-round traffic must be multiplied by the expected round count before federation can claim a bandwidth saving.


The local-work schedule and update encoding jointly determine communication cost. Figure 14 compares uncompressed 32-bit values (Panel A) with uniform 8-bit quantization (Panel B), which gives a \(4\times\) reduction in value bytes before scales and other metadata are counted. Top-\(\Glyph{k}\) sparsification with retained error feedback (Panel C) must encode coordinate identities as well as selected values. Error feedback retains one residual value per update coordinate between transmissions. Its storage depends on the update size and residual precision and must fit the device allowance alongside training and replay state. The receiving path must reconstruct or aggregate these encodings consistently, with separate compatibility requirements when secure aggregation hides individual updates.

The quantization panel’s “zero client state” means no persistent error-feedback residual; encoding buffers, scales, and temporary workspace still enter the device budget. Compression is useful when its reduction in total communication outweighs encoding work and any extra rounds needed to reach the quality target. A smaller upload helps a round only if transfer was what made clients miss the deadline or excluded a cohort, and the round’s completion logs show which. Smaller payloads can let clients on slow or congested uplinks finish before their resource window closes, so compression is judged by completed participation and cohort outcomes, not by bytes saved alone. Even when transfer becomes feasible, the shared model may still fail to capture local variation.



Compressing updates lets more devices finish a round, but clients that complete compatible updates can still pull the shared model in opposite directions when a dialect phrase, a regional keyboard shortcut, or an individual’s wrist-worn sensor placement conflicts with the population mean. A single global model may serve the average user adequately while concealing persistent accuracy losses for specific cohorts. Personalized federated learning retains shared representation learning while allowing selected parameters or models to specialize locally, trading added local state, training cost, and overfitting risk on sparse user data against per-user quality.
Let \(\ModelParameters_k\) denote the model parameters on client \(\ClientIndex\), and \(\GlobalModelParameters\) the aggregated global model. For \(\ParticipatingClientCount\) clients, counted as in equation 3, traditional FL seeks to minimize a global objective: \[
\min_\ModelParameters\sum_{k=1}^{\ParticipatingClientCount} \ClientObjectiveWeight_k \LossFunction_k(\ModelParameters)
\] where \(\LossFunction_k(\ModelParameters)\) is the local loss on client \(\ClientIndex\), and \(\ClientObjectiveWeight_k\) is a weighting factor (e.g., proportional to local dataset size). This formulation optimizes the weighted average loss of a shared model \(\ModelParameters\); it does not guarantee acceptable performance for every client. Local loss landscapes \(\LossFunction_k\) can differ across clients, reflecting non-IID data distributions and varying task requirements.
Personalization modifies this objective to allow each client to maintain its own adapted parameters \(\ModelParameters_k\), optimized with respect to both the global model and local data: \[
\min_{\ModelParameters_1, \ldots, \ModelParameters_{\ParticipatingClientCount}} \sum_{k=1}^{\ParticipatingClientCount} \left( \LossFunction_k(\ModelParameters_k) + \PersonalizationPenaltyWeight\cdot \GlobalDeviationPenalty(\ModelParameters_k, \GlobalModelParameters) \right)
\]
Here, \(\GlobalDeviationPenalty\) penalizes deviation from the global model, and \(\PersonalizationPenaltyWeight\) controls the strength of that penalty. The displayed objective describes local specialization around a given global reference; a complete protocol must additionally specify how that reference is trained and refreshed. The penalty trades local fit against proximity to the shared model, without guaranteeing improvement for every client.
In a wearable health monitor that classifies physical activities from physiological signals, this objective separates shared motion features from individual gait signatures, resting baselines, and sensor placements. Finetuning the final classification layer or low-rank adapters around the global reference \(\GlobalModelParameters\) addresses those user-specific differences, provided evaluation establishes that the local examples actually improve accuracy on rare activity classes with little supervision.
Several personalization strategies address the trade-offs between compute overhead, information exposure, and adaptation speed. One widely used approach is local finetuning, in which each client downloads the latest global model and performs a small number of gradient steps using its local data. This method avoids transmitting those examples during adaptation, but the resulting local state and any later update remain privacy-sensitive. It may also yield suboptimal results when the global model is poorly aligned with the client’s data distribution or when the local dataset is extremely limited.
Another effective technique involves personalization layers, where the model is partitioned into a shared backbone and a lightweight, client-specific head, typically the final classification layer (Arivazhagan et al. 2019). In FedPer, clients train both the shared base and their personal head, but only the shared base participates in server aggregation; the head remains local. A separate head-only adaptation policy can freeze a downloaded backbone to reduce local training cost when the relevant variation lies mainly in output categories or decision boundaries.

Clustered federated learning offers an alternative by grouping clients according to similarities in their data or performance characteristics, and training separate models for each cluster. This strategy can enhance accuracy within homogeneous subpopulations, though it introduces additional system complexity and may require exchanging metadata to determine group membership. Finally, meta-learning approaches, such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML),15 aim to produce a global model initialization that can be quickly adapted to new tasks with a few local updates (Finn et al. 2017). This is especially useful when clients have limited data or operate in environments with frequent distributional shifts.
Each strategy occupies a different point in the personalization trade-off space. Local finetuning, personalization layers, clustered federated learning, and meta-learning differ in compute overhead, information exposure, and adaptation latency (table 7). The mechanism determines what state is shared; a privacy guarantee requires separately specified controls and assumptions.

Two protective measures address that leakage. Secure aggregation17 protocols reveal a combined result while hiding individual updates beyond what that result itself reveals, subject to the protocol’s assumptions about collusion and participating clients. Differential privacy, a formal bound on how much any one protected user’s or record’s inclusion can change a released result, is obtained by clipping each contribution and adding noise calibrated to that bound. The deployment must specify which unit receives that protection.
These controls solve different problems. Secure aggregation limits what the coordinator learns about each submitted update, whereas differential privacy bounds how much a declared privacy unit can affect a released result. A deployment therefore needs a privacy accounting log that records the unit of protection, clipping rule, noise mechanism, sampling assumptions, \((\PrivacyBudget,\PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) expenditure for every release, and cumulative composition across training and federated analytics (Abadi et al. 2016; Kairouz and McMahan 2021). Clipping bounds each contribution before noise is calibrated. The parameters \(\PrivacyBudget\) and \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) describe the permitted change in output probabilities when the protected user or record is included or removed; composition accounts for repeated releases involving that unit. Resetting a round counter does not reset privacy loss for a user who participates again.

Secure aggregation also creates a robustness conflict. Byzantine-resilient rules such as Krum, coordinate-wise filtering, or per-client anomaly inspection need access to individual updates, while secure aggregation deliberately hides those updates (Blanchard et al. 2017; Bonawitz et al. 2017). A system cannot claim both arbitrary per-client inspection and conventional secure aggregation over the same messages. It must instead validate clients before masking, use attested execution and bounded local updates, compute only aggregation-compatible checks, or adopt a protocol designed to evaluate approved robust statistics without revealing raw client contributions. Figure 16 models this cryptographic boundary through pairwise zero-sum masking. Clients A and B negotiate a shared random mask \(\PairwiseMaskSecret\) via Diffie-Hellman key agreement. They perturb their local updates into pseudo-random vectors (\(\FirstClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters+ \PairwiseMaskSecret\) and \(\SecondClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters- \PairwiseMaskSecret\)) before crossing into the server domain. When the aggregation server sums the received vectors, the symmetric masks cancel (\(\PairwiseMaskSecret - \PairwiseMaskSecret = 0\)), yielding the exact unmasked aggregate \(\FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters+ \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters\). This two-client illustration assumes both clients complete the exchange and neither reveals its mask to the server. It demonstrates cancellation, not a complete protocol for collusion resistance or dropout recovery.
A real round has many clients, and some drop out after agreeing on masks but before uploading. Each dropped client leaves its pairwise masks uncancelled in the sum. The full protocol therefore has every client split the secret seeds of its masks into shares held by the other clients, and any threshold number of those shares can rebuild a seed (Bonawitz et al. 2017). After the upload deadline, surviving clients send the shares of the dropped clients’ seeds, and the server regenerates and subtracts the dangling masks. Recovery therefore costs an extra message round and computation that grows with the number of dropouts, and it succeeds only if at least the threshold number of clients survive; otherwise the round is abandoned. That threshold is one reason for a participation floor. The other is the sum itself, because an aggregate over a few clients reveals too much about each of them. The coordinator must therefore invite enough clients that the expected survivors clear the floor, and a cohort that falls short is held for a later round rather than aggregated.

Summing them cancels the mask and yields exactly \(\FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters\). The server learns only the aggregate, which can still leak information unless differential privacy bounds it.



Secure aggregation and differential privacy can protect different boundaries, but their composition must follow the threat model. If a trusted server adds noise after receiving an exact aggregate, the privacy guarantee applies to the released noisy result; it does not hide that exact aggregate from the server. A protocol designed for distributed noise can instead let the server receive only a noisy aggregate. Clipping, noise calibration, dropout assumptions, and repeated-release accounting must match the chosen protocol. Neither mechanism establishes that local data or updates are trustworthy.

A round that selects a million phones overnight will see some fraction overheat, lose connectivity, or be unplugged before they report, and a few may submit corrupted or deliberately malicious updates. Coordinating that population requires protocols that handle Byzantine clients, network partitions that temporarily cut participants off, and constrained communication. These challenges differ from controlled data center training, where high-bandwidth networks and managed infrastructure narrow the trust and availability envelope.


Federated learning inherits failures from distributed systems and machine learning, but its coordination objective is not consensus, the problem of making replicated servers agree on one ordered log of operations. Federated clients agree on no such log. A coordinator instead decides which stochastic client updates are eligible, how stale updates are weighted, and which aggregation rule can tolerate faulty participants without letting them steer the model. Devices crash, lose power, or disconnect during rounds, while compromised clients can submit poisoned updates crafted to push the shared model toward an attacker’s goal. Robust aggregation can reduce the influence of some faulty participants, but its assumptions, compute cost, and compatibility with secure aggregation must be explicit.
The trust chain begins before aggregation. A production coordinator authenticates the device and application instance, verifies the signed model and training-policy version, checks eligibility and freshness, binds the returned update to that version and round nonce, and records whether the update passed protocol-level bounds. Hardware-backed attestation can strengthen claims about code identity on supported devices, but it cannot prove that local examples are benign or representative. The resulting update-integrity record supports rejection, rollback, and incident analysis without treating device identity as evidence that the gradient is correct.
Network partitions are the harder case. Unlike a data center network, a federated fleet must absorb clients that stay offline for hours or days while traveling, out of coverage, or powered down. Asynchronous coordination protocols keep training moving despite missing participants, but they must balance staleness (accepting outdated contributions) against freshness (prioritizing recent but possibly sparse updates). Buffered asynchronous aggregation (Nguyen et al. 2021) shows the mechanism. It removes the round barrier, letting each client train whenever its admission test passes and upload when done, while the server accumulates arriving updates in a buffer and applies their aggregate once a fixed number have arrived. Each update is down-weighted by its staleness, the number of server versions published since the client downloaded its starting model, so a slow client still contributes without dragging the shared model back toward an old state.

Recovery must distinguish coordinator state from device-local state. The coordinator checkpoints the global model and the optimizer and protocol state needed to resume accepted progress; this does not require a simultaneous checkpoint on every device. An incomplete round needs an explicit acceptance or abandonment rule, followed by evaluation of the population represented by its completed updates. State reconciliation identifies a returning device’s base version and determines which shared state it must download and which personal state remains compatible. Server-side load balancing can redistribute coordination work, but replacing an unavailable client with a faster one also changes the local data contributing to training. Whereas convergence guarantees for synchronous training assume that every participant completes each round, a federated coordinator must treat stragglers18 and dropouts as the normal case and state what its convergence argument assumes about them.



Million-device orchestration is a tiering decision, in which the system decides which clients can train, which can only report lightweight updates, and how much bias that selection introduces. The difficulty is that hardware capabilities, network conditions, data distributions, and availability patterns vary simultaneously, challenging traditional distributed machine learning assumptions about homogeneous participants operating under similar conditions.
Across these four dimensions, illustrative peak compute ratings differ by about 1,200× between flagship smartphones rated at 35 TOPS and, below Archetype C’s phone-class clients, IoT microcontrollers rated at 0.03 TOPS. These ratings do not translate into a training-speed ratio, because supported precision, backward operators, memory traffic, and sustained execution determine update time. Memory spans the same 65,536× range from microcontroller SRAM to flagship phone RAM met in section 11.3.2, and at fleet scale that range decides which update state each tier can retain at all. Energy budgets further restrict when that work can run. Background adaptation in this example targets roughly 500–1000 mW, while phones may sustain 2–3 W for foreground ML workloads and burst higher briefly. Network throughput, latency, and interruption patterns must likewise be measured for the participating clients before selecting update frequency and compression.
Measured scores show a spread of the same order among phones alone, without counting microcontrollers. The AI Benchmark from ETH Zurich runs a fixed suite of quantized and floating-point inference workloads on each phone processor through its Android acceleration path (Ignatov et al. 2019; ETH Zurich Computer Vision Lab 2026). Among processors released from 2020 on, which a client fleet can still contain, the scores span about 400×, from the Snapdragon 460 (2020) to the Dimensity 9600 Pro (2026), and figure 17 plots every processor in the ranking. The Tensor G4 result runs through Android’s generic neural-network interface, while the leaders use their vendors’ own runtimes. These are inference scores, not training speeds, but they bound the problem from the side that matters for scheduling. No single local-work quota fits devices that differ by two orders of magnitude in measured throughput.

Tiered participation can assign different amounts of local work while preserving a compatible shared-update contract. A capable phone may complete more steps, while a constrained client contributes a smaller update or a separately defined aggregate statistic. These outputs are not interchangeable simply because they come from the same fleet. More work on strong devices also cannot replace the observations held by weak devices, so the policy must evaluate both computational contribution and population coverage.
The scale challenges extend beyond device heterogeneity to coordination overhead. Federated learning does not run a consensus protocol among millions of clients, nor does hierarchical aggregation perform local consensus. Regional aggregators reduce fan-in by validating an eligible cohort and combining updates before forwarding a partial aggregate; agreement on an ordered replicated log, if needed for the coordinator’s own metadata, remains a separate control-plane service. Edge infrastructure can provide aggregation points, but each added tier creates another trust boundary and another place where weighting, clipping, privacy accounting, and failure recovery must remain consistent.
Tiering interacts with the participation bias analyzed under client scheduling (section 11.7.1). Capability-based selection shortens rounds but concentrates completed updates on strong devices, so stratified sampling across tiers must be paired with per-cohort evaluation of completed participation and model quality. Availability also has a daily rhythm; devices that charge overnight in one time zone form a different cohort from those available during another zone’s working hours.
Orchestration brings client scheduling, update compression, personalization, privacy, and tiering into a coherent policy for a single federated round. Deployed systems, however, do not stop after one round: devices continue collecting streams of mostly unlabeled sensor data and applying local and federated updates week after week, so continual learning must bound how those updates compound over time rather than treat each window as an isolated event.

A keyboard model that adapts each night for a year passes through hundreds of admitted update windows, and each window moves it a little further from the version that was validated at release. Every update the chapter has built so far was judged one at a time, by whether it fit the memory budget, passed the admission test, and improved a local metric. Repeated across a deployment’s lifetime, those individually acceptable updates compound. Earlier changes alter what later updates start from, the replay buffer decides which old observations still count, and participation decides which devices shape the next shared version.
The mechanisms that keep this trajectory stable are the ones already introduced, now applied over time. Selective updates bound how far any one window can move the model, and they save work only when the execution path can skip it. Replay protects earlier behavior at the cost of retained examples and additional training. Opportunistic admission delays learning until device conditions permit it. Each needs a resource budget and an outcome check on retained behavior alongside the newest data. The long-lived stream that drives this learning is mostly unlabeled, which sets the first design question.


A camera stream running continuously at 30 frames per second produces roughly 2.6 million frames daily before retention filtering. An accelerometer sampling at 100 Hz generates 8.6 million readings, almost none of them accompanied by a user label. Cameras, accelerometers, location sensors, and touch interactions all supply data that can support self-supervised learning, turning continual learning into a storage and scheduling decision. The engineering question is which traces encode stable structure worth learning from and which should expire before they crowd out model state, replay buffers, or user-facing storage.
Learning from such traces without labels requires the supervision to come from the data’s own structure. Contrastive learning is the common way to manufacture it on a sensor stream, training a representation to bring designated positive pairs closer and distinguish them from designated negative pairs. Nearby camera frames or augmented views of one frame can supply positives when they preserve the task-relevant content; scene changes can invalidate that assumption. Different frames or replay entries can supply negatives, but may depict the same underlying event. The pair-selection policy therefore defines a learning signal that needs validation. Other devices’ samples are not automatically available under a federated data-locality policy, and stored pairs or representations compete with replay and model state for memory.



A model that adapts continually to recent summer lighting, a new work commute, or a shift in user vocabulary can overwrite the weights it needed for winter weather or older commands if each update moves parameters purely to minimize recent loss. When a deployment uses continual adaptation to address changing environments, user behavior, or task requirements, each update must balance new evidence against previously learned behavior. This is the stability-plasticity trade-off: models must remain stable enough to preserve useful knowledge while plastic enough to learn new patterns.
Continual learning on edge devices faces several interconnected challenges. Catastrophic forgetting (section 11.5.2) is magnified when devices cannot store or revisit historical training data. Task interference compounds it when several learning objectives compete for limited parameter capacity, and distribution shift between pretraining and local deployment demands continued adaptation without eroding the model’s core representations. Restricted device memory rules out the comprehensive replay buffers that centralized infrastructure can afford.
Three families of mechanisms manage the stability-plasticity trade-off during continual learning. Elastic weight consolidation19 (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017) mitigates catastrophic forgetting by penalizing changes to weights important for previous tasks. Experience replay (section 11.5.2) maintains stability during adaptation by interleaving new training with replayed examples from previous tasks. Progressive neural architectures allocate new capacity for new tasks rather than forcing all knowledge into fixed-capacity networks (Rusu et al. 2016). That last option is attractive when interference is severe, but it consumes additional memory and therefore fits only devices with enough spare capacity.

Compared with replay, EWC trades stored examples for parameter-sized statistics; which uses less memory depends on model size, retained history, precision, and the penalty implementation.

The earlier mechanisms bound each step without guaranteeing the trajectory. Meta-learned initializations (section 11.7.3) and few-shot adaptation (section 11.5.1) reach useful local behavior in few updates. Restricting updates to bias terms, adapters, or heads (section 11.4) keeps the base parameters intact, while useful pretrained representations reduce what the device must learn (Bommasani et al. 2021). Even a single update to a head or adapter can alter predictions on earlier tasks, and a year of individually small updates can accumulate into significant behavioral drift. The acceptance test for each window must therefore measure retained capability alongside improvement on the new data, against a recoverable baseline, because neither a small update count nor a frozen backbone is a stability guarantee.
Once the update footprint is bounded, the runtime must decide when the update can execute and whether it should be shared. The admission condition in equation 2 already governs when a continual update may run; what changes over a long deployment is that each admitted window also moves the device further from its last validated state. When the device also shares updates, the compression and selective transmission of section 11.7.2 keep that repeated traffic inside the bandwidth and energy budgets (Konečný et al. 2016).

Stability then becomes a state-management problem. Replay buffers, support sets, adaptation logs, and model update metadata must be protected against unauthorized access or tampering because they encode the local evidence that shaped the model. Lightweight encryption or hardware-backed secure storage can reduce that exposure, but security controls do not prove that adaptation remains beneficial. Lightweight validation techniques, including confidence scoring, drift detection heuristics (Gama et al. 2014), and shadow model evaluation, monitor adaptation dynamics and can hold an update for validated review before severe degradation occurs. Robust rollback procedures require a trusted baseline checkpoint that can be restored quickly, especially in safety-important and regulated domains where failure recovery must be provable.
Privacy and compliance requirements close the loop. User consent, data minimization, retention limits, and the right to erasure must be designed into the adaptation pipeline rather than added after deployment. Meeting regulatory obligations at scale demands on-device learning workflows in which the model can adapt in place while the operator can still explain, bound, and reverse each change. Because a fleet applies these rules on flagship phones, budget phones, and microcontroller sensors at once, the pillars and their stability controls must be assembled into one policy whose terms change with the device that runs it.
