text:
Self-Check: Answer

A mobile robotics vision system must process each frame within \(33\text{ ms}\), while cloud network round-trip time is \(80\text{–}150\text{ ms}\). Why must the foreground perception path execute locally even if model training remains in the cloud?

Network round-trip latency alone exceeds the foreground deadline, so a frame cannot wait for a cloud response.
Cloud data centers are physically incapable of computing backpropagation gradients on batch sizes of one within milliseconds.
The on-device camera sensor cannot serialize video frames into digital packets without first running an on-device forward-backward training pass.
On-device adaptation reduces model parameter count to zero before sending updates across the cellular uplink.

Answer: The correct answer is A. An \(80\text{–}150\text{ ms}\) round trip cannot fit inside a \(33\text{ ms}\) foreground deadline, regardless of server compute speed. This establishes the need for local inference; it does not establish the need for local training, which requires a separate adaptation benefit and resource budget.
Learning Objective: Distinguish latency-driven local inference requirements from the separate justification for on-device training.
Before investing in an on-device gradient-based learning pipeline for a mobile news app, an ML systems architect considers feature-based personalization (local feature caching with a frozen global model) versus on-device gradient fine-tuning. Under what systems criteria is feature-based personalization preferred, and what eliminates the need for local backpropagation?
Answer: Feature-based personalization is preferred when local preference vectors, interaction histories, or lookup embeddings give a frozen model the useful context it needs. Its parameters do not change, so this path avoids weight-gradient, backward-pass, and optimizer-state costs. Local feature state and inference buffers still consume resources. Compare validated personalization quality and the complete footprint against a gradient-based candidate; the chapter’s 4–12x range describes particular full-model training configurations relative to weight storage, not a universal amplification.
Learning Objective: Compare feature-based personalization against on-device gradient adaptation in terms of systems overhead and implementation complexity.
In comparing learning paradigms across edge fleets, what fundamental systems distinction separates isolated on-device learning from federated learning?

Isolated on-device learning transmits raw private data to centralized servers, whereas federated learning processes data locally without communication.
Isolated on-device learning restricts parameter updates entirely to a single node, preventing collective fleet knowledge sharing, whereas federated learning coordinates model updates across devices while preserving data locality.
Federated learning trains models from scratch on client devices without a pretrained base model, whereas isolated on-device learning requires continuous cloud synchronization.
Isolated on-device learning uses only INT4 integer arithmetic, whereas federated learning requires double-precision FP64 hardware accelerators on all mobile clients.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Isolated adaptation updates one device without aggregating knowledge from its peers. Federated learning coordinates local updates while keeping raw training data local. A shared initialization may be pretrained or initialized for federated training; pretraining is not a defining requirement. Neither approach requires FP64 arithmetic.
Learning Objective: Contrast isolated on-device adaptation and federated learning in terms of knowledge aggregation and communication boundaries.
True or False: Because on-device learning keeps raw user observations (such as typed keystrokes or biometric sensor traces) on the client device, it inherently guarantees full compliance with privacy regulations like GDPR and HIPAA without requiring any additional cryptographic or governance safeguards.
Answer: False. Keeping raw data on-device significantly reduces privacy exposure and data transmission risks, but it does not automatically guarantee full regulatory compliance. First, intermediate artifacts such as gradient updates or adapter checkpoints can still leak sensitive private information via gradient inversion or membership inference attacks if transmitted or observed. Second, regulatory frameworks like GDPR and HIPAA impose strict obligations regarding lawful basis, user consent, purpose limitation, auditability, data retention limits, and secure local storage of protected health information (PHI) or personal data on the physical device.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the privacy and regulatory compliance boundaries of on-device learning beyond simple raw data localization.
Compare the coordination responsibilities of isolated on-device learning, centralized cloud training, and cross-device federated learning. Why does the paradigm alone not establish a universal ranking of implementation complexity?
Answer: Isolated learning keeps the update loop on one device. Centralized training coordinates data ingestion, training infrastructure, and artifact release. Cross-device federation adds client eligibility, compatible versions, partial participation, aggregation, and population coverage across intermittent devices. These responsibilities differ, but deployment scale, trust boundaries, and reliability requirements determine implementation complexity; a large cloud training service need not be simpler than a small federated deployment.
Learning Objective: Distinguish coordination responsibilities across learning paradigms without inferring a universal complexity ordering.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A mobile engineering team observes that fine-tuning a 10M parameter vision model on a smartphone with 8 GB of RAM causes the background training process to be killed by the operating system’s out-of-memory (OOM) killer during backpropagation. Why does training memory demand spike so severely compared to inference for the exact same model?

The base model weights dynamically expand by \(100\times\) during the forward pass due to weight unpacking.
Floating-point units on mobile SoCs automatically convert all INT8 weights to FP64 double precision during training.
Training adds gradients, optimizer state, and saved backward activations to the weights; the simultaneous peak can exceed the app’s budget even when inference fits.
The mobile operating system creates a separate virtual machine sandbox for every individual neuron in the neural network.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Training can retain activations needed for backward computation, gradients, and optimizer state in addition to weights. Their simultaneous peak can exceed a background process budget even when total device RAM is much larger. The amplification is configuration-dependent; inference also requires activation buffers and workspace, not necessarily only one layer of activations.
Learning Objective: Analyze the sources of memory amplification in edge training compared to inference-only execution.
A quantized 7B-parameter language model achieves 12 tokens/sec on a mobile SoC advertised at 45 peak TOPS. Profiling shows that low-batch decode saturates available DRAM bandwidth while arithmetic units wait. Which hardware resource is the binding constraint?

Insufficient CPU integer arithmetic capacity for calculating cross-entropy loss.
Thermal throttling of the wireless 5G modem during token generation.
Flash storage read latency when loading the token tokenizer vocabulary.
Mobile LPDDR5/LPDDR5X memory bandwidth (\(51\text{–}77\text{ GB/s}\)), which is roughly \(44\text{–}65\times\) lower than data-center HBM3, causing the memory streaming term \((D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW})\) to dominate execution time per token.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Low-batch autoregressive decode often streams a large weight volume per token, so limited mobile DRAM bandwidth can dominate despite high peak TOPS. The stated peak rates alone do not prove the measured bottleneck: profiling must check achieved bandwidth, operator support, and thermal limits. Tokenizer initialization and loss computation do not explain steady-state decode throughput.
Learning Objective: Analyze why memory bandwidth, rather than peak TOPS, is the binding constraint for on-device autoregressive transformer decoding.
A proposed background personalization task on a smartphone draws \(4.5\text{ W}\) of sustained SoC power and requires 30 minutes to complete. Calculate the total energy consumed (in \(\text{Wh}\)) and the percentage drain on an idealized \(15\text{ Wh}\) smartphone battery. Explain why this result mandates opportunistic scheduling.
Answer: The task consumes \(4.5\text{ W}\times0.5\text{ h}=2.25\text{ Wh}\), or \(15\%\) of the idealized battery. That is a substantial background cost, motivating charging, idle, and thermal eligibility gates. Network restrictions are needed when the workflow communicates; the exact scheduling policy depends on the deployment rather than following from the energy calculation alone.
Learning Objective: Calculate battery energy consumption of background on-device training and justify opportunistic scheduling constraints.
True or False: Gradient checkpointing reduces the total electrical energy consumed by an on-device training workload because it reduces peak SRAM/DRAM memory allocation.
Answer: False. Checkpointing trades saved activations for recomputation. The extra arithmetic can increase energy, while reduced memory traffic or avoiding spill may offset that cost. Lower peak allocation alone therefore does not determine energy per update; measure the complete workload on the target device.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the compute, memory, and energy trade-offs of gradient checkpointing in edge training.
**Consider the end-to-end memory lifecycle of a single gradient update during on-device backpropagation for a convolutional layer. Order the following operational stages from first to last in execution sequence:


Discard intermediate activations and compute parameter updates in optimizer state
Forward pass computes and caches layer activations
Fetch batch inputs into SRAM buffer
Loss evaluation and backward pass calculates layer gradients using cached activations**

Answer: The correct order is (3) -> (2) -> (4) -> (1). First, (3) Fetch batch inputs into SRAM buffer prepares the raw or preprocessed batch tensors in accessible working memory. Second, (2) Forward pass computes and caches layer activations sequentially through the network layers, saving feature maps needed for gradient calculation. Third, (4) Loss evaluation and backward pass calculates layer gradients using cached activations, traversing backward from the loss through the computation graph. Finally, (1) Discard intermediate activations and compute parameter updates in optimizer state applies the optimizer step (e.g., SGD or Adam) to update weights, freeing cached activations and gradients.
Learning Objective: Analyze the chronological memory allocation and deallocation stages of an on-device backpropagation training step.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why does Tiny Transfer Learning (TinyTL) freeze convolutional backbone weights and adapt biases with optional lite residual modules?

Freezing removes backbone weight-gradient and optimizer state; suitable activation and normalization choices also reduce saved backward state.
Microcontroller hardware units physically short-circuit if matrix multiplications are performed in reverse during backpropagation.
Bias parameters have mathematical properties that prevent all forms of numerical underflow in 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic.
Training bias parameters modifies the underlying kernel weights directly through implicit singular value decomposition.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Frozen weights need no weight gradients or optimizer state, but they remain part of the deployed model. Gradients may still traverse frozen operators, and nonlinearities can require saved state. TinyTL reduces these costs through its adaptation path and operator choices; it does not guarantee an arbitrary backbone fits microcontroller SRAM. Bias updates do not modify frozen kernels.
Learning Objective: Explain how TinyTL reduces trainable and saved activation state without eliminating the full deployment memory budget.
A mobile vision engineer chooses between Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Residual Bottleneck Adapters for on-device camera personalization. The system requires zero additional inference latency during real-time 60 FPS video capture, while another use case requires hot-swapping between 10 user contexts without reloading the base model. How do LoRA and Residual Adapters compare across these requirements?

Residual Adapters introduce zero inference latency because they replace the backbone, while LoRA requires recomputing matrix inverses on every video frame.
LoRA updates can be merged into compatible base weights to remove the adapter execution path, while residual adapters retain separate computation and support modular context switching.
LoRA updates require storing 10 full copies of the 7B base model in SRAM, whereas Residual Adapters operate without trainable parameters.
Both methods require identical memory footprints and add exactly 50 ms of inference latency per layer.

Answer: The correct answer is B. A compatible linear LoRA update can be merged as \(W_{\text{final}}=W_{\text{base}}+BA\), removing separate adapter operations. Residual adapters retain their own computation, whose latency must be measured. Unmerged LoRA also supports context switching; the distinction is mergeability, not exclusive access to hot-swapping. Neither method requires copies of the entire base model per context.
Learning Objective: Compare LoRA and Residual Bottleneck Adapters regarding inference latency, weight merging, and multi-tenant context swapping.
A smart camera supports 10 personalization contexts. Its base model has 10M parameters (\(40\text{ MB}\) in FP32), and assume each complete adapter checkpoint occupies \(200\text{ KB}\). Compare storage for 10 full fine-tuned models with one shared base plus 10 adapters. Explain the architectural advantage.
Answer: Ten full models require \(400\text{ MB}\). One \(40\text{ MB}\) base plus ten \(0.2\text{ MB}\) adapter checkpoints requires \(42\text{ MB}\). The incremental per-context checkpoint is \(200\times\) smaller, while total storage is about \(9.5\times\) smaller. Sharing the base enables compact context switching; the stated checkpoint size is an assumption, not a consequence of adapter rank alone, and excludes training state.
Learning Objective: Calculate storage savings of multi-tenant adapter personalization over full model fine-tuning.
In structured parameter adaptation, a technique that approximates a full weight matrix update \(\FiniteChange\WeightMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\WeightMatrixRowCount \times \WeightMatrixColumnCount}\) as the product of a low-rank up-projection \(\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\WeightMatrixRowCount \times \AdapterRank}\) and down-projection \(\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\AdapterRank \times \WeightMatrixColumnCount}\) (where \(\AdapterRank \ll \min(\WeightMatrixRowCount, \WeightMatrixColumnCount)\)) is known as ____ (low-rank adaptation).
Answer: LoRA. Low-rank factors restrict the trainable update to a compact subspace, reducing parameter and optimizer-state storage relative to full-matrix adaptation.
Learning Objective: Apply low-rank matrix decomposition principles to parameter-efficient edge fine-tuning.
**Task-adaptive sparse updates use individual-layer profiling to propose a trainable subset. Order the steps from profiling to deployment:


Fine-tune each candidate layer separately and measure its validation gain and resource cost
Freeze the pretrained model to establish a baseline
Deploy the jointly validated subset with other parameters frozen
Rank layers by gain per unit cost and propose a subset
Measure the selected combination against memory, energy, foreground-latency, and quality budgets, including profiling cost**

Answer: The correct order is (2) establish the frozen baseline, (1) profile individual layers, (4) rank and propose a subset, (5) measure the combined update, then (3) deploy the validated subset. Individual gains need not add, and shared backward dependencies change combined resource cost. Deploying directly from the ranking skips the joint feasibility and quality test; a subset that fails it must be revised or rejected.
Learning Objective: Design a task-adaptive sparse parameter selection workflow using layer contribution profiling.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A developer of a keyword spotting (KWS) system for smart home appliances wants users to configure custom wake words using 5 to 10 spoken samples. Why is few-shot adaptation of a classification head on top of a frozen acoustic encoder preferred over end-to-end retraining?

End-to-end retraining of acoustic encoders produces audio waveforms that violate device speaker impedance limits.
Spoken custom wake words cannot be processed by neural networks unless the entire encoder architecture is expanded by \(10\times\).
Updating only the head restricts trainable state and preserves frozen encoder representations, reducing adaptation cost and overfitting risk relative to full retraining.
The Fourier transform algorithm only converges when supervised labels exceed 100,000 samples.

Answer: The correct answer is C. A pretrained encoder can supply reusable acoustic features while a small head adapts to a few user examples. Freezing the encoder reduces trainable state and preserves its parameters, but does not guarantee accuracy or a particular power and memory footprint. Measure the adaptation path separately from always-on inference; speaker impedance and Fourier-transform convergence do not govern this choice.
Learning Objective: Apply few-shot transfer learning principles to always-on keyword spotting adaptation under severe data and energy scarcity.
An edge health tracker adapts a continuous activity classifier to a user’s walking gait over several weeks. When the user starts cycling, the device adapts its model, but suddenly misclassifies normal walking as cycling. What core failure mode has occurred, and why did it happen?

Overfitting on a single static batch caused by excessive L2 regularization.
Numerical floating-point overflow in the hardware accelerometer sensor buffer.
Model inversion attack where cycling data erased the operating system kernel.
Catastrophic forgetting, where sequential gradient updates on new data distributions overwrite the weight configurations responsible for preserving performance on previously learned tasks.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Catastrophic forgetting is the fundamental stability failure of sequential learning in neural networks: when a model updates parameters on a new data stream (cycling) without mechanisms to preserve prior distributions (walking), gradient steps overwrite the representations that encoded the old task. Overfitting on a single batch does not describe sequential task erosion. Sensor overflow is a hardware I/O fault, and model inversion is an adversarial privacy attack, not a continuous learning stability failure.
Learning Objective: Analyze catastrophic forgetting in streaming on-device adaptation.
In on-device continuous learning, why do production experience-replay implementations store compressed feature embeddings (e.g., penultimate-layer activations or MFCCs) in a circular ring buffer rather than saving raw sensor observations (such as raw images or audio waveforms)?
Answer: Compact embeddings can retain useful replay information with less storage than raw sensor streams, allowing a bounded ring buffer. Discarding raw samples reduces one exposure path, but embeddings may still reveal sensitive information and need access and retention controls. Replay quality also depends on representation stability: changing the encoder can make stored embeddings stale, so this design is easiest with a stable feature extractor.
Learning Objective: Justify the use of compressed feature embeddings over raw inputs in edge experience replay buffers.
True or False: In on-device experience replay, maintaining a small buffer of 100 uniformly sampled past examples guarantees that the adapted model will not suffer from catastrophic forgetting across rare or long-tail edge cases.
Answer: False. A bounded uniform sample does not guarantee coverage of rare classes or preservation of earlier behavior. A ring buffer favors recent observations; reservoir sampling gives historical examples an equal inclusion probability but a small reservoir can still contain few or no rare examples. Compare retention policies, capacity, and regularization under retained-task and rare-event evaluation; none is a universal forgetting guarantee.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the limitations of naive uniform experience replay for long-tail robustness in edge learning.
In continuous edge adaptation, the fundamental trade-off between retaining previously acquired knowledge and acquiring new patterns from dynamic local data is known as the stability-____ trade-off.
Answer: plasticity. Stability preserves previously learned behavior; plasticity allows adaptation to new observations. Continual learning must balance both rather than maximize either alone.
Learning Objective: Explain the stability-plasticity dilemma in continual on-device learning.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In the Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm, what is the primary algorithmic trade-off when tuning the number of local training epochs (\(\LocalEpochCount\)) on client devices?

Increasing local work can amortize communication, but may increase client drift on non-IID data; rounds and elapsed time to the same quality target must be measured.
Increasing \(\LocalEpochCount\) forces the central server to store full training datasets from all participating clients in server DRAM.
Increasing \(\LocalEpochCount\) eliminates the need for clients to compute backward passes during local training.
Increasing \(\LocalEpochCount\) increases the size (in megabytes) of the transmitted model parameter vector by a factor of \(\LocalEpochCount^2\).

Answer: The correct answer is A. More local epochs can reduce communication frequency, but do not guarantee fewer rounds or less time to a fixed quality target. Non-IID local updates can increase client drift. Compare candidate \(\LocalEpochCount\) values under matched data and participation conditions, recording validated target quality, elapsed round times, bytes, and energy. More epochs neither transfer raw data nor change the parameter vector dimension.
Learning Objective: Analyze the trade-off between local computation epochs (\(\LocalEpochCount\)) and communication rounds in FedAvg under non-IID data.
A mobile federated learning deployment encounters severe client drift due to extreme non-IID typing patterns across users, causing standard FedAvg to oscillate and fail to converge. Which algorithmic modification directly addresses client drift by constraining local updates to stay close to the global model?

Switching from 32-bit floating-point to 1-bit stochastic sign quantization without error compensation.
Adding a proximal regularization term \(\frac{\mu}{2} \|w - w_t\|^2\) to the local client objective (as in FedProx) to penalize excessive deviation from the global server model \(w_t\).
Increasing the local learning rate by \(10\times\) to accelerate convergence on outlier devices.
Dropping the central aggregation server and allowing devices to train purely in isolation without synchronization.

Answer: The correct answer is B. FedProx adds \(\frac{\mu}{2}\|w-w_t\|^2\) to penalize departure from the current global reference. This can mitigate client drift, but does not guarantee convergence for every workload or hyperparameter choice; evaluate matched quality and resource budgets. Raising the learning rate can worsen drift, while isolated training abandons the federated objective.
Learning Objective: Apply algorithmic regularizers (FedProx proximal term) to mitigate client drift in non-IID federated optimization.
Contrast cross-silo federated learning and cross-device federated learning across three dimensions: participant scale/reliability, network connectivity, and client incentive/governance.
Answer: 1. Participant scale and reliability: Cross-silo FL involves a small, fixed number of known, highly reliable institutional organizations (e.g., 2–100 hospitals or banks) that participate in almost every round. Cross-device FL involves massive fleets of millions of anonymous, unreliable mobile or IoT devices with high dropout and churn rates.
Network connectivity: Cross-silo participants connect via high-speed, reliable data-center or enterprise WAN connections. Cross-device clients connect over unmetered/metered mobile Wi-Fi or cellular networks with asymmetric bandwidth and frequent disconnects.
Incentive and governance: Cross-silo systems operate under formal legal data-sharing agreements and regulatory audits (e.g., BAA/HIPAA consortia). Cross-device systems operate under consumer platform operating policies (e.g., opt-in telemetry, strict opportunistic gating when idle/charging).
Learning Objective: Compare cross-silo and cross-device federated learning across infrastructure, reliability, and governance characteristics.
In federated optimization, the phenomenon where multiple local gradient steps on non-identically distributed client data cause local models to diverge toward disparate local optima is called client ____.
Answer: drift. Repeated local steps on different client distributions move models toward different objectives, making their aggregated update less aligned with the global objective.
Learning Objective: Explain the mechanism and consequences of client drift in federated optimization.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In production cross-device federated learning (such as Google Gboard), why do systems implement Over-Selection of clients (selecting \(\CandidateClientCount \approx 1.3 \times \TargetUpdateCount\) devices per round) rather than selecting exactly \(\TargetUpdateCount\) devices?

Over-selection ensures that every mobile client receives \(1.3\times\) the monetary payment for participating.
Over-selection forces client devices to increase their CPU clock frequencies by \(30\%\) during training.
Selecting surplus candidates can reach the target number of valid reports earlier than waiting for every selected device, provided enough clients complete; a deadline and incomplete-round policy are still required.
The aggregation server requires exactly \(30\%\) redundant updates to perform parity-bit error correction on the GPU memory bus.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Over-selection accommodates dropout and slow completion. If enough valid reports arrive, the round can proceed at the target-th completion rather than waiting for the slowest selected device. A surplus pool does not guarantee that the target is reached or prevent a stalled round by itself. The coordinator also needs a deadline, acceptance or abandonment rules, and evaluation of the completed cohort. The approximate 1.3 factor is a deployment example, not a universal setting.
Learning Objective: Design client selection and straggler mitigation mechanisms using over-selection in large-scale federated systems.
How does the Secure Aggregation (SecAgg) cryptographic protocol protect individual client privacy during federated aggregation on a central server?

Clients transmit raw unencrypted updates, and the server permanently deletes its hard drive after every round.
Clients train on synthetic dummy data generated by the server, ensuring real gradients are never computed.
The server encrypts all client devices using a remote ransomware key until the global round terminates.
Participating client pairs agree on shared pseudo-random masks that are added by one client and subtracted by the other; when the server sums all received masked updates, the masks algebraically cancel out, revealing the exact global aggregate without exposing any individual update.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Clients establish pairwise secrets and generate opposite masks, so masks cancel when the protocol forms an authorized aggregate. Dropout recovery requires additional protocol steps. Individual-update confidentiality depends on the participant threshold and threat model; it does not make the released aggregate differentially private. Deleting a server disk after receiving raw updates offers no comparable protection.
Learning Objective: Explain the algebraic masking and cancellation mechanism of Secure Aggregation (SecAgg).
In Differential Privacy for Federated Learning (DP-FedAvg), explain why gradient clipping to a fixed threshold \(S\) (\(\|\Delta \theta_k\|_2 \le S\)) is a mandatory prerequisite before adding calibrated Gaussian noise to the aggregate.
Answer: Clipping bounds each client update norm by \(S\), making sensitivity finite. The bound depends on the aggregation rule and neighboring-dataset definition: replacing one contribution in a fixed-size mean can change it by at most \(2S/K\). Noise must be calibrated to the chosen bound, sampling procedure, and privacy budget, with composition across rounds; clipping alone does not establish an \((\PrivacyBudget,\PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) guarantee.
Learning Objective: Analyze why \(L_2\) norm clipping is essential for establishing sensitivity bounds in DP-FedAvg.
True or False: In top-\(k\) gradient sparsification for federated learning, discarding all gradient components outside the top \(1\text{–}10\%\) by magnitude without maintaining a local error accumulation buffer preserves the exact convergence rate of uncompressed SGD.
Answer: False. Dropping unsent components need not preserve the convergence rate of uncompressed SGD and can introduce optimization bias. Error feedback carries those components into subsequent compression steps, but its update-sized residual consumes persistent device memory. Neither immediate transmission of every component nor convergence for every optimizer and workload is guaranteed; compare quality, rounds, and total communication under the chosen assumptions.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the role of error accumulation buffers in gradient sparsification for federated learning.
In a federated camera-personalization deployment, a user captures \(200\text{ MB}\) of compressed images per week. A 4-bit quantized model update for the 5M-parameter on-device model requires \(2.5\text{ MB}\) per uplink round. Calculate the single-round communication savings of transmitting model updates versus uploading raw weekly data, and explain why cumulative round counts must be accounted for in production network budgets.
Answer: The single-round upload reduction is \(200\text{ MB} / 2.5\text{ MB} = 80\times\) less data transferred on the uplink. However, this \(80\times\) factor represents only a single training round. Over the course of training, if a device participates in 80 federated uplink rounds (\(80 \times 2.5\text{ MB} = 200\text{ MB}\)), cumulative update uploads alone equal the total raw data volume, before accounting for downlink global-model broadcasts, dropped-round retransmissions, or protocol handshake metadata. Therefore, production network planning must evaluate total communication cost over the entire convergence trajectory rather than single-round ratios.
Learning Objective: Calculate single-round versus cumulative communication volume in federated learning deployments.
**For a round using secure aggregation and a trusted server that adds differential-privacy noise, order these stages. Assume protocol participation thresholds and dropout recovery are satisfied:


Select eligible clients and distribute a compatible global model and training policy
Form the authorized aggregate and add noise calibrated to bounded client contributions and the declared privacy unit
Clients train, clip their contributions under the policy, and apply protocol masks
Update the global model and evaluate progress and completed-cohort coverage
Receive enough valid masked reports before the round deadline, or apply the incomplete-round policy**

Answer: The correct order is (1) -> (3) -> (5) -> (2) -> (4). Eligibility and compatible state precede local work; clipping precedes calibrated noise. Secure aggregation forms an authorized aggregate under its threshold and dropout rules, rather than relying on arbitrary masks to cancel after clients are dropped. In this trusted-server design, differential privacy protects the released noisy result, not the exact aggregate from that server. Repeated releases require privacy accounting. Failure to meet the deadline or threshold follows the incomplete-round policy rather than proceeding with an unauthorized aggregate.
Learning Objective: Synthesize the complete end-to-end execution lifecycle of a production federated learning round.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A keyboard adapts nightly for a year. Each update fits its device budget and improves a metric on recent typing. Why must acceptance also check previously learned behavior against a recoverable baseline?

Passing the memory and energy tests guarantees that earlier-task predictions remain unchanged.
Freezing the backbone prevents head or adapter updates from changing any earlier-task prediction.
Individually useful updates can accumulate into forgetting; retained-task evidence and a compatible recovery point remain necessary.
Improving the recent-data metric establishes quality for all past tasks, so a recovery point is unnecessary.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Repeated updates can erode earlier behavior even when each improves recent data. A frozen backbone does not freeze predictions when its head or adapters change. Acceptance therefore needs retained-task evaluation and a compatible baseline to restore if the accumulated trajectory becomes unacceptable.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why repeated local improvements require retained-behavior checks and a recoverable baseline.
In lifelong on-device learning without catastrophic forgetting, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Experience Replay offer distinct memory-compute trade-offs. Under which deployment condition is EWC architecturally preferred over Experience Replay?

When model weights exceed 100 billion parameters and local RAM is strictly 64 KB.
When the device has unlimited flash storage but cannot perform floating-point addition.
When the device must continuously store raw 4K video feeds for retrospective auditing.
When the model is relatively compact and storing past private data samples in a replay buffer violates strict privacy regulations or storage constraints.

Answer: The correct answer is D. EWC replaces a replay buffer with parameter-sized importance scores and reference values. A compact model may make that state affordable when retaining examples is prohibited. Memory depends on precision and retained task history; a basic same-precision implementation adds two parameter-sized arrays beyond current weights, and separate task penalties can add more. Very large models can therefore make EWC impractical.
Learning Objective: Compare Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Experience Replay in terms of memory scaling and privacy trade-offs.
An on-device sensor application receives a continuous unlabeled stream. Explain how contrastive learning can construct a useful local training signal while respecting memory, energy, and retention limits. What must be checked before treating nearby observations as positive pairs?
Answer: Positive pairs must preserve task-relevant content; nearby frames across a scene change may not, and apparent negatives may depict the same event. A bounded pair or feature buffer limits retention, but the complete update still needs profiled model, activation, optimizer, energy, and foreground budgets. Training from fixed cached features changes only the downstream trainable path; changing the encoder requires compatible replay state or refreshed features. Pair validity and retained-task quality need separate evaluation.
Learning Objective: Design a self-supervised contrastive learning workflow for continuous on-device sensor adaptation.
True or False: In lifelong edge learning, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) requires zero additional memory overhead beyond the standard model weights because Fisher Information scores are computed and discarded instantaneously during the forward pass.
Answer: False. In addition to current parameters, a basic EWC implementation stores importance scores and reference parameter values. At equal precision, these two extra arrays add twice the current parameter storage, making three times that storage in total before other training state. Separate task histories can require more.
Learning Objective: Calculate the memory overhead incurred by Elastic Weight Consolidation on edge devices.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A production voice assistant is deployed across a heterogeneous fleet of 10 million devices comprising 20% flagship smartphones, 50% mid-tier phones, and 30% budget devices. How does the three-pillar integration framework structure model adaptation across this fleet?

It mandates that all 10 million devices execute full 32-bit fine-tuning of the 7B-parameter backbone during active voice calls.
It restricts learning exclusively to cloud data centers, disabling all on-device learning across all device tiers.
It proposes tier-specific LoRA ranks and replay allowances, with bias-only updates for budget devices, then validates joint resource fit and useful adaptation for each permitted path.
It assigns the highest-rank adapters to budget microcontrollers because microcontrollers have no operating system overhead.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Tier assignments are candidates, not proof of fit. Profiling must count the resident base, trainable and backward state, replay, runtime support, and foreground reserve; live admission then checks energy, heat, and latency. Validation must establish useful adaptation. An available NPU does not establish backward support, and inference-only operation remains valid when learning fails these tests.
Learning Objective: Design a tiered edge-learning architecture that integrates model adaptation, data efficiency, and federated coordination across device capability tiers.
In a multi-pillar edge architecture, an explicit priority policy is established to arbitrate runtime resource contention between active user inference and background adaptation. What is the fundamental operational rule enforced by this control?

Background gradient updates take absolute priority over interactive user requests to maximize training convergence speed.
When battery drops below 5%, the device shuts down display output to continue running backpropagation.
Memory buffers for experience replay are allowed to grow dynamically until they consume 100% of physical system RAM.
Interactive user inference strictly preempts background training tasks, and training is immediately suspended if memory pressure, thermal limits, or QoS latency thresholds are approached.

Answer: The correct answer is D. In edge systems, user experience and interactive Quality of Service (QoS) are paramount. The explicit priority control mandates that foreground inference tasks (e.g., wake-word detection, keyboard typing, camera rendering) strictly preempt background training tasks. If memory headroom shrinks, device temperature crosses thermal limits, or frame latency degrades, background gradient updates and replay processing are throttled or suspended immediately. Prioritizing training over user interaction or exhausting battery/memory violates fundamental edge engineering principles.
Learning Objective: Apply explicit priority policies and graceful degradation controls to prevent resource conflicts in edge learning systems.
In the integrated voice assistant case study, participating devices exchange LoRA adapter updates (\(50\text{ MiB}\)) rather than full model updates (\(14\text{ GB}\) in FP16). Explain how this parameter-efficient adaptation strategy simultaneously satisfies constraints across all three pillars: Model Adaptation, Data Efficiency, and Federated Coordination.
Answer: Compact adapter updates reduce trainable parameter and optimizer-state storage, although frozen weights and backward activation state still require memory. Restricting the update space can help with scarce data, but does not guarantee freedom from overfitting or forgetting. For the stated checkpoints, \(14\text{ GB}\) divided by \(50\text{ MiB}\) is roughly \(267\times\) per transfer. Total communication still includes participation frequency, downloads, and protocol overhead.
Learning Objective: Synthesize how parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA) simultaneously resolves bottlenecks across model adaptation, data efficiency, and federated coordination.
When a mobile device experiences poor cellular connectivity, high thermal load, or battery depletion during deployment, an edge-learning control mechanism known as graceful ____ ensures the device seamlessly transitions into a minimal or inference-only adaptation mode without disrupting active user functionality.
Answer: degradation. The controller reduces or suspends background adaptation when resources become scarce, preserving foreground inference and user-facing service requirements.
Learning Objective: Explain graceful degradation mechanisms under adverse edge operating conditions.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In traditional cloud MLOps, a deployment pipeline releases a single monolithic model binary to uniform server clusters. How does this deployment artifact transform when shipping an on-device learning system across a heterogeneous mobile fleet?

The deployable artifact becomes a policy bundle containing a shared base model along with device-tier adaptation strategies (e.g., bias-only for microcontrollers, LoRA for mid-tier, selective layers for flagship), resource execution rules, and rollback thresholds.
The artifact is replaced by an uncompiled Python script executed directly on bare-metal microcontroller sensors.
The deployment pipeline requires manual per-device flashing over USB cables for every smartphone in the world.
The deployment artifact eliminates model weights entirely, transmitting only random seeds to client operating systems.

Answer: The correct answer is A. On-device learning systems operate across heterogeneous hardware tiers with vast differences in memory, compute, and power. Consequently, MLOps cannot release a single monolithic binary; it ships a validated policy bundle that specifies the base model backbone, tier-specific adaptation mechanisms (e.g., bias-only updates for extreme constraints, LoRA rank configurations for mid-tier devices), opportunistic execution policies (battery, thermal, and network triggers), and automated validation/rollback gates. The other choices mischaracterize production software deployment.
Learning Objective: Analyze how MLOps deployment pipelines transform from static model artifacts into tiered policy bundles for edge fleets.
What can a frozen shadow model establish when compared with a locally adapted model without labeled outcomes or a validated task-quality proxy?

The Shadow Model connects to cloud labeling services via satellite to annotate live user keystrokes in real time.
Prediction and confidence differences reveal behavioral change and can suspend an update for evaluation, but do not by themselves establish which model is more accurate.
The Shadow Model inverts user biometric features into cryptographic tokens to bypass operating system security firewalls.
The Shadow Model permanently deletes the active model whenever the device battery drops below 90%.

Answer: The correct answer is B. A shadow comparison detects disagreement, confidence shifts, latency changes, and resource regressions. Without labels or a validated quality proxy, lower confidence is not proof of lower accuracy, and agreement can hide shared errors. Automatic rollback needs an established outcome criterion or safety invariant, rather than confidence comparison alone.
Learning Objective: Distinguish unlabeled shadow-model change detection from validated quality and rollback decisions.
A production edge ML team cannot collect raw user inputs or ground-truth prediction labels due to privacy policies. Explain how Federated Analytics and privacy-preserving telemetry allow the platform team to monitor fleet-wide model health and detect cohort regressions.
Answer: Devices can compute confidence histograms, task proxies, and locally available outcome metrics without exporting raw observations. Secure aggregation hides individual contributions under its protocol assumptions, while differential privacy bounds release leakage through clipping, calibrated noise, and accounting. Cohort summaries help detect regressions, but small cohorts need disclosure controls and unlabeled confidence statistics remain change signals rather than direct accuracy measurements.
Learning Objective: Design a privacy-preserving telemetry and observability pipeline using federated analytics.
True or False: In production edge learning systems, tracking global fleet-wide average accuracy is sufficient to ensure high quality, because individual device variances cancel out across millions of deployed nodes.
Answer: False. Tracking only global fleet-wide averages masks critical cohort-specific failures. Because edge fleets exhibit extreme heterogeneity, high-performing flagship devices with fast networks can skew the global average upward, completely hiding severe regressions or adaptation failures occurring on budget devices, specific geographic regions, or underrepresented device demographics. Production monitoring requires segmented cohort tracking across hardware tiers, connectivity types, and participation frequencies.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why global fleet metrics fail to capture cohort-specific regressions in heterogeneous edge deployments.
**A production MLOps system executes a federated A/B deployment to validate a new on-device adaptation algorithm before fleet-wide rollout. Order the stages of this validation workflow from first to last:


Gradually expand rollout across the general population once treatment confirms statistically significant quality gains without regressions
Deploy candidate adaptation strategy to treatment cohort while control cohort retains baseline strategy
Stratify device fleet into statistically balanced treatment and control cohorts across hardware capability tiers
Aggregate differentially private validation metrics and compare convergence speed and user task-proxy satisfaction**

Answer: The correct order is (3) -> (2) -> (4) -> (1). First, (3) Stratify device fleet into statistically balanced treatment and control cohorts across hardware capability tiers to ensure fair comparative groups. Second, (2) Deploy candidate adaptation strategy to treatment cohort while control cohort retains baseline strategy under identical operating policies. Third, (4) Aggregate differentially private validation metrics and compare convergence speed and user task-proxy satisfaction between cohorts. Finally, (1) Gradually expand rollout across the general population once treatment confirms statistically significant quality gains without regressions.
Learning Objective: Design a federated A/B testing workflow for safe production rollout on edge fleets.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A mobile keyboard application allows continuous, unconstrained on-device model adaptation on all typed keystrokes. After several months of deployment, users report that the keyboard frequently suggests misspelled words and typos as high-confidence autocomplete options. What failure mode has occurred, and what is the standard architectural mitigation?

Unbounded adaptation drift and autocorrection feedback loop; mitigated by bounding parameter update ranges, filtering user corrections, and validating against a frozen shadow model.
Cryptographic hash collision in the secure aggregation protocol; mitigated by increasing RSA key size to 4096 bits.
Memory leak in the LPDDR5X DRAM controller; mitigated by rewriting the keyboard in assembly language.
Quantization underflow in the NPU matrix multipliers; mitigated by disabling all integer arithmetic.

Answer: The correct answer is A. When an adaptive system trains naively on streaming user inputs without validation, it cannot distinguish between intentional typing and accidental typos. If users accept or correct typos, the model adapts to its own mistakes, causing unbounded adaptation drift and creating an autocorrection feedback loop. The mitigation requires bounded adaptation ranges, input filtering (e.g., ignoring unverified corrections), task-proxy gating, and shadow evaluation against a frozen baseline model. RSA key size, DRAM memory leaks, and NPU quantization do not address adaptation drift.
Learning Objective: Analyze unbounded adaptation drift and feedback loops in on-device text prediction systems and identify mitigation controls.
In a federated learning fleet of 100,000 devices, malicious or compromised clients attempt to corrupt the global model by uploading maliciously crafted gradient vectors with extreme magnitudes. Which aggregation defense mitigates this Byzantine attack?

Standard arithmetic mean aggregation with no client filtering.
Byzantine-resilient aggregation rules (such as coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, or Krum) combined with gradient norm clipping.
Increasing the local training epochs on all clients to \(E = 100\).
Disabling secure aggregation and publishing all client IP addresses to an open web dashboard.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Clipping limits update magnitude, while robust aggregation can reduce the influence of outliers under assumptions about malicious participation and honest-data variation. These methods do not guarantee stability against arbitrary attacks. Many require access to individual updates, creating a design tension with secure aggregation. Unfiltered averaging remains vulnerable; extra local epochs do not remove poisoned updates.
Learning Objective: Apply Byzantine-resilient aggregation techniques (trimmed mean, median, Krum) to protect federated systems against poisoned updates.
Explain the mechanism of ‘participation bias amplification’ in large-scale mobile federated learning, and describe how it creates a digital inequality feedback loop across user cohorts.
Answer: Participation bias amplification occurs when client eligibility requirements (e.g., connected to Wi-Fi, fully charged, idle overnight) are systematically met more frequently by users with high-end flagship devices, high-speed home broadband, and regular charging habits. As a result, the global model receives a disproportionate volume of updates from this privileged cohort, becoming heavily optimized for their language patterns, accents, and usage contexts. Conversely, budget devices with irregular charging or limited connectivity participate rarely, causing global model quality to degrade for those underserved populations. This degradation reduces app engagement among budget users, causing them to participate even less and amplifying digital inequality across the fleet.
Learning Objective: Analyze the sociological and algorithmic causes of participation bias amplification in federated learning fleets.
What does the 2016 Williston Tesla crash illustrate about relying on human supervision as the fallback for an automated driving feature?
Answer: The NTSB identified the truck driver’s failure to yield and the car driver’s inattention associated with overreliance on automation; the automation design permitted prolonged disengagement and use outside guidance. The engineering lesson is to enforce operational limits and the supervision contract. A fast local inference loop alone cannot ensure that a disengaged driver will intervene when needed.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why operational limits and enforceable supervision are part of a safety-critical edge deployment.
True or False: Because on-device learning decentralizes computation to user hardware, platform engineering teams no longer need to budget for server-side orchestration, verification, or monitoring infrastructure.
Answer: False. Decentralizing learning to edge devices actually increases server-side and platform engineering complexity. The central infrastructure must manage complex client selection protocols, secure aggregation handshakes, straggler mitigation, differential privacy accounting, multi-stage cryptographic verification of updates, distributed telemetry aggregation (Federated Analytics), shadow model tracking, and tiered rollback mechanisms across millions of heterogeneous clients.
Learning Objective: Analyze the server-side orchestration and platform infrastructure required to support decentralized edge learning fleets.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A product manager asserts: ‘Because our smart home devices keep all audio recordings strictly on the local device and only upload federated gradient updates to the cloud, our architecture is mathematically immune to user privacy leakage.’ What technical fallacy does this statement commit?

It ignores that raw model updates and gradients directly expose training-step information, enabling adversaries to reconstruct private training samples via gradient inversion attacks or verify user participation via membership inference unless protected by secure aggregation and differential privacy.
It ignores that audio recordings stored in flash memory are automatically broadcast over FM radio frequencies by microcontrollers.
It incorrectly assumes that federated learning requires quantum computers to achieve privacy.
It assumes that gradient vectors always have a mathematical magnitude of zero on edge devices.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Keeping raw observations local does not make transmitted updates immune to inference attacks. Reconstruction and membership inference depend on attacker access, auxiliary information, and the training configuration. Secure aggregation can hide individual updates under its threat-model assumptions, while differential privacy bounds a declared privacy unit’s influence on released results through clipping, calibrated noise, and composition. Required controls follow the deployment’s disclosure policy and threat model; locality alone supplies neither guarantee.
Learning Objective: Analyze the fallacy that data locality in federated learning guarantees privacy without cryptographic masking or differential privacy.
A development team attempts to deploy an on-device personalization algorithm across an IoT ecosystem spanning both 64 MHz ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers (with 256 KB SRAM) and flagship mobile phones (with 12 GB RAM). The team uses identical full-model fine-tuning hyperparameters across all endpoints. What pitfall does this design encounter?

Mobile phones will refuse to execute floating-point operations because microcontrollers only understand binary code.
It ignores differences in available working memory, supported update operators, and energy budgets; an identical policy needs a separate feasibility and quality check on each device class.
Microcontroller clock speeds will accelerate to 3 GHz due to thermal resonance with mobile phones.
Full-model fine-tuning requires all microcontrollers to be physically connected via optical fiber cables.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The stated memory capacities differ by several orders of magnitude, but they do not establish a CPU-throughput ratio or NPU underutilization. The same model can have different residency, backward support, and sustained costs on each device. Compare measured update paths under matched tasks and operating states, then choose and validate feasible tier-specific policies; full fine-tuning is not automatically admissible on either class.
Learning Objective: Analyze system failures resulting from ignoring hardware heterogeneity across microcontroller and mobile edge tiers.
Explain why performing on-device personalization on scarce, noisy, or uncurated local data can actually degrade model performance compared to a static, well-trained centralized base model.
Answer: A well-trained base can generalize better than a locally adapted candidate when local examples are scarce, noisy, or unrepresentative. Unconstrained updates may overfit accidental inputs or distort useful decision boundaries. This is a risk to test, not an inevitable result: evaluate local improvement and retained behavior against a trusted baseline, using validated outcomes and a compatible recovery path. Centralized training also does not inherently guarantee balanced data or broad generalization.
Learning Objective: Explain the conditions under which local on-device adaptation degrades model accuracy relative to static base models.
A common fallacy in federated learning treats the central coordinator as a simple stateless aggregation server, ignoring that production fleet coordination is an active control loop that must manage client ____ criteria (such as verifying that devices are charging, on unmetered Wi-Fi, and thermally stable).
Answer: eligibility. Admission checks enforce device resource and availability requirements before local training, protecting foreground service and reducing round failures.
Learning Objective: Analyze client eligibility filtering and admission control requirements in production federated orchestration.

← Back to Questions

title: 9 Fleet Efficiency
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a fleet that is fully allocated and visibly busy still turn only a fraction of its compute into training progress and served requests?
Expensive accelerators can spend much of a training step or a request waiting for data, software dispatch, or communication while their arithmetic units remain underused. Adding more machines may raise cost without removing the delay, and a faster isolated kernel may leave the step’s or request’s critical path unchanged. The engineering stakes are useful fleet capacity, the training progress and completed service an existing fleet produces while preserving model quality. A dashboard that counts every held accelerator as busy cannot see that waste, so a fleet can look fully used while turning only a fraction of its capacity into useful work. These interactions make optimization a question of measured constraints rather than a search for the fastest component. On one machine, a local improvement can be tested against a relatively contained execution path. Across a fleet, its value also depends on scheduling, recovery, communication, synchronization, and the distribution of work across devices. The cost of a mistaken diagnosis grows when the same inefficient execution repeats across many replicas and many weeks of training, and when the remedy is applied by a team that does not own the loss. A saving that looks large in isolation is worth only the part that survives along the complete step or request path. In C³ terms, fleet efficiency holds every compute gain accountable to the communication and coordination costs that decide how much of a fleet’s capacity becomes useful work.

Learning Objectives

Explain how a job’s or fleet’s useful output decomposes into scheduling, runtime, and program goodput, with each loss charged to exactly one factor
Measure goodput under a reproducible contract and localize the lost factor from scheduler records, job timelines, and step traces
Attribute scheduling and runtime losses using the owners’ results, without re-deriving them
Measure program goodput with MFU and MBU and find the Fleet Law term a fix must shorten
Select fleet-level program levers (compiler partitioning, overlap under contention, compilation) and recognize kernel-level levers by the term they shorten
Evaluate a change that trades one factor against another by its effect on the product, and place the result on the efficiency frontier



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



A fleet can be fully allocated and visibly busy while most of its capacity never becomes training progress or completed service. When thousands of accelerators run a single workload, losses accumulate before a job starts, between the steps it executes, and inside the steps it keeps. The size of that gap is clearest in a run whose engineering is not in doubt.

Lighthouse 9.1: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): Held capacity versus progressMeta’s pretraining of Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100 GPUs is one of the best-documented large training runs, and its two most quoted efficiency numbers measure different things. Across a 54-day snapshot, the job kept more than 90 percent of its elapsed time as effective training time despite hundreds of unexpected interruptions, as Recovery automation pipeline records. In the steps it kept, its arithmetic achieved a model FLOPs utilization (MFU) of about 41 percent of the accelerators’ peak rate (Dubey et al. 2024). Multiplied, the two figures show the run turning roughly 37 percent of the peak-rate capacity it held into training progress. Because the two figures come from different measurement windows, the product is only an estimate. Yet it shows one of the most carefully engineered runs on record losing about two-thirds of the capacity it held, mostly to steps that ran below the hardware’s rate rather than to the failures that dominate its reputation. Its two figures therefore bound what a well-run job of this archetype loses during execution.


Even that one-third figure overstates what a shared cluster delivers, because the Llama 3 numbers begin only after the job holds its accelerators. On a multi-tenant fleet, the setting of Fleet Orchestration, capacity is also lost before a job starts. Accelerators sit unallocated when no queued job fits the free pool, or a job holds part of its gang while waiting for the remaining members and cannot execute a single step. The orchestrator’s accounting separates allocated capacity from productive work, yet it cannot see where inside a running job the missing work went. Allocated capacity is where fleet-efficiency accounting begins, not evidence that the fleet used those accelerators well.


↩︎ The allocated, active, and productive tiers of fleet resource accounting are established in Allocated, active, and productive utilization.
Earlier chapters examined the mechanisms of a fleet one layer at a time: data delivery (Data Storage), collective communication (Collective Communication), parallel work partitioning (Distributed Training), fault recovery (Fault Tolerance), and cluster scheduling (Fleet Orchestration). Each subsystem reports performance in its own local unit—input stall ratio, link bandwidth, scaling efficiency, availability, or cluster occupancy—and none of those isolated metrics tells an organization what fraction of its fleet investment becomes useful progress. Worse, when subsystem reports are read separately, their denominators overlap in some places and leave gaps in others. An hour lost to a restart can be penalized in two reports at once, while accelerators held idle by an incomplete gang vanish between the scheduler’s log and the job’s step timer. As we enter the Serving band of The Fleet Stack, performance engineering requires a single end-to-end accounting framework that follows every accelerator-hour from offered hardware to useful output and ranks every optimization lever across the stack on one common scale.


↩︎ The Fleet Law, where these multiplicative efficiency factors are first previewed, is established in The Fleet Law.
To make that accounting concrete, one recurring training job carries the numbers through this chapter: pretraining Llama 2 70B, a smaller Archetype A model than the archetype’s 175B reference, on 128 GPUs (16 nodes of eight GPUs each) in a shared cluster. The job uses 8-way tensor parallelism within each node and data parallelism across nodes. Because it competes with other teams for complete gang allocations, absorbs cluster failures and preemptions, and executes steps whose exposed communication grows with node count, every stage of fleet loss appears in a single workload on a single pool.


↩︎ Archetype A and its 175B-parameter reference model are established in Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3).
A serving replica of the same model provides the running example’s inference twin. The replica spans one node of eight H100 GPUs, so a single tensor-parallel node forms one complete serving unit. Because a dense Archetype A transformer cannot fit on one accelerator, the eight GPUs exchange activations in every layer. The cluster scheduler must place the replica as an indivisible gang, the replica must load weights and warm up before taking traffic, and its decode steps can leave most of the node’s arithmetic idle while weights stream from high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Its capacity losses therefore arise at the same stages as those of the training job.
The serving twin also marks where fleet-efficiency accounting stops and request-level serving design begins. In production serving, requests share execution across dynamically formed batches, occupy key-value cache memory, and must satisfy tail-latency targets; Serving at Scale develops how a serving engine manages uneven arrivals under those constraints. Here, the boundary test is whether a loss would persist even under a steady, uncontended stream of work. A replica held off-line while loading weights, or a decode step that reads weights more slowly than the node’s memory bandwidth allows, fails to use held hardware even without arrival bursts and is counted here over windows of hours to weeks. By contrast, a request delayed behind an oversized batch is a queueing phenomenon caused by uneven arrivals and belongs to serving analysis. Headroom that a replica holds in reserve to absorb traffic spikes appears in goodput accounting as ready capacity running below its ideal rate, whereas choosing how much headroom a latency target requires is a serving decision.
This chapter builds the measurement and optimization discipline that turns those scattered losses into one engineering budget. We begin by defining ML goodput (section 9.2), which factors useful fleet output into scheduling, runtime, and program goodput on non-overlapping boundaries. We then establish the reproducible measurement contract and hierarchical fleet profiling needed to localize which factor moved without drowning the cluster in trace data (section 9.3). From there, we trace the three factors in chronological order. We attribute scheduling losses (section 9.4) and runtime losses (section 9.5) to the orchestration and fault-tolerance mechanisms developed in earlier chapters, and then diagnose (section 9.6) and recover (section 9.7) the program-goodput losses that this chapter owns directly. Finally, we compose all three factors into a whole-fleet waterfall and cost per useful accelerator-hour (section 9.8) and evaluate optimizations that trade one goodput factor against another along the fleet’s efficiency frontier (section 9.9).

Across a fleet, capacity disappears at three successive stages in the life of a job. First, a job must acquire a complete set of devices: an accelerator produces no progress while it sits unallocated, while cluster fragmentation strands it in a shape no queued gang can use, or while a partially allocated gang holds it idle waiting for the rest of its peers. Second, once a job holds a complete allocation, its execution must produce durable progress: initialization, input stalls, synchronous checkpoint pauses, failure recovery, and steps re-executed after a rollback all consume held device-hours without advancing the last saved checkpoint. Third, the steps that do survive in a checkpoint must execute near the rate the hardware can sustain. A step that exposes collective communication, waits on a straggling rank or a pipeline bubble, stalls on memory traffic, or dispatches long chains of tiny kernels occupies healthy accelerators while extracting only a fraction of their capability.


Run-level goodput, introduced with the Coordination dimension in Orchestration coordination layer, tracks a single job across its execution and discounts time lost to failures and replayed steps. Because that measure starts only after the job holds its accelerators and stops at the boundary of a completed step, it misses both the capacity the job never received and the execution efficiency of the steps the job kept. Google’s fleet-efficiency framework extends the measurement window backward to the capacity offered by the fleet and forward to the ideal execution time of each retained step, factoring useful fleet output into three multiplicative terms (Wongpanich et al. 2025).1

The paper reports the factors across the whole fleet and segmented by job size and by workload phase, with real-time serving and bulk inference alongside training. The boundaries themselves name no accelerator, so this chapter applies them to any accelerator fleet, for serving replicas as well as training jobs.

Definition 9.1: ML productivity goodput (MPG)
ML productivity goodput (MPG) is the fraction of a fleet’s capacity-time that becomes useful work at the hardware’s ideal rate, expressed as the product of scheduling, runtime, and program goodput, each measured on a fixed accounting boundary so that every lost interval is charged to exactly one factor (Wongpanich et al. 2025).

Significance: It converts the losses that scheduling, recovery, and execution each report in their own units into one fraction of fleet capacity, so a loss at one boundary can be compared directly with an equal loss at another, and an accelerator-hour’s price divided by it is the cost of one ideal-rate hour of useful work.
Distinction: Unlike utilization, which counts an accelerator as used whenever it is allocated or busy, it counts only retained work at its ideal rate. Unlike run-level goodput, it also charges the capacity a job never received and the rate at which its kept steps ran.
Common pitfall: A frequent mistake is to multiply factors measured over different windows or against overlapping denominators, such as a run-averaged MFU that already includes restart time and a runtime factor that charges the same restarts again. The product is meaningful only when each factor divides by exactly what the previous one passed.



The three factors follow a job chronologically, and each factor takes as its denominator the capacity-time that survived the stage before it. Scheduling goodput (\(\SchedulingGoodput\)) is the fraction of fleet capacity-time held by complete allocations—intervals in which a job holds every resource its synchronous execution requires, which the fleet-efficiency literature calls all-allocated time (Wongpanich et al. 2025). Runtime goodput (\(\RuntimeGoodput\)) is the fraction of that all-allocated time spent on steps that a checkpoint retains, excluding initialization, input stalls, synchronous checkpoint pauses, failure recovery, and work discarded after the last checkpoint; its numerator is productive time. Program goodput (\(\ProgramGoodput\)) is the ratio of the predicted ideal execution time of those retained steps to their actual productive time, capturing the efficiency of code, compiler, and communication against a named hardware ideal. In the Llama 3 405B run, effective training time serves as runtime goodput and MFU serves as program goodput; on a shared multi-tenant cluster, a scheduling factor below one multiplies both. Equation 1 combines the three factors into MPG:
\[\MlProductivityGoodput = \SchedulingGoodput \times \RuntimeGoodput \times \ProgramGoodput \tag{1}\]
The three factors multiply cleanly because each factor’s denominator is the preceding factor’s numerator. Scheduling goodput divides held all-allocated time by offered capacity-time, runtime goodput divides retained productive step time by all-allocated time, and program goodput divides predicted ideal time by productive step time. Adjacent numerators and denominators cancel, leaving the ideal-rate time of useful work divided by the total capacity-time the fleet offered (figure 1). MPG is therefore a dimensionless fraction of fleet capacity rather than a raw throughput rate: useful fleet output equals peak capacity multiplied by MPG, and the effective cost per unit of useful work equals the cost of raw capacity divided by MPG. That telescoping cancellation also defines when the product is valid. If two factors include the same lost interval in their denominators, that loss is counted twice; if a gap falls between one factor’s numerator and the next factor’s denominator, the loss goes uncounted in both.

The dashed slice at the end of each row is the capacity-time lost at the boundary above that row, and the losses beside it are charged there and at no other boundary, so the three factors multiply into the share of offered capacity-time that becomes useful work. Each factor captures the losses from one stage of a job’s lifecycle (section 9.1), and the three goodput boundaries cut across the C\(^3\) taxonomy rather than mapping one-to-one onto its axes. Hiding collective communication behind computation raises program goodput, whereas checkpointing and failure recovery—which the Fleet Law places under Coordination—reduce runtime goodput. Goodput factors identify when in a job’s execution capacity was lost, while the C\(^3\) dimensions identify which physical mechanism caused the loss; diagnosing a fleet bottleneck therefore names the goodput factor first and the C\(^3\) mechanism inside it second.
Because the three factors multiply, the share of total fleet capacity lost at any boundary equals that boundary’s fractional loss weighted by the capacity share that reached it. Equation 2 partitions the total efficiency gap \(1 - \SchedulingGoodput\RuntimeGoodput\ProgramGoodput\) into three additive shares—the scheduling loss on offered capacity, the runtime loss on held capacity, and the program loss on retained step time:
\[\begin{aligned} 1 - \SchedulingGoodput\RuntimeGoodput\ProgramGoodput &= (1-\SchedulingGoodput) \\ &\quad + \SchedulingGoodput(1-\RuntimeGoodput) \\ &\quad + \SchedulingGoodput\RuntimeGoodput(1-\ProgramGoodput) \end{aligned} \tag{2}\]
The three right-hand terms sum to the total gap, reflecting the rule that every lost device-hour is charged at exactly one boundary. Although the product \(\SchedulingGoodput\RuntimeGoodput\ProgramGoodput\) is commutative, the additive share attributed to each stage depends on the order in which capacity passes through the boundaries. The decomposition therefore follows the chronological order in which a workload encounters the three losses. Applied to the published Llama 3 405B telemetry, equation 2 shows immediately which boundary consumed most of the cluster’s held capacity.

Hardware activity counters cannot measure how efficiently a retained step ran, because an accelerator registers as busy whether it is waiting on a collective, recomputing dropped activations, or executing arithmetic far below its peak rate. Measuring program goodput instead requires comparing actual step time against a named hardware ideal for the resource that limits the workload. For training steps and for the prefill pass over a prompt, arithmetic dominates, so the ideal time of a step is the time the accelerators would need to execute the model’s required mathematical operations at their peak rate. MFU measures against that ideal by counting only the operations the model architecture requires.3 In Google’s fleet-efficiency methodology, the ideal operation count is fixed before compilation from the program as written—before the compiler fuses kernels or rematerializes activations—so that a compiler optimization that shortens the step raises program goodput instead of shifting its own baseline (Wongpanich et al. 2025). For the same reason, program goodput is not measured against a per-operation roofline. A per-operation roofline rewards kernels that run near their local ceiling and would therefore penalize a rewrite that executes fewer operations at lower utilization while finishing the step sooner. The roofline remains a diagnostic for individual kernels (section 9.6.3) rather than the efficiency measure of a whole program.
3 MFU and HFU: The PaLM report proposed MFU in place of hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU), which counts every executed operation, because the executed count depends on implementation and compiler choices, most visibly rematerialization, which recomputes activations to save memory (Chowdhery et al. 2022). MFU’s reference rate depends only on the model architecture and the published peak rate, so runs of one model on different software stacks compare directly. For goodput accounting, the choice means that recomputation which lets a layout fit in memory is charged to program goodput as lost time rather than credited as work.
