For tenant \(\TenantIndex\), define its dominant share as \(\DominantShare_i=\max_\ResourceTypeIndex(\TenantResourceAllocation/\FleetResourceCapacity)\), where \(\TenantResourceAllocation\) is its allocation of resource \(\ResourceTypeIndex\) and \(\FleetResourceCapacity\) is fleet capacity for that resource. The calculation equalizes \(\DominantShare_i\), not every resource share. One A replica raises A’s dominant share by \(1/8\); one B worker raises B’s by \(2/8\). Progressive filling therefore grants roughly two A replicas for each B worker until both dominant shares reach \(0.50\). This is a fair policy target, but it is not yet a feasible placement. If B’s two workers form one four-GPU gang, the four GPUs must become available atomically. If tensor parallelism requires one NVLink domain, four free GPUs scattered across nodes do not satisfy the allocation. If the job requires 80 GB HBM accelerators, four incompatible GPUs do not count at all. A production scheduler therefore applies capability, gang, and topology constraints to the feasible set, then uses DRF to choose fairly among allocations that can actually run. The order is not a convenience. Feasibility comes before fairness (principle \(\ref{pri-feasibility-before-fairness}\)) because a fair share of accelerators on which the job cannot run delivers no progress to the tenant who holds it. When no equal-share placement exists, the scheduler should report the constraint causing the deviation rather than silently presenting an infeasible entitlement as service delivered.

Lighthouse 8.1: Lighthouse archetypes: Placement changes fairnessThe same resource share has different meaning across the three lighthouse workloads introduced in Three systems archetypes:

Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) needs a rigid, topology-compatible gang. Fractional allocations below its minimum parallel configuration deliver no progress, so fairness must include maximum feasible wait for a contiguous placement rather than GPU-hours alone.
Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) couples accelerator memory to sparse-routing bandwidth. A nominal GPU allocation is infeasible when embedding shards or network capacity cannot follow it, so network and memory must enter the dominant share and placement must protect the serving-latency envelope.
Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) schedules participation rather than data-center GPUs. Eligibility filters for power, connectivity, and device capability can systematically exclude parts of the population, so fairness must be audited through participation and outcome rates across device and user groups, not equal device counts in a round.

The common rule is to define the feasible bundle first and assess fairness over useful progress second. Treating every accelerator or client as interchangeable would conceal the constraint that makes each archetype difficult.





Even when a cluster has dozens of free GPUs in total, a pending 8-GPU job will sit blocked if previous placements scattered those free GPUs in 1- and 2-GPU remnants across partially occupied nodes. Fitting jobs of varying sizes into fixed-capacity nodes without stranding capacity is an instance of bin packing.3 Because general bin packing is NP-hard, no known algorithm finds optimal solutions in polynomial time. Practical heuristics such as first-fit decreasing and best-fit decreasing offer tractable choices, but their performance depends on job sizes and placement constraints. How much usable capacity a heuristic recovers in a heterogeneous ML fleet has to be measured against that fleet’s job mix, because the classical guarantees cover only one-dimensional packing.
3 Bin packing: First-fit decreasing has a classical asymptotic \(11/9\) approximation ratio for one-dimensional bin packing, with an additive constant in the finite-instance bound. That result does not guarantee the same ratio for ML placement with several resource dimensions, topology constraints, and indivisible gangs. A scheduler must evaluate its heuristic against feasible placements and the stranded capacity it leaves.Consider a 64-node cluster with 8 GPUs per node, totaling 512 GPUs. If every job requires 6 GPUs within one node, only one such job fits per node, leaving 2 GPUs unused and reducing effective capacity for this workload to 75 percent. The remaining 2 GPUs per node cannot be combined across nodes into another feasible six-GPU allocation, although smaller compatible jobs could use them. With a mix of 1-GPU, 3-GPU, and 7-GPU jobs, fragmentation depends on the placement and the pending requests; total free capacity can exceed a waiting job’s demand while no individual node has enough space. Figure 3 maps this stranded capacity across an \(8{\times}8\) allocation grid. Although 19 slots (30 percent of cluster capacity, dashed white cells) sit idle across nodes 0 through 7, active allocations (J1 through J15) leave every node partially occupied, which blocks a pending 8-GPU job that requires an entire unfragmented node.
ML placement is a multi-dimensional packing problem. Jobs require GPUs together with CPU cores for data preprocessing, host memory for data loading and augmentation pipelines, local SSD storage for dataset caching, and network bandwidth for gradient synchronization. A job requesting 4 GPUs, 32 CPU cores, and 256 GB of RAM may not fit on a node that has 4 free GPUs but only 16 free CPU cores because other jobs have consumed the host CPU for preprocessing. The scheduler must simultaneously satisfy all resource dimensions, and the job fits only if every dimension has sufficient capacity on the selected node. A bottleneck in any one dimension can therefore strand capacity in the others.
Locality constraints further restrict placement beyond simple resource availability. A training job may require tensor-parallel groups to remain within NVLink-connected nodes when its communication budget cannot tolerate the lower per-endpoint bandwidth of the external fabric (450 GB/s per direction intra-node vs. 50 GB/s per port inter-node). On this topology, where NVLink does not connect the nodes, a job requesting “4 GPUs with NVLink connectivity” cannot use 2 GPUs from node A and 2 from node B, even if all 4 GPUs are individually available and the total capacity is sufficient. These topology constraints turn resource counts into a placement problem where which specific resources are available matters as much as how many. A capacity-feasible packing must also pass the job’s locality constraints.
Schedulers address fragmentation through several complementary strategies, each targeting a different aspect of the problem. The first, backfill, lets smaller jobs run in the gaps while a large job waits for contiguous resources; section 8.4.3 develops it together with the reservation it must protect and the runtime estimates it depends on. A second strategy, periodic defragmentation, migrates or preempts low-priority jobs to consolidate free resources into contiguous blocks, analogous to memory compaction in operating systems. The scheduler identifies nodes where partial allocations leave stranded resources, preempts the jobs occupying those resources, and re-schedules them on nodes where they can be packed more efficiently. The cost includes state transfer and restart, plus replay of work not captured by a valid checkpoint. A graceful checkpoint can preserve recent progress, but still takes time and storage bandwidth. The scheduler must weigh these costs against the benefit of starting large jobs sooner, and low-demand periods reduce the number of competing jobs affected by the move.
A third strategy, over-subscription, admits more demand than a capacity dimension can sustain simultaneously, but only where the resource is divisible and the scheduler can bound interference. Average activity of a GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs), its compute units, does not create fractional whole GPUs. A job that reserves device memory, requires an exclusive CUDA context, or belongs to a rigid gang still occupies its assigned device while kernels are idle. Statistical multiplexing can be safe for explicitly shareable CPU, network, storage, or partitioned GPU capacity when tenants have measured, weakly correlated peaks and enforceable limits. It is unsafe to convert 70 percent average GPU utilization into a 1.4\(\times\) device overcommit ratio. Whole-device capacity should instead be recovered through preemption, elastic resizing, or an isolation mechanism such as Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) hardware partitioning or NVIDIA’s Multi-Process Service (MPS), which lets several processes’ kernels share one device. Either mechanism helps only if the scheduler models its memory, compute, and fault-sharing contract explicitly. Both reappear with the serving workloads they suit best in section 8.10.1.

In the left panel of figure 4, jobs J1 and J2 each hold 4 of the 8 GPUs they require, and the whole pool stalls. Atomic gang scheduling (right panel) instead grants J1 all 8 GPUs as one allocation while J2 waits without holding any, which prevents this allocation deadlock.






Figure 4: The Distributed Deadlock (Hold and Wait): In a non-gang scheduler (left), job J1 acquires half the cluster and waits for the rest, while job J2 acquires the other half and waits for J1 to release its GPUs. Neither can proceed, and 100 percent of the cluster sits idle. Gang scheduling (right) solves this by mandating atomic allocation: a job is either granted its entire \(\DeviceCount\)-GPU requirement simultaneously or it waits in the queue without holding any resources.




Definition 8.1: Gang scheduling
Gang scheduling is the ML cluster scheduling policy that atomically allocates the resources required by a job’s minimum viable execution group, so a rigid group either receives its complete allocation or waits without retaining a partial one.

Significance: A rigid synchronous job configured for 1,024 GPUs but holding only 512 GPUs completes zero training steps, not half as many: each collective stalls until every rank in its communication group arrives, so the held GPUs consume power and capital at zero useful output. Without atomic allocation, two such jobs can each acquire half the cluster and deadlock, both at zero progress while consuming the full cluster’s operating cost.
Distinction: Unlike a malleable service or parallel job that can make progress across a resource range, rigid synchronous training has step-function utility: the minimum viable gang or nothing. The distinction is a property of the execution graph, not of whether the workload is labeled ML, cloud, or HPC.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that priorities or quotas alone solve this. Atomicity must extend to every co-scheduled resource the job needs to make progress (accelerators, high-bandwidth interconnect domains, network capacity for collectives); enforcing it at GPU granularity alone recreates the deadlock one resource layer down.





↩︎ Ring and tree AllReduce schedules, each of which completes only after every rank’s contribution has been reduced, are established in AllReduce Algorithms and Topologies.
4 Hold-and-wait: One of the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait), all of which must hold for deadlock to occur (Coffman et al. 1971). Gang scheduling removes hold-and-wait through atomic allocation, which is why it prevents this deadlock by construction; the price is reduced packing flexibility.
Coffman, Edward G., Michael Elphick, and Arie Shoshani. 1971. “System Deadlocks.” ACM Computing Surveys 3 (2): 67–78. https://doi.org/10.1145/356586.356588.
The partial-allocation pattern is a hold-and-wait deadlock4 in which two jobs each hold half the cluster and neither can proceed. Its price is the whole allocation for as long as the cycle persists. At the scale of the chapter’s reference workload, two 1,024-GPU gangs that have each acquired 900 GPUs from a pool too small to complete either one burn about $1,800 per hour apiece. The limiting case is two jobs that each request the entire cluster, the example OpenAI used to motivate group admission (war story 8.1). On the 10,000-GPU cluster, a deadlock that strands every device wastes $20,000 per hour at the chapter’s rate while producing no progress for either job. Measured against the stake computed at the start of the chapter, raising utilization from 50 percent to 80 percent recovers about $144,000 per day in equivalent capacity value. About 7 hours of such a deadlock therefore erase a full day of that gain. Gang scheduling does not create the gain, but it protects it. For a rigid job \(\RigidGangJob\) requiring \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs, the scheduler must grant all \(\DeviceCount\) GPUs atomically or leave the job queued without a partial allocation. This removes hold-and-wait for the resources covered by that allocation; it does not prevent later deadlocks in application code or auxiliary resources.
Naive gang scheduling is wasteful in predictable ways. Atomic allocation means the waiting job holds nothing, yet a large gang will never assemble if every freed GPU goes to a smaller job. The scheduler therefore places a reservation for the job at the head of the queue, draining capacity toward it by declining to start new work on GPUs that the gang will need. If the cluster has 900 free GPUs and that job requests 1,024, the reservation keeps the 900 GPUs idle until 124 more become available, potentially wasting thousands of GPU-hours. Backfill scheduling addresses this by identifying jobs in the queue that can fit within the 900 available GPUs without delaying the large job’s expected start time (figure 5), an idea popularized in the ANL/IBM SP scheduling system (Lifka 1995). A 128-GPU job with an estimated runtime of 2 hours is a backfill candidate if the 124 additional GPUs needed by the large job will remain unavailable for at least 2 hours. Protecting the reservation requires an enforced runtime bound or a preemption contract that releases the backfill allocation in time, including any checkpoint and cleanup delay. The estimate identifies an opportunity; the release contract makes the reservation enforceable.

Lifka, David A. 1995. “The ANL/IBM SP Scheduling System.” In Job Scheduling Strategies for Parallel Processing, edited by Dror G. Feitelson and Larry Rudolph, vol. 949. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-60153-8_35.






Figure 5: Backfill under a Reservation: The head-of-queue gang holds a reservation that begins when the running jobs release their GPUs. Until then, the free GPUs form a backfill window. A short job that ends before the reservation start runs in that window, while a job whose runtime bound would carry it past the start is held, because admitting it would delay the gang. The schematic carries no measured values.



The accuracy of runtime estimates determines backfill effectiveness, and this creates a game-theoretic challenge. If users overestimate runtimes, fewer jobs appear to fit a backfill window. If they underestimate, the scheduler may need to preempt a backfilled job to honor the reservation, paying recovery costs and losing unsaved progress. A policy that kills jobs at their declared limit encourages conservative estimates. Tiresias (Gu et al. 2019), discussed in section 8.9.1, avoids duration estimates when setting priority by using observed resource consumption. That choice addresses ordering under uncertainty, while reservation protection still needs an enforced runtime bound or release contract that says when a backfilled job will give its capacity back.



Gang scheduling eliminates the hold-and-wait condition for the atomically allocated bundle, but it does not immunize the cluster against all forms of resource contention. Later requests for auxiliary resources can still create a cycle of dependencies. Priority rules can also prevent a resource holder from making progress without creating a cycle. Distinguishing these cases matters because breaking a deadlock and providing a starved job with enough resources to exit require different interventions.
Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority job waits on a low-priority resource holder whose progress other work delays. Consider the 64-GPU fine-tuning run of the 175B-parameter model, submitted at high priority. The scheduler has reserved 60 available GPUs, but the remaining 4 are held by a low-priority data processing job. Normally, the scheduler would preempt the low-priority job to satisfy the high-priority request. However, if a stream of medium-priority development jobs saturates the cluster’s CPU or network bandwidth, starving the low-priority job of the resources it needs to checkpoint and exit, the low-priority job stalls. Its graceful release path cannot complete. The high-priority job waits for the low-priority job, which is effectively blocked by the medium-priority jobs. The 60-GPU idle block persists until the exit path receives resources or an enforced termination policy reclaims the remaining GPUs, potentially losing uncheckpointed work.



Priority inversion: the high-priority job waits on a low-priority holder that medium-priority work starves.

Definition 8.2: Priority inversion
Priority inversion is an ML cluster scheduling pathology in which a high-priority task is forced to wait for a lower-priority task to release a shared resource.

Significance: It ties the progress of a high-priority job, and the accelerators reserved for it, to the progress of the lowest-priority job in the wait-for chain. In ML clusters, this typically occurs when a low-priority job holding GPUs is starved of auxiliary resources (for example, bandwidth for checkpointing), preventing it from finishing and releasing the accelerators needed by high-priority workloads.
Distinction: Unlike standard queuing (where tasks wait their turn), priority inversion involves an active blockage: the high-priority task is ready to run but is transitively dependent on a task that the scheduler does not prioritize.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that strict priority levels solve this. Raising the waiting job’s priority does not supply the CPU or bandwidth that its lower-priority resource holder needs to exit; the preemption policy must protect that release path.



Prevention and detection address different parts of this problem. Atomic allocation prevents hold-and-wait for the resources included in the gang, while reserving checkpoint bandwidth allows a preempted job to complete its exit path. Timeouts instead bound how long the system waits before investigating or reclaiming an allocation; they do not prevent deadlock states from arising. Monitoring can trigger recovery when progress stops, but safe reclamation still requires enforcing the new ownership decision.
Detection, unlike exact placement search, is computationally cheap. Before feasibility filtering, a cluster with 10,000 GPUs and 500 pending jobs can have more than \(10^{15}\) candidate allocations, which puts exhaustive allocation search out of reach. Detection instead works on a wait-for graph, a directed graph with one vertex per job and an edge from job A to job B whenever A waits for a resource that B holds. A cycle identifies a potential deadlock. It establishes deadlock when every edge is an unavoidable blocking dependency and no alternative resource allocation can let a member proceed. Finding a cycle in an already constructed graph takes time linear in its vertices and edges. The difficulty lies in construction. Resource state changes continuously across a distributed control plane, so the scheduler rarely holds a complete, current graph, and a cycle detected on stale state may already have resolved while a real one goes unseen.
Large-scale schedulers therefore supplement wait-for detection with mechanisms that preserve liveness under incomplete state. A lease-based resource gives every allocation a time-to-live; expiry authorizes reclamation only when the resource manager enforces revocation and cleanup before reuse. Progress monitoring checks advancement through signals such as completed-step counters, using GPU utilization and heartbeats as supporting observations rather than proof of useful work. When the scheduler must preempt a lower-priority job, holistic preemption reserves the CPU, network, and storage bandwidth needed for that job to checkpoint and exit cleanly; otherwise, the victim can be too starved to release the accelerators. False failure suspicions can cost useful work, but must not bypass the ownership checks required for safe recovery.



In preference-training pipelines such as reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), allocating the policy-training GPUs while the rollout-generation or reward-scoring workers sit queued stalls the workflow just as completely as a missing AllReduce rank. Homogeneous gang scheduling allocates \(\DeviceCount\) identical workers executing the same compute graph. Heterogeneous workflows instead combine trainers, evaluators, and inference-style workers that need different GPU counts, memory footprints, and lifetimes, yet still must run together as a single job.


↩︎ The models that alignment training co-locates, and their unequal resource demands, are established in Multi-Model Training for Alignment and RLHF.

Systems Perspective 8.1: Routing over synchronyHeterogeneous gang scheduling extends atomic allocation to the roles that must coexist for a workflow to progress. A viable group might pair high-HBM nodes for memory-bound generation with compute-oriented nodes for policy updates. The orchestration problem then shifts from packing a homogeneous ring toward routing data. Rather than reducing gradients among identical workers, the job streams rollouts from generation workers to the workers that compute policy updates, so placement must also support the data exchanged between those roles. Rollout and training stages may exchange work in batches or through a buffered pipeline; their measured production and consumption rates determine where queues grow or accelerators wait. The scheduler needs a minimum viable resource bundle and a supported scaling policy for each role, rather than an assumption that all workers are interchangeable or perfectly balanced.


Homogeneous and heterogeneous jobs share an allocation requirement: the scheduler must assemble a viable group before expecting progress. Backfill can use capacity while that group waits, provided runtime estimates or preemption contracts protect the reservation. Enforcing these policies requires a control plane that represents ownership and reconciles allocations after failures.

A pending gang and a queue of small backfill jobs need both a policy for sharing capacity and a control plane that can enforce it. The policies just developed apply across platforms; the orchestration paradigm determines how the platform represents allocations and recovers when observed state diverges from them. Slurm, shaped by HPC batch systems, favors explicit resource requests and predictable allocation. Kubernetes, shaped by cloud-native service management, favors declared desired state and continuous reconciliation. The choice is therefore not Slurm vs. Kubernetes as products; it is which control model best matches the workload mix, failure behavior, and operational culture of the fleet.
The two platforms embody two control models (figure 6). Slurm follows an imperative batch model, in which the user states the resources a job needs and the central slurmctld dispatches that allocation through per-node slurmd daemons. Kubernetes follows a declarative model, in which the user states what should be running and controllers reconcile observed state toward that declaration through the API server and node agents. Both platforms accept explicit resource requirements and track execution state, so the useful distinction is which lifecycle the platform manages directly: an allocated batch job or a collection of workloads maintained by controllers. That distinction shapes how ML workloads are admitted, monitored, and recovered from failure, and distributed training still needs framework-level coordination under either model.






Figure 6: Architectural Paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes: Slurm (left) uses an imperative batch model where users submit explicit resource requests to a centralized controller (slurmctld) providing deterministic atomic allocation. Kubernetes (right) uses a declarative service model where controllers continuously reconcile observed cluster state in etcd against desired state specifications.





When a multi-node job needs an exclusive, non-overlapping block of accelerators for days at a time without partial-allocation deadlocks or conflicting node ownership, a centralized batch allocator is the most direct control plane. The Slurm Workload Manager5 originated at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to solve that problem for Linux supercomputers (Yoo et al. 2003): long-running jobs, expensive shared hardware, and users who can specify resource needs in advance. In ML infrastructure, the same batch model maps to GPU training through partitions for heterogeneous accelerator pools and predictable atomic allocations for long-running distributed jobs.
5 Slurm Workload Manager: Originally “SLURM,” an acronym for Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management, the project dropped the acronym capitalization in 2012. Developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory beginning in 2002, Slurm’s centralized controller (slurmctld) maintains a single authoritative view of resource allocations. At very large scale, operators may partition fleets or federate schedulers to keep scheduling latency, policy isolation, and failure domains manageable.

Slurm’s batch submission model makes resource requirements explicit. Users submit job scripts, and the scheduler allocates resources within eligible partitions according to policy and availability. A submission of sbatch --gres=gpu:8 --nodes=4 requests 8 GPUs on each of 4 nodes, a 32-GPU allocation. The request supplies a capacity contract, but useful execution still depends on the selected hardware and the application’s launch configuration. Overstating requirements strands resources; understating them can cause memory failures or poor performance.
Slurm’s architecture consists of a central controller daemon (slurmctld) that maintains the global view of cluster state and makes scheduling decisions, and per-node daemons (slurmd) that manage local resources and execute jobs. This centralized architecture provides the authoritative allocation model discussed in section 8.2: the controller is the source of truth for resource assignments, reducing the risk of conflicting allocations. The cost is a potential single point of failure (addressed through active-passive failover) and a scheduling-throughput limit. As fleets grow, organizations may partition the cluster or federate schedulers to bound scheduling latency and failure impact; within a cluster, a typical ML configuration defines Slurm partitions by accelerator type and interconnect (table 2).

Within a partition, a request specifies both the number of GPUs a job needs and the allocation shape: how those GPUs are distributed across nodes. In Slurm, --gres=gpu:N or --gpus-per-node=N requests a per-node count, while --gpus=N requests a job-wide total. Whether the scheduler may split a node between jobs is a separate consumable-resource policy (Slurm’s select/cons_tres plugin), and a node-exclusive policy strands the unused devices in the six-on-eight example of section 8.4.2. Shape decides communication. In an eight-GPU-per-node pool, a 16-GPU request that also fixes eight GPUs per node (--gpus-per-node=8) yields two fully populated nodes, whose NVLink domains follow from the node hardware rather than the count. A request for 16 GPUs with no per-node constraint gives the scheduler more freedom, so it can start sooner on partially occupied nodes, but it may spread the group across several of them. Whether that flexibility is useful depends on the parallelism configuration and its communication budget. Tensor-parallel groups with frequent exchanges may justify compact placement, while data-parallel groups with well-overlapped communication may tolerate a wider allocation.
The fair-share scheduling mechanism uses past consumption to influence future priority under contention. An illustrative heuristic combines base priority, the user’s target fair share (\(\TargetFairShare\)), recent actual consumption (\(\RecentUsageShare\)), and a small stabilizing constant (\(\FairShareStabilizingConstant\)); it illustrates the feedback without reproducing Slurm’s multifactor priority calculation:
\[\text{Priority}_{\text{effective}} = \text{Priority}_{\text{base}} \times \frac{\TargetFairShare}{\RecentUsageShare+ \FairShareStabilizingConstant} \tag{1}\]
With base priority and target share fixed, equation 1 lowers priority as recent consumption increases. Doubling consumption approximately halves this illustrative priority when the stabilizing constant is negligible. Actual admission also depends on other priority factors and feasible resources; low recent usage does not guarantee an immediate start.
The time decay of usage history determines how quickly the system “forgives” past heavy usage. A half-life of one week means that a researcher’s heavy usage from two weeks ago contributes only 25 percent to their current usage calculation. Short half-lives make the policy more responsive to recent changes but can encourage alternating bursts of usage. Long half-lives retain the effect of a completed large project when its researchers return with smaller jobs. The useful decay window depends on the fleet’s job durations and the period over which the organization intends to balance access. Usage itself need not count every device alike. Trackable resources (TRES) let accounting charge different accelerator classes different billing weights in fair-share usage, an administrative valuation that tracks economic cost only as far as the chosen weights do.
Preemption policies enable high-priority jobs to reclaim resources from running workloads, and for ML training the reclaim must leave time to save state. Slurm expresses that time as a grace period. It signals the selected job (SIGTERM), waits the configured GraceTime, and only then kills it (SIGKILL); under PreemptMode=REQUEUE it can also requeue an eligible job to run again later. Neither the signal nor the requeue saves model state. The application must handle the signal, publish a valid checkpoint within the grace period, and restore it on restart. If termination precedes completion of that save, recovery uses the last valid checkpoint and replays subsequent work. Preemption therefore buys access for high-priority work with the victim’s replay and restart time, a price that section 8.8.1 develops.


↩︎ Checkpointing for progress preservation, including the checkpoint interval and coordination patterns, is established in Checkpointing and Progress Preservation.
Several Slurm features expose ML structure to the batch system. A hyperparameter sweep is the opposite of a gang. Job arrays submit many trials as one record (for example, --array=0-99), and each trial reads its index from the SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID environment variable to select its configuration. Slurm schedules the elements independently, so individual trials become ideal backfill candidates that fill small gaps in capacity, while the array keeps submission and management overhead low without making the trials one indivisible gang.
Heterogeneous jobs carry the heterogeneous gang of section 8.4.5 into a batch allocation. One job can contain components with distinct resource requests, admitted together. The 64-GPU fine-tuning run of the 175B model, for example, could request 8 GPU nodes for training and 2 CPU-only nodes for on-the-fly tokenization as a single allocation. It could then launch training on the GPU component and data workers on the CPU component (srun --het-group=0 and --het-group=1). This separation helps only if the data workers and transfer path sustain the training stage’s consumption rate; a heterogeneous allocation exposes that choice but does not itself balance the pipeline. At the boundaries of each allocation, prolog and epilog scripts turn job transitions into health checks. A prolog tests reported topology, ECC counters, and link status on each allocated node and drains a failing node before launch. An epilog removes the job’s orphan processes and shared-memory segments. They apply the quarantine idea of section 8.6.4 at job boundaries, reducing exposure to known faults without establishing delivered bandwidth.
Slurm’s strengths for ML training include explicit batch allocations, configurable fair-share policies, and integration with MPI-based distributed training frameworks. A mixed training-serving fleet also needs a service lifecycle that maintains ready replicas as demand and failures change. Inside a batch scheduler, adding or removing an inference replica means submitting or canceling a job, a far heavier operation than a controller adjusting a replica count, and a failed replica stays down until something resubmits it. Operators must integrate replica health, replacement, and demand-driven scaling with the batch scheduler, or assign those responsibilities to a service orchestration platform. Kubernetes starts from that service contract, in which users declare the desired state of services and jobs and controllers continuously reconcile the cluster toward it.



When a cluster runs always-on inference services alongside training jobs, managing serving replicas as batch scripts forces operators to rebuild health checks, rolling updates, and replica replacement by hand. Kubernetes addresses this mixed workload by managing both services and batch jobs through a declarative model that expresses a workload’s desired state and uses control loops to reconcile observations with that state (Burns et al. 2016; Cloud Native Computing Foundation 2024). The unit it places is the pod, one or more containers that share a node and a network identity, and its default scheduler places pods one at a time. The name collides with the hardware pod of The Pod, the many racks joined under one fabric. A Kubernetes pod is a software unit that never spans more than one node, so a 64-pod training job is 64 container groups placed onto nodes, all of which can sit inside one hardware pod. Controllers above the scheduler give groups of pods a purpose: a Deployment keeps a set number of identical replica pods running, while a Job runs pods until they complete, retrying failures under a stated policy. The workload controller therefore determines what completion, replacement, or continued availability means.

Burns, Brendan, Brian Grant, David Oppenheimer, Eric Brewer, and John Wilkes. 2016. “Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes.” Communications of the ACM 59 (5): 50–57. https://doi.org/10.1145/2890784.

Cloud Native Computing Foundation. 2024. Kubernetes: Production-Grade Container Orchestration.
Failure handling reveals the importance of the workload contract. Slurm can detect node failures and requeue eligible jobs when configured to do so. Kubernetes controllers maintain workload-specific goals, such as a Deployment’s replica count or a Job’s completion and retry policy. A replacement pod still has to be placed, become ready, and rejoin the distributed training run before progress resumes. Training operators can coordinate worker creation, while the framework remains responsible for valid state and group recovery. Both platforms therefore require an explicit agreement between allocation, process lifecycle, and application recovery.
Kubernetes’ control loop architecture uses the controller pattern:6 controllers observe and update API objects through the API server, which persists cluster state in etcd, a replicated key-value store. Those objects contain desired state and reported observations, not instantaneous physical truth. The pattern repeats at every level: the Deployment controller reconciles the number of pod replicas, the scheduler binds pending pods to nodes, the kubelet (the agent on each node) keeps its assigned containers running, and the node controller marks nodes that stop reporting. Each component acts independently and communicates only through API objects, which makes the system resilient to the failure of any single controller. The price of that independence is that their interactions require clear ownership and retry behavior, particularly when a failed node’s last reported state no longer describes its execution.
6 Controller pattern (reconciliation loop): A “level-triggered” design reconciles the current desired and observed states rather than depending on every intermediate event. A restarted controller can resume from durable state if its actions tolerate retries and its observations expose unfinished work. In the device-plugin model, device plugins expose accelerators as schedulable extended resources. The NVIDIA device plugin registers GPUs with the kubelet, enabling pod specifications that request GPU resources declaratively through the standard Kubernetes resource model. A pod then asks for whole GPUs by naming the nvidia.com/gpu resource in its limits (listing 1).

When the device plugin exposes exclusive whole GPUs, a small model serving occasional requests can reserve a device while using only a fraction of its compute and memory capacity. Whole-device allocation suits workloads that need the capacity or isolation, but can strand resources for smaller workloads. The resource unit exposed by the plugin therefore matters, because sharing or partitioning changes what the scheduler can allocate and what isolation each allocation receives. Device plugins can also expose hardware partitions, such as MIG instances, as schedulable units, a choice that section 8.10.1 develops with the serving workloads it suits.
Kubernetes’ default scheduler places pods independently, so it does not supply the group admission that section 8.4.3 requires. Under that default, a 64-pod training job receives 64 separate placement decisions, with no guarantee that all will succeed. If the cluster has resources for 60 pods but not 64, those 60 can occupy capacity while the remaining 4 wait. The platform must therefore configure a group-level admission and placement contract for a rigid job. PodGroup-style abstractions give that contract a unit matching the job’s minimum viable execution group rather than an individual pod.
The mechanism that closes this gap is group admission. A PodGroup declares a group’s minimum runnable membership. The scheduler tentatively reserves a placement for each member as it finds one but binds none of them to nodes until the minimum membership is placed, and it releases every reservation if the attempt fails or times out. Admission and placement thereby become two decisions, with the group admitted only when placement has succeeded for enough of it. The Volcano7 batch scheduler and the Coscheduling scheduler plugin both implement this pattern. Group admission does not make physical launches simultaneous; nodes can still fail or start at different times, so the framework must establish the communication group before training proceeds.
7 Volcano: Volcano provides a scheduler with batch and gang-scheduling mechanisms. Pods select it through their scheduler name, so it can coexist with Kubernetes’ default scheduler. The operational contract must account for interactions between schedulers sharing the same nodes; installing Volcano does not automatically transfer every workload’s scheduling to it.
War Story 8.1: OpenAI's gang-scheduling example (2021)Context: OpenAI scaled Kubernetes clusters to 7,500 nodes for workloads including GPT-3, CLIP, and DALL-E. Its account explains that MPI-coordinated optimizer groups needed all members scheduled before training could progress (Sigler 2021).
Mechanism: The account illustrates the risk with two experiments each requesting the entire cluster. Incremental pod placement could allocate half the capacity to each, leaving neither with a complete group.
Impact: In that example, both jobs hold capacity without making progress. It demonstrates the deadlock mechanism rather than documenting a particular pair of stalled production runs.
Fix: OpenAI reports adopting the coscheduling plugin to add group-aware admission to the Kubernetes scheduler.
Systems lesson: Distributed ML scheduling must encode the job’s execution semantics. For MPI-style training, “some pods scheduled” is not partial progress; it is wasted allocation. Production schedulers need gang scheduling, quota controls, and workload-aware policies rather than generic pod placement alone.


Priority classes control scheduling precedence and preemption eligibility. A fleet might give inference higher priority than training to help protect serving service-level objectives (SLOs), but priority cannot replace ready capacity during a demand spike. With preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority, a pending pod can displace lower-priority pods when their removal makes placement feasible. With preemptionPolicy: Never, it retains queue precedence without initiating preemption and remains subject to higher-priority preemption. Termination, cleanup, and replacement startup take time. Training applications also need a checkpoint-aware shutdown path that fits the allowed grace period; assigning priorities does not create that path. The policy must balance serving readiness against repeated interruption of training.
Kueue8 makes admission a separate control decision. It manages when workloads may consume quota, while a compatible scheduler binds their pods to nodes. The admission policy and placement policy must agree on resource types, group requirements, and topology. Separating these responsibilities lets each layer run its own policy, at the price of keeping the two consistent. Kueue represents each team or project as a queue with a configured quota (a ClusterQueue) and groups queues into cohorts whose members may lend one another unused quota, under the borrowing and reclaim contract of section 8.11.2.
8 Kueue: Kueue separates workload admission from pod placement. Its all-or-nothing mechanisms include waiting for admitted pods to become ready and requeuing workloads that exceed the configured timeout. Aggregate quota admission alone does not prove that a gang fits the physical topology; the guarantee depends on the configured readiness, topology, and placement mechanisms.


Group admission handles one constraint that microservice orchestration leaves implicit and distributed training cannot. Four more remain. Workers must launch knowing their peers, collective traffic must avoid network layers built for request traffic, checkpoint writes need bandwidth rather than only storage capacity, and progress must be observable below the container. Operators and plugins add each constraint to the platform; the mechanism matters more than the product that happens to implement it.
Peer discovery is the job of the training operator ecosystem, which extends Kubernetes with job-specific resource types (custom resource definitions). In the Kubeflow Training Operator, a PyTorchJob declares the number of workers, the container image, and resource requirements. The operator creates the pods and injects the rendezvous address (MASTER_ADDR and MASTER_PORT), the group size, and each worker’s rank (WORLD_SIZE and RANK), which the framework uses to form its communication group. If a worker pod fails, the operator can detect the deviation and create a replacement pod to restore the desired replica count, but training-state recovery still depends on the framework’s checkpoint and rendezvous logic.
Collective traffic is the second constraint. The pod overlay network that the Container Network Interface (CNI) configures, designed for microservice requests, routes packets through software switching on the host CPU, which adds latency and caps bandwidth when it sits on the critical gradient-synchronization path. For bandwidth-sensitive training, host networking (hostNetwork: true) places pods in the host’s network namespace, bypassing the ordinary pod overlay path. It does not itself allocate remote direct memory access (RDMA) devices or grant permission to use them; device exposure, resource requests, drivers, and access controls require separate configuration. Operators such as NVIDIA’s Network Operator automate that exposure through RDMA device plugins and GPUDirect RDMA configuration, letting containerized workloads approach bare-metal interconnect performance once the rest of the stack is configured.
Checkpoint bandwidth is the third constraint, because storage integration must account for the checkpoint storm of definition \(\ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}\), in which many workers write large amounts of state together. Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) request capacity on a configured storage system but do not reserve checkpoint throughput. A 1,024-GPU training job writing the 2.45 TB resumable checkpoint of the 175B model needs a measured write budget shared with other workloads. Backend bandwidth controls, client throttling, or staggered writes can limit interference; the platform must verify which controls the storage implementation enforces.
Visibility into progress is the fourth. The observability stack for training clusters combines general-purpose cluster monitoring (commonly Prometheus and Grafana) with accelerator telemetry such as the Data Center GPU Manager (DCGM) exporter, which reports utilization, memory bandwidth, temperature, and ECC errors. These observations locate symptoms. Correlating them with step progress, input waits, and communication traces is what distinguishes useful computation from stalls and identifies which dependency limits a training job.


↪ Fleet telemetry across device, network, and facility levels, and the correlation that narrows a failure domain, is developed in Fleet telemetry and hardware observability.
The 1,024-GPU pretraining run for our 175B model illustrates how these responsibilities fit together. One possible deployment defines a PyTorchJob with 128 worker pods, each requesting 8 GPUs. Host networking removes the pod overlay from the gradient path, and the Network Operator exposes each node’s InfiniBand adapters to the workers through RDMA device plugins. A PVC backed by Lustre provides access to the 6 TB tokenized training corpus and a checkpoint path whose sustained bandwidth must be validated. DCGM metrics stream to Prometheus, supporting alerts on uncorrectable ECC errors and deviations from workload-specific communication baselines.



Selecting a control plane requires matching its allocation and recovery contract to the workload mix. Rigid training groups need reliable atomic placement and checkpoint-aware interruption; serving replicas need readiness checks and continuous recovery. Existing operational expertise and the cost of running a second control plane also shape the choice. A fleet dedicated to long, homogeneous training runs that use bare-metal collectives, operated by a team fluent in batch scheduling, gains most from Slurm’s authoritative allocation and mature fair-share. A fleet that mixes training with always-on serving, and already runs cloud-native deployment and observability tooling, gains more from Kubernetes with a gang-admission layer added for its rigid jobs. The Slurm vs. Kubernetes trade-off organizes around the dimensions most relevant to ML workloads (table 3).

The gang-scheduling row of the table compresses a naming collision that is easy to miss. This chapter uses gang scheduling for atomic allocation of a whole execution group, which is the requirement distributed training imposes. Slurm reserves the name for the older, Ousterhout-style meaning of the term, in which co-scheduled jobs share nodes by time-slicing in synchronized rounds. Slurm provides atomic multi-node allocation under its ordinary job model, so the requirement is met even though Slurm’s “gang scheduling” option means something else.
The choice of scheduling paradigm also reflects organizational trajectory. Teams starting with HPC-focused training infrastructure may begin with Slurm and add Kubernetes for serving. Teams starting from cloud-native application infrastructure may begin with Kubernetes and add HPC-oriented extensions (Volcano, Kueue) for training. Slurm has meanwhile added a REST interface and container support, so the two platforms now overlap in capability. Either path can reach a functional hybrid architecture, but the starting point determines which capabilities are strongest and which require the most investment to develop.



While the choice between Slurm and Kubernetes often appears binary, engineering organizations can deploy hybrid architectures that use the strengths of both systems. The relevant boundary again follows workload semantics rather than labels. Rigid, topology-sensitive jobs fit a batch scheduler’s atomic allocation contract, while malleable services fit a reconciliation loop that adjusts replica count continuously. Some training jobs are elastic, and some serving replicas are rigid multi-accelerator gangs, so neither “training” nor “serving” selects a control plane by itself.
The Kubernetes-over-Slurm pattern wraps the HPC scheduler within a cloud-native control plane. Kubernetes manages the lifecycle of training jobs through custom operators while delegating batch admission and placement to Slurm. The central engineering problem is ownership: exactly one control plane must authorize each placement, while the outer controller reconciles lifecycle state without issuing a conflicting allocation. The arrangement combines a declarative management surface with Slurm’s batch and topology policies, but it also creates a cross-control-plane failure boundary that operators must fence explicitly.
The Slurm-alongside-Kubernetes pattern takes a coarser-grained approach, maintaining separate clusters for training and serving that draw from a shared pool of physical nodes. A meta-scheduler or capacity broker acts as an arbitrator, dynamically reassigning nodes between the Slurm partition and the Kubernetes cluster based on demand signals. During intensive training campaigns, nodes are drained from Kubernetes and joined to Slurm; during product launches or traffic spikes, the flow reverses. The primary challenge is the mode-switching cost: draining a node, changing its ownership and configuration, and admitting it to the other control plane takes much longer than an ordinary placement decision. This latency limits sharing to planned capacity shifts rather than second-by-second inference bursts.
A shared application runtime such as Ray provides task and actor abstractions for both training and serving. Ray’s placement groups, unlike the cloud network-locality abstraction of the same name, reserve bundles of logical resources for work that must run together, and serving replicas can also require multi-device groups. Inside a shared runtime the workloads keep their different state, latency, and recovery requirements, so the platform must still coordinate Ray’s logical allocations with the underlying resource manager and validate the isolation and recovery behavior needed by each workload.
Threading these patterns together, consider the lifecycle of our 175B parameter model. A hybrid platform can allocate the training gang through Slurm and later place serving replicas through Kubernetes. The orchestration boundary concerns resource ownership: the training job releases its allocation, and the serving control plane admits replicas against its own capacity and readiness requirements. Deciding whether the trained artifact is ready for production requires validation and release policy beyond the scheduler; CI/CD for ML at Scale develops those validation gates and rollout policies.
A hybrid platform is useful when its separate allocation contracts justify the additional ownership and recovery boundary. The cost to measure is the coordination between control planes, including node draining and reassignment, rather than a presumed performance advantage from either product name. Because Slurm and Kubernetes now overlap in capability, the paradigm choice is a workload-specific design decision, and teams must establish the allocation and recovery guarantees they need before layering physical placement constraints on top of them.

Two allocations of the same size can meet very different communication budgets depending on where the devices sit in the cluster fabric. The next layer of the scheduler must therefore weigh physical location alongside resource count.

A scattered allocation can place frequent collective traffic on shared cross-rack paths, exposing latency or bandwidth limits that a more compact allocation avoids. The penalty is set by how much of the job’s traffic crosses those paths and how much capacity the fabric provisions there, not by the rack count itself. The earlier feasibility rules already required compatible topology; topology-aware scheduling makes that requirement explicit in the placement objective, accounting for communication paths as well as raw compute.


Splitting a tensor-parallel group across node boundaries moves its per-layer activation exchanges off intra-node NVLink onto the external network fabric, where an H100’s per-direction NVLink rate is 9× the rate of one NDR port (Bandwidth hierarchy). Each level of a cluster’s communication hierarchy comes from the hardware that builds it and sets a distinct bandwidth and latency budget. GPUs inside a node exchange data over NVLink, the tier fast enough for the per-layer exchanges of tensor parallelism. Nodes under one leaf switch communicate over an external fabric such as InfiniBand or RoCE. Racks joined through spine switches add switch hops whose delivered bandwidth depends on concurrent flows and oversubscription even in a fat-tree. Cross-rack communication also adds tail latency variability: while median latency may be only slightly higher, p99 latency can spike during congestion events, creating straggler effects in synchronous training where the slowest communicator determines the pace for all workers.


↩︎ Bisection bandwidth and fat-tree network topologies are established in Fat-tree (Clos) networks.
A 64-GPU job within one rack can avoid cross-rack paths that a spread allocation must use. It outperforms the spread allocation only when those paths add exposed latency or bandwidth contention; a non-blocking, uncongested spine need not reduce sustained throughput. The performance difference stems directly from the hierarchical communication analysis in Hierarchical AllReduce: a flat ring AllReduce runs at the speed of the slowest link in the ring, and cross-rack hops introduce both higher latency and increased contention risk. For synchronous training, every iteration waits for the slowest worker to complete its AllReduce, so even occasional cross-rack congestion inflates the Fleet Law’s communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) (equation 1.3) on every step it touches.
The scheduler must therefore model the cluster as a hierarchical graph with discrete bandwidth boundaries (figure 7). In the illustrated H100 fleet, per-direction bandwidth steps down from 450 GB/s across the NVSwitch inside a node to 50 GB/s per port under a leaf switch, and to roughly 12.5–25 GB/s per endpoint when balanced traffic saturates an oversubscribed spine. A node boundary can introduce a large bandwidth reduction, but a non-blocking rack or pod boundary need not reduce per-endpoint bandwidth. Oversubscription adds a separate constraint when traffic saturates shared uplinks. Topology-aware placement minimizes the communication cost of the job’s actual traffic pattern rather than applying a fixed penalty to every boundary.

Under balanced load saturating a 2:1 to 4:1 oversubscribed spine, the external per-endpoint share falls to approximately 12.5–25 GB/s. A non-blocking spine need not impose this reduction. The bar in each domain’s header draws its bandwidth on one shared linear scale.



For a 4-GPU collective group, the routing paths make that cost concrete (figure 8). In the illustrated contended fabric, scattering ranks across Rack A and Rack B forces a 3-hop leaf-spine-leaf path with about 12.5 GB/s of effective bandwidth per endpoint, a share of contended uplinks rather than a physical link rate. Consolidating all four ranks (G0–G3) under Rack A’s leaf switch avoids those shared uplinks and provides about 50 GB/s per GPU under the example’s load assumptions.

The illustrated 4× bandwidth difference between the 1-hop leaf path and the 3-hop spine route (figure 8) stretches the transfer component by the same factor when transfer time is bandwidth-dominated. Crossing a spine does not impose that ratio independently of load and topology. Whether communication exceeds computation also depends on the model and overlap schedule, and repeated exchanges can amplify the exposed cost. Topology-aware placement algorithms assign jobs to nodes that reduce this cost, turning resource packing into graph optimization over the physical topology. A simple locality cost, defined in equation 2, penalizes allocations spanning multiple topology domains:
\[ \text{Cost}_{\text{locality}} = \sum_{i < j} \LocalityPenaltyFunction(\GpuTopologicalDistance(\AssignedJobGpu_i, \AssignedJobGpu_j))  \tag{2}\]
where \(\AssignedJobGpu_i\) and \(\AssignedJobGpu_j\) are GPUs assigned to the job, \(\GpuTopologicalDistance(\AssignedJobGpu_i, \AssignedJobGpu_j)\) is their topological distance (0 for same node, 1 for same rack, 2 for different racks), and \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(\cdot)\) is a weighting function that increases with distance. The scheduler minimizes this score when selecting an allocation from the set of feasible placements. An illustrative heuristic assigns locality penalties of \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(0) = 0\) (same node, NVLink, no penalty), \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(1) = 1\) (same rack, one switch hop), and \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(2) = 10\) (different racks, multiple switch hops). These dimensionless weights are policy assumptions rather than measured latency or bandwidth ratios, so a deployment must calibrate them to its traffic and topology. An unweighted pairwise score still cannot distinguish heavily communicating rank pairs from pairs that rarely exchange data.
More sophisticated algorithms distinguish the communication requirements of different parallelism strategies. Frequent tensor-parallel activation exchanges favor a high-bandwidth, low-latency domain that meets the measured communication budget; that domain need not coincide with one server. Pipeline parallelism exchanges activations across stage boundaries rather than between every layer, but its tolerance for link delay depends on microbatch size and the pipeline schedule. Data-parallel gradient synchronization can overlap computation, making wider placement feasible when the exposed communication remains within budget. These patterns guide placement without establishing a universal ranking for every model or fabric.
Algorithm 1 combines the all-or-nothing gang constraint of section 8.4.3, the locality cost of equation 2, and an illustrative parallelism-to-topology mapping. Its enumeration expresses the decision conceptually: construct feasible rank mappings, score their allocations, and choose the lowest illustrative locality score, leaving the job queued when none fits. This surrogate does not guarantee minimum communication time or completion time. A fleet-scale implementation must restrict that search using heuristics rather than enumerate every allocation.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Topology-aware placement}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require job requesting $N$ accelerators with tensor-, pipeline-, and data-parallel groups; cluster topology with illustrative per-level locality weights $w(\cdot)$
\Ensure an all-or-nothing feasible placement with the lowest illustrative locality score, or the job stays queued
\State enumerate candidate slots: sets of $N$ free accelerators that satisfy every resource dimension \Comment{gang: all or nothing}
\State retain only slots that admit a rank mapping satisfying the job's tensor-, pipeline-, and data-parallel communication constraints
\If{no feasible slot exists}
    \State leave the job queued without holding any accelerators \Comment{prevents hold-and-wait deadlock}
    \State \Return no placement
\EndIf
\For{each feasible slot}
    \State use a feasible rank mapping: tensor-parallel ranks within an NVLink domain, pipeline stages within a rack, data-parallel replicas across racks where permitted
    \State score the slot by $\text{Cost}_{\text{locality}} = \sum_{i < j} w(d(g_i, g_j))$
\EndFor
\State \Return the feasible slot of least $\text{Cost}_{\text{locality}}$ \Comment{minimum score among enumerated feasible placements; atomic allocation}
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

Applied to a whole job, the same reasoning ranks placement strategies. The latencies in this comparison are illustrative, not derived. They are constructed to stay above the ring-AllReduce bandwidth bound for the payload, and they show the order in which placement removes delay rather than values a reader could recompute from topology names. For a 0.5 GB gradient synchronization on 64 GPUs, random placement spans multiple racks and spine switches and takes an assumed 120 ms. Each successive strategy removes a source of delay that the previous one leaves. Confining the group to a single rack removes spine hops and reduces latency to 85 ms. Rail-optimized alignment maps ranks so that every member of each collective group sits at the same local GPU index and therefore on the same network rail (developed in section 8.6.3). Traffic that previously hopped between rails through the spine now stays within one rail’s switches, which cuts latency to 40 ms. Topology-optimal placement additionally avoids leaf ports that other jobs are using and reaches 25 ms, a 4.8× reduction (figure 9, where each bar also carries its algorithm throughput). This ratio compares whole collectives under four assumed placements, so it need not match the link-bandwidth ratio of the two-rack paths above.

A hierarchical placement algorithm applies these constraints from the most restrictive communication domain outward, matching each 3D parallelism dimension to the interconnect tier its traffic can tolerate (figure 10). In the illustrated fleet, it places each tensor-parallel group within an NVLink-connected node, where the per-layer activation exchanges run at 450 GB/s. It places consecutive pipeline stages under the same leaf switch, where stage boundaries cross at 50 GB/s. It distributes data-parallel replicas across racks only when the once-per-step gradient synchronization fits the roughly 12.5–25 GB/s per endpoint that an oversubscribed spine leaves. This alignment reduces costly boundary crossings, but placement alone cannot reserve the fabric’s full bisection bandwidth against other jobs.






Figure 10: Hierarchical Placement for 3D Parallelism: This placement example maps distributed training dimensions to physical interconnect layers. Tensor parallelism (TP), which exchanges activations at every layer, stays inside a node on NVLink (450 GB/s); pipeline parallelism (PP) maps across adjacent nodes under one leaf switch (50 GB/s); and data parallelism (DP), which exchanges gradients only once per step, spans racks through the oversubscribed spine. Bandwidths are per direction, as in figure 7.



Evaluating all possible placements for a 256-GPU job across a 10,000-GPU cluster is combinatorially intractable, so production schedulers rely on heuristic approaches. Common choices include greedy algorithms that build placements bottom-up (first fill NVLink domains, then fill racks, then spread across racks), tree-search algorithms with pruning that explore the most promising placements first, and scoring-based approaches that evaluate a sample of feasible placements and select the best. Long jobs can amortize a more expensive search, but frequent submissions, short jobs, and recovery bursts also consume scheduler capacity, making end-to-end completion time, including placement delay, the useful comparison rather than execution throughput alone.

Good placement (topology-aware):

Tensor parallel groups: 32 groups of 8 GPUs, each confined to one 8-GPU node (NVLink: 450 GB/s per direction)

Math: The tensor parallel communication alone illustrates the impact. With NVLink delivering 450 GB/s per direction, a 1 GB activation transfer takes approximately 2.2 ms. Over InfiniBand at 50 GB/s, the same transfer takes approximately 20 ms, a 9× slowdown.
Systems insight: This calculation prices only the tensor-parallel component of the bad placement. Splitting a tensor-parallel group across nodes makes each activation exchange 9× slower, and the group performs such exchanges at every transformer layer of every step, so the penalty multiplies with model depth rather than appearing once. How much of it reaches step time depends on how much of the exchange was hidden behind computation, and it is why hierarchical placement gives tensor-parallel groups the fastest tier first. The scattered pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas add their own penalties on top, and the scheduler must profile the complete job before assigning a throughput benefit to the placement.





Even when two nodes sit in the same pod, placing corresponding data-parallel shards on mismatched local GPU indices forces their gradient collective to cross between network rails through the spine instead of staying on a single rail switch. In rail-optimized topologies, corresponding GPU positions across nodes connect through parallel network “rails” that a suitable rank mapping can use concurrently. Balanced bandwidth depends on distributing traffic across those paths rather than concentrating it on a subset. Keeping a collective group on one rail avoids cross-rail transfers for that group, while the placement of other groups determines how much rail capacity it must share.


↩︎ Rail-optimized fabric architectures and rail-to-rail traffic isolation are established in Rail-optimized topology.
Rail-aware scheduling assigns corresponding model shards across data-parallel replicas to GPUs attached to the same rail. When intra-node parallelism partitions a model replica across the eight GPUs of a node, each data-parallel gradient collective reduces only one shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) across replicas rather than combining all eight GPUs on the node. In the eight-GPU-per-node example, local GPU index \(\LocalRankIndex\) connects to rail \(\LocalRankIndex\). Placing every replica’s copy of shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) at that same local index on its selected node means the data-parallel replica rank varies across nodes rather than across local GPU indices, so the collective for shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) stays entirely within rail \(\LocalRankIndex\). This alignment removes cross-rail transfers for that group, though other groups or tenants can still contend for the same rail’s links, and full dedicated bandwidth requires an explicit capacity and sharing contract.
Rail alignment therefore acts at two levels, and they belong to different components. Within a node it is a rank-mapping decision. The launcher or framework must give every member of a data-parallel group the same local GPU index on its node, which is what removes the cross-rail hops in the placement comparison above. A mapping that puts shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) at index \(\LocalRankIndex\) on one node and at another index elsewhere sends that group’s traffic between rails. Across nodes it constrains the scheduler only when allocations are smaller than a node. When each replica’s pipeline stage occupies a complete node and every node wires local GPU \(\LocalRankIndex\) to rail \(\LocalRankIndex\), any free node already offers every rail, so rail alignment does not narrow which racks the scheduler can choose. With partial-node allocations, a job can receive different local indices on different nodes, and the scheduler must then choose GPU positions as well as nodes so that each group’s members share a rail. Those positions can conflict with the tensor-parallel budget and the paths between pipeline stages when only particular GPU positions remain free. The packing cost therefore follows the allocation granularity and the available topology rather than an inherent conflict among the three parallelism dimensions. Even a single-node allocation can have meaningful topology constraints when GPUs occupy different interconnect, PCIe, or non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domains, so packing efficiency should be optimized only among placements that satisfy the job’s local and external communication contract.



When a spine switch fails or an optical link degrades and begins retransmitting, a static configuration file such as Slurm’s topology.conf or Kubernetes node labels still reports the rack as healthy and full-bandwidth. The scheduler then places communication-heavy gangs onto a crippled path. Runtime topology discovery supplements static maps with information exposed by the operating system and device libraries. NCCL uses system topology information, including the PCIe hierarchy and network devices exposed through paths such as /sys/class/infiniband, to identify communication paths and network interface card (NIC) proximity. The discovered graph describes reported connectivity; health checks and traffic measurements must establish whether those paths deliver the expected performance.
Cluster topology is an operating state, not a fixed schematic. Hardware failures, maintenance windows, and thermal throttling change the paths and effective capacity available to the scheduler. A spine switch failure in a redundant Clos network can leave connectivity intact while removing capacity. The effect on our 175B parameter model’s data-parallel AllReduce depends on rerouting, concurrent traffic, and how much bandwidth the job was using. If the failure increases exposed communication time, the scheduler must compare continuing at reduced throughput with the cost of moving to a healthier allocation. A degraded link can also pass binary up/down probes while cutting delivered bandwidth, so the scheduler needs performance evidence such as retransmission counts and collective bandwidth, the link-level telemetry of Link-level telemetry, as well as reachability.
A checkpoint-and-restart migration spends time saving state, releasing the old allocation, obtaining a new one, and restoring execution. Its value depends on measured transition cost and remaining work. If migration takes 10 minutes and restores throughput after a sustained 20 percent penalty, it pays back in less than an hour of subsequent training. That comparison assumes a healthy destination is available and the gain persists. A practical policy also accounts for queue delay and requires evidence that placement causes the slowdown, such as rising collective time on the affected path, before it moves the job.

War Story 8.2: Performance-aware health checks (2021)Context: OpenAI’s account of scaling Kubernetes describes automated health checks that remove misbehaving nodes from the schedulable pool (Sigler 2021).
Mechanism: Passive checks monitor reachability, disks, and GPU errors, but error codes do not expose every hardware or driver problem. Active GPU tests exercise the device before admitting ordinary workloads and periodically during its lifetime.
Fix: Nodes enter with a preflight taint, a node marking that repels ordinary pods, which blocks normal scheduling until the tests pass. Failed passive checks cordon a node; more serious failures can trigger eviction requests.
Systems lesson: Reachability alone is not a sufficient admission test. A scheduler needs health evidence that reflects the resources its jobs depend on, together with a policy for removing suspect nodes from placement.

Rather than treating resource allocation as fixed for a job’s lifetime, elastic training allows logical jobs to grow, shrink, and recover. Whether worker processes restart depends on the framework; TorchElastic restarts its worker group when membership changes.


↩︎ Slow components that pass liveness checks while setting the pace of every synchronous step, and how to tell them from fail-stop failures, are established in Stragglers versus fail-stop failures.
