title: 8 Fleet Orchestration
text:
A scattered allocation can place frequent collective traffic on shared cross-rack paths, exposing latency or bandwidth limits that a more compact allocation avoids. The penalty is set by how much of the job’s traffic crosses those paths and how much capacity the fabric provisions there, not by the rack count itself. The earlier feasibility rules already required compatible topology; topology-aware scheduling makes that requirement explicit in the placement objective, accounting for communication paths as well as raw compute.


Splitting a tensor-parallel group across node boundaries moves its per-layer activation exchanges off intra-node NVLink onto the external network fabric, where an H100’s per-direction NVLink rate is 9× the rate of one NDR port (Bandwidth hierarchy). Each level of a cluster’s communication hierarchy comes from the hardware that builds it and sets a distinct bandwidth and latency budget. GPUs inside a node exchange data over NVLink, the tier fast enough for the per-layer exchanges of tensor parallelism. Nodes under one leaf switch communicate over an external fabric such as InfiniBand or RoCE. Racks joined through spine switches add switch hops whose delivered bandwidth depends on concurrent flows and oversubscription even in a fat-tree. Cross-rack communication also adds tail latency variability: while median latency may be only slightly higher, p99 latency can spike during congestion events, creating straggler effects in synchronous training where the slowest communicator determines the pace for all workers.


↩︎ Bisection bandwidth and fat-tree network topologies are established in Fat-tree (Clos) networks.
A 64-GPU job within one rack can avoid cross-rack paths that a spread allocation must use. It outperforms the spread allocation only when those paths add exposed latency or bandwidth contention; a non-blocking, uncongested spine need not reduce sustained throughput. The performance difference stems directly from the hierarchical communication analysis in Hierarchical AllReduce: a flat ring AllReduce runs at the speed of the slowest link in the ring, and cross-rack hops introduce both higher latency and increased contention risk. For synchronous training, every iteration waits for the slowest worker to complete its AllReduce, so even occasional cross-rack congestion inflates the Fleet Law’s communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) (equation 1.3) on every step it touches.
The scheduler must therefore model the cluster as a hierarchical graph with discrete bandwidth boundaries (figure 7). In the illustrated H100 fleet, per-direction bandwidth steps down from 450 GB/s across the NVSwitch inside a node to 50 GB/s per port under a leaf switch, and to roughly 12.5–25 GB/s per endpoint when balanced traffic saturates an oversubscribed spine. A node boundary can introduce a large bandwidth reduction, but a non-blocking rack or pod boundary need not reduce per-endpoint bandwidth. Oversubscription adds a separate constraint when traffic saturates shared uplinks. Topology-aware placement minimizes the communication cost of the job’s actual traffic pattern rather than applying a fixed penalty to every boundary.






Figure 7: Physical Topology Hierarchy and Bandwidth Cliffs: Hardware boundaries dictate communication performance across three distinct domains. The example compares a 450 GB/s per-direction NVLink endpoint budget with a 50 GB/s per-direction external port. Under balanced load saturating a 2:1 to 4:1 oversubscribed spine, the external per-endpoint share falls to approximately 12.5–25 GB/s. A non-blocking spine need not impose this reduction. The bar in each domain’s header draws its bandwidth on one shared linear scale.



For a 4-GPU collective group, the routing paths make that cost concrete (figure 8). In the illustrated contended fabric, scattering ranks across Rack A and Rack B forces a 3-hop leaf-spine-leaf path with about 12.5 GB/s of effective bandwidth per endpoint, a share of contended uplinks rather than a physical link rate. Consolidating all four ranks (G0–G3) under Rack A’s leaf switch avoids those shared uplinks and provides about 50 GB/s per GPU under the example’s load assumptions.






Figure 8: Topology-Unaware vs. Topology-Aware Placement: An illustrative 4-GPU job that permits inter-node placement and uses an oversubscribed cross-rack fabric, placed across two racks (left, topology-unaware) must traverse leaf-spine-leaf hops: 3 switch hops per AllReduce message at about 12.5 GB/s effective bandwidth. The same 4-GPU job packed within one rack (right, topology-aware) uses a single leaf switch: 1 hop at about 50 GB/s, roughly 4× faster. Blue squares are the job’s GPUs; gray squares are GPUs held by other jobs.






The illustrated 4× bandwidth difference between the 1-hop leaf path and the 3-hop spine route (figure 8) stretches the transfer component by the same factor when transfer time is bandwidth-dominated. Crossing a spine does not impose that ratio independently of load and topology. Whether communication exceeds computation also depends on the model and overlap schedule, and repeated exchanges can amplify the exposed cost. Topology-aware placement algorithms assign jobs to nodes that reduce this cost, turning resource packing into graph optimization over the physical topology. A simple locality cost, defined in equation 2, penalizes allocations spanning multiple topology domains:
\[ \text{Cost}_{\text{locality}} = \sum_{i < j} \LocalityPenaltyFunction(\GpuTopologicalDistance(\AssignedJobGpu_i, \AssignedJobGpu_j))  \tag{2}\]
where \(\AssignedJobGpu_i\) and \(\AssignedJobGpu_j\) are GPUs assigned to the job, \(\GpuTopologicalDistance(\AssignedJobGpu_i, \AssignedJobGpu_j)\) is their topological distance (0 for same node, 1 for same rack, 2 for different racks), and \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(\cdot)\) is a weighting function that increases with distance. The scheduler minimizes this score when selecting an allocation from the set of feasible placements. An illustrative heuristic assigns locality penalties of \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(0) = 0\) (same node, NVLink, no penalty), \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(1) = 1\) (same rack, one switch hop), and \(\LocalityPenaltyFunction(2) = 10\) (different racks, multiple switch hops). These dimensionless weights are policy assumptions rather than measured latency or bandwidth ratios, so a deployment must calibrate them to its traffic and topology. An unweighted pairwise score still cannot distinguish heavily communicating rank pairs from pairs that rarely exchange data.
More sophisticated algorithms distinguish the communication requirements of different parallelism strategies. Frequent tensor-parallel activation exchanges favor a high-bandwidth, low-latency domain that meets the measured communication budget; that domain need not coincide with one server. Pipeline parallelism exchanges activations across stage boundaries rather than between every layer, but its tolerance for link delay depends on microbatch size and the pipeline schedule. Data-parallel gradient synchronization can overlap computation, making wider placement feasible when the exposed communication remains within budget. These patterns guide placement without establishing a universal ranking for every model or fabric.
Algorithm 1 combines the all-or-nothing gang constraint of section 8.4.3, the locality cost of equation 2, and an illustrative parallelism-to-topology mapping. Its enumeration expresses the decision conceptually: construct feasible rank mappings, score their allocations, and choose the lowest illustrative locality score, leaving the job queued when none fits. This surrogate does not guarantee minimum communication time or completion time. A fleet-scale implementation must restrict that search using heuristics rather than enumerate every allocation.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Topology-aware placement}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require job requesting $N$ accelerators with tensor-, pipeline-, and data-parallel groups; cluster topology with illustrative per-level locality weights $w(\cdot)$
\Ensure an all-or-nothing feasible placement with the lowest illustrative locality score, or the job stays queued
\State enumerate candidate slots: sets of $N$ free accelerators that satisfy every resource dimension \Comment{gang: all or nothing}
\State retain only slots that admit a rank mapping satisfying the job's tensor-, pipeline-, and data-parallel communication constraints
\If{no feasible slot exists}
    \State leave the job queued without holding any accelerators \Comment{prevents hold-and-wait deadlock}
    \State \Return no placement
\EndIf
\For{each feasible slot}
    \State use a feasible rank mapping: tensor-parallel ranks within an NVLink domain, pipeline stages within a rack, data-parallel replicas across racks where permitted
    \State score the slot by $\text{Cost}_{\text{locality}} = \sum_{i < j} w(d(g_i, g_j))$
\EndFor
\State \Return the feasible slot of least $\text{Cost}_{\text{locality}}$ \Comment{minimum score among enumerated feasible placements; atomic allocation}
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(N\)

Applied to a whole job, the same reasoning ranks placement strategies. The latencies in this comparison are illustrative, not derived. They are constructed to stay above the ring-AllReduce bandwidth bound for the payload, and they show the order in which placement removes delay rather than values a reader could recompute from topology names. For a 0.5 GB gradient synchronization on 64 GPUs, random placement spans multiple racks and spine switches and takes an assumed 120 ms. Each successive strategy removes a source of delay that the previous one leaves. Confining the group to a single rack removes spine hops and reduces latency to 85 ms. Rail-optimized alignment maps ranks so that every member of each collective group sits at the same local GPU index and therefore on the same network rail (developed in section 8.6.3). Traffic that previously hopped between rails through the spine now stays within one rail’s switches, which cuts latency to 40 ms. Topology-optimal placement additionally avoids leaf ports that other jobs are using and reaches 25 ms, a 4.8× reduction (figure 9, where each bar also carries its algorithm throughput). This ratio compares whole collectives under four assumed placements, so it need not match the link-bandwidth ratio of the two-rack paths above.














Figure 9: Topology Placement Impact: Assumed AllReduce latency across four placement strategies (Random, Rack-Aware, Rail-Optimized, and Topology-Optimal) for a 0.5 GB gradient sync on 64 GPUs. The assumed latency falls from 120 ms to 25 ms, a 4.8\(\times\) ratio. Labels report payload divided by completion time (algorithm throughput), not physical link bandwidth. The dashed ghost above each bar names the source of delay that strategy removes.



A hierarchical placement algorithm applies these constraints from the most restrictive communication domain outward, matching each 3D parallelism dimension to the interconnect tier its traffic can tolerate (figure 10). In the illustrated fleet, it places each tensor-parallel group within an NVLink-connected node, where the per-layer activation exchanges run at 450 GB/s. It places consecutive pipeline stages under the same leaf switch, where stage boundaries cross at 50 GB/s. It distributes data-parallel replicas across racks only when the once-per-step gradient synchronization fits the roughly 12.5–25 GB/s per endpoint that an oversubscribed spine leaves. This alignment reduces costly boundary crossings, but placement alone cannot reserve the fabric’s full bisection bandwidth against other jobs.






Figure 10: Hierarchical Placement for 3D Parallelism: This placement example maps distributed training dimensions to physical interconnect layers. Tensor parallelism (TP), which exchanges activations at every layer, stays inside a node on NVLink (450 GB/s); pipeline parallelism (PP) maps across adjacent nodes under one leaf switch (50 GB/s); and data parallelism (DP), which exchanges gradients only once per step, spans racks through the oversubscribed spine. Bandwidths are per direction, as in figure 7.



Evaluating all possible placements for a 256-GPU job across a 10,000-GPU cluster is combinatorially intractable, so production schedulers rely on heuristic approaches. Common choices include greedy algorithms that build placements bottom-up (first fill NVLink domains, then fill racks, then spread across racks), tree-search algorithms with pruning that explore the most promising placements first, and scoring-based approaches that evaluate a sample of feasible placements and select the best. Long jobs can amortize a more expensive search, but frequent submissions, short jobs, and recovery bursts also consume scheduler capacity, making end-to-end completion time, including placement delay, the useful comparison rather than execution throughput alone.

Napkin Math 8.2: Placement impact on 3D-parallel trainingScenario: Consider a 256-GPU training job using 3D parallelism: 8-way tensor parallel, 4-way pipeline parallel, 8-way data parallel.
Good placement (topology-aware):

Tensor parallel groups: 32 groups of 8 GPUs, each confined to one 8-GPU node (NVLink: 450 GB/s per direction)
Pipeline stages: 4 consecutive nodes within the same rack (1 switch hop, InfiniBand: 50 GB/s per direction)
Data parallel replicas: 8 racks (3 switch hops through leaf-spine-leaf paths)

Bad placement (topology-unaware):

Tensor parallel groups split across 2 nodes (InfiniBand instead of NVLink)
Pipeline stages scattered across racks (3 switch hops instead of 1)
Data parallel replicas randomly distributed

Math: The tensor parallel communication alone illustrates the impact. With NVLink delivering 450 GB/s per direction, a 1 GB activation transfer takes approximately 2.2 ms. Over InfiniBand at 50 GB/s, the same transfer takes approximately 20 ms, a 9× slowdown.
Systems insight: This calculation prices only the tensor-parallel component of the bad placement. Splitting a tensor-parallel group across nodes makes each activation exchange 9× slower, and the group performs such exchanges at every transformer layer of every step, so the penalty multiplies with model depth rather than appearing once. How much of it reaches step time depends on how much of the exchange was hidden behind computation, and it is why hierarchical placement gives tensor-parallel groups the fastest tier first. The scattered pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas add their own penalties on top, and the scheduler must profile the complete job before assigning a throughput benefit to the placement.





Even when two nodes sit in the same pod, placing corresponding data-parallel shards on mismatched local GPU indices forces their gradient collective to cross between network rails through the spine instead of staying on a single rail switch. In rail-optimized topologies, corresponding GPU positions across nodes connect through parallel network “rails” that a suitable rank mapping can use concurrently. Balanced bandwidth depends on distributing traffic across those paths rather than concentrating it on a subset. Keeping a collective group on one rail avoids cross-rail transfers for that group, while the placement of other groups determines how much rail capacity it must share.


↩︎ Rail-optimized fabric architectures and rail-to-rail traffic isolation are established in Rail-optimized topology.
Rail-aware scheduling assigns corresponding model shards across data-parallel replicas to GPUs attached to the same rail. When intra-node parallelism partitions a model replica across the eight GPUs of a node, each data-parallel gradient collective reduces only one shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) across replicas rather than combining all eight GPUs on the node. In the eight-GPU-per-node example, local GPU index \(\LocalRankIndex\) connects to rail \(\LocalRankIndex\). Placing every replica’s copy of shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) at that same local index on its selected node means the data-parallel replica rank varies across nodes rather than across local GPU indices, so the collective for shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) stays entirely within rail \(\LocalRankIndex\). This alignment removes cross-rail transfers for that group, though other groups or tenants can still contend for the same rail’s links, and full dedicated bandwidth requires an explicit capacity and sharing contract.
Rail alignment therefore acts at two levels, and they belong to different components. Within a node it is a rank-mapping decision. The launcher or framework must give every member of a data-parallel group the same local GPU index on its node, which is what removes the cross-rail hops in the placement comparison above. A mapping that puts shard \(\LocalRankIndex\) at index \(\LocalRankIndex\) on one node and at another index elsewhere sends that group’s traffic between rails. Across nodes it constrains the scheduler only when allocations are smaller than a node. When each replica’s pipeline stage occupies a complete node and every node wires local GPU \(\LocalRankIndex\) to rail \(\LocalRankIndex\), any free node already offers every rail, so rail alignment does not narrow which racks the scheduler can choose. With partial-node allocations, a job can receive different local indices on different nodes, and the scheduler must then choose GPU positions as well as nodes so that each group’s members share a rail. Those positions can conflict with the tensor-parallel budget and the paths between pipeline stages when only particular GPU positions remain free. The packing cost therefore follows the allocation granularity and the available topology rather than an inherent conflict among the three parallelism dimensions. Even a single-node allocation can have meaningful topology constraints when GPUs occupy different interconnect, PCIe, or non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domains, so packing efficiency should be optimized only among placements that satisfy the job’s local and external communication contract.



When a spine switch fails or an optical link degrades and begins retransmitting, a static configuration file such as Slurm’s topology.conf or Kubernetes node labels still reports the rack as healthy and full-bandwidth. The scheduler then places communication-heavy gangs onto a crippled path. Runtime topology discovery supplements static maps with information exposed by the operating system and device libraries. NCCL uses system topology information, including the PCIe hierarchy and network devices exposed through paths such as /sys/class/infiniband, to identify communication paths and network interface card (NIC) proximity. The discovered graph describes reported connectivity; health checks and traffic measurements must establish whether those paths deliver the expected performance.
Cluster topology is an operating state, not a fixed schematic. Hardware failures, maintenance windows, and thermal throttling change the paths and effective capacity available to the scheduler. A spine switch failure in a redundant Clos network can leave connectivity intact while removing capacity. The effect on our 175B parameter model’s data-parallel AllReduce depends on rerouting, concurrent traffic, and how much bandwidth the job was using. If the failure increases exposed communication time, the scheduler must compare continuing at reduced throughput with the cost of moving to a healthier allocation. A degraded link can also pass binary up/down probes while cutting delivered bandwidth, so the scheduler needs performance evidence such as retransmission counts and collective bandwidth, the link-level telemetry of Link-level telemetry, as well as reachability.
A checkpoint-and-restart migration spends time saving state, releasing the old allocation, obtaining a new one, and restoring execution. Its value depends on measured transition cost and remaining work. If migration takes 10 minutes and restores throughput after a sustained 20 percent penalty, it pays back in less than an hour of subsequent training. That comparison assumes a healthy destination is available and the gain persists. A practical policy also accounts for queue delay and requires evidence that placement causes the slowdown, such as rising collective time on the affected path, before it moves the job.

War Story 8.2: Performance-aware health checks (2021)Context: OpenAI’s account of scaling Kubernetes describes automated health checks that remove misbehaving nodes from the schedulable pool (Sigler 2021).
Mechanism: Passive checks monitor reachability, disks, and GPU errors, but error codes do not expose every hardware or driver problem. Active GPU tests exercise the device before admitting ordinary workloads and periodically during its lifetime.
Fix: Nodes enter with a preflight taint, a node marking that repels ordinary pods, which blocks normal scheduling until the tests pass. Failed passive checks cordon a node; more serious failures can trigger eviction requests.
Systems lesson: Reachability alone is not a sufficient admission test. A scheduler needs health evidence that reflects the resources its jobs depend on, together with a policy for removing suspect nodes from placement.



Sigler, Eric. 2021. Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 Nodes. OpenAI Blog.
9 Taints and tolerations: Node taints can block scheduling of pods without matching tolerations. A toleration permits consideration of a node but neither requires placement there nor reserves it exclusively for training. Dedicated GPU pools also need controlled toleration assignment and placement constraints; removing existing workloads requires an eviction or drain policy appropriate to the taint’s effect.The general scheduling idea is quarantine: when runtime evidence says a node, rack, or link is degraded, the scheduler should stop placing sensitive work there even if the nominal resource count still looks available. Kubernetes implements this pattern through taints and tolerations,9 while Slurm clusters commonly use drain states, node features, or partition rules. The complementary problem is how jobs adapt when available resources change dynamically. Rather than treating resource allocation as fixed for a job’s lifetime, elastic training allows logical jobs to grow, shrink, and recover. Whether worker processes restart depends on the framework; TorchElastic restarts its worker group when membership changes.


↩︎ Slow components that pass liveness checks while setting the pace of every synchronous step, and how to tell them from fail-stop failures, are established in Stragglers versus fail-stop failures.

Self-Check: Question

When scheduling a 3D-parallel large language model across a multi-rack GPU cluster, how should Tensor Parallelism (TP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), and Data Parallelism (DP) be mapped across the topology hierarchy to maximize throughput?

Map DP strictly within intra-node NVLink domains, TP across inter-rack spine switches, and PP across rail-aligned network switches.
Map PP strictly within intra-node NVLink domains, DP across Top-of-Rack switches, and TP across multi-hop spine switches.
Map TP to the highest-bandwidth domain, place PP stages along suitable low-contention paths, and align corresponding DP shards with network rails while checking available capacity.
Map TP, PP, and DP uniformly at random across all available nodes to balance switch thermal loads across the datacenter fabric.

A persistent degraded switch path lowers measured end-to-end training throughput by 30 percent. A checkpoint-and-migration pause would take 10 minutes, healthy replacement capacity is available, and days of training remain. What is the appropriate orchestration response?

Continue running the job indefinitely because a 10-minute checkpoint-and-reschedule migration would cost more compute than a 30% slowdown over a multi-week run.
Rely on the GPU driver to disable NVLink and route all tensor-parallel traffic through host memory over PCIe.
Trigger a performance-aware topology quarantine via taints or drain states, checkpoint the running job, and migrate it to healthy nodes where the break-even time is under an hour.
Terminate the job and permanently de-allocate all 10,000 GPUs in the datacenter until all network transceivers are manually replaced.

In an 8-GPU-per-node cluster with eight network rails, how should rail-aware placement map corresponding model shards across replicas, and what contention limits remain?
Why are static topology configuration files (such as Slurm’s topology.conf or static Kubernetes node labels) insufficient on their own for optimal collective placement in large-scale ML clusters?
For the illustrated eight-GPU-per-node fleet, explain how a scheduler combines tensor-parallel locality, pipeline paths, and data-parallel rail alignment when selecting a placement. Why does minimizing the chapter’s illustrative locality score not establish minimum communication time?
In cloud orchestration environments such as AWS and GCP, a user specifies a ____ to request close placement of virtual machine instances for high-bandwidth, low-latency communication.

See Answers →

title: 8 Fleet Orchestration
text:
When cluster demand fluctuates, rigid allocation creates two categories of waste. During off-peak hours, a job running on 256 GPUs cannot absorb idle resources to speed up training. During peak demand, the same job cannot release excess resources to accommodate higher-priority work without being fully preempted. The scheduler’s only options are “let it keep all its resources” or “kill it entirely,” with nothing in between.
Elastic scheduling expands this binary choice. The recovery mechanics of elastic training show how a distributed job can adjust its worker count, adapt its batch policy, and reconstruct its communication group after a failure. From the scheduler’s perspective, the same capability solves a resource-allocation problem under fluctuating demand. A training job might start with 128 GPUs, scale up to 256 when resources become available, and scale back to 192 when higher-priority work arrives, provided each allocation supports a viable worker group. Resizing may pause training and restart workers from saved state. The scheduler therefore chooses among supported allocation sizes, each with a transition cost, rather than assuming uninterrupted progress at any resource level.


↩︎ Batch-size and learning-rate adjustment and communication-group contraction during elastic recovery are established in Recovery adaptation mechanisms.


If a scheduler reclaims four nodes from a running job by abruptly killing their containers, or adds four idle nodes without triggering a new rendezvous, the surviving ranks treat the change as a fatal collective timeout rather than an elastic resize. Resizing a live job without crashing it requires an explicit contract between the scheduler and the training framework. For planned resizing, the scheduler and framework coordinate resource release through defined signals and an agreed adaptation window. Unexpected failures can bypass that window, so the framework must also recover from valid saved state. Its recovery path reconstructs communication groups and either preserves the global batch or applies a validated batch-size and learning-rate policy. The worker-membership lifecycle therefore behaves as a state machine centered on active training (figure 11). Idle GPUs trigger scale-up, preemptions trigger scale-down, and host timeouts or ECC errors divert ranks to worker replacement; each path returns to active training once the communication group is rebuilt or a spare node joins.






Figure 11: Elastic Training Worker Lifecycle and State Machine: The state machine governing dynamic worker membership. Active training loops on step completion and leaves that state along three paths: idle GPUs trigger scale up, a preemption for higher-priority work triggers scale down, and a host timeout or ECC error triggers worker replacement. Each path rebuilds the communication group and returns to active training (dashed arrows), and a spot reclamation deadline can force a shrinking job straight into replacement. Worker processes may restart during resizing, so recovery requires the application to restore valid training state.



From the scheduler’s perspective, this contract is defined by three governing parameters: the elastic range, the transition cost, and the scaling efficiency curve. The elastic range, \([\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount, \ElasticMaximumWorkerCount]\), specifies lower and upper worker bounds; the job’s parallelism layout determines the valid allocation increments within them. The transition cost includes any checkpoint, restart, state redistribution, and rendezvous required by the runtime. Measuring the full interruption determines how frequently the scheduler can trigger reallocations before transition overhead wipes out any throughput advantage. Finally, the scaling efficiency curve quantifies the marginal throughput gained from each added worker, indicating whether assigning idle GPUs to this job yields more aggregate progress than holding them for an assembling gang-scheduled workload. Together, these parameters provide the scheduler with the quantitative bounds needed to resize jobs dynamically without treating elasticity as free capacity.
The scheduler must also account for the effect of worker count on global batch size (\(\GlobalBatchSize = \PerWorkerBatchSize\times \DeviceCount\)), where the per-worker batch counts examples contributing to one optimizer update, including gradient accumulation. Holding the global batch constant requires each remaining worker to process more examples after a shrink. Larger microbatches consume more memory; additional accumulation steps extend the update time. Preserving the batch removes one source of optimization change but does not guarantee identical convergence. Allowing the global batch to change instead requires validating the learning-rate policy and resulting model quality, so throughput alone cannot determine the best allocation.



Listing 2: TorchElastic Launch Configuration: The --nnodes=4:16 range configures the elastic worker group to admit 4 to 16 nodes, or 32 to 128 workers. A separate cluster scheduler or operator must acquire, launch, and release nodes within that range.


# Launch elastic training with min 32 to max 128 workers
torchrun \
  --nnodes=4:16 \
  --nproc_per_node=8 \
  --rdzv_backend=c10d \
  --rdzv_endpoint=head-node:29500 \
  --max_restarts=3 \
  train.py



TorchElastic sets the elastic range in its launch configuration as a minimum and maximum node count (listing 2). There, the --nnodes=4:16 specification configures TorchElastic’s rendezvous and worker-membership range as 4 to 16 nodes (32 to 128 workers with 8 processes per node). It does not acquire or resize cluster resources; a separate cluster scheduler or operator must place the nodes and start or stop elastic agents as capacity changes.

Systems Perspective 8.2: Elastic vs. rigid schedulingConsider a congested cluster where a 128-GPU job waits 8 hours for a full gang allocation. This first comparison assumes throughput scales linearly with worker count, equivalent learning progress per processed example, and negligible resize overhead; the later scaling decision relaxes the throughput and transition assumptions.
Rigid scheduling: Wait 8 hours, then train for 24 hours at full throughput. Total wall-clock: 32 hours.
Elastic scheduling (min 32, max 128):

Start immediately with 32 GPUs (throughput = 25 percent of full)
At hour 2, when 64 GPUs free, scale to 64 (throughput = 50 percent)
At hour 8, when the full gang frees and the rigid job would also start, scale to 128 (throughput = 100 percent)

Work completed during the 8-hour queue wait, in hours of full-scale training:

Hours 0 to 2: 25 percent throughput \(\times\) 2 hours = 0.5
Hours 2 to 8: 50 percent throughput \(\times\) 6 hours = 3
Total: 3.5 hours of equivalent full-scale work

The elastic job completes in approximately 28.5 hours (8 hours of partial-scale training plus 20.5 hours at full scale), saving 3.5 hours compared to rigid scheduling. This improvement of about 11 percent comes entirely from using resources productively during what would otherwise be idle queue time.


The scheduler cannot treat every worker count as a valid elastic configuration. Model parallelism constrains the allocation increment when the resize policy keeps tensor and pipeline layouts fixed and adds or removes whole data-parallel replicas. For a 175B-parameter job that relies on 8-way tensor parallelism within each node and 8 pipeline stages across nodes, this policy operates at the granularity of a whole model replica of 64 GPUs. The pipeline depth of 8 is the smallest power of two at which each GPU’s share of the mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) training state fits in its HBM when that state is not sharded across replicas. The feasible layout of Distributed Training instead uses a shallower pipeline and shards optimizer state across the data-parallel group with ZeRO (Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP). Keeping each replica’s state self-contained costs memory, but it lets the scheduler add or remove a replica without redistributing every other replica’s optimizer shards. The job can scale between 128 nodes (1,024 GPUs) and 32 nodes (256 GPUs) one replica at a time, changing the data-parallel degree. Removing a single GPU from a tensor-parallel group would instead require a new sharding layout and redistribution of training state. Changing the pipeline degree would also require repartitioning stages and rebuilding the pipeline schedule. A runtime that supports these transitions can expose them to the scheduler, but their feasibility and measured costs belong in the resize contract rather than following automatically from data-parallel elasticity.
The transition cost also constrains the scheduler’s resize frequency. Each scaling event can interrupt useful work while the framework reconstructs its communication group and restores or redistributes state. The duration must be measured for the chosen runtime and checkpoint path. The scheduler must amortize this cost over the subsequent run duration, so small resize increments are only worthwhile if the job will run at the new scale for significantly longer than the transition window. Section 8.7.3 shows the thrashing that results when a policy ignores this amortization.



Without scheduler integration, a job that declares an elastic range \([\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount, \ElasticMaximumWorkerCount]\) in its launch script still waits in the queue for its full node count and still gets killed outright when a higher-priority job arrives. Integrating the \([\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount, \ElasticMaximumWorkerCount]\) bounds into the scheduler lets it start a job early at the minimum, expand the job into newly idle capacity, or shrink it to release borrowed capacity without terminating the logical job. Which action wins depends on the job’s scaling curve and transition cost, and the policies below compare the choices by the work completed over the same time window.
Each action must respect the framework contract. The most consequential of the three is graceful preemption: when higher-priority work arrives, the scheduler first shrinks an elastic job toward \(\ElasticMinimumWorkerCount\), reclaiming whole replicas at the next resize boundary, and resorts to checkpoint-and-preempt only when the final viable group itself must yield. Quota borrowing across teams, developed in section 8.11, depends on this primitive whenever an owner reclaims capacity it lent. Scaling curves and transition costs determine whether the extra progress repays the disruption. Because batch changes can affect convergence, the test of a resize is time to target model quality, not throughput.



Adding resources to a running job does not always accelerate time-to-convergence. Communication and synchronization overhead limit throughput gains, requiring the scheduler to enforce elastic scaling policies based on empirical efficiency curves rather than resource availability alone. With fixed global work per step, a job’s scaling efficiency \(\ScalingEfficiency(\ScalingCurveWorkerCount)\) at \(\ScalingCurveWorkerCount\) workers (definition \(\ref{dfn-distributed-training-scaling-efficiency}\)) typically passes through three regimes. In the near-linear regime, per-worker computation dwarfs every fixed per-step cost. In the sublinear regime, pipeline fill and drain and the unhidden part of gradient synchronization become a visible share of each step. In the saturation regime, those fixed costs rival the shrinking computation itself. Assigning available GPUs to a saturated job can yield less useful progress than serving queued work. The lower allocation bound answers a different question. Below its minimum viable scale, a job may lack the memory or complete parallel groups needed to execute at all. A policy can impose a higher minimum to meet a deadline, even when a smaller allocation remains computationally efficient.



Throughput falls away from ideal linear scaling and saturates.
The 175B reference job shows these regimes with the chapter’s own numbers. Modeled at a fixed global batch with the step-time decomposition of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3), its scaling efficiency falls from 87 percent at 256 GPUs to 83 percent at 1,024 GPUs and 69 percent at 4,096 GPUs (figure 12, panel a). Efficiency falls, yet quadrupling from 1,024 to 4,096 GPUs still raises throughput 3.3×, so a lower efficiency is a declining marginal return rather than a slowdown. Panel (b) locates the loss. Tensor-parallel communication shrinks along with each worker’s computation, so its share of the step never rises above 11 percent. The decline comes instead from pipeline fill and drain and unhidden gradient synchronization, which take roughly fixed time per step while each worker’s share of the batch shrinks. The pipeline bubble grows fastest of the three, for a reason the bubble fraction \((\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\MicrobatchCount+\PipelineParallelDegree-1)\) of Pipeline parallelism makes explicit. With the global batch fixed, each added replica takes a share of the sequences, so the microbatch count \(\MicrobatchCount\) per replica falls while the stage count stays at 8, and the idle fraction rises. The shaded window from 256 to 1,024 GPUs is therefore a policy choice, not an interval derived from these efficiencies alone. A minimum allocation could follow from a completion deadline or the job’s declared resource contract. It does not follow from insufficient per-worker computation at smaller scale, since with fixed global work fewer workers generally perform more work each. The upper limit likewise requires comparing additional useful progress with resize cost and the value of serving queued jobs. A real scheduler must obtain those inputs from profiling and the workload’s quality target.














Figure 12: Modeled Scaling Efficiency and Elastic Operating Range: (a) Scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)) of the 175B reference job from 64 to 4,096 GPUs, computed with 8-way tensor parallelism within each DGX H100 node, 8 pipeline stages, HDR InfiniBand, and a fixed global batch of 1,536 sequences. The shaded window is an assumed admission policy; efficiency alone establishes neither its minimum nor its maximum. (b) Share of each step lost to tensor-parallel communication, pipeline bubble, and exposed gradient synchronization. Lower efficiency does not imply that adding workers reduces throughput.



This logic extends to the temporal dimension, where the scheduler must weigh the immediate progress of a smaller allocation against waiting for a larger one. If a 512-GPU job can start immediately with 128 GPUs or wait for the full request, the better choice depends on the integration of throughput over time. The resize overhead (the cost of stopping, checkpointing, and restarting when the runtime requires them) must be amortized over the subsequent run duration. A policy of “opportunistic scaling” that resizes a job every time a single node becomes free can lose its throughput advantage to repeated interruptions, completing less useful work than a stable allocation.

Napkin Math 8.3: The elastic scaling decisionThe comparison of elastic and rigid scheduling above assumed linear scaling and free resizing; this decision drops both assumptions. Consider a training job with a target batch size that requires 512 GPUs for the highest throughput among the configurations considered. Three scheduling strategies are evaluated over a window of 24 hours.
Given: Throughput at 128 GPUs is 1 epoch/hour (baseline). Throughput at 256 GPUs is 1.8 epochs/hour (90 percent scaling efficiency relative to that baseline). Throughput at 512 GPUs is 3.2 epochs/hour (80 percent scaling efficiency). Re-scaling cost is 10 minutes (0.17 hours) to checkpoint, re-shard, and restart.
Strategy 1 (immediate start, no scaling): The job starts immediately with 128 GPUs and runs for the full 24 hours. Total work: \(24 \times 1.0 = 24\) epochs.
Strategy 2 (wait for the full allocation): The job waits in the queue for 4 hours until 512 GPUs become available, then runs for 20 hours. Total work: \(20 \times 3.2 = 64\) epochs.
Strategy 3 (elastic step-up): The job starts immediately with 128 GPUs. After 4 hours, the capacity that lets Strategy 2 start frees up, but the elastic policy caps growth at 256 GPUs so that the remaining GPUs stay available to queued jobs. The job pauses, scales up, and resumes. Phase 1: \(4 \times 1.0 = 4\) epochs. Phase 2: \((24 - 4 - 0.17) \times 1.8 \approx 35.7\) epochs. Total work: 4 + 35.7 = 39.7 epochs.
The elastic strategy completes nearly 1.7× the epoch-equivalent work of the immediate small-scale run, but still trails the full allocation by about 38 percent. That comparison counts this job’s epochs, not the GPU-hours spent on them. Strategy 2 holds twice as many GPUs as Strategy 3 for most of the window and runs them at 80 percent scaling efficiency against Strategy 3’s 90 percent. The elastic job therefore does more work per GPU-hour, and the GPUs it leaves free serve queued jobs. Which strategy wins therefore depends on whether the fleet values this job’s completion time or the total work completed across all jobs. That gap shrinks when queue waits grow or peak capacity stays scarce. Re-scaling overhead is only 10 minutes, so the step-up strategy keeps its lead over the immediate small-scale run unless slow checkpoint transfer or compilation stretches that overhead beyond about 9 hours.


Placement and elasticity determine which allocations are feasible and how much useful progress they produce across competing jobs. Fleet economics adds the price of those choices. Every placement, preemption, and reservation consumes capacity that could serve another workload, so the scheduler must compare both useful progress and opportunity cost.

Self-Check: Question

When an elastic scheduler resizes a distributed training job from 64 GPUs to 128 GPUs, what trade-off exists between maintaining a constant global batch size versus scaling batch size proportionally with worker count?

Constant global batch size halves the effective examples per worker per optimizer update, removing one source of optimization change without guaranteeing identical convergence; proportional batch scaling preserves that per-worker count but changes optimization and requires a validated learning-rate policy.
Constant global batch size requires restarting the model weights from epoch zero, whereas proportional batch size allows continuous gradient descent without learning rate adjustment.
Constant global batch size disables NVLink communication across workers, whereas proportional batch size enables ring AllReduce.
Constant global batch size doubles the learning rate automatically via PyTorch hooks, whereas proportional batch size keeps the learning rate fixed to prevent divergence.

An elastic job running on 64 GPUs at 100 steps/minute can scale to 128 GPUs, reaching 180 steps/minute. If resizing triggers a dynamic rendezvous and checkpoint-sync transition pause of 60 seconds (0 steps during pause), what is the break-even duration the job must run after the pause at 128 GPUs to recover the lost progress in total steps completed?

At least 15 seconds.
At least 30 seconds.
At least 45 seconds.
At least 75 seconds.

What three parameters define the operational contract between an elastic scheduler and an elastic training framework (such as TorchElastic), and why is each necessary?
True or False: Under a supported resize and checkpoint contract, an elastic scheduler can reclaim capacity by shrinking a training job to a smaller viable configuration without terminating the logical job, although worker processes may restart.
A worker encounters an unhandled CUDA fault during a TorchElastic training run. Explain the dependencies that must hold before useful training resumes, and why recovery cannot require every surviving worker to finish a clean step boundary.

title: 8 Fleet Orchestration
text:
An idle accelerator in an enterprise fleet incurs operational costs every hour whether computing or blocked in a queue, turning placement and preemption decisions into direct financial trade-offs. The orchestrator translates this utilization-to-dollars relationship from section 8.1 into an online scheduling signal, balancing resource prices, reservation commitments, interruption risk, checkpoint cost, and job deadlines to decide whether to admit, delay, preempt, or resize work. Capital planning, portfolio return, cost attribution, and lifecycle total cost of ownership are larger, slower decisions developed in Fleet Economics and Utilization; the scheduler consumes their outcomes as prices and constraints.
At a fixed utilization, idle capacity grows linearly with fleet size, so the dollar cost of a scheduling inefficiency grows with every procurement (figure 13). At 10,000 GPUs operating at 50 percent utilization, annual waste reaches $87.6M under the chapter’s $2/GPU-hour accounting scenario. Published measurements show that such underutilization occurs in production. Microsoft’s Philly cluster study (Jeon et al. 2019) measured mean GPU utilization of approximately 52 percent. The 30 to 70 percent shaded band in the figure is an illustrative operating range for the cost model, not a universal empirical claim about all production clusters. Moving from 50 percent to 80 percent utilization, the improvement priced in the chapter opening, recovers over $52M annually in equivalent capacity value. That is the same 3,000 GPU-equivalents the opening counted as waste at 30 percent idle, and it becomes cash savings only when it avoids billed usage or a planned purchase.














Figure 13: The Cost of Idle GPUs: Annual wasted cost as a function of cluster size for different GPU utilization levels, assuming $2/GPU-hour (cloud equivalent). The shaded region between 30 percent and 70 percent is an illustrative operating range for the scenario analysis. At 10,000 GPUs with 50 percent utilization, the model yields $87.6M in annual wasted capacity. The thin violet line traces the published Microsoft Philly mean GPU utilization of 52 percent across all cluster sizes; it is a utilization reference, not a measured cluster size or cost. Data source: Jeon et al. (2019).


Jeon, Myeongjae, Shivaram Venkataraman, Amar Phanishayee, Junjie Qian, Wencong Xiao, and Fan Yang. 2019. “Analysis of Large-Scale Multi-Tenant GPU Clusters for DNN Training Workloads.” 2019 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC 19), 947–60.


Recovering that idle capacity requires pricing each scheduling lever against the disruption it causes. Because reclaiming GPUs from running jobs is the most direct way to admit higher-value work, the cost of a single preemption and the cascades it can trigger come first. Discounted spot capacity then lowers the hourly price of restart-tolerant training, diversification and checkpoint policies keep correlated reclamations from erasing that discount, and capacity-reservation tiers combine with workload cost policies to route jobs across reserved, on-demand, and interruptible pools.





Each eviction can evict again, so one admission reaches \(\PreemptionFanoutCount + \PreemptionFanoutCount^2\) jobs.
When a high-priority job enters a saturated cluster, the scheduler must decide which running workloads to terminate to free up resources. This decision is rarely isolated. In tightly packed clusters, evicting a medium-priority job to accommodate a high-priority request often triggers a preemption cascade, where the evicted job immediately attempts to reschedule itself by displacing lower-priority workloads. The disruption multiplies with each level. If the urgent job displaces \(\PreemptionFanoutCount\) medium-priority jobs and each of those, on rescheduling, displaces \(\PreemptionFanoutCount\) lower-priority jobs, one admission interrupts \(\PreemptionFanoutCount+ \PreemptionFanoutCount^2\) jobs after two levels. Every one of them pays the preemption overhead quantified below and adds a checkpoint reload to the storage system at the same moment. Two dampening controls cap that growth. A rule that evicted jobs requeue without preempting anyone themselves stops the chain at the first level, so one admission costs at most \(\PreemptionFanoutCount\) interruptions. A preemption budget limits how often any single job, or what fraction of capacity, may be displaced in a time window, which protects the jobs at the bottom of the priority order that every chain would otherwise reach.
The engineering cost of preemption extends beyond scheduling latency. The preemption overhead depends on the exit path. A successful graceful checkpoint adds the time to save and restart while preserving completed progress; a forced stop can instead discard work since the last durable checkpoint. Consider such a victim, a forced interruption of the 64-GPU fine-tuning run for our 175B parameter model. The scenario assumes lost work equivalent to 15 minutes of execution. The restart then repeats the cold-restart steps of the recovery budget in Recovery procedures, without its detection step because the scheduler itself stopped the job. These steps take 3 minutes to relaunch, 24.5 seconds to reload the 2.45 TB checkpoint with its optimizer state, and 2 minutes of warmup as data pipelines refill and just-in-time (JIT) compilation and runtime initialization complete. The calculation prices replay and restart across the same allocation; it does not also charge for a successful final save.
Reconstructing the distributed data pipeline also belongs in the preemption contract. The checkpoint must preserve the sampling and loader state needed to resume the intended data order, alongside model and optimizer state. If the restart path omits that state, it can repeat or skip samples and lose exact replay of the training trajectory. A different shuffle order does not by itself prove statistical corruption, but the recovery policy must specify which changes are acceptable. The scheduler should therefore measure restoration and pipeline warmup as part of recovery cost, rather than assume that reloading model weights alone makes the job productive.
The resulting 20.4-minute overhead combines discarded execution, its larger part, with relaunch, reload, and warmup time; it is not a measurement of continuous kernel activity after eviction. Spread over the run, it belongs to the Fleet Law’s coordination term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) (equation 1.3), which counts scheduling decisions and failure recovery alongside barrier waits, so frequent preemption lengthens the average step exactly as frequent failure does. At $2/GPU-hour, the scenario values each event at $44 in allocation time. A low-priority run sits at the bottom of every cascade, so without a budget it can be struck many times a day. At the scenario’s 12 forced preemptions per day, it loses 4.1 hours of equivalent allocation time, or 261 GPU-hours for this 64-GPU run. A per-job budget bounds that loss directly. When a budget binds, the scheduler must consider waiting, another placement, or a defined emergency exception. The trade-off is reduced recovery churn against delayed admission, measured under the workload’s deadlines.



Renting on-demand cloud GPUs for a multi-week training run protects the job from provider reclamation, but pays full price even when spare GPUs sit idle in the provider’s data center. Renting interruptible capacity cuts the hourly rate by 60 to 90 percent, but lets the provider reclaim those GPUs on best-effort notice. Cloud providers sell this spare capacity through spot instances10 (AWS) or preemptible VMs (GCP), where actual discounts depend on the resource and market. The reference interruption windows range from up to 30 seconds for GCP preemptible shutdown to 2 minutes for AWS stop or termination notices, with best-effort delivery rather than a guaranteed recovery interval. At the scenario rates of $0.70/GPU-hour instead of $2/GPU-hour, the worked comparison below shows how savings can exceed half the on-demand cost after accounting for its assumed interruption overhead.
10 Spot instances: The scenario’s 60 to 90 percent discount purchases reclaimable capacity, not a guaranteed interval for saving state. AWS’s best-effort stop or termination notice targets 2 minutes, while GCP preemptible shutdown allows up to 30 seconds; AWS hibernation begins immediately. If a job’s measured checkpoint time exceeds the reference 30-second window, a notice-triggered save cannot be its only recovery path.The viability of spot instances for ML training depends on two factors that determine whether the discount translates into actual savings. The first is the cost of each interruption (checkpoint overhead plus restart time plus lost work since the last checkpoint). The second is the frequency of interruption (which varies by instance type, region, time of day, and overall cloud demand). Equation 3 gives the effective cost of spot training:
\[ \EffectiveSpotTrainingCost= \SpotHourlyPrice\times \frac{\BilledAllocationTime}{\RetainedProductiveTime}  \tag{3}\]
where \(\BilledAllocationTime\) is billed allocation time, including checkpointing, recovery, and work later discarded after an interruption, and \(\RetainedProductiveTime\) is the equivalent training time represented by retained progress. The ratio assumes a fixed allocation size and price, with unchanged useful throughput while training; variable allocations require summing the cost of each allocation interval. Waiting for replacement capacity extends completion time but contributes to billed time only while resources remain allocated. When checkpointing and interruption losses consume a small fraction of billed time, effective cost stays near the spot price. Frequent interruptions, expensive recovery, or substantial replay can instead erase the discount.
Spot savings and fault tolerance infrastructure are coupled. Fault tolerance mechanisms (frequent asynchronous checkpointing, fast checkpoint loading, elastic recovery) make spot capacity usable by lowering the cost of each interruption. Elastic training can resume a logical job with fewer workers after reclamation, provided the remaining allocation is viable, although the framework may still restart worker processes and restore checkpointed state, so elasticity reduces recovery cost rather than eliminating it. The same infrastructure therefore earns a double return. It protects against hardware losses, and it enables the deliberate use of interruptible capacity. Both benefits require measurement. The scheduler combines observed interruption rates, recovery costs, and retained training progress with resource prices to estimate whether spot savings repay the additional recovery infrastructure. The same evidence supports valuing protection against hardware failures; neither benefit follows from the discount or checkpoint mechanism alone.



Spot capacity pays off only when an interruption rarely removes the whole job at once, so schedulers that use it diversify where capacity comes from instead of simply retrying on failure. Availability zone diversification reduces the probability of simultaneous fleet-wide reclamation. Cloud providers typically manage spot pools independently per availability zone (AZ). If a training job requires 1,024 GPUs, allocating them as a single block in one zone exposes the job to a complete stop if that specific zone’s spot pool is reclaimed. Diversifying independent jobs or restart destinations across zones reduces exposure to one exhausted pool. Splitting a single synchronous gang across zones also changes its communication paths, so the scheduler must include cross-zone bandwidth, latency, and transfer costs before accepting that placement. The scheduler still must model correlation carefully: independent per-instance interruptions make large simultaneous losses unlikely, but pool-level or AZ-level reclamations can remove hundreds of GPUs at once and must be treated as elastic-shrink or failover events rather than ordinary isolated failures.
Instance type diversification expands the set of capacity pools a job can use, though availability across those pools can remain correlated. A job that requests only one instance type cannot use spare capacity in another pool. Accepting alternatives therefore requires a compatibility list that includes memory capacity, runtime support, communication paths, and measured throughput. An instance with more memory can still be an unsuitable substitute if its runtime support, communication paths, or throughput differ. The scheduler compares each feasible alternative’s price and recovery cost per unit of retained progress; mixing devices within a synchronous gang also requires accounting for unequal worker speeds.
Spot capacity signals can guide placement but do not necessarily predict interruption frequency. For example, the AWS Spot Placement Score estimates the current likelihood that a capacity request will succeed in a region or availability zone; it explicitly does not predict interruption risk. A scheduler can use this signal to choose where to request capacity, but estimating interruptions per day requires separate historical measurements for the instance type and region. If the resulting workload-specific recovery model shows that interruption overhead erases the discount, the scheduler should migrate the job to on-demand capacity or a different region.
Checkpoint frequency optimization for spot instances extends the reliability logic. The Young-Daly formula developed in The Young-Daly checkpoint interval models losses from unpredicted interruptions, whether caused by hardware failure or reclamation without a usable warning. Provider notices offer an additional opportunity to save state, using the reference windows of 2 minutes on AWS and up to 30 seconds on GCP preemptible VMs. A two-tier checkpointing approach combines periodic checkpoints, with an interval chosen for the workload’s interruption model, and a best-effort checkpoint triggered by a notice. The notice-triggered checkpoint reduces lost work only if it becomes durable before reclamation; otherwise, the job restores its last durable state, whether produced by a periodic, asynchronous, or incremental checkpoint, and replays subsequent work. That contingency planning matters more when spot interruptions are correlated across a pool rather than isolated to single machines.

Systems Perspective 8.3: Correlated spot riskContext: Spot capacity is cheap because it is reclaimable. That risk is not independent across instances: cloud regions, instance types, product launches, and deadline cycles can create correlated demand.
Failure mode: A fleet that concentrates all interruptible training in one region and one instance type can lose a large fraction of workers at once, even if each individual worker appears restartable.
Consequence: Checkpointing handles isolated interruptions; it does not solve fleet-wide preemption when every retry targets the same exhausted pool.
Systems insight: A robust scheduler diversifies compatible restart destinations, monitors interruption risk, and plans an on-demand fallback when spot capacity cannot meet the job’s deadline or cost target. That fallback still depends on available capacity and the time needed to restore state.





Committing to long-term reserved capacity for 100 percent of peak demand leaves expensive GPUs idle whenever traffic dips, while relying solely on spot or on-demand pools risks capacity shortages during product launches and sudden reclamations during deadline crunches. To avoid paying for idle reservations or starving urgent workloads, organizations that rely on cloud infrastructure (or that price on-premises capacity in economic terms) combine three tiers of compute capacity. Each tier trades cost and commitment against availability and interruption risk (table 4).



Table 4: Cloud Capacity Reservation Tiers: Capacity tiers trade cost and commitment against availability guarantees and interruption risk, giving the scheduler a price ladder for routing workloads by urgency and restart tolerance.











Capacity tier
Cost and commitment
Availability and interruption risk
Best-fit workloads




Reserved capacity
Capacity reservation; price discounts require a separate purchasing contract.
Capacity assurance within the reservation terms; startup still takes time.
Predictable continuous workloads: 24/7 inference, scheduled training, CI and regression testing, jobs under service-level agreements (SLAs).


On-demand capacity
Full price with no long-term commitment.
Admission depends on available capacity; provisioning and startup add delay.
Urgent retraining, interactive debugging, and short-lived jobs that do not justify spot management.


Spot capacity
Discounted interruptible capacity.
Availability varies with cloud demand, and workers can be reclaimed.
Restart-tolerant jobs: hyperparameter sweeps, ablations, checkpointed pretraining, and exploratory research.






The constructed portfolio in figure 14 divides capacity into a reserved tier covering the steady 60 percent baseline, an on-demand band between 60 and 80 percent, and an interruptible spot tier serving peaks up to 92 percent. An organization with 60 percent steady-state utilization and 40 percent burst demand might reserve capacity for 60 percent of peak need, use on-demand for bursts whose deadlines tolerate admission and startup delay, and use spot for restart-tolerant work. These shares illustrate a policy rather than establish an optimal portfolio. The scheduler must match each workload’s deadline and recovery contract to the capacity tier. Reserved capacity can support the steady serving load or a training job’s base allocation, while spot can support elastic replicas or independent experiments that tolerate reclamation. A peak in urgent demand cannot automatically be assigned to spot merely because it lies above the reserved band.






Figure 14: Capacity Reservation Tiers and Portfolio Optimization: This constructed portfolio combines reserved physical capacity, on-demand acquisitions, and interruptible workers. Reserved capacity covers the steady 60 percent base, on-demand the next 20 percent, and spot the peak; these shares and the demand curve are scenario assumptions. A discount commitment alone does not reserve capacity, and on-demand admission is not instantaneous. Schedulers map steady-state baseline demand to reserved capacity, diurnal spikes to on-demand instances, and restart-tolerant training to discounted spot pools. Hatching marks reserved capacity that is held while demand sits below it.




Systems Perspective 8.4: Spot vs. on-demand trainingConsider training a 70B parameter model, a smaller workload than the chapter’s 175B reference, on 512 GPUs for 14 days. The scenario fixes the event budget at 196 interruptions over the run and treats each as graceful, so no progress is replayed.
On-Demand: 512 GPUs \(\times\) 336 hours \(\times\) $2/GPU-hour = $344,064
Spot (65 percent discount, 5 percent checkpoint overhead, 14 interruptions per day of useful training with 30 minutes restart):

Base cost: 512 GPUs \(\times\) 336 hours \(\times\) $0.70/GPU-hour = $120,422
Checkpoint overhead: \(5\%\) \(\times\) 336 hours = 16.8 hours
Restart overhead: 196 interruptions \(\times\) 0.5 hours = 98 hours
Total time: 336 hours + 16.8 hours + 98 hours = 450.8 hours
Total cost: 512 GPUs \(\times\) 450.8 hours \(\times\) $0.70/GPU-hour = $161,567

Savings: $182,497 (53.0 percent), at the cost of approximately 34.2 percent longer wall-clock time.
These savings assume fault tolerance infrastructure is already in place. Without checkpointing, a single interruption forces restart from scratch, potentially wasting days of compute and negating all savings.





Once a fleet spans reserved, on-demand, and spot tiers, a newly submitted job can often launch immediately on reserved A100 GPUs or wait two hours for spot H100 instances that deliver twice the throughput at half the execution cost. Deciding whether those savings repay the two-hour delay and interruption risk turns the purchasing tiers into an online scheduling decision. Alongside completion time, utilization, and fairness, a cost-aware orchestrator evaluates three recurring trade-offs: waiting versus running immediately, preempting lower-priority work on reserved capacity (such as a hyperparameter sweep) versus routing a high-priority training run to more expensive on-demand instances, and replacing reclaimed spot instances with on-demand nodes versus shrinking elastically. Each choice requires the costs of waiting, recovery, and displaced work as well as the price of the new allocation.
These decisions require the scheduler to model both the time-value of computation (the organizational cost of a 2-hour delay in researcher productivity, product launch schedules, or competitive position) and the financial cost of different resource allocations. Delaying a production model retrain by 2 hours might violate a service level agreement (SLA), while the same delay to an exploratory experiment can postpone a research decision or block dependent work. A workload class’s delay tolerance is therefore a policy input grounded in its dependencies and deadlines, not an assumption that exploratory work has no time cost.
Production systems can define cost policies per workload class that encode these trade-offs as configuration rather than requiring per-decision human judgment. One policy places steady inference demand on reserved capacity and maintains ready replicas to meet its latency target; the reservation alone does not guarantee application availability or latency. Large training runs can combine a reserved minimum viable allocation with interruptible elastic expansion, requesting on-demand replacements when a deadline justifies the cost and capacity is available. Exploratory workloads with flexible deadlines can use spot capacity while accepting interruptions and variable completion times. These assignments express the organization’s priorities rather than a universal mapping from workload type to purchasing tier.
The scheduler does not implement the organization’s financial accounting system. It consumes the resulting price and policy signals: the marginal price of each capacity tier, the reservation a project may claim, the interruption risk it may accept, and the deadline it must meet. Showback, chargeback, and attribution belong to that accounting system; the scheduler uses their outputs only to rank feasible scheduling actions. Lifecycle total cost of ownership (TCO) reaches the scheduler the same way, as per-resource opportunity costs and constraints that record whether capacity is owned, reserved, on demand, or interruptible, rather than as a scheduling mechanism.


↪ Tag-based cost attribution, shared-cost allocation, and chargeback are developed in Cost visibility and attribution.

↪ The lifecycle TCO framework, which combines training, inference, data, and iteration costs, is developed in ML systems TCO framework.


Checkpoint 8.2: Cost-aware scheduling trade-offs
Before moving to ML-specific schedulers, review how the cost-optimization mechanisms interact:

Spot break-even: identify the additional inputs needed to compute a break-even checkpoint interval for the 512-GPU, 14-day training job of the spot comparison above (65 percent spot discount, 14 interruptions per day, 30-minute restart overhead), including checkpoint duration, the interruption-rate clock, and lost-progress assumptions.
Double return: explain why fault tolerance infrastructure has a “double return” for reliability and cost savings, and identify the minimum fault tolerance investment needed to make spot instances viable.
Reservation sizing: starting from the constructed portfolio that reserves 60 percent of peak, identify the demand history, reservation terms, unit prices, and unused-capacity costs needed to decide whether raising the reserved share to 70 percent reduces total spending.



Spot pricing and reservation strategy reduce the cost of capacity, but they do not determine which competing job should receive it. Runtime uncertainty, unequal completion delays, and the cost of interrupting an iteration remain even when prices are known. Resolving them requires signals from the workload itself, such as how much service a job has consumed, where its iteration boundaries fall, or how fast it is learning. A scheduler that tracks learning progress can optimize time-to-accuracy, the wall-clock time until a run reaches a target validation metric, rather than execution speed alone.

Self-Check: Question

What is a preemption cascade in a shared GPU cluster, and which control stops it at the first level?

A cascade is a burst of hardware failures in one rack; spare-capacity reservation stops it.
A cascade is a high-priority admission that evicts medium-priority jobs, each of which then evicts lower-priority jobs to reschedule itself; requiring evicted jobs to requeue without preempting anyone stops it after the first level.
A cascade is a queue of jobs waiting behind a large gang; backfill scheduling stops it.
A cascade is repeated checkpointing by one job; lengthening its checkpoint interval stops it.

A training job moves from on-demand to spot capacity at the chapter’s scenario discount. According to the effective-cost relation, in which effective cost equals the spot price times billed allocation time divided by retained productive time, what determines whether the discount survives?

Only the advertised discount, because interruptions are free once a provider sends a notice.
The ratio of billed allocation time to retained productive time, which grows with checkpoint overhead, restart time, and work replayed after each interruption.
The number of GPUs in the job, because larger jobs always receive deeper spot discounts.
The provider’s capacity-placement score, which predicts how many interruptions the job will see per day.

An organization runs steady 24/7 inference, urgent retraining with tight deadlines, and a large hyperparameter sweep. Which assignment of these workloads to reserved, on-demand, and spot capacity matches each workload’s deadline and recovery contract?

Inference on spot, retraining on reserved, sweep on on-demand.
Inference on reserved, retraining on on-demand, sweep on spot.
All three on spot, because the discount outweighs any interruption risk.
Inference on on-demand, retraining on spot, sweep on reserved.

This chapter treats lifecycle total cost of ownership (TCO) as an input to the scheduler rather than as a scheduling mechanism. What does the scheduler consume from TCO analysis and cost accounting, and how does it use those inputs?
A low-priority 64-GPU fine-tuning run is forcibly preempted. What makes up the preemption overhead for that event, and why does a per-job preemption budget matter more for this run than for a high-priority job?
True or False: Because each VM instance in a cloud provider has an independent lifecycle, placing worker nodes of a 64-node distributed training job across different instance types within the same Availability Zone guarantees that preemption events will remain uncorrelated and statistically independent.
