When a model fits on one accelerator but training takes weeks, replicating its computation lets several workers process examples concurrently. The initial data-parallel baseline gives each worker the same model state and a local portion of one global minibatch. Combining those local contributions before the optimizer update preserves the intended global-batch estimator; the sampling and weighting conditions below explain when that equivalence holds.

Definition 6.2: Data parallelism
Data parallelism distributes training examples across workers that execute the model and combine their contributions to its optimization updates.

Significance: With \(\DeviceCount\) workers each processing a local batch of \(\LocalBatchSize\) examples once per update, the global batch size is \(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\). At fixed local work, 1,024 workers offer an ideal 1,024\(\times\) throughput increase before exposed overhead. A 1B-parameter model with BF16 gradients contributes a 2 GB gradient payload; ring AllReduce moves \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times that payload per worker. Realized speedup depends on local compute, collective service, overlap, and load balance.
Distinction: The replicated synchronous baseline keeps a full model copy on each worker and aggregates gradients before each optimizer update. Model parallelism instead partitions the model’s computation. Sharded data parallelism, developed below, retains data-parallel computation while distributing training-state storage.
Common pitfall: Data parallelism does not scale indefinitely with worker count. Holding the local batch \(\LocalBatchSize\) fixed while adding workers grows the global batch. Beyond the workload-dependent critical batch size, additional examples yield diminishing reductions in the steps needed to reach target quality (Shallue et al. 2019). The crossover developed in section 6.4.6 therefore limits the statistical benefit even when gradient variance continues to decrease.




He, Kaiming, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. 2016. “Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition.” 2016 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 770–78. https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr.2016.90.
Data parallelism applies when examples can be processed independently, as in training a ResNet model (He et al. 2016) on ImageNet. Each replica computes its local loss gradient, and the workers combine those contributions to reproduce the intended global-batch gradient. The averaging rule makes the sampling and weighting assumptions explicit.
Consider a model with parameters \(\ModelParameters\) training on a dataset \(\TrainingDataset\). The loss function for a single data point \(\ModelInput_i\) is \(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)\). In standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with batch size \(\BatchSize\), the gradient update for a minibatch is: \[
\MinibatchGradient= \frac{1}{\BatchSize} \sum_{i=1}^\BatchSize\nabla_{\ModelParameters} \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)
\]
In data parallelism with \(\DeviceCount\) devices, each device \(\WorkerIndex\) computes gradients on its own minibatch \(\MiniBatchSet_k\): \[
\MinibatchGradient_k = \frac{1}{|\MiniBatchSet_k|} \sum_{\ModelInput_i \in \MiniBatchSet_k} \nabla_{\ModelParameters} \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)
\]
When all workers use the same local batch size, the global update averages these local gradients: \[
\GlobalBatchGradient= \frac{1}{\DeviceCount} \sum_{k=1}^\DeviceCount\MinibatchGradient_k
\]
Under that equal-batch assumption, the averaging is mathematically equivalent to computing the gradient on the combined batch \(\CombinedBatch= \bigcup_{k=1}^\DeviceCount \MiniBatchSet_k\): \[
\GlobalBatchGradient= \frac{1}{|\CombinedBatch|} \sum_{\ModelInput_i \in \CombinedBatch} \nabla_{\ModelParameters} \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput_i)
\]
For unequal local batch sizes, the combined-batch gradient is the weighted average \(\GlobalBatchGradient= (1/|\CombinedBatch|)\sum_k |\MiniBatchSet_k|\MinibatchGradient_k\). Data parallelism therefore maintains the statistical properties of SGD training, because sampling the intended global batch across devices, computing local gradient sums independently, and normalizing by the aggregate denominator reproduces its estimator. The reduction step uses an AllReduce over local gradient sums and valid-item counts.
Three batch quantities recur from here on, and the chapter keeps them apart. A worker’s local batch \(\LocalBatchSize\) is the set of examples it processes for one update, playing the role of \(\MiniBatchSet_k\) above. The global batch \(\GlobalBatchSize= \DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) is the set the update averages over. Pipeline parallelism later splits a batch into \(\MicrobatchCount\) microbatches of size \(\MicrobatchSize\) that flow through stages one after another; the word microbatch is reserved for those pipeline slices.

The method parallels gradient accumulation, where a device accumulates contributions from multiple forward and backward passes before one optimizer update. Both techniques use gradient addition and the intended loss denominator to process a larger effective batch. Distribution adds communication, partial failures, and coordination to that arithmetic. The implementation must preserve the update while accounting for those costs.


The implementation details matter because the SGD equivalence only holds when each phase preserves the intended aggregate sampling and weighting, complete local gradient contributions, and a single synchronized update. The concrete workflow follows the dataflow from assigning local batches to synchronizing the computed gradients. The five-stage execution pipeline in figure 3 follows four GPU swimlanes. Identical model replicas ingest disjoint batch shards and compute local gradients (\(\MinibatchGradient_0\)–\(\MinibatchGradient_3\)). They then synchronize through a ring AllReduce collective before applying uniform parameter updates.







Figure 3: Data Parallelism Implementation Pipeline: The five-stage workflow for data-parallel training: (1) partition the global batch, (2) assign sharded mini-batches to individual GPUs, (3) compute independent forward and backward passes to produce local gradients \(\MinibatchGradient_i\), (4) execute an AllReduce collective across the cluster to obtain the average gradient \(\GlobalBatchGradient\), and (5) update parameters identically across all devices. This strategy preserves the mathematical semantics of single-device SGD while distributing the compute burden.



The gradient synchronization stage of figure 3 (stage 4) creates a dependency, because each rank must receive the completed reduction before applying its optimizer update. The exposed wait can reflect bandwidth, collective startup, or a late contribution. Measuring that wait determines whether synchronization limits scaling; the dependency alone does not identify the binding resource.


Data splitting is the first place where the SGD equivalence can fail, but uniqueness and equal-sized shards are sufficient conditions rather than the invariant itself. The aggregate examples or tokens, their sampling probabilities, and their gradient weights must reproduce the intended global-batch estimator. Uniform sampling without replacement can assign disjoint shards. Sampling with replacement can legitimately repeat examples. Variable-length batches can assign unequal token counts if the reduction weights each worker by its valid-example or valid-token denominator. An unweighted mean of unequal local means instead overweights workers with smaller denominators.
The sampler is therefore an integral component of the distributed training system rather than merely an input-loader convenience. A distributed sampler coordinates workers by rank and can deterministically partition or draw indices from a seeded sampling stream. The 1.28 million training images of ImageNet-1k do not divide evenly across 32 GPUs. A sampler that pads by repeating examples gives each GPU 40,037 examples per epoch and adds 17 repeats across the job. The loss normalization or sample weights must account for those repeats when exact epoch-level weighting matters. A recorded seed and deterministic index stream make sample assignment repeatable. Bitwise run reproducibility additionally depends on kernel determinism, collective reduction order, numerical precision, and checkpointed random-number-generator state.



For a replicated model whose local forward and backward operations require no cross-worker state, the computation phase is embarrassingly parallel. Each GPU executes the model on its local batch; synchronized normalization or additional model partitioning can introduce communication within that phase. To isolate the activation term, consider an unpartitioned 175B reference model at a local batch of 4 sequences and sequence length 2048. This is a hypothetical memory budget, not a feasible one-GPU training configuration, because weights and optimizer state must fit as well. Without optimization, storing these activations for backpropagation would consume roughly 1.1 TB of HBM, an order of magnitude beyond the capacity of even an H100 GPU. Activation checkpointing recomputes selected activations during the backward pass rather than retaining them, reducing this example’s footprint to ~19.3 GB at the cost of extra computation.
The capacity test must include activations rather than stopping at bytes per parameter. Numeric Precision and Training Memory tabulates the 16-byte-per-parameter training state from which this test starts. At the point of peak residency, \[
\TotalMemoryFootprint = \WeightMemory + \GradientMemory + \OptimizerStateMemory + \ActivationMemory,
\] with communication buffers and temporary workspaces consuming additional headroom. Sharding reduces the first three terms according to its stage, whereas sequence length, local batch size, and pipeline scheduling govern \(\ActivationMemory\). Activation checkpointing reduces that last term by retaining only selected boundaries and recomputing the omitted forward operators during backpropagation (Narayanan et al. 2021). Full recomputation re-executes about one extra forward pass per step. Because a backward pass costs roughly two forward passes, a step that needed three forward-pass equivalents of arithmetic now needs four, about a third more (Chen et al. 2016). Selective recomputation re-executes only operators whose activations are large but cheap to produce, such as the attention softmax and dropout, and keeps most of the memory saving for a few percent of extra arithmetic (Korthikanti et al. 2023). Recomputed operations raise hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU) but not model FLOPs utilization (MFU), which credits only the model’s own forward and backward work. A plan that buys feasibility with full recomputation therefore pays for it in useful throughput. The memory saved is purchased with additional FLOPs and a longer critical path. A feasible parallelism plan must budget both effects.

As the backward pass traverses the computation graph in reverse, it produces gradients for the parameters held by each replica or shard. Under pure data parallelism, a full 175B FP16 replica would imply a 350 GB gradient tensor per worker, which exceeds single-accelerator memory budgets. Large runs therefore combine data parallelism with sharding, tensor parallelism, or pipeline parallelism. Each local gradient contributes to the intended global-batch estimator. Aggregation can begin as gradient tensors become ready, overlapping later backward computation, but the optimizer must wait for the completed contributions it consumes. This readiness schedule connects local computation to collective communication.



Gradient synchronization combines local contributions into the synchronous update. Each replica must receive the aggregate before applying that update. In a centralized parameter-server design with fixed per-worker payload and update frequency, the server receives \(\mathcal{O}(\DeviceCount)\) incoming traffic. That concentration becomes a bottleneck when demand exceeds the server tier’s service capacity; sharding the server state or changing the communication pattern can relieve it.
The replicated synchronous baseline distributes aggregation through collective communication. AllReduce lets each worker contribute its local gradient tensor and receive the same reduced result, which the training loop normalizes to obtain the global average. In sharded variants such as ZeRO and FSDP, ReduceScatter and AllGather change which result each worker retains, leaving each worker only its own shard of the reduced gradient and reconstructing full parameters on demand. Small messages emphasize startup latency; large messages emphasize sustained bandwidth. Centralized aggregation remains another design choice, particularly for the sparse workloads developed later.

Parameter updating closes the replicated synchronous contract. After the gradient AllReduce (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009), every worker holds the same global gradient and applies it to its own replica with SGD, momentum, or Adam, so the update stays decentralized without losing equivalence to single-device training. Identical gradients alone are insufficient, because optimizer moments, learning rates, and step counts must also match across replicas. Frameworks automate the cycle of splitting data, computing gradients, synchronizing, and updating, but they cannot remove the ordering constraint that keeps the replicas coherent: every worker must finish aggregating the current step’s gradient before any replica computes from the updated weights.



Whether every worker must wait for that barrier on every step defines the job’s synchronization model. The baseline is bulk synchronous parallel (BSP), the superstep-and-barrier model just described, in which workers compute from one parameter version, combine their gradient contributions, and complete the update before computing from the next version. This is a dependency order, not a requirement that every device update at the same wall-clock instant. Relaxing it changes the optimization process as well as the waiting time.


↩︎ Bulk synchronous parallel execution and its barrier cost are established in How ML Networking Inverts Data-Center Assumptions.
BSP provides synchronous update semantics, in which every worker computes from the same parameter version and reaches the next update boundary together. With the same global batch and reduction, this matches the corresponding synchronous single-device update mathematically. It does not by itself guarantee bitwise reproducibility. Floating-point reduction order, nondeterministic kernels, data-order state, and failure recovery can still change the result. The synchronization cost is that the slowest worker determines iteration time. A worker that keeps producing correct results but runs markedly slower than its peers is a straggler, and under BSP every straggler delays the entire step.
Stale synchronous parallel (SSP) relaxes this constraint by allowing workers to proceed up to \(\StalenessBound\) iterations ahead of the slowest worker before blocking. This bounds staleness while reducing synchronization delays. SSP requires careful learning rate tuning since workers compute gradients on slightly different parameter versions. The bounded staleness guarantee provides a middle ground between BSP’s strong consistency and fully asynchronous approaches (Ho et al. 2013).
Asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier, allowing a worker’s contribution to be applied while others continue computing; asynchronous SGD is the optimizer run under that protocol. Less barrier waiting can improve update throughput, but communication and shared-state contention remain. Gradients computed from older parameter versions introduce staleness that can affect convergence. Section 6.4.4 develops the objective and delay assumptions needed to evaluate that trade-off. The three models lie on one spectrum, from the strong consistency of BSP to the barrier-free updates of ASP (table 2).

Throughput and time to target quality depend on the workload and implementation. Reproducibility requires a separate deterministic-execution contract.

Middle: stale synchronous parallel (SSP) allows workers to proceed up to \(\StalenessBound\) steps ahead of the slowest worker. Bottom: asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier while allowing gradient staleness; communication and resource contention can still delay progress.






An optimizer update that consumes an AllReduce result must wait for every required contribution. Workers can execute independent computation while a collective is in flight, but they must issue compatible collectives in the same group order and wait for completion before consuming the result. This coupling creates failure modes absent from single-device training.
A worker failure can leave peers waiting for a contribution that will never arrive. The runtime may report a communication error, or the operation may remain blocked until a timeout detects the failure. Watchdogs bound that wait so the job can enter recovery rather than retain an unusable allocation indefinitely.



One missing worker stalls the entire AllReduce barrier.
Collective mismatches occur when workers issue incompatible operations, tensor shapes, or ordering within a communication group. Conditional computation can create such a mismatch if some workers omit an expected reduction. Variable sequence lengths or different expert routes do not inherently violate the protocol; the runtime must construct a compatible communication schedule for those varying local computations.
Stragglers extend an iteration when their late work lies on its critical path. Thermal throttling, network congestion, or OS jitter can delay a required contribution even when other workers are ready. At 1,000 GPUs with a 1 percent straggler probability per GPU per step, the expected count is 10 stragglers per step, but the number that matters under BSP is the chance of a step with none at all. That chance is the per-GPU on-time probability raised to the GPU count, about 0.004 percent. Almost every step therefore waits for at least one slow worker, which is why the slowest worker, not the typical one, sets step time. The resulting exposed wait depends on how late that contribution arrives and what independent work remains. Deployed systems bound these waits with timeouts and heartbeat monitoring, and elastic training lets a job continue with a resized worker group after a failure.


↪ Heartbeat and collective-timeout failure detection, and the trade-off between restarting healthy workers and leaving peers blocked, are developed in Failure detection mechanisms.




Data parallelism is the simplest way to add accelerators because it leaves each replica’s model computation intact, but adding workers eventually hits either a communication wall or a statistical wall (Ben-Nun and Hoefler 2019). Near-linear throughput scaling requires local compute efficiency, balanced input delivery, and small exposed synchronization costs. Which wall arrives first depends on whether the global batch stays fixed or grows as workers are added. Holding the global batch fixed while adding workers is strong scaling: each worker’s local batch shrinks, so communication must hide behind less computation. Holding the local batch fixed so that the global batch grows with \(\DeviceCount\) is weak scaling: per-worker computation stays constant, but each update averages more examples, which eventually stops reducing the number of updates needed. The rest of the chapter refers to the two regimes by these names.

Ben-Nun, Tal, and Torsten Hoefler. 2019. “Demystifying Parallel and Distributed Deep Learning: An in-Depth Concurrency Analysis.” ACM Computing Surveys 52 (4): 1–43. https://doi.org/10.1145/3320060.
Weak scaling pays off when the larger global batch still reaches the target accuracy. Goyal et al. (2017) trained ResNet-50 on ImageNet in about one hour on 256 GPUs at a global batch of 8,192 images; the learning-rate rules that let that batch reach the target accuracy are developed in section 6.4.5. Replicated data parallelism retains the model’s local operators, and frameworks can trigger gradient reductions as backward computation produces them. Each replica executes a complete forward and backward pass, avoiding the layer-stage fill and drain bubbles of pipeline parallelism. Input stalls, imbalance, and exposed reductions can still leave devices idle.
These advantages hold only until replication runs into memory capacity, communication bandwidth, or statistical diminishing returns. The memory wall binds first on large models because a replicated worker holds every parameter, gradient, and optimizer state, demanding more than 1 TB per replica for the 175B-parameter example before activations. Even when the state fits, communication limits useful scaling once its exposed cost grows relative to local work. As \(\DeviceCount\) increases, the ideal ring bandwidth term \(\frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \frac{\GradientPayload}{\LinkBandwidth}\) approaches a constant for a fixed gradient payload \(\GradientPayload\) and link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), while startup latency, topology, and shrinking local computation worsen the balance. Statistical efficiency then sets the ceiling under weak scaling, because growing \(\GlobalBatchSize= \DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) with \(\DeviceCount\) eventually yields diminishing reductions in update count. Strong scaling avoids that batch-size ceiling only by shrinking each worker’s local batch, which exposes the communication trade-off sooner.

Replicated data parallelism stores an identical copy of weights, gradients, and optimizer state on every GPU, so a 7B-parameter model demands 112 GB on each device and overflows an 80 GB accelerator before a single activation is allocated. The Zero Redundancy Optimizer (ZeRO) (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) and PyTorch’s Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) (Zhao et al. 2023) remove that duplication by sharding training state across workers while keeping each worker’s full forward and backward computation.3 Sharding can make a model fit in memory without splitting its layer computations across devices.

Definition 6.3: Sharded data parallelism
Sharded data parallelism partitions optimizer state, gradients, and at the deepest stage the parameters themselves across data-parallel workers. Each worker processes its own minibatch shard and uses collectives to obtain the parameters and reduced gradients it needs. Full sharding reduces each worker’s persistent state toward \(1/\DeviceCount\) of the replicated training state; activations and temporary buffers still contribute to peak memory.

Significance: Under the mixed-precision Adam convention used here, 16 bytes of state per parameter gives a 7B-parameter model 112 GB of training state, exceeding a 80 GB accelerator before activations. ZeRO Stage 3 across 64 workers reduces persistent state per device to 1.75 GB (0.25 bytes per parameter). The resulting AllGather and ReduceScatter traffic trades memory capacity for communication whose exposed cost depends on the interconnect and available overlap.
Distinction: Unlike vanilla data parallelism, which replicates training state, sharded data parallelism partitions its storage. Unlike model parallelism, it retains each worker’s full forward and backward computation. Fully sharded execution gathers parameters for the current computation; the resharding schedule determines when it releases them.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that sharding is free memory. The on-demand AllGathers place parameter traffic on the critical path of every layer in every step. On slower interconnects or at small per-worker batch sizes, the exposed communication erodes throughput faster than the memory savings help. Capacity is purchased with bandwidth.



The scale of the savings is clearest on a model whose replicated training state only modestly overflows one accelerator, so that the effect of each sharding stage stays visible. The 175B reference returns after this trace when the question becomes whether sharding alone is enough.

The first step, ZeRO-1, shards optimizer states across GPUs so each GPU stores only \(1/\DeviceCount\) of the Adam optimizer-related state. During backpropagation, each worker still materializes the full 2 bytes/param gradient buffer locally, which is why gradient memory remains unsharded in table 3. Once gradients are ready, however, they need only be reduced to the worker responsible for each parameter shard via a ReduceScatter, and after each worker updates its owned shard, an AllGather broadcasts the updated parameters to restore the full replicas. This two-phase schedule (one gradient ReduceScatter plus one parameter AllGather) matches the table’s \(1\times\) baseline communication volume, whereas running a full gradient AllReduce followed by a parameter AllGather would add 50 percent more traffic. Under the 12-byte convention that counts FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance, sharding the optimizer state reduces cluster-wide storage from \(12\DeviceCount\) bytes/param to \(12\) bytes/param in total.
Building on that owner-update contract, ZeRO-2 eliminates persistent full-model gradient buffers by streaming the ReduceScatter during the backward pass. As each layer or communication bucket finishes its backward computation, workers immediately ReduceScatter that bucket’s gradients and free the slices owned by other ranks, leaving each GPU with only its \(1/\DeviceCount\) persistent shard of reduced gradients. Each worker then updates its \(1/\DeviceCount\) parameter partition using the corresponding optimizer state, and an AllGather restores the updated parameter replicas. In the ideal ring accounting, the gradient ReduceScatter and the parameter AllGather each transfer \(\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) elements per worker, for \(2\Parameters(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) across both phases, matching DDP’s byte volume (\(1\times\)) when gradient and parameter communication widths match. Replicated parameters avoid forward parameter gathers, although model operations may still communicate. Under the FP16-gradient convention, persistent gradient storage falls from \(2\DeviceCount\) bytes per parameter across \(\DeviceCount\) workers to \(2\) bytes per parameter in total, or \(2/\DeviceCount\) per GPU, apart from transient bucket buffers.
At the deepest stage, ZeRO-3 and FSDP partition the parameters as well, leaving each GPU with a \(1/\DeviceCount\) persistent slice of all three training states. Because workers no longer hold full parameter replicas between steps, the post-update parameter AllGather disappears and is replaced by two on-demand parameter AllGathers during computation. Each sharded unit gathers its parameters before the forward pass and immediately releases the non-local slices, then gathers them a second time before the backward pass and releases them again once local gradients are computed, and finally runs a ReduceScatter to deliver the completed gradients to each shard’s owner for the local optimizer update. Across four ranks (figure 7) and under matching communication widths, ZeRO-1 (\(\OptimizerStateMemory/4\)) and ZeRO-2 (\(\OptimizerStateMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4\)) each execute two collective phases per step and retain the baseline \(1\times\) communication volume. ZeRO-3 (\(\WeightMemory/4, \GradientMemory/4, \OptimizerStateMemory/4\)) executes three collective phases of one parameter-equivalent payload each (forward AllGather, backward AllGather, and gradient ReduceScatter), which yields \(3/2 = 1.5\times\) the baseline two-phase volume in this accounting.







Figure 7: ZeRO State Partitioning across GPU Ranks: Which copy of each training state every GPU holds, for 4 workers. A filled full-width tile is a replicated copy; a quarter-width segment inside a dashed outline is that GPU’s shard, stepping one quarter per rank. ZeRO-1 shards optimizer state (\(\OptimizerStateMemory/4\)), ZeRO-2 adds gradients (\(\GradientMemory/4\)), and ZeRO-3 shards parameters too (\(\WeightMemory/4\)). The footers give per-worker communication volume relative to DDP: only ZeRO-3 pays more, for the parameter AllGathers.



Full sharding adds parameter-readiness dependencies that replicated DDP avoids. With one sharding unit per layer, the forward pass needs an AllGather to reconstruct parameters (\(\LayerParameterPayload\) bytes). Resharding after forward requires another gather before backward (\(\LayerParameterPayload\) bytes), followed by a ReduceScatter for gradients (\(\LayerParameterPayload\) bytes under equal communication precision). For a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers, this schedule performs about \(3\LayerCount\) collective operations per step. DDP instead AllReduces gradient buckets as they become ready. At large worker counts, the ideal per-worker transfer volumes approach \(3\ParameterPayload\) bytes versus \(2\ParameterPayload\) for DDP. Here \(\ParameterPayload\) is the model’s parameter bytes at the communication precision, not full training state, and it equals \(\GradientPayload\) when parameters and gradients travel at the same width. These volumes do not determine elapsed time alone. While layer \(\LayerIndex\) computes, layer \(\LayerIndex+1\) can prefetch parameters, subject to memory headroom and fabric contention.
The allocation lifetimes in figure 8 separate persistent ownership from the temporary buffers needed to execute one sharding unit.






Figure 8: FSDP Parameter Lifetimes: One rank executes a sharding unit under a policy that reshards parameters after forward computation. Gathered parameters disappear between forward and backward, while saved activations remain until backward consumes them. Dashed cells show optional prefetch of another unit; these allocations can coexist with the current unit. The cells describe logical lifetimes, not byte totals or operation durations. Implementations may alias shard storage or reuse buffers.



A model fits only when all simultaneously live allocations fit. The persistent shards therefore establish a floor, while gathered units, saved activations, and prefetch determine how far the execution peak rises above it.
The choice between FSDP and DDP begins with peak memory. If replicated state, activations, and working buffers fit, DDP avoids repeated parameter gathers. When optimizer and gradient storage are the obstacle, ZeRO-2 offers savings while leaving parameters replicated. If parameters themselves do not fit, ZeRO-3/FSDP, offload, or partitioned computation must address that remaining constraint. For a 70B+ model on 80 GB devices, the need for tensor parallelism depends on the gathered layer size, activation budget, and throughput target; parameter count alone does not decide it.
Memory-efficient data parallelism requires careful tuning of sharding strategy (by layer, by transformer block, or flat) and mixed precision settings. Finer sharding reduces per-GPU memory but increases communication frequency, because more AllGather and ReduceScatter operations must execute per training step. Replicated or sharded, a data-parallel design earns its added workers only when they turn into faster progress toward target quality, and scaling efficiency measures that conversion.

Data parallelism and ZeRO sharding show how communication and synchronization enter every training step, yet raw step throughput alone cannot judge a distributed run. When doubling the number of GPUs yields only 1.5\(\times\) speedup for the same work, scaling efficiency is 75 percent, and if the larger global batch also requires more optimizer updates to reach the same loss, wall-clock time to quality degrades further. Evaluating a distributed configuration therefore requires separating two questions: how efficiently added devices execute each step, and how batch growth or stale updates affect the number of steps to convergence. The hardware scaling metrics below apply to every parallelism strategy; the convergence analysis that follows concerns data-parallel batch growth and synchronization slack, establishing a batch-size constraint that tensor and pipeline configurations must also respect when combined with data parallelism.


That first question is answered by scaling efficiency, the fleet-level ratio introduced with the Fleet Law in The Fleet Law. If a model trains in time \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) on one device, ideal (linear) scaling would train it in time \(\SingleDeviceRunTime/\DeviceCount\) on \(\DeviceCount\) devices; communication overhead, pipeline bubbles, and load imbalance widen the gap between that ideal and the realized time \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\). Equation 1 formalizes the ratio:
\[\ScalingEfficiency = \frac{\SingleDeviceRunTime}{\DeviceCount\times \MultiDeviceRunTime} \tag{1}\]
where \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\) is the training time on \(\DeviceCount\) devices. Measured per step of the same work, \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) is the quantity the Fleet Law writes as \(\IronLawComputeTime\), the single-device compute time that its compute term divides by \(\DeviceCount\). An efficiency of 1.0 means perfect linear scaling; an efficiency of 0.5 means the run achieves only half the ideal speedup.

Definition 6.4: Scaling efficiency
Scaling efficiency \((\ScalingEfficiency)\) is the ratio of actual training throughput to ideal linear throughput when increasing the number of ML compute devices (\(\DeviceCount\)).

Significance: The ratio in equation 1 measures added devices against the specified baseline. At 0.50 efficiency, a 10,000-GPU run delivers the throughput that 5,000 perfectly scaled devices would, so half of the accelerator-hours buy no progress relative to ideal scaling. The equivalence is to an idealized baseline. A real 5,000-GPU run would have its own, typically higher, efficiency, and the loss is spread across every device as waiting rather than concentrated in idle ones.
Distinction: Unlike single-node efficiency, which captures local bottlenecks like \(\Bandwidth\), scaling efficiency measures how performance changes with device count. Communication time \((\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount))\) and synchronization contribute, but changing local kernel shapes or input delivery can also affect the ratio.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that scaling efficiency is constant. In reality, it depends on both device count and problem size. For a fixed model, the communication-to-compute ratio typically worsens as \(\DeviceCount\) increases (Amdahl’s Law). At a fixed \(\DeviceCount\), a smaller model or local batch leaves less computation per device to hide startup latency and coordination, so its efficiency falls sooner.



The Fleet Law leads to the scaling efficiency metric for fixed global work. Substituting its step time (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)) for \(\MultiDeviceRunTime\) in equation 1, with \(\IronLawComputeTime\) standing for \(\SingleDeviceRunTime\) per step as noted there, gives equation 2:
\[ \ScalingEfficiency = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount\times \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)} = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{\DeviceCount(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime)}{\IronLawComputeTime}}  \tag{2}\]
This form states the scaling efficiency bound (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)), under which perfect linear scaling \((\ScalingEfficiency = 1.0)\) is a theoretical limit, not a practical target. Real systems fall short of it by an amount that depends on the configuration and grows with \(\DeviceCount\). The 175B data-parallel example below reaches only 15 percent, and the hybrid layouts later in the chapter recover much of that loss without reaching 1.0. The gap between \(\ScalingEfficiency = 1.0\) and the achieved efficiency is the price of distributed execution, paid in communication and coordination.
The equation also exposes the scaling wall. As \(\DeviceCount\) increases, the compute term \((\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\) shrinks, but the communication and synchronization terms can remain constant or grow. A ring AllReduce’s bandwidth term, for example, stays near its bound however many workers join (principle \(\ref{pri-allreduce-bandwidth-bound}\)). Eventually, the denominator is dominated by overhead, driving efficiency toward zero.
For data-parallel training of the 175B reference model, the per-step communication cost is dominated by the AllReduce of 350 GB of gradients, and how much of that exchange hides behind computation decides the efficiency. The scaling efficiency depends on computation per communicated byte. At fixed tokens per update, increasing parameter count raises both transformer computation and gradient bytes roughly proportionally, so model size alone does not guarantee better scaling. Larger batches raise computation per optimizer step without changing gradient size. The catch is that large batches can harm convergence and so require learning-rate tuning and warmup schedules. Network bandwidth enters directly because doubling InfiniBand bandwidth halves the bandwidth term, but efficiency changes according to the full step-time denominator rather than in direct proportion. The network fabric is therefore a first-order determinant of cluster productivity, not a secondary concern. Every point of scaling efficiency it recovers is returned across the much larger accelerator investment, which is why fabric spending is judged by the efficiency it buys rather than by its own price.
These factors interact, so efficiency cannot be inferred from model size or GPU count alone. The following worked model fixes the parameter count, tokens per update, accelerator count, effective bandwidth, local compute efficiency before communication, and overlap before calculating one efficiency point. Changing any of those inputs requires recomputing the full step-time model.

Per-GPU compute time on 1,024 GPUs, each at 1,979 TFLOP/s peak in the 8-bit floating-point (FP8) format developed in section 6.4.8 (50 percent local compute efficiency before communication). The general matrix multiplications (GEMMs) run in FP8 while the gradients below still cross the wire in FP16, because the collective’s data type is chosen independently of the arithmetic’s: \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount \approx 2.1\) seconds
AllReduce time (for 350 GB of gradients using ring-AllReduce with overlap): \(\ExposedCommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) \approx 11.9\) seconds (raw ring transfer takes \(2 \times (N-1)/N \times 350 / 50\), about 14 seconds; the schedule could hide 75 percent of that transfer, but the available compute window caps hidden communication at 15 percent of raw transfer time)
Scaling efficiency: \(\ScalingEfficiency = \PerDeviceComputeTime/(\PerDeviceComputeTime+ \ExposedCommunicationTime)\), which is equation 2 with the per-device compute window \(\PerDeviceComputeTime= \IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) and the exposed term standing for \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime\). Here the numerator is 2.1 s and the complete denominator is 14 s, giving 15 percent. The exposed communication term already subtracts the hidden portion from the raw transfer time and includes collective synchronization; subtracting overlap again would double-count the same saving.

Systems insight: The low efficiency (15 percent) shows why naive data parallelism at this scale is insufficient. It is one operating point, fixed by 2M per update, 1,024 GPUs, and 15 percent overlap, not a universal threshold. Another cluster size requires recomputing per-device compute time, collective cost, overlap, and topology. Hierarchy-aware systems recover much of the lost efficiency by combining data parallelism with tensor parallelism, which communicates over NVLink, and pipeline parallelism, which overlaps computation with communication.




↩︎ The compute window that bounds how much of a collective can hide is established in Overlap limits and exposed communication.


The scaling efficiency of a run is set by the interaction between the model’s communication requirements and the infrastructure’s bandwidth hierarchy, not by the model architecture alone. Recovering the efficiency that pure data parallelism lost above means mapping each parallelism dimension onto the bandwidth tier that can carry its traffic. Section 6.6 works through three concrete configurations once tensor and pipeline parallelism have been developed.
The collective algorithm adds its own dependence on message size. Tree-based AllReduce reaches every rank in \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) steps and suits small, latency-bound messages, whereas large gradient buffers favor the bandwidth-optimal ring; message size, topology, and contention decide between them.


↩︎ The message size at which ring AllReduce overtakes tree AllReduce, derived from the latency and bandwidth terms of each algorithm, is established in The algorithm crossover point.
Even for pre-frontier transformers, those algorithm choices translate into substantial link-bandwidth requirements. BERT-Base (110M parameters) requires approximately 440 MB of gradient synchronization per iteration in FP32, while BERT-Large (340M parameters) requires approximately 1.4 GB. Because a ring AllReduce across 64 GPUs moves nearly twice the gradient bytes through each GPU’s link, finishing BERT-Large synchronization within 50 ms demands roughly 54 GB/s of sustained per-GPU bandwidth, and BERT-Base about a third of that. At 175B parameters, meeting the step budget requires combining 3D parallelism, gradient accumulation, and overlap rather than relying on a single flat collective, and whatever communication remains unhidden acts as the unscalable residual that Amdahl’s Law prices next.




Even a small unscalable cost in a single-device step eventually dominates distributed execution, because adding \(\DeviceCount\) devices shrinks the parallelizable compute share (\(\SingleDeviceRunTime / \DeviceCount\)) while leaving the fixed residual untouched. An Amdahl-style model separates that scalable work from the fixed residual fraction \(\SerialFraction\) of the single-device baseline (Amdahl's Law at fleet scale).
That baseline fraction is not the synchronization share a profiler reports for a distributed step (the distributed Amdahl pitfall of The Fleet Law), because the compute share has been divided by \(\DeviceCount\) while the residual has not. A residual of 1 percent of the single-device step occupies about 84 percent of each step on 512 GPUs. Reading the observed share as \(\SerialFraction\) would therefore overstate the residual many times over and predict a far lower speedup ceiling than the model implies.
Plotted on log-log axes up to 512 GPUs, the same fixed-residual model shows how much speedup each residual fraction gives up (figure 9), complementing the scaling efficiency bound (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)). In this illustrative model, a small baseline fraction (\(\SerialFraction= 0.1\%\)) stays closer to ideal scaling than a larger fraction (\(\SerialFraction= 1\%\)). A residual equal to a tenth of baseline time (\(\SerialFraction= 0.10\)) limits asymptotic speedup to \(1/\SerialFraction= 10\times\). Actual collective and coordination costs can change with worker count, so predicting a training run requires the full step-time accounting of equation 2.

Published benchmark runs show the same shortfall in practice. MLPerf Training times complete runs to a fixed quality target, and several submitters report the same system at several sizes within one round (Mattson et al. 2020; MLCommons 2025). Each of 5 such series for the GPT-3 and Llama 3.1 405B benchmarks falls below the ideal line drawn through its smallest configuration (figure 10). On NVIDIA’s Eos cluster, GPT-3 trained in about 58 minutes on 512 H100 GPUs and 3.9 minutes on 10,752. A 21× increase in accelerators therefore cut the time 14.9×, a scaling efficiency (equation 1, measured relative to the smallest configuration rather than one device) of 71 percent. Across the series, the largest configuration keeps 71–84 percent of ideal. Two effects compound in these numbers. Communication and coordination grow with worker count, and the larger configurations also train with larger global batches, which can require more samples to reach the target (section 6.4.6). Separating the two requires the step-level accounting of equation 2.

Predicting a run means pricing each term of equation 2 for the configuration at hand. For a large-message ring AllReduce, the communication term’s bandwidth contribution is \(\frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \frac{\DataVolume}{\LinkBandwidth}\). This is the fleet counterpart of the single-machine iron law’s data-movement ratio \(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\). Here \(\DataVolume\) is the payload being reduced (the gradient bytes \(\GradientPayload\) under data parallelism, or a shard of model state under sharding), and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is sustained per-link bandwidth. The expression omits per-message startup latency. Each wait must enter the accounting once.


↪ The single-machine iron law and its data-movement term are developed in Iron Law Mapping.


Communication energy climbs from HBM out to the network.

This communication overhead costs energy as well as wall-clock time, and the energy cost of communication grows with the physical distance between devices. At the scale of 10,000 GPUs, moving data is itself a power load. A full H100 NVLink envelope of roughly 9 PB/s at 7.5 pJ/bit represents about 540 kW before cooling and switch overhead. The smaller NDR InfiniBand envelope (500 TB/s at 35 pJ/bit) still represents about 140 kW. The per-boundary accounting behind these per-bit costs is developed in The Physics of Data Movement. Overlap hides communication time but not its energy, so avoiding unnecessary movement is the direct way to reduce the power term.
As the device count grows for a fixed workload, the balance can move from a linear scaling regime toward a communication-bound regime. The transition has no universal GPU count, because it depends on compute per device, message sizes, topology, and overlap. Coordination overhead becomes consequential when its exposed time is no longer small relative to useful computation. Measurements at the intended workload and placement must establish the efficiency curve.



More GPUs shrink each step’s compute, not its communication.
The efficiency metrics directly influence the choice of parallelism strategy. Data parallelism works well in the linear scaling regime but becomes communication bound at scale. The model-parallel strategies developed after this section replace part of that gradient traffic with other costs, which the same efficiency equation prices once each mechanism is in place. Hardware efficiency metrics govern throughput, yet convergence theory determines whether distributed training reaches the same solution quality as single-device training. Parallelism affects optimization convergence in three ways: convergence rate changes with batch size, adding workers yields diminishing returns beyond the critical batch size, and learning-rate schedules must be revalidated when the global batch changes.



Averaging gradients across \(\DeviceCount\) workers processes \(\DeviceCount\) times as many examples per step, but only reduces the number of steps to convergence when gradient noise—rather than loss curvature—is what holds back a larger step size. Formally, let \(\LossFunction\) be lower bounded by \(\LossLowerBound\) and have \(\SmoothnessConstant\)-Lipschitz gradients, so the smoothness constant limits how sharply the gradient can change as parameters move. Each worker computes gradients from \(\LocalBatchSize\) independent samples. At update \(\OptimizerStepIndex\), the aggregated estimator \(\MinibatchGradient_t\), the average of the \(\DeviceCount\) workers’ local gradients, is unbiased, and its conditional variance satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\|\MinibatchGradient_t-\nabla\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_t)\|^2\mid\ModelParameters_t]\leq\SampleGradientStandardDeviation^2/(\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize)\). When averaging reduces that noise, synchronous SGD makes steady progress toward parameters where the gradient is small. These assumptions bound progress toward a small gradient norm, not convergence to a global minimizer or a particular validation accuracy.

Theorem 6.1: Convergence rate for distributed SGDFor the update \(\ModelParameters_{t+1}=\ModelParameters_t-\LearningRate\MinibatchGradient_t\) with constant step size \(0<\LearningRate\leq 1/\SmoothnessConstant\), after \(\OptimizerUpdateCount\) synchronized updates,
\[
\frac{1}{\OptimizerUpdateCount}\sum_{t=0}^{\OptimizerUpdateCount-1}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\nabla\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_t)\|^2\right]
\leq
\underbrace{\frac{2\bigl(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_0)-\LossLowerBound\bigr)}{\LearningRate \OptimizerUpdateCount}}_{\text{optimization term}}
+
\underbrace{\frac{\LearningRate \SmoothnessConstant\SampleGradientStandardDeviation^2}{\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize}}_{\text{stochastic-variance term}}.
\]
Choosing \(\LearningRate=\min\!\left\{1/\SmoothnessConstant,\sqrt{2(\LossFunction(\ModelParameters_0)-\LossLowerBound)\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize/(\SmoothnessConstant\SampleGradientStandardDeviation^2\OptimizerUpdateCount)}\right\}\) balances the two terms. Before the smoothness cap becomes active, the stochastic contribution scales as \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\DeviceCount \LocalBatchSize \OptimizerUpdateCount})\).


The theorem isolates the benefit that follows from the assumptions. With equal local batch size \(\LocalBatchSize\), synchronous data-parallel SGD computes the same minibatch estimator as one worker using batch size \(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) for that update, and the estimator variance decreases as \(1/(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize)\). It does not say that every increase in batch size proportionally reduces time to a target loss; learning-rate limits and critical-batch-size effects still apply. This distinction is the statistical efficiency of distributed training, separate from hardware efficiency. Because the theorem assumes perfect synchronization (BSP), convergence guarantees degrade as staleness increases whenever workers proceed at different rates or apply stale gradients.



When a slow worker applies a gradient computed on an older parameter version, the update pushes the model along a direction that the current parameters may have already outgrown. The staleness parameter \(\GradientStaleness\) counts how many updates occur between computing and applying a gradient, tying the barrier savings of BSP, SSP, and ASP (section 6.3.1.5) to solution quality (Ho et al. 2013; Dutta et al. 2018). Because the damage from stale gradients depends on the objective, step-size schedule, worker count, and delay distribution, no single additive penalty applies across all runs.

Definition 6.5: Gradient staleness
Gradient staleness (\(\GradientStaleness\)) is the number of parameter updates that occur between the time a gradient is computed and the time it is applied to the global model state.

Significance: It represents the synchronization error in distributed optimization. Increasing \(\GradientStaleness\) can improve throughput by reducing barrier waits \((\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount))\), but it typically degrades the rate of convergence, requiring more optimizer steps, and therefore more FLOPs, to reach the same accuracy.
Distinction: Unlike network latency, which is a physical delay, staleness is an algorithmic offset that arises from the choice of synchronization protocol (e.g., ASP, SSP).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that staleness is “always bad.” In reality, it is a throughput-convergence trade-off: for some large-scale workloads, allowing bounded staleness is one practical way to keep thousands of GPUs in use.



The convergence behavior differs across these models in ways that directly affect training cost and solution quality. In BSP (\(\GradientStaleness=0\)), all workers compute on the same parameter version and aggregate before updating. Under the assumptions of theorem 6.1, the synchronized estimator inherits the \(\DeviceCount\times \LocalBatchSize\) minibatch guarantee.
SSP (\(\GradientStaleness\leq \StalenessBound\)) allows workers to proceed up to \(\StalenessBound\) iterations ahead of the slowest worker. Ho et al. (2013) bound the average regret of their SSP update sequence at \(\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{(\StalenessBound+1)\DeviceCount/\OptimizerUpdateCount})\) for \(\DeviceCount\) workers and \(\OptimizerUpdateCount\) updates. Average regret is the per-update gap between the loss its iterates incur and the loss of the best fixed parameters chosen in hindsight. The bound assumes convex Lipschitz component functions, a bounded domain, and a decreasing step size. It makes the staleness dependence explicit, since the bound grows with \(\StalenessBound\). It measures a different quantity from the gradient-norm bound of theorem 6.1, which covers nonconvex objectives, so the two rates cannot be compared directly.

Dutta, Sanghamitra, Gauri Joshi, Soumyadip Ghosh, Parijat Dube, and Priya Nagpurkar. 2018. “Slow and Stale Gradients Can Win the Race: Error-Runtime Trade-Offs in Distributed SGD.” Proceedings of the Twenty-First International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics 84: 803–12.
Asynchronous SGD imposes no protocol-wide finite delay bound. Removing the barrier can improve update throughput, but a convergence rate requires additional assumptions about realized delays, the objective, and the step-size schedule. Dutta et al. (2018) analyze this as an error-runtime trade-off in which worker speed and gradient staleness jointly determine whether accepting a delayed update helps. Therefore neither a fixed square-of-average-delay penalty nor the complete loss of \(\DeviceCount\)-worker variance reduction follows from asynchronous execution alone. The protocol fixes each model’s delay control, but the strength of its convergence guarantee depends on further assumptions (table 4).

Even under zero-staleness BSP (\(\GradientStaleness=0\) in table 4), scaling out across \(\DeviceCount\) workers changes the optimization trajectory whenever the global batch grows with the cluster. Multiplying the global batch by \(\BatchScalingFactor\) cuts the number of optimizer updates per epoch by the same factor, so keeping the single-GPU learning rate leaves the model under-trained, while jumping straight to a \(\BatchScalingFactor\)-fold larger step size can destabilize early epochs. Whenever data parallelism changes the effective batch size, the learning-rate schedule must be revalidated against the target quality; two scaling rules provide starting points for that adjustment.
The linear scaling rule (Goyal et al. 2017) proposes that when batch size is multiplied by \(\BatchScalingFactor\), learning rate also increases by \(\BatchScalingFactor\):
\[
\ScaledLearningRate = \BatchScalingFactor\cdot \BaseLearningRate\]
The approximation compares one large-batch step at learning rate \(\BatchScalingFactor\LearningRate\) with \(\BatchScalingFactor\) consecutive small-batch steps at learning rate \(\LearningRate\). At batch size \(\BatchScalingFactor\times \BatchSize\), independent gradient contributions reduce estimator variance by factor \(\BatchScalingFactor\), but lower variance alone does not establish stability. The approximation also requires gradients to change little over the corresponding \(\BatchScalingFactor\) small-batch steps. Goyal et al. (2017) validated the recipe for ResNet-50/ImageNet at global batch size 8,192 with gradual warmup. Layer-wise adaptive rate scaling (LARS) and layer-wise adaptive moments based optimizer (LAMB) provide related large-batch approaches for ImageNet and BERT-style pretraining (You et al. 2017; You et al. 2020). A warmup period increases the learning rate from \(\BaseLearningRate\) to \(\BatchScalingFactor\cdot \BaseLearningRate\) over the first \(\WarmupStepCount\) iterations to reduce early instability; the schedule still requires validation:
\[
\LearningRate_t = \BaseLearningRate+ \frac{\OptimizerStepIndex}{\WarmupStepCount}(\BatchScalingFactor\cdot \BaseLearningRate- \BaseLearningRate) \quad \text{for } \OptimizerStepIndex< \WarmupStepCount\]
The rule and the warmup were introduced together, and the run that introduced them shows why the scaled learning rate needs the warmup. A learning-rate schedule tuned for an eight-GPU run need not reach the same accuracy at 256 GPUs once the global batch grows with the worker count.

War Story 6.1: The one-hour ImageNet run (2017)Context: Facebook AI Research set out to train ResNet-50 on ImageNet in one hour using 256 GPUs, pushing data parallelism far beyond the batch sizes that earlier practice treated as safe (Goyal et al. 2017).
Mechanism: Scaling the global batch to 8,192 cut the number of optimizer updates per epoch by the same factor. Keeping the small-batch learning rate left too few effective updates to reach the target accuracy, while scaling the learning rate up by the same factor destabilized optimization in the first epochs, when the loss surface changes fastest.
Impact: Without the gradual warmup recipe, the large-batch runs reported higher training and validation error than the small-batch baseline. Higher hardware throughput alone did not preserve the quality target.
Fix: The team introduced the linear learning-rate scaling rule paired with a 5-epoch gradual warmup schedule, stabilizing optimization at batch size 8,192.
Systems lesson: Distributed training demands more than parallel hardware alone. Scaling changes the optimization regime, so the cluster, communication schedule, batch size, and learning-rate schedule must be tuned as one system.


The square root scaling rule is an alternative learning-rate heuristic to test when increasing batch size:
\[
\ScaledLearningRate = \sqrt{\BatchScalingFactor} \cdot \BaseLearningRate\]
This rule increases the learning rate more slowly than linear scaling. Its suitability depends on the optimizer, schedule, and training regime; exceeding a critical-batch estimate does not make it mandatory or guarantee convergence. The learning rate must be validated against the same target quality.
LARS (You et al. 2017) scales each layer’s update relative to its weight norm. The simplified LARS expression below illustrates the ratio of weight norm to gradient norm with weight decay. LAMB (You et al. 2020) applies a related layer-wise adaptation to an Adam-based update rather than using this raw-gradient denominator:
\[
\LearningRate_\ell = \LarsGlobalLearningRate\cdot \frac{\|\LayerWeights_\ell\|}{\|\MinibatchGradient_\ell\| + \WeightPenaltyStrength\|\LayerWeights_\ell\|}
\]
Here \(\WeightPenaltyStrength\) is the weight-decay coefficient in the illustrated LARS expression, distinct from the failure-rate parameter used in reliability analysis. Layer-wise scaling controls update magnitude relative to parameter magnitude, but does not guarantee convergence for arbitrary batches. Its systems role is to extend the range of validated batch sizes over which added data-parallel workers can reduce time to quality.



Increasing the global batch eventually yields diminishing reductions in the optimization steps needed to reach a fixed target quality. The critical batch size \(\CriticalBatchSize\) marks the transition point beyond which increasing batch size yields diminishing returns in convergence per sample seen.

Definition 6.6: Critical batch size
Critical batch size \((\CriticalBatchSize)\) is a workload-dependent crossover batch size beyond which further batch growth yields diminishing reductions in optimization steps per added sample (McCandlish et al. 2018; Shallue et al. 2019).

Significance: It characterizes statistical scaling, separately from hardware throughput. In the gradient-noise model, batches well below \(\CriticalBatchSize\) can reduce step count approximately in proportion to batch growth; above it, additional samples buy progressively smaller step-count reductions.
Distinction: Unlike the memory-limited batch size (determined by memory capacity and activation footprint), the critical batch size depends on the model, data, optimizer, training phase, and target quality.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that training can be sped up indefinitely by adding GPUs. In reality, \(\CriticalBatchSize\) is a guide to diminishing statistical returns, not a hard physical ceiling or a universal optimum in wall-clock time.




Shallue, Christopher J, Jaehoon Lee, Joseph Antognini, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, Roy Frostig, and George E Dahl. 2019. “Measuring the Effects of Data Parallelism on Neural Network Training.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 20: 1–49.
The gradient-noise-scale proxy for the critical batch size can be estimated as:
\[
\CriticalBatchSize\approx \frac{\text{tr}(\GradientCovarianceMatrix)}{\|\nabla \LossFunction(\ModelParameters)\|^2}
\]
where \(\text{tr}(\GradientCovarianceMatrix)\) is the trace of the gradient covariance matrix (total gradient variance) and \(\|\nabla \LossFunction(\ModelParameters)\|^2\) is the squared gradient norm (signal strength). Intuitively, \(\CriticalBatchSize\) is the batch size at which averaging reduces gradient variance to the level of the true gradient magnitude.
Published large-batch regimes illustrate the scale rather than providing fixed thresholds. On ImageNet, Goyal et al. (2017) stabilized ResNet-50 at global batch 8,192 with warmup, and LARS extends ImageNet large-batch training further in some settings (You et al. 2017). For BERT-Large pretraining, LAMB reports training at 32K–64K batch sizes with layer-wise adaptive updates (You et al. 2020). Across other domains, McCandlish et al. (2018) show useful batch-size limits ranging from tens of thousands in ImageNet-like settings to millions in reinforcement-learning workloads, so new frontier-language-model thresholds should be measured rather than copied.

The gradient-noise model separates statistical efficiency from hardware efficiency. Well below \(\CriticalBatchSize\), increasing batch size can reduce optimization steps almost proportionally while preserving similar total sample use. Near \(\CriticalBatchSize\), the trade-off between fewer updates and more samples becomes material. Above it, step count approaches a lower limit while sample use continues to increase. Neither maximum samples per second nor minimum training time necessarily occurs at \(\CriticalBatchSize\): those objectives also depend on device utilization, communication, and the validated learning-rate schedule.
On log-log axes, the gradient-noise trade-off appears as a divergence between optimization step count and total sample consumption (figure 11). Below the critical threshold (\(\BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize< 1\)), increasing batch size yields near-linear reductions in optimization steps with negligible sample waste. Past the crossover point at \(\BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize= 1\) (where both normalized costs equal 2), the step count curve asymptotically flattens toward 1 while total examples processed climb steeply along the \(1 + \BatchSize/\CriticalBatchSize\) trajectory.

Dividing the critical batch by the per-worker batch \(\LocalBatchSize\) estimates where worker growth leaves the near-proportional statistical scaling regime. With one local batch per update and its size held fixed, the crossover occurs around \(\DeviceCount\approx \CriticalBatchSize/\LocalBatchSize\) workers. Past that point, additional workers mainly raise sample throughput that the optimizer cannot convert into proportionally fewer steps. Gradient accumulation increases each worker’s contribution per update and lowers the corresponding worker count. Shrinking \(\LocalBatchSize\) moves the crossover outward but leaves less computation per worker to hide communication, coupling statistical and hardware efficiency.
That crossover informs a cost-time trade-off rather than setting a mandatory worker count. Larger batches may still reduce time to target even as they consume more examples. That benefit must be established with measured step time and a validated learning-rate schedule at the same target quality. Changing synchronization or compression also changes the optimization process, so its communication savings must be weighed against any additional steps required.

Moving a job along this cost-time frontier requires shrinking each message, synchronizing less often, or relaxing the global reduction topology. Instead of shrinking each payload, Local SGD lowers synchronization frequency by letting workers perform \(\LocalUpdateCount\) local updates before averaging, which cuts collective calls per local update by a factor of \(\LocalUpdateCount\). Results for smooth, strongly convex objectives can recover synchronous SGD’s asymptotic rate under specified learning-rate and local-update-interval conditions (Stich 2019), so the synchronization interval remains part of the convergence contract rather than an unrestricted communication saving.
Where Local SGD keeps a global AllReduce at wider intervals, Decentralized SGD replaces the global collective with sparse neighbor exchanges along a communication graph. Immediate bandwidth demand drops, at the cost of taking additional rounds to spread information across the group. Graph connectivity, link service time, and the optimization effect of delayed mixing determine whether that trade-off helps a geographically distributed workload.
Choosing among these three levers depends on which bottleneck binds and how many extra iterations the altered update costs. Each candidate must be judged by measured time to the same target quality. A narrower numeric format offers one more way to shrink the payload without changing the collective schedule, under conditions that FP8 makes precise.



Running matrix multiplications in 8-bit floating point (FP8) accelerates local compute, which can make a distributed job more communication-bound if gradients still cross the network in 16-bit precision. Compute precision and communication precision are separate choices: casting GEMM operands to half as many bytes reduces operand storage and local memory traffic, but it halves a collective payload only when the communication path explicitly transmits that narrower representation.


↩︎ The throughput that narrower precisions buy on current accelerators is established in Precision and throughput trade-offs.
FP8 matters to distributed training only after four dtypes are distinguished: the stored parameter dtype, the GEMM operand dtype, the accumulator or master-state dtype, and the collective wire dtype. Traditional mixed-precision training commonly retains FP32 optimizer or master state while using FP16/BF16 operands. FP8-capable accelerators add E4M3 (four exponent bits and three mantissa bits) and E5M2 (five exponent bits and two mantissa bits) operand formats optimized for different tensor distributions (Micikevicius et al. 2022).
The two FP8 formats trade precision against range. E4M3 keeps an extra mantissa bit for scaled weights and activations, which cluster within a predictable range, while E5M2 keeps an extra exponent bit for scaled gradients, which can span many orders of magnitude during backpropagation. Because tensor magnitudes drift during training, each tensor is multiplied before conversion by a scale, commonly derived from its recent maximum absolute value, a policy called dynamic scaling. Neither the format nor the scaling policy guarantees that every value survives conversion, so training quality must be validated for each workload.


↪ Per-parameter training memory under each of these formats is collected for reference in Numeric Precision and Training Memory.

Micikevicius, Paulius, Dusan Stosic, Neil Burgess, Marius Cornea, Pradeep Dubey, Richard Grisenthwaite, Sangwon Ha, et al. 2022. “FP8 Formats for Deep Learning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2209.05433.
An FP8 training contract pairs FP32 master or optimizer state and FP8 GEMM operands with higher-precision accumulation, and it can approach FP16 training quality on suitable workloads (Micikevicius et al. 2022). FP8 halves bytes only for tensors actually stored or transmitted in FP8, so a collective that reduces FP16 gradients still moves FP16 bytes even when every preceding GEMM ran in FP8. FP8 therefore earns its place in distributed training when lower-precision compute shortens the local critical path, or when an explicit communication cast shrinks payloads while the accumulation and scaling policy protects convergence. It changes representation, not the parallelization axis. Compression, local updates, and narrower formats all make each data-parallel step cheaper, yet none of them partitions an individual layer or its activations; that remaining capacity constraint motivates model parallelism.

Sharded data parallelism distributes stored state but still asks each worker to execute every layer on its local examples. If one layer’s gathered parameters and working memory exceed device capacity, or its execution is too slow for the target schedule, splitting that computation becomes a candidate. Model parallelism addresses this form of the memory capacity gap (principle \(\ref{pri-memory-capacity-gap}\)) by assigning different computations to different devices. Its value must be compared with offload, recomputation, and smaller local batches under the same throughput and quality requirements.

Definition 6.7: Model parallelism
Model parallelism is a distributed training strategy that partitions a single neural network’s parameters or operations across multiple devices so each device computes a distinct portion of the model.

Significance: If a model with parameter state \(\WeightMemory\) is split across \(\TensorParallelDegree \PipelineParallelDegree\) model-parallel devices, the ideal per-device parameter footprint falls toward \(\WeightMemory/(\TensorParallelDegree \PipelineParallelDegree)\), enabling training of models that exceed single-device memory. The cost is extra communication for activations and gradients plus idle time from sequential dependencies, so the memory gain must exceed the transfer and pipeline-bubble overhead introduced by the partition.
Distinction: Unlike data parallelism, which replicates the full model on every worker and shards the minibatch, model parallelism shards the model itself. Pipeline parallelism and tensor parallelism are implementation forms of model parallelism: one partitions layers into stages, while the other partitions individual tensor operations.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that model parallelism automatically speeds up training. Its primary benefit is capacity, not throughput; without careful scheduling and overlap, downstream devices wait for upstream activations and utilization can fall below a single-device baseline.






Weights are only a small slice of the full Adam training state.
Memory fit alone does not settle whether a model needs this kind of partition. For a 175B-parameter model, weights alone occupy 350 GB, or about 5.5 GB per GPU across a 64-GPU group, one-sixteenth of the 1,024-GPU reference cluster. Full mixed-precision Adam training state is much larger, 2,800 GB globally, yet ZeRO-3 across the same 64 GPUs reduces it to roughly 43.8 GB per GPU before activations, which fits an 80 GB accelerator. ZeRO-3 can therefore make the static state fit, as the notebook below confirms. It pays for that fit in traffic, because every step regathers every layer’s parameters across the data-parallel fabric, roughly three times the model’s parameter bytes per worker (section 6.3.3). It also cannot split an individual layer’s computation or activations across devices. Tensor parallelism addresses both limits by partitioning individual weight matrices across devices, using the column-then-row pairing of figure 16, detailed in section 6.5.3, which confines collective communication to block boundaries. Pipeline parallelism instead stages sequential layers across devices (section 6.5.2).
Activations add a separate memory requirement. Under the earlier unchecked-storage assumptions, a 2048-token sequence through 175B parameters produces roughly 1.1 TB at a local batch of 4 sequences; optimizer sharding does not reduce that storage. Recomputation trades memory for extra FLOPs, partitioning distributes activations, and offload moves them to another memory tier. Kernel and batch-size choices also change the budget. Full activation checkpointing brings the same modeled case down to ~19.3 GB. The following notebook, which uses a single-sequence local batch, checks whether ZeRO-3 plus checkpointing fits the model without partitioning its computation.

Math:

Parameter storage: 175B params \(\times\) 2 bytes (FP16) = 350 GB.
Gradients and optimizer state: Gradients add 175B params \(\times\) 2 bytes = 350 GB, while Adam FP32 master weights, momentum, and variance add 175B params \(\times\) 12 bytes = 2,100 GB.
Total static memory: 2,800 GB.
ZeRO-3 sharding: With 64 GPUs, per-GPU static memory = 2,800 GB/64 GPUs \(\approx\) 43.8 GB.

Systems insight: 43.8 GB (static) + 4.8 GB (dynamic) = 48.6 GB. Under this simplified accounting, ZeRO-3 plus full activation checkpointing fits within the 80 GB A100 capacity, leaving material headroom for framework buffers and transient layer gathers. If those additional allocations exceed the remaining HBM, the design can reduce the local batch, offload state, increase the sharding degree, or add tensor or pipeline parallelism; tensor parallelism is not the only recourse.


In this example, sharding and checkpointing make the modeled state fit, leaving two distinct reasons to partition the model itself. One is regather traffic: on the 1,024-GPU reference cluster, ZeRO-3 moves about 1.1 TB per worker per step for this model, which on one NDR InfiniBand port takes about 10× as long as the step’s computation. The other is layer execution, since full sharding gathers parameters on demand without ever splitting a single layer’s computation or activations across devices. Model parallelism instead cuts the computation graph directly, either between sequential layer groups (such as layers 1–4 and layers 5–8) or inside a layer across channels and attention heads. Layer cuts introduce pipeline dependencies that leave downstream devices idle while an upstream stage computes, creating the pipeline bubble that governs utilization for this partition. Channel and head cuts instead expose concurrent work within a layer at the price of intra-layer exchanges. Other workloads still need these cuts to fit peak memory capacity.
These cuts enable the large-scale cases that exceed a single device for different reasons. GPT-3, with 175B parameters, was trained with model parallelism within each matrix multiplication and across layers (Brown et al. 2020), avoiding a full-parameter regather on every step. Vision transformers processing high-resolution \(16\Glyph{k}{\times}16\Glyph{k}\) pixel images use model parallelism to bound activation memory. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, whose sparsely activated feed-forward blocks are developed in section 6.5.5, distribute their conditional computation paths across hardware (Shazeer et al. 2017; Lepikhin et al. 2021; Fedus et al. 2022).

Each partitioning strategy trades single-device memory overflow for a different systems cost: layer-wise partitioning pays in idle time, pipeline parallelism pays in scheduling complexity to hide that idle time, and tensor parallelism pays in NVLink bandwidth to split individual layers. Sequence and context parallelism, expert parallelism, and sparse embedding sharding then extend the same trade-off to long-context activations, sparsely activated experts, and sparsely touched embedding tables.
