Even when a framework makes switching from single-node DDP to multi-node execution a one-line configuration change, the underlying physics still governs the step time. In the GPT-2 scale-out of notebook 6.1 and notebook 6.2, moving the same model from one NVLink node to four Ethernet-connected nodes quadrupled the GPU count but cut parallel efficiency from 99.4 percent to 27.9 percent. The following misconceptions generalize that error, each treating one term of the step-time accounting as if it were the whole budget.

Fallacy: Linear speedup is achievable with sufficient engineering effort.
Amdahl’s Law limits speedup when a fixed serial component remains exposed. Synchronous gradient aggregation creates an update dependency, but some of its work can overlap backward computation. As section 6.4 shows, \(\ScalingEfficiency = 1/(1 + \DeviceCount(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime)/\IronLawComputeTime)\) depends on the exposed overhead relative to useful compute as \(\DeviceCount\) changes. A 1,000-GPU allocation therefore does not by itself justify a 1,000\(\times\) speedup forecast. Local kernel efficiency, memory feasibility, communication, and convergence must be evaluated against the specified baseline. Linear scaling is a result to demonstrate for an operating range, not a return guaranteed by device count.


Pitfall: Optimizing MFU without considering scaling efficiency.
A single-node MFU measurement does not predict fleet throughput by itself. For a fixed workload and hardware peak convention, scaling efficiency compares measured distributed throughput with ideal replication of that single-node baseline. Multiplying the baseline MFU by this scaling efficiency gives distributed MFU; multiplying an already measured distributed MFU by the same scaling efficiency counts communication and synchronization losses twice. The chapter’s own numbers make the difference concrete. A single node running at 50 percent MFU, scaled with the 83 percent scaling efficiency of the overlapped TP-8 layout in section 6.6, delivers about 41 percent MFU across the fleet. A planner who measures that 41 percent on the full cluster and then applies the 83 percent again would budget for about 34 percent and buy capacity the job does not need. Capacity planning must state the device count and measurement window for each metric. Checkpointing, recovery, and replay require additional accounting only when those losses fall outside that window. Useful goodput must count retained model progress rather than repeated work, under the accounting boundaries of Accounting boundaries.


Fallacy: Hyperparameters tuned on small clusters transfer directly to large-scale training.
Engineers tune hyperparameters on 8-GPU workstations then deploy to 256-GPU clusters expecting identical behavior. At scale, convergence behavior changes. The most sensitive hyperparameter is learning rate. As section 6.3 explains, global batch increases with GPU count when local batch and accumulation depth remain fixed, so the learning-rate schedule must be revalidated. The linear scaling rule of section 6.4.5, which the one-hour ImageNet run established, suggests \(\ScaledLearningRate = \BaseLearningRate\times (\ScaledBatchSize/\BaseBatchSize)\), but this relationship holds only within bounds. As models scale, they eventually encounter the critical batch size of section 6.4.6, where adding more data per step yields diminishing returns in convergence.
Beyond the critical batch size, this relationship breaks down in a model-, data-, and optimizer-dependent way. A team that takes a small-cluster learning rate, multiplies it mechanically with GPU count, and jumps directly to a much larger global batch may see lower final quality or slower sample efficiency even though hardware throughput improved. Warmup schedules, weight decay adjustment, layer-wise optimizers such as LARS/LAMB, and careful momentum tuning can recover accuracy in some regimes, but require systematic experimentation at target scale. Organizations that skip these scaling studies waste thousands of GPU-hours on suboptimal runs.


Pitfall: Adding GPUs to data-parallel jobs without modeling communication.
More GPUs improve time to target only if the gain in processing rate outweighs communication overhead and any additional sample use. With fixed local batch size, adding data-parallel workers increases the global batch; fixing the global batch instead reduces local work and can expose more communication. The critical-batch analysis in section 6.4.6 supplies a workload-dependent statistical guide, not universal GPU-count or model-size thresholds. Compare complete learning curves and cost at the same target quality before committing to a larger allocation.


Fallacy: Memory capacity alone determines the parallelism strategy.
A model that exceeds device capacity needs a feasible partition, but memory fit does not select the fastest one. Tensor parallelism exchanges partial results within layers, while pipeline parallelism transfers stage-boundary activations and introduces scheduling bubbles. Their relative cost depends on layer shapes, microbatch count, placement, and overlap. Compare complete training-state and activation budgets together with measured time to target; an unsupported throughput percentage or a weights-only fit cannot settle the choice.


Pitfall: Applying FSDP or ZeRO without measuring efficiency trade-offs.
Engineers adopt FSDP universally after reading that it “reduces memory and enables larger models.” Sharding trades memory capacity for communication overhead: full-shard FSDP gathers parameters before layer execution and reduces gradient shards during backward, with another parameter gather when the forward pass resharded them. The relevant comparison begins with the complete training-state budget. Under the mixed-precision Adam convention established here, the 7B worked example exceeds single-device capacity before activations, so standard DDP cannot fit that state on an A100-80 GB. A weights-only fit does not establish a feasible training baseline. When the complete state, activations, and workspaces fit without sharding, DDP can avoid the repeated gathers; when they exceed the 80 GB capacity, the comparison must include a feasible alternative such as sharding or offload. FSDP provides value when it enables training at all or when the larger local batch it permits offsets its communication cost. ZeRO-Offload extends capacity through CPU memory but adds transfers of its own. The decision therefore requires measuring peak memory and exposed communication for the same workload and optimizer contract.


Fallacy: Parallelism overhead is roughly constant regardless of model size.
Engineers benchmark parallelism strategies on convenient small models then apply those conclusions to large-scale training. For dense transformers at fixed tokens per update, computation and gradient bytes both grow roughly proportionally with parameter count, as the earlier scaling analysis established. Larger parameter count alone therefore does not imply a better computation-to-communication ratio. Architecture, sequence length, local batch size, partition degree, and kernel efficiency determine how much useful work each rank performs; gradient representation and process-group membership determine how much it communicates. A larger model can also require a different partition that introduces new layer collectives or pipeline bubbles. Reliable strategy selection holds the workload and target quality explicit, then recomputes memory fit, local compute time, communication volume, and the available overlap window at the target scale. A small-model benchmark becomes transferable evidence only when those governing terms remain comparable.


Pitfall: Treating scaling efficiency as a property of the hardware alone.
A vendor benchmark might report 85 percent scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs, and procurement teams then plan capacity as if that number were a cluster constant. Scaling efficiency is a joint property of four things: the workload’s communication-to-computation ratio, the parallelism strategy (data, pipeline, tensor, hybrid), the network topology (fat-tree vs. torus vs. dragonfly), and the software stack (NCCL version, kernel fusion, overlap quality). Reference numbers from dense large-language-model benchmarks transfer poorly to other workloads and fabrics. They may overstate scaling for graph neural networks with irregular communication and for embedding-heavy recommendation models, whose AllToAll embedding exchanges and many small random lookups load the fabric differently from dense gradient AllReduce (section 6.5.6). They also say nothing about a commodity-Ethernet placement like the GPT-2 scale-out, which lost most of its parallel efficiency on leaving the node. Capacity planning should use measured scaling on the target workload, not a vendor hero benchmark.


Fallacy: Gradient accumulation is free.
Gradient accumulation can reduce synchronization from every microstep to once per window of \(\AccumulationStepCount\) microsteps, eliminating \((\AccumulationStepCount-1)/\AccumulationStepCount\) of those synchronization events when the implementation defers reduction. The saving has costs. A resident gradient buffer remains live throughout the accumulation window; for the 7B model, the FP16 buffer occupies 14 GB. Retaining graphs across microsteps or increasing the local batch size can add activation pressure. Accumulating eight microsteps makes updates 8\(\times\) less frequent per processed microstep, but wall-clock spacing also depends on the communication saved. Larger effective batches can change convergence, and narrow accumulation formats can lose small contributions or overflow. The dtype, loss normalization, and reduction schedule must therefore be validated at the intended batch size. Accumulation trades communication frequency against update spacing, memory residency, and numerical stability.

Scaling laws keep pushing frontier training budgets past what one machine can hold or finish in time, and distributed training is how the fleet absorbs that growth. It confronts the scaling wall, the workload-dependent operating point beyond which communication and coordination can consume the compute time saved by adding accelerators. A feasible design must preserve the intended optimization update while satisfying model-state, activation, batch-size, and interconnect constraints. Hardware throughput alone is insufficient; the comparison must also account for time to the target model quality.
Each partition relocates cost along the C³ axes. Data parallelism divides compute across replicas and pays in communication, the gradient aggregation whose exposed share set the scaling efficiency of the 175B communication example. Tensor parallelism divides work inside a layer and pays in communication on the critical path, which confines it to a fast domain. Pipeline parallelism divides layer depth and pays mostly in coordination, the fill and drain bubble that only more microbatches, better balance, or a smarter schedule can shrink. The 3D parallelism cube in figure 2 unites these trade-offs in one coordinate space (\(\DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\)). A feasible point must satisfy peak memory and global-batch constraints as well as communication and coordination budgets.
Sharding and model partitioning make different parts of the training state fit, while synchronization and precision policies determine whether the resulting updates remain useful. Hybrid layouts compose these choices within the bandwidth hierarchy. The alignment workload extends the same reasoning to multiple models and alternating generation and update phases, where peak memory depends on which state is live together.
The chapter’s strategies are complementary dimensions of one design space rather than alternatives. Systems such as Megatron-LM map tensor, pipeline, data, and expert exchanges to the communication domains that can carry them, and that matching is what delays the communication-bound regime as the fleet grows. The workload archetypes weight those dimensions differently. Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) combines dense-model partitioning with state sharding and, at long contexts, sequence or context partitioning. Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) shards sparse embedding state and pays in lookup traffic rather than layer collectives. Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) moves the coordination problem onto unreliable edge devices. In each case the binding constraint, not the archetype label, selects the configuration.

Key Takeaways: Parallelism relocates overhead

Splitting work moves the bottleneck: Distributed training does not make the underlying computation smaller; it converts memory pressure into communication volume, synchronization delay, or idle pipeline time (principle \(\ref{pri-scaling-efficiency}\)). The winning strategy is the split that sends overhead to the least binding part of the fleet.
The slowest worker sets synchronous step time: Under bulk-synchronous updates every step waits for its last required contribution, so a rare per-worker delay becomes a near-certain per-step delay at thousands of workers. Stale and asynchronous protocols trade that waiting for staleness, which can cost extra steps to the same target quality.
Throughput must serve convergence: Larger global batches can improve hardware efficiency while yielding diminishing progress per sample. Compare time to the same target quality, and treat the critical-batch estimate as a workload-dependent guide for selecting batch size and update schedules.
Sharding buys memory with messages: ZeRO and FSDP partition optimizer state, gradients, and parameters (principle \(\ref{pri-memory-capacity-gap}\)), reducing replicated storage. Peak memory must still include activations, temporary gathers, and workspaces; exposed ReduceScatter and AllGather costs determine whether the capacity gain also improves throughput.
Tensor parallelism needs a fast domain: Splitting operations inside layers creates frequent communication on the dependency path. Place those groups on links with sufficient bandwidth and low latency; the relevant boundary is the communication domain, which may span nodes, rather than the server enclosure.
Pipeline parallelism trades bytes for bubbles: Layer staging reduces communication frequency, but fill and drain slots leave accelerators idle (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)). Microbatching with \(\MicrobatchCount\gg \PipelineParallelDegree\) is the mechanism that turns model depth into throughput rather than pipeline slack.
Hybrid layouts are joint decisions: Combine only the partitioning and sharding strategies needed to satisfy the workload’s constraints (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)). Model divisibility, batch size, peak memory, communication groups, and failure domains must form one feasible configuration; improving one axis can expose a limit on another.



The displacement of overhead (principle \(\ref{pri-conservation-overhead}\)) makes a feasible partition the beginning of the design problem. A memory-saving split is useful only if its communication and schedule still meet the run’s time-to-quality budget. Every mechanism in this chapter shrinks the per-device compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) or the per-device training state, and pays for it in \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), in \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) through barriers, stragglers, and pipeline bubbles, or in lost overlap. In C³ terms, no partition removes the overhead of scale; it only relocates that overhead among compute, communication, and coordination. The engineering judgment is therefore to compare complete configurations, including their exposed dependencies, rather than optimize each parallelism axis independently.

What’s Next: From logic to resilienceThe fleet now has its traffic patterns (communication) and its logic (parallelism). Every configuration in this chapter, however, assumed that all ranks in each communication group arrive, on time and with correct data. A collective is not a barrier, but each dependent consumer still waits for every contribution, so one crashed node, failed link, or GPU that slows down without failing stalls the whole synchronous group. A contribution corrupted in transit is reduced into every replica’s update. Across thousands of accelerators such events stop being rare. Fault Tolerance begins by computing how often they arrive, then builds the checkpointing, recovery, and elastic training that keep the computation making progress on imperfect hardware.

Answer: The 16-byte-per-parameter state totals \(175\times10^9\times16=2{,}800\) GB. Tensor parallelism alone leaves \(2{,}800/8=350\) GB per GPU, exceeding 80 GB. Adding 16 balanced pipeline stages reduces the static state to \(2{,}800/(8\times16)=21.875\) GB per GPU. Activations, temporary parameter gathers, communication buffers, and uneven layer placement require additional headroom.
Learning Objective: Calculate per-GPU static memory requirements in a 3D hybrid parallelism configuration
**For one rank in a balanced 3D layout with eight transformer layers per pipeline stage, 32 microbatches per update, two tensor-parallel reductions per layer in each pass, and one unbucketed data-parallel reduction after accumulation, order these communication patterns by invocation count per update, highest to lowest:


Data-parallel gradient reduction
Tensor-parallel reductions
Pipeline stage-boundary transfers**

Answer: (2) -> (3) -> (1). Tensor reductions recur within each layer of each microbatch. Pipeline transfers recur at stage boundaries for each microbatch. The specified unbucketed data-parallel reduction occurs once after accumulation. This ordering depends on the supplied layer count, schedule, and bucketing; it is not a universal ranking of bandwidth demand or exposed time.
Learning Objective: Compare communication invocation counts under an explicitly specified hybrid schedule

In a 16,384-GPU cluster configured with \(\text{TP}=8\), \(\text{PP}=16\), and \(\text{DP}=128\), how many GPUs participate in each individual data-parallel AllReduce communicator group?

\(16{,}384\text{ GPUs}\), because all accelerators in the cluster must synchronize in a single global collective
\(128\text{ GPUs}\), because each rank communicates only with its corresponding tensor-and-pipeline shard position across the 128 model replicas
\(8\text{ GPUs}\), matching the tensor-parallel degree within each local node
\(16\text{ GPUs}\), matching the pipeline stage depth across the cluster spine

Answer: The correct answer is B. In 3D parallelism, the cluster contains \(\text{DP}=128\) complete model replicas, each partitioned across \(\text{TP} \times \text{PP} = 8 \times 16 = 128\) distinct shard positions. For each shard position, the corresponding rank in every replica forms an independent data-parallel group of 128 GPUs that AllReduces its specific parameter shard. Participating in a single global collective of 16,384 GPUs would discard 3D partitioning. Confining DP groups to 8 or 16 GPUs confuses data-parallel replica count with tensor or pipeline dimensions.
Learning Objective: Analyze communicator group sizes and partitioning in a large-scale 3D parallelism cluster
True or False: A uniform fat-tree network topology providing equal bisection bandwidth between all node pairs is always more cost-effective than a rail-optimized topology when training large language models with hierarchy-aware 3D parallelism.
Answer: False. A rail-optimized fabric can reduce hardware and cabling costs when its connectivity matches the intended pipeline and data-parallel groups. The saving requires a workload and placement comparison; expert AllToAll traffic, mixed jobs, routing constraints, and contention can change the required fabric. Neither topology is always more cost-effective.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how network topology design interacts with hierarchy-aware parallelism communication locality

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why does Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in multi-model RLHF create an infrastructure asymmetry challenge that does not exist in standard pretraining?

It combines policy and value-model training with policy-generated autoregressive rollouts and forward-only scoring by frozen reference and reward models.
All four models in PPO must be trained with identical optimizer hyperparameters on the same GPU
PPO requires all models to be converted to INT4 precision to enable cross-node gradient synchronization
PPO eliminates backward passes entirely, turning distributed training into a stateless inference service

Answer: The correct answer is A. The policy generates autoregressive rollouts, requiring a generation-time KV cache; policy and value updates require backward passes and optimizer state. Frozen reference and reward models score generated sequences without generating those sequences themselves. These phases have different memory and compute demands. Freezing scoring models does not eliminate the policy and value-model training work.
Learning Objective: Analyze the infrastructure asymmetry between training and inference models in multi-model RLHF
Explain how Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) simplifies cluster infrastructure compared to PPO, detailing which models and computational phases are eliminated.
Answer: Standard offline DPO removes separate reward and value models and online autoregressive rollouts from the update loop. It trains on fixed preference pairs using a policy and a frozen reference, whose scores may be precomputed. Static-state savings depend on the PPO model sizes and placement. Removing rollout KV state eliminates a generation peak; it does not by itself enlarge update microbatches because both methods still need policy activations and other live buffers.
Learning Objective: Compare the memory and execution pipeline requirements of PPO and DPO alignment architectures
During the autoregressive generation phase of PPO alignment for a 70B-parameter model, which growing runtime state can limit generation concurrency in accelerator memory?

FP32 Adam momentum and variance buffers stored on CPU hosts
Key-Value (KV) cache memory in GPU HBM, bounded by memory bandwidth during token-by-token generation
AllReduce gradient communication buffers across InfiniBand switches
Host filesystem NVMe write bandwidth for checkpoint dumping

Answer: The correct answer is B. The KV cache grows with concurrent sequence count, context length, layer count, and KV-head width. It can limit how many rollouts fit beside model weights and other resident state. Small-batch decoding is often memory-bandwidth bound, but cache capacity and compute limits must be evaluated separately. Optimizer buffers and checkpoint I/O do not explain this per-sequence growth.
Learning Objective: Identify the binding resource bottleneck during the generation phase of online RLHF
The scheduling approach in RLHF distributed systems where the accelerator fleet alternates between an autoregressive rollout phase dominated by KV cache memory and a backward training phase dominated by matrix GEMM compute is known as ____.
Answer: temporal multiplexing. Temporal multiplexing reconfigures hardware resources dynamically between inference-shaped sequence generation and training-shaped gradient backpropagation.
Learning Objective: Define temporal multiplexing as the scheduling strategy for alternating execution phases in RLHF
True or False: Because Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) eliminates reward and value models and avoids online sequence generation, it is strictly superior to PPO for all model alignment and exploration tasks.
Answer: False. DPO is restricted to optimizing against a static offline dataset of preference pairs, preventing the policy from generating novel outputs and exploring beyond the provided data. For tasks requiring iterative self-improvement and exploration (such as multi-step mathematical reasoning), PPO’s online rollout and reward feedback loop can discover superior trajectories, justifying its higher infrastructure overhead.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the functional trade-offs between static DPO optimization and dynamic PPO exploration

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

According to the chapter’s parallelism decision framework, which condition indicates that standard DistributedDataParallel (DDP) is a sensible baseline to evaluate over FSDP, TP, or PP?

The model’s single layer weight matrices exceed the HBM capacity of an individual GPU
The cluster is connected by slow 10 Gb/s commodity Ethernet across 1,024 nodes
The entire model state (parameters, gradients, and optimizer state) fits comfortably within single-device memory with sufficient headroom for activations
The model architecture contains sparse Mixture-of-Experts routing layers

Answer: The correct answer is C. Comfortable full-state and activation fit makes DDP a sensible baseline because it avoids sharded parameter reconstruction and pipeline bubbles. Memory fit alone does not prove maximum throughput; exposed communication and useful batch size still need evaluation. An oversized layer makes tensor parallelism a candidate, while offload or recomputation may enable other layouts. Slow Ethernet requires a workload-specific communication budget; accumulation or a faster fabric may help. Sparse MoE routing motivates evaluating expert placement and its AllToAll demand.
Learning Objective: Identify the binding constraint criteria that validate using standard Data Parallelism
An engineering team observes that an 8-GPU training job using pure pipeline parallelism achieves only 35 percent Model Flops Utilization (MFU), while interconnect links are largely idle. Using the bubble formula \(F_{\text{bubble}} = \frac{p-1}{m+p-1}\), explain how to assess the pipeline-bubble hypothesis and propose two adjustments if the trace confirms it.
Answer: Low MFU and idle interconnect links make pipeline bubbles a candidate, but they do not prove the cause. Measure stage timelines and the microbatch count, and compare observed fill/drain idle slots with the bubble formula. Stage imbalance, input stalls, or inefficient local kernels can also lower MFU. If bubbles bind, increasing microbatch count can reduce their fraction, subject to activation memory and useful global batch size. Reducing stage count can also help when the revised memory budget fits; replacing some intra-node stages with tensor parallelism additionally requires a suitable communication budget.
Learning Objective: Analyze pipeline bubble underutilization and propose architectural remedies
**Order the following parallelism strategies by their structural granularity from coarsest (whole model / batch level) to finest (intra-operator level):


Tensor Parallelism (Megatron column/row splits)
Standard Data Parallelism (batch dimension splitting)
Pipeline Parallelism (inter-layer stage splitting)**

Answer: (2) -> (3) -> (1). First, (2) Standard Data Parallelism operates at the coarsest granularity, replicating the entire model and partitioning only the outer batch loop. Next, (3) Pipeline Parallelism partitions at the inter-layer boundary (assigning sequential layer groups to stages). Finally, (1) Tensor Parallelism operates at the finest intra-operator granularity, partitioning individual weight matrices within each layer.
Learning Objective: Rank distributed parallelism strategies by their structural decomposition granularity
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In distributed training framework runtimes (such as PyTorch DDP), what mechanism combines multiple small layer gradient tensors into contiguous memory buffers before launching collective communication?

Activation checkpointing
ZeRO Stage 3 parameter gathering
Temporal multiplexing
Gradient bucketing

Answer: The correct answer is D. Gradient bucketing groups individual layer gradient tensors into larger contiguous memory buffers (typically 25–50 MB buckets) during the backward pass. Launching an AllReduce on a single aggregated bucket amortizes collective invocation latency and saturates network link bandwidth far more effectively than issuing hundreds of tiny per-tensor transfers. Activation checkpointing recomputes activations to save memory. ZeRO-3 parameter gathering reconstructs sharded weights on demand. Temporal multiplexing alternates execution modes in multi-model RLHF.
Learning Objective: Explain the role of gradient bucketing in amortizing collective communication latency
Contrast the collective communication primitive invocation frequency of standard DDP against full-shard FSDP with resharding for a model with \(N_L\) layers during a single training step.
Answer: DDP launches one AllReduce per ready gradient bucket, often overlapping those calls with backward computation. Full-shard FSDP with layer-level wrapping and resharding after forward typically adds an AllGather before forward, another before backward, and a ReduceScatter after backward: approximately \(3N_L\) calls. Actual counts depend on wrapping, bucketing, prefetch, and resharding policy.
Learning Objective: Compare collective communication primitive invocations between standard DDP and full-shard FSDP
Explain why framework optimizations such as CUDA graphs and asynchronous communication streams cannot eliminate the physical scaling penalty of distributed training as the cluster size \(N\) becomes very large.
Answer: Framework optimizations can reduce launch overhead and change readiness, overlap, and effective communication service time. They cannot make a required payload cross a finite-bandwidth link instantaneously. At fixed global work, adding ranks reduces local compute while required transfers and coordination can remain exposed. A scaling prediction therefore needs the actual workload, collective schedule, and critical path; a fixed-residual Amdahl ceiling applies only under that model’s assumptions.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the physical limits of framework-level communication optimizations

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team achieves 50 percent Model Flops Utilization (MFU) on a single node, scales to 1,024 GPUs, and measures a scaling efficiency \((\eta_{\text{scaling}})\) of 50 percent on their communication-heavy workload. What is the cluster’s realized model-FLOP rate during distributed execution as a fraction of peak hardware compute?

25 percent of peak compute (delivering 256 GPU-equivalents of model computation)
50 percent of peak compute (delivering 512 GPU-equivalents of useful work)
100 percent of peak compute (delivering 1,024 GPU-equivalents of useful work)
12.5 percent of peak compute (delivering 128 GPU-equivalents of useful work)

Answer: The correct answer is A. Starting from the single-node MFU baseline, the distributed model-FLOP rate is \(0.50\times0.50=0.25\) of fleet peak, or 256 peak-GPU equivalents. The scaling factor accounts for losses relative to that baseline. A measured distributed MFU would already include those losses and must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again. Retained-progress goodput additionally requires accounting for replay and recovery outside this measurement.
Learning Objective: Calculate distributed model-FLOP rate from a local MFU baseline and scaling efficiency without double-counting losses
A procurement team plans capacity for a graph neural network workload using a vendor benchmark that reports 85 percent scaling efficiency at 1,024 GPUs for large-language-model training. Explain why this figure cannot be treated as a property of the cluster and what the team should measure instead.
Answer: Scaling efficiency is a joint property of the workload’s communication-to-computation ratio, the parallelism strategy, the network topology, and the software stack (collective library version, kernel fusion, overlap quality). The benchmark fixes all four for a language model; a graph neural network with irregular communication changes the first and likely the second, so the same hardware can deliver much lower efficiency. The team should measure scaling on the target workload, at the intended device count and parallelism layout, and plan capacity from that measured curve rather than from a hero benchmark.
Learning Objective: Explain why scaling efficiency must be measured on the target workload rather than inherited from vendor benchmarks.
Why is gradient accumulation NOT a cost-free substitute for true physical scale-out even though it reduces gradient AllReduce communication frequency by a factor of \(k\)?

It is mathematically incompatible with the Adam optimizer
It keeps a live gradient buffer resident, spaces optimizer updates by \(k\) microsteps, and requires appropriate accumulation precision and normalization
It requires dedicated InfiniBand links between CPU and GPU for each microstep
It forces batch normalization layers to synchronize across all nodes on every forward pass

Answer: The correct answer is B. One optimizer update follows \(k\) forward/backward microsteps, but this does not imply \(k\) times the wall-clock update latency: saved synchronization and the comparison schedule affect elapsed time. A live gradient buffer remains resident during the window. Unscaled FP16 accumulation can overflow; accumulation precision and loss normalization must preserve the intended update. Changes in effective batch size must be evaluated at matched target quality. Accumulation is compatible with Adam and requires neither special CPU-GPU links nor mandatory cross-node batch normalization.
Learning Objective: Analyze the memory, latency, and numerical stability trade-offs of gradient accumulation
The largest global batch size beyond which adding more samples per step yields diminishing reductions in the number of steps needed to reach target quality is called the ____.
Answer: critical batch size. Beyond this workload-dependent point, larger global batches can raise hardware throughput without proportionally reducing the steps to target quality, so hardware scaling and statistical scaling must be evaluated separately.
Learning Objective: Identify the critical batch size as the statistical limit on useful data-parallel scale-out.
True or False: If a 7B-parameter model fits comfortably in single-GPU memory with high compute utilization under standard DDP, universally enabling ZeRO-3 / FSDP full sharding will always increase training throughput by reducing per-GPU memory consumption.
Answer: False. FSDP trades memory capacity for parameter-gather and gradient-reduction traffic. If its memory savings do not enable a more efficient batch or layout, the exposed communication can lower throughput. The outcome depends on wrapping, resharding, overlap, and network capacity, so neither a universal gain nor a fixed percentage penalty follows from sharding.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the performance pitfall of applying FSDP when memory capacity is not binding

← Back to Questions

title: 6 Distributed Training
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can adding accelerators make training slower?
Splitting a training job across machines creates more compute capacity, but it also requires those machines to exchange state and agree on updates. Each accelerator may finish its local work sooner while spending more of the step waiting for other workers. Once communication and waiting consume the time saved by parallel execution, adding accelerators raises the bill without shortening the run. Single-node optimization remains necessary, yet faster local arithmetic cannot remove a dependency on data that another machine has not delivered. Memory pressure complicates the decision, because a model may require distribution simply to fit, even when the resulting exchanges are expensive. Dividing its state across more devices can relieve that limit while exposing another in network bandwidth or scheduling. Conversely, replicating a model can process more examples at once without reducing the memory needed for each copy. Neither improvement alone establishes that training will finish sooner. Changing how examples are grouped or when updates become available can change the work required to reach the target quality. Engineers must therefore compare complete training configurations, accounting for memory, communication, update behavior, and elapsed time together. The practical question is where additional hardware buys useful progress and where it merely creates more coordination. That judgment determines which models and experiments fit the available schedule and budget. In C³ terms, each partitioning strategy trades parallelized compute against network-bound communication and coordination across workers.

Learning Objectives

Apply the Fleet Law to diagnose compute-, memory-, communication-, or coordination-bound distributed training regimes
Calculate scaling efficiency, estimate useful batch size, and budget synchronization overhead for data-parallel training
Design memory-sharding plans that trade accelerator capacity for additional communication
Map tensor, pipeline, sequence, expert, and data parallelism onto hardware bandwidth tiers and model structure
Analyze microbatch pipeline schedules for bubble overhead, activation residency, and synchronous update ordering
Evaluate synchronization and low-precision policies under staleness, straggler, and numerical-stability constraints
Synthesize hybrid parallelism configurations for frontier, recommendation, and alignment training constraints

title: 6 Distributed Training
text:
A 175B-parameter reference model cannot load onto a single accelerator, because its FP16 weights alone exceed the memory of the device that must hold them (Data Storage). The empirical scaling law (principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\)) keeps pushing frontier models further past what one machine can store or finish in calendar time. The accelerator hierarchy, network fabric, and storage pipeline form the physical foundation of the fleet, and Collective Communication priced the collective operations that move state across it. The remaining challenge is deciding how to partition the training job: which intermediate results and gradients must cross that fabric, and when workers must synchronize, while preserving the optimization process a single device would have followed.


↩︎ The power-law relationship between quality and compute, data, and parameters, and the compute-optimal allocation it implies, are established in AI Scaling Laws.
In the fleet stack (The Fleet Stack), distributed training occupies the Distributed Execution row of the Distribution band, the logic that partitions the mathematical workload across the physical fleet. Data, tensor, pipeline, and hybrid parallelism create different traffic patterns for the interconnect to carry, and selecting among them requires evaluating the reference workload against finite high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, compute throughput, and input bandwidth.
Three distinct limits push a training workload past a single accelerator. Memory exhaustion hits first when model parameters, optimizer states, and activation storage exceed single-device capacity. For full mixed-precision training with Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), the convention of 16 bytes per parameter can exceed an 80 GB accelerator at roughly 5 billion parameters before activations. Larger 10–20B models therefore need sharding, offload, or another memory-saving approach (Rajbhandari et al. 2020). The failed allocation establishes a capacity problem without by itself choosing the remedy.

↪ Accelerator HBM capacity, the ceiling these per-parameter budgets are measured against, is developed in Accelerator Memory Hierarchy.

Even when a model fits in memory, unacceptable training duration can still force distribution because a single device may require weeks or months to converge, turning wall-clock time itself into a systems constraint. GPT-3’s 175B-parameter training run used a cluster of V100 GPUs (Brown et al. 2020), illustrating why the calendar, alongside HBM capacity, drives scale-out.
Input demand at dataset scale adds a third pressure: dataset bytes govern storage capacity, whereas the training schedule governs the required delivery rate. As The Data Pipeline Equation showed, either can motivate distributed data services, although a large dataset alone does not require distributing model computation. Together, capacity, calendar, and input delivery define the constraints a training configuration must satisfy.
The first signal, memory exhaustion, has a long history, traced in figure 1. Over the plotted span, single-accelerator memory grew about 15× from the K80 to the B200, while the memory needed to train a state-of-the-art model grew by roughly 4 orders of magnitude. Among the plotted models, the curves cross in 2020 at GPT-3, whose training state exceeded the largest accelerator then available by about 35×. GPT-3 marks where the gap passed an order of magnitude, and every later plotted frontier model also sits far above the capacity curve. For those models, spreading state beyond one device’s memory is a precondition for training at all rather than a way to train faster.














Figure 1: The Memory Wall: Accelerator memory capacity plotted against the memory a state-of-the-art model needs to train. Capacity climbs steadily while demand climbs faster, and the widening gap is why weights, gradients, and optimizer state must be split across devices rather than merely compressed. Training memory assumes 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam state; parameter counts are from Epoch AI (2026) and capacities are vendor specifications.


Epoch AI. 2026. Notable AI Models.


Whichever signal motivates distribution, the system must state which optimization update it implements. The synchronous baseline is developed first. In it, the 1,024 GPUs of the volume’s Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) reference cluster combine their contributions before advancing to the next parameter version. The running instance in this chapter is a GPT-3-class 175B-parameter dense transformer. Matching the global batch, loss normalization, and optimizer state preserves the corresponding single-device update mathematically. Later synchronization models deliberately relax that update ordering and must be evaluated under their own convergence assumptions.


↩︎ The three systems archetypes and their binding constraints are established in Three systems archetypes.

Definition 6.1: Distributed training
Distributed training partitions the optimization loop across multiple compute nodes, distributing data or model computation and coordinating contributions according to a specified update protocol.

Significance: Partitioning training state across devices can meet a memory budget that exceeds one accelerator. GPT-3 (175B parameters) requires approximately 350 GB in BF16 (FP16 also stores 2 bytes per value, so the chapter’s byte counts hold for either format), more than 4× the 80 GB capacity of a single H100. If weights remain entirely in HBM, their aggregate capacity lower bound is 5 H100s. Adding BF16 gradients plus FP32 Adam master weights and moments gives about 2.8 TB, or at least 35 H100s before activations. These lower bounds do not establish a runnable placement; offload changes the capacity calculation, and the time budget can require more accelerators than memory alone.
Distinction: CPU threads can share a coherent address space, while accelerators generally hold separate training-state allocations even within one node. Distributed training extends coordination across those devices and node boundaries through collectives or point-to-point transfers governed by the chosen update protocol.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that distributed training scales linearly with node count. In practice, communication overhead grows with cluster size and the serial fraction of each step (Amdahl’s Law): a fixed serial fraction of the single-device baseline bounds strong-scaling speedup.



Distribution expands three costs that determine whether a partition is viable. Communication overhead includes gradient aggregation through AllReduce, which returns the same reduced tensor to each participant, or rank. For \(\Parameters\) parameters across \(\DeviceCount\) devices, a ring AllReduce, in which each worker passes gradient chunks only to its neighbor in a logical ring, sends approximately \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\times \GradientPayload\) bytes per worker per step. Here the gradient payload \(\GradientPayload\) is the \(\Parameters\) gradient values times their storage width. That payload is not total fleet traffic.


↩︎ The ring schedule and the derivation of its \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) volume are established in Collective Communication.
Fault tolerance becomes more demanding as the number of failure sources grows. Under independent constant-rate failures, 1,024 GPUs that each have a mean time to failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours produce a GPU failure about every 49 hours, the cluster’s mean time between failures (MTBF). Whether each event interrupts training depends on recovery and redundancy; The MTBF cascade develops the assumptions.
Algorithmic stability adds a separate constraint when the partition changes global batch size or update ordering. Learning-rate scaling and warmup are candidate responses to large-batch behavior (Goyal et al. 2017), not requirements unique to multiple machines. A viable design must satisfy all three budgets.
Communication and coordination costs enter every step through the Fleet Law (principle \(\ref{pri-distributed-step-time}\)), which decomposes the per-step time:
\[ \DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \]


↩︎ The Fleet Law and its compute, communication, and coordination terms are established in The Fleet Law.
The communication-computation ratio, \(\CommunicationComputeRatio= \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)/(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\), compares communication time with ideally partitioned compute time for fixed global work. It is the time consequence of communication intensity \(\CommunicationIntensity\) (equation 1.1), the bytes moved per operation of the workload. When transfers run at link bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\) and each device computes at sustained rate \(\PeakRate\EfficiencyHw\), \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\approx \CommunicationIntensity \times \PeakRate\EfficiencyHw/\LinkBandwidth\), so the same workload becomes more communication-bound on faster accelerators or slower links. This ratio identifies the pressure to overlap communication; the complete step time also depends on how much exchange is hidden and how much coordination remains exposed.


↩︎ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) message model, with startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and sustained bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\), is established in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model.

↪ The communication-computation ratio, evaluated for representative data-parallel and point-to-point transfers and related to communication intensity, is developed in The communication-computation ratio.

Two regimes follow from this ratio. When \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\gg \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), the cluster is compute-bound, and communication is small relative to useful computation, provided coordination and input delivery do not introduce another limit. Large-batch training of a dense convolutional model such as ResNet commonly sits here. When \(\CommunicationComputeRatio\gtrsim 1\), \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) matches or exceeds \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) and the cluster is communication-bound. Insufficient overlap then leaves substantial time waiting for gradients or activations. Large language models (LLMs) with billions of parameters to synchronize, and Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM)-style workloads whose embedding exchanges saturate the network, frequently land in this regime. These are typical operating points rather than fixed labels. Batch size, partitioning, and placement can move the same workload across the boundary, so the ratio must be measured for the configuration at hand. Where a workload lands also depends on how its training loop is cut across devices, the choice each parallelism strategy makes.


↪ The optimizations that help, and the ones that are wasted, for a compute-bound, communication-bound, or coordination-bound fleet are collected for reference in The bottleneck diagnostic table.

Self-Check: Question

A research team is training a 3B-parameter transformer that fits comfortably in one H100 GPU’s 80 GB of memory, but projected single-GPU training would take 18 months to reach target loss. The dataset is 3 TB and fits on local NVMe storage. Which signal makes distributed training necessary in this scenario?

Dataset exceeding GPU HBM capacity, which automatically mandates tensor parallelism regardless of execution time
The presence of NVLink inside the node, which makes multi-machine scaling mandatory by default
Unacceptable wall-clock training duration, even though single-device memory capacity and local storage are sufficient
Fault tolerance limitations, because single-GPU training cannot survive hardware restarts

A team doubles a data-parallel cluster from 64 to 128 GPUs and observes that total step time drops by only 12 percent even though per-worker compute time halves. Using the distributed step-time equation \(T_{\text{step}}(N) = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}}\), explain what the observation establishes and what measurement would distinguish possible causes.
True or False: A cluster of 1,024 GPUs, each with a 50,000-hour mean time to failure, should expect a GPU failure roughly every two days if failures are independent, even though any single GPU fails only about once every five to six years.
The dimensionless ratio \(\rho = T_{\text{comm}}(N) / (T_{\text{compute}}/N)\), which screens communication demand relative to per-worker compute time, is defined as the ____.

title: 6 Distributed Training
text:
Once a model or its training time outgrows a single GPU, the training loop offers three nested axes to split across devices: the examples in a batch, the layers of the model, and the matrix operations inside each layer. Data parallelism assigns different examples to model replicas; pipeline parallelism assigns successive layer groups to different devices; tensor parallelism splits the operations inside a layer. Because every split adds inter-device communication and synchronization overhead on top of single-machine compute and memory limits (The D·A·M Taxonomy), profiling and design must treat these three strategies as loop transformations applied by a cluster-level compiler.
In compiler terms, data parallelism acts like a parallel for-loop that assigns different batch indices to devices running the same model. Tensor parallelism resembles vectorization, or single instruction, multiple data (SIMD), by partitioning the work inside matrix operations. This is an analogy for the work split rather than for a shared instruction stream or register file, since the devices still exchange tensor shards over an interconnect. Pipeline parallelism instead resembles instruction pipelining, assigning successive layer groups to stages so that overlapping microbatches keep those stages active, subject to dependency delays and load balance.
Whichever loop a strategy unrolls, distributed training1 spreads the workload across machines that must coordinate to train a single model. Coordination here means keeping every model shard or replica on a compatible training step. Basic barriers can keep a small research run ordered, but long-running training jobs also need timeout, checkpoint, and recovery mechanisms so one failed worker does not waste days of compute.
1 Distributed training: Google’s DistBelief (2012) was an early framework for training neural networks across thousands of machines, but its parameter server architecture created bandwidth bottlenecks at central nodes. This limitation drove the shift to decentralized AllReduce patterns in successors such as Horovod and PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP), where each data-parallel worker sends and receives about \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\) times the gradient size per step rather than concentrating traffic at a single server (Dean et al. 2012; Sergeev and Balso 2018; Li et al. 2020; Patarasuk and Yuan 2009).
Dean, Jeffrey, Greg Corrado, Rajat Monga, Kai Chen, Matthieu Devin, Quoc V. Le, Mark Z. Mao, et al. 2012. “Large Scale Distributed Deep Networks.” In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), edited by Peter L. Bartlett, Fernando C. N. Pereira, Christopher J. C. Burges, Léon Bottou, and Kilian Q. Weinberger, vol. 25. Curran Associates.

Sergeev, Alexander, and Mike Del Balso. 2018. “Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow.” CoRR abs/1802.05799.

Li, Shen, Yanli Zhao, Rohan Varma, Omkar Salpekar, Pieter Noordhuis, Teng Li, Adam Paszke, et al. 2020. “PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 13 (12): 3005–18. https://doi.org/10.14778/3415478.3415530.

Patarasuk, Pitch, and Xin Yuan. 2009. “Bandwidth Optimal All-Reduce Algorithms for Clusters of Workstations.” Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 69 (2): 117–24. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2008.09.002.

↪ Checkpointing and recovery for long-running training jobs are developed in Fault Tolerance.
2 NVLink: NVIDIA’s point-to-point GPU interconnect delivers 300 GB/s–450 GB/s per-direction bandwidth, roughly 12×–18× InfiniBand HDR per port. This bandwidth gap is why tensor parallelism, which requires AllReduce on every layer, favors the fast NVLink domain, while pipeline and data parallelism can tolerate slower links when their traffic budgets fit. NVLink Switch systems can extend that fast domain beyond one server.
Mapping those three loop transformations onto hardware follows the cluster’s interconnect hierarchy. Within a single node, multiple GPUs coordinate across separate device memories over high-bandwidth NVLink or PCIe links,2 with collective libraries such as NCCL scheduling the transfers.
Crossing node boundaries adds slower inter-node network links, fault-tolerance exposure, and cluster orchestration, so single-GPU kernel and memory efficiency must be tuned first rather than multiplied as waste across the fleet. Matching the three loop splits to these intra-node and inter-node tiers decomposes the design space onto a three-dimensional grid, \(\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\), that partitions cluster execution across tensor parallelism (\(\TensorParallelDegree\), intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism (\(\PipelineParallelDegree\), sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism (\(\DataParallelDegree\), batch replication). Each cell of the grid is one accelerator coordinate (figure 2).







Figure 2: The 3D Parallelism Cube: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism (\(\TensorParallelDegree\), intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism (\(\PipelineParallelDegree\), sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism (\(\DataParallelDegree\), batch replication). Each cell is one accelerator, identified by its \((\DataParallelDegree, \PipelineParallelDegree, \TensorParallelDegree)\) coordinate, so the cube holds \(\DeviceCount = \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\) devices. A feasible point must jointly satisfy model divisibility, per-device memory limits, and the network hierarchy that carries each axis’s traffic.



Under the three-dimensional partitioning of figure 2, called 3D parallelism, the total accelerator allocation scales as the product \(\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\). The axes represent distinct mathematical partitions, but they are not independent configuration knobs. Tensor and pipeline degrees must divide the model structure, the data-parallel degree and microbatch schedule must produce a viable global batch, every partition must fit memory, and each communication group must map onto an adequate topology and acceptable failure domain. Training systems therefore select a jointly feasible coordinate rather than tuning \(\DataParallelDegree\), \(\PipelineParallelDegree\), and \(\TensorParallelDegree\) in isolation.


A parallelism strategy that places frequent, high-volume exchanges on a slow link fails before it leaves the whiteboard, because communication stalls the accelerators it was meant to feed. Choosing a strategy is therefore a constraint satisfaction problem governed by parameter count \((\Parameters)\), batch size \((\BatchSize)\), and interconnect bandwidth. A first feasibility screen compares the traffic each strategy creates against the hardware topology (table 1). In that screen, \(\LayerCount\) denotes layer count, \(\SequenceLength\) sequence length, and \(\HiddenDimension\) hidden width. The table identifies traffic sources rather than complete byte budgets; datatype width, partition degree, and communication frequency enter the worked mechanisms below.



Table 1: Parallelism Communication Costs: Tensor parallelism exchanges partial layer results frequently and favors a fast communication domain, which can span servers. Pipeline parallelism transfers boundary activations; its bandwidth need depends on tensor shape and microbatch schedule. Data parallelism synchronizes gradient bytes, whose exposed cost depends on overlap and topology. Memory sharding addresses capacity but does not automatically reduce communication.

Those bandwidth requirements impose a hard constraint on hardware placement: each parallelism axis must map onto an interconnect tier that can sustain its traffic within the compute budget. A quick back-of-envelope bandwidth feasibility check catches a mismatch before any code is written.


↩︎ The communication domains and bandwidth hierarchy used to evaluate placement are established in Bandwidth hierarchy.

Systems Perspective 6.1: Bandwidth feasibility checkFrequent tensor-parallel collectives must fit the layer-time budget. The test compares the time one layer’s local share of computation takes with the time its collectives take on each candidate link. For the forward pass of one GPT-3 layer split 8 ways, processing one 2,048-token sequence at half of an H100’s dense FP16 peak:

Local compute per layer: about 1.9 ms
Tensor-parallel transfer per layer over NVLink: about 0.4 ms
The same transfer over one NDR InfiniBand port: about 3.5 ms

On NVLink the exchange is a fraction of the layer’s compute; across InfiniBand it would take longer than the compute it serves. The amount hidden depends on independent work available in the execution schedule. NVLink is one suitable fast domain, but the test uses message bytes, exposed latency, and sustained link rate rather than an interconnect brand or chassis boundary. Cross-rack placement may favor pipeline or data parallelism when the available fabric cannot meet the tensor-parallel budget; their activation and gradient traffic must also be checked.


The communication costs in table 1 already narrow the choice before any mechanism has been developed, because a strategy is viable only when its traffic fits the tier that must carry it. What each formula implies in practice depends on the mechanics of data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism developed over the rest of the chapter, and section 6.8 turns the same constraints into a decision procedure once those mechanics are in place.

Self-Check: Question

Framing distributed parallelism strategies as compiler loop transformations across the training loop’s iterators (batches, layers, and operations), which distributed strategy corresponds to vectorization (SIMD) of inner matrix multiplications?

Tensor parallelism, which partitions inner matrix-multiplication operations across devices and exchanges partial results over the interconnect
Data parallelism, which unrolls the outer batch loop across devices so each rank processes independent data indices
Pipeline parallelism, which stages sequential layer operations across devices analogous to CPU instruction pipelining
Model replication, which duplicates the entire forward and backward execution redundantly across machines

In the 3D parallelism cube, where the device count equals the product of the data-, pipeline-, and tensor-parallel degrees, how do the three scaling axes interact to allocate cluster accelerators for large models?

The three axes are mutually exclusive; choosing data parallelism precludes using tensor or pipeline parallelism in the same cluster
Tensor and pipeline parallelism can combine within a node, but data parallelism can only be used if model parallelism is disabled
The total accelerator count is the sum of the three degrees, with each parallelism type requiring a disjoint node pool
The axes compose multiplicatively, so one layout can split layers (TP), stage the layer stack (PP), and replicate the pipeline across data shards (DP), and its device count is the product of the three degrees

True or False: If a neural network’s parameters exceed a single GPU’s memory capacity, tensor parallelism can be scaled across standard commodity Ethernet switches between server racks, provided the global batch size is made large enough.
For one GPT-3 layer split eight ways, the chapter’s bandwidth feasibility check finds about 1.9 ms of local compute, about 0.4 ms of tensor-parallel transfer over NVLink, and about 3.5 ms for the same transfer over one NDR InfiniBand port. Explain what these numbers imply for where the tensor-parallel group should be placed and what a planner must still check before accepting that placement.
