Network performance problems in ML clusters are insidious because they show up as silent waste rather than explicit failures. A degraded transceiver causing a 10 percent reduction in effective bandwidth might slow each training iteration by only 2–3 percent. The slowdown is small because the lost bandwidth stretches only the exposed communication share of the step (the 30 percent assumed in the oversubscription estimate, less whatever overlap hides), and stretches it by roughly the inverse of the bandwidth that remains. A drift that small is easily masked by the natural variance of checkpointing or data loading. Over a 30-day training run on 1,024 GPUs, this invisible drag accumulates to roughly 15,000–22,000 wasted GPU-hours, burning about $30,000–$44,000 at $2/GPU-hour without triggering a single alarm. Traditional IT monitoring tools like SNMP or ICMP ping measure connectivity, not the sustained throughput required by RDMA. Effective observability requires a three-layer approach: physical monitoring (FEC errors, signal attenuation), transport monitoring (PFC pause frames, retransmission rates), and application monitoring (NCCL algorithmic bandwidth) (Jeaugey 2017; Gangidi et al. 2024). The three layers retrace the five-level model from the top down. Application monitoring observes the collective that Level 5 integrates, transport monitoring observes the Level 2 recovery and Level 4 congestion machinery, and physical monitoring observes the Level 1 wire. Only by correlating signals across these layers can operators detect that a “slow training run” is caused by a single degraded cable in one rack.

Jeaugey, Sylvain. 2017. NCCL 2.0. GPU Technology Conference presentation.


A marginal cable or overheating transceiver rarely drops the link outright; instead, it accumulates symbol errors, triggers transmit discards, or retrains to a slower link state while the job keeps running. Catching that physical drift requires polling switch and NIC port counters, which report transmitted and received data, transmit discards, symbol errors, and link-down events; on InfiniBand a utility such as perfquery reads them, and Ethernet/RoCE devices expose the equivalent telemetry through their own management interfaces (Linux man-pages project 2026). Data counters measure utilization, discards warrant investigation against the port’s traffic and recovery policy, and symbol errors and link-down events are evidence of a degrading signal. Correlating those counters with link rate, lane state, and transport behavior narrows the cause; a counter alone does not identify a defective cable or transceiver.

Linux man-pages project. 2026. Perfquery(8): Query InfiniBand Port Counters on a Single Port.
Polling link state alongside traffic counters can reveal silent degradation. A link operating at HDR (200 Gb/s) rather than the expected NDR rate (400 Gb/s) can remain connected while offering half the expected bandwidth. A link that trains with two of its four lanes active after a connector fault fails the same way: it stays up while its bandwidth is halved. Both cases are visible only when negotiated rate and lane state are compared with the deployment baseline. For 1,024 GPUs and roughly 3,000 links, the assumed 0.1 percent point-in-time degradation probability gives 3 degraded links in expectation and, under independent events, a 95 percent probability of at least one degradation. This probability measures something different from the daily figure in notebook 3.4. That notebook asks how often a new degradation begins; this one asks how many degraded links are present at any moment. Standing prevalence is roughly the onset rate times how long a degraded link stays in service, and silent degradation, by definition, stays in service until someone looks, so prevalence can far exceed what a small daily onset rate suggests. Both rates are scenario assumptions rather than measured fleet data. A job slows when an affected path limits its required traffic; fleet-wide exposure alone does not determine the job’s slowdown. When the degraded link lies on a ring AllReduce’s path, however, the cost reaches every participant, because each round waits for its slowest hop and the whole ring proceeds at the pace of that one link.


↪ Gray failure, the general case of a component that degrades without failing, and why a synchronous job feels it as a straggler, is developed in Stragglers versus fail-stop failures.



Clean port counters and an active 50 GB/s NDR link state still do not guarantee that a node pair can deliver that rate to a training job: a degraded PCIe path, a cross-socket NUMA bounce, or a congested spine cut can throttle RDMA transfers without incrementing a single physical error counter. Active validation must therefore measure the bandwidth and latency the job can actually achieve across the complete host-to-host path. Pairwise tests such as ib_write_bw can populate an all-pairs bandwidth matrix, or a sampled subset for a large fleet (linux-rdma project 2026). A low-throughput pair identifies a path to investigate. Comparing the affected pairs with routing and physical telemetry helps distinguish a shared switch or cable problem from endpoint limitations.

linux-rdma project. 2026. perftest: InfiniBand Verbs Performance Tests.
For latency-sensitive synchronization, ib_write_lat runs a ping-pong test with small RDMA writes and reports half the measured round-trip time as one-way latency. Values such as 2 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\)s, 5 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\)s, or 100 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\)s must be compared with a baseline for the same endpoints, message size, path, and load; they are not universal fault thresholds or evidence of a particular fallback. Application-level tests such as nccl-tests then exercise collective communication across the intended worker group. Point-to-point results establish a path baseline, while collective tests reveal costs from concurrent traffic and scheduling that isolated pairs cannot expose.



When a training job reports lower-than-expected throughput, the diagnostic order should preserve the layer model rather than starting with cables. The following sequence moves from application symptoms toward physical causes:

Check GPU utilization: Rule out compute bottlenecks with accelerator telemetry (nvidia-smi, for example). High SM utilization alone does not rule out a network bottleneck, because communication kernels can also keep SMs active. Correlate utilization with the compute and collective portions of the step timeline. Low utilization does not automatically implicate the fabric, however. A starved input pipeline (data loading or storage) produces the same symptom, so confirm the data path is keeping the accelerators fed before investigating the network.
Inspect collective-library logs: Enable the library’s debug output (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO in NCCL, for example) to reveal which network transport was selected, the detected bandwidth between nodes, and any fallbacks to slower protocols.
Run point-to-point tests: Run a pairwise bandwidth test (such as ib_write_bw) between specific nodes in the job. A single degraded link can bottleneck the entire ring in a ring AllReduce.
Check PFC/ECN counters: Inspect switch counters along the path. Sustained PFC activity indicates persistent congestion that should be investigated at the scheduler or routing level.
Validate physical layer: Check symbol errors and CRC counts to identify failing transceivers or cables.

In this order, application symptoms identify the failing path, transport counters show whether congestion or fallback is involved, and physical telemetry confirms whether the wire itself is degrading. Applying the sequence to a concrete slowdown shows how each layer narrows the search before any hardware is replaced.

Monitoring keeps deployed fabrics honest, but it cannot push past the physical ceilings it measures, such as the reach and power limits that copper approaches at high signaling rates. New fabric technologies earn attention only when they move one of those bounds. As clusters scale toward 100,000 nodes, the durable design variables are power per bit, reach, and the ratio of compute to memory to network capacity, not the product names attached to a particular roadmap.


Standard RoCEv2 forces operators to wrestle with fragile PFC pause thresholds and ECMP hash collisions that were never designed for synchronized elephant flows, while InfiniBand locks the fabric into a single-vendor stack. The Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) addresses these reliability and load-balancing limits for AI/HPC traffic over Ethernet. Its Ultra Ethernet Transport design combines packet spraying across multiple paths, flexible ordering, multiple transport delivery services, congestion-control changes, and telemetry (Ultra Ethernet Consortium 2025). The architectural question is how the selected service delivers the required completion and ordering semantics under congestion or loss. Packet trimming (cutting an overflowing packet down to its header instead of dropping it, so the receiver learns of the loss at once), retry, and endpoint recovery should therefore be judged by their effect on completion-time tails and resource cost. Whether the design reproduces a lossless-fabric mechanism is not the test.

Higher switch capacity attacks hop count as well as raw bandwidth. XDR InfiniBand pushes 800 Gb/s per port, and Ethernet roadmaps include 800GbE and 1.6TbE link speeds (NVIDIA 2026c; Ethernet Alliance 2025). Ethernet switch silicon with 1.6 Tb/s ports pushes aggregate capacity to 102.4 Tb/s in current Tomahawk 6-class designs (Broadcom Inc. 2025). A single 1.6 Tb/s port delivers the bandwidth of 4 400G ports, so the same ASIC can instead expose 4 times as many 400G ports. Spending that capacity on radix rather than port rate is what flattens the topology, because fat-tree host count grows as \(\SwitchRadix^2/2\) at two tiers and \(\SwitchRadix^3/4\) at three. A cluster that previously required three tiers of switches may then be served by two when radix, port rate, and placement constraints line up, potentially reducing the number of optical links and switching stages. The transceiver savings require explicit port and cable accounting; removing one tier does not automatically halve the module count, and the latency benefit depends on the resulting paths and traffic.






Each extra meter pushes the fabric from copper toward optics.
Pushing ports from 400 Gb/s to the 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s rates of section 3.10.1 doubles per-lane signaling from the 100 Gb/s class of current NDR and 800G Ethernet links to the 200 Gb/s class, which sharply increases the insertion loss per meter of passive copper. As that usable reach shrinks, in line with the link-budget example in section 3.3.3, the SerDes must spend more energy per bit on equalization to recover the signal. Active electrical cables, which add retimer chips to regenerate the signal mid-cable, extend that reach but add latency and power of their own, leaving optical interconnects as the primary lever on power per bit and reach.
Co-packaged optics (CPO) places optical engines close to the switch or accelerator on a shared package substrate. Moving the optical engine from the switch faceplate to the package shortens the SerDes-to-optics electrical path from centimeters of board trace to millimeters, which reduces the signal-conditioning burden before transmission over fiber. The receiving optical engine converts the signal back to electrical form. Fiber still introduces propagation delay and has a loss budget; packaging the optics closer to the processor does not remove those constraints.
Co-packaged optics therefore changes the electrical portion of the link budget while retaining the reach advantages of optical transmission. Usable reach still depends on the fiber, connectors, optical power, and receiver design. The relevant comparison holds payload capacity and error targets fixed, then measures the power saved by the shorter electrical path against the packaging and maintenance costs of integration. The power side of that comparison can be estimated port by port for a single switch.

Napkin Math 3.5: The optical dividendProblem: Calculate the power savings of moving a 51.2 Tb/s switch from pluggable transceivers to co-packaged optics.

Pluggable architecture: 128 ports \(\times\) 20 W = 2.56 kW for optics alone.
CPO architecture: 128 engines \(\times\) 10 W = 1.28 kW.
Savings: The savings reach 1.28 kW of power per switch.

Systems insight: Across 1,000 switches, the assumed pluggable modules consume 2.56 MW. The modeled CPO configuration saves 1.28 MW, equivalent to the reference power budget of roughly 1,800 H100 GPUs. That equivalence measures the scale of the saving; using it for additional accelerators also requires compute capacity, power delivery, and cooling in the right locations. Optics power constrains both operating cost and the equipment a facility can support.


The spine example for 10,000 GPUs assigns 400 kW to pluggable optics. That subtotal counts only the selected spine-side endpoints. Applying the same fractional saving to those endpoints would require a CPO implementation with the assumed per-port power and capacity; opposite-end optics remain outside the comparison. Integration also changes serviceability: replacing a failed optical component may involve a larger assembly than swapping a pluggable module. The energy benefit must be evaluated alongside packaging, repair, and spare-capacity costs.
For ML infrastructure, CPO could flatten the bandwidth hierarchy by narrowing the gap between intra-node and inter-node bandwidth. If inter-node links achieve bandwidth comparable to NVLink-class local fabrics (hundreds of GB/s per GPU), the bandwidth penalty for extending tensor parallelism beyond a single node would shrink. Cross-node tensor parallelism would then become economical for more workloads, provided that startup latency and collective frequency also fit the step-time budget.
However, CPO introduces new challenges. Optical components are sensitive to temperature (laser wavelength shifts with temperature, requiring active thermal management), and integrating photonics on the same package as a 1,000 W GPU creates a hostile thermal environment for the optical components. The manufacturing processes for silicon photonics and CMOS transistors are similar but not identical, requiring separate fabrication steps that increase package cost and complexity. Hybrid integration, which places the photonics chiplet on a cooler region of the package substrate and thermally isolates it from the GPU die, is one way to manage that environment, at the cost of a longer electrical path than full co-location.



Narrowing the gap between package-level and rack-level interconnects also tempts architects to relax the fixed compute-to-memory ratio of the server node itself, which otherwise leaves compute or memory underused when workloads need different resource ratios. Compute Express Link (CXL) memory pooling allows supported hosts to access assigned memory capacity through a CXL path, while disaggregated designs make some resource allocations independent of the chassis boundary. This changes which links lie on the workload’s critical path. It does not merge CXL memory access, NVLink communication, and InfiniBand transport into one interchangeable service; each path retains its own supported operations, bandwidth, and latency.


↩︎ CXL memory pooling, which makes node memory capacity less rigid but remains a capacity tier rather than a high-bandwidth memory (HBM) replacement, is established in Compute express link (CXL).
A composed node therefore needs a new traffic budget. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) distinction between startup and transfer cost remains useful, but each path requires its own parameters and access model. Remote memory traffic can compete with other transfers, and fine-grained dependent accesses can expose latency that a bulk-bandwidth estimate hides. Disaggregation improves resource flexibility only when these added costs fit the workload’s execution budget. Composition relocates the synchronization backbone onto new paths rather than eliminating it.

Designing and operating high-performance fabrics for ML requires unlearning assumptions from traditional data-center networking. The following fallacies and pitfalls capture the most common errors that stall training and degrade cluster productivity.

Fallacy: More bandwidth always means faster training.
Engineers assume upgrading from HDR (200 Gb/s) to NDR (400 Gb/s) will yield proportional gains, but the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (section 3.4.4) reveals this is only true in the bandwidth-dominated regime. For small models or the small-message phases of pipeline parallelism, the startup term \(\MessageStartupLatency\) (1.5 μs in this chapter’s NDR scenario, including NIC processing, switch hops, and FEC) dictates performance. If a workload is latency-bound, a 2\(\times\) bandwidth increase may deliver only a small fraction of the line-rate gain while adding substantial power and transceiver cost.
Consider a 10 KB message (typical for control synchronization). On 200 Gb/s InfiniBand, it takes 1.90 μs. Upgrading to 400 Gb/s reduces this to 1.70 μs, a 10.5 percent improvement despite doubling the link rate.


Fallacy: Lossless Ethernet is as reliable as InfiniBand.
RoCE over Ethernet can achieve throughput comparable to InfiniBand for large transfers, but lossless operation depends on the configuration and interaction of PFC, ECN, routing, buffers, and NIC behavior (section 3.6.1). A forwarding loop, cyclic buffer dependency, or firmware defect can trigger a PFC storm, where PAUSE frames spread beyond the original queue. InfiniBand’s per-hop credit mechanism avoids this specific reactive PAUSE-frame cascade, but the fabric still requires deadlock-free routing, sound virtual-lane configuration, and congestion management (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000). Both fabrics require validation and telemetry; RoCE adds particular sensitivity to the configuration of Ethernet losslessness. Procurement should therefore compare complete transport stacks rather than link rates, because the stack determines where flow-control state and operational risk reside even when nominal rates match.

InfiniBand Trade Association. 2000. InfiniBand Architecture Specification Volume 1. InfiniBand Trade Association.


Pitfall: Accepting data-center oversubscription ratios for synchronous training.
Oversubscription relies on the traffic crossing a shared boundary fitting its available capacity. Bulk-synchronous training can violate that assumption with coordinated bursts. In the cut-saturating scenario of section 3.5.2, 4:1 oversubscription increases the modeled communication bound by 4×. Applied to a $300M cluster with the assumed 30 percent communication fraction, the resulting idle-capacity estimate exceeds $142.1M. This is an equivalent-capacity comparison under the stated schedule, not an equipment loss or a universal penalty for every collective.


Fallacy: TCP bandwidth tests are sufficient for ML fabric validation.
Standard benchmarks like iperf measure kernel-based TCP/IP performance. TCP throughput depends on host processing, offloads, and tuning as well as wire speed; it has no fixed throughput ceiling independent of that configuration. An RDMA training job exercises a different data path, so a low TCP result does not establish that the RDMA path is slow, and a high TCP result does not validate collective performance. Validation protocols must use RDMA-specific tools from the perftest suite to match the workload’s data path.


Pitfall: Relying on adaptive routing instead of topology-aware placement.
Adaptive routing can distribute traffic across available paths, but it cannot increase their total capacity. For a 1,024-GPU job spanning two oversubscribed spine groups, the group-to-group links become limiting when the collective sends more crossing traffic than those links can carry within its time budget. Placement can reduce that traffic, and routing can reduce path imbalance. Both must be evaluated against the actual collective schedule.



↪ Topology-aware gang placement that keeps collective traffic off contended cross-rack paths is developed in Placement algorithms.

Fallacy: Network fabric problems always appear as hard failures.
Network performance issues in ML clusters often show up as subtle training slowdowns rather than errors, because jobs continue to run while gradients arrive late. The silent-waste estimate in section 3.9 shows how a small bandwidth loss accumulates into wasted GPU-hours over a long run without raising a single alarm. Detection therefore depends on comparing delivered throughput with a baseline, not on waiting for an error.


Pitfall: Treating PFC and ECN counters as optional production details.
Discard counters and PFC pause durations should be correlated with collective completion time and the affected paths. Rising values can reveal queue pressure or recovery activity, but they do not establish a failing transceiver or predict an inevitable job failure. Physical error counters, traffic load, routing, and configured watchdog actions help distinguish the causes and select a response.

The five-level model of figure 3 bridges physical reach, transport primitives, switch topologies, congestion dynamics, and cluster integration into a single system contract. A fabric must provide both enough capacity for the workload’s traffic and predictable completion at its synchronization boundaries. InfiniBand and RoCE distribute this responsibility differently across links, endpoints, and operational policy; the production cases show why neither port rate nor protocol name determines delivered performance.
Three numerical anchors show how to apply the model. One GPU’s NVLink bandwidth exceeds its own external port’s per-direction bandwidth by 9×; the modeled NDR path has equal startup and transmission costs near 75 KB; and the 4:1 oversubscribed cut increases the fixed-payload transfer bound by 4×. Each result depends on its stated configuration and traffic assumptions. In the Fleet Law, transfer time contributes to \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and residual synchronization waiting to \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\); consistent timeline accounting prevents counting one delay in both. The communication and coordination axes of C³ meet where those dependencies determine useful compute progress.
The same model guides design and diagnosis. Message sizes determine whether startup latency or bandwidth dominates; communication patterns determine which paths must carry that traffic. During operation, application throughput, transport counters, and physical telemetry distinguish inadequate capacity from contention or a degraded component. These measurements also test whether a proposed optical or composable architecture removes the binding constraint or merely moves it.

Key Takeaways: The fabric decides useful compute

Synchronous training inverts data-center traffic: A bulk-synchronous step releases a few large, correlated flows whose completion gates a barrier, so the fabric is judged by collective completion time and its p99 tail rather than by average per-flow throughput. Static ECMP hashing turns flow collisions into persistent hot spots.
Link speed is not fabric speed: For traffic that crosses a fabric cut, available capacity bounds transfer time (principle \(\ref{pri-bisection-bandwidth}\)). Workload placement and collective schedules determine how much data must cross, so advertised port speed alone cannot predict useful training throughput.
Latency and bandwidth bind differently: The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model of section 3.4.4 separates startup cost from per-byte transfer cost, with \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\) marking the regime change. Message-size distributions, not vendor peak numbers, determine whether to optimize software latency or hardware bandwidth.
Reliable delivery moves the risk: RDMA transports need reliable completion and bounded recovery, not one universal lossless-fabric mechanism. InfiniBand normally suppresses loss with link-level credits; many RoCE deployments use PFC and ECN, while PFC-free designs place more recovery responsibility at the endpoints. Each choice trades hardware flexibility against tail latency and operational complexity.
Topology must match traffic: Fat-trees buy flexible bisection bandwidth, rail-optimized designs give same-rank AllReduce traffic its own isolated switch network, and dragonfly or torus designs trade cabling and locality differently. The right fabric depends on whether the workload stresses AllReduce, AllToAll, or multi-tenant sharing.
Losslessness and load create their own failures: PFC prevents drops by pausing senders, which can spread one slow drainer’s congestion to victim flows or freeze a lossless class in a cyclic buffer dependency. Under synchronized load, end-to-end congestion control is a latency requirement, adaptive routing repairs hash collisions without adding capacity, and incast is spread in time, space, and priority rather than eliminated.
Telemetry saves GPU-hours: PFC counters, link error rates, bandwidth baselines, and application throughput must be correlated across layers. Without that observability, a degraded transceiver or congestion storm silently converts a high-end fleet into a queue of waiting accelerators.



At fleet scale, the interconnect is part of the computer. Its value lies in how much useful computation it allows the participating accelerators to complete together. A fabric decision therefore has to be judged against the workload’s communication pattern and synchronization schedule, because additional capacity helps only where those dependencies expose a communication limit.

What’s Next: From wires to data pipelinesA fabric that completes every collective on time still leaves two flows of bytes unaccounted for. Each step needs its next input batch in place before the accelerators ask for it, and the fleet’s training state must outlive the next hardware failure, which at this scale means writing multi-terabyte checkpoints on a schedule. Those checkpoint bursts are the traffic class this chapter isolated from the synchronization path, and for text pretraining they can outweigh the training corpus itself. Data Storage treats storage as the fleet’s fuel line, sizing the tiers and pipelines that deliver inputs ahead of demand and persist model state without stalling the step.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Symbol errors and reduced data counts are evidence of a degrading signal on that link, but a counter alone does not identify a defective cable or transceiver. Correlating the counters with negotiated rate, lane state, and transport behavior, and checking that the link lies on the slow collective’s path, narrows the cause. Replacing hardware on counter evidence alone skips that confirmation, retuning PFC and ECN assumes congestion that the symbol errors do not show, and dismissing the counters ignores the physical-layer evidence they carry.
Learning Objective: Interpret fabric port counters as evidence to correlate across layers rather than as a diagnosis.
Explain the concept of ‘silent degradation’ in an AI cluster fabric, give a concrete physical example of how it occurs, and describe its economic impact on a large synchronous training run.
Answer: Silent degradation occurs when a network link suffers severe bandwidth or latency degradation without failing completely or generating an explicit link-down alert. For example, a damaged connector pin or optical transceiver fault may cause a link to negotiate at HDR (\(200\text{ Gb/s}\)) instead of NDR (\(400\text{ Gb/s}\)), or silently drop from 4 physical lanes to 2. If the affected path limits a required collective transfer and extends its critical path, the participating workers can lose useful compute time while waiting. The chapter’s assumed \(2\text{--}3\%\) iteration slowdown illustrates the resulting GPU-hour and dollar cost over a month-long 1,024-GPU run; neither that slowdown nor its propagation to every worker follows from the link fault alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze silent network degradation and evaluate its economic impact on synchronous training.
What is the primary purpose of constructing an ‘All-Pairs Bandwidth Matrix’ before launching a distributed training job?

To run point-to-point bandwidth benchmarks (such as ib_write_bw) across all node pairs and visualize a heatmap of underperforming node pairs that warrant investigation of paths and endpoints
To pre-allocate GPU memory buffers for all possible tensor-parallel communication patterns
To calculate the exact gradient loss trajectory of the neural network architecture
To calibrate the clock frequency of the CPU PCIe root complex

Answer: The correct answer is A. An All-Pairs Bandwidth Matrix is generated by executing point-to-point RDMA throughput tests (e.g., using ib_write_bw) between every pair of nodes in a cluster allocation. The resulting heatmap identifies underperforming node pairs for investigation before a multi-week training job. Routing information and matched physical, transport, and endpoint telemetry are needed to distinguish a shared switch or cable problem from endpoint limitations; the matrix alone does not identify the failed component. The option proposing pre-allocation of GPU memory buffers describes a runtime memory pool task rather than network validation. The choice regarding gradient loss trajectory confuses training convergence with network testing. The option regarding CPU PCIe clock calibration is unrelated to cluster-wide network benchmarking.
Learning Objective: Apply all-pairs network benchmarking tools to detect fabric performance anomalies.
**Order the recommended diagnostic steps when investigating an unexpected slowdown in a multi-node GPU training job, moving from application symptoms down to physical causes:


Inspect switch PFC pause and ECN congestion counters along the network path
Run point-to-point RDMA bandwidth tests (ib_write_bw) between candidate nodes
Check GPU compute and SM utilization (using nvidia-smi or dcgmi)
Validate physical layer health by checking symbol errors and CRC discard counters
Enable NCCL debug logging (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO) to identify transport selection and detected topology**

Answer: The correct sequence is: (3) Check GPU compute and SM utilization (using nvidia-smi or dcgmi) -> (5) Enable NCCL debug logging (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO) to identify transport selection and detected topology -> (2) Run point-to-point RDMA bandwidth tests (ib_write_bw) between candidate nodes -> (1) Inspect switch PFC pause and ECN congestion counters along the network path -> (4) Validate physical layer health by checking symbol errors and CRC discard counters.
Learning Objective: Order the systematic debugging workflow for distributed training network bottlenecks.

True or False: In a healthy, properly configured lossless InfiniBand or RoCEv2 fabric, the PortXmitDiscards counter on switch ports should periodically increment under heavy AllReduce traffic to signal senders to back off.
Answer: False. Packet discards are not the intended congestion signal in a fabric configured to avoid overflow loss. Operators should investigate new discard increments, while checking the counter definition and interval. Credits, ECN, and configured PFC provide the normal flow-control and congestion signals; a historical nonzero counter alone does not diagnose an active fault.
Learning Objective: Evaluate error and discard counter baselines in lossless network fabrics.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

How does Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) physically reduce interconnect power consumption compared to traditional pluggable optical transceivers?

It replaces optical lasers with superconducting RF antennas that operate without electrical resistance
It integrates silicon photonics directly onto the processor or switch package substrate, shortening the electrical SerDes trace from centimeters to millimeters and eliminating power-hungry signal conditioning
It removes the need for fiber optic cables by transmitting data through free-space infrared beams inside the server rack
It downsamples 16-bit floating-point tensors to 1-bit integers directly inside the optical waveguide

Answer: The correct answer is B. In traditional pluggable architectures, high-speed electrical signals must travel several centimeters across PCBs from the switch ASIC to the faceplate transceiver, requiring high-power SerDes equalization and retimers. Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) integrates silicon photonics chiplets directly onto the same substrate as the switch/compute ASIC, reducing the electrical trace to millimeters and saving approximately \(50\%\) of transceiver power (roughly \(1.28\text{ kW}\) per \(51.2\text{ Tb/s}\) switch). The option alleging superconducting RF antennas is science fiction. The choice proposing free-space infrared beams inside racks misidentifies guided optical fiber architectures. The option describing tensor downsampling inside waveguides confuses optical transmission with algorithmic quantization.
Learning Objective: Explain the physical mechanism and efficiency gains of Co-Packaged Optics.
How does increasing switch ASIC capacity to \(102.4\text{ Tb/s}\) with \(1.6\text{ Tb/s}\) ports impact the topology and latency of a multi-thousand GPU cluster compared to building the same cluster with \(400\text{ Gb/s}\) switches?
Answer: A \(102.4\text{ Tb/s}\) ASIC offers aggregate capacity equivalent to 256 ports at \(400\text{ Gb/s}\), or 64 ports at \(1.6\text{ Tb/s}\). These are bandwidth equivalents, not automatically interchangeable physical port counts. A flatter topology becomes possible when usable radix, breakout support, endpoint rates, and placement permit it. Removing a tier then reduces switch traversals and optical links, but neither a two-tier design nor a halving of transceiver count follows from aggregate ASIC bandwidth alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze the topological and latency impact of higher-radix, next-generation switch silicon.
What is the primary design goal of the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) transport specification for AI and HPC workloads?

To mandate standard TCP Reno congestion control across all high-performance computing clusters
To replace physical Ethernet cabling with proprietary wireless mesh interconnects
To develop an open, multi-vendor Ethernet transport featuring multi-path packet spraying, flexible packet ordering, and improved congestion control and recovery to reduce reliance on PFC
To deprecate GPU-to-GPU direct memory access in favor of host CPU centralized message queues

Answer: The correct answer is C. Ultra Ethernet Transport combines multipath packet spraying, flexible ordering, congestion-control changes, and AI/HPC telemetry within an open Ethernet ecosystem. Its reliability goal is to bound the completion-time penalty of congestion and loss while reducing dependence on PFC. These design goals do not guarantee immunity from every congestion or recovery failure. TCP Reno and centralized host message queues do not describe this transport architecture.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the architecture and design goals of the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) specification.
True or False: Disaggregated composable architectures using CXL memory pooling eliminate the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) communication costs between processors and remote memory pools.
Answer: False. While CXL memory pooling decouples compute and memory into composable resource pools with load/store semantics, cross-chassis memory access still traverses physical wires and switches. It remains governed by physical \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) latency and bandwidth constraints, SerDes power limits, and bisection capacity; disaggregation relocates the synchronization boundary rather than eliminating physical transfer costs.
Learning Objective: Evaluate physical communication limits in disaggregated and composable architectures.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why is using standard TCP benchmark tools like iperf to validate an ML cluster network fabric considered a major operational fallacy?

iperf measures the TCP path, whose throughput depends on host processing, offloads, and tuning; it does not validate the RDMA path exercised by distributed training
iperf only operates over wireless IEEE 802.11 interfaces and cannot bind to physical QSFP56 ports
iperf automatically enables InfiniBand credit-based flow control on standard Ethernet switches
iperf encrypts all network packets with 4096-bit RSA keys, causing false GPU thermal throttling

Answer: The correct answer is A. TCP and RDMA exercise different transport and host-processing paths, so a TCP benchmark cannot establish RDMA or collective performance. TCP throughput depends on host configuration and has no universal fixed ceiling. RDMA-specific tools such as ib_write_bw test the relevant data path; collective benchmarks then test synchronization and topology effects. The wireless-only and automatic InfiniBand flow-control claims are incorrect.
Learning Objective: Analyze why TCP benchmarks are inadequate for validating RDMA-based ML fabrics.
An infrastructure team claims: ‘Adaptive routing completely eliminates the need for topology-aware job placement in our GPU cluster.’ Why is this assertion a critical pitfall?

Adaptive routing only functions when all GPU servers are manufactured by the same vendor
Adaptive routing disables link-layer CRC error checking on optical switches
Adaptive routing forces all AllReduce operations to execute sequentially across a single ring
Adaptive routing balances traffic across existing paths, but it cannot synthesize bisection bandwidth that does not exist if a job is split across an oversubscribed or constrained network boundary

Answer: The correct answer is D. Adaptive routing can direct packets away from congested queues onto less loaded eligible paths, reducing imbalance from static hash collisions. However, it cannot generate physical bandwidth where none exists. For a tightly coupled 1,024-GPU job spanning two spine pods, a collective is limited by their boundary when its crossing traffic exceeds what the boundary can deliver within the communication budget. Adaptive routing can reduce path imbalance but cannot increase that capacity; topology-aware placement can reduce crossing traffic. Both must be evaluated against the actual collective schedule, and neither guarantees efficient delivery by itself. The choices claiming single-vendor restrictions, CRC disabling, or forced sequential ring execution are factually incorrect.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the complementary roles and limitations of adaptive routing versus topology-aware scheduling.
Explain why upgrading an InfiniBand fabric from HDR (\(200\text{ Gb/s}\)) to NDR (\(400\text{ Gb/s}\)) yields less than a \(15\%\) reduction in transfer time for a \(10\text{ KB}\) control message, and state the condition under which bandwidth upgrades deliver linear performance gains.
Answer: For a \(10\text{ KB}\) message, transfer time is governed by the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) model (\(T(n) = \alpha + n/\beta\)). With the same assumed \(\alpha = 1.5\,\mu\text{s}\) on both paths, HDR takes \(1.5 + 0.4 = 1.9\,\mu\text{s}\) and NDR takes \(1.5 + 0.2 = 1.7\,\mu\text{s}\), a reduction of about \(10.5\%\). Startup contributes about \(79\%\) of the HDR total and \(88\%\) of the NDR total. Doubling bandwidth halves the transmission term while leaving startup unchanged. Bandwidth upgrades deliver near-linear speedups only in the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(n \gg n^*\)), such as multi-megabyte to gigabyte gradient AllReduce transfers.
Learning Objective: Explain the diminishing returns of network bandwidth upgrades in latency-dominated regimes.
True or False: Lossless RoCEv2 Ethernet fabrics provide the exact same operational simplicity and fault immunity as InfiniBand fabrics because both support zero-packet-loss guarantees.
Answer: False. InfiniBand uses native credit-based flow control, while many RoCE deployments use Ethernet PFC with endpoint congestion control and recovery. PFC introduces pause-based storms and cyclic-dependency risks, but credits alone do not make InfiniBand immune to deadlock: routing and resource dependencies still matter. PFC-free RoCE designs make a different recovery trade-off.
Learning Objective: Compare operational risk and failure modes in lossless Ethernet versus InfiniBand.

← Back to Questions

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can the network connecting accelerators matter more than the accelerators themselves at scale?
A single accelerator can perform trillions of operations per second, but distributed training requires devices to exchange results before dependent work can proceed. When network capacity cannot keep pace with computation, accelerators sit idle, and adding more devices can increase the waiting instead of shortening the run. The resulting cost extends beyond the network equipment: an inexpensive connection can leave expensive compute capacity unused throughout a long experiment. Single-node intuition is insufficient because data that once traveled through a local interconnect must now cross cables, switches, and shared paths. A fast connection between two machines does not establish that the same performance will hold when the entire fleet communicates at once. The arrangement of those paths determines which groups can exchange data together and where competing transfers accumulate. Large transfers need sustained bandwidth, while frequent dependent exchanges can remain limited by the time required to start and complete each message. A delayed participant can hold up others even when most links appear healthy. Network design therefore has to follow the workload’s communication pattern, and validation must reflect the traffic that will actually run. Choices about placement, sharing, and failure recovery affect whether available bandwidth becomes useful progress or recurring delay. In C³ terms, the fabric connects compute through communication, while coordination determines when the fleet must wait for that communication to finish.

Learning Objectives

Explain how synchronized collective traffic inverts data-center assumptions about flows, loss, and oversubscription
Model network communication cost using the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) framework and identify bandwidth-dominated vs. latency-dominated regimes
Compare high-performance transport protocols by latency, loss-recovery behavior, and operational complexity
Compare network topologies using \(\BisectionBandwidth\), hop count, and the workload’s collective communication pattern
Evaluate congestion-control mechanisms and their impact on tail latency during distributed training
Compare network partitioning and traffic-isolation mechanisms for concurrent training and inference workloads
Diagnose network performance bottlenecks using RDMA counters, link-level telemetry, and bandwidth testing tools

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
One slow link stalls every peer that waits on it.
Compute Infrastructure traced the bandwidth hierarchy down to the node boundary, where each GPU’s NVLink bandwidth narrows to a single external network port. How much that narrowing costs depends on what the training job must push through the port, and how often. Consider the running instance of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), a 175B-parameter GPT-3-class dense transformer partitioned across the 1,024 GPUs of the reference cluster. Each training step must combine gradient contributions so that corresponding model replicas apply the same update. This operation, called AllReduce, returns the combined result to every participating worker. The model has 350 GB of gradient data at two bytes per parameter, the 16-bit gradients of mixed-precision training that this chapter assumes throughout (FP32 gradients would double the figure). That model-wide figure is not what any one GPU sends. When a reduction partitions the gradient across all 1,024 ranks, each rank owns a 1/1,024 share, a few hundred megabytes, which is the gradient-shard size the transport examples below use; the job’s tensor, pipeline, and data-parallel split (Distributed Training) sets each GPU’s actual payload. Worked examples that switch to another model, precision, or payload state their parameters explicitly. A delayed transfer on the step’s critical path can leave the other 1023 GPUs waiting at a job-wide synchronization boundary. The fabric’s contribution to training time therefore depends on which transfers the next computation needs and how much of their cost remains exposed. In that role the fabric is not auxiliary infrastructure; it is the synchronization backbone that decides whether the cluster trains as one machine.
Within the multi-tier fleet hierarchy framed by The Fleet Stack, the fabric turns isolated accelerator nodes into a coherent training system. Accelerators, power delivery, cooling, racks, and pods define what each node can compute in isolation; the fabric determines whether the nodes can act together before communication cost overwhelms computation. That design space organizes into a five-level model of co-dependent tiers, developed in section 3.2.1.
At scale, communication cost can dominate computation cost. The fleet-law decomposition in The Fleet Law makes this explicit: the nonoverlapped communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime\) determines how much of each training step is exposed to the network fabric. The fabric influences the layers above it by determining whether communication can run while independent computation continues, which collective algorithms are viable, and how network partitions interact with node failures. That concurrency, communication-computation overlap, is what the \(\OverlappedTime\) term credits, because transfer time that proceeds behind useful arithmetic does not lengthen the step.


↪ How layer-by-layer scheduling achieves that overlap, and how much communication it still leaves exposed, is developed in Communication-Computation Overlap.
A collective is a communication operation performed by a group of workers. Its name specifies the result each worker receives, while an algorithm determines the messages that produce that result. The physical network fabric carries three recurring collective communication patterns:

AllReduce: Combines corresponding values from all participants and returns the same result to each; synchronous training uses a sum, followed by normalization, to average gradient contributions across workers.
AllGather: Collects a distinct portion from each participant and returns the concatenated collection to every participant, as required when reconstructing a sharded parameter tensor.
AllToAll: Lets each participant send a distinct portion to every other participant, an exchange central to expert parallelism when workers host different expert subnetworks and must route tokens to their assigned destinations.

Collective communication algorithms orchestrate these patterns, while the fabric layer supplies the physical wires and switches that carry them. The distinction matters because the fabric’s physical properties (bandwidth, latency, and topology) determine which patterns are efficient and which become bottlenecks.


↪ The full set of collective primitives, with the output contract each one guarantees, is developed in The six core primitives.

Systems Perspective 3.1: The network as a gradient busIn a single machine, the memory bus moves data between the processor and memory. In a distributed training cluster, the network fabric serves an analogous role as the gradient bus that carries contributions between workers. When those exchanges limit progress, the job encounters the network wall mapped across the pod tier in The Four Infrastructure Walls. Protocols, topologies, congestion control, and collective schedules determine how effectively the job uses the available paths. This bus has a narrow segment. Since NVLink appeared, the external ports that join machines have offered less bandwidth than the interconnect inside each machine in every generation (figure 1). How much of that gap a job actually feels depends on its message sizes, port provisioning, routing, and contention, so the link ratio bounds the problem rather than predicting a transfer time.




↩︎ Communication dominance at scale, the network wall, is established in Communication dominance and the network wall.














Figure 1: Historical Network Bandwidth Scaling: Intra-node NVLink, inter-node InfiniBand and Ethernet, and the PCIe host bus, plotted per direction on a common log scale by the year each generation first shipped, 2010 to 2025. The aggregate NVLink budget exceeds the external-port budgets in these configurations; collective completion time also depends on payloads, provisioning, routing, and overlap. Rates and first-product years from IEEE 802.3, InfiniBand Trade Association, PCI-SIG, and NVIDIA specifications and product announcements.



The reference hardware gives the gradient bus analogy a concrete scale. A single H100 has a precision-specific FP16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s and memory bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s. Each GPU’s NVLink ports together provide 900 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth to its peers within the node. The comparison that matters is per GPU and per direction. In the reference node each GPU has its own network interface card (NIC) with one NDR InfiniBand port, so a tensor leaving the node through that GPU drops from 450 GB/s of NVLink bandwidth to 50 GB/s at the port. This 9× gap is the node boundary’s cliff that the bandwidth hierarchy of Bandwidth hierarchy already identified. The model-wide 350 GB gradient state does not all pass through every 50 GB/s port; partitioning and the collective schedule determine each port’s traffic. Converting that gap into a step-time estimate requires the workload’s local payloads and communication dependencies.


↪ The network hierarchy ratio between intra-node and inter-node bandwidth, with the reference NVLink and InfiniBand values behind it, is developed in Numbers Every Fleet Engineer Should Know.
Which traffic must cross that gap depends on how the job is partitioned. The same hierarchy keeps tensor parallelism, with its per-layer exchanges, inside the NVLink domain and lets pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas span nodes, the combination called 3D parallelism whose schedules are developed in The 3D training loop. The fabric adds one lever to that placement. Each data-parallel replica can sum gradients over several microbatches before an exchange (gradient accumulation), reducing how often it must cross the node boundary at the cost of changing the batch and update schedule.
Exposed communication leaves gaps between dependent compute phases. Two assumed training schedules on a common 230 ms axis, each containing 100 ms forward and backward compute phases, make that cost visible (figure 2). The 8-GPU intra-node case assumes a 1 ms AllReduce and spends 99.5 percent of the step in those compute phases; the 64-GPU inter-node case assumes a 30 ms AllReduce and spends 87 percent in computation. The two AllReduce durations are illustrative inputs chosen to show the effect, not values derived from the link rates above, and the percentages are shares of the schedule rather than measured arithmetic utilization.






Figure 2: The Bandwidth Cliff in a Training Step: Illustrative timelines on a common millisecond axis for the same compute phases: an 8-GPU intra-node job (top) with an assumed 1 ms AllReduce, and a 64-GPU inter-node job (bottom) with an assumed 30 ms AllReduce. These durations illustrate an exposed communication cost rather than predict a particular fabric. The AllReduce phase (red) grows from a thin sliver to a larger share of the step. Without overlap, model computation waits during AllReduce. The compute phases occupy 99.5 percent and 87 percent of these illustrative schedules, a gap of 12.5 percentage points; these shares are not arithmetic utilization measurements.



In Fleet Law terms, the widened red block is the part of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) that no \(\OverlappedTime\) has hidden. In the inter-node schedule it is 30 ms of every 230 ms step, about 13 percent, and that share applies to every accelerator-hour the cluster spends for the life of the run. Network fabric design therefore belongs at the center of distributed-training design rather than at its edge, and keeping that exposed window small requires rethinking the traffic assumptions that govern conventional data-center fabrics.

Self-Check: Question

On an H100 GPU server, why does moving gradient synchronization across node boundaries create a severe ‘bandwidth cliff,’ and by what factor does per-direction bandwidth drop when transitioning from local NVLink to a single NDR InfiniBand port?

Bandwidth drops by roughly \(2\times\) because optical conversion adds latency while maintaining similar wire transfer rates
Bandwidth drops by roughly \(50\times\) because inter-node links must encapsulate packets in kernel TCP/IP stacks
Bandwidth drops by roughly \(9\times\) (from \(450\text{ GB/s}\) per direction to \(50\text{ GB/s}\) per port) due to the physical distance and switching constraints of inter-node cables
Bandwidth drops by roughly \(100\times\) because inter-node communication requires staging all gradients through CPU system RAM

In a 1,024-GPU synchronous training job on a 175B-parameter model, a degraded inter-node link carries a required collective transfer. Explain when its delay can leave the other participating GPUs waiting, and why the link fault alone does not establish a job-wide slowdown.
True or False: AllToAll collective communication is less demanding on network fabric bisection bandwidth than AllReduce because each GPU only sends data to a single designated peer.
In a distributed training cluster, the network fabric functions as the global ______, analogous to the internal memory bus in a single workstation, moving parameter updates and activation tensors between accelerators.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
A conventional cloud network built for millions of independent web requests breaks down when a training job releases its gradient exchanges in lockstep at the end of a backward pass. Statistical multiplexing relies on traffic peaks not all coinciding, whereas synchronized workers demand the same switch paths at the same microsecond. Web services also have dependency chains and tail-latency requirements, but a bulk-synchronous training job binds every participating worker to a single shared completion boundary.
The ML networking inversion in table 1 concerns this change in traffic dependencies. Synchronous collective phases can generate correlated bursts and long-lived flows whose completion gates the next computation. Fabric validation must therefore measure collective completion under the expected load; average per-flow throughput alone does not establish that the job can meet its step-time budget.



Table 1: ML Networking Inverts Traditional Data-Center Assumptions: The comparison contrasts independent-request traffic with synchronized collective phases. Correlated demand and shared completion boundaries change the fabric’s capacity and latency requirements.










Workload pattern
Traditional data-center assumption
ML reality




Traffic pattern
Independent requests can arrive asynchronously
Collective phases can release correlated bursts


Flow type
Many short transfers can share available paths
Large collective transfers can create persistent “elephant” flows


Performance metric
Per-request completion and throughput
Collective completion and exposed step time


Loss tolerance
Recovery delays affected requests
Recovery can delay dependent workers at a barrier


Congestion
Statistical multiplexing relies on noncoincident peaks
Shared paths and fan-in can concentrate synchronized traffic






The bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)1 model, the lockstep at step barriers already met at the scale of one node (The Node), makes the dependency in table 1 explicit. In the synchronous training example, all 1,024 GPUs must complete the required gradient exchange before the next step can proceed. A 100 ms transfer delay adds 100 ms to that step only if it extends the critical path by the full interval; other computation or communication may hide part of it. At a barrier that waits for the last required result, tail latency, the slow end of the completion-time distribution (commonly reported as its 99th percentile, p99), decides when the step ends, so at such a barrier the tail cannot be dismissed as an outlier.
1 BSP (bulk synchronous parallel): Proposed by Valiant (1990) as a bridging model between parallel hardware and software. Synchronous data-parallel training follows the same barrier structure (Goyal et al. 2017; Li et al. 2020).
Valiant, Leslie G. 1990. “A Bridging Model for Parallel Computation.” Communications of the ACM 33 (8): 103–11. https://doi.org/10.1145/79173.79181.

Goyal, Priya, Piotr Dollár, Ross Girshick, Pieter Noordhuis, Lukasz Wesolowski, Aapo Kyrola, Andrew Tulloch, Yangqing Jia, and Kaiming He. 2017. “Accurate, Large Minibatch SGD: Training ImageNet in 1 Hour.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1706.02677 abs/1706.02677.

Li, Shen, Yanli Zhao, Rohan Varma, Omkar Salpekar, Pieter Noordhuis, Teng Li, Adam Paszke, et al. 2020. “PyTorch Distributed: Experiences on Accelerating Data Parallel Training.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 13 (12): 3005–18. https://doi.org/10.14778/3415478.3415530.

Definition 3.1: Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)
Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) is a parallel execution model in which every worker completes a local computation phase, exchanges the data required by the next phase, and then waits at a global barrier before any worker begins the next phase, which makes the slowest participant the pacing constraint for the entire cluster.

Significance: The slowest required computation or communication determines when a superstep can complete. Faster workers wait at the barrier, so a localized delay can consume idle accelerator time across the entire participating group.
Distinction: BSP organizes execution into synchronized supersteps; it does not itself prescribe a learning algorithm or a particular exchange pattern. Synchronous data-parallel updates match a single-device reference only under compatible global batches, update rules, and numerical assumptions.
Common pitfall: Removing barriers does not by itself establish faster time-to-quality. Asynchronous training trades waiting against stale updates, and the convergence and wall-clock comparison depends on the workload and update schedule.





↩︎ Synchronous tight coupling, the shared step barrier that lets the slowest worker pace a training fleet, is established in Independent tasks vs. synchronous training steps.
2 Elephant and mice flows: The model-wide gradient size is not the size of one network flow. A collective can split each worker’s local gradient shard across channels and transport connections; the resulting long-lived flows can still collide under ECMP when their static hashes select the same path.The flow inversion compounds this problem. Traditional networks are designed for fairness among millions of “mice flows,”2 yet ML training is dominated by a few “elephant flows” corresponding to the gradient AllReduce. The full 175B model has 350 GB of gradient state at the assumed precision, but a sharded job distributes that state across workers. Each collective operates on its participating group and local payload; its algorithm determines how much each worker sends. Standard flow control and routing mechanisms like equal-cost multi-path (ECMP), which hash each flow onto one of several equal-cost paths, are poorly suited to this traffic pattern. A static hash cannot subdivide one elephant flow across all available links, and it can inadvertently map multiple elephant flows to the same link, creating massive congestion while other links sit idle.
The loss inversion completes the picture. TCP was designed to recover across an unreliable network, and an occasional retransmission delays only the request it belongs to. In a synchronous collective, a lost packet delays the transfer that every waiting worker needs, and some NICs that implement remote direct memory access (RDMA), called RDMA NICs or RNICs, recover by resending everything after the missing packet rather than only the lost region (Go-Back-N-style recovery). ML fabrics therefore aim to make loss rare and recovery bounded, either by preventing buffer overflow at the link layer or by building transports that recover quickly from it. Level 2 (section 3.4.3) develops both approaches.
Correlated demand also makes oversubscription, provisioning less uplink capacity at a switch tier than the downlink capacity it serves (written as a downlink:uplink ratio such as 2:1), a workload decision. A fabric with spare capacity under independent requests can become saturated when a collective releases traffic across the same cut. Designing for that traffic requires tracing the constraint from the wire through transport, topology, and congestion control to the job’s synchronization boundary.


Provisioning fast NICs or buying a non-blocking switch tier in isolation routinely fails to speed up training: a 400 Gb/s link still stalls if host TCP copies starve the PCIe bus, an unaligned rack layout exhausts the copper link budget, or static ECMP hashing piles two elephant flows onto one spine port. Tracing why a collective slows down requires following the packet across five coupled layers, from serializer/deserializer (SerDes) signaling and copper or optical reach at Level 1 to the integration of a production cluster at Level 5 (figure 3). Each level is developed at the point where its physical or protocol limit becomes the binding constraint.






Figure 3: The Five-Level Network Model for ML Training: Read from the bottom up, each level builds on the one below and becomes more abstract. Level 1 moves bits over wires and optics; Level 2 turns links into reliable, low-overhead transfers between accelerators; Level 3 arranges switches into a topology; Level 4 governs how the fabric behaves under load and congestion; and Level 5 integrates all of them into a production cluster.



Each inversion of table 1 traces back to a specific physical or protocol constraint, and the five levels locate where each one is paid:

Level 1: wire and link (section 3.3). Signal integrity (PAM4, SerDes), forward error correction, and the reach of copper and optics impose hard constraints on per-hop latency and cluster geometry.
Level 2: transport (section 3.4). InfiniBand and RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) provide RDMA primitives; the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model quantifies the latency-vs.-bandwidth trade-off for different message sizes.
Level 3: switch and topology (section 3.5). Fat-trees, rail-optimized designs, and dragonflies achieve the \(\BisectionBandwidth\) needed for global collectives through different structural trade-offs.
Level 4: fabric behavior (section 3.6). Link-level flow control and end-to-end congestion control determine whether theoretical bandwidth translates to realized throughput; adaptive routing and incast behavior determine whether that throughput survives real collective traffic (Alizadeh et al. 2010; Zhu et al. 2015; Li et al. 2019; Gangidi et al. 2024).
Level 5: cluster design (section 3.7). Production supercomputers like the NVIDIA SuperPOD and Meta Grand Teton integrate these layers into a unified gradient bus (NVIDIA 2023; Meta Engineering 2024).


Alizadeh, Mohammad, Albert Greenberg, David A. Maltz, Jitendra Padhye, Parveen Patel, Balaji Prabhakar, Sudipta Sengupta, and Murari Sridharan. 2010. “Data Center TCP (DCTCP).” Proceedings of the ACM SIGCOMM 2010 Conference, 63–74. https://doi.org/10.1145/1851182.1851192.
The levels are not an inventory of networking topics; they are the causal chain that turns synchronous ML traffic into infrastructure requirements. Large gradient messages first stress the wire and transport, then force topology choices that preserve bisection bandwidth, then expose congestion behavior that ordinary enterprise networks can hide, and finally determine whether the whole cluster behaves like one training machine.
The traffic pattern determines which fabric metric matters. A global reduction stresses bisection bandwidth and the slowest path; a point-to-point pipeline transfer sits on the critical path, so its full transfer time and hop count matter; an expert exchange stresses path diversity and egress balance; and checkpoint or tenant traffic stresses isolation from the synchronization path (table 2). The remaining levels develop each of these pairings in turn.

Mapping workload semantics to physical constraints shows why ML fabric design must proceed from the physical layer up. Before higher-level topologies or routing protocols can organize traffic, the physical layer must reliably deliver bits between endpoints without excessive signal attenuation or prohibitive power consumption. Level 1 begins where all fabric architecture originates: at the physical wire.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
At 400 Gb/s and beyond, the physics of signal transmission imposes hard limits on cable length, power consumption, and error rates. Signal attenuation in copper and chromatic dispersion in fiber dictate how far an accelerator can sit from its switches before communication fails. Every higher-level protocol and topology is ultimately constrained by what the physical wire can carry; these limits shape the geometry of the entire cluster. To meet throughput demands without raising the signaling rate into worse attenuation, link designs must carry more bits in each transmitted symbol.


Achieving 400 Gb/s and higher line rates requires balancing signaling speed against channel loss and detection errors. The symbol rate counts transmitted symbols per second; consecutive symbols need not produce a voltage transition. Raising the symbol rate raises the frequencies the channel must carry, and copper loses more signal at higher frequencies. Carrying more bits in each symbol, by using more than two signal levels, raises the bit rate without that penalty, and PAM4 is the scheme high-speed links use to do it.

Definition 3.2: PAM4 signaling
PAM4 signaling is a modulation scheme that represents two bits per symbol with four signal levels, doubling the raw bit rate relative to binary signaling at the same symbol rate.

Significance: PAM4 increases the raw \(\Bandwidth\) available at a given symbol rate. The reduced separation between levels makes error-control design part of that gain. High-speed Ethernet uses forward error correction (FEC), including Reed-Solomon RS(544,514), with processing latency that depends on the physical-layer (PHY) design and implementation (Anslow 2016; Yin et al. 2022). FEC contributes to the fixed path budget modeled by the \(\MessageStartupLatency\) term in section 3.4.4; it is one component alongside propagation, switching, and endpoint processing.
Distinction: At equal symbol rate and voltage swing, NRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero) binary signaling carries one bit per symbol with greater separation between levels. PAM4 carries two bits per symbol with smaller level spacing; the link must compensate through its signal-quality and error-correction design.
Common pitfall: Doubling bits per symbol does not guarantee twice the usable payload throughput or a fixed latency penalty. Coding overhead, channel quality, and the chosen PHY implementation determine delivered performance.




Anslow, Pete. 2016. RS(544,514) FEC Performance Including Precoding. IEEE P802.3cd Task Force.

Yin, Shuang, Xiang Zhou, and Cedric Lam. 2022. FEC Requirements for 800GbE/1.6TbE Optics: An Operator’s Perspective. IEEE 802.3df Task Force.
The price is noise margin. With four levels packed into the same voltage swing, the gap between adjacent levels in PAM4 shrinks to one third of the NRZ gap (figure 4), making the link highly susceptible to noise. Consequently, high-speed links operate near the physical limits of reliable detection and require forward error correction (FEC) at the physical layer, commonly using Reed-Solomon RS(544,514)-family codes in high-speed Ethernet designs (Anslow 2016; Ethernet Alliance 2025). FEC processing is an implementation-dependent latency term; IEEE 802.3df operator material treats roughly 100 ns of host-side FEC with the RS(544,514) code (called KP4 in the standard) and hundreds of nanoseconds of end-to-end module latency as meaningful at AI/HPC fabric timescales (Yin et al. 2022). Because each switch on a path decodes and re-encodes the signal, the FEC cost accumulates with the number of switches a packet traverses. A path’s length is its hop count, counted as switch traversals or as inter-switch links; where the two counts differ, each example states which one it uses. A packet that traverses three switches, the leaf-spine-leaf route of a two-tier fabric, incurs a scenario budget of 300 ns–600 ns of one-way FEC latency, or 600 ns–1200 ns for a round trip. Against the 350 GB gradient of the 175B job, a few hundred nanoseconds are negligible, because bulk transfers are governed by bandwidth. The cost lands instead on small, latency-bound messages, such as the control handoffs that coordinate pipeline stages, and on collectives whose many sequential steps each pay it. This physical-layer latency sets a floor on the fabric’s fixed startup latency, formalized in section 3.4.4 as the \(\MessageStartupLatency\) term, that no software optimization can remove.






Figure 4: From NRZ to PAM4 Signaling: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric’s fixed \(\MessageStartupLatency\) latency.



Doubling line rate without doubling the symbol rate therefore trades signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for bandwidth, and forward error correction is what lets the link operate that close to the channel limit. Because that tighter margin leaves less room for channel attenuation, it also shortens the distance a passive copper cable can span before the link must switch to optics.



Past one to three meters, passive copper attenuates high-frequency PAM4 signals beyond what even FEC can recover, forcing any link that exits a rack onto active optical cables or pluggable optics at a steep jump in cost and power. The choice of physical medium therefore determines how far a link can reach before latency, power, and cabling budgets reshape the cluster geometry, and the recurring cable and optics options differ along exactly those attributes (table 3).

The high-speed copper and optical paths considered here both include FEC, so choosing optics does not by itself remove error-correction overhead. The ranges in table 3 describe representative placements rather than fixed boundaries between media. Optical interconnects can extend the layout beyond a passive copper channel’s budget, while pluggable optics also permit separate replacement of modules and fiber. Reach, delivered latency, power, and serviceability jointly determine the choice.

Systems Perspective 3.2: The cost of distanceIn an ML fleet, distance is money. Assuming two spine-layer optical links per accelerator, a cluster of 10,000 GPUs requires ~20,000 optical links at the spine layer alone. At $500 per complete link, that represents $10 million in cabling. For power, count one selected spine-side pluggable module per link at 20 W per module, giving 400 kW for those endpoints alone. Each optical link also has a module at its opposite end; this subtotal excludes those modules, switch electronics, and cooling, so it is not the full fabric power budget. The cost dictates cluster geometry: architects pack accelerators as densely as possible (70–100 kW per rack) to maximize cheap copper and minimize expensive optics.





Driving thousands of high-speed links across a cluster burns tens of kilowatts just to serialize bits onto the wire, rivaling a noticeable share of the accelerators’ own thermal budget. Every port depends on a serializer/deserializer (SerDes) circuit that converts parallel data from the switch application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) into a serial stream, and its power cost accumulates across the provisioned ports. For the 1,024 GPUs reference cluster, assume a full-\(\BisectionBandwidth\) fabric with roughly 3,000 high-speed links across its host and switch tiers. Count one selected switch-side port per link in this power subtotal. Each counted 400 Gb/s port is assigned 25 W, more than the 20 W pluggable-module figure in the cost-of-distance estimate because it also counts the switch-side SerDes that drives the module. The model totals 75 kW, equivalent to 10.5 percent of the accelerators’ combined thermal design power. This comparison isolates the assumed power of the selected switch-side ports, excluding the opposite endpoints and the rest of the switch chassis; it does not establish total fabric power or the fraction of measured cluster energy consumed by networking.
The link budget allocates the signal loss a path can tolerate while meeting its error target. Losses are counted in decibels (dB), a logarithmic power ratio in which every 10 dB is a further tenfold attenuation (3 dB is roughly a halving), so the losses of cables and connectors in series add directly. In this simplified accounting, a lane has a 30 dB allowance. A 3-meter DAC cable contributing 18 dB of loss and connectors contributing 2 dB leave 10 dB of margin. Higher signaling frequencies increase copper loss, so preserving reach can require more signal conditioning, a different cable, or optics. Aggregate port speed alone does not determine cable reach; lane rate, channel construction, and active components matter. The design must meet both the signal-quality target and the power budget before the transport layer can rely on the link.
