title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
Closing the physical link budget delivers raw bits between adjacent ports, but a single AllReduce across 1,024 GPUs still stalls if host software sits in the path of every transfer or if a dropped packet triggers a multi-millisecond recovery pause. Turning raw wire rate into predictable step time requires a transport layer that offloads memory-to-memory delivery and bounds loss recovery (a contract met either through a physically lossless fabric or through loss-tolerant endpoint recovery), together with a performance model that separates fixed per-message startup latency from sustained link bandwidth.


A conventional kernel TCP path charges the host for every byte it moves. Interrupt processing, protocol work, and payload copies consume CPU cycles and memory bandwidth that the training process also needs for data loading and preprocessing, and the charge grows with aggregate I/O as many streams or NICs drive a host at 400 Gb/s link rates. Modern TCP stacks reduce the charge with segmentation offload, receive-side scaling, zero-copy interfaces, and careful non-uniform memory access (NUMA) placement, so a single stream need not exhaust a server’s memory bandwidth. They do not remove it, and the contention becomes harder to provision predictably as nodes add NICs.

Definition 3.3: Remote direct memory access (RDMA)
Remote direct memory access (RDMA) is a networking technology that offloads transport processing to network interface hardware, allowing access to registered remote memory without per-transfer kernel processing of the payload.

Significance: RDMA can reduce end-to-end message latency from tens of microseconds for a kernel TCP path to low-single-digit microseconds on a tuned fabric, shrinking the fixed startup cost that every message adds to the Fleet Law’s communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\).
Distinction: Unlike a conventional kernel TCP path, RDMA offloads transport processing to NIC hardware and permits user-space access to registered memory. The resulting CPU-core and memory-bandwidth savings depend on the host, NIC, I/O path, message size, and software configuration rather than on link rate alone.
Common pitfall: RDMA is an access and offload model, not one loss-recovery algorithm. Reliable InfiniBand and RoCE transports detect loss and retransmit (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000). Some RNIC generations use the Go-Back-N-style recovery noted with the loss inversion, which makes a drop expensive (section 3.4.3 quantifies the cost), while other designs support stronger selective recovery or tolerate lossy Ethernet without the link-layer pause mechanism (priority flow control) that many RoCE deployments rely on (Mittal et al. 2018). The requirement is reliable completion with a recovery tail that the synchronized workload can tolerate, not a physically lossless Ethernet fabric in every implementation.



3 GPUDirect RDMA: Introduced by NVIDIA for Kepler-class GPUs and CUDA 5.0, GPUDirect RDMA enables a direct PCIe path between GPU memory and third-party peer devices such as network interfaces (NVIDIA 2026b). Before GPUDirect, every gradient transfer had to stage through host memory, consuming CPU memory bandwidth that competes with data loading. Eliminating this bounce path is one reason overlapping communication with backward-pass computation is feasible at scale.
NVIDIA. 2026b. GPUDirect RDMA.
RDMA bypasses the kernel data path. Offloading transport logic to the NIC allows applications to read and write registered remote memory without per-message kernel intervention. For ML, GPUDirect RDMA,3 the path that dense nodes pair with one NIC per GPU (Dense node designs), extends this principle to accelerator memory (NVIDIA 2026b). Within a sending node (figure 5), GPUDirect RDMA routes an \(\PointToPointMessageSize\)-byte payload (what one participant sends, not the model-wide gradient state) along the solid green peer-to-peer path through the PCIe switch straight to the RDMA NIC, bypassing host memory entirely. Without this direct memory access (DMA) bypass, the dashed gray staging path must first copy \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and subsequently read \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes out to the NIC, generating roughly \(2\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes of redundant host-memory bus traffic. The network still transfers the payload, and the PCIe path may comprise multiple DMA transactions; the optimization removes staging copies rather than collapsing the transfer into one transaction.






Figure 5: GPUDirect RDMA Data Path: Without GPUDirect (dashed), a sending node first writes the \(\PointToPointMessageSize\)-byte payload from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and the NIC then reads it back out, about \(2\PointToPointMessageSize\) bytes of host-memory traffic per payload. With GPUDirect RDMA (solid), the NIC reads GPU memory directly over the PCIe peer-to-peer path, so the host-memory bounce disappears.






GPU clusters commonly choose between two RDMA transport stacks, and the decision is a reliability-versus-operations trade-off. Both stacks must keep switch buffers from overflowing under synchronized bursts, and they do so in different places. InfiniBand uses credit-based flow control. Each receiver advertises its free buffer space to the sender at the other end of the link in units called credits, and the sender transmits only into space that has been advertised. A buffer therefore cannot overflow; congestion appears as senders waiting for credits rather than as dropped packets. Ethernet was designed to drop packets when buffers fill, so RoCE deployments that want the same behavior add two mechanisms. Priority flow control (PFC) lets a filling switch port send a PAUSE frame that stops its upstream neighbor for one traffic class, and explicit congestion notification (ECN) marks packets that pass through a filling queue so that their senders slow down before a pause is needed. InfiniBand thus builds losslessness into the link layer, while RoCE assembles it from switch configuration and end-to-end congestion control (table 4); section 3.6.1 develops PFC’s failure modes.



Table 4: RDMA Transport Stack Trade-Offs: InfiniBand and RoCE expose RDMA semantics through different operational contracts, one built around native losslessness and the other around Ethernet compatibility.











Stack
Fabric behavior
Operational burden
Typical fit




InfiniBand (IB)

a central subnet manager computes routes, and virtual lanes (VLs), separate buffer and credit pools on one link, isolate traffic

RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet)

The InfiniBand4 row reflects a protocol heritage that favors hardware-managed losslessness over Ethernet compatibility, while both RDMA stacks share the same user-space bypass across the user-space, kernel, and hardware boundary (figure 6). The conventional copied TCP/IP path on the left uses two software copies across kernel buffer boundaries and runs the protocol in software. The RDMA stack on the right traces a single amber bypass arrow from the collective communication library (such as the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, or NCCL) and the user-space verbs API straight to the RDMA NIC, which keeps the operating system off the active data path.
4 InfiniBand: Formed in 1999 from the merger of two competing server I/O standards (Future I/O and NGIO), InfiniBand was originally designed to replace PCI as a general-purpose system interconnect. Its pivot to HPC networking preserved the credit-based, hardware-managed flow control that server I/O demanded, and that heritage is why InfiniBand provides native losslessness without the PFC fragility of Ethernet-based RDMA fabrics.





Figure 6: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA Verbs Stacks: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC’s transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. With RDMA verbs over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 (right), the collective library posts work requests from user space, the kernel stays off the data path, and the RDMA NIC runs the reliable transport in hardware, reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect instead of staging a host copy.






By routing the user-space verbs API directly to hardware (figure 6), the architecture decouples collective library calls from the operating system, leaving the transport hardware and fabric to arbitrate reliable delivery and packet loss. Reliable connected transports in both InfiniBand and RoCE detect loss and retransmit (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000); credits and PFC exist to make that retransmission rare (Guo et al. 2016; Gangidi et al. 2024). Losslessness is therefore a deployment contract rather than a property of RDMA as a family. Designs that operate over lossy Ethernet without PFC shift more responsibility to endpoint congestion control, packet reordering, and selective recovery (Mittal et al. 2018).
Recovery granularity therefore matters. On an RNIC with Go-Back-N-style recovery and no out-of-order retention, a lost packet invalidates every packet that arrives after it, and the sender must retransmit from the missing sequence point. The penalty is everything the sender transmitted between the lost packet and the moment it learned of the loss, so it equals link rate times detection delay. If the receiver’s negative acknowledgment reaches the sender after one 5 μs round trip, a sender at 50 GB/s has meanwhile sent 250 KB, all of which it must send again; a drop 900 MB into a 1 GB transfer wastes that window, not the 900 MB already delivered. When detection instead waits for a retransmission timeout, the delay, and with it the resent window, grows with that timeout. An RNIC with selective recovery retransmits only the missing packets, so the same physical loss produces a shorter tail (Mittal et al. 2018). Because the window is line rate times detection delay, resending it takes about as long as detecting the loss did, so a faster link resends more bytes per drop without shortening the stall. Either way the stall spans many packet wire times, and a synchronous collective exposes the slowest recovery to every waiting worker. Fabric designers can reduce that tail by suppressing drops with PFC, by using a loss-tolerant transport with bounded endpoint recovery, or by combining congestion control and admission policy so queues rarely overflow. Each choice moves state and failure modes between switches and endpoints.



Even on a lossless RDMA path with zero packet drops, doubling the link rate barely speeds up a few-kilobyte pipeline control handoff while cutting a multi-hundred-megabyte gradient transfer nearly in half. Separating those two behaviors requires a cost model that distinguishes fixed per-message overhead from per-byte transmission rate. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)) decomposes message transfer time as \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\), where \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) is the message size in bytes, \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the fixed startup latency, and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is the sustained bandwidth in bytes per unit time (Hockney 1994). The physical topology influences both parameters through path length and available capacity. A collective built from many sequential rounds of messages pays \(\MessageStartupLatency\) once per round, so its startup cost can grow with the number of participants even when the underlying fabric provides short physical paths.

Hockney, Roger W. 1994. “The Communication Challenge for MPP: Intel Paragon and Meiko CS-2.” Parallel Computing 20 (3): 389–98. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0167-8191(06)80021-9.

↪ The same decomposition, multiplied by each schedule’s round count and traffic factor, is developed for collective algorithms in Pricing Collectives by Rounds and Chunks.

The model reveals two regimes that call for different engineering responses. When \(\PointToPointMessageSize< \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\), the startup cost \(\MessageStartupLatency\) exceeds the transmission cost, placing small control messages deep in the latency-bound region, whereas when \(\PointToPointMessageSize> \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth\), the \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) term dominates and large gradient transfers sit deep in the bandwidth-bound region. Near the crossover both terms matter, and where a collective lands also depends on how its algorithm divides the payload into messages and schedules them across rounds.


↪ The crossover message size that separates the latency-dominated and bandwidth-dominated regimes, with a worked InfiniBand NDR example, is developed in Latency-dominated vs. bandwidth-dominated regimes.
For the modeled NDR InfiniBand path with \(\MessageStartupLatency=\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth=\) 50 GB/s, the crossover point \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\approx\) 75 KB. Measured startup latency and delivered bandwidth vary with the NIC, switch path, software stack, and contention, so these parameters describe a scenario rather than a protocol constant. Far below the crossover, more bandwidth removes only a small part of transfer time; far above it, lower startup latency removes only a small part. Shorter paths can lower \(\MessageStartupLatency\), while additional delivered path bandwidth raises \(\LinkBandwidth\); their value depends on the message sizes the workload actually exchanges.

Napkin Math 3.1: The alpha-beta crossoverProblem: A fabric designer is comparing a modeled InfiniBand NDR path (1.5 μs, 50 GB/s) against a modeled RoCE path over slower Ethernet (5 μs, 12.5 GB/s). The comparison deliberately bundles a higher-latency stack with a slower link, so a third path, RoCE on a 400 Gb/s link, separates the two effects. For a 4 KB control message and a 350 MB gradient shard, which part of \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)=\MessageStartupLatency+\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) dominates, and why does the first path help for different reasons in each regime?
Math: Apply \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) for a 4 KB control message and a 350 MB gradient shard.

Small message (4 KB):

InfiniBand: \(1.5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s} + 4\,\text{KB}/50\,\text{GB/s} = 1.5 + 0.08 = \mathbf{1.58}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)
RoCE (100G): \(5.0\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s} + 4\,\text{KB}/12.5\,\text{GB/s} = 5.0 + 0.32 = \mathbf{5.32}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\)
Result: Under these assumed path parameters, the NDR path is 3.4× faster because its modeled \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is lower.

Large message (350 MB):

InfiniBand: \(\PointToPointTransferTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth=\) 7.0 ms
RoCE (100G): \(\PointToPointTransferTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth=\) 28.01 ms
Result: Under these assumed path parameters, the NDR path is 4× faster because its modeled \(\LinkBandwidth\) is higher. That factor is the ratio of the two line rates, so it measures the faster link rather than the transport.

Same line rate (RoCE at 400 Gb/s, RoCE \(\MessageStartupLatency\)):

Small message: 5.08 μs, still 3.2× the NDR time, because \(\MessageStartupLatency\) alone separates the stacks.
Large message: 7.0 ms, essentially the NDR time, because at equal \(\LinkBandwidth\) nothing but a few microseconds of \(\MessageStartupLatency\) separates them.


Systems insight: This scenario places the crossover \((\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth)\) near 75 KB. Because gradients are megabytes to gigabytes, their transfers are usually bandwidth dominated, whereas pipeline coordination can remain latency dominated. A higher line rate produces little benefit for a message whose startup term dominates; transport processing, topology, and hop count then govern the improvement.


The two message sizes in notebook 3.1 map directly onto the 175B training job. For the 4 KB control message that notifies a pipeline stage its next microbatch is ready (\(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx\) 1.58 μs on NDR), the transmission term contributes only 5.1 percent of the total, so faster links offer little benefit. For the 350 MB shard that each of the 1,024 GPUs owns from the 350 GB gradient (\(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx\) 7.0 ms), transmission dominates, and doubling bandwidth to 100 GB/s approximately halves the transfer time.
Across the full range of message sizes, each path traces a flat latency-dominated plateau that bends into a linear bandwidth-dominated regime (figure 7). On the modeled NDR path, the knee at 75 KB marks where transmission time overtakes the 1.5 μs startup latency; the 100 Gb/s RoCE path sits on a higher floor of 5 μs and bends near 62.5 KB. The exact positions reflect the assumed \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) scenario parameters rather than invariant protocol constants. On both paths, startup latency governs sub-kilobyte control handoffs, whereas multi-megabyte gradient shards sit well inside the bandwidth-bound regime.














Figure 7: The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) Crossover: Modeled transfer time as a function of message size for an NDR InfiniBand path and a 100 Gb/s RoCE baseline using the scenario parameters in the text. Small messages are latency dominated (flat region), while large messages are bandwidth dominated (linear region); on the InfiniBand path the dotted asymptotes show the knee sitting where the two terms are equal. Measured crossover points vary with the end-to-end path.



A measured collective shows both regimes and where the two-parameter model needs care. NVIDIA publishes the full output of the standard NCCL AllReduce benchmark on one node of eight H100 GPUs connected by NVLink, sweeping message sizes from 8 bytes to 16 GB (NVIDIA 2026a). The two-parameter model can be built from two summary values of that sweep, the median time of the small messages as \(\MessageStartupLatency\) and the delivered rate of the largest message as \(\LinkBandwidth\), and set beside the measured time (figure 8). The small messages sit on a floor of about 17 µs regardless of size, and the largest messages approach 274 GB/s of algorithm bandwidth, defined as the tensor size divided by completion time. Because an eight-GPU ring AllReduce sends \(2(8-1)/8 = 1.75\) bytes across each GPU’s links per tensor byte reduced, multiplying by that factor gives 480 GB/s of bus bandwidth, the benchmark’s hardware-normalized rate on the physical links. Between the two extremes, the model places the knee near 5 MB, but the measured time runs up to 1.7× the model’s prediction for messages of 8 to 128 MB. Across that middle range, chunks are not yet large enough to fill every parallel NVLink channel and amortize per-round protocol overhead, so delivered bandwidth is still ramping toward its peak. The model is therefore close at the two ends and optimistic in the middle, and that middle range is where the gradient buckets of data-parallel training often fall.














Figure 8: Measured AllReduce Time against the Two-Parameter Model: NCCL AllReduce time on one node of eight H100 GPUs over NVLink for message sizes from 8 bytes to 16 GB, on logarithmic axes (points), with the two-parameter model built from the measured small-message floor and the largest message’s delivered bandwidth (solid line) and its two asymptotes (dotted). The model is close at both ends; between roughly 1 MB and 1 GB the measurement runs above it. One early small-message point is a timing outlier. Data from NVIDIA (2026a); whether NVLink SHARP was enabled for this run is not stated.


NVIDIA. 2026a. Exemplar Performance: NCCL Microbenchmarks.



Checkpoint 3.1: Protocol selection
Consider the 175B job on the 1,024-GPU reference cluster. Its gradient exchanges move messages of hundreds of megabytes, while its pipeline stages coordinate through frequent control messages of a few kilobytes.

Protocol fit: use the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) crossover to recommend a transport stack, and justify the choice for both the large gradient messages and the small control messages.
RoCE requirements: compare the infrastructure required by PFC-based and PFC-free RoCE designs with InfiniBand’s credit-based fabric.
Line rate vs. startup cost: explain why moving the control messages from a 100 Gb/s path to a 400 Gb/s path with the same \(\MessageStartupLatency\) would barely change their transfer time.



Beyond classifying individual transfers, the same model identifies when communication overtakes computation. A ring AllReduce passes chunks around a logical cycle of participants, in a ReduceScatter phase and then an AllGather phase, with no requirement that the physical switches form a ring. The scaling laws that push training toward more parameters (AI Scaling Laws) enlarge, in direct proportion, the gradient that every data-parallel step must reduce. The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) cost of each transfer, multiplied by the ring’s round count and traffic factor, then decides when that collective outlasts the step’s computation. At that point the network becomes the pacing constraint for the entire job.


↪ The ring AllReduce derivation, and the schedules that compete with it, are developed in Ring AllReduce.
The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model quantifies the speed of a single link, but the 175B-parameter model requires 1,024 GPUs to work in concert. Scaling these transport primitives from a pair of nodes to a warehouse-scale supercomputer demands a network topology: a specific pattern of connections that maximizes \(\BisectionBandwidth\) while minimizing the hop count and cabling cost for global collective operations.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
A cluster can have thousands of fast links at the edge and still starve its AllReduce operations if the cross-sectional capacity at the narrowest point in the switching hierarchy is insufficient. The physical arrangement of switches determines whether that cross-section throttles collective communication or sustains full line-rate exchange across all participating workers. Two properties govern this capability: bisection bandwidth \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and whether the fabric is non-blocking, a constraint captured by the bisection bandwidth theorem (principle \(\ref{pri-bisection-bandwidth}\)). Bisection bandwidth quantifies the worst-case throughput ceiling that the topology imposes on global collectives.

Definition 3.4: Bisection bandwidth
Bisection bandwidth is a network topology metric defined as the minimum aggregate link capacity crossing any partition that divides the cluster into two equal halves, representing the worst-case throughput ceiling for traffic that must cross that partition, including global collectives.

Significance: Bisection bandwidth \(\BisectionBandwidth\) directly sets the cluster-scale bandwidth ceiling for global synchronization. A 1,024-GPU fat-tree with 400 Gb/s links at 1:1 subscription provides \(\text{BW}_{\text{bisect}} = 512 \times 50\,\text{GB/s} = 25.6\,\text{TB/s}\) per direction; a 4:1 oversubscribed spine reduces this to 6.4 TB/s, increasing the transfer-time lower bound for a fixed cut-crossing payload by 4×. Actual AllReduce slowdown depends on rank placement, the collective schedule, and which links are saturated.
Distinction: Unlike aggregate bandwidth (the sum of all edge link speeds, which can be high even in a poorly connected topology), \(\BisectionBandwidth\) measures global connectivity. A star topology with 1,000 edge links all meeting at one central switch has high aggregate bandwidth but \(\BisectionBandwidth\) limited by that switch’s backplane capacity.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that adding more leaf switches always increases \(\BisectionBandwidth\). In a three-tier fat-tree, oversubscribing the spine layer (giving each spine switch fewer uplinks to the core than downlinks to its leaves) reduces \(\BisectionBandwidth\) below the edge-link total regardless of how many leaf switches are present.



ML training includes global collectives and AllToAll phases that can drive traffic across topology partitions, making full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) a useful capacity target. A smaller cut becomes a bottleneck when the workload’s crossing traffic exceeds what it can deliver within the communication budget, and rank placement together with the collective schedule determines how much traffic crosses that cut.
Bisection bandwidth measures cut capacity; a non-blocking fabric provides paths that can sustain simultaneous input-output pairings at line rate with suitable routing. Full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and balanced uplink capacity support that goal, but routing must also spread traffic across the available paths. In the oversubscribed designs considered here, reducing a cut’s capacity reduces its effective \(\BisectionBandwidth\), increasing the transfer-time bound for a fixed payload that saturates it, whereas a collective that keeps most traffic within each half need not experience the same slowdown.


↪ A slower cut lengthens the training step only when the extra transfer time cannot hide behind computation. The communication-to-compute diagnostic that tests this is developed in Compute \cap communication.

Definition 3.5: Non-blocking fabric
Non-blocking fabric is a network with sufficient internal path capacity to support any permutation of input-output port pairs simultaneously at full line rate under a suitable routing assignment.

Significance: In ML fleets, a non-blocking fabric can support full-rate permutation traffic with suitable routing, preserving the available \(\BisectionBandwidth\) term for global collectives. A 2:1 oversubscribed spine halves the effective \(\BisectionBandwidth\), doubling the communication time when that cut is the saturated bottleneck and dropping scaling efficiency \(\ScalingEfficiency\) accordingly. In a scenario workload assumed to spend 30 percent of each step communicating, doubling that share while the computation share stays fixed lengthens each step, and the longer step costs roughly 23.1 percent of total cluster throughput. This definition uses 2:1, a common data-center compromise, whereas the bisection definition above and notebook 3.2 use 4:1, a cost-optimized spine; the notebook writes out the throughput formula behind both results.
Distinction: The guarantee concerns a permutation, in which each input and output belongs to one pairing. It does not promise full line rate from every sender to every receiver at once, nor does it make an arbitrary routing assignment free of contention.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that non-blocking means zero congestion. Endpoint congestion (incast) can still occur if multiple senders simultaneously target the same receiver port, regardless of how much internal fabric capacity is available.



Fat-trees build on Clos-style non-blocking network principles to supply full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) (Clos 1953), rail-optimized networks trade some global routing flexibility for lower cabling cost, and dragonfly topologies reduce optical link counts while introducing workload-placement constraints (Kim et al. 2008). This trade-off between guaranteed bisection bandwidth and cabling cost drives every topology decision in large-scale ML clusters, as the comparisons in section 3.5.2, section 3.5.3, and section 3.5.4 show, and every switched design begins at the first-hop switch that aggregates a rack or rail of servers.


Consider a rack containing four nodes with eight GPUs each: if all 32 accelerators attach to a single top-of-rack (ToR) switch with no alternate path, losing that switch disconnects the entire rack from the job at once. Because the ToR aggregates every server link in the rack, it becomes a shared failure domain, one level of the physical hierarchy defined in Node health and reliability, and recovery then depends on available paths, surviving state, and the job’s recovery policy. This one-switch-per-rack wiring is the simpler baseline used here to teach radix and failure domains. The reference cluster itself wires each GPU to a rail switch, a layout developed in section 3.5.3. That layout reshapes the failure domain, because losing one rail switch cuts one GPU in each of many nodes rather than every GPU in one rack.
The switch radix,5 its number of ports, determines how many endpoints and uplinks it can connect. In the reference allocation, a 64-port switch assigns 32 ports to servers, one for each of 32 GPUs, and 32 ports to the spine. With equal port rates, the 1:1 ratio avoids oversubscription at that boundary; delivered throughput still depends on forwarding and the paths beyond it. The 1,024 GPUs-GPU cluster therefore requires approximately 32 such endpoint groups, although the physical rack count also depends on node density and the cabling layout.
5 Switch radix: High-end switches such as NVIDIA Quantum-2 offer a radix of 64 ports, each at 400 Gb/s. As model scale pushes toward 100,000 GPUs, higher radix (128 or 256 ports), larger local accelerator domains, or accepted topology constraints are the main ways to avoid adding switch tiers, each of which adds switch latency and cost.The same boundary shapes state placement. To survive a rack-wide outage, a job needs recoverable state outside that rack and a way to resume on available capacity. Topology-aware scheduling must therefore consider both fast communication paths and the failures that several nearby resources share.


↪ Nested failure domains, and why redundant state must span them to survive a correlated rack or ToR outage, are developed in Correlated failures.



The ToR provides non-blocking bandwidth within a single rack, but connecting the reference cluster’s 32 endpoint groups into a cluster that preserves full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) across every possible communication pair requires a topology that scales cross-sectional capacity with cluster size. The fat-tree (also called a Clos network) achieves this by adding parallel spine switches at each tier, so the aggregate uplink capacity always matches the total edge bandwidth feeding into it. In this vocabulary, leaf switches attach servers or racks, spine switches connect leaves within a pod, and core switches connect multiple pods when a third tier is needed; other sources call the leaf and spine tiers edge and aggregation. A pod here is a switching domain, the group of leaves that one set of spines joins, which can be narrower than the multi-rack pod of The Pod. A multi-rack pod in that sense can contain several fat-tree pods.

Definition 3.6: Fat-tree
Fat-tree is a hierarchical ML cluster network topology in which the number of parallel paths (and therefore aggregate cross-sectional capacity) increases at each switch tier toward the spine, providing full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and multiple equal-cost routes between any two nodes (Al-Fares et al. 2008).

Significance: A \(\SwitchRadix\)-ary fat-tree built from radix-\(\SwitchRadix\) switches supports \(\SwitchRadix^2/2\) hosts in a standalone two-tier configuration and \(\SwitchRadix^3/4\) hosts in a three-tier configuration with full \(\BisectionBandwidth\). With 64-port switches, a standalone two-tier fabric supports 2,048 GPUs and a three-tier fabric supports 65,536 hosts. This is a capacity bound for suitable routing and admissible traffic; it does not eliminate endpoint contention or guarantee that a particular AllReduce implementation reaches line rate.
Distinction: Unlike a standard tree (where bandwidth at the root is a single bottleneck shared by all leaves), a fat-tree replaces each root with multiple spine switches whose combined uplink capacity matches the total edge bandwidth, eliminating the bottleneck.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that fat-trees guarantee zero network cost. They require \(\mathcal{O}(\TopologyEndpointCount\log \TopologyEndpointCount)\) switches and dense cabling, so a non-blocking three-tier fat-tree at the 4,000-GPU scale needs hundreds of switches and more than ten thousand links before a single accelerator is purchased.




Al-Fares, Mohammad, Alexander Loukissas, and Amin Vahdat. 2008. “A Scalable, Commodity Data Center Network Architecture.” ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 38 (4): 63–74. https://doi.org/10.1145/1402946.1402967.
A three-tier radix-4 fabric (\(\SwitchRadix=4\)) shows the non-blocking structure at a scale small enough to draw (figure 9), with four core switches interconnecting four dashed pod modules. Leaf and spine switches split their ports between the tiers below and above; core switches use all their ports to connect pods. Each tier boundary therefore carries 16 links. The highlighted route traverses five switches and is one of \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = 4\) equal-cost routes from a GPU in Pod 1 to Pod 4. Parallel paths supply the capacity, while routing must distribute traffic across them to use it.






Figure 9: Non-blocking Fat-Tree Topology: A three-tier fat-tree built from radix-4 switches (\(\SwitchRadix=4\)) connects \(\SwitchRadix^3/4 = 16\) GPUs through four pods. Leaf and spine switches split their ports equally between the tiers below and above; core switches use all their ports to connect pods. Each tier boundary carries 16 links, supporting full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) with suitable routing. The highlighted leaf-spine-core-spine-leaf route between pod 1 and pod 4 is one of \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = 4\) equal-cost paths (the other three are drawn lighter), and exploiting those alternatives without excessive reordering requires compatible switch and endpoint mechanisms.



The fat-tree6 is a common default for ML clusters because a non-blocking design can provide full \(\BisectionBandwidth\) across arbitrary partitions. This capacity benefits global AllReduce even though implementations such as rings and trees do not require every pair of ranks to communicate at once. The number of hosts that the guarantee can cover depends on switch radix and tier count.
6 Fat-tree (Clos network): The underlying multi-stage switching theory was invented by Clos (1953) at Bell Labs to minimize the number of electromechanical crosspoints in telephone exchanges. Leiserson (1985) at MIT generalized the concept as the “fat-tree,” where the tree is “fat” because link bandwidth increases toward the root, proving it could emulate any network of equal hardware volume. The same cost-minimization logic that drove 1950s telephony now drives ML cluster design: minimize switch count while guaranteeing non-blocking connectivity for global AllReduce.
Clos, C. 1953. “A Study of Non-Blocking Switching Networks.” Bell System Technical Journal 32 (2): 406–24. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1953.tb01433.x.

Leiserson, Charles E. 1985. “Fat-Trees: Universal Networks for Hardware-Efficient Supercomputing.” IEEE Transactions on Computers C-34 (10): 892–901. https://doi.org/10.1109/tc.1985.6312192.
A fat-tree built from switches with radix \(\SwitchRadix\) supports \(\FatTreeHostCount= \SwitchRadix^{3}/4\) hosts at three tiers. A standalone two-tier non-blocking fabric can instead use \(\SwitchRadix\) leaves, each with \(\SwitchRadix/2\) host ports and \(\SwitchRadix/2\) uplinks, connected to \(\SwitchRadix/2\) spines. Each spine uses all \(\SwitchRadix\) ports to reach the leaves, providing \(\SwitchRadix^{2}/2 =\) 2,048 host ports for radix-64 switches. In the three-tier design, each spine switch reserves half of its ports for the core tier and uses the other \(\SwitchRadix/2\) ports to connect to leaves, so one pod has \(\SwitchRadix/2\) leaves and \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 =\) 1,024 host ports. Because each radix-\(\SwitchRadix\) core switch connects one port to each pod, the core tier can join up to \(\SwitchRadix\) pods for the full \(\SwitchRadix \times (\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = \SwitchRadix^3/4\) host capacity. These are different port allocations and switch counts rather than two ways of counting the same fabric, and while the 1,024-GPU reference cluster fits within a standalone two-tier design, the distinction matters as soon as a cluster outgrows that limit. A 4,096-GPU deployment cannot join two fully populated standalone 2,048-host fabrics at their spines, because every spine port is already occupied by a leaf connection. Instead, it is built as four 1,024-host pods of the three-tier design, joined through a core tier. A concrete bisection estimate shows how quickly oversubscription at that spine or core boundary turns into synchronization delay.

Napkin Math 3.2: Bisection bandwidth: The cost of oversubscriptionProblem: A cluster designer is choosing between a “non-blocking” (1:1) fat-tree and a “cost-optimized” (4:1) spine for a $300M cluster of 1024 GPUs. This is a separate economics scenario rather than the running 175B job: each GPU contributes a 5 GB gradient payload, and the workload is assumed to spend \(\CommunicationTimeFraction=\) 30 percent of each step communicating. That share is a scenario input. It is larger than the 13 percent of the illustrative schedule in figure 2 and far smaller than the exposed share in the introduction’s GPT-3 synchronization example (The energy accounting boundary), which assumes pure data parallelism with no overlap; none of the three is a measured share of the reference job. How much slower will the AllReduce be on the cheaper network, and what does that cost?
Math: Bisection bandwidth (\(\BisectionBandwidth\)) is the minimum pipe diameter between halves of the cluster. Assume a unidirectional ring whose ranks alternate between the two halves of the cluster. Every ring edge then crosses the cut, with \(\AcceleratorCount/2\) senders in each direction. Assume balanced routing, no competing traffic, and negligible startup latency. ReduceScatter plus AllGather contributes a traffic factor \(2(\AcceleratorCount-1)/\AcceleratorCount\) = 1.998 per GPU; multiplying by \(\AcceleratorCount/2\) gives the bytes crossing the cut in each direction. A ring that groups ranks within each half would have fewer crossing edges and a different cut-load bound.

Non-blocking (1:1): \(\BisectionBandwidth =\) 512 \(\times\) 50 GB/s \(=\) 25,600 GB/s per direction.

Time: 5,115 GB / 25,600 GB/s \(\approx\) 0.200 s.

Oversubscribed (4:1): \(\BisectionBandwidth =\) 25,600 GB/s divided by 4 = 6,400 GB/s per direction.

Time: 5,115 GB / 6,400 GB/s \(\approx\) 0.799 s.

Throughput: If the communication share stretches by the slowdown factor \(\CommunicationSlowdownFactor\) while computation stays fixed, then \(\text{relative throughput} = \frac{1}{(1-\CommunicationTimeFraction) + \CommunicationTimeFraction\,\CommunicationSlowdownFactor} = \frac{1}{0.70 + 0.30 \times 4} = \frac{1}{1.90} \approx 0.53\), a loss of about 47.4 percent of cluster throughput.
Cost: That loss times the $300M capital cost is about $142.1M.

Systems insight: For this cut-saturating placement, saving money on core switches creates a 4× bottleneck for global synchronization, and on a $300M cluster that bottleneck idles about $142.1M of compute. The same formula gives the 23.1 percent loss of the 2:1 spine in the non-blocking definition. This is an equivalent-capacity cost under the stated workload assumptions, not a direct equipment loss. Oversubscription must be evaluated against the collective traffic actually crossing the constrained cut.


The subscription ratio at each tier therefore determines whether a fat-tree can sustain global collectives, and the tier count determines how far it can grow. Scaling beyond the 2,048-host two-tier limit requires a three-tier architecture with core switches, enabling the fabric to reach 65,536 hosts, but the added scale carries both cost and latency. Each of the \(\SwitchRadix\) pods contains \(\SwitchRadix/2\) leaf switches and \(\SwitchRadix/2\) spine switches (\(\SwitchRadix^2\) switches across all pods), and their \(\SwitchRadix/2\) spines each send \(\SwitchRadix/2\) uplinks into \((\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = \SwitchRadix^2/4\) core switches. A non-blocking \(\SwitchRadix=64\) three-tier tree therefore requires \(5\SwitchRadix^2/4 =\) 5,120 switches across the core, spine, and leaf layers. At $10,000 to $50,000 per switch, the switching layer alone represents $51M to $256M. Typical hop counts also rise, from two inter-switch links and three switch traversals for intra-pod traffic (leaf-spine-leaf) to four inter-switch links and five switch traversals for inter-pod traffic (leaf-spine-core-spine-leaf), adding serialization delay and switch processing time to the \(\MessageStartupLatency\) latency term across thousands of synchronization steps. Rail-optimized topologies respond to both pressures by matching the physical cabling pattern to the collective communication pattern.

Checkpoint 3.2: Fat-tree topologies
These questions check whether hierarchical switch-fabric trade-offs are clear:

Radix and scale: compute the maximum number of GPUs a radix-64 two-tier fat-tree can connect without core switches.
Non-blocking ratio: explain why a non-blocking fabric requires a 1:1 subscription ratio at every tier of the network.
Tier vs. latency: determine how \(\MessageStartupLatency\) (startup latency) changes when moving from a two-tier to a three-tier fat-tree.
Aggregate vs. bisection: distinguish aggregate bandwidth from \(\BisectionBandwidth\) and identify the metric that matters for AllReduce.






When tensor-parallel groups stay inside each node’s high-bandwidth NVSwitch domain, data parallelism exchanges gradients only between GPUs that hold the same model shard in the same local slot position across nodes, yet a standard fat-tree wires all eight GPUs of a node into a shared ToR switch. A rail-optimized topology instead cables external network ports by local slot position (figure 10): GPU 0 in every node connects to the Rail 0 switch, GPU 1 connects to Rail 1, and so on across the cluster.






Figure 10: Rail-Optimized Physical Wiring: In dense accelerator nodes such as the DGX H100, each GPU’s network port is cabled by local slot position: GPU 0 in every node connects to the rail 0 switch, GPU 1 to the rail 1 switch, and so on. Three nodes and four of each node’s eight GPUs are drawn, with the rail 0 cables emphasized; further nodes attach to the same rail switches. Tensor-parallel traffic stays on each node’s NVSwitch, same-rank data-parallel traffic stays on its own rail, and a spine layer (not drawn) bridges the rails for cross-rank traffic.



This slot-aligned wiring exploits the stratified traffic that 3D parallelism produces. Because each node holds a tensor-parallel group, each data-parallel replica assigns the corresponding model shard to the same local GPU slot (where the slot number is a local rank within a node, distinct from the worker’s global rank in the distributed job). During data-parallel AllReduce, GPU 0 on one node synchronizes its shard’s gradients with GPU 0 on other nodes, but rarely communicates with GPU 1. Isolating each local rank onto its own rail switch fabric removes same-rank traffic from shared rack switches and, when a rail fits on a single switch, shortens the path between corresponding GPUs. A simple hop-count estimate shows the payoff.

Napkin Math 3.3: The rail-optimized dividendProblem: A team is synchronizing per-rank data-parallel gradients across 128 nodes. In a standard fat-tree, each message between same-rank GPUs traverses its source leaf switch, a spine switch, and the destination leaf switch (3 switch traversals). In a rail-optimized network built from rail switches with at least one port per node, all corresponding GPUs sit on the same rail switch (one traversal). On the reference cluster that requires rail switches with more ports than the radix-64 switch used so far, so the estimate describes a higher-radix design. How much latency dividend does the rail design earn when a rail fits on one switch?
Math: This estimate counts only the switch-traversal contribution to communication latency (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)), using the same assumed delay for each traversal.

Standard latency: 3 traversals \(\times\) 0.6 μs = 1.8 μs.
Rail-optimized: 1 traversal \(\times\) 0.6 μs = 0.6 μs.
Result: 3× lower latency.

Systems insight: For synchronous data-parallel AllReduce, this 3× reduction applies to the modeled switch-latency contribution, not to total collective time. Its effect on scaling efficiency (\(\ScalingEfficiency\)) depends on payload size, delivered bandwidth, compute time, and overlap. The single-switch rail in this example avoids the spine traversal for same-rank traffic. The dividend is conditional. On the reference cluster’s radix-64 switches each rail outgrows one switch and regains the extra traversals, so what rails reliably buy there is isolation, developed below.


The hop saving is only part of the case for rails. Large language model fleets adopt the pattern because it matches how their parallelism plan divides traffic.

Lighthouse 3.1: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): The rail-optimized fleetArchetype A’s use of 3D parallelism generates two distinct traffic patterns that pull in opposite directions: (1) large, bandwidth-hungry gradient averaging for data parallelism, and (2) high-frequency, latency-sensitive activation exchanges for tensor parallelism. Keeping tensor parallelism inside each node’s NVLink domain leaves data-parallel gradient traffic on the fabric, and rails give each same-rank data-parallel group its own switch network. A rail can provide a single switch hop between nodes when its endpoint count fits the available switch ports. Larger rails require additional switching stages, so rail alignment alone does not guarantee single-hop communication. Either way, the lesson for Archetype A is that how the fabric is wired to the parallelism plan matters as much as how many accelerators it connects.


For the cluster of 1,024 GPUs spanning 128 nodes, this creates 8 parallel networks of 128 GPUs each, requiring at least one switch port per endpoint in each rail. A single-switch realization therefore needs a radix at least as large as the rail endpoint count; the earlier radix-64 switch cannot realize this rail alone, which is why notebook 3.3 assumed higher-radix rail switches. Built from radix-64 switches instead, each rail becomes a small two-tier fabric that preserves rank alignment but adds hops. For the bandwidth-hungry gradient exchanges of data parallelism, the larger benefit is isolation: each rail carries only its own rank’s traffic, so the eight rail networks operate concurrently without competing for shared spine capacity. When a rail fits on one switch, the shorter path also trims the startup cost a ring pays on every round. That same isolation creates a sharp trade-off, because traffic that must reach GPUs of different ranks (such as expert routing in mixture of experts (MoE), or pipeline-stage handoffs that do not align with the rail wiring) requires bridging across rails. Large clusters therefore often employ a hybrid approach, using rail-optimized leaves for same-rank data-parallel traffic while bridging the rails with a full fat-tree spine to support cross-rank communication patterns.

Checkpoint 3.3: Rail-optimized networks
These questions check whether workload-specific network-design trade-offs are clear:

Rail beneficiary: identify the dimension of 3D parallelism (tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, or data parallelism) that benefits most from a rail-optimized design.
Switch hops: explain when a rail-optimized network reduces the number of switch hops for gradient exchanges compared to a standard fat-tree, and what it still provides when a rail needs more ports than one switch offers.
Traffic isolation: explain the traffic isolation benefit of placing all GPU 0s on one rail and all GPU 1s on another.
Core switch need: classify the claim as true or false: a rail-optimized network eliminates the need for high-bandwidth core switches connecting different rails.






At tens of thousands of endpoints, a non-blocking three-tier fat-tree forces a third layer of core switches and tens of thousands of long optical cables into the budget, driving network capital expenditure into the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. Two alternative topologies attack that cost wall from opposite directions: tapering the global switch tier or removing external fabric switches altogether. A dragonfly7 topology organizes high-radix routers (the dragonfly literature’s name for switches) into fully connected groups joined by global optical links. Each group has \(\DragonflyGroupRouterCount\) routers, and each router has \(\DragonflyTerminalPortCount\) terminal ports and \(\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\) global channels. The ratio of \(\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\) to \(\DragonflyTerminalPortCount\) sets how much global bandwidth each group receives relative to the traffic its terminals can inject, so global bandwidth is a design parameter rather than a fixed percentage of aggregate injection bandwidth. The balanced configuration analyzed by Kim et al. (2008), \(\DragonflyGroupRouterCount=2\DragonflyTerminalPortCount=2\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\), is one setting of that knob. The routers in a group are fully connected, and the groups are joined by global links. A minimal route between two groups therefore takes at most one local hop to the router holding the right global link, one global hop, and one local hop in the destination group. No minimal path exceeds three router-to-router hops, regardless of system size. Short paths come cheaply, but performance for jobs spanning groups depends on the chosen \(\DragonflyTerminalPortCount/\DragonflyGlobalChannelCount\) ratio, routing, and traffic matrix, because every inter-group transfer shares the provisioned global links.
7 Dragonfly topology: Introduced by Kim et al. (2008) at ISCA 2008, the dragonfly uses high-radix routers grouped into fully connected “super-nodes.” For systems with at least 16,000 terminals, the architecture achieves a 52 percent network-cost reduction relative to a folded Clos (the fat-tree of section 3.5.2) of equivalent bandwidth, though global optical link oversubscription can create AllToAll bottlenecks during MoE token routing.
Kim, J., W. J. Dally, S. Scott, and D. Abts. 2008. “Technology-Driven, Highly-Scalable Dragonfly Topology.” 2008 International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 77–88. https://doi.org/10.1109/isca.2008.19.
A torus topology connects each node directly to its neighbors in a multidimensional grid, most commonly a 3D torus where every node links to its six adjacent peers (up/down, left/right, front/back). The design offers full local bandwidth with minimal switching hardware, because every neighbor is a single hop away. However, global communication requires traversing the diameter of the mesh (\(\mathcal{O}(\TopologyEndpointCount^{1/3})\) hops), making latency scale poorly with cluster size. Google adopted this architecture for its Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) pods because the collectives that dominate its training workloads can be scheduled as rings along each torus dimension, a nearest-neighbor pattern that maps naturally onto the physical grid. The limitation becomes apparent with MoE, which relies on AllToAll communication patterns. On a torus, these random permutations can congest the limited \(\BisectionBandwidth\) of the mesh and degrade performance relative to a non-blocking switch fabric.
The trade-off becomes concrete for the 4,096-endpoint deployment that the three-tier fat-tree reached with four pods. Arranged as a \(16 \times 16 \times 16\) torus with wraparound links, the same endpoints need no external switching stages. Splitting the cube in half across one axis cuts a \(16 \times 16\) plane of interior links and an equal plane of wraparound links, so only \(2 \times 16^2 =\) 512 links cross the bisection, against 2,048 in the non-blocking fat-tree. With 50 GB/s per link and direction, the torus offers 25.6 TB/s across the cut against the fat-tree’s 102.4 TB/s, a 4× gap. Because wraparound links cap the distance along each 16-node axis at 8 hops, the torus’s worst-case path across all three axes crosses \(3 \times 8 =\) 24 neighbor hops against the fat-tree’s five switch traversals. Because a cubic torus’s cut grows only as \(\TopologyEndpointCount^{2/3}\) while its endpoint count grows as \(\TopologyEndpointCount\), that capacity gap widens at fixed link rate. Whether the gap matters depends on the traffic. A ring AllReduce scheduled along each torus dimension moves data only between neighbors and combines contributions before forwarding them, so it leans little on the narrow cut. An MoE AllToAll or an embedding exchange instead sends a large share of its traffic between distant endpoints and drives it straight into the cut, with the exact pressure set by placement and message sizes. Consequently, the collective schedule and traffic matrix determine whether the torus’s lower cross-sectional capacity limits completion time.


↪ AllToAll schedules and their cost at scale, where every rank sends a distinct share to every other rank, are developed in AllToAll Exchanges at Scale.
At the scale of the 1,024-GPU reference cluster, the four families range in cut capacity from 25.6 TB/s in the non-blocking fat-tree down to 6.4 TB/s in a 3D torus, while an assumed interconnect cost runs from $1.5/Gb/s for the switchless torus to $4/Gb/s for the tapered dragonfly (figure 11). The cheapest capacity is also the least capacity, which is the trade every topology decision prices. The dragonfly’s assumed cost per Gb/s is the highest here because its savings come from replacing long optical runs and switch tiers at large scale, which Kim et al. (2008) reports for systems of at least 16,000 terminals; at 1,024 GPUs it has few such runs to replace. Radix, endpoint count, link speed, routing mechanisms, and equipment pricing all shift these trade-offs; the topology family alone dictates neither raw cross-sectional capacity nor operational capital cost.














Figure 11: An Illustrative Bandwidth-Cost Scenario for ML Network Topologies: \(\BisectionBandwidth\) (TB/s, horizontal axis) against assumed cost per Gb/s (vertical axis) for four topology configurations on a 1,024-GPU cluster: fat-tree (25.6 TB/s, $3/Gb/s), dragonfly with tapered global links (19.2 TB/s, $4), rail-optimized with a 2:1 bridging spine (12.8 TB/s, $2), and a 3D torus (6.4 TB/s, $1.5). The bandwidths follow from the stated structures at one link rate; the costs are scenario inputs that illustrate the comparison method rather than universal properties of each topology family.






Every topology compared in figure 11 is fixed when the facility is cabled, locking the cluster into a single physical graph regardless of which workload runs on it. A statically cabled Clos hierarchy (section 3.5.2) fixes the oversubscription ratio and bisection pattern whether the active job is pipeline-dominated, data-parallel, or AllToAll expert-routed. A statically cabled torus (section 3.5.4) is equally rigid: it fits dimension-ordered rings, but it congests under MoE AllToAll traffic and cannot rewire its links to match the job.
Switching those multi-tier fabrics electrically also extracts a recurring power tax at every hop. Each electrical packet switch inspects headers and chooses an outgoing link only after an Optical-Electrical-Optical (OEO) conversion: incoming photons hit a photodiode, high-speed SerDes circuits deserialize the electrical signal, switch ASICs buffer and route packets across crossbars, and output SerDes drive lasers to re-transmit light over optical fiber. At 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s per-port data rates, SerDes and transceiver electronics consume significant energy (section 3.3.3), and every additional switch tier repeats that conversion cost for each bit that crosses it. Changing the physical connections between node groups in light, for the duration of a workload allocation rather than packet by packet, avoids both static wiring and per-hop OEO conversion.

Definition 3.7: Optical circuit switching
Optical circuit switching (OCS) is a physical networking architecture that routes optical signals directly using Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) mirror arrays without Optical-Electrical-Optical (OEO) conversion, enabling dynamic, software-defined topology reconfiguration and high energy efficiency at warehouse scale.

Significance: An optical circuit bypasses packet-by-packet electronic processing in the switching path. The complete system still consumes power for actuators, control, and transceivers. Its compatibility across line rates depends on optical loss, wavelengths, and endpoint budgets, so protocol transparency does not imply unrestricted upgrades.
Distinction: Unlike electrical packet switches (which inspect headers, buffer packets in SRAM, and make nanosecond routing decisions per packet), an OCS establishes semi-static physical optical circuits with millisecond-scale switching latency (\(10\)–\(30\) ms), making it suitable for topology-level reconfiguration rather than dynamic packet routing.
Common pitfall: Assuming OCS replaces packet switching entirely. OCS operates at circuit granularity: it configures cluster-scale topologies (such as 3D tori or job-specific sub-clusters) and routes around hardware faults, while packet switching or accelerator-native interconnects handle fine-grained, intra-step message routing.



Google’s TPU v4 supercomputer (Jouppi et al. 2023) deployed optical circuit switching in production. Instead of wiring 4,096 chips into an inflexible electrical fat-tree, the system groups accelerators into \(4{\times}4{\times}4\) node cubes and routes the inter-cube links through an array of 3D MEMS optical circuit switches (codenamed Palomar).

Jouppi, Norm, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Peter Ma, Rahul Nagarajan, Lifeng Nai, Nishant Patil, et al. 2023. “TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589350.
The optical layer serves two purposes, adapting the topology to the workload and recovering from faults. For workload adaptation, the physical interconnect can be reconfigured to match the communication structure of the running model. A training run using 1D pipeline parallelism can configure its slice as an elongated cylinder to streamline stage-to-stage transfers. Conversely, a 2D or 3D tensor-parallel partition can configure a compact cubic 3D torus that minimizes average hop count, while an MoE workload can maximize bisection bandwidth across specific expert groups.
Optical switching also supports fault isolation by changing connections around unavailable hardware where spare connectivity permits. The capability matters because in a statically cabled torus, a single failed link or node can break a ring along an entire dimension and degrade every job that spans it. With optical circuit switching, the mirrors can be redirected to bypass the failed cube or fiber and splice healthy cubes into a complete, smaller torus slice without manual recabling. The fabric manager must first detect the fault, choose a feasible allocation, and establish the new circuits, which means circuit-switching time is only one part of recovery; a training job may also need to rebuild its process groups and restore state before computation resumes, so optical reconfiguration latency alone does not specify recovery time.
The trade-off is switching latency. Because MEMS mirrors physically rotate to steer collimated light beams, reconfiguration occurs on a mechanical timescale that is much longer than packet forwarding in an established electrical path. Circuit setup changes connectivity, while packet forwarding uses connectivity already in place. Consequently, OCS raises the power and protocol ceiling of the switching layer while leaving reconfiguration latency as the binding constraint, so it is deployed for job-level topology allocation and fault isolation, not for per-message dynamic routing. Within that limit, OCS turns the choice of topology from a decision fixed when the fabric is cabled into one made for each job.
Each topology comparison so far has considered one traffic pattern at a time. In practice, clusters serve multiple workloads with different communication patterns, and topology selection must balance their competing demands.

Checkpoint 3.4: Topology selection for your workload
The choice of network topology dictates the upper bound of training efficiency. Warm up by matching each single-workload pattern to its ideal topology, then design a fabric that must serve several at once.
Single-workload picks

AllReduce bandwidth: select the topology that maximizes \(\BisectionBandwidth\) for a standard data-parallel job dominated by AllReduce.
MoE traffic: select the topology that best sustains a mixture-of-experts model’s AllToAll-dominant, bursty communication, in which any rank may send to any other.
Neighbor locality: select the topology that best fits a ring AllReduce scheduled along each dimension of the machine, where every transfer goes to a physical neighbor.

Designing for a mixed cluster
You are designing the network for a new ML cluster that will run two primary workloads: (1) training a 175B-parameter language model using 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism), and (2) serving a mixture-of-experts model that relies heavily on AllToAll communication to route tokens to the correct experts.

Training topology: select the topology (fat-tree, rail-optimized, or hybrid) that best matches tensor parallelism within groups of 8 GPUs and data parallelism across all nodes, then justify the choice.
MoE topology: revise the topology choice for unpredictable AllToAll traffic where any GPU may need to communicate with any other GPU.
Oversubscription risk: identify which workload suffers more under 2:1 spine-layer oversubscription and propose a scheduling strategy to mitigate the impact.



Topology provides the structural capacity for the cluster of 1,024 GPUs to communicate, but structure alone does not guarantee performance. When the 1,024 GPUs synchronize contributions to the model’s 350 GB gradient state, that theoretical capacity collides with the reality of fabric behavior: congestion control and routing dynamics determine whether this traffic flows smoothly or gridlocks under the strict synchronization of the BSP model.

Self-Check: Question

A cluster designer builds a three-tier non-blocking fat-tree network using radix-64 switches (\(k = 64\)). What is the maximum number of hosts this fabric can support at 1:1 bisection bandwidth subscription, and how many total switches are required across all tiers?

\(2{,}048\) hosts and \(128\) switches
\(16{,}384\) hosts and \(1{,}024\) switches
\(65{,}536\) hosts and \(5{,}120\) switches
\(262{,}144\) hosts and \(20{,}480\) switches

Why does a rail-optimized network topology significantly reduce synchronization latency for 3D-parallel training jobs compared to a standard uniform fat-tree?

It replaces optical fiber cables with liquid-cooled copper buses across all rows
It physically connects all GPUs of the same local rank (e.g., all GPU 0s) across server nodes to dedicated rail switches, allowing same-rail transfers within a leaf group to use a single switch hop
It eliminates the need for intra-node NVLink by routing all tensor-parallel traffic through Top-of-Rack switches
It dynamically routes all AllReduce packets through the GPU display engine to bypass PCIe contention

A cluster operator considers saving capital expenditure by building a \(4:1\) oversubscribed spine in a 1,024-GPU training cluster. Explain the quantitative and economic impact of this design on a 100 GB per GPU AllReduce collective during distributed training.
Why did Google adopt a 3D torus topology for its TPU Pods, and what communication workload exposes the primary structural limitation of this topology?

The 3D torus minimizes cabling cost and external switch hardware by leveraging direct neighbor-to-neighbor links that suit structured transformer collectives, but suffers high hop count (\(\mathcal{O}(N^{1/3})\)) and bisection congestion under irregular AllToAll traffic from Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models
The 3D torus provides full non-blocking bisection bandwidth for random permutation traffic, but fails when running ring AllReduce due to cyclic buffer dependencies
The 3D torus eliminates Forward Error Correction requirements, but cannot support FP16 numerical precision
The 3D torus reduces power consumption by disabling physical link SerDes, but restricts cluster scale to 32 nodes

True or False: In a data center network, aggregate bandwidth (the sum of all endpoint link rates) and bisection bandwidth (\(\text{BW}_{\text{bisect}}\)) are identical metrics.
