Adaptive routing disables link-layer CRC error checking on optical switches
Adaptive routing forces all AllReduce operations to execute sequentially across a single ring
Adaptive routing balances traffic across existing paths, but it cannot synthesize bisection bandwidth that does not exist if a job is split across an oversubscribed or constrained network boundary

Explain why upgrading an InfiniBand fabric from HDR (\(200\text{ Gb/s}\)) to NDR (\(400\text{ Gb/s}\)) yields less than a \(15\%\) reduction in transfer time for a \(10\text{ KB}\) control message, and state the condition under which bandwidth upgrades deliver linear performance gains.
True or False: Lossless RoCEv2 Ethernet fabrics provide the exact same operational simplicity and fault immunity as InfiniBand fabrics because both support zero-packet-loss guarantees.

See Answers →

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
The five-level model of figure 3 bridges physical reach, transport primitives, switch topologies, congestion dynamics, and cluster integration into a single system contract. A fabric must provide both enough capacity for the workload’s traffic and predictable completion at its synchronization boundaries. InfiniBand and RoCE distribute this responsibility differently across links, endpoints, and operational policy; the production cases show why neither port rate nor protocol name determines delivered performance.
Three numerical anchors show how to apply the model. One GPU’s NVLink bandwidth exceeds its own external port’s per-direction bandwidth by 9×; the modeled NDR path has equal startup and transmission costs near 75 KB; and the 4:1 oversubscribed cut increases the fixed-payload transfer bound by 4×. Each result depends on its stated configuration and traffic assumptions. In the Fleet Law, transfer time contributes to \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and residual synchronization waiting to \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\); consistent timeline accounting prevents counting one delay in both. The communication and coordination axes of C³ meet where those dependencies determine useful compute progress.
The same model guides design and diagnosis. Message sizes determine whether startup latency or bandwidth dominates; communication patterns determine which paths must carry that traffic. During operation, application throughput, transport counters, and physical telemetry distinguish inadequate capacity from contention or a degraded component. These measurements also test whether a proposed optical or composable architecture removes the binding constraint or merely moves it.

Key Takeaways: The fabric decides useful compute

Synchronous training inverts data-center traffic: A bulk-synchronous step releases a few large, correlated flows whose completion gates a barrier, so the fabric is judged by collective completion time and its p99 tail rather than by average per-flow throughput. Static ECMP hashing turns flow collisions into persistent hot spots.
Link speed is not fabric speed: For traffic that crosses a fabric cut, available capacity bounds transfer time (principle \(\ref{pri-bisection-bandwidth}\)). Workload placement and collective schedules determine how much data must cross, so advertised port speed alone cannot predict useful training throughput.
Latency and bandwidth bind differently: The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model of section 3.4.4 separates startup cost from per-byte transfer cost, with \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\) marking the regime change. Message-size distributions, not vendor peak numbers, determine whether to optimize software latency or hardware bandwidth.
Reliable delivery moves the risk: RDMA transports need reliable completion and bounded recovery, not one universal lossless-fabric mechanism. InfiniBand normally suppresses loss with link-level credits; many RoCE deployments use PFC and ECN, while PFC-free designs place more recovery responsibility at the endpoints. Each choice trades hardware flexibility against tail latency and operational complexity.
Topology must match traffic: Fat-trees buy flexible bisection bandwidth, rail-optimized designs give same-rank AllReduce traffic its own isolated switch network, and dragonfly or torus designs trade cabling and locality differently. The right fabric depends on whether the workload stresses AllReduce, AllToAll, or multi-tenant sharing.
Losslessness and load create their own failures: PFC prevents drops by pausing senders, which can spread one slow drainer’s congestion to victim flows or freeze a lossless class in a cyclic buffer dependency. Under synchronized load, end-to-end congestion control is a latency requirement, adaptive routing repairs hash collisions without adding capacity, and incast is spread in time, space, and priority rather than eliminated.
Telemetry saves GPU-hours: PFC counters, link error rates, bandwidth baselines, and application throughput must be correlated across layers. Without that observability, a degraded transceiver or congestion storm silently converts a high-end fleet into a queue of waiting accelerators.



At fleet scale, the interconnect is part of the computer. Its value lies in how much useful computation it allows the participating accelerators to complete together. A fabric decision therefore has to be judged against the workload’s communication pattern and synchronization schedule, because additional capacity helps only where those dependencies expose a communication limit.

What’s Next: From wires to data pipelinesA fabric that completes every collective on time still leaves two flows of bytes unaccounted for. Each step needs its next input batch in place before the accelerators ask for it, and the fleet’s training state must outlive the next hardware failure, which at this scale means writing multi-terabyte checkpoints on a schedule. Those checkpoint bursts are the traffic class this chapter isolated from the synchronization path, and for text pretraining they can outweigh the training corpus itself. Data Storage treats storage as the fleet’s fuel line, sizing the tiers and pipelines that deliver inputs ahead of demand and persist model state without stalling the step.

title: 3 Network Fabrics
text:
Self-Check: Answer

On an H100 GPU server, why does moving gradient synchronization across node boundaries create a severe ‘bandwidth cliff,’ and by what factor does per-direction bandwidth drop when transitioning from local NVLink to a single NDR InfiniBand port?

Bandwidth drops by roughly \(2\times\) because optical conversion adds latency while maintaining similar wire transfer rates
Bandwidth drops by roughly \(50\times\) because inter-node links must encapsulate packets in kernel TCP/IP stacks
Bandwidth drops by roughly \(9\times\) (from \(450\text{ GB/s}\) per direction to \(50\text{ GB/s}\) per port) due to the physical distance and switching constraints of inter-node cables
Bandwidth drops by roughly \(100\times\) because inter-node communication requires staging all gradients through CPU system RAM

Answer: The correct answer is C. On an H100 system, per-direction NVLink bandwidth is \(450\text{ GB/s}\) (half of its \(900\text{ GB/s}\) bidirectional total), whereas a single NDR InfiniBand port delivers \(50\text{ GB/s}\) (\(400\text{ Gb/s}\)), representing an approximate \(9\times\) bandwidth cliff. The assertion of a \(2\times\) drop significantly underestimates the physical disparity between on-chassis copper traces and multi-meter inter-node cabling. The claim of a \(50\times\) drop mistakenly assumes inter-node traffic uses kernel TCP/IP rather than RDMA. The assertion of a \(100\times\) drop confuses GPUDirect RDMA transfers with legacy CPU bounce buffering.
Learning Objective: Compare intra-node and inter-node interconnect bandwidths across GPU generations.
In a 1,024-GPU synchronous training job on a 175B-parameter model, a degraded inter-node link carries a required collective transfer. Explain when its delay can leave the other participating GPUs waiting, and why the link fault alone does not establish a job-wide slowdown.
Answer: If the degraded link delays the last required collective completion on the job’s critical path, workers that finish their dependent work earlier wait at the synchronization boundary. The exposed delay depends on the participating group, routing, collective schedule, and overlap with independent computation; a fault on an unused path or a transfer whose delay remains hidden need not lengthen the step. The relevant evidence is a matched step and transfer timeline, not the existence of a degraded link elsewhere in the fleet.
Learning Objective: Explain how synchronous collective communication creates a bulk-synchronous bottleneck in multi-GPU training.
True or False: AllToAll collective communication is less demanding on network fabric bisection bandwidth than AllReduce because each GPU only sends data to a single designated peer.
Answer: False. In AllToAll, each participant sends a distinct portion to every other participant, creating many simultaneous source-destination pairs. This can stress bisection bandwidth and path diversity. Ring AllReduce exchanges with logical neighbors at each step, but its physical cross-sectional traffic still depends on rank placement and routing.
Learning Objective: Analyze the communication demands of AllToAll versus AllReduce collective patterns.
In a distributed training cluster, the network fabric functions as the global ______, analogous to the internal memory bus in a single workstation, moving parameter updates and activation tensors between accelerators.
Answer: gradient bus. The fabric carries parameter updates between workers, making its bandwidth and synchronization delays central constraints on distributed training throughput.
Learning Objective: Identify the conceptual role of the network fabric in distributed machine learning architectures.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why can standard Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing produce persistent hot spots when a distributed ML training job has a small number of large gradient flows?

ECMP hashes each flow to one path, so several large gradient flows can collide on one link while other equal-cost paths remain underused
ECMP introduces non-deterministic packet reordering that corrupts the internal state of GPU tensor cores
ECMP relies on centralized SDN controllers that cannot update routing tables at microsecond timescales
ECMP requires all switches in the fabric to maintain complete copies of the global model parameters

Answer: The correct answer is A. A large population of independent small flows can distribute load more evenly under hashing, but ECMP does not guarantee balance. With few long-lived gradient flows, several hashes can select the same path, and the imbalance can persist through the collective while other paths remain underused. The actual result depends on the flow population, hashes, traffic volumes, and provisioned paths. The statement regarding packet reordering corrupting GPU tensor cores misattributes network-layer reordering to hardware compute corruption. The option referencing slow centralized SDN controllers confuses distributed IP routing with SDN control planes. The claim about switch hardware holding model parameters confuses network routing state with accelerator memory.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why static flow hashing fails under large-scale ML collective traffic.
Contrast how packet loss is handled in traditional web-scale TCP/IP networks versus RDMA-based ML fabrics (such as RoCEv2), and explain why packet loss in an ML cluster can cause a large performance drop.
Answer: TCP with selective acknowledgments can retransmit missing regions. Reliable RDMA transports also recover loss, but the recovery granularity depends on the RNIC implementation. A Go-Back-N-style RNIC can retransmit data after the missing packet, extending the completion tail seen by synchronized workers; selective-recovery implementations can repair a smaller region. The performance penalty therefore depends on recovery behavior and the collective critical path, rather than following from RDMA alone.
Learning Objective: Compare packet loss recovery mechanisms and their performance implications in TCP/IP versus RDMA fabrics.
**Arrange the five levels of the high-performance ML network fabric model in ascending order of abstraction, from physical signaling up to cluster orchestration:


Switch and Topology
Cluster Design
Wire and Link
Fabric Behavior
Transport and Performance Model**

Answer: The correct sequence is: (3) Wire and Link -> (5) Transport and Performance Model -> (1) Switch and Topology -> (4) Fabric Behavior -> (2) Cluster Design.
Learning Objective: Classify networking mechanisms within the five-level ML fabric model.

Which performance metric is the primary optimization target in an ML training network fabric, and why?

Average per-flow throughput, because web data centers maximize aggregate data volume across millions of independent users
Jitter buffer depth, because audio and video streaming protocols require bounded inter-packet arrival gaps
Maximum hop count across the core, because reducing total cable length minimizes physical fiber deployment costs
Collective completion time under load, because a Bulk Synchronous Parallel barrier waits for the last required transfer; p99 transfer latency helps characterize the tail

Answer: The correct answer is D. In distributed ML training under the Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) paradigm, all GPUs must reach a synchronization barrier before any worker can proceed. Consequently, the last required transfer can determine barrier completion and extend the step. The p99 transfer latency summarizes a distribution; it is not the maximum completion time of a particular collective. The choice focusing on average per-flow throughput reflects traditional web-service optimization rather than synchronous ML collectives. The option mentioning jitter buffers pertains to real-time multimedia streaming rather than RDMA bulk transfers. The choice concerning physical fiber deployment costs addresses cabling economics rather than the operational performance metric governing synchronization.
Learning Objective: Analyze why tail latency dominates network fabric design under synchronous training workloads.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

What is the primary physical trade-off introduced by adopting PAM4 (Pulse Amplitude Modulation 4-level) instead of NRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero) signaling in \(400\text{ Gb/s}\) and \(800\text{ Gb/s}\) network fabrics?

PAM4 triples the baud rate on the physical wire but eliminates the need for receiver equalization
PAM4 doubles the data rate per symbol by using four voltage levels, but the reduced noise margin requires Forward Error Correction (FEC) with an implementation-dependent latency cost
PAM4 replaces electrical copper signaling with optical coherent modulation, restricting maximum cable length to under \(50\text{ cm}\)
PAM4 eliminates link-level bit errors entirely, removing the need for physical layer error detection at the cost of doubling SerDes power consumption

Answer: The correct answer is B. PAM4 transmits 2 bits per symbol using 4 discrete voltage levels, doubling throughput without doubling the symbol rate. However, the voltage gap between adjacent levels shrinks by a factor of 3 compared to NRZ, requiring Reed-Solomon Forward Error Correction (RS-FEC) whose processing latency depends on the PHY and module implementation. The choice claiming PAM4 triples the baud rate while eliminating equalization is incorrect because PAM4 maintains the symbol rate while requiring more complex equalization. The option stating PAM4 replaces copper with optical coherent modulation confuses electrical modulation with optical transceivers. The assertion that PAM4 eliminates bit errors contradicts the physical reality that smaller noise margins increase raw bit error rates.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the trade-offs between PAM4 and NRZ signaling in high-speed network fabrics.
Why can increasing per-lane signaling rate shorten passive Direct Attach Copper reach, and how should the resulting link budget constrain AI rack design?
Answer: Higher signaling frequencies increase copper attenuation, consuming the available loss margin. Usable reach depends on lane rate, cable construction, connectors, and active components rather than aggregate port rate alone. Designers keep passive paths within the validated channel budget and consider active cables or optics when the required distance exceeds it; a rack boundary by itself does not determine the medium.
Learning Objective: Analyze link budget and attenuation constraints on high-speed copper cabling in dense AI racks.
In a modern multi-thousand GPU cluster using \(400\text{ Gb/s}\) pluggable optical transceivers, why is transceiver power consumption a critical design constraint at the facility level?

Pluggable transceivers require cryogenic cooling to prevent optical fiber dispersion
Optical transceivers consume no power during active data transfer but draw high surge currents during idle states
Counting one selected spine-side module on each of 20,000 links at \(20\text{ W}\) per module gives a \(400\text{ kW}\) endpoint subtotal, before opposite-end modules and other fabric power
Optical modules dissipate heat directly into the switch ASIC die, reducing switch processing clock frequencies by \(50\%\)

Answer: The correct answer is C. The scenario counts one selected spine-side module per physical link, giving \(20{,}000 \times 20\text{ W} = 400\text{ kW}\) for those endpoints. A complete optical link has a module at each end; the opposite endpoints, switch electronics, and cooling are outside this subtotal. The separate \(25\text{ W}\) per-port budget also includes the selected switch-side SerDes. Standard datacom optics do not require cryogenic cooling, and active conversion consumes power while data moves.
Learning Objective: Calculate and evaluate the power overhead of optical interconnects in large-scale AI clusters.
True or False: Direct Attach Copper (DAC) cables introduce higher propagation and serialization latency than Active Optical Cables (AOC) over a 2-meter intra-rack link because copper has higher electrical resistance than optical fiber.
Answer: False. Passive DAC avoids electrical-to-optical and optical-to-electrical conversion, but both high-speed copper and optical paths can include PHY and FEC processing. Actual latency depends on the complete path, signaling, and implementation; electrical resistance alone does not establish a latency ordering or a universal under-3-meter winner.
Learning Objective: Compare latency profiles of Direct Attach Copper versus optical cabling.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

How does GPUDirect RDMA optimize the end-to-end data path during a multi-node AllReduce gradient exchange compared to traditional host-staged network transfers?

It allows the network interface card (NIC) to read and write GPU High Bandwidth Memory directly over the PCIe bus without staging data through host CPU system RAM
It compresses floating-point tensors in GPU L2 cache before writing them directly to the optical switch buffer
It enables the GPU to execute TCP/IP checksum offloading in CUDA streaming multiprocessors
It re-routes inter-node gradient traffic over host SATA storage buses to bypass network switch congestion

Answer: The correct answer is A. Traditional network transfers require copying gradient data from GPU memory to CPU system RAM, and then through the OS kernel buffer before reaching the NIC. GPUDirect RDMA enables peer-to-peer DMA over PCIe between the GPU memory and the NIC, eliminating intermediate host copies, reducing CPU utilization and host-staging overhead. The choice claiming tensor compression in GPU L2 cache describes a data compression technique rather than RDMA DMA bypass. The option regarding GPU-executed TCP/IP checksums is incorrect because GPUDirect RDMA offloads the data path to the NIC rather than executing transport checksums on GPU cores. The claim regarding SATA storage buses confuses storage interfaces with accelerator network interconnects.

True or False: Disaggregated composable architectures using CXL memory pooling eliminate the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) communication costs between processors and remote memory pools.
Answer: False. While CXL memory pooling decouples compute and memory into composable resource pools with load/store semantics, cross-chassis memory access still traverses physical wires and switches. It remains governed by physical \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) latency and bandwidth constraints, SerDes power limits, and bisection capacity; disaggregation relocates the synchronization boundary rather than eliminating physical transfer costs.
Learning Objective: Evaluate physical communication limits in disaggregated and composable architectures.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why is using standard TCP benchmark tools like iperf to validate an ML cluster network fabric considered a major operational fallacy?

iperf measures the TCP path, whose throughput depends on host processing, offloads, and tuning; it does not validate the RDMA path exercised by distributed training
iperf only operates over wireless IEEE 802.11 interfaces and cannot bind to physical QSFP56 ports
iperf automatically enables InfiniBand credit-based flow control on standard Ethernet switches
iperf encrypts all network packets with 4096-bit RSA keys, causing false GPU thermal throttling

Answer: The correct answer is A. TCP and RDMA exercise different transport and host-processing paths, so a TCP benchmark cannot establish RDMA or collective performance. TCP throughput depends on host configuration and has no universal fixed ceiling. RDMA-specific tools such as ib_write_bw test the relevant data path; collective benchmarks then test synchronization and topology effects. The wireless-only and automatic InfiniBand flow-control claims are incorrect.
Learning Objective: Analyze why TCP benchmarks are inadequate for validating RDMA-based ML fabrics.
An infrastructure team claims: ‘Adaptive routing completely eliminates the need for topology-aware job placement in our GPU cluster.’ Why is this assertion a critical pitfall?

Adaptive routing only functions when all GPU servers are manufactured by the same vendor
Adaptive routing disables link-layer CRC error checking on optical switches
Adaptive routing forces all AllReduce operations to execute sequentially across a single ring
Adaptive routing balances traffic across existing paths, but it cannot synthesize bisection bandwidth that does not exist if a job is split across an oversubscribed or constrained network boundary

Answer: The correct answer is D. Adaptive routing can direct packets away from congested queues onto less loaded eligible paths, reducing imbalance from static hash collisions. However, it cannot generate physical bandwidth where none exists. For a tightly coupled 1,024-GPU job spanning two spine pods, a collective is limited by their boundary when its crossing traffic exceeds what the boundary can deliver within the communication budget. Adaptive routing can reduce path imbalance but cannot increase that capacity; topology-aware placement can reduce crossing traffic. Both must be evaluated against the actual collective schedule, and neither guarantees efficient delivery by itself. The choices claiming single-vendor restrictions, CRC disabling, or forced sequential ring execution are factually incorrect.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the complementary roles and limitations of adaptive routing versus topology-aware scheduling.
Explain why upgrading an InfiniBand fabric from HDR (\(200\text{ Gb/s}\)) to NDR (\(400\text{ Gb/s}\)) yields less than a \(15\%\) reduction in transfer time for a \(10\text{ KB}\) control message, and state the condition under which bandwidth upgrades deliver linear performance gains.
Answer: For a \(10\text{ KB}\) message, transfer time is governed by the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) model (\(T(n) = \alpha + n/\beta\)). With the same assumed \(\alpha = 1.5\,\mu\text{s}\) on both paths, HDR takes \(1.5 + 0.4 = 1.9\,\mu\text{s}\) and NDR takes \(1.5 + 0.2 = 1.7\,\mu\text{s}\), a reduction of about \(10.5\%\). Startup contributes about \(79\%\) of the HDR total and \(88\%\) of the NDR total. Doubling bandwidth halves the transmission term while leaving startup unchanged. Bandwidth upgrades deliver near-linear speedups only in the bandwidth-dominated regime (\(n \gg n^*\)), such as multi-megabyte to gigabyte gradient AllReduce transfers.
Learning Objective: Explain the diminishing returns of network bandwidth upgrades in latency-dominated regimes.
True or False: Lossless RoCEv2 Ethernet fabrics provide the exact same operational simplicity and fault immunity as InfiniBand fabrics because both support zero-packet-loss guarantees.
Answer: False. InfiniBand uses native credit-based flow control, while many RoCE deployments use Ethernet PFC with endpoint congestion control and recovery. PFC introduces pause-based storms and cyclic-dependency risks, but credits alone do not make InfiniBand immune to deadlock: routing and resource dependencies still matter. PFC-free RoCE designs make a different recovery trade-off.
Learning Objective: Compare operational risk and failure modes in lossless Ethernet versus InfiniBand.

← Back to Questions

title: Fleet Principles
text:
Fleet Principles
The scaling laws of AI Scaling Laws reward more parameters, more training tokens, and more compute together, so each further gain in model quality asks the fleet for more memory, more arithmetic, more bytes moved between machines, and more data stored and read. With that demand set, Part I builds the physics of supply: the silicon, the wires, the cooling systems, and the storage hierarchies of the warehouse-scale machine learning fleet, where the network is the bus, power density limits deployment, and component failures are routine at scale. The broader fleet also includes geographically distributed serving systems and heterogeneous edge devices, whose constraints appear in Part III. Across this physical foundation, the focus shifts from the single accelerator to the data-center-scale machine, and the engineering question is no longer how to compute on one device but how to move energy and information at a scale that challenges the limits of the physical infrastructure.
At this scale the individual accelerator becomes one component of a larger, tightly coupled system. The principles of the fleet are therefore not best practices for cluster management. They are constraints, most of them physical, that dictate what kind of models can be trained and how they can be served. These constraints range from the efficiency of specialized silicon and the heat a rack can shed to the bisection bandwidth of the network fabric. They define the boundaries of the Infrastructure band of the fleet stack, the two rows (Facility and Accelerators, Fabric and Storage) on which every other part of the book rests. The C³ taxonomy tracks costs across Compute, Communication, and Coordination. An optimization can reduce total execution time while shifting which cost dominates; reducing local compute, for example, can expose communication that was previously hidden. The engineering obligation is to measure the complete path rather than assume that a local saving yields the same fleet-wide gain.
The principles below preview the constraints that Part I makes concrete through compute infrastructure, network fabrics, and storage, in the order those chapters develop them. Their implications name some mechanisms developed later in the book; those names are signposts, not prerequisites for reading this part. The first constraint applies before any machine is assembled, because the choice of accelerator decides how much of its silicon and power go to useful arithmetic.

Principle 1: The generality taxInvariant: For workloads with stable computation patterns, specialization can improve performance per watt by reducing general-purpose overhead, while also reducing programmability and workload flexibility. \[ \SpecializedEnergyProductivity\gg \GeneralPurposeEnergyProductivity\quad \text{for a fixed power budget} \] Here, \(\FleetEnergyProductivity\) denotes useful computation per unit energy; the comparison illustrates the potential advantage for a workload suited to the specialized design.
Implication: The trajectory from CPU to GPU to Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) to fixed-function ASIC is a workload-dependent architecture trade-off, not a universal physical law. Each step can trade programmability for efficiency, and the fleet architect must choose the right point on this curve for each workload.


A specialized accelerator still holds only as much model state as its memory allows, and that capacity gives the first reason to divide a model. When parameters, gradients, and optimizer states outgrow a single package, the computation can proceed only by splitting that state across multiple devices.

Principle 2: The memory capacity gapInvariant: Frontier model memory requirements have grown faster and more irregularly than single-accelerator HBM capacity.
Implication: When a model and its training state exceed one device’s memory, the system must divide that state across devices. Part II develops the parallelism strategies for doing so: tensor parallelism divides individual operations, and pipeline parallelism assigns groups of layers to different devices. Complementary data parallelism distributes training examples across model replicas. Because per-device bandwidth falls roughly tenfold at each physical boundary, from device memory to the node interconnect to the cluster fabric, the division that exchanges the most data, tensor parallelism, stays inside the fastest domain. Part I establishes the capacity and communication constraints those strategies must respect.


Dividing a model across more accelerators packs more of them into each rack, and the rack’s power budget is the first limit on that density. Keeping latency-sensitive peers close enough for high-bandwidth copper links concentrates electrical draw into a narrow physical footprint.

Principle 3: The power density wallInvariant: Cluster scaling is constrained by thermal dissipation limits (watts per rack) and cooling capacity, not just silicon area or floor space.
Implication: Watts per rack, together with power-delivery losses and the cooling class the facility installs, bound how many accelerators can share a rack, and therefore how large a fast interconnect domain can be. Accelerator power has risen faster than rack power budgets, so installable compute is set by the rack envelope rather than by peak FLOP/s.


Every watt the rack draws becomes heat that the facility must remove. Sustaining that electrical load therefore turns a power-delivery specification into a continuous heat-rejection requirement.

Principle 4: The thermodynamic limitInvariant: Irreversible computation and data movement dissipate electrical energy as heat; at data-center scale, the practical limit is the rate at which that heat can be removed. \[ \InformationTechnologyHeatLoad\leq \FacilityHeatRemovalCapacity(\text{facility},\text{cooling configuration}) \] where \(\InformationTechnologyHeatLoad\) is the heat produced by IT equipment and \(\FacilityHeatRemovalCapacity\) is the maximum heat-removal rate of the installed facility and cooling configuration.
Implication: A rack can operate only while its heat output remains within the installed cooling system’s capacity. The cooling class is chosen to match that heat load. Engineered air cooling remains viable for configurations designed for its airflow, while denser configurations need cold-plate or immersion liquid loops, which carry the same heat with far less flow at a cost in serviceability and leak and loss-of-flow risk.


Once a model is divided across devices, the network becomes part of the execution path. The time to move a single message has a structure of its own, which determines whether a transfer is limited by fixed startup cost or by bandwidth.

Principle 5: The bandwidth-latency trade-off (α-β model)Invariant: In the latency-bandwidth model, communication time combines fixed startup latency (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) with the transfer time for a message of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) at effective bandwidth \(\LinkBandwidth\). \[ \PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \]
Implication: Small messages (for example, routing metadata or control signals) are latency-bound; large messages (for example, gradients) are bandwidth-bound. Optimization strategies must match the regime: fuse small messages to amortize \(\MessageStartupLatency\), compress large messages to reduce \(\PointToPointMessageSize\).


The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model prices one message on one path. When every worker communicates at once, those messages compete for the links that join one half of the cluster to the other, and the capacity of that cut bounds their aggregate rate.

Principle 6: The bisection bandwidth theoremInvariant: Communication that crosses a network cut is limited by the aggregate bandwidth of that cut. For traffic that must cross between two halves of a cluster, the minimum bisection bandwidth bounds the achievable transfer rate.
Implication: Synchronized training requires bisection bandwidth commensurate with the traffic crossing the fabric. A collective operation coordinates communication among a group of workers; AllReduce, for example, combines their contributions and returns the result to every worker. Part I explains how network topology limits this traffic; Part II develops the collective algorithms that generate it.


A fabric that carries every exchange on time still helps only if the training pipeline can keep the accelerators fed. Every training step begins by pulling fresh batches from storage, so an underprovisioned input path stalls the cluster before arithmetic or gradient exchange even starts.

Principle 7: The I/O wallInvariant: When storage throughput cannot deliver training data as fast as accelerators consume it, accelerators idle regardless of their computational power. \[ \text{Utilization} = \min\!\left(1,\;\frac{\StorageBandwidth}{\AcceleratorCount \times \AcceleratorDataConsumptionRate}\right) \] where \(\StorageBandwidth\) is aggregate storage bandwidth, \(\AcceleratorCount\) is the number of accelerators, and \(\AcceleratorDataConsumptionRate\) is each accelerator’s data-consumption rate.
Implication: A storage system that was adequate for 8 accelerators can become the bottleneck at 64 if its provisioned throughput cannot meet the higher aggregate demand. The I/O wall scales with the number of accelerators: at a fixed per-device consumption rate, every accelerator added raises the throughput floor that storage must sustain. Without matching capacity, the data pipeline can become the limiting factor.


Meeting that demand requires a hierarchy rather than a single undifferentiated storage pool. No single storage medium offers both the petabyte capacity of a training corpus and the terabyte-per-second bandwidth of an accelerator pod.

Principle 8: The storage hierarchy principleInvariant: Storage hierarchies are designed so that tiers farther from the accelerator typically trade higher access latency and lower per-stream bandwidth for greater capacity and lower cost per byte; aggregate throughput still depends on provisioning and parallelism.
Implication: The systems engineer’s task is to ensure that the right data is on the right tier at the right time. Data format choices, caching strategies, prefetch buffer sizing, and tiering policies all exist to manage movement upward through the hierarchy so that accelerators do not starve.


These constraints make the fleet a first-class engineering object. Following the introduction’s account of why single machines no longer suffice, Part I builds the physical machine from the ground up, starting with the silicon, power, and cooling systems of the AI data center and the network fabrics that connect the fleet. It then turns to the storage hierarchy that feeds the training pipeline, preserves its checkpoints, versions the artifacts a run depends on, and serves retrieval at inference time. Each chapter sets one or more terms of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3). Compute infrastructure sets the per-device rate behind \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) and the failure exposure that later surfaces in \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\). Network fabrics set \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) and the barrier tail. Storage adds the input stalls and checkpoint pauses that the step pays whenever prefetching and asynchronous writes cannot hide them. Together, these chapters fix the physical rates within which the communication, partitioning, and recovery mechanisms of Part II must work, for each of the lighthouse archetypes (Three systems archetypes) traced across this book.




 Back to top

title: SocratiQ AI
text:
Welcome to SocratiQ (pronounced ``Socratic’’), an AI learning assistant seamlessly integrated throughout this resource. Inspired by the Socratic method of teaching—emphasizing thoughtful questions and answers to stimulate critical thinking—SocratiQ is part of our experiment with what we call Generative Learning. By combining interactive quizzes, personalized assistance, and real-time feedback, SocratiQ is meant to reinforce your understanding and help you create new connections. SocratiQ is still a work in progress, and we welcome your feedback.
Learn more: Read our research paper SocratiQ: A Generative AI-Powered Learning Companion for Personalized Education and Broader Accessibility.
Listen to this AI-generated podcast about SocratiQ. 

    
    
    
    
You can enable SocratiQ by clicking the button below:


SocratiQ: OFF









TipDirect URL access



You can directly control SocratiQ by adding ?socratiq= parameters to your URL:

To activate: mlsysbook.ai/?socratiq=true
To deactivate: mlsysbook.ai/?socratiq=false

This gives you quick access to toggle SocratiQ’s functionality directly from your browser’s address bar, without needing to return here.


SocratiQ’s goal is to adapt to your needs while generating targeted questions and engaging in meaningful dialogue about the material. Unlike traditional textbook study, SocratiQ offers an interactive, personalized learning experience that can help you better understand and retain complex concepts. It is only available as an online feature.




Enable SocratiQ using the button below or URL parameters
Use keyboard shortcut (Cmd/Ctrl + /) to open SocratiQ anytime
Set your academic level in Settings
Start learning! Look for quiz buttons at the end of sections

title: A Note on AI Assistance
text:
A Note on AI Assistance
Every chapter of this book was researched, written, and rewritten by me. I also used artificial intelligence tools throughout the process. What follows is more than the disclosure MIT Press requires of authors who use AI. It is an honest statement of how AI assisted in navigating fleet-scale systems engineering, and the rigorous human verification standard applied to the result.
In an era of generative AI, defining what authorship really means has become genuinely difficult. When tools can draft prose, crunch cluster arithmetic, unearth research papers, and generate visual sketches, where does the machine end and the author begin?
In developing this text, AI tools served as an accelerator across computation, literature review, and drafting. On the infrastructure side, this involved extending the MLSysIM infrastructure modeling engine from single-node execution to the fleet level: modeling 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and data parallel strategies), collective communication fabrics, cluster network topologies, and fault-tolerance protocols. AI helped formulate complex cluster-level equations, write executable Python cells, and implement automated pre-commit checks.
AI proved especially valuable in digging into the vast literature of distributed systems, unearthing seminal, classical papers and historical foundations that modern AI literature often overlooks. In the writing itself, I used AI to draft initial chapter outlines, generate preliminary explanations, and synthesize dense research papers into first-pass text, which I then evaluated, restructured, and substantially rewrote to ensure conceptual rigor.
Beyond code and prose, AI fundamentally shifted how I developed the book’s visual language. In previous work, sketching architectural diagrams was a slow, manual bottleneck. For this book, I used generative AI to produce initial conceptual drafts and rough schematics of cluster topologies. While these AI-generated sketches were far from publication-ready, they served as an effective conceptual boilerplate, helping clarify and communicate the architectural concepts and communication patterns for the ongoing illustration and refinement process.
Yet mechanical computation, literature synthesis, and AI-assisted drafting are only the starting point. The most critical and time-intensive phase of writing this book was human validation. To ensure that the analytical models reflect the reality of warehouse-scale computing rather than idealized abstractions, I conducted extensive one-on-one review meetings with domain experts: distributed systems researchers, ML fleet operators, and hardware architects. In these sessions, we walked through chapters, stress-tested assumptions, scrutinized performance equations, and debated design trade-offs. This human feedback loop is the longest and most demanding part of the authoring process, but it is indispensable. Without that expert review, a systems book risks teaching clean abstractions that fail on real silicon.
Writing a textbook is an act of synthesis, not a claim of personal invention. The fundamental breakthroughs in distributed systems and hardware architecture belong to the researchers and engineers cited throughout these chapters. My name appears on the cover not out of ego, but because authorship is the assumption of human responsibility. It is the demanding process of vetting these ideas against real-world hardware, and it means providing a single human being whom readers, students, and engineers can hold accountable, someone to reach out to for clarifications, debates, and corrections.
Machine learning systems cannot be certified the way deterministic logic can. That verification gap applies to AI-assisted authoring with equal force. The standard held here is the standard we must demand of every fleet we build: the tool can propose, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.




 Back to top

title: Preface
text:
This book is for anyone who understands machine learning on a single machine and now faces the challenge of making it work at scale. The problems of scale are not the problems of a single node, only bigger. They are qualitatively different: networks partition, hardware fails as a statistical certainty, and the societal impact of every design decision is amplified by millions of users.
The assumed foundation is what an introductory ML systems course or equivalent experience supplies, with no particular prior textbook required. The advanced scope here is the transition from that single node to a coordinated fleet. That scope ranges from designing the physical substrate of an AI data center, to scaling training beyond the limits of a single accelerator, to reasoning about what happens when a production fleet serves a global user base. Throughout, the focus is on the physics of distribution, the invariants that govern every fleet-scale ML system regardless of the framework, the model, or the era.



Readers should bring the following background:

Single-machine ML systems: Understanding of ML workflows, neural network training, model optimization, and deployment on a single machine. Readers should be comfortable reasoning about memory hierarchies, computational graphs, accelerator execution, and hardware-software interactions. The D·A·M Taxonomy recaps the single-machine performance model (the iron law, arithmetic intensity, and the Roofline Model), the memory hierarchy, training memory per parameter, and transformer compute that later chapters assume.
Programming: Fluency in Python, including functions, classes, and data manipulation with NumPy. Familiarity with at least one ML framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX).
Mathematics: Comfort with linear algebra, basic calculus, and probability at the undergraduate level. Probability tools for failure analysis restates the probability results that the failure analysis uses, and Queuing theory for batched inference develops the queuing results that serving analysis uses.

The following background is helpful but not required:

Distributed systems: Familiarity with networking concepts (TCP/IP, bandwidth, latency), parallelism, and basic distributed computing deepens understanding of the fleet infrastructure and training chapters.
Cloud infrastructure: Experience with containerization and orchestration (Docker and Kubernetes) or cluster schedulers (Slurm) provides useful operational context.
Production engineering: Understanding of monitoring, observability, and site reliability practices will enrich the deployment and operations chapters.




In 2012, training AlexNet took five to six days on two GPUs (Krizhevsky et al. 2012). By 2023, public GPT-4-class estimates placed frontier training at roughly 25,000 GPUs running for about three months (Patel and Wong 2023); OpenAI did not disclose the actual hardware configuration (OpenAI et al. 2023). This is not the same engineering problem at a larger scale. It is a categorically different engineering problem.

Krizhevsky, Alex, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2012. “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 25.

Patel, Dylan, and Gerald Wong. 2023. GPT-4 Architecture, Infrastructure, Training Dataset, Costs, Vision, MoE. SemiAnalysis Blog.

OpenAI, Josh Achiam, Steven Adler, Sandhini Agarwal, Lama Ahmad, Ilge Akkaya, Florencia Leoni Aleman, et al. 2023. “GPT-4 Technical Report.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2303.08774, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.08774.
On a single machine, performance is governed by the memory wall, the gap between processor speed and memory bandwidth. In a distributed cluster, a new limit emerges. Bisection bandwidth, the total bandwidth across the narrowest cut that divides the cluster into two halves, caps the throughput of any traffic that must cross that cut. Data no longer moves through local hierarchies alone; it traverses optical fabrics governed by the speed of light between racks and across continents. Hardware failures, rare enough on a single machine to be treated as exceptions, become routine statistical events at fleet scale. Long training runs must plan for interruptions rather than rely on every component remaining available until completion.
These are not operational annoyances. They are physical constraints, as fundamental and as permanent as the memory wall, Amdahl’s Law, or the energy cost of data movement. They require their own engineering discipline, built on the invariants this book develops:

The Empirical Scaling Law: Within empirically validated regimes, model loss falls as a power law in training compute, data, or parameters, so each further improvement demands multiplicatively more resources. This is the pressure that moves machine learning from single machines onto fleets.
The Bisection Bandwidth Theorem: For communication patterns that must cross the minimum bisection, throughput is bounded by that bisection bandwidth.
The Fleet Law: Under fixed-work scaling, reduced per-node computation competes with communication and coordination costs, so adding workers does not guarantee proportional speedup.
The Young-Daly Checkpoint Interval: The optimal checkpoint interval balances the cost of writing state against the expected cost of lost work due to failure.
Serving Cost Dominance: For high-traffic production models, cumulative inference operational expenditure can exceed the one-time training cost, making serving efficiency a lifecycle optimization target.
The Fairness Impossibility Theorem: With unequal group base rates and imperfect prediction, risk scores cannot satisfy groupwise calibration and equal mean scores across groups within both outcome classes simultaneously. Thresholded error-rate parity and demographic parity are distinct requirements with their own trade-offs.

If single-machine ML systems engineering asks “what can one machine build?”, then fleet-scale ML systems engineering asks “what can a thousand machines build together, and at what cost to reliability, efficiency, and society?” That final clause is what sets fleet-scale engineering apart. A single machine affects its user; a fleet affects everyone its outputs touch, across millions of decisions per second. At that scale, reliability, efficiency, and fairness stop being features and become engineering constraints as binding as bandwidth or power. A system that scales but cannot be trusted has not been engineered. It has only been enlarged.
This book develops that discipline. It follows the Hennessy and Patterson pedagogical model, extending the quantitative, principles-first approach to the distributed scale (Hennessy and Patterson 2011; Hennessy and Patterson 2019, 2017). Just as their work taught a generation to reason about processor performance from first principles, this book teaches the reader to reason about fleet performance, replacing intuition about distributed systems with measurement, and ad hoc scaling with engineering.

Hennessy, J. L., and D. A. Patterson. 2011. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. Morgan Kaufmann.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2019. “A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture.” Communications of the ACM 62 (2): 48–60. https://doi.org/10.1145/3282307.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2017. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. 6th ed. Morgan Kaufmann.
The architectural priorities and operational failure modes explored in these chapters did not originate in an academic vacuum. They were gathered directly from practitioners in industry, through technical exchanges at conferences, engineering meetups, and conversations with colleagues. These colleagues generously made the time to explain what breaks when scaling models across thousands of accelerators and what practicing systems engineers must understand.
Single-node foundations supply the bricks of those systems: tensors, kernels, memory hierarchies, and optimization loops. What breaks at fleet scale is rarely an individual brick, because a fleet is closer to an orchestra than to a larger wall. An orchestra is not simply many musicians playing at once. It needs a conductor, a score, precise synchronization, and the ability to recover when a player drops out, none of which governs a solo performer. A training cluster, a serving fleet, and an edge deployment are vastly different systems, but beneath them sit the same building blocks: parallelism strategies, collective communication primitives, checkpoint protocols, scheduling algorithms, and the trade-offs between throughput, latency, fault tolerance, and cost.



This book focuses on the machine learning fleet: coordinated machines that jointly train, serve, or maintain ML models. Warehouse-scale training clusters are one form; geographically distributed serving replicas and heterogeneous edge devices are others. Across these forms, communication and coordination couple local execution to fleet behavior, while reliability, resource budgets, and governance constrain the design. The scope is the fleet as it exists today and the governance of operating it at scale. Research-frontier topics such as fully autonomous fleet management, next-generation interconnects, neuromorphic computing at scale, and formal verification of fleet-level safety properties lie beyond it.
The content is organized into four parts:

Part I: The Fleet builds the physical substrate of the AI data center from the ground up: the silicon and cooling of compute infrastructure, the network fabrics that connect thousands of accelerators, and the scalable data storage that feeds training pipelines.
Part II: Distributed ML establishes the logic of distribution beyond a single machine: the collective communication primitives that synchronize gradients, the parallelism strategies (data, tensor, and pipeline) for training models too large for single devices, the fault tolerance mechanisms that ensure reliability when failure is routine, and the orchestration systems that manage the fleet.
Part III: The Fleet in Production takes the trained model from the cluster to the world: fleet efficiency, which measures how much of a fleet’s capacity becomes useful work, serving at scale for millions of concurrent requests, edge intelligence across heterogeneous and federated devices, and the operational lifecycle required to manage production fleets.
Part IV: The Responsible Fleet confronts the forces that determine whether the fleet serves its users or harms them: security and privacy, robust system design, environmental sustainability, and responsible engineering as constraints as fundamental as power density or bisection bandwidth.

These four parts trace a path through the fleet stack, a layered abstraction that organizes an ML system at distributed scale, from the physical facility up to its governance. The stack has eight rows grouped into four bands, and each band is one part of the book. At the base, the Infrastructure band (Part I) holds Facility & Accelerators and Fabric & Storage, the physical substrate. On top of that hardware, the Distribution band (Part II) adds Distributed Execution and Reliability & Control to manage parallel work, communication, scheduling, and recovery. Once a model can be trained reliably, the Serving band (Part III) provides Runtime & Serving and Operations to take models to users and manage the production lifecycle. At the top, the Governance band (Part IV) layers Assurance (security, privacy, and robustness) and Governance & Sustainability to turn trust, risk, policy, and environmental cost into engineering constraints. Each row provides an abstraction to the row above and consumes the row below. Engineering decisions in the Infrastructure band constrain what is possible in the bands above it, while governance requirements constrain choices throughout the stack. Privacy, acceptable risk, and environmental budgets enter the design from the beginning; Part IV develops their enforcement mechanisms after the infrastructure and operational dependencies are available.
Where the fleet stack locates responsibility, a second framework diagnoses cost. The C³ taxonomy divides the wall-clock time of distributed execution into Compute, Communication, and Coordination, and the Fleet Law turns that division into an equation for distributed step time. Every chapter applies this lens to its own layer of the stack. Three recurring workloads, the archetypes, keep the analysis concrete: a large dense language model (Archetype A), a recommendation model with very large embedding tables (Archetype B), and a model trained by federated learning across phone-class devices (Archetype C). Each stresses a different part of the fleet, and the chapters return to whichever one exposes their central constraint.
Each part builds on the previous one, so sequential reading is recommended. The reading paths below offer alternatives for readers with specific goals.



The chapters are ordered so that each can draw on everything before it, but not every chapter consumes the one immediately before it. A dependency map derived from the chapters’ own cross-references records which chapters build directly on which (figure 1). An arrow in the map means the later chapter uses a model, mechanism, or constraint that the earlier one establishes. Two features of the map guide the choice of path. First, every chapter lies on a route to Conclusion, whose six principles cite every chapter of Parts I through IV, so no chapter is a dead end. Second, several dependencies cross part boundaries: distributed training builds on both the storage pipeline of Data Storage and the collectives of Collective Communication, and fleet efficiency (Fleet Efficiency) builds on Fleet Orchestration. Consecutive chapters without an arrow mark a change of thread rather than a gap. Collective Communication, for example, builds on the fabric model of Network Fabrics rather than on the storage chapter that precedes it.






Figure 1: Chapter Dependency Map: Each arrow points from a chapter to a later chapter that builds on its results, derived from the book’s cross-references with transitive links omitted. Every chapter lies on the core path the conclusion builds on, so the map draws no optional branch. Book order is one valid reading order; a missing arrow between consecutive chapters means the later chapter does not directly consume the earlier one’s results.



Each path below begins with the introduction, assumes the single-machine prerequisites listed earlier in this preface, and keeps every chapter that its destination depends on in the map:

The Complete Path (all chapters, in sequence): Follows the causal chain of constraints that governs the ML fleet from first principles of distribution. After the introduction, progress through Parts I, II, III, and IV.
The Infrastructure Path (physical fleet and orchestration): Focuses on Part I (Compute Infrastructure, Network Fabrics, Data Storage), then Fleet Orchestration. Before orchestration, use the collective traffic patterns in Collective Communication, the workload partitioning in Distributed Training, and the checkpoint/recovery model in Fault Tolerance to establish what the scheduler must place, connect, and preserve.
The Scaling Path (distributed training depth): Establishes the memory-capacity, network-bandwidth, and storage-throughput models in Part I before focusing on Collective Communication, Distributed Training, Fault Tolerance, Fleet Orchestration, and Fleet Efficiency. Readers already comfortable estimating those limits can use Part I as a reference.
The Production Path (deployment and operations): Uses Part I for fleet capacity and network constraints. It then establishes collective communication in Collective Communication, model partitioning in Distributed Training, failure and recovery in Fault Tolerance, placement and isolation in Fleet Orchestration, and how much of the fleet’s capacity becomes useful work in Fleet Efficiency. Continue through Serving at Scale, Edge Intelligence, ML Operations at Scale, and Part IV (Security & Privacy, Robust AI, Sustainable AI, and Responsible AI).




Across any of those reading paths, recurring visual cues in the margins orient the reader within the fleet stack. At every chapter opening, a margin figure highlights which rows of the stack the chapter addresses. The full stack below shows each row with its scope, grouped into the four parts of the book:

The Roman numerals (I–IV) mark those four parts, while the row intensity marks emphasis. The stack uses one accent color throughout so that shade, not hue, carries the chapter-focus signal.
In the margin figures throughout the book, the intensity of each row reflects how strongly the chapter engages it. Brighter (higher intensity) marks the chapter’s primary focus; dimmer (lower intensity) marks contextual relevance as constraints propagate upward. Consider three chapters that illustrate how the emphasis shifts:






Compute Infrastructure







Distributed Training







Responsible AI





In Compute Infrastructure, the bottom row dominates because the chapter is about silicon, power, cooling, and physical deployment. In Distributed Training, Distributed Execution is brightest while Reliability & Control remains visibly relevant because large training runs depend on scheduling and recovery. In Responsible AI, Governance & Sustainability is primary while Assurance stays strong because accountability depends on measurable trust and risk controls. The same stack tells three different stories, and in each one a decision made in one row ripples through the rows above and below it.
Small visual notes sit in the margins wherever a relationship is fastest to grasp by eye. They are reading aids, not figures to cite later. At fleet scale, this visual grammar makes bandwidth gaps, failure blast radius, checkpoint ratios, and edge-energy trade-offs visible without interrupting the argument. When a miniature uses a log scale, it says so inside the image.
















Alongside these visual miniatures, the margins carry unnumbered marginal navigation pointers that trace architectural dependencies across the fleet without interrupting the reading flow of the prose:

↩︎ Backward pointer: Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a physical limit, hardware contract, or analytical model was established.
↪ Forward pointer: Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to the appendix, where the current idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
⇄ Contrast: Marks a place where two chapters treat the same problem differently, so the comparison is visible at a glance.

A pointer only orients. When a sentence depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.
The appendices are the last reading aid. Beyond the single-machine recap in The D·A·M Taxonomy, they collect the diagnostic tables, the communication, reliability, and serving models, and the reference numbers the chapters use.



This book uses a small set of typographic conventions to mark what each piece of prose is doing.


A term in bold within body prose is its formal first introduction in the book. Each term receives this treatment exactly once. Subsequent appearances are unbolded; by then the term is part of the working vocabulary the chapter carries forward.

The Fleet Law decomposes the time of one distributed step into local computation, exposed communication, and synchronization.

The bold is a contract: register this term because it will recur. A matching index entry in the back of the book points to the defining occurrence (under the definition subentry), providing a way to return to it. Key technical terms are also compiled in the glossary.
Bold also appears in a second, structural role: as a functional label at the start of an item inside a callout box or a summary bullet, for example Recommendation, Trade-off, or Result. In that context, the bold is scaffolding rather than a first definition.



Italics are not used for general emphasis. Every italic span in this book performs one of five specific jobs:

Direct opposition: training vs. inference, allocated vs. productive accelerator time.
Impossibility, stated as physical, mathematical, or logical law: “a synchronous step cannot finish before its slowest worker does.”
Word used as word: “the term gradient refers to a vector of partial derivatives.”
Titles of works: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach.
Thesis punchline: A single italicized sentence that captures the controlling insight of a section, for example, At scale, failure is the normal operating condition.

An italicized word is performing one of these jobs. A word that is not italicized carries no implicit emphasis.



Callout boxes are not decoration. Each type signals a specific kind of content, so the visual identity tells the reader what the box contains before they read it.








Callout
Contains




Definition
Formal definition of a key term, with its significance, distinction from the nearest neighbor concept, and a common pitfall


Example
Historical case or concrete scenario, structured as context, insight, and systems lesson


Systems Perspective
Analytical observation or mathematical nuance that enriches the surrounding argument


Napkin Math
Worked calculation walked through step by step, with values computed inline from the book’s constants; intermediate tables and equations are the math itself


Checkpoint
Self-check questions to verify understanding of the preceding section


War Story
Documented engineering incident with a sourced failure mode, structured as context, failure, consequence, and lesson


Lighthouse
Recurring workloads characterized by a profile (parameters, FLOPs, dominant constraint), used as anchored case studies across multiple chapters


Principle
Canonical book principle or invariant referenced from later chapters


Theorem
Formal, equation-backed result or bound, stated with its conditions and applied in later quantitative analysis


Key Takeaways
Four to seven most important results from a chapter, in summary form


Learning Objectives
Skills and concepts that readers should be able to explain or apply after completing the chapter


What’s Next
Bridge from the chapter just ended to the chapter beginning, naming the open question the next chapter addresses




When a callout contains a table, figure, or equation, that artifact is part of the callout’s pedagogical unit, not decoration. A lighthouse’s profile is its characterization. A napkin math box’s intermediate tables are the worked math. Reading these as separated artifacts loses the teaching arc. Standalone reference tables, by contrast, sit between paragraphs as numbered artifacts the reader returns to through cross-references. Both forms are valid; the visual marker (callout vs. standalone) tells the reader which one they are looking at.




Whichever path readers choose, this book is one component of a broader learning ecosystem. The complete text, interactive notebooks, lecture slides, exercises, hands-on labs, and supplementary materials for every chapter are freely available at mlsysbook.ai.



This book is built in the open. Its full text, figures, and build system live at mlsysbook.ai/git, and contributions are welcome from every reader.
This is a deliberate choice. If AI engineering is to become a shared discipline rather than a collection of isolated practices, its foundational texts must be accessible to everyone. ML systems is a field shaped by practitioners across industry, academia, and the open-source community worldwide. A textbook covering this field should reflect that breadth and be available to all, regardless of geography or institutional affiliation.
Contributions from readers, whether fixing an error, suggesting a clearer explanation, adding a worked example, or proposing new content, have materially improved every chapter. Readers who find something that could be better are encouraged to open an issue or submit a pull request. This book improves because readers participate in building it.



This book grew out of CS249r at Harvard University and the TinyML edX professional certificate program. That teaching reinforced an insight that shapes the curriculum here: bandwidth, energy, and failure set the limits on a microcontroller and on a data center alike, and what changes with scale is which limit binds. Because the physics is continuous while the engineering changes at each scale boundary, the book is structured to support a one-semester advanced course covering the full distributed ML systems stack, while allowing instructors to select individual parts for shorter modules:

Parts I–II (The Fleet and Distributed ML) suit an advanced half-semester on distributed training infrastructure.
Parts III–IV (The Fleet in Production and The Responsible Fleet) suit an applied half-semester on production ML at scale. Such a module should first review Collective Communication and Fleet Orchestration, which fleet efficiency and serving build on (figure 1).

For survey courses or executive programs, the four part introductions provide a condensed map of the constraints that govern fleet-scale ML systems. Their principle statements are previews; the chapters supply the assumptions, worked reasoning, and mechanisms needed to apply them.
