title: Preface
text:
This book is for anyone who understands machine learning on a single machine and now faces the challenge of making it work at scale. The problems of scale are not the problems of a single node, only bigger. They are qualitatively different: networks partition, hardware fails as a statistical certainty, and the societal impact of every design decision is amplified by millions of users.
The assumed foundation is what an introductory ML systems course or equivalent experience supplies, with no particular prior textbook required. The advanced scope here is the transition from that single node to a coordinated fleet. That scope ranges from designing the physical substrate of an AI data center, to scaling training beyond the limits of a single accelerator, to reasoning about what happens when a production fleet serves a global user base. Throughout, the focus is on the physics of distribution, the invariants that govern every fleet-scale ML system regardless of the framework, the model, or the era.

title: Preface
text:
Readers should bring the following background:

Single-machine ML systems: Understanding of ML workflows, neural network training, model optimization, and deployment on a single machine. Readers should be comfortable reasoning about memory hierarchies, computational graphs, accelerator execution, and hardware-software interactions. The D·A·M Taxonomy recaps the single-machine performance model (the iron law, arithmetic intensity, and the Roofline Model), the memory hierarchy, training memory per parameter, and transformer compute that later chapters assume.
Programming: Fluency in Python, including functions, classes, and data manipulation with NumPy. Familiarity with at least one ML framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, or JAX).
Mathematics: Comfort with linear algebra, basic calculus, and probability at the undergraduate level. Probability tools for failure analysis restates the probability results that the failure analysis uses, and Queuing theory for batched inference develops the queuing results that serving analysis uses.

The following background is helpful but not required:

Distributed systems: Familiarity with networking concepts (TCP/IP, bandwidth, latency), parallelism, and basic distributed computing deepens understanding of the fleet infrastructure and training chapters.
Cloud infrastructure: Experience with containerization and orchestration (Docker and Kubernetes) or cluster schedulers (Slurm) provides useful operational context.
Production engineering: Understanding of monitoring, observability, and site reliability practices will enrich the deployment and operations chapters.

title: Preface
text:
In 2012, training AlexNet took five to six days on two GPUs (Krizhevsky et al. 2012). By 2023, public GPT-4-class estimates placed frontier training at roughly 25,000 GPUs running for about three months (Patel and Wong 2023); OpenAI did not disclose the actual hardware configuration (OpenAI et al. 2023). This is not the same engineering problem at a larger scale. It is a categorically different engineering problem.

Krizhevsky, Alex, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey E. Hinton. 2012. “ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 25.

Patel, Dylan, and Gerald Wong. 2023. GPT-4 Architecture, Infrastructure, Training Dataset, Costs, Vision, MoE. SemiAnalysis Blog.

OpenAI, Josh Achiam, Steven Adler, Sandhini Agarwal, Lama Ahmad, Ilge Akkaya, Florencia Leoni Aleman, et al. 2023. “GPT-4 Technical Report.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2303.08774, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2303.08774.
On a single machine, performance is governed by the memory wall, the gap between processor speed and memory bandwidth. In a distributed cluster, a new limit emerges. Bisection bandwidth, the total bandwidth across the narrowest cut that divides the cluster into two halves, caps the throughput of any traffic that must cross that cut. Data no longer moves through local hierarchies alone; it traverses optical fabrics governed by the speed of light between racks and across continents. Hardware failures, rare enough on a single machine to be treated as exceptions, become routine statistical events at fleet scale. Long training runs must plan for interruptions rather than rely on every component remaining available until completion.
These are not operational annoyances. They are physical constraints, as fundamental and as permanent as the memory wall, Amdahl’s Law, or the energy cost of data movement. They require their own engineering discipline, built on the invariants this book develops:

The Empirical Scaling Law: Within empirically validated regimes, model loss falls as a power law in training compute, data, or parameters, so each further improvement demands multiplicatively more resources. This is the pressure that moves machine learning from single machines onto fleets.
The Bisection Bandwidth Theorem: For communication patterns that must cross the minimum bisection, throughput is bounded by that bisection bandwidth.
The Fleet Law: Under fixed-work scaling, reduced per-node computation competes with communication and coordination costs, so adding workers does not guarantee proportional speedup.
The Young-Daly Checkpoint Interval: The optimal checkpoint interval balances the cost of writing state against the expected cost of lost work due to failure.
Serving Cost Dominance: For high-traffic production models, cumulative inference operational expenditure can exceed the one-time training cost, making serving efficiency a lifecycle optimization target.
The Fairness Impossibility Theorem: With unequal group base rates and imperfect prediction, risk scores cannot satisfy groupwise calibration and equal mean scores across groups within both outcome classes simultaneously. Thresholded error-rate parity and demographic parity are distinct requirements with their own trade-offs.

If single-machine ML systems engineering asks “what can one machine build?”, then fleet-scale ML systems engineering asks “what can a thousand machines build together, and at what cost to reliability, efficiency, and society?” That final clause is what sets fleet-scale engineering apart. A single machine affects its user; a fleet affects everyone its outputs touch, across millions of decisions per second. At that scale, reliability, efficiency, and fairness stop being features and become engineering constraints as binding as bandwidth or power. A system that scales but cannot be trusted has not been engineered. It has only been enlarged.
This book develops that discipline. It follows the Hennessy and Patterson pedagogical model, extending the quantitative, principles-first approach to the distributed scale (Hennessy and Patterson 2011; Hennessy and Patterson 2019, 2017). Just as their work taught a generation to reason about processor performance from first principles, this book teaches the reader to reason about fleet performance, replacing intuition about distributed systems with measurement, and ad hoc scaling with engineering.

Hennessy, J. L., and D. A. Patterson. 2011. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. Morgan Kaufmann.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2019. “A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture.” Communications of the ACM 62 (2): 48–60. https://doi.org/10.1145/3282307.

Hennessy, John L., and David A. Patterson. 2017. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach. 6th ed. Morgan Kaufmann.
The architectural priorities and operational failure modes explored in these chapters did not originate in an academic vacuum. They were gathered directly from practitioners in industry, through technical exchanges at conferences, engineering meetups, and conversations with colleagues. These colleagues generously made the time to explain what breaks when scaling models across thousands of accelerators and what practicing systems engineers must understand.
Single-node foundations supply the bricks of those systems: tensors, kernels, memory hierarchies, and optimization loops. What breaks at fleet scale is rarely an individual brick, because a fleet is closer to an orchestra than to a larger wall. An orchestra is not simply many musicians playing at once. It needs a conductor, a score, precise synchronization, and the ability to recover when a player drops out, none of which governs a solo performer. A training cluster, a serving fleet, and an edge deployment are vastly different systems, but beneath them sit the same building blocks: parallelism strategies, collective communication primitives, checkpoint protocols, scheduling algorithms, and the trade-offs between throughput, latency, fault tolerance, and cost.

title: Preface
text:
This book focuses on the machine learning fleet: coordinated machines that jointly train, serve, or maintain ML models. Warehouse-scale training clusters are one form; geographically distributed serving replicas and heterogeneous edge devices are others. Across these forms, communication and coordination couple local execution to fleet behavior, while reliability, resource budgets, and governance constrain the design. The scope is the fleet as it exists today and the governance of operating it at scale. Research-frontier topics such as fully autonomous fleet management, next-generation interconnects, neuromorphic computing at scale, and formal verification of fleet-level safety properties lie beyond it.
The content is organized into four parts:

Part I: The Fleet builds the physical substrate of the AI data center from the ground up: the silicon and cooling of compute infrastructure, the network fabrics that connect thousands of accelerators, and the scalable data storage that feeds training pipelines.
Part II: Distributed ML establishes the logic of distribution beyond a single machine: the collective communication primitives that synchronize gradients, the parallelism strategies (data, tensor, and pipeline) for training models too large for single devices, the fault tolerance mechanisms that ensure reliability when failure is routine, and the orchestration systems that manage the fleet.
Part III: The Fleet in Production takes the trained model from the cluster to the world: fleet efficiency, which measures how much of a fleet’s capacity becomes useful work, serving at scale for millions of concurrent requests, edge intelligence across heterogeneous and federated devices, and the operational lifecycle required to manage production fleets.
Part IV: The Responsible Fleet confronts the forces that determine whether the fleet serves its users or harms them: security and privacy, robust system design, environmental sustainability, and responsible engineering as constraints as fundamental as power density or bisection bandwidth.

These four parts trace a path through the fleet stack, a layered abstraction that organizes an ML system at distributed scale, from the physical facility up to its governance. The stack has eight rows grouped into four bands, and each band is one part of the book. At the base, the Infrastructure band (Part I) holds Facility & Accelerators and Fabric & Storage, the physical substrate. On top of that hardware, the Distribution band (Part II) adds Distributed Execution and Reliability & Control to manage parallel work, communication, scheduling, and recovery. Once a model can be trained reliably, the Serving band (Part III) provides Runtime & Serving and Operations to take models to users and manage the production lifecycle. At the top, the Governance band (Part IV) layers Assurance (security, privacy, and robustness) and Governance & Sustainability to turn trust, risk, policy, and environmental cost into engineering constraints. Each row provides an abstraction to the row above and consumes the row below. Engineering decisions in the Infrastructure band constrain what is possible in the bands above it, while governance requirements constrain choices throughout the stack. Privacy, acceptable risk, and environmental budgets enter the design from the beginning; Part IV develops their enforcement mechanisms after the infrastructure and operational dependencies are available.
Where the fleet stack locates responsibility, a second framework diagnoses cost. The C³ taxonomy divides the wall-clock time of distributed execution into Compute, Communication, and Coordination, and the Fleet Law turns that division into an equation for distributed step time. Every chapter applies this lens to its own layer of the stack. Three recurring workloads, the archetypes, keep the analysis concrete: a large dense language model (Archetype A), a recommendation model with very large embedding tables (Archetype B), and a model trained by federated learning across phone-class devices (Archetype C). Each stresses a different part of the fleet, and the chapters return to whichever one exposes their central constraint.
Each part builds on the previous one, so sequential reading is recommended. The reading paths below offer alternatives for readers with specific goals.

title: Preface
text:
The chapters are ordered so that each can draw on everything before it, but not every chapter consumes the one immediately before it. A dependency map derived from the chapters’ own cross-references records which chapters build directly on which (figure 1). An arrow in the map means the later chapter uses a model, mechanism, or constraint that the earlier one establishes. Two features of the map guide the choice of path. First, every chapter lies on a route to Conclusion, whose six principles cite every chapter of Parts I through IV, so no chapter is a dead end. Second, several dependencies cross part boundaries: distributed training builds on both the storage pipeline of Data Storage and the collectives of Collective Communication, and fleet efficiency (Fleet Efficiency) builds on Fleet Orchestration. Consecutive chapters without an arrow mark a change of thread rather than a gap. Collective Communication, for example, builds on the fabric model of Network Fabrics rather than on the storage chapter that precedes it.






Figure 1: Chapter Dependency Map: Each arrow points from a chapter to a later chapter that builds on its results, derived from the book’s cross-references with transitive links omitted. Every chapter lies on the core path the conclusion builds on, so the map draws no optional branch. Book order is one valid reading order; a missing arrow between consecutive chapters means the later chapter does not directly consume the earlier one’s results.



Each path below begins with the introduction, assumes the single-machine prerequisites listed earlier in this preface, and keeps every chapter that its destination depends on in the map:

The Complete Path (all chapters, in sequence): Follows the causal chain of constraints that governs the ML fleet from first principles of distribution. After the introduction, progress through Parts I, II, III, and IV.
The Infrastructure Path (physical fleet and orchestration): Focuses on Part I (Compute Infrastructure, Network Fabrics, Data Storage), then Fleet Orchestration. Before orchestration, use the collective traffic patterns in Collective Communication, the workload partitioning in Distributed Training, and the checkpoint/recovery model in Fault Tolerance to establish what the scheduler must place, connect, and preserve.
The Scaling Path (distributed training depth): Establishes the memory-capacity, network-bandwidth, and storage-throughput models in Part I before focusing on Collective Communication, Distributed Training, Fault Tolerance, Fleet Orchestration, and Fleet Efficiency. Readers already comfortable estimating those limits can use Part I as a reference.
The Production Path (deployment and operations): Uses Part I for fleet capacity and network constraints. It then establishes collective communication in Collective Communication, model partitioning in Distributed Training, failure and recovery in Fault Tolerance, placement and isolation in Fleet Orchestration, and how much of the fleet’s capacity becomes useful work in Fleet Efficiency. Continue through Serving at Scale, Edge Intelligence, ML Operations at Scale, and Part IV (Security & Privacy, Robust AI, Sustainable AI, and Responsible AI).

title: Preface
text:
Across any of those reading paths, recurring visual cues in the margins orient the reader within the fleet stack. At every chapter opening, a margin figure highlights which rows of the stack the chapter addresses. The full stack below shows each row with its scope, grouped into the four parts of the book:

The Roman numerals (I–IV) mark those four parts, while the row intensity marks emphasis. The stack uses one accent color throughout so that shade, not hue, carries the chapter-focus signal.
In the margin figures throughout the book, the intensity of each row reflects how strongly the chapter engages it. Brighter (higher intensity) marks the chapter’s primary focus; dimmer (lower intensity) marks contextual relevance as constraints propagate upward. Consider three chapters that illustrate how the emphasis shifts:






Compute Infrastructure







Distributed Training







Responsible AI





In Compute Infrastructure, the bottom row dominates because the chapter is about silicon, power, cooling, and physical deployment. In Distributed Training, Distributed Execution is brightest while Reliability & Control remains visibly relevant because large training runs depend on scheduling and recovery. In Responsible AI, Governance & Sustainability is primary while Assurance stays strong because accountability depends on measurable trust and risk controls. The same stack tells three different stories, and in each one a decision made in one row ripples through the rows above and below it.
Small visual notes sit in the margins wherever a relationship is fastest to grasp by eye. They are reading aids, not figures to cite later. At fleet scale, this visual grammar makes bandwidth gaps, failure blast radius, checkpoint ratios, and edge-energy trade-offs visible without interrupting the argument. When a miniature uses a log scale, it says so inside the image.
















Alongside these visual miniatures, the margins carry unnumbered marginal navigation pointers that trace architectural dependencies across the fleet without interrupting the reading flow of the prose:

↩︎ Backward pointer: Directs the reader back to the earlier chapter where a physical limit, hardware contract, or analytical model was established.
↪ Forward pointer: Directs the reader ahead to the later chapter, or to the appendix, where the current idea is developed, measured, or enforced.
⇄ Contrast: Marks a place where two chapters treat the same problem differently, so the comparison is visible at a glance.

A pointer only orients. When a sentence depends on another chapter, the reference stays in the text.
The appendices are the last reading aid. Beyond the single-machine recap in The D·A·M Taxonomy, they collect the diagnostic tables, the communication, reliability, and serving models, and the reference numbers the chapters use.

title: Preface
text:
This book uses a small set of typographic conventions to mark what each piece of prose is doing.


A term in bold within body prose is its formal first introduction in the book. Each term receives this treatment exactly once. Subsequent appearances are unbolded; by then the term is part of the working vocabulary the chapter carries forward.

The Fleet Law decomposes the time of one distributed step into local computation, exposed communication, and synchronization.

The bold is a contract: register this term because it will recur. A matching index entry in the back of the book points to the defining occurrence (under the definition subentry), providing a way to return to it. Key technical terms are also compiled in the glossary.
Bold also appears in a second, structural role: as a functional label at the start of an item inside a callout box or a summary bullet, for example Recommendation, Trade-off, or Result. In that context, the bold is scaffolding rather than a first definition.



Italics are not used for general emphasis. Every italic span in this book performs one of five specific jobs:

Direct opposition: training vs. inference, allocated vs. productive accelerator time.
Impossibility, stated as physical, mathematical, or logical law: “a synchronous step cannot finish before its slowest worker does.”
Word used as word: “the term gradient refers to a vector of partial derivatives.”
Titles of works: Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach.
Thesis punchline: A single italicized sentence that captures the controlling insight of a section, for example, At scale, failure is the normal operating condition.

An italicized word is performing one of these jobs. A word that is not italicized carries no implicit emphasis.



Callout boxes are not decoration. Each type signals a specific kind of content, so the visual identity tells the reader what the box contains before they read it.








Callout
Contains




Definition
Formal definition of a key term, with its significance, distinction from the nearest neighbor concept, and a common pitfall


Example
Historical case or concrete scenario, structured as context, insight, and systems lesson


Systems Perspective
Analytical observation or mathematical nuance that enriches the surrounding argument


Napkin Math
Worked calculation walked through step by step, with values computed inline from the book’s constants; intermediate tables and equations are the math itself


Checkpoint
Self-check questions to verify understanding of the preceding section


War Story
Documented engineering incident with a sourced failure mode, structured as context, failure, consequence, and lesson


Lighthouse
Recurring workloads characterized by a profile (parameters, FLOPs, dominant constraint), used as anchored case studies across multiple chapters


Principle
Canonical book principle or invariant referenced from later chapters


Theorem
Formal, equation-backed result or bound, stated with its conditions and applied in later quantitative analysis


Key Takeaways
Four to seven most important results from a chapter, in summary form


Learning Objectives
Skills and concepts that readers should be able to explain or apply after completing the chapter


What’s Next
Bridge from the chapter just ended to the chapter beginning, naming the open question the next chapter addresses




When a callout contains a table, figure, or equation, that artifact is part of the callout’s pedagogical unit, not decoration. A lighthouse’s profile is its characterization. A napkin math box’s intermediate tables are the worked math. Reading these as separated artifacts loses the teaching arc. Standalone reference tables, by contrast, sit between paragraphs as numbered artifacts the reader returns to through cross-references. Both forms are valid; the visual marker (callout vs. standalone) tells the reader which one they are looking at.

title: Scaling Machine Learning Systems
text:
At scale, machine learning changes its engineering requirements: models grow too large for a single accelerator, services span continents, and deployments carry responsibilities to society. At this scale, the costs of distribution limit AI capability as much as the model does, and every system in this book is engineered under both the physical limits of distributed infrastructure and the statistical behavior of learning. This book addresses AI engineering at scale. The treatment follows the lifecycle of a large-scale system: defining the distributed architecture, building the physical infrastructure fleet, ensuring operational reliability, deploying to global users, and hardening the system for safety and responsibility.
  

  
    
    Scaling Machine Learning Systems
    Publisher: The MIT Press (2027)
  


What You Will Learn

The four parts extend ML systems foundations into production-scale systems by following the fleet stack from bottom to top:

  Part I: The Fleet. The data-center infrastructure, high-bandwidth network fabrics, and scalable storage that every distributed ML deployment runs on.
  Part II: Distributed ML. How computation is coordinated across thousands of devices, through collective communication primitives, parallelism strategies, fault tolerance mechanisms, and fleet orchestration.
  Part III: The Fleet in Production. How much of the fleet's capacity becomes useful work, the shift from training to serving, ML at the edge, and the operational lifecycle of production fleets.
  Part IV: The Responsible Fleet. Security, robustness, environmental sustainability, and responsible engineering in large-scale operations.


Prerequisites

This book assumes:

  Foundational or equivalent background in single-machine ML systems
  Programming proficiency in Python with familiarity in NumPy
  Mathematics foundations in linear algebra, calculus, and probability
  Familiarity with distributed systems concepts (networking, parallelism) is helpful for advanced topics


Learn by Doing

Within the broader AI engineering curriculum, this volume is the scale and governance spine. Pair the chapters with Labs for fleet-scale trade-off exercises, MLSys·im for first-principles infrastructure modeling, and StaffML for systems design practice. Instructors can adopt the full scale sequence through Instructor Hub.

title: Author’s Note
text:
Author’s Note

When a new model is announced, the world looks at the model. It almost never looks at the fleet.
Behind many frontier models, however, stand thousands of accelerators held in lockstep across a network where one slow link can stall the whole run, cooled by systems that move megawatts of heat, kept alive by protocols that treat failure not as an exception but as a scheduled event. None of this fits in the announcement. The model gets the paper. The fleet gets a footnote, if that.
This book is an argument that the fleet deserves more than a footnote. We have built vast distributed systems before, but none quite like this one, because none of the others had to be right about two things at once. The telephone network had to stay available; it never had to converge. The internet had to deliver the packet; it never had to preserve the gradient inside it. A fleet has to do both. It must move data the way any distributed system does, and it must keep the mathematics of learning intact while it moves. A node that drops out does not only cost capacity; it can break the synchronization a training step depends on and force a rollback that wastes work since the most recent checkpoint. That double obligation, computational and statistical, sustained at the scale of a small campus, is the engineering this book makes visible.
The obligation does not end when training does. A model that cannot be trained is an idea, not a system. A model that cannot be served is a research result, not a product. A model that cannot be governed is a liability, not an asset. At every stage, from the first allocated node to the last served request, the fleet decides what is possible and what remains imagined.
The problem under every chapter is easy to state and hard to solve: what it takes to build not one machine learning system but a thousand, make them work as one, and run them responsibly. I believe that is a defining engineering problem of this generation, and that the people who take it on, the ones who rarely get the headline, deserve a book that treats it as one.
— Vijay Janapa Reddi
Cambridge, Massachusetts
2026

title: Acknowledgments
text:
Earlier teaching on TinyML grew out of the realization that the constraints governing milliwatt devices are the same constraints governing data-center accelerators. This book grew out of a different realization, one that came from working on ML Fleet Efficiency as a visiting researcher at Google. Peter Mattson, who had been a collaborator on MLPerf, made that opportunity possible. What I encountered there changed how I think about ML systems: the engineering required to coordinate thousands of accelerators into a single coherent system is a discipline unto itself, and that discipline had no textbook.
That work introduced me to the ML Productivity Goodput (MPG) metric, fleet-level heterogeneity at a scale I had not seen before, and the daily reality of failure as a statistical certainty rather than an exception. The gap between what practitioners knew and what was written down was enormous. The researchers who built these systems published individual results, but the connective tissue between those results, the principles that made them cohere into a discipline, existed only in the heads of the people doing the work. This book is an attempt to document that connective tissue.



I learned most of what I know about fleet-scale systems from the ML Fleet Efficiency team at Google: Arissa Wongpanich, Tayo Oguntebi, Jose Baiocchi Paredes, Yu Emma Wang, Phitchaya Mangpo Phothilimthana, Ritwika Mitra, and Zongwei Zhou. Naveen Kumar led that effort, and the way he thought about fleet-level optimization shaped how I think about it still. Robert Hundt pushed my understanding of performance engineering at scale. Together, Naveen and Robert showed me what fleet-level efficiency looks like from the inside. David Kanter continued the MLPerf collaboration, and our discussions on benchmarking distributed systems sharpened the quantitative methodology that runs through every chapter. Greg Diamos provided invaluable perspective on scaling laws and their origins at Baidu, where some of the earliest work on large-scale distributed training took shape.
The researchers whose papers fill the bibliography of this book deserve particular acknowledgment. The principles taught here were not invented for this textbook; the practitioners and researchers who built the systems, measured the failures, and published what they learned discovered them. This book synthesizes their work into a coherent narrative. The debt is to them.



The Harvard Data Science Initiative, Harvard Extension School, and the National Science Foundation supported this work. The Edge AI Foundation and ICTP supported educational outreach and scholarships, while our industry partners provided the infrastructure and tooling that enabled practical experimentation.
At MIT Press, Susan Hartman believed in this project from the beginning and guided it from an open-source experiment to a published textbook. Her editorial judgment and support made this book real. I am equally grateful to MIT Press for agreeing to keep this book available as open access. A textbook about a discipline shaped by the open-source community should be accessible to everyone in it.
An open-source community shaped this book in ways that no single author could. Dozens of contributors caught errors, improved explanations, filed issues, and submitted pull requests. The book improved because people who owed it nothing chose to make it better. I am grateful to every one of them.
For the complete and most up-to-date list of all contributors, please visit the GitHub contributors page. For those interested in contributing, please consult our contribution guidelines.
Every GitHub star is a signal that someone cares about this material, is learning from it, and believes the work matters. The online community of learners, with their questions, their curiosity, and their willingness to engage with an unfinished textbook, kept this project moving when the scope felt overwhelming.
Finally, I thank my wife and my children. I wrote this book in the hours that belonged to them: weekends that disappeared into revisions, evenings that stretched past midnight, mornings when I was present but not quite there. They never complained. They asked how the writing was going, brought me coffee, and gave me the space to finish. Whatever merit this book has, their patience and their support made it possible.

Greg Diamos provided invaluable perspective on scaling laws and their origins at Baidu, where some of the earliest work on large-scale distributed training took shape.
The researchers whose papers fill the bibliography of this book deserve particular acknowledgment. The principles taught here were not invented for this textbook; the practitioners and researchers who built the systems, measured the failures, and published what they learned discovered them. This book synthesizes their work into a coherent narrative. The debt is to them.

text:

I am equally grateful to MIT Press for agreeing to keep this book available as open access. A textbook about a discipline shaped by the open-source community should be accessible to everyone in it.
An open-source community shaped this book in ways that no single author could. Dozens of contributors caught errors, improved explanations, filed issues, and submitted pull requests. The book improved because people who owed it nothing chose to make it better. I am grateful to every one of them.
For the complete and most up-to-date list of all contributors, please visit the GitHub contributors page. For those interested in contributing, please consult our contribution guidelines.

The online community of learners, with their questions, their curiosity, and their willingness to engage with an unfinished textbook, kept this project moving when the scope felt overwhelming.
Finally, I thank my wife and my children. I wrote this book in the hours that belonged to them: weekends that disappeared into revisions, evenings that stretched past midnight, mornings when I was present but not quite there. They never complained. They asked how the writing was going, brought me coffee, and gave me the space to finish. Whatever merit this book has, their patience and their support made it possible.

title: Notation
text:
To a machine learning researcher, \(\Glyph{B}\) denotes batch size, while to a network engineer, \(\Glyph{B}\) denotes bandwidth. In distributed systems, \(\Glyph{N}\) represents the count of worker accelerators, whereas in statistics, \(\Glyph{N}\) denotes sample count. In high-performance computing, \(\Glyph{P}\) is commonly used for processor count, but in deep learning, \(\Glyph{P}\) is reserved for model parameter count. Similarly, in this book’s communication models, \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) denotes per-message network latency and \(\Glyph{\beta}\) denotes link bandwidth, whereas in statistical learning, \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) represents a power-law scaling exponent and \(\Glyph{\beta}\) represents optimizer momentum.
These collisions arise because machine learning at scale combines three fields that developed their mathematical conventions independently: machine learning, distributed systems, and high-performance data center networking. Training and serving modern foundation models requires orchestrating workloads across thousands of accelerators connected by high-speed networks, which places symbols from all three fields into the same equation.
This book establishes a unified mathematical notation for distributed machine learning systems. The conventions defined below eliminate ambiguity across scaling laws, collective communication algorithms, parallel execution schedules, and cluster reliability models.


A distributed training step or serving request spends time both inside each accelerator and across the network that connects them, so performance modeling follows a two-tier hierarchy: the single-device execution foundation and its fleet-wide composition. The subsections that follow state each governing equation and define the symbols that appear in its terms.


Every distributed training step or inference pass builds on local execution on individual accelerators. For serialized execution phases on a single accelerator, the iron law of ML systems decomposes execution time into memory access, arithmetic computation, and latency overhead:
\[\Time = \underbrace{\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth}}_{\text{Memory Time}} + \underbrace{\frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}}_{\text{Compute Time}} + \underbrace{\Latency}_{\text{Latency Overhead}}\]
Each symbol was chosen deliberately to preserve machine learning conventions while maintaining architectural precision. The table below records the definition, physical unit, and collision-avoidance rationale for each term:










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\Time\)
Execution Time
seconds
Total serialized execution time in the iron-law performance decomposition.


\(\Bandwidth\)
Bandwidth
bytes/s
Avoids collision with \(\BatchSize\) (Batch Size). Systems literature often uses \(\Glyph{B}\) for bandwidth, while ML literature often uses \(\Glyph{B}\) for batch size. The notation preserves the ML convention.


\(\DataVolume\)
Data Volume
bytes
Avoids collision with \(\DatasetSize\) (Dataset Size). In scaling laws, \(\Glyph{D}\) means training tokens. Here we need bytes moved through memory. The subscript disambiguates.


\(\EfficiencyHw\)
Efficiency
—
Hardware utilization \((0 \le \EfficiencyHw \le 1)\). Avoids collision with learning rate \((\LearningRate)\).


\(\Latency\)
Latency
seconds
Avoids collision with \(\Glyph{L}\) (Loss). Fixed overhead time (kernel launch, network RTT). The subscript distinguishes from the loss function.


\(\Operations\)
Operations
FLOPs
Total floating-point operations. Clean in equations (vs. “\(\text{Ops}\)”).


\(\PeakRate\)
Peak Rate
FLOP/s
Avoids collision with \(\Parameters\) (Parameters). Roofline presentations often use \(\Glyph{P}\) for performance, while ML literature commonly uses \(\Glyph{P}\) for parameter count. The notation preserves the ML convention.


\(\AsymptoticTightBound\)
Asymptotic Tight Bound
Operator
Asymptotic tight bound: grows at the same rate as its argument, up to constant factors.


\(\BatchDataVolume\)
Batch Data Volume
bytes
Bytes of input data one batch carries to the accelerator.


\(\ClockFrequency\)
Clock Frequency
hertz
Rate at which a processor’s clock ticks, setting how many switching cycles occur per second.


\(\FiniteChange\)
Finite Change
Operator
Finite change in the quantity it prefixes, between two states, configurations or points in time.


\(\MicroUnitPrefix\)
Micro Unit Prefix
Operator
SI unit prefix micro, one millionth, written before a unit such as seconds.


\(\NumericBitWidth\)
Numeric Bit Width
Integer
Number of bits used to represent one numeric value, such as an arithmetic operand or a quantized weight or activation.


\(\PipelinedExecutionTime\)
Pipelined Execution Time
seconds
Execution time of a workload whose data movement and computation overlap, set by the slower of the two plus fixed latency.


\(\SequentialExecutionTime\)
Sequential Execution Time
seconds
Execution time when data movement, computation and fixed overhead run one after another with no overlap, the sum of the iron-law terms.


\(\StepIoTime\)
Step I/O Time
seconds
Time the input pipeline needs to read, decompress, decode and stage the data for one training step.


\(\StorageBandwidth\)
Storage Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which the storage system delivers bytes to the input pipeline.


\(\TrainingStepTime\)
Training Step Time
seconds
Wall-clock time of one training step, bounded below by the slower of compute and input I/O.


\(\UnitAliasMultiplier\)
Unit Alias Multiplier
Dimensionless
Number of base units in one unit alias, the conversion multiplier of a unit-conventions table row.






Without careful notation, statements about distributed systems become ambiguous. Consider a typical unsubscripted claim:

“Reducing \(\Glyph{D}\) improves performance.”

In distributed machine learning, this could mean reducing the dataset size (fewer training samples), shrinking the data-parallel degree \(\DataParallelDegree\), or reducing the data volume \(\DataVolume\) moved across the memory bus through quantization. With our notation, we distinguish them precisely:

“Reducing \(\DataVolume\) through FP8 quantization cuts memory traffic across the interconnect while \(\DatasetSize\) (training tokens) and \(\DataParallelDegree\) remain unchanged.”




The root symbol names the fundamental physical quantity, while an upright subscript specifies the precise domain or measurement point. Three recurring families illustrate this convention across this book:

\(\Glyph{\text{BW}_{\text{memory}}}\), \(\NetworkBandwidth\), \(\Glyph{\text{BW}_{\text{interconnect}}}\): bandwidth across distinct tiers of the distributed memory and fabric hierarchy.
\(\DataVolume\), \(\PeakRate\), \(\Latency\), \(\EfficiencyHw\): single-node iron-law terms, held clear of shared ML symbols.
\(\EnergyPerByteMoved\), \(\EnergyPerOperation\), \(\TotalEnergy\): energy budget components across distributed compute nodes.

The subscript therefore carries part of the claim. Memory and network bandwidth differ by orders of magnitude, so a figure is reproducible only when the subscript says where it was measured.




When scaling a model across a fleet of \(\DeviceCount= \AcceleratorCount\) accelerators, single-device compute time is distributed across workers, while communication and synchronization overheads are introduced. Under partitioned execution of fixed work, the governing equation is the Fleet Law (the distributed step-time model, equation 1.3):
\[\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\DeviceCount, \AcceleratorCount\)
Number of Devices
Integer
Accelerator count in a distributed job, the core’s \(\AcceleratorCount\) (\(\DeviceCount= \AcceleratorCount\)); also the rank count of a collective. (Not parameters, use \(\Parameters\).)


\(\AcceleratorsPerNode\), \(\ClusterNodeCount\)
Accelerators per Node, Node Count
Integer
Hierarchical collectives split the fleet as \(\DeviceCount= \AcceleratorsPerNode \ClusterNodeCount\). (Bare \(\Glyph{G}\) is the LogGP gap per byte.)


\(\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)\)
Distributed Step Time
seconds
Wall-clock time for one training step at scale \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\IronLawComputeTime\)
Single-Device Compute Time
seconds
The core’s compute term for one training step (forward + backward pass) on one device.


\(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\)
Communication Time
seconds
Time for collective operations (AllReduce, AllGather); depends on payload, topology, and \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\OverlappedTime\)
Overlapped Time
seconds
Communication hidden behind computation. Reduces effective overhead.


\(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\)
Synchronization Time
seconds
Total nonoverlapped synchronization or coordination cost per step at scale \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\CommunicationComputeRatio\)
Communication-Computation Ratio
Dimensionless
\(\CommunicationComputeRatio= \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)/(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount)\). Values near or above 1 indicate communication-bound scaling.


\(\CommunicationIntensity\)
Communication Intensity
bytes/FLOP
Network bytes moved per local FLOP, \(\CommunicationIntensity = \CollectivePayloadSize/\Operations\); the fleet analogue of arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\).


\(\FleetCommunicationTaxonomyAxis\)
Communication Axis
Set
Communication axis of the C\(^3\) taxonomy, data movement across the network fabric, viewed as the set of techniques it covers so that axis intersections name zones of the taxonomy.


\(\FleetComputeTaxonomyAxis\)
Compute Axis
Set
Compute axis of the C\(^3\) taxonomy, local arithmetic and memory within a node, viewed as the set of techniques it covers so that axis intersections name zones of the taxonomy.


\(\FleetCoordinationTaxonomyAxis\)
Coordination Axis
Set
Coordination axis of the C\(^3\) taxonomy, synchronization, failure recovery and scheduling across the fleet, viewed as the set of techniques it covers so that axis intersections name zones of the taxonomy.


\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension\)
Operational Dimension
Record
One of the three operational dimensions of the C\(^3\) taxonomy, indexed 1 to 3 as compute, communication and coordination.







Scaling laws anchor the book’s account of why machine learning moved onto fleets. The single-resource power law and the dense-transformer compute rule are:
\[\LossFunction(\ScaledResource) = \ScaleCoefficient \ScaledResource^{-\ScalingExponent} + \IrreducibleLoss, \qquad \TrainingCompute \approx 6\Parameters \DatasetSize\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\ScaledResource\)
Scaled Resource
varies
Training compute, parameter count \(\Parameters\), or training tokens \(\DatasetSize\), depending on the fitted law.


\(\ScalingExponent\)
Scaling Exponent
Dimensionless
Fitted power-law exponent; valid only within the regime in which it was measured. (Not network latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\).)


\(\ScaleCoefficient\)
Scale Coefficient
loss units
Task-dependent fitted constant.


\(\IrreducibleLoss\)
Irreducible Loss
loss units
Loss floor that added resources do not remove within the fitted regime.


\(\TrainingCompute\)
Training Compute
FLOPs
About \(6\Parameters \DatasetSize\) for a dense transformer: \(2\Parameters\) per token forward and \(4\Parameters\) backward.


\(\BaseBatchSize\)
Base Batch Size
Integer
Reference batch size at which the base learning rate was tuned.


\(\BaseLearningRate\)
Base Learning Rate
Dimensionless
Learning rate tuned at the reference batch size before linear scaling.


\(\EpochCount\)
Epoch Count
Integer
Number of full passes a training run makes over its dataset.


\(\ScaledBatchSize\)
Scaled Batch Size
Integer
Batch size a training recipe is scaled to under the linear scaling rule.


\(\ScaledLearningRate\)
Scaled Learning Rate
Dimensionless
Learning rate used at a new batch size under the linear scaling rule.


\(\ScalingLawLoss\)
Scaling Law Loss
Function
Loss a trained model reaches as a function of the resource scaled, such as parameters, training tokens or compute, in an empirical power-law scaling law.







At data center scale, energy and power delivery are primary system constraints. For \(\DeviceCount\) devices that each move the same \(\DataVolume\) bytes and execute the same \(\Operations\) FLOPs over a workload interval, effective per-byte data-movement costs and per-operation compute costs give the following fleet energy model. Here the work and traffic terms are per-device quantities, so multiplying by \(\DeviceCount\) sums the device contributions:
\[\TotalEnergy \approx \DeviceCount\times \left( \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved + \Operations \times \EnergyPerOperation \right)\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\EnergyPerByteMoved\)
Energy per Byte Moved
joules/byte
Effective movement cost; total energy also depends on bytes moved and operations executed.


\(\EnergyPerOperation\)
Energy per Operation
joules/FLOP
Energy cost of a single arithmetic operation.


\(\TotalEnergy\)
Total Energy
joules
Total energy consumed by an ML workload, decomposed into data-movement and compute terms.


\(\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent\)
Accelerator Supply Current
amperes
Electrical current an accelerator draws from its power supply.


\(\ActiveInferencePower\)
Active Inference Power
watts
Average power an accelerator draws while actively running inference.


\(\AveragePower\)
Average Power
watts
Power drawn averaged over a stated period.


\(\CloudOffloadEnergy\)
Cloud Offload Energy
joules
Energy a device spends transmitting an input to the cloud for remote inference.


\(\CoolantHeatLoad\)
Coolant Heat Load
watts
Heat per unit time that a liquid cooling loop must carry away from a rack, the load that sets its coolant mass flow.


\(\CoolantMassFlowRate\)
Coolant Mass Flow Rate
kg/s
Mass of coolant, liquid or air, passing through a cooling loop per second.


\(\CoolantTemperature\)
Coolant Temperature
kelvin
Temperature of the liquid or air coolant in a cooling loop, whose finite change is its rise from inlet to outlet.


\(\DevicePower\)
Device Power
watts
Electrical power one device draws.


\(\DynamicPower\)
Dynamic Power
watts
Power a chip draws switching its transistors, proportional to switched capacitance, supply voltage squared and clock frequency.


\(\ElectricalResistance\)
Electrical Resistance
ohms
Electrical resistance of a circuit or winding.


\(\FacilityHeatRemovalCapacity\)
Facility Heat Removal Capacity
watts
Largest rate at which an installed facility and cooling configuration can remove heat.


\(\FacilityPower\)
Facility Power
watts
Total electrical power a data center facility draws from the grid, its IT load plus cooling, power conversion, lighting and other overhead.


\(\GeneralPurposeEnergyProductivity\)
General-Purpose Energy Productivity
FLOP/J
Useful floating-point operations general-purpose silicon delivers per joule on a given workload.


\(\InferenceDutyCycle\)
Inference Duty Cycle
Dimensionless
Fraction of time an accelerator actively runs inference rather than waiting in standby.


\(\InformationTechnologyHeatLoad\)
IT Heat Load
watts
Rate at which a facility’s information technology equipment (servers, accelerators, network gear) produces heat.


\(\InformationTechnologyPower\)
IT Power
watts
Electrical power delivered to a data center’s IT equipment: servers, accelerators, storage and networking.


\(\LeakageCurrent\)
Leakage Current
amperes
Current that leaks through a chip’s transistors when they are not switching.


\(\LeakagePower\)
Leakage Power
watts
Static power a chip dissipates through leakage current regardless of switching.


\(\LocalInferenceEnergy\)
Local Inference Energy
joules
Energy a device spends running one inference on its own hardware.


\(\NetworkEnergy\)
Network Energy
joules
Energy the network fabric, its switches, links and adapters, consumes over a stated interval.


\(\ParasiticLoopInductance\)
Parasitic Loop Inductance
henries
Unintended inductance of the current loop that feeds an accelerator’s core rail, which turns current slew into voltage droop.


\(\SpecializedEnergyProductivity\)
Specialized Energy Productivity
FLOP/J
Useful floating-point operations specialized, domain-specific silicon delivers per joule on a workload suited to its design.


\(\SpecificHeatCapacity\)
Specific Heat Capacity
J/(kg K)
Heat needed to raise one kilogram of a coolant by one kelvin at constant pressure.


\(\StandbyPower\)
Standby Power
watts
Power a device draws in standby, when it is not running inference.


\(\SupplyVoltage\)
Supply Voltage
volts
Supply voltage that powers a digital circuit, the quantity dynamic voltage and frequency scaling lowers.


\(\SwitchedCapacitance\)
Switched Capacitance
farads
Capacitance of the wires and gates a circuit charges when it switches.


\(\SwitchingActivityFactor\)
Switching Activity Factor
Dimensionless
Average fraction of a chip’s gate capacitance that switches each clock cycle.


\(\TotalChipPower\)
Total Chip Power
watts
Total power a chip dissipates, the sum of dynamic switching power and static leakage power.








Collective communications (AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, AllToAll) move payloads across the network fabric, following ring or tree schedules over topologies such as the fat tree. The models below price those transfers by separating fixed per-message latency from bandwidth-proportional transmission time.


In the standard first-order model, network communication time decomposes into fixed message startup latency and bandwidth-dependent transfer. For a single point-to-point message, transfer time is the sum of those two terms:
\[\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\PointToPointMessageSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\]
The model keeps its literature’s letters as aliases of core concepts: \(\MessageStartupLatency\) is the per-message \(\Latency\) and \(\LinkBandwidth\) is a link’s \(\Bandwidth\), written in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form. Inside \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) formulas, write \(\Glyph{\alpha}\) and \(\Glyph{\beta}\); elsewhere, write \(\Latency\) and a subscripted \(\Bandwidth\).










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\)
Point-to-Point Transfer Time
seconds
Wall-clock time to transmit one message of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) across one link.


\(\PointToPointMessageSize\)
Point-to-Point Message Size
bytes
Size of one message in \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\).


\(\MessageStartupLatency\)
Per-Message Latency
seconds
The core’s \(\Latency\) for one message, in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form: the fixed startup cost. (Not significance level or Rényi order, which carry subscripts.)


\(\LinkBandwidth\)
Link Bandwidth
bytes/s
The core’s \(\Bandwidth\) for one link (\(\SingleLinkBandwidth\)), in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form: effective throughput per link.


\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\)
Crossover Point
bytes
\(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize= \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\). Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\): latency-bound. Above: bandwidth-bound.


\(\CollectivePayloadSize\)
Collective Payload Size
bytes
Per-rank gradient, model-state, activation, or compressed payload that a collective moves. Not a memory footprint (those are \(\TotalMemoryFootprint\), \(\WeightMemory\), and so on) and not the core’s GEMM dimension \(\GemmRowDimension\), which appears only in GEMM shape statements.


\(\CollectiveTensorSize\)
Collective Tensor Size
bytes
Full tensor acted on by Broadcast, Reduce, or AllReduce, reconstructed by AllGather, or partitioned by ReduceScatter. An equally sharded AllGather starts with \(\CollectiveTensorSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes per rank; AllToAll uses the per-rank payload \(\CollectivePayloadSize\).


\(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime\), \(\TreeAllReduceCompletionTime\)
Collective Completion Time
seconds
AllReduce time under the ring or tree algorithm in \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) form, for example \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = 2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency+ 2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\). \(\AllReduceCompletionTime\) names an AllReduce whose algorithm the text leaves open.


\(\RingTreeCrossoverPayload\)
Ring-Tree Crossover Payload
bytes
Payload at which \(\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = \TreeAllReduceCompletionTime\); approximately \(\DeviceCount\MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth/\log_2 \DeviceCount\) for large \(\DeviceCount\).


\(\AllReduceCompletionTime\)
AllReduce Completion Time
seconds
Time to complete one AllReduce collective over a group of devices, whatever algorithm implements it.


\(\AllToAllCompletionTime\)
AllToAll Completion Time
seconds
Time to complete one AllToAll collective, in which every device exchanges a distinct share of its payload with every other device.


\(\BisectionBandwidth\)
Bisection Bandwidth
bytes/s
Total bandwidth across the narrowest cut that divides a network’s nodes into two equal halves.


\(\LocalRankIndex\)
Local Rank Index
Integer
Position of an accelerator within its node, its local rank, which in a rail-optimized fabric also names the rail it attaches to.


\(\NetworkBandwidth\)
Network Bandwidth
bytes/s
Sustained rate at which a network path delivers bytes between machines.


\(\NetworkTrafficVolume\)
Network Traffic Volume
bytes
Bytes one worker moves across the network over a stated interval, such as one training step.


\(\RankCountBinaryExponent\)
Rank Count Binary Exponent
Dimensionless
Integer exponent for which the rank count equals two raised to it, the condition algorithms such as butterfly AllReduce require.


\(\RankIndex\)
Rank Index
Integer
Position of one rank, a device or worker, within a collective communication group, counted from zero.


\(\SingleLinkBandwidth\)
Single Link Bandwidth
bytes/s
Bandwidth of one network link in one direction, written in the core bandwidth notation outside alpha-beta formulas.


\(\SwitchRadix\)
Switch Radix
Integer
Number of ports on one network switch, its radix.


\(\TopologyEndpointCount\)
Topology Endpoint Count
Integer
Number of endpoints, accelerators or hosts, that one network topology connects, the size variable of its scaling relations.







LogGP refines the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model by separating network transit latency, processor initiation overhead, and long-message injection gaps. The book uses descriptive subscripts for the highest-collision terms; the bare letters \(\Glyph{g}\) and \(\Glyph{G}\) keep their LogGP meanings inside this model only.










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\LoggpLongMessageTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)\)
LogGP Long-Message Time
seconds
Transfer time for an \(\PointToPointMessageSize\)-byte long message. Reuses \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) from the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model.


\(\LogpNetworkLatency\)
LogP/LogGP Network Latency
seconds
Network transit time of one message, the part of the core’s \(\Latency\) that excludes processor overhead, so \(\MessageStartupLatency\approx \SenderOverhead + \LogpNetworkLatency + \ReceiverOverhead\). The subscript avoids bare \(\Glyph{L}\) collisions.


\(\SenderOverhead\)
Sender Overhead
seconds
Processor/NIC overhead to initiate a message.


\(\ReceiverOverhead\)
Receiver Overhead
seconds
Processor/NIC overhead to complete a message. Symmetric LogP writes \(\SymmetricMessageOverhead= \SenderOverhead = \ReceiverOverhead\), so one message costs \(2\SymmetricMessageOverhead\).


\(\MessageInjectionGap\)
Message Injection Gap
seconds
Minimum interval between consecutive message injections. (Gradients are bold, \(\Glyph{\mathbf{g}}\).)


\(\LongMessageGapPerByte\)
Long-Message Gap per Byte
seconds/byte
Per-byte long-message gap; distinct from \(\LinkBandwidth\) link bandwidth. (Accelerators per node are \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\).)


\(\SymmetricMessageOverhead\)
Symmetric Message Overhead
seconds
Processor time spent initiating or completing one message in the symmetric LogP model, where sender and receiver overheads are equal, during which the processor cannot compute.







Gradient and activation compression trade local computation for reduced network traffic. The resulting models compare codec overhead against the communication time saved by shrinking the payload:










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\TransferTimeForPayload\)
Transfer Time for Payload
seconds
Communication time for an \(\Glyph{x}\)-byte payload: \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\Glyph{x})\) for one link, or the relevant collective time.


\(\CompressedCommunicationTime\)
Compressed Communication Time
seconds
Total time after encode, transfer of \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\CompressionRatio\), and decode.


\(\CodecEncodeTime\)
Codec Encode Time
seconds
Local compression overhead before transfer.


\(\CodecDecodeTime\)
Codec Decode Time
seconds
Local decompression overhead after transfer.


\(\QuantizationBlockSize\)
Quantization Block Size
Integer
Number of tensor elements in one block of block-wise quantization, all sharing one scale.


\(\QuantizationScale\)
Quantization Scale
Varies
Real-valued step between adjacent integer levels of a uniform quantizer.


\(\RetainedGradientElementCount\)
Retained Gradient Element Count
Integer
Number of largest-magnitude gradient elements top-k sparsification keeps and transmits.








Scaling large foundation models requires combining multiple parallelism strategies across device dimensions. The notation below tracks how devices are partitioned across those dimensions and how efficiently the combined schedule converts added hardware into speedup.


A single parallelism strategy rarely scales across an entire cluster without hitting memory or bandwidth limits. To stay within both bounds, 3D parallelism partitions the training workload across three orthogonal dimensions:
\[\DeviceCount= \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree\]










Symbol
Definition
Unit
Notes




\(\DataParallelDegree\)
Data-Parallel Degree
Integer
Number of model replicas. (Bare \(\Glyph{d}\) stays the core’s hidden dimension.)


\(\PipelineParallelDegree\)
Pipeline-Parallel Degree
Integer
Number of physical pipeline stages in model-depth partitioning.


\(\TensorParallelDegree\)
Tensor-Parallel Degree
Integer
Degree of intra-layer partitioning (model width). (Bare \(\Glyph{t}\) stays time or a step index.)


\(\MicrobatchCount\)
Microbatch Count
Integer
Number of microbatches used to fill and drain the pipeline.


\(\PipelineBubbleFraction\)
Pipeline Bubble Fraction
Dimensionless
Fraction of pipeline GPU-time spent idle, \(\PipelineBubbleFraction = (\PipelineParallelDegree-1)/(\PipelineParallelDegree-1+\MicrobatchCount)\); avoids bare \(\Glyph{b}\).


\(\VirtualPipelineStagesPerDevice\)
Virtual Pipeline Stages per Device
Integer
Number of interleaved virtual chunks assigned to each physical pipeline stage. (The attention value matrix is bold, \(\AttentionValuesMatrix\).)


\(\GradientStaleness\)
Gradient Staleness
steps
Number of parameter updates between the parameters a gradient was computed on and the parameters it updates; \(\GradientStaleness = 0\) is synchronous training.


\(\AccumulationStepCount\)
Accumulation Step Count
Integer
Number of micro-batches whose gradients are accumulated before one optimizer update.


\(\ClientIndex\)
Client Index
Integer
Position of one client among the clients of a federated round or secure aggregation.


\(\ExpertCapacityFactor\)
Expert Capacity Factor
Dimensionless
Multiplier on an expert’s uniform share of token assignments that sets how many assignments it may accept per step.


\(\ExpertCount\)
Expert Count
Integer
Number of expert subnetworks in one mixture-of-experts layer.


\(\FederatedRoundCount\)
Federated Round Count
Integer
Number of communication rounds a federated training run performs, or needs to reach a quality target.


\(\GlobalBatchSize\)
Global Batch Size
Integer
Number of examples one synchronous optimizer update averages over across all data-parallel workers.


\(\LocalGradient\)
Local Gradient
Vector
Gradient vector one data-parallel worker computes from its local batch in one step, its contribution to the gradient collective.


\(\MicrobatchSize\)
Microbatch Size
Integer
Number of examples in one micro-batch, the unit run through a single forward and backward pass.


\(\ParticipatingClientCount\)
Participating Client Count
Integer
Number of clients whose updates one federated round aggregates.


\(\RoutedExpertCount\)
Routed Expert Count
Integer
Number of experts a mixture-of-experts router sends each token to.


\(\RouterGateProbability\)
Router Gate Probability
Dimensionless
Probability a mixture-of-experts router assigns to the expert it selects for a token.

At cluster scale, hardware component failures are standard operating conditions rather than rare anomalies. The symbols in this section quantify failure rates, checkpoint intervals, recovery overheads, and their net effect on fleet goodput.


When a job requires many components to remain healthy simultaneously, individual failure hazards compound across the fleet. Assuming independent components with exponential failure distributions, system reliability across \(\RequiredComponentCount\) components is:
\[\SystemReliability(\TimeInstant) = e^{-\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant}\]
The aggregate exponent uses the system-level rate \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate\), where \(\ComponentFailureRate\) is the per-component failure rate under the independent, identical-component assumption. The exponent \(\RequiredComponentCount\ComponentFailureRate \TimeInstant\) is dimensionless, so the elapsed time \(\TimeInstant\) must use the same time unit as \(\ComponentFailureRate\) (hours, when \(\ComponentFailureRate\) comes from the FIT-derived rates below).
Checkpointing too frequently wastes wall time writing state to storage, whereas checkpointing too rarely loses long stretches of training work when a node fails. The optimal checkpoint interval balances that I/O overhead against recomputation rework:
\[\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\]
The formula uses the system-wide mean time between failures (the failure interval for the whole job), not a component lifetime; substituting the per-component value would overestimate \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) by \(\sqrt{\RequiredComponentCount}\). For dimensional consistency, \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) and \(\SystemMtbf\) must be in the same time unit. Industry-standard \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\) is reported in hours; to combine it with seconds-scale write times, multiply the hour value by 3600. The result \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) then carries the time unit chosen for the inputs.
