Because the bottlenecks move rather than disappear, compute infrastructure teams often optimize the visible specification while missing the binding physical constraint. Each fallacy and pitfall below turns a node, rack, pod, or facility lesson into an operational warning.

Fallacy: More GPUs always means faster training.
Fallacies and Pitfalls warned against reading a compute budget as a wall-clock prediction. The hardware form of the same error assumes that training time scales linearly with GPU count, so that doubling the GPUs halves the training time. In practice, communication overhead grows with cluster size, and this chapter’s modeled scaling efficiencies show how fast.
Amdahl’s law bounds speedup when a fixed workload has a fixed serial fraction. Distributed training also incurs communication, pipeline, and I/O costs that can change with partitioning and scale; these are not all an invariant serial fraction. For a 175B-parameter model with 350 GB of gradients, the AllReduce at each training step must combine contributions across the participating group. It can do so through ring or tree exchanges; direct transfers between every pair are not required.
Even for a carefully engineered fabric, the modeled scaling efficiency of the running model falls from 0.87 at 256 GPUs to 0.83 at 1,024 GPUs and 0.56 at 8,192. Growing from the reference cluster to the 8,192-GPU scenario of section 2.7 therefore multiplies the hardware 8× but the speed only 5.4×, and 44 percent of the larger cluster’s locally achievable throughput is lost to communication and pipeline bubbles. That run still finishes in days, so the scale is worth buying for a deadline, but each added GPU returns less than the one before it; without an engineered fabric and overlapped communication, the curve flattens far sooner.
The correct approach is to profile useful compute time, exposed communication time, and idle time at the current scale before buying the next pod. If the added GPUs mostly increase exposed communication, procurement is buying idle time rather than training progress. The mathematics of scaling efficiency turns this local ratio into a scaling-efficiency estimate before committing to procurement.


Pitfall: Planning training throughput from peak FLOP/s alone.
Peak FLOP/s describes only one roofline ceiling. At the H100 FP16 ridge point of approximately 295.2 FLOP/byte, the bandwidth and arithmetic ceilings meet; lower-intensity operations cannot reach the arithmetic peak through more compute alone. In the chapter’s batch-1 weight-streaming estimate, decode near 1 FLOP/byte uses well under 1 percent of the arithmetic peak. Prefill and training supply more reuse, yet even well-tuned large training runs commonly sustain only 30–50 percent of peak once memory-bound attention and normalization kernels, activation recomputation, dependencies, and communication are counted. Procurement needs those measurements for the intended execution phase.


Fallacy: Power and cooling constraints can be handled after accelerator purchase.
Teams that plan GPU purchases from compute requirements without verifying that the target facility can deliver the required power and cooling run into hard physical limits with long lead times. A single rack of four DGX H100 systems requires 33.5 kW of power. Upgrading a data center’s electrical infrastructure (new transformers, switchgear, and UPS capacity) and its cooling plant (chillers, piping, pumps) are construction projects planned in months, not days. Even seemingly simple changes, such as upgrading the PDU in a single rack from 20 kW to 60 kW, can require new cabling and circuit breaker panels. Organizations that order hardware without confirming facility readiness risk having millions of dollars of GPUs sitting in shipping containers in the parking lot while the building is retrofitted. Accelerators can arrive faster than a facility can be upgraded to power and cool them, which makes this mismatch a practical planning risk.


Pitfall: Buying a newer accelerator without checking the workload’s arithmetic intensity.
Suppose a team deploys B200 GPUs (4,500 TFLOP/s FP8 peak) for an inference workload serving a 7B-parameter model at batch size 1, where an arithmetic intensity of approximately 1 FLOP/byte places the workload deep in the memory-bound region. The B200’s memory bandwidth (8 TB/s) is 2.4× higher than the H100’s (3.35 TB/s). Comparing B200 FP8 against H100 FP16/BF16-class throughput gives a peak arithmetic ratio of about 4.6×, but also changes the precision convention. At a fixed weight footprint, the bandwidth-only model instead predicts a gain of about 2.4×. The low intensity limits the fraction of arithmetic peak that this model can use, though it does not measure idle time; the comparison that matters is bandwidth per dollar at the measured serving rate, and the larger arithmetic peak alone does not establish better value.


Fallacy: Air cooling is sufficient for AI workloads.
Operators of legacy facilities may assume that adding fans and chiller capacity is sufficient for any denser AI rack. In practice, the cooling choice depends on the system’s heat-rejection design and the facility’s available airflow, pressure, inlet temperature, and containment. Engineered air remains viable for some dense configurations, while higher rack densities can require direct liquid cooling to avoid thermal throttling or exceeding facility limits.


Fallacy: All GPU-hours are equivalent.
A common error in cost comparisons is to treat one GPU-hour on an H100 as interchangeable with one GPU-hour on an A100 or V100. Under the same dense FP16 peak convention, H100 offers 3.2× the arithmetic rate of A100 and 7.9× that of V100. If a workload sustained the same fraction of those peaks with the same operation count and target quality, 10,000 V100 GPU-hours would correspond to approximately 1,264 H100 GPU-hours. That is a conditional compute-only comparison, not a predicted training time, because memory, communication, numerical recipes, and software can change sustained efficiency. Procurement must compare measured cost per useful computation or per completed run, rather than rental price or peak FLOP/s alone.


Pitfall: Upgrading the network before identifying the training bottleneck.
A network upgrade from 200 Gb/s to 400 Gb/s InfiniBand changes training time only through the communication it accelerates on the critical path, the mirror image of the faster-accelerator fallacy in Fallacies and Pitfalls. In a no-overlap example with 20 seconds of computation and 2 seconds of communication, doubling transfer bandwidth reduces the estimated step from 22 to 21 seconds, an improvement of 4.5 percent. That result assumes the communication term scales with bandwidth and other terms remain fixed. Adding GPUs or optimizing kernels requires a separate estimate because either can change communication and overlap. The Fleet Law keeps those costs visible when comparing investments.


Fallacy: Average power draw is sufficient for cooling design.
Accelerator power draw varies across communication, memory, and compute phases. A workload average below the configured sustained envelope does not establish the cooling requirement because synchronized compute phases can raise many devices toward that envelope together. Thermal design must use the vendor’s sustained design target under the intended inlet and cooling conditions, while the electrical path must separately tolerate documented transients. Otherwise thermal throttling can reduce sustained throughput without producing a crash or explicit application error.


Pitfall: Selecting accelerators by HBM capacity without checking bandwidth.
Capacity and bandwidth answer separate feasibility questions, and a model that fits in HBM but cannot be served within its latency target is as unusable as one that does not fit. Consider two hypothetical options for a 70-billion-parameter model: (a) 192 GB of HBM2e at 2.04 TB/s, and (b) 80 GB of HBM3 at 3.35 TB/s. Option (a) holds the 141 GB FP16 weight payload, whose streaming floor is 141 GB/2.04 TB/s = 69.2 ms. Option (b) cannot hold 141 GB in its 80 GB capacity, but the 71 GB INT8 payload fits before other live state is counted. Its weight-transfer floor is 71 GB/3.35 TB/s = 21 ms, a 3.3× ratio between the two estimates. That ratio combines faster memory with fewer bytes; option (a) could also use a validated INT8 recipe. Selection must compare like-for-like quality, complete live-state capacity, and measured latency at the intended concurrency.


Fallacy: Data loading can be fixed after deployment.
Teams that optimize only GPU kernels and communication can still find their accelerators waiting for input. The data loading pipeline must sustain the cluster’s consumption rate across storage, preprocessing, and host-to-GPU transfer. The chapter’s pre-tokenized language-model example needs modest raw bandwidth, but tokenization, sequence packing, and shuffling can change the host-side demand. Size CPU workers, buffering, and storage concurrency from the actual pipeline. Local NVMe staging and prefetching are useful when they relieve the measured bottleneck; neither substitutes for testing the complete path at fleet concurrency.


Pitfall: Buying homogeneous clusters without modeling workload diversity.
Uniform hardware simplifies support and placement, but that benefit must be weighed against the useful work existing devices can still perform. For our 175B model, training and low-batch decode stress different resources. Separate pools can exploit that difference without placing mismatched devices in the same tightly synchronized group.
The A100’s 2.04 TB/s and the H100’s 3.35 TB/s supply different bandwidth ceilings. Retaining older devices for an inference pool can reduce cost when their measured throughput, power, and support costs compare favorably at the required latency. The distinction is between job-level balance within a synchronized group and cluster-level hardware uniformity. A heterogeneous fleet can preserve balanced groups, but its matching benefit must cover the added scheduling and operational complexity.


Pitfall: Treating commissioning and burn-in as schedule slack.
Commissioning is part of the system build, not a buffer that can be consumed when hardware delivery slips. Burn-in tests, cable validation, firmware qualification, thermal soak, and NCCL stress runs are the first time the node, rack, network, and facility layers operate as one machine. Compressing that phase turns installation defects into production failures, where each debugging cycle idles the full fleet rather than a small acceptance-test window.

Training our 175B-parameter model exposes a constraint cascade: accelerator capacity and throughput shape the node, node power shapes rack cooling, rack density shapes pod layout, and pod topology and reliability determine how much useful work the fleet sustains. At the device level, the generality tax (principle \(\ref{pri-generality-tax}\)) explains the trade between flexibility and workload-specific efficiency. A GPU delivers 10–100\(\times\) the matrix throughput of a CPU on suitable workloads, but that specialization pays only when the workload and software stack can use the dedicated arithmetic over the deployment’s lifetime. The roofline in section 2.3.2 identifies the binding compute or memory ceiling, while the bandwidth hierarchy in section 2.5.1 guides where communicating work belongs. Together, these models connect software choices to the physical limits of the fleet.
Our 175B-parameter model connects the decisions at each level. Its low-batch decode estimate requires about 350 billion floating-point operations per token, but moving the 350 GB FP16 weight payload through one hypothetical 3.35 TB/s HBM path takes over 100 ms. A feasible partition changes that path budget as well as solving capacity. At the node level, training state exceeds 2 TB, requiring additional sharding or reductions in resident state. At the rack level, 32 accelerators at 700 W each, plus modeled host and network overhead, require 33.5 kW of qualified power and cooling capacity. The reference cluster coordinates 1,024 GPUs, while the worked pod scenario uses eight times that number. Communication, failure recovery, and sustained utilization determine how much of the purchased capacity becomes completed work. The model’s size exposes these interactions, but the same accounting applies whenever a workload crosses physical resource boundaries.
The method transfers beyond this model. At each level, identify the binding constraint, quantify its effect, and propagate the consequence upward. A faster accelerator is counterproductive if cooling cannot remove its heat; a denser rack is futile if the grid cannot supply it; and a wider network is wasteful if the workload cannot use its bandwidth. Infrastructure engineering is thus a quantitative discipline for tracing chip-level choices into rack power, facility cooling, network topology, reliability, and ownership cost.

Key Takeaways: The data center is the computer

Capacity and bandwidth are separate tests: Capacity decides whether model state fits; bandwidth decides how fast low-reuse phases run. For single-request LLM decode, weight traffic commonly sets the latency floor. The ridge point (\(\RooflineRidgePoint\) = peak FLOP/s divided by memory BW) separates bandwidth- from compute-bound operation, but batch shape, fusion, precision, reuse, and the modeled memory level determine where each training or inference phase lies.
Bandwidth hierarchy guides parallelism placement: The 9× per-direction bandwidth gap in the NVLink–InfiniBand example favors keeping frequent tensor-parallel exchanges inside the fast interconnect domain. Pipeline and data parallelism can span slower links, but their traffic and synchronization still have to fit the workload’s time budget.
A node aggregates private memories: Eight accelerators multiply HBM capacity, but each device’s memory stays private, so the running model’s 2.8 TB of persistent training state forces tensor parallelism, optimizer sharding, activation checkpointing, and memory tiering to be combined.
Peak vs. sustained: Capacity planning must use sustained throughput measured with a consistent model-FLOP convention, precision, system scale, and workload shape, not peak specifications.
Rack power and cooling bound installable compute: Watts per rack, delivery losses, and cooling class, not FLOP/s, set how much compute a facility can install and sustain; at pod scale, network topology, cooling, and power delivery must be co-designed for the dominant workload.
Failure exposure grows with fleet size: With independent failures and a per-GPU MTTF of 50,000 hours, the 10,000-GPU example has a mean interval of about five hours between GPU failures. Recovery and checkpoint storage therefore belong in infrastructure planning from the start.
Price useful work, not hardware: GPU-hours from different generations, an FP8 peak that doubles advertised capacity, and bandwidth per dollar for decode compare only through sustained throughput on the target workload. Power, cooling, facilities, and utilization then set the lifetime cost of that useful work, so hardware price alone cannot settle a purchase.



Applied through C³, choosing liquid cooling for a dense accelerator rack changes more than heat removal. It raises the compute a rack can hold, which concentrates communication onto fewer top-of-rack links and adds coordination work for power capping, failure isolation, and maintenance. In the Fleet Law’s accounting, the hardware in this chapter fixes the per-device rate behind \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) and the link bandwidths behind \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), while rack and pod reliability decide how often synchronization and recovery interrupt the step. Removing one physical ceiling therefore requires checking the rest of the fleet again; otherwise the investment creates capacity that the workload cannot use.

What’s Next: From silicon to wiresPhysical infrastructure spans from Tensor Core transistors to megawatt data-center substations. A fleet of disconnected nodes, however, is not yet a computer; it is a warehouse of expensive accelerators. The network fabric turns those nodes into a unified training system by carrying gradients, activations, and checkpoints between them. At every scale above the node, this chapter met the same limit in a new form. The bandwidth hierarchy showed a 9× cliff between NVLink and InfiniBand, and the pod showed why usable bandwidth depends on the communication pattern and where it is placed. Every training step of our 175B model ends by combining gradients across all 1,024 GPUs of the reference cluster, so the slowest required transfer sets when the next step can begin. Network Fabrics starts from that synchronization and climbs from signaling on a single link through transport protocols, switch topology, and congestion behavior to the integrated cluster. At each level it asks whether the fabric lets those GPUs train as one coherent machine or leaves them waiting as isolated devices.

What physical constraint is this transition primarily designed to bypass, and what trade-off does it introduce?

The area and energy devoted by a processor to capabilities outside the dominant neural network matrix-multiplication workload, such as out-of-order scheduling, branch prediction, and complex hardware caches, is called the ____.

ML accelerators reduce this generality tax by allocating 50–90%+ of silicon area to dense arithmetic units (Tensor Cores or systolic arrays), trading general-purpose programmability for matrix compute density.

Use SRAM-sized attention tiles and fusion to avoid materializing the full score matrix in HBM and reduce intermediate HBM round-trips.
Overclocking Tensor Cores to increase peak FP16 TFLOP/s, raising the horizontal ceiling of the roofline.
Adding dummy memory reads to artificially raise the measured memory traffic of the kernel.
Offloading the layer normalization and attention operations to host CPU DRAM over PCIe Gen5.

A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workload routes tokens dynamically across experts, producing heavy AllToAll collective traffic where every GPU in a node sends distinct token buffers to every other GPU. Why does an NVSwitch crossbar topology significantly outperform a physical GPU ring topology for this workload?

NVSwitch provides non-blocking full bisection bandwidth enabling any-GPU-to-any-GPU communication in a single hop, whereas a ring forces non-neighbor transfers through intermediate hops, causing link contention and \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) latency.
NVSwitch converts AllToAll network collectives into local register-file reads, eliminating inter-GPU data transfer entirely.
Ring topologies cannot support mixed precision, forcing all token embeddings to be cast to FP64.
NVSwitch increases individual GPU HBM3 bandwidth from \(3.35\text{ TB/s}\) to \(19\text{ TB/s}\).

Answer: The correct answer is A. In an AllToAll collective, all \(N\) GPUs simultaneously exchange unique data with all other \(N-1\) GPUs (\(N \times (N-1)\) distinct streams). An NVSwitch crossbar fabric provides non-blocking, full-bisection single-hop connectivity between all 8 GPUs. In contrast, a ring topology forces traffic between non-adjacent GPUs to traverse intermediate nodes, creating severe link contention and \(\mathcal{O}(N)\) multi-hop latency. The claim that NVSwitch eliminates inter-GPU communication is false because NVSwitch is a network switch. The claim that rings force FP64 is fabricated. The claim that NVSwitch raises on-package HBM bandwidth confuses the intra-node interconnect with on-package memory.
Learning Objective: Compare intra-node topologies by mapping their connectivity structure to the communication patterns of AllToAll-heavy workloads.

Gray failures disable FP8 Tensor Cores, silently falling back to double-precision FP64 and exhausting memory.

Answer: The correct answer is C. A late required participant can delay dependent work in its synchronous job or process group. A hard failure has a bounded interruption only under the stated detection and recovery assumptions; an undetected slowdown accumulates loss for as long as it persists. Which costs more depends on the exposed delay, its duration, and recovery cost. This does not imply that unrelated jobs wait, that detection is immediate, or that every gray failure preserves numerical correctness.
Learning Objective: Contrast the impact of gray failures versus hard crashes on cluster-wide throughput in synchronous distributed training.
A pod fabric that uses tiers of switches to supply full bisection bandwidth across node uplinks, in contrast to a direct-connect torus, is called a ____ topology.
Answer: The correct answer is Fat-Tree (or fat-tree). In a fully provisioned design, uplink capacity supports the endpoint rate across an equal cut. This removes the modeled oversubscription limit at that boundary; it does not guarantee congestion-free execution or an optimal AllReduce. Collective schedule, routing, traffic placement, and competing load still determine performance.
Learning Objective: Identify the Fat-Tree network topology and its role in delivering non-blocking full bisection bandwidth for distributed training.
Arrange the stages in the worked scenario’s accounting sequence: begin with the compute-only baseline, add the distributed-step losses, then checkpointing, restart, and maintenance allowances. (1) Checkpoint I/O overhead (\(\approx 3\%\)), (2) Compute-only training time (\(6PD\) FLOPs divided by aggregate peak throughput times assumed local compute efficiency), (3) Hardware failure and restart overhead (\(\approx 10\%\)), (4) Scaling efficiency covering communication and pipeline bubbles (\(\approx 0.56\)), (5) Maintenance overhead (\(\approx 5\%\)). Each additive percentage is relative to the preceding subtotal.
Answer: The correct order is: (2) Compute-only baseline, (4) Scaling efficiency, (1) Checkpoint I/O overhead, (3) Failure and restart overhead, (5) Maintenance overhead. Starting near 12 hours gives successive subtotals near 21.4, 22.1, 24.3, and 25.5 hours. The scaling factor already includes pipeline fill and drain, so adding a separate bubble step would count that loss twice. This is an illustrative accounting convention, not a physical chronology or universal minimum. Local compute efficiency excludes the distributed losses added here; using measured distributed MFU would double-count them.
Learning Objective: Sequence the worked training-time accounting model and distinguish its local efficiency and incremental overhead denominators.

Self-Check: Answer

A team will serve a dense language model at batch size 1 with a strict per-token latency target. Which metric should dominate its comparison of candidate accelerators?

Peak FP8 TFLOP/s per dollar, because decode performs two floating-point operations per parameter.
Memory bandwidth per dollar, confirmed by measured throughput at the required latency, because batch-1 decode streams the weights with little reuse.
Host DRAM capacity per dollar, because the weights should be served from host memory.
Bisection bandwidth of the cluster fabric, because every request crosses the network.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Batch-1 decode sits near 1 FLOP/byte, far below the ridge point, so the weight-streaming time set by memory bandwidth dominates and more arithmetic barely changes it. Peak FLOP/s raises a nonbinding ceiling, host memory is far slower than HBM, and independent replicas need not send every request across the cluster fabric. Measured throughput at the latency target confirms the screen.
Learning Objective: Select the procurement metric that matches the binding constraint of a serving workload.
The 175B running model needs about 350 GB for FP16 weights. Using 80 GB accelerators, how many devices are needed for the weights alone at FP16, INT8, and INT4, and why does a fourfold smaller payload not guarantee a fourfold lower token latency?
Answer: The weights need at least five devices at FP16 (350 GB), three at INT8 (175 GB), and two at INT4 (87.5 GB). These are weight-only capacity bounds; quantization metadata, key-value cache, and workspace also need memory. Reading 4-bit instead of 16-bit weights quarters the raw payload, but kernel support, dequantization work, other memory traffic, any change in device count and communication, and validation of model quality determine the realized latency gain.
Learning Objective: Calculate how quantization changes serving device counts and explain why payload reduction does not translate directly into latency.
True or False: A workload whose binding constraint on each device is arithmetic throughput cannot be communication-bound across the cluster.
Answer: False. The decision matrix names the per-device constraint, what one accelerator must supply. Whether the fleet as a whole is limited by compute, communication, or coordination is a separate question. Large-batch LLM training can be compute-bound on each device and still be communication-bound across the cluster, as Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) is.
Learning Objective: Distinguish the per-device binding constraint from the constraint that binds the fleet as a whole.
MLPerf results that fix the workload and the quality target so that different implementations can be compared belong to the ____ division.
Answer: The correct answer is closed. The open division permits broader changes. Neither predicts a deployment automatically, so a procurement team must compare the submission’s workload, software, precision, hardware count, and quality target with the intended system.
Learning Objective: Interpret benchmark results under the measurement rules that produced them.

Self-Check: Answer

A representative CXL memory path over PCIe Gen5 x16 delivers roughly \(64\text{ GB/s}\) of bandwidth, approximately \(50\times\) lower than an H100’s \(3.35\text{ TB/s}\) HBM3 bandwidth. Which infrastructure bottleneck is CXL memory pooling designed to relieve, and which bottleneck does it explicitly not solve?

It relieves peak Tensor Core throughput shortages, but does not solve the memory capacity limit.
It relieves rack cooling limits by eliminating electrical resistance, but does not solve chip-to-chip latency.
It relieves the memory capacity ceiling by holding phase-local optimizer state in shared pooled memory, but explicitly does not replace HBM for bandwidth-critical forward and backward pass weight streaming.
It relieves wafer-scale weight injection bottlenecks, but does not solve semiconductor yield.

Answer: The correct answer is C. CXL memory expansion and pooling can relieve host capacity pressure; accelerator access requires a supported platform, device type, data path, and software placement. Phase-local optimizer shards are candidates only when their transfer schedule fits the update budget. The representative PCIe-based path remains far slower than local HBM and does not replace its bandwidth-critical working set. The other choices confuse memory capacity with arithmetic, cooling, or wafer-scale injection.
Learning Objective: Analyze how CXL relieves memory-capacity pressure without displacing HBM for bandwidth-critical computation.
A systems team proposes moving a 1.8-trillion parameter LLM training workload to a Wafer-Scale Engine (such as Cerebras WSE-3) to eliminate chip-to-chip network communication delays. Explain why this move changes rather than eliminates communication constraints and identify the resulting capacity and bandwidth budgets.
Answer: Wafer-scale integration removes package- and board-level transfers for operations mapped onto one wafer, but communication remains. A 1.8-trillion-parameter model requires several terabytes for weights alone, exceeding \(44\text{ GB}\) of on-wafer SRAM. External weight streaming introduces an injection-bandwidth constraint, while training must also schedule activations, gradients, and updates. The planner must budget external data movement and power density rather than assume that a larger chip eliminates the network or memory problem.
Learning Objective: Analyze the capacity and injection-bandwidth constraints introduced by wafer-scale integration when model size exceeds on-wafer memory.
Advanced packaging technologies (such as 2.5D silicon interposers and 3D chiplet stacking) enable dense die-to-die interconnects on a single package. According to systems engineering principles, how does advanced packaging alter the landscape of infrastructure bottlenecks?

It allows accelerators to run uncooled at ambient room temperature by eliminating electrical resistance across die boundaries.
It permanently eliminates both the memory wall and the power wall by integrating optical waveguides directly onto the silicon substrate.
It eliminates the need for distributed training frameworks because all model parameters can fit permanently in on-die SRAM caches.
It shortens die-to-die paths while requiring package power density, current transients, and heat removal to be checked against the intended configuration.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Dense package-level interconnects can reduce communication distance while concentrating compute and memory power. The resulting design must qualify power delivery, current transients, and cooling; which constraint binds still depends on workload and configuration. Packaging does not eliminate switching energy, permit uncooled operation, or make arbitrary model state fit in SRAM.
Learning Objective: Explain how advanced packaging changes communication paths and power-density budgets without determining one universal binding constraint.
True or False: Emerging infrastructure technologies such as CXL memory pooling, wafer-scale integration, and 2.5D packaging eliminate physical infrastructure constraints, allowing data center operators to deploy dense ML clusters without modifying cooling or power delivery.
Answer: False. Emerging infrastructure technologies do not eliminate physical constraints; they relocate them. CXL moves memory capacity into a shared fabric but leaves interconnect bandwidth as the limiting factor. Wafer-scale integration removes some inter-package transfers for mapped operations but leaves on-wafer communication, external streaming bandwidth, and power concentration as constraints. Advanced packaging compresses die-to-die distances but concentrates thermal flux, requiring cooling and power delivery qualified for the package and rack.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the principle that emerging technologies relocate rather than eliminate physical infrastructure bottlenecks.

Self-Check: Answer

A 175B-parameter model training run on 1,024 GPUs has a step time of \(1{,}000\text{ ms}\), broken down into \(700\text{ ms}\) of compute (\(T_{\text{compute}}\)) and \(300\text{ ms}\) of gradient AllReduce communication (\(T_{\text{comm}}\)). If the team scales out to 2,048 GPUs (assuming compute scales linearly to \(350\text{ ms}\), while AllReduce communication time remains constant at \(300\text{ ms}\)), what is the resulting scaling efficiency?

100% (ideal linear speedup, halving step time to \(500\text{ ms}\)).
\(\approx 77\%\) (speedup of \(\approx 1.54\times\) from \(1{,}000\text{ ms}\) to \(650\text{ ms}\), demonstrating diminishing returns on the \(2\times\) hardware investment).
50% (step time remains completely unchanged at \(1{,}000\text{ ms}\)).
\(\approx 125\%\) (superlinear speedup due to increased aggregate L2 cache capacity).

Answer: The correct answer is B. At 1,024 GPUs, step time is \(T_1 = 700 + 300 = 1{,}000\text{ ms}\). At 2,048 GPUs, the compute term halves to \(700 / 2 = 350\text{ ms}\), while the communication term remains \(300\text{ ms}\), yielding a new step time of \(T_2 = 350 + 300 = 650\text{ ms}\). The realized speedup is \(S = 1{,}000 / 650 \approx 1.538\times\). Scaling efficiency is \(\eta = S / 2.0 = 1.538 / 2.0 \approx 76.9\%\). The team pays for \(2\times\) the hardware to achieve only a \(1.54\times\) speedup, illustrating the fallacy that doubling GPUs halves training duration when communication is non-trivial. The choice predicting 100% efficiency ignores the unscaled communication bottleneck (violating Amdahl’s law). The choice predicting 50% efficiency assumes zero compute speedup. The choice predicting superlinear speedup invents unphysical scaling for communication-limited training.
Learning Objective: Calculate the scaling efficiency of a distributed training cluster to quantify diminishing returns caused by communication bottlenecks.
Explain how neglecting facility readiness and commissioning can delay an ML training program by months even after GPUs have been delivered to the loading dock. Identify two concrete critical-path failure modes.
Answer: Power, cooling, cabling, firmware qualification, and integrated burn-in belong on the deployment critical path. First, unresolved utility or transformer readiness can leave delivered accelerators unpowered. Second, compressing cable validation, thermal soak, and collective stress checks can move installation defects into production, where diagnosis idles an active job or shared infrastructure. Commissioning duration must be planned from the actual acceptance work; the chapter does not establish a universal percentage of project time.
Learning Objective: Analyze how facility-readiness and commissioning failures create hidden delays in ML infrastructure deployment and identify concrete critical-path failure modes.
A team serving a 70B-parameter LLM at batch size 1 on H100s observes poor token generation latency and proposes upgrading to a B200 (\(4{,}500\text{ FP8 TFLOP/s}\) peak, \(\approx 8\text{ TB/s}\) HBM3e) primarily to capture the \(\approx 2.3\times\) boost in peak arithmetic throughput. Which hidden assumption in their reasoning is fundamentally flawed?

Assuming liquid-cooled racks are capable of hosting high-density B200 servers.
Assuming checkpoint storage bandwidth is necessary during inference serving.
Assuming InfiniBand switches are required for single-node inference deployments.
Assuming that peak arithmetic throughput governs performance when the modeled batch-1 decode workload is limited by weight bandwidth; the HBM bandwidth ratio is the relevant first estimate.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Under the stated weight-streaming model, token throughput is bounded by HBM bandwidth divided by bytes per token. Holding precision, payload, and partition fixed, the bandwidth ratio changes that bound; it does not guarantee the measured token-rate gain. Low arithmetic intensity limits the usable fraction of peak without measuring how much time arithmetic units are idle. Procurement must compare sustained serving throughput at the required quality and latency, rather than pay for a larger arithmetic peak alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze when peak-performance specifications mislead infrastructure procurement for memory-bandwidth-bound inference.
A cost analyst evaluates cloud GPU pricing by comparing hourly rates: H100 at $4.00/GPU-hour vs. V100 at $0.80/GPU-hour, concluding that V100 is \(5\times\) cheaper. Using throughput equivalence (an H100 delivers \(\approx 7.9\times\) the FP16 Tensor throughput of a V100), explain why this hourly rate comparison is a procurement fallacy.
Answer: At dense FP16, the peak ratio is about \(989/125 \approx 7.9\). If both devices sustain the same fraction of those peaks on this workload, \(10{,}000\) V100 GPU-hours become about \(1{,}264\) H100 GPU-hours: roughly $5,056 rather than $8,000 at the stated rates. The H100 is then about 1.6 times cheaper per completed workload despite its higher hourly rate. Actual procurement must compare measured useful throughput at consistent precision and quality; mixed FP8/FP16 peaks are not interchangeable.
Learning Objective: Compare accelerator total cost of ownership using throughput-normalized cost per useful TFLOP-hour rather than nominal hourly GPU rental rates.

title: 2 Compute Infrastructure
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why does infrastructure, not algorithms alone, determine who can participate in advancing machine learning at scale?
Machine learning systems have a physical reality beyond their code. Public algorithms do not make large-scale training equally accessible: executing them requires power, cooling, memory, and communication capacity that organizations must build and sustain. A model that outgrows one machine turns a local resource problem into a shared infrastructure commitment. Buying more accelerators adds arithmetic capacity, but it also adds data transfers, heat, and components whose failures can interrupt collective work. The useful capacity of the fleet depends on whether those demands can be met together. Hardware that appears attractive in isolation may spend much of its deployment waiting for data or operating below its advertised speed. A facility that can house equipment may lack the electrical or cooling capacity to run it at the intended density. These mismatches consume both capital and operating budgets while reducing the experiments that can finish on schedule. Infrastructure decisions also outlast individual models, so an organization must weigh the efficiency of specialization against the flexibility needed for future workloads. Single-machine performance remains part of that judgment, but multiplying it by the number of machines cannot establish what the complete installation will deliver. Participation at scale therefore depends on turning purchased hardware into sustained, usable capacity within physical and financial limits. In C³ terms, the physical substrate sets the compute and communication bounds within which the fleet must coordinate useful work.

Learning Objectives

Explain how the memory, communication, power, and reliability walls bind at successive physical scales and cascade upward
Compare GPU, TPU, and ASIC specialization as a bet on workload stability against refresh cycles and facility lifetime
Distinguish memory capacity from memory bandwidth as separate procurement tests, using roofline placement to find bandwidth-bound phases
Calculate token-latency floors, memory budgets, and pod training time from accelerator specifications and sustained utilization
Match tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism to the available interconnect bandwidth hierarchy
Evaluate rack and pod designs using power density, cooling limits, topology, and facility reliability constraints
Select accelerator infrastructure using sustained throughput, power constraints, workload fit, and deployment cost

title: 2 Compute Infrastructure
text:
The scaling laws of AI Scaling Laws are why demand outruns any single device. Loss falls predictably as parameters, training tokens, and compute grow together, so each step up in capability multiplies both the memory a model occupies and the arithmetic its training consumes; a GPT-3-class model already needs several accelerators merely to store its FP16 weights. A model that exceeds one accelerator’s memory capacity forces a hardware decision before training begins. Adding accelerators supplies capacity, but also creates transfers between devices, increases power demand, and couples progress to more components that can fail. The familiar single-node compute and memory limits therefore become inputs to fleet design. Four recurring physical constraints appear at escalating physical scales, from an eight-GPU node to a 25K-accelerator fleet (figure 1). Memory bandwidth, rack power, pod communication, and fleet failure exposure provide the examples; the workload and configuration determine which constraint binds at each scale. These are the memory, energy, and network walls of the scale moment and the fleet’s reliability gap, seen from the hardware that imposes them. Because this chapter studies the hardware, it names each constraint by the physical resource that runs out. It uses these four names from here on: the memory wall, the power wall (the energy wall as power delivery and heat removal), the communication wall (the network wall as link bandwidth), and the reliability wall (the reliability gap as a failure interval).


↩︎ The memory, network, and energy walls of the scale moment are established in The Scale Moment.
The 175B model anchors this progression. It is the chapter’s running instance of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), a GPT-3-class dense transformer trained with mixed precision and the Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer, whose reference training cluster is 1,024 H100 GPUs in 128 eight-GPU nodes. Accelerator selection establishes the compute rate, memory capacity, and power envelope that a fleet can buy. The node must connect enough of those accelerators to hold and execute the workload; the rack must power and cool them; the pod must sustain communication and survive component failures. This is the hardware contribution to C³: useful fleet compute depends on the communication and coordination costs created at each physical boundary.


↩︎ The three fleet workload archetypes are established in Three systems archetypes.

↪ The running model’s parameters and reference cluster are developed in Reference Workload.

One naming refinement accompanies the fourth wall: the reliability calculation starts from a per-GPU failure figure that The Scale Moment calls an MTBF. A failed GPU is replaced rather than repaired, so this chapter calls the per-device figure a mean time to failure (MTTF) and reserves mean time between failures (MTBF) for nodes and fleets, which keep running through repeated failures and replacements. The number is the same; only the label records what is being counted.






Figure 1: The Four Infrastructure Walls: Read left to right, the examples illustrate four constraints at increasing physical scales; the workload and configuration determine which one binds. The node compares 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 with about 2,000 TFLOP/s of FP8 arithmetic; the four-node DGX H100 rack draws 33.5 kW; the pod compares per-direction NVLink bandwidth with one InfiniBand port, a ninefold budget gap; and the fleet assumes independent GPU failures, reducing a 50,000-hour per-GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) to about 2 hours between failures at 25K GPUs.



The chapter climbs the same scale ladder, so the four walls arrive in the order the figure reads, though not one wall per section. The memory wall begins at the accelerator and is developed in section 2.3. The communication wall first appears inside the node, where section 2.5.1 measures the cliff between local and inter-node links, and returns at pod scale in section 2.7. The power wall binds at the rack (section 2.6.1), and the reliability wall accumulates from node health (section 2.5.5) through facility controls to the fleet-scale failure interval of section 2.7.1.

Self-Check: Question

Which statement correctly describes representative constraints and mitigation mechanisms across the accelerator, node, rack, and pod hierarchy, without assigning one universally dominant wall to each tier?

Accelerator: arithmetic throughput vs. generality tax \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by specialized silicon; Node: single-chip memory capacity limit \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by high-speed intra-node fabrics aggregating HBM; Rack: thermal and power density \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by facility cooling and power distribution; Pod: network bisection and fleet MTBF \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by pod-scale fabrics and fault-tolerant orchestration.
Accelerator: network latency \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by InfiniBand; Node: transistor count \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by photolithography; Rack: memory bandwidth \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by PCIe Gen5; Pod: power delivery \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by running jobs asynchronously without barriers.
Accelerator: single-chip memory capacity wall \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by on-die branch predictors; Node: power wall \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by host underclocking; Rack: communication wall \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by standard commodity Ethernet; Pod: memory bandwidth wall \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by building-wide CXL pooling.
Accelerator: storage I/O capacity \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by local NVMe drives; Node: compilation time \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by JIT compilers; Rack: clock jitter \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by atomic clocks; Pod: software bug rate \(\rightarrow\) mitigated by unit testing frameworks.

Explain how relieving a constraint at one physical level of the compute infrastructure stack can expose another constraint. Use the accelerator, node, rack, and pod hierarchy, and explain why it is not a fixed one-wall-per-tier sequence.
True or False: In a warehouse-scale training cluster, the reliability wall implies that as the cluster scales to tens of thousands of GPUs, the aggregate fleet Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) remains bounded primarily by the lifetime of the most resilient server chassis.

title: 2 Compute Infrastructure
text:
The progression begins with the accelerator, because every wall above it is measured against the rates one device can compute, store, and draw. An accelerator purchase commits the fleet to a workload and software stack for longer than one experiment. A research group changing model operations frequently needs programmability; a service executing a stable computation at sustained volume can justify more specialization. The familiar trade-off between control flexibility and arithmetic efficiency matters here because an architectural mismatch is replicated across the fleet. Comparing programmable and specialized accelerators therefore starts with how much of the workload and compiler stack can remain stable over the deployment’s lifetime.

Systems Perspective 2.1: The generality taxGeneral-purpose CPUs allocate silicon to caches and control logic as well as arithmetic. Branch predictors, reorder buffers, and instruction decoders support code with irregular control flow and data access. Matrix multiplication has a more regular schedule, so some of that flexibility contributes little to its dominant computation. The generality tax (principle \(\ref{pri-generality-tax}\)) is the area and energy devoted to capabilities outside the dominant workload.
Specialized accelerators reduce this tax by replacing general-purpose control with a dataflow matched to the workload. In the approximate shares of figure 2, the arithmetic fraction of the die rises from roughly 5–10 percent on a CPU to 50–60 percent on a GPU, 70–80 percent on a Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), and over 90 percent on a custom application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). The shares mark a direction rather than measured proportions for any product. The selection question is how much of the complete workload can use the specialized hardware.








Figure 2: The Accelerator Spectrum: Each die is drawn as a grid of 100 cells divided between arithmetic units (dark) and control, cache, and other logic (light), with the medium cells marking the spread of each approximate, illustrative share. Read left to right, the arithmetic share grows from 5 to 10 percent on a CPU to over 90 percent on a custom ASIC, because hardwired dataflow replaces instruction fetch, decode, and scheduling; each step buys throughput per watt by narrowing the range of model architectures the silicon runs well.



Along the spectrum of figure 2, GPUs retain substantial programmability and provide 10–100\(\times\) the matrix throughput of CPUs, while custom ASICs at the far end hardwire a specific dataflow for maximum efficiency at the cost of flexibility. The spectrum is not a ranking from “bad” (general-purpose CPU) to “good” (custom ASIC). It is a continuum of trade-offs in which each position is the best match for a different combination of workload characteristics and deployment constraints.
GPUs represent the first major step away from general-purpose computing toward large-scale parallelism while retaining programmability. An NVIDIA H100, for example, contains 16,896 CUDA cores organized into 132 streaming multiprocessors (SMs). The SMs keep thousands of threads in flight under the single instruction, multiple threads (SIMT) model, so a programmer-written kernel can express any mathematical operation, from convolutions to attention to custom loss functions. Neural network operations have uniform enough control flow that this programmability costs the GPU little on ML workloads.
TPUs specialize the matrix dataflow while retaining other units for operations that do not map onto it. Google’s Tensor Processing Units use a systolic array1 architecture, a fixed grid of multiply-accumulate (MAC) units that pass operands and partial results between neighboring cells on a regular schedule, so local reuse replaces per-operation instruction fetch and memory traffic. The complete accelerator still needs control, data movement, and execution of nonmatrix operations.
1 Systolic array: From Greek systole (contraction), the name describes data pulsing through a grid of processing elements in a heart-like rhythm. Kung and Leiserson (1979) proposed the design for VLSI chips whose limiting resource was memory access rather than logic (Kung 1982): each operand fetched once is reused by every cell it passes. That ratio of computation to memory traffic is exactly what matrix multiplication at ML scale rewards.
Kung, Hsiang Tsung, and Charles E Leiserson. 1979. “Systolic Arrays (for VLSI).” Sparse Matrix Proceedings 1978 1: 256–82.

Kung, H. T. 1982. “Why Systolic Architectures?” Computer 15 (1): 37–46. https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.1982.1653825.
The cost of this efficiency is reduced programmability. Models must be compiled through Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA), which maps high-level operations onto the fixed dataflow. Workloads with irregular control flow or dynamic shapes may not map well to this architecture, and the compilation process itself can be time-consuming (minutes to hours for complex models), which slows the iteration cycle during model development.
The programming model distinction between GPUs and TPUs has practical implications for organizational decisions. A research team that frequently adds custom operations, such as new attention patterns or activation functions, needs a path to implement them as kernels without waiting for compiler support, and must check how each platform expresses and optimizes those operations. A team running a stable computation at scale can place more weight on sustained utilization and compilation cost amortized over many runs. CUDA kernel support and XLA graph compilation offer different development paths, but neither establishes a utilization advantage without evaluating the workload and implementation. Software fit belongs in the hardware comparison because unsupported or poorly mapped work can leave specialized arithmetic idle.

Example 2.1: The TPU origin storyScenario: In 2013, Google projected that if users spoke to Android phones for 3 minutes per day using voice search, handling the inference load on general-purpose CPUs would require doubling data center compute capacity at prohibitive cost (Jouppi et al. 2017).
Diagnosis: Standard CPU architectures paid a heavy generality tax, spending significant silicon area and power on out-of-order execution, branch prediction, and complex caches rather than matrix multiplication throughput.
Systems lesson: Hardware specialization is economically justified when a workload is large, stable, and dominated by a single mathematical kernel (MatMul). The TPU v1 hardwired a \(256 \times 256\) systolic array to deliver 92 TOPS (INT8) within a 75 W footprint, establishing custom ASIC accelerators in production serving infrastructure.


Custom ASICs occupy the specialized end of the spectrum, where the economics of silicon can justify giving up much of the general-purpose programmability. When an organization runs a stable workload at enormous scale, designing a chip specifically for that workload may become economically rational. A custom ASIC can improve energy per operation and sustained utilization on its target workload by removing features that computation does not require.
Tesla’s Dojo D1 chip, for example, is optimized for the spatial and temporal structure of video-based vision models. Its hundreds of tightly coupled processing nodes are designed around the dataflow needs of Tesla’s vision pipeline, with on-chip SRAM sized to keep spatial tiles close to the compute units. This reduces the repeated round-trips to off-chip memory that a general-purpose GPU would require for the same computation. AWS Trainium takes a different approach, targeting the broad category of Transformer training rather than a single model. Trainium systems combine compiler-managed memory scheduling with hardware-assisted collective communication, so common training patterns such as tensor-parallel synchronization and data-parallel reductions can be optimized in the accelerator fabric rather than handled entirely by host software.
The risk of custom silicon follows from the same specialization. A change in the dominant model architecture can reduce the value of a fixed dataflow if the new operators, tensor shapes, or memory demands map poorly onto it. Sharing matrix operations across model families can preserve some of that investment, so a change from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to Transformers does not by itself make an accelerator unusable. The forecasting window is long. Even Google’s first TPU, a high-priority project, took 15 months to design, verify, build, and deploy (Jouppi et al. 2017), and a chip then serves for several years more. The design decision must therefore anticipate which operations will remain useful years after the workload was profiled, and how much flexibility is needed for the rest. In 2015, few would have predicted that attention-based Transformers would replace CNNs as the dominant architecture within five years, a span of only a few ASIC design cycles.
Custom silicon is therefore a bet on workload stability, and the organizations that make this bet are typically those with enough scale to justify a large up-front design investment and enough workload volume to amortize that NRE (nonrecurring engineering) cost across many chips. Google can justify the TPU’s development cost because high-volume services such as Search, YouTube recommendations, and Gmail spam filtering can amortize a shared accelerator platform. A research lab running a few hundred GPUs cannot justify the same investment.
The bet can pay off when workloads are stable. The first-generation TPU reported 30–80\(\times\) the performance per watt of contemporary GPUs and CPUs on its inference workloads (Jouppi et al. 2017), and TPU v4 reported 1.3–1.9\(\times\) lower power than the A100 for similar-sized training systems (Jouppi et al. 2023). A workload shift can strand that advantage because the chip’s fixed dataflow may not accommodate a substantially different computational pattern. Pushing the locality argument further raises a question of physical scale: whether the compute fabric can expand to the size of an entire wafer.

Jouppi, Norman P., Cliff Young, Nishant Patil, David Patterson, Gaurav Agrawal, Raminder Bajwa, Sarah Bates, et al. 2017. “In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit.” Proceedings of the 44th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, ISCA ’17, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1145/3079856.3080246.

Jouppi, Norm, George Kurian, Sheng Li, Peter Ma, Rahul Nagarajan, Lifeng Nai, Nishant Patil, et al. 2023. “TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589350.


Slicing a silicon wafer into discrete chips forces every exchange between accelerators to leave the die and cross slower, higher-energy package, board, or rack links. Wafer-scale engines (WSE) avoid those crossings by keeping most of a silicon wafer intact as one continuous compute fabric the size of a dinner plate, as in the Cerebras WSE-3, rather than dicing the wafer and reconnecting the pieces across packages and boards.
For its 2024 WSE-3 configuration, Cerebras reported 900,000 AI-optimized cores, 44 GB of distributed on-chip SRAM, and 21 PB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth in its registration filing (Cerebras Systems 2024). These specifications are not directly comparable to GPU-cluster peak FLOP/s or high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth because the architectures expose different dataflows, memory organizations, precisions, and workload mappings. The durable comparison is topological: on-wafer links avoid package-, board-, and rack-level transfers for work that maps onto the fabric.

Cerebras Systems. 2024. Cerebras Systems, Inc. Registration Statement on Form S-1.

Systems, Cerebras. 2021. “Wafer-Scale Deep Learning Acceleration with the Cerebras CS-2.” Cerebras Technical Paper 2021.
A multi-GPU chassis and a wafer-scale engine draw their package and board boundaries in different places (figure 3). The eight GPUs of a chassis exchange state through NVSwitch, and transfers to other nodes cross the external network. A wafer-scale engine instead routes between 900,000 on-wafer cores on the 300 mm wafer. Defect-aware routing lets the fabric use working regions despite local manufacturing flaws. In the documented CS-2 configuration, twelve power supplies in a 9+3 redundant arrangement could deliver up to 23 kW to the WSE-2 (Systems 2021). That configuration-specific design illustrates why wafer-scale power delivery and cooling require system-level liquid-cooling hardware rather than a conventional accelerator heatsink.






Figure 3: Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE) Architecture: A DGX H100 node (left) joins eight separately packaged GPUs through an NVSwitch fabric and must leave the chassis over InfiniBand to reach other nodes, so every exchange crosses a package, board, or network boundary. A WSE (right) instead uses most of a 300 mm wafer as one routed mesh of cores, each with local SRAM; defect-aware routing steers traffic around unusable cores, and the on-wafer mesh replaces off-package transfers for mapped operations. The WSE-3 figures are the vendor’s reported totals and are not directly comparable to GPU HBM bandwidth.



Wafer-scale engines specialize the physical architecture while retaining flexibility in the computational model through programmable cores. That trade-off exchanges manufacturing complexity and defect-aware routing for an on-wafer fabric that replaces package- and board-level communication between its cores, though SRAM capacity and data injection still constrain which parts of a workload can benefit from that locality. Where the wafer-scale engine removes the package boundary by never dicing the wafer, chiplet designs keep the package and change what goes inside it.



Once a monolithic processor die grows to the optical exposure limit of a lithography scanner, adding more arithmetic units or HBM controllers on a single piece of silicon becomes impossible without stitching exposures at lower yield and sharply higher cost. Chiplet architectures, exemplified by NVIDIA’s Blackwell and AMD’s Instinct MI300 series, break through that ceiling by partitioning the processor into smaller dies connected by a high-bandwidth die-to-die interconnect on a common package substrate. This approach addresses two physical limits that constrain monolithic designs.
First, the maximum die size is capped by the photolithographic reticle limit, the largest area that a lithography scanner can pattern in a single exposure. The limit comes from the optics of photolithography, because the lens system of an extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) scanner projects a pattern onto a field of only about \(26{\times}33\) mm (858 mm²). A larger die would need multiple exposures stitched together, which is technically possible but sharply raises cost and lowers yield. The limit caps the number of Tensor Cores, SMs, and HBM stacks a monolithic GPU can integrate. Chiplet designs bypass this limit by placing multiple dies on a single package, with the B200’s two reticle-limited dies effectively creating a processor of about 1,700 mm².
Second, manufacturing yield depends on die area and defect density. Under the standard Poisson defect model, the fraction of defect-free dies falls exponentially with die area at a fixed defect density, because a single killer defect anywhere on the die can render it unusable. Smaller dies expose less area to each defect, and testing can select known-good chiplets before package assembly, so one defect discards a small die rather than a reticle-sized one. The resulting yield advantage must be weighed against the cost and yield of the package, its interconnects, and the additional testing. Chiplets change the manufacturing trade-off; they do not guarantee a lower cost per unit of compute.
The trade-off is the die-to-die interconnect. Communication between chiplets within a package is faster than communication between packages (NVLink) but slower than communication within a single monolithic die (the on-die mesh network). Workloads that generate frequent, fine-grained communication between processing elements (such as operations that share data between nonadjacent SMs) may experience a latency penalty when those SMs reside on different chiplets. GPU vendors mitigate this by making the die-to-die link transparent to the programmer, so the software sees a single logical GPU regardless of the underlying chiplet topology. Seeing why modern accelerators reached that multi-die boundary requires tracing how successive GPU and TPU generations spent their single-die transistor budgets first.



NVIDIA’s data center GPUs show the specialization bet placed one generation at a time. Each generation added hardware aimed at a bottleneck that production ML workloads had exposed, rather than more transistors of the same kind. The Volta architecture (2017) introduced the first-generation Tensor Core, dedicated matrix-multiply-accumulate hardware placed beside the existing CUDA cores, because neural network training spends most of its time in matrix multiplications. Volta accelerated that dominant pattern without giving up the general-purpose programmability that made GPUs attractive for research.
The Ampere architecture (2020) expanded Tensor Core support to TF32 and BF16 and introduced Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), which partitions one GPU into up to seven isolated instances so that several inference workloads can share it. The change that mattered most for infrastructure was Ampere’s third-generation NVLink, which doubled per-GPU bandwidth to 600 GB/s from Volta’s 300 GB/s, the bandwidth that tensor parallelism needs because it splits each layer’s matrices across GPUs.
The Hopper architecture (2022) added the Transformer Engine, whose FP8 recipes and autocast integration run supported Transformer operations in FP8 with managed scaling while retaining higher precision where the configured recipe or implementation requires it. Hopper also introduced NVLink 4.0 at 900 GB/s per GPU and the NVLink Switch, enabling NVLink connectivity beyond the 8-GPU boundary.
The Blackwell architecture (2024) takes the chiplet route of section 2.2.2 past the 858 mm² reticle limit. The B200 pairs two GPU dies in one package over a 10 TB/s die-to-die link, fast enough that the two dies appear to software as a single logical GPU for many operations, and its fifth-generation NVLink doubles intra-node bandwidth again to 1800 GB/s per GPU. Its FP8 rating in table 1 is not an FP16/BF16 figure; those comparisons should use the lower precision-specific vendor rate.
Each generation thus targeted the bottleneck its predecessor exposed. Volta added dedicated matrix hardware, Ampere widened mixed-precision support, Hopper added FP8 for Transformer workloads, and Blackwell worked around the die-size limit with two dies in one package. Because architects choose those targets by profiling the workloads of their era, accelerator design follows model architecture, which is why Transformer workloads have shaped accelerator design since 2017.
Because accelerator generations turn over faster than the facility that houses them, a data center must anticipate refresh cycles before the first rack arrives. Those generations also changed interconnect capacity and power (table 1). From V100 to B200, dense FP16 throughput rose 18\(\times\), memory bandwidth 8.9\(\times\), and thermal design power (TDP) 3.3\(\times\) (figure 4). These are growth multiples over the whole span, not annual rates, and their ratios carry the planning lesson. Each byte delivered from memory must now feed about twice as many operations, and each watt of the power allowance supplies more than five times as many peak operations. That first ratio raises the data reuse a workload needs to approach peak throughput. Even with the fivefold gain in peak operations per watt, reaching the 18\(\times\) compute multiple still required raising per-device TDP by 3.3\(\times\), and that higher per-device wattage multiplied by device count sets the proposed rack load. A facility refreshed one-for-one for compute density therefore outruns both its memory delivery and its cooling envelope.

Compute rises 18\(\times\), bandwidth 8.9\(\times\), and TDP 3.3\(\times\), so the endpoint gains in arithmetic exceed the gains in memory bandwidth and power allowance. These are peak specifications, not measured application throughput. Specifications come from the MLSysIM hardware registry.

Because table 1 mixes FP16 and FP8 peaks, its per-watt efficiency must be read at fixed precision. At dense FP16, dividing each generation’s peak throughput by its TDP (table 2) gives a V100-to-B200 gain of 5.4× in peak throughput per watt, the more-than-fivefold figure above, against 18× in raw throughput. The rest of the raw gain came from a power allowance that itself rose 3.3×. The same caution applies between adjacent generations. The H100’s FP8 peak per watt of TDP is 6.8× the V100’s FP16 figure, but a factor of two of that comes from the change of precision, and at equal FP16 precision the gain is 3.4×. Facilities must therefore accommodate higher device power as well as greater arithmetic capacity, which connects this trend to the power wall in section 2.6.1.

The four generations in table 2 sit on a broader and slower trend. Across the 64 accelerator models released since 2017 for which Epoch AI records both a dense FP16 tensor rate and a TDP, from every major vendor, peak arithmetic per watt improved about 1.2× per year, doubling roughly every 4 years (figure 5) (Epoch AI 2026b). The leading NVIDIA parts improved faster, 5.4× from the V100 to the B200 in seven years (the fixed-precision gain noted earlier), because frontier devices adopt new process nodes and tensor formats first. A fleet on a 4-year refresh cycle therefore gains about 2× in peak arithmetic per watt each cycle on the broad trend. Peak ratios bound what a refresh can deliver, and only measurements at the workload level decide how much of it a given fleet realizes.

The dashed line is a least-squares fit across all devices; the four GPUs of table 2 are circled and labeled. The ratio compares arithmetic ceilings, not measured energy per workload. Faster per-chip arithmetic leaves a cluster stalled if inter-chip collectives still have to traverse host CPUs and general-purpose PCIe switches. Google’s TPU trajectory attacked that bottleneck directly by treating the multi-rack pod, rather than the individual chip, as its unit of design from its second generation onward. While GPUs emphasize peak per-chip throughput and software flexibility (CUDA), every TPU chip since TPU v2 integrates dedicated inter-chip interconnect (ICI) links that route traffic directly between accelerators without touching the host CPU.
The generation sequence shows how that pod-first design moved from inference to training. After the inference-only TPU v1 of the origin story, TPU v2 (2017) and TPU v3 (2018) shifted the architecture toward training. They added bfloat16 (BF16), which avoids the dynamic range problems of standard FP16, and they scaled the pod concept until a TPU v3 pod joined 1,024 chips with about 126 PFLOP/s of aggregate BF16 peak. TPU v4 (2021) extended the same logic into the network itself. It added an optical circuit switch so the physical topology could be reconfigured for different workloads, introduced SparseCore units that accelerate embedding lookups, and raised per-chip BF16 throughput to 275 TFLOP/s.
The TPU v5p (2023) continued this pod-scale design for high-end training. It features 459 TFLOP/s of BF16 compute, 95 GB of HBM2e with 2,760 GB/s memory bandwidth, and 1,200 GB/s bidirectional ICI bandwidth per chip. The ICI figure matters for hardware selection because collectives such as AllReduce run over those links. AllReduce combines values such as gradient sums across a group of accelerators and returns the result to every participant. AllReduce develops the complexity model and algorithm choices that determine when those exchanges limit training throughput. The pod-first design took shape over successive TPU generations (table 3).

The GPU and TPU lines follow two design philosophies (table 1, table 3). GPU evolution packs more arithmetic, in ever lower-precision Tensor Core formats, onto one package, and turns to chiplets once a single die reaches its size limit. TPU evolution treats the pod as the product. Per-chip arithmetic matters, but inter-chip bandwidth and reconfigurability decide how much of it a large training job can use. Both lines combine local computation with memory and interconnect improvements; they place those resources differently. The warehouse-scale perspective of The shift to the warehouse-scale computer treats chip throughput, collective bandwidth, and reconfigurability as parts of one system (Barroso et al. 2019), so the useful comparison is how each candidate sustains the intended workload across that complete system.



Both lines concentrate their peak arithmetic in specialized matrix units, called Tensor Cores on NVIDIA GPUs and Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs) on Google TPUs. A Tensor Core executes matrix-multiply-accumulate instructions of the form \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination = \GemmLeftOperand\times \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\) on small tile matrices, concentrating the dominant neural-network operation in dedicated hardware that supplies most of the chip’s peak arithmetic.
With 528 Tensor Cores across the chip (4 per SM, 132 SMs), the H100 reaches its 989 TFLOP/s dense FP16/BF16 peak. The important systems point is the architectural specialization rather than the exact per-cycle instruction accounting. The die dedicates a large fraction of its arithmetic area to dense tiled matrix operations rather than general-purpose scalar execution.
Google’s MXUs organize multiply-accumulate units into the systolic array introduced with the TPU above. In the MXU’s weight-stationary dataflow, a weight tile stays resident in the array while activations stream through it. Every operand fetched from memory is therefore reused by an entire row or column of cells, which is the reuse that a Tensor Core kernel obtains by staging tiles in shared memory and registers. Each TPU v5p chip contains two TPU cores (which Google calls TensorCores, a name unrelated to NVIDIA’s Tensor Cores) with four \(128{\times}128\) MXUs each, together providing 459 TFLOP/s of BF16 throughput. Approaching that peak requires compatible tile shapes and a sustained operand supply; pipeline fill, partial tiles, and dependencies can leave cells idle. Vector and scalar units handle other operations, so complete-workload efficiency depends on how computation maps across the accelerator.
For our 175B model, compiler and kernel support determine how much work reaches the specialized arithmetic units. CUDA kernels can combine matrix operations with thread-level work, while XLA maps the computation graph onto the TPU dataflow. In either stack, fusion keeps intermediate results in registers or shared memory instead of repeatedly writing them to HBM. Sustained throughput therefore depends on operation coverage and data reuse as well as the matrix units themselves.

Definition 2.1: Tensor core
Tensor Core is a specialized ML accelerator hardware unit that performs a fused matrix-multiply-accumulate operation \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination = \GemmLeftOperand\times \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\) on small tiles (for example, \(16{\times}8{\times}16\) in BF16) as a single hardware instruction, delivering dramatically higher throughput than general-purpose CUDA cores by trading programmability for fixed-function matrix arithmetic.

Significance: Tensor Cores provide the bulk of the H100’s 989 TFLOP/s FP16/BF16 peak (and ~1,979 TFLOP/s at FP8), roughly 14.8× the ~67 TFLOP/s delivered by CUDA (vector) cores alone. This comparison changes both the execution unit and precision. Reductions and element-wise operations in layer normalization or softmax require a different performance model; their throughput is not a fixed fraction of the matrix peak.
Distinction: A Tensor Core is a fixed-function matrix-multiply-accumulate unit, not a faster general-purpose core. CUDA cores execute arbitrary scalar and vector work; Tensor Cores execute only the tiled \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination = \GemmLeftOperand\times \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\) primitive, which is why peak throughput and delivered throughput diverge so sharply by workload.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that all GPU operations benefit from Tensor Cores. Operations must map to the \(\MatrixMultiplyDestination = \GemmLeftOperand\times \GemmRightOperand+ \GemmOutputMatrix\) tile computation to use those units. Element-wise activations, normalization, and embedding lookups have different execution and data-access demands. A fixed 10–30\(\times\) penalty per FLOP is not a workload-independent model for their runtime.

Across the whole spectrum, from CPU to custom ASIC, the architectures differ in arithmetic core, execution model, and memory control (table 4). For the 175B running model, the choice among these columns is not purely about peak FLOP/s. A research lab experimenting with novel architectures weekly can justify the GPU’s generality tax by its flexibility. An organization deploying a fixed Transformer at scale for years may find that the TPU’s dataflow efficiency or a custom ASIC’s power advantage dominates total cost. The accelerator spectrum is ultimately an economic question of how much flexibility can be surrendered, given the stability of the workload. Even when the H100’s arithmetic engine reaches 1,979 TFLOP/s in its advertised low-precision mode, eligible operations approach that throughput only when data reaches the compute units fast enough. Accelerator selection therefore requires a second comparison, between the workload’s data demand and the memory system that feeds the arithmetic.

Self-Check: Question

A hardware vendor transitions their next-generation accelerator from a monolithic \(800\text{ mm}^2\) die to a dual-die chiplet architecture (such as the NVIDIA B200 with an equivalent area of about \(1{,}700\text{ mm}^2\)) connected on a single package. What physical constraint is this transition primarily designed to bypass, and what trade-off does it introduce?

It bypasses the memory wall by moving all memory on-chip, but introduces warp divergence because threads must synchronize across the die boundary.
It bypasses the photolithographic reticle limit (\(\approx 858\text{ mm}^2\)) and improves manufacturing yield, but introduces a die-to-die interconnect that is slower than a continuous on-die mesh.
It bypasses the maximum TDP limit of a single package by separating thermal loads into different server chassis, but requires developers to write separate CUDA kernels for each chiplet.
It bypasses the communication wall by replacing electrical copper signaling with optical waveguides, but increases the generality tax of control logic.

A research lab frequently experiments with novel, custom attention patterns and dynamic sparsity, while a production platform team trains a fixed standard Transformer at massive scale for months. Compare the systems trade-offs of choosing GPUs (CUDA) versus TPUs (XLA) for these two organizational teams.
Comparing the V100 and B200 at dense FP16 separates peak throughput growth from growth in throughput per TDP watt. Which statement correctly captures that difference and its infrastructure consequence?

Peak throughput per TDP watt grew faster than peak throughput, allowing higher-density clusters to ignore power delivery.
Both peak throughput and power efficiency scaled linearly at exactly the same rate, confirming that Dennard scaling remains fully active in modern 4nm nodes.
Peak dense FP16 throughput grew about 18 times while peak throughput per TDP watt grew about 5.4 times, so facilities must accommodate higher device power as well as greater arithmetic capacity.
Peak throughput plateaued after Volta (V100), meaning all recent performance gains stem exclusively from host CPU software optimizations.

The area and energy devoted by a processor to capabilities outside the dominant neural network matrix-multiplication workload, such as out-of-order scheduling, branch prediction, and complex hardware caches, is called the ____.
Arrange the following processor architectures in ascending order of the approximate percentage of their die area devoted strictly to arithmetic units (from lowest arithmetic die allocation to highest): (1) Google TPU (systolic array), (2) Purpose-built custom ASIC, (3) General-purpose server CPU, (4) NVIDIA GPU (with Tensor Cores).
