title: 2 Compute Infrastructure
text:
That comparison between arithmetic supply and data delivery exposes a structural divergence: because transistor scaling has multiplied logic throughput far faster than off-chip interconnects can supply operands, specialized matrix units routinely spend more time waiting for bytes than executing math. This divergence is the memory wall (Wulf and McKee 1995), and the weight and activation streams of large neural networks make memory bandwidth rather than peak compute the governing constraint across major inference and training regimes.

Wulf, Wm. A., and Sally A. McKee. 1995. “Hitting the Memory Wall: Implications of the Obvious.” ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 23 (1): 20–24. https://doi.org/10.1145/216585.216588.

↪ The diagnostic table that maps memory-bound, compute-bound, and latency-bound symptoms to the optimizations that help is developed in Bottleneck diagnostic.

Single-request inference on our 175B running model turns that divergence into a user-visible delay. Its weights occupy 350 GB in FP16. In dense autoregressive decode at batch size 1, each generated token uses all of those weights, whose footprint far exceeds on-chip storage, so every token must stream them in from memory. Suppose, hypothetically, that one H100 could hold them. Streaming the whole 350 GB through that device’s HBM at about 3.35 TB/s takes over 100 ms per token, long enough to be a perceptible pause between generated words. No real H100 holds the model, so the figure is a floor on bandwidth demand rather than a prediction of deployed latency, but it shows that the memory wall is a delay a user can notice, not an abstract architectural ratio.
Three levers lower that floor. Sharding spreads the weights across more memory paths, so each path streams fewer bytes. Quantization shrinks the bytes themselves. Reuse lets each fetched byte feed more arithmetic, which HBM’s bandwidth and on-chip tiling make possible. The Roofline Model, recapped for one machine in The roofline bound, tests whether the resulting data supply can feed the arithmetic units. Its ridge point, peak arithmetic divided by memory bandwidth, is the number of operations a kernel must perform per byte fetched before arithmetic rather than memory becomes the limit. The ridge point recurs throughout the analysis below, and section 2.3.2 evaluates it for the H100. Where each architecture places its bytes sets how much bandwidth those levers can draw on (figure 6), because moving the active working set closer to arithmetic increases available bandwidth while reducing the capacity that can reside there.














Figure 6: Accelerator Memory Tiers: Peak memory bandwidth and capacity separate local-SRAM designs (solid stars), HBM accelerators (half-tone filled circles), and edge and shared-LPDDR devices (hollow squares); all three are memory, so they share one hue and differ by marker. The dotted arrow marks the design trade-off: moving data closer to compute raises bandwidth but reduces capacity.



Accelerators do not line up along a single performance axis; they fall into structural clusters according to where each architecture places its bytes (figure 6). Edge devices in the lower band keep memory cheap and compact, but their bandwidth remains constrained, and the devices of Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) sit in that corner. On each device, the binding limit is the power envelope that bounds compute. A phone-class device sustains only 2 W to 3 W, while one H100’s thermal envelope is about 233× larger. A federated fleet therefore grows by adding devices rather than by moving up the memory tiers, and at fleet scale, as Three systems archetypes noted, communication and which devices participate in each round limit progress as well.
Within the data center tiers, HBM moves memory onto the accelerator package, buying enough capacity and enough bandwidth for active model state. Local-SRAM designs push the working set still closer to arithmetic, buying extraordinary bandwidth at the cost of much smaller resident capacity. That tier map explains why HBM is the next engineering response. HBM is not the fastest memory in the system, but it is the highest-bandwidth tier that can hold tens to hundreds of gigabytes next to the compute die.


↪ The power, thermal, and memory limits of phone-class edge devices are developed in Design Constraints.


An H100 can execute 1,979 TFLOP/s of low-precision matrix arithmetic, but the batch-1 weight-streaming example for our 175B model supplies too little reuse to approach that peak. In a bandwidth-floor model its arithmetic units would use well under 1 percent of the matrix peak while the weights stream in. The limiting resource is the speed of delivery relative to multiplication. Once weights fit through sharding or compression, the serving path must still deliver the active shards at the required rate. Additional arithmetic capacity alone does not raise a binding bandwidth ceiling. HBM increases that data supply within the package.2
2 HBM origin: Standardized by JEDEC in 2013 as a joint development between AMD and SK Hynix, originally for graphics cards. ML accelerators adopted HBM because neural networks share the same bandwidth-hungry, capacity-moderate access pattern as high-end rendering. Each HBM generation has roughly doubled bandwidth (128 GB/s in HBM1 to 1.2 TB/s per stack in HBM3e), yet the gap between memory bandwidth and arithmetic throughput continues to widen, which makes HBM a necessary but never sufficient response to the memory wall.3 SRAM energy (pJ/bit): Reading a bit from an 8–32 KB on-chip SRAM array costs roughly 0.15–0.3 pJ at the 45 nm node (Horowitz 2014), while fetching a bit from HBM2 costs about 4 pJ (O’Connor et al. 2017). This order-of-magnitude energy difference is the physical driver behind kernel fusion: every intermediate result kept in SRAM instead of written to HBM saves both time and significant power and thermal headroom.
Horowitz, Mark. 2014. “1.1 Computing’s Energy Problem (and What We Can Do about It).” 2014 IEEE International Solid-State Circuits Conference Digest of Technical Papers (ISSCC), 10–14. https://doi.org/10.1109/isscc.2014.6757323.

O’Connor, Mike, Niladrish Chatterjee, Donghyuk Lee, John Wilson, Aditya Agrawal, Stephen W. Keckler, and William J. Dally. 2017. “Fine-Grained DRAM: Energy-Efficient DRAM for Extreme Bandwidth Systems.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, 41–54. https://doi.org/10.1145/3123939.3124545.
HBM is the bottom on-package tier of the accelerator memory hierarchy, beneath the register file, the L1 and shared memory (SRAM),3 and the L2 cache. Aggregate bandwidth falls from hundreds of TB/s at the registers to the 3.35 TB/s of the H100’s 80 GB of HBM3, while capacity grows in the opposite direction.


↪ The single-accelerator memory hierarchy, from registers and shared memory through HBM to host memory, is collected for reference in Accelerator Memory Hierarchy.
The bandwidth gap between registers and HBM is approximately 100\(\times\), but that ratio alone does not specify stalled time. Utilization depends on arithmetic intensity, the floating-point operations performed per byte moved from memory (FLOP/byte), which tiling raises by staging matrix blocks on chip so that each fetched operand feeds many multiply-accumulate operations. Kernel-Level Levers collects tiling with the other kernel-level levers for reference.


↪ Arithmetic intensity and the boundary it draws between memory-bound and compute-bound work are collected for reference in Arithmetic Intensity Boundary.

Definition 2.2: HBM
HBM is a 3D-stacked DRAM architecture used by ML accelerators, with through-silicon vias (TSVs) connecting memory dies vertically within each stack and a wide interface across the package interposer connecting the stack to the processor.

Significance: HBM3 in the H100 delivers approximately 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth (roughly 17× DDR5’s ~200 GB/s) at roughly 4 pJ/bit for an HBM2-class stack (O’Connor et al. 2017) vs. roughly 20 pJ/bit for off-package DRAM (Horowitz 2014). This bandwidth sets the \(\Bandwidth\) term of the single-machine iron law given in Iron Law Mapping. The H100’s FP16 ridge point is approximately \(989\,\text{TFLOP/s} / 3.35\,\text{TB/s} \approx 295\) FLOP/byte, so any operator with arithmetic intensity below 295 FLOP/byte (for example, single-request decode, which performs two FLOPs for every two-byte FP16 weight it reads) remains memory-bound even with HBM.
Distinction: Unlike socketed DDR memory, which communicates across centimeters of printed circuit board (PCB) trace, an HBM stack sits beside the processor on the package. Its micrometer-scale vertical connections can be 1,000\(\times\) shorter than board traces, but the complete processor-to-memory path also crosses the interposer. The wide, short on-package interface raises bandwidth without relying on a proportionate increase in per-pin signaling rate.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that HBM solves the memory wall. HBM moves the wall rather than eliminating it. From the V100 (900 GB/s with 125 TFLOP/s FP16) to the H100 (3.35 TB/s with 989 TFLOP/s FP16), peak arithmetic \((\PeakRate)\) grew faster than HBM bandwidth.



Traditional DDR memory connects to the processor through pins on the edge of a printed circuit board. Each DIMM communicates over a 64-bit bus, and even with multiple channels (8 channels is typical for a high-end server CPU), a modern server tops out at roughly 200 GB/s of aggregate memory bandwidth.
The physical distance from the DIMM slot to the processor die is measured in centimeters, and every centimeter of copper trace introduces capacitance, signal attenuation, and energy loss. At DDR5 data rates (4,800–6,400 MT/s per pin), the signal conditioning circuits must compensate for significant channel impairment, consuming substantial power per bit transferred. Increasing the data rate on these long traces requires progressively more power for signal conditioning, creating a diminishing-returns curve that DDR5 is already approaching.
HBM sidesteps that board-level degradation through 2.5D integration (figure 7). Instead of driving signals horizontally across centimeters of motherboard trace over a narrow 64-bit bus, it stacks DRAM dies vertically and places the stack beside the processor on a silicon interposer.






Figure 7: HBM 3D-Stacked Architecture: Left: high-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies on a base logic die, links them vertically with through-silicon vias (TSVs), and places the stack on a silicon interposer beside the GPU die, so each stack reaches the GPU over a 1,024-bit interface only millimeters long. Right: DDR5 instead sits on a DIMM across the motherboard, reached over a 64-bit channel through centimeters of board trace. The wider, shorter path raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit, but HBM bandwidth and capacity remain finite, so the memory wall moves rather than disappears.



The vertical stacking changes how bandwidth scales. Rather than pushing signals faster through long copper traces (the DDR approach, which has diminishing returns), HBM multiplies the number of parallel signal paths. A single HBM stack bonds 8–12 DRAM dies, threading thousands of through-silicon vias (TSVs),4 copper pillars etched through each die, to form a 1024-bit-wide interface per stack, compared to 64 bits for a DDR5 channel. This 16\(\times\) wider interface is the main source of HBM’s bandwidth advantage; HBM need not exceed DDR’s per-pin signaling rate. The processor and HBM stacks share a package and communicate across the silicon interposer, shortening the electrical path relative to socketed DIMMs. This packaging primarily improves bandwidth and energy per transferred bit; it does not by itself imply that complete HBM load latency is only a few nanoseconds.
4 TSV (through-silicon via): A vertical copper pillar, 5–10 micrometers in diameter, etched through a silicon die to connect stacked layers. Originally developed for CMOS image sensors in smartphone cameras, TSVs enabled HBM by replacing centimeters of PCB trace with tens of micrometers of vertical silicon, roughly a 1,000\(\times\) shorter signal path, which is what lets a stack expose a 1024-bit interface within an accelerator’s power budget.The shorter path also lowers transfer energy per bit by roughly 5\(\times\), from approximately 20 pJ/bit for off-package DRAM (Horowitz 2014) to about 4 pJ/bit for HBM2 (O’Connor et al. 2017), because the short interconnects present less capacitance and need less driving current. The same reduced loading lets the 1024-bit interface run at moderate per-pin rates instead of the high-power signaling that long board traces require. Propagation delay shrinks by only a fraction of a nanosecond, small next to the DRAM array and controller delays that dominate access latency, so HBM’s advantage lies in bandwidth and energy per bit rather than in latency. Modern accelerators therefore widen the memory interface across an interposer rather than driving off-package pins faster; set side by side in table 5, the bandwidth, interface-width, and energy differences all trace to placement and width rather than to faster signaling.

Checkpoint 2.1: HBM and the memory wall
These questions check whether the physical benefits of 3D-stacked memory are clear:

This bandwidth advantage comes at a price. HBM costs approximately $10–$15 per GB, compared to roughly $3 per GB for DDR5 server memory. For an H100 with 80 GB of HBM3, the memory alone represents approximately $800–$1,200 of the accelerator’s manufacturing cost. For a B200 with 180 GB of HBM3e, the memory cost rises to $1,800–$2,700 per accelerator, making HBM one of the most expensive components in the system.
Packaging adds manufacturing stages beyond fabricating the memory dies. The stacking process includes thinning, alignment, bonding, and vertical interconnection, so usable stack yield depends on both the dies and their assembly. Those yields compound, because a 12-high HBM3e stack is usable only if every die and every bonding step succeeds, so even small per-step losses multiply into a complete-stack yield below that of a single DRAM die. The silicon interposer must also accommodate the processor and multiple HBM stacks. With each stack occupying roughly 100 mm², an illustrative large package that pairs a reticle-sized processor with several stacks needs an interposer exceeding 1,000 mm². Testing, repair provisions, and assembly yield all affect cost; die count alone does not determine how many complete stacks remain usable. Supply is a constraint as well as cost: HBM production is concentrated among a few manufacturers whose stacking steps need specialized equipment, so memory availability can pace accelerator delivery, a lead-time risk that Capacity lead time as operational risk plans for.
For our 175B model, this cost-capacity trade-off explains why accelerators typically offer 80 GB to 192 GB of HBM while the host server provides 512 GB to 2 TB of DDR. The fast memory holds state touched every step (weight shards, activations, gradients, and usually the sharded optimizer state), while the cheap memory holds staging buffers, data loading queues, and colder state that capacity pressure forces out, such as offloaded optimizer shards.
The boundary between what resides in HBM and what resides in DDR is a critical design parameter for training frameworks, and managing this boundary efficiently is one of the key challenges addressed by ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) sharding and offloading strategies. Sharding divides optimizer, gradient, and parameter state across workers; offloading places colder state in host DRAM or Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) when HBM capacity is the binding limit. Getting this boundary wrong in either direction is costly. Placing too much data in HBM wastes expensive capacity, while placing too much in DDR creates bandwidth stalls that idle the arithmetic units.


↪ Memory-efficient sharding of optimizer, gradient, and parameter state is developed in Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP.

Lighthouse 2.1: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): The capacity wallArchetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) has so far exposed the bandwidth side of the memory wall. Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) exposes the capacity side, the boundary between fast and cheap memory just examined. An embedding table of 10 TB or more cannot fit into the 80 GB HBM of a single H100, nor can it fit into the aggregate HBM of a single 8-GPU node (640 GB nameplate, about 687 GB in decimal bytes). Capacity alone requires at least 15 such nodes before accounting for replication, hot-table headroom, and bandwidth balance. Sharding makes lookup routing and result exchange part of the request path. An AllToAll exchange sends distinct portions to different participants; its traffic depends on the batch and placement. Clearing the capacity limit therefore creates a second question about bandwidth and latency.




Data movement also dominates energy. At 3.97 pJ per bit, the HBM2 access energy that O’Connor et al. estimate (2017), reading one 16-bit operand costs about 64 pJ. One FP16 multiply-accumulate costs roughly 1.5 pJ at the 45 nm node (Horowitz 2014). The raw fetch therefore costs about 42× the arithmetic it feeds, until tiling and reuse spread it across many operations. From off-package DRAM at about 20 pJ per bit, the same fetch costs roughly 5× more again. That ratio is why accelerators devote so much silicon to reuse, and why the levers that cut bytes, such as quantization and fusion, improve power efficiency as well as speed. The Physics of Data Movement extends the per-boundary accounting to collective communication, and Arithmetic intensity and energy roofline turns these per-byte costs into an energy roofline.


Data movement dwarfs arithmetic in energy cost.




HBM has grown alongside model sizes, but far more slowly than parameter counts, which is why capacity pressure keeps pushing models across devices. Each generation increases the number of stacked dies, the signaling rate per pin, and the total capacity per stack. The projected HBM4 generation in table 6 marks the scaling boundary, doubling the interface width from 1024 to 2048 bits for the first time since HBM’s introduction, because pin-rate increases alone no longer sustain the required bandwidth growth. The wider bus also needs more interposer area for routing, one reason accelerator packages have grown as bandwidth targets rise.

The generations in table 6 move both capacity and bandwidth for our running example, and the step to HBM3e matters most. Using decimal bytes consistently, an A100 with 85.9 GB of HBM2e holds 24.5 percent of our 175B model’s FP16 weights. An H100 with 85.9 GB of HBM3 holds the same fraction while delivering the data 64 percent faster. A B200 with 193.3 GB of HBM3e raises the resident share to 55.2 percent at about 8 TB/s. Because even HBM3e leaves nearly half the model outside a single package, multiple accelerators are still needed in a node (section 2.5).
Quantization changes the capacity story for inference. Storing weights in INT8 or INT4 halves or quarters the footprint, and section 2.8.1 works through how many accelerators the running model then needs. The capacity constraints that drive multi-accelerator nodes for training, where FP16 or BF16 precision is typically required, are substantially relaxed for inference, where INT8 or INT4 quantization is often acceptable, which is one reason training and inference infrastructure have different optimal configurations.
Aggregate package bandwidth scales with the number of HBM stacks that can sit beside the processor die on the silicon interposer. The H100 has 5 HBM3 stacks, each providing approximately 670 GB/s, for a total of 3.35 TB/s aggregate bandwidth. A B200-class Blackwell GPU package uses 8 HBM3e stacks for an aggregate of about 8 TB/s. The number of stacks is constrained by the interposer area available for HBM placement. Each HBM stack occupies approximately 100 mm² of interposer area, and the total interposer must accommodate both the processor die(s) and all HBM stacks. Larger interposers allow more HBM stacks (and therefore higher bandwidth and capacity) but are more expensive and harder to manufacture.
The interposer area constraint creates a concrete design tension. Making the processor die larger (more Tensor Cores, more SMs) leaves less interposer area for HBM stacks, potentially reducing bandwidth. Making the processor die smaller (fewer Tensor Cores) frees interposer area for more HBM but reduces peak compute throughput. The optimal balance depends on the target workload’s position relative to the ridge point. Compute-bound workloads, whose arithmetic intensity sits above it, benefit from a larger processor die (more Tensor Cores). Bandwidth-bound workloads below it benefit from more HBM stacks, so a workload’s arithmetic intensity predicts which side of the balance it falls on before any silicon is committed.



Adding or upgrading HBM stacks raises both memory capacity (how many gigabytes the package can store) and memory bandwidth (how many terabytes per second it can deliver), which answer two separate procurement questions. Capacity determines whether a model’s weights fit, with headroom for the remaining live state; bandwidth limits how fast the model can run when data movement sets the critical path. Dense autoregressive decode at batch size 1 isolates the second question because each weight serves only one token before the next weight load. The next three calculations step down from the running model to Llama-3 70B. Its FP16 weights span two H100s rather than the running model’s five, and the H200 comparison that follows needs a model whose serving behavior a real memory upgrade can change; the arithmetic carries over to the 175B model by scaling the bytes.

Napkin Math 2.1: The physics of token latencyProblem: A weight-only model of batch-1 decode for Llama-3 70B uses 141.2 GB of FP16 weights. To isolate the two resource demands, assume hypothetical capacity sufficient to hold them while retaining one H100-equivalent compute rate and HBM path. Which term gives the larger time estimate: arithmetic or weight transfer?

Compute time: Each token requires \(2 \times 70.6 \times 10^9 = 1.41 \times 10^{11}\) floating-point operations. At 989 TFLOP/s of FP16/BF16 Tensor Core peak throughput, the arithmetic takes \(\IronLawComputeTime \approx \text{\textbf{0.14}}\text{ ms}\).
Memory time: Loading 141.2 GB of weights from HBM at 3.35 TB/s takes \(\IronLawMemoryTime \approx \text{\textbf{42.1}}\text{ ms}\).

Systems insight: The memory term accounts for 99.7 percent of the sum of these two idealized times. That ratio identifies a bandwidth-dominated estimate; it is not a measurement of cycles spent idle. Raising compute throughput alone barely changes this estimate. A faster memory path reduces the weight-transfer floor, while actual token latency also includes the other memory traffic, communication, and execution costs omitted here.


Holding that weight load fixed and changing only the memory system shows how directly each HBM generation moves the floor. For the same 70.6B FP16 model, with 141 GB of weights, the single-path streaming floor is roughly 141 GB/2.04 TB/s = 69.2 ms at A100-class bandwidth. At H100-class bandwidth (the notebook’s memory term) it is 141 GB/3.35 TB/s = 42.1 ms, and at B200-class bandwidth it is 141 GB/8 TB/s = 17.7 ms. The floor falls nearly in proportion to each bandwidth gain. As in the notebook, each case isolates one accelerator-equivalent HBM path even though the full FP16 model does not fit on one A100 or H100. These bounds screen memory bandwidth against a latency target; whether token latency improves by the same ratio depends on the other work on the request’s critical path.
The same floor at trillion-parameter scale shows the limit of bandwidth gains alone, even at the projected 12–16 TB/s of an HBM4-class package. A dense 1T-parameter model requires roughly 2 TB of FP16 weight storage. Streaming those weights through one B200-class path at about 8 TB/s gives 2000 GB/8 TB/s = 250 ms for one batch-1 weight load. At the assumed 16 TB/s, that floor becomes roughly 125 ms. Neither path has been shown to hold the full model, and even the faster floor limits a single path to about eight tokens per second for one request. A responsive trillion-parameter service must therefore split its weights across many memory paths, shrink them with reduced precision, or both; which combination depends on the latency target and the quality the reduced precision preserves. The cleanest test of how far a memory upgrade moves real latency compares two accelerators that differ only in their memory system.

Napkin Math 2.2: The memory wall: H100 vs. H200Comparing the NVIDIA H100 against the H200 isolates a memory-system upgrade for large language models (LLMs). While both chips share the same compute cores (same peak TFLOP/s), the H200 provides 1.4× higher memory bandwidth and 1.8× more HBM capacity.
This comparison uses a Llama 3 model with 70.6B parameters, sequence length 2,048, and batch size 1. Both cases retain FP16 weights and the hypothetical capacity convention of notebook 2.1: each streams the complete payload through one accelerator-equivalent HBM path, even though it cannot fit on one H100. The comparison isolates path latency rather than establishing two feasible single-device deployments.
The reported speedup comes from a serving-latency model whose inter-token latency adds two terms to the weight-streaming time, the key-value cache reads for the request’s context and a fixed per-layer kernel-launch overhead, so it is not a raw bandwidth ratio alone. The weight-only estimate provides a comparison. Its memory term accounts for 99.7 percent of the summed compute and transfer times, so reducing that term suggests a gain near the HBM bandwidth ratio, 4.8 TB/s \(\div\) 3.35 TB/s \(\approx\) 1.4×.
Systems insight: For the modeled configuration, the latency model predicts an H200 speedup of 1.4× over the H100 despite equal peak arithmetic throughput. Its agreement with the bandwidth ratio supports the memory-bound diagnosis for this case. Changing batch size, context length, or partitioning requires evaluating the new configuration; the estimate does not establish one bottleneck for all autoregressive models.


The modeled memory-time share, 99.7 percent in this example, indicates the memory-boundedness of this workload under the stated assumptions. A workload this memory-bound gains almost nothing from more TFLOP/s and nearly proportionally from more TB/s, which is what the H200 comparison shows, so bandwidth per dollar rather than peak arithmetic is the useful procurement metric for this regime. A measured execution timeline is still needed to determine how much transfer overlaps computation and which delays remain exposed, which keeps a hardware-screening calculation separate from a performance forecast. For training workloads, reusing weights across more tokens can instead shift the constraint toward arithmetic throughput; the Roofline Model tests the compute and bandwidth ceilings for the actual operation and batch shape before either specification becomes a procurement metric.




The token latency calculation in notebook 2.1 makes memory bandwidth the relevant procurement metric for the batch-1 workload. The Roofline Model of Williams, Waterman, and Patterson (Williams et al. 2009) tests whether that diagnosis survives a change in batch shape, precision, or accelerator by relating the workload’s arithmetic intensity to the candidate accelerator’s compute and bandwidth ceilings.

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
For an H100 (989 TFLOP/s FP16, 3.35 TB/s HBM), the ridge point is about 295 FLOP/byte. Most LLM inference operators fall well below this threshold, which is why the roofline remains the first diagnostic tool for identifying whether more compute or more bandwidth will improve performance. The quantity that places a workload on the plot is the arithmetic intensity introduced with tiling above, written \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) in FLOP/byte.


↪ Placing measured kernels on the roofline by arithmetic intensity is developed in Drilling into the step.


Decode sits deep in the memory-bound regime, far below the ridge.

As the single-machine recap in The roofline bound derives, the Roofline Model expresses the maximum achievable performance of a workload as the lesser of two ceilings:
\[ \text{Achievable FLOP/s} = \min\left(\PeakRate,\ \Bandwidth \times \ArithmeticIntensity\right)  \tag{1}\]
In equation 1, below the ridge point the sloped bandwidth ceiling, which grows with \(\ArithmeticIntensity\), is the lower one; above it the flat compute roof binds, and a measured kernel can sit below either.

Definition 2.3: Ridge point
Ridge point is the ML accelerator arithmetic intensity where the memory bandwidth ceiling meets the compute ceiling \((\RooflineRidgePoint = \frac{\PeakRate}{\Bandwidth})\).

Significance: It is the accelerator’s efficiency threshold. Below the ridge point, bandwidth supplies the lower modeled ceiling \((\Bandwidth)\); above it, arithmetic supplies the lower ceiling \((\PeakRate)\).
Distinction: Unlike peak FLOP/s, which describes only the horizontal ceiling, the ridge point describes the balance between arithmetic and memory delivery in the architecture. A rising ridge point over hardware generations indicates that compute is growing faster than bandwidth, making utilization harder.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that an accelerator has a single ridge point. In reality, it varies by precision: because \(\PeakRate\) is higher for INT8 than FP32 while \(\Bandwidth\) is constant, the ridge point for INT8 is much higher, requiring more data reuse to saturate the hardware.



Machine learning workloads land in different regions of the roofline plot depending on the operation and the batch configuration, not on the model family. Single-request autoregressive decode streams the full weight tensor (two bytes per parameter in FP16) from HBM to perform two floating-point operations per parameter, an arithmetic intensity of about 1 FLOP/byte, far below the H100’s ridge point of 295 FLOP/byte. The token-latency calculation in notebook 2.1 showed that the arithmetic finishes in microseconds while the weight movement takes milliseconds. Every other regime in table 7 comes from reusing each byte fetched from HBM across more operations. Decode also reads the key-value (KV) cache, the stored attention keys and values of earlier tokens, and because each request has its own cache, batching does not amortize that traffic.



Table 7: Roofline Placement by Workload Phase: Language-model intensities count only weight traffic at the HBM level, the same idealization used for figure 8, against an H100 FP16 ridge point of 295 FLOP/byte; the convolution value is a representative scenario figure rather than a derived count. Attention is not plotted in the figure because its placement depends on shape. Measured placement must also count activation, key-value cache, and optimizer traffic.

The table’s intensities are idealized reuse counts that classify an execution phase and batch shape, not a model family, and tensor layout, fusion, precision, and cache residency move the measured point. Which kernel-level change then helps, more reuse and fewer bytes below the ridge or a cheaper operation above it, is a diagnosis that Drilling into the step develops.
A measured workload point below its roofline ceiling needs further diagnosis. Dependencies, insufficient parallel work, irregular accesses, synchronization, and power limits can all prevent a kernel from approaching that ceiling. The gap identifies a question for profiling; it does not establish that software optimization can recover the entire difference.
Whole phases spread even wider than individual operators. The idealized intensities of decode and training differ by 2,048×, which is why the same hardware shows widely different utilization across them. Batch-1 decode sits near 1 FLOP/byte, far left of the ridge and deeply bound by memory bandwidth, while large-batch training near 2,048 FLOP/byte crosses the ridge and reaches the compute roof (figure 8). The training point assumes that 2048 tokens on one accelerator share each weight read, the local reuse that a large global batch alone does not guarantee, so it counts tokens rather than sequences and local rather than global batch. It is a contrast case, not a universal intensity for training. Actual placement requires counting bytes at the memory level being modeled and accounting for tensor shapes, fusion, and reuse.














Figure 8: The H100 Roofline Landscape: Attainable FP16 throughput is the lower of two ceilings, the memory-bandwidth slope (blue) and the compute roof (orange), which meet at the dashed ridge point. Each dot places a representative workload by its arithmetic intensity; workloads left of the ridge stay capped by bandwidth however much compute the chip offers, and only those to its right can approach peak throughput.



The table’s batching rows can be turned into a utilization bound. For inference serving, batching multiple requests together moves the workload point rightward on the plot, because each weight read is multiplied against more activations. Under the weight-traffic-only bound, batch-1 decode on an H100 can use at most 0.34 percent of the FP16 peak. At batch size 64, each weight read from HBM serves every request in the batch, the intensity rises to 64 FLOP/byte, and the bound climbs to about 22 percent of peak, a 64× gain that still leaves the workload below the ridge. The linear growth holds only in this approximation; key-value cache traffic, which batching does not amortize, activation traffic, and capacity limits lower both figures in practice. The gain has a cost. Waiting to assemble a batch can introduce queuing latency, although a serving policy can instead dispatch a smaller batch when a latency deadline approaches. Serving systems must carefully balance this trade-off between throughput (larger batches, higher utilization) and latency (smaller batches, faster response per request).
For fleet procurement, the roofline is a screening test rather than a throughput forecast. It rules out upgrades that raise a nonbinding ceiling, while the gap below the relevant ceiling identifies work still needed in software or communication. Collected into a single procurement comparison for the running model, the two ends of the landscape give opposite hardware answers, and that diagnostic becomes most valuable when a proposed upgrade changes the wrong ceiling. Memory capacity and bandwidth therefore screen out infeasible accelerator choices, while for the candidates that remain, fleet sizing also needs a sustained compute rate at a precision the workload can use, within the node’s memory budget, the interconnect, and the facility power envelope.

Example 2.2: Roofline analysis: Training vs. inferenceScenario: An engineering team evaluates hardware choices for serving (decode batch size 1) vs. training (batch size 2048) a 175B parameter model on an H100 GPU (ridge point 295.2 FLOP/byte).
Diagnosis: The weight-traffic model gives single-token decode arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity=\) 1 FLOP/byte \(\ll\) 295.2 FLOP/byte, bounding throughput to 0.34 percent of the selected peak FLOP/s. The assumed training reuse raises intensity to \(\ArithmeticIntensity=\) 2,048 FLOP/byte \(\gg\) 295.2 FLOP/byte, making arithmetic the lower roofline ceiling. This placement identifies the relevant bound without establishing achieved throughput.
Systems lesson: Hardware selection starts with the phase’s arithmetic intensity and memory footprint. The modeled training phase benefits from arithmetic capacity, while batch-1 decode benefits from bandwidth. Sustained throughput at the required quality and latency determines whether either advantage justifies its cost.



Checkpoint 2.2: Roofline diagnosis
A team is serving a 13B-parameter model at batch size 1 on an H100 and observing 25 ms per token. The profile shows low tensor-core utilization during decode.

Arithmetic intensity: estimate the arithmetic intensity of the workload.
Peak-throughput upgrade: explain what the roofline estimate can establish about a higher peak-TFLOP/s accelerator and what requires measured execution.
Binding constraint: identify the profile measurements needed to distinguish exposed HBM transfers from communication, launch overhead, or insufficient parallel work before selecting an improvement.

title: 2 Compute Infrastructure
text:
A fleet sized from advertised matrix throughput can miss its training deadline when operations cannot use the advertised precision or keep the matrix units of section 2.2.5 busy. The relevant hardware contract includes both the eligible matrix operations and their sustained contribution to the complete workload.
Tensor Core precision support widened with each generation traced in section 2.2.3, from FP16 on Volta to FP8 on Hopper, because neural network training and inference tolerate lower numerical precision than was once assumed. Transformer Engine recipes and FP8 autocast decide which supported operations run in FP8, recording tensor ranges and applying scale factors so values fit the format, but they do not establish that a layer is numerically safe at that precision. Precision policy therefore remains a software configuration and validation decision, which FP8 for distributed training develops for training.
The relationship between numerical precision and hardware throughput matters for infrastructure planning because it directly affects how much useful work each accelerator can perform per second. Lower precision representations use fewer bits per number, which has two compounding benefits: more numbers fit in the same HBM capacity (reducing memory pressure), and the arithmetic units can process more operations per cycle (increasing throughput). Each format an H100-class accelerator supports unlocks a different dense peak rate and plays a usual role in training or inference (table 8).

TF32 preserves the FP32 exponent width but reduces mantissa precision so Tensor Cores can accelerate common FP32 training workloads.

For training, many workloads use the standard mixed-precision recipe, which decouples storage from arithmetic precision by keeping FP32 master weights while the forward and backward passes run in BF16 or FP16 at full Tensor Core throughput. The node memory examples in section 2.5.3 assume retained FP16 gradients; implementations that retain a full FP32 accumulation buffer must add that buffer to their peak budget. The FP8 recipes described earlier extend the same decoupling one step further, running eligible matrix operations in eight bits while the master weights stay in FP32.


↪ The byte widths of each format and the per-parameter memory of mixed-precision training are collected for reference in Numeric Precision and Training Memory.
The practical implication for fleet design is that peak TFLOP/s specifications are precision-dependent. The H100 delivers 989 TFLOP/s in FP16 but twice that (1,979 TFLOP/s) in FP8. FP8 therefore doubles the advertised arithmetic ceiling for supported operations on the same hardware. The complete training run gains less when communication, memory traffic, or higher-precision operations remain on the critical path. Precision engineering is therefore a primary optimization lever for infrastructure planners, alongside its effect on model accuracy.
Approaching peak throughput requires pipeline balance. Operand staging and reuse must supply the arithmetic units at the rate the operation requires. Kernel fusion and tiled attention such as FlashAttention improve that balance by keeping intermediate values on chip instead of making separate HBM round-trips, mechanisms that Kernel-Level Levers collects for reference. For our 175B model, the fleet-level gain depends on how much step time the affected kernels consume. A faster attention kernel shortens the step only in proportion to attention’s share of it, the same Amdahl accounting that bounds every partial speedup.


A training run budgeted for 1,000 GPU-hours from datasheet TFLOP/s will consume 2,500 GPU-hours in practice when the workload sustains only 40 percent of peak throughput. Infrastructure planning therefore separates peak throughput (the maximum rate for the vendor-specified operation and precision) from sustained throughput (what the complete workload delivers). Peak TFLOP/s assumes that eligible arithmetic units remain fed under the stated sparsity, precision, and clock conditions; it does not include memory stalls, ineligible operations, communication, or software overhead. Sustained fractions therefore vary with model shape, batch size, precision, implementation, and scale. The gap arises from several sources, each representing a different physical or software limitation.
Memory stalls occur when the Tensor Cores complete their current tile multiplication before the next tile has been loaded from HBM. Even with the H100’s 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, the Tensor Cores can consume data faster than HBM can deliver it for certain matrix dimensions, creating idle cycles while the arithmetic units wait for data.
Dependency stalls arise when one operation must complete before the next can begin, leaving some processing elements idle. In a Transformer layer, the attention computation must complete before the feed-forward network can begin, and the feed-forward computation must complete before the next layer’s attention can start. These sequential dependencies create brief periods where some hardware resources are unused, even within one accelerator. When the model is split into sequential stages on different accelerators (pipeline parallelism), the same dependencies become pipeline bubbles, idle slots in which a whole stage waits for its predecessor. Splitting each batch into microbatches reduces the waste by feeding later microbatches into stages that would otherwise wait. The term pipeline bubble refers only to this cross-device case, whose scheduling Distributed Training develops. At the infrastructure level, the lesson is that peak throughput assumes every unit stays busy, while real training includes dependency gaps that lower sustained utilization.
AllReduce operations used in tensor parallelism and gradient synchronization used in data parallelism can likewise delay computations that depend on their results; even when communication overlaps computation on separate streams, operations that depend on the collective output cannot proceed until the transfer completes. Kernel submission, memory allocation, and framework control also consume time, and when each kernel completes in microseconds, launch overhead of a similar size becomes a comparable share of the step that only a host-and-device execution trace can separate from slow arithmetic or memory access. Achieving high sustained utilization is therefore largely a matter of minimizing the time Tensor Cores spend idle between operations, which is why kernel fusion and specialized kernel libraries such as FlashAttention and the Transformer Engine exist.
The last source of the gap is the device itself, and no kernel change removes it. Device variation, sometimes called the silicon lottery, means that nominally identical accelerators sustain different clocks. Clock behavior also depends on the configured power limit, temperature, and workload, so a slow participant should not be diagnosed from its product label or frequency alone. In synchronous training, a participant that finishes dependent work late delays its whole process group. One device sustaining a clock about 2.5 percent below its peers can slow every synchronous step it joins by up to that fraction, because the other participants wait for it at each collective. Fleet management systems therefore track per-device sustained throughput and can move persistent underperformers to pools, such as inference serving, where they do not gate a synchronized group. Profiling must determine whether local arithmetic, memory, communication, or a power limit caused that delay before changing placement or replacing hardware.
Capacity planning must use a measured or conservatively modeled sustained rate, not the peak specification. A run estimated at 1,000 GPU-hours from peak FLOP/s requires \(1/\EfficiencyHw\) times that estimate when its measured utilization fraction is \(\EfficiencyHw\). Infrastructure teams track model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the useful model computation per second divided by the selected hardware peak, as the standard measure of \(\EfficiencyHw\), but comparisons remain meaningful only when model-FLOP conventions, precision, hardware peak, and system scale match.


↪ MFU as the measure of program goodput, one factor of fleet-level ML goodput, is developed in Program goodput and its measure.
The accelerator’s physics establish a concrete problem. Our 175B model requires 350 GB of memory for its weights alone in FP16, and Adam-style training state raises the requirement to multiple terabytes once optimizer moments, gradients, and activations are included. A single H100 provides 80 GB of HBM. No single accelerator can hold this model, an instance of the memory capacity gap (principle \(\ref{pri-memory-capacity-gap}\)), in which frontier memory requirements outgrow single-accelerator HBM. The system must expand to the next physical level: the node.

Self-Check: Question

An H100 advertises twice the dense arithmetic rate in FP8 that it advertises in FP16. A team sizes a training run’s GPU-hours by assuming the full FP8 rate. Which statement best describes the planning error?

FP8 halves the bytes per weight, so memory-bound phases also run exactly twice as fast and the plan is correct.
The FP8 rating is a ceiling for eligible matrix operations; ineligible operations, memory stalls, communication, and the need to validate the precision policy keep the sustained rate below it, so the plan must use a measured sustained rate.
FP8 Tensor Core rates apply only to inference, so a training plan must use the FP32 rate instead.
FP8 runs slower than FP16 on Tensor Cores because of scaling overhead, so the plan overestimates the time.

A training run is estimated at 1,000 GPU-hours from peak FLOP/s. Profiling a representative window shows a model FLOPs utilization (MFU) of 0.4. How many GPU-hours should the plan budget, and what must match before this MFU can be compared with another team’s figure?
True or False: In synchronous training, an accelerator that sustains a clock about 2.5 percent below its peers costs the job at most 2.5 percent of that one device’s throughput.
The standard mixed-precision recipe runs the forward and backward passes in BF16 or FP16 but keeps a full-precision FP32 copy of the parameters, called the ____ weights, so that updates much smaller than a weight are not lost to FP16 rounding.

See Answers →

title: 2 Compute Infrastructure
text:
The running model needs more memory than one accelerator provides. A node supplies several accelerators in one chassis, but each retains its own memory; dividing the work creates communication that the local fabric must sustain. Tensor parallelism divides an operation across accelerators, pipeline parallelism assigns successive model stages to different groups, and data parallelism assigns different training examples to model replicas whose updates must be combined. These strategies impose different traffic patterns, and the node’s internal fabric decides which of them it can carry at the speed the partition needs.
Aggregating accelerators solves the capacity problem only if the interconnect between them is fast enough that the group behaves as one machine rather than as several machines passing messages. The 175B model’s weights span at least five accelerators, and the full training state spans an entire 8-H100 node and more, so some model state must live on different chips. Depending on the partition, execution exchanges partial results, activations, gradients, or parameter shards. Whether those exchanges are cheap or ruinous depends on the local fabric, which is why the node is the first scale level where the accelerator’s specifications matter less than the wires between accelerators. The training system can combine tensor parallelism, optimizer sharding, and memory offload as needed to meet its capacity budget, and each strategy places a different demand on the interconnect.

Definition 2.4: Node
Node is the ML training cluster’s physical server chassis that aggregates multiple accelerators (typically 8) through a high-speed intra-node interconnect (NVLink or ICI), providing a physical packaging and failure boundary. The fast communication domain can coincide with one chassis or extend across several, depending on the fabric.

Significance: The NVLink bandwidth within a DGX H100 node reaches 900 GB/s bidirectional, or 450 GB/s per direction, while inter-node InfiniBand NDR provides 50 GB/s, a 9× per-direction gap that constrains where each parallelism strategy can run. For this DGX H100 topology, frequent tensor-parallel collectives favor the intra-node NVLink domain; pipeline parallelism can span nodes when the network sustains stage-boundary activation traffic. The node is also the primary failure domain: a single node failure in a bulk synchronous parallel training job, where workers advance in lockstep at step barriers, idles the entire cluster until recovery.
Distinction: Unlike a single accelerator (which provides fast HBM bandwidth but limited capacity), a node aggregates 8\(\times\) the HBM capacity and 8\(\times\) the compute of a single chip. That is enough to place large FP16 weight shards (8 \(\times\) 80 GB = 640 GB on DGX H100), but not enough to keep the full Adam training state in HBM.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that nodes in a distributed training job operate independently. In bulk synchronous parallel training, all nodes are synchronously coupled at every step barrier: a performance degradation on one node (from thermal throttling, a faulty NIC, or a slow storage read) stalls the entire cluster and drops overall MFU for the duration of that step.



Why not hold the overflow in host DRAM instead of wiring eight accelerators together? A server’s DDR5 channels supply ample capacity (512 GB to 2 TB per node) at a fraction of HBM’s cost, but their bandwidth is orders of magnitude too slow to feed Tensor Cores on the active forward and backward path. Pooling the HBM of eight accelerators inside one chassis keeps the active working set in high-bandwidth memory, with the crucial caveat that each accelerator’s HBM remains private to its own package. Software must shard or replicate tensors explicitly and invoke collectives or peer-to-peer transfers whenever an operation crosses device boundaries, so an eight-GPU node delivers 8\(\times\) aggregate capacity and 8\(\times\) aggregate compute without ever behaving like a single shared-memory processor.
The capacity arithmetic also explains the appeal of multiple packages. Holding a 175B model’s 350 GB of FP16 weights on one accelerator, at the example 17–24 GB per HBM stack, would require 350 GB spread across roughly 15–21 stacks. That exceeds the 5-stack H100 and 8-stack B200-class configurations used here. Such a package would need its own area, yield, power, and cooling analysis. Distributing capacity across 8 accelerators instead uses available packages and pays for communication between their private memories.


Placing a layer-by-layer tensor-parallel collective across a 50 GB/s inter-node link instead of a 450 GB/s intra-node link multiplies its transfer floor ninefold and stalls every accelerator in the group. Multi-accelerator systems are governed less by the number of chips than by the speed at which they can exchange data across physical boundaries. Data movement speed drops by orders of magnitude as it crosses package, board, and rack boundaries, each with a different physical medium, connector technology, and signaling constraint. This physical ordering of data transfer rates, from on-chip SRAM at the fast end to the wide-area network at the slow end, is the bandwidth hierarchy; this ordering dictates where in the hierarchy each type of parallelism can operate efficiently.
The hierarchy reflects the physical cost of distance. Shorter signal paths over denser wiring achieve higher throughput at lower energy per bit, so at each boundary the effective bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\) drops by roughly an order of magnitude while latency \((\Latency)\) rises. The exact size of each gap depends on link count, signaling, and the measurement boundary, but the gradient itself sets a scaling ceiling for distributed training. The common mistake is to treat all cluster communication as equal. Parallelism placement must be hierarchy-aware, because putting high-frequency synchronization such as tensor parallelism on a slow tier leaves the arithmetic units \((\PeakRate)\) waiting and collapses scaling efficiency \((\ScalingEfficiency)\).
The bandwidth hierarchy can be read as concentric zones around each accelerator (figure 9), losing 7.4\(\times\) to 9\(\times\) of bandwidth at each physical boundary on the way out through NVLink, InfiniBand, and remote storage. The innermost zone is the HBM on the same package, with terabytes per second of bandwidth and sub-microsecond access latency. The next zone holds the other accelerators in the node’s NVLink domain, reachable at hundreds of gigabytes per second per GPU with microsecond-scale transfer latency. The outermost zone spans the other nodes in the cluster, reached through InfiniBand ports that each supply tens of gigabytes per second per direction, with point-to-point latency measured in single-digit microseconds. Latency figures are comparable only when they measure the same thing (a memory access, a link transfer, or a complete collective), and bandwidth ratios only when they compare matching endpoints and directions, as the representative paths of table 9 do.



Table 9: The Bandwidth Hierarchy: These representative paths have different bandwidth budgets. Link bandwidths are per direction; link count, signaling, and system configuration determine the gap between tiers. These example bandwidth gaps favor placing frequent tensor-parallel collectives within the fast communication domain, which need not coincide with a server boundary.

HBM (3.35 TB/s) sits at the center; the outward tiers are NVLink/NVSwitch (450 GB/s per direction per GPU), one InfiniBand NDR port (50 GB/s per direction), and an illustrative 7 GB/s storage path. Each step outward cuts bandwidth by roughly 7.4, 9, and 7.1 times, not by a universal tenfold law. Exploiting this hierarchy through tiered algorithms is the primary task of distributed systems engineering.




Napkin Math 2.3: The physics of the staircaseProblem: A 10 GB buffer must move one hop at each tier of the hierarchy, with a local HBM read as the reference point. How much does the tier it crosses change the transfer time?
Math: Transfer time is \(\TransferTimeForPayload= \DataVolume / \Bandwidth\).

HBM (local read, the reference point): 10 GB / 3,350 GB/s \(\approx\) 3.0 ms.
NVLink (intra-node): 10 GB / 450 GB/s \(\approx\) 22.2 ms.
InfiniBand (inter-node): 10 GB / 50 GB/s \(\approx\) 200 ms.

Systems insight: For the same payload, the example inter-node path has a transfer-time lower bound 9× larger than the example intra-node path. Size alone does not decide which traffic may cross that cliff; frequency and overlap do. Tensor parallelism exchanges activations inside every layer, on the critical path, so it favors the fast local NVLink domain in this configuration. Data parallelism moves the largest buffer, the full gradient, but only once per step and overlapped with the backward pass, so it can cross the scarce InfiniBand tier. A partition that fits in memory can still spend much of a step waiting if its exposed exchanges exceed the communication budget.


Each cliff in the bandwidth staircase has a physical cause at its distance scale. Millimeter-long traces on a silicon interposer can carry a wide, slow-clocked parallel interface without serializer/deserializer (SerDes) transceivers. NVLink crosses tens of centimeters of board copper, which requires SerDes transceivers with equalization to recover the signal at high per-lane rates. PCIe pays for universal compatibility with protocol overhead (packet headers, flow-control credits, and error checking). InfiniBand crosses meters of cable between racks, adding optical conversion on longer runs, forward error correction, and switch hops. SerDes, link budget, and power develops the signaling physics behind these cliffs. For node design, link count and sustained bandwidth must be evaluated together with the power and cooling load of the components that provide them.
The practical consequence for model partitioning is that tensor parallelism (TP), which splits individual matrix multiplications across accelerators and requires collective exchanges within layers, generates communication volume proportional to the model’s hidden dimension hundreds of times per second. Over NVLink, each of these exchanges takes under a millisecond for the running model (section 2.5.2 computes the idealized lower bound). At the reference InfiniBand port rate, the bandwidth-only lower bound for the same exchange is 9× as large; the step-time effect also depends on startup, routing, and overlap. For this topology TP therefore stays within a node, although a system whose fast scale-up fabric spans several chassis can place a tensor-parallel group across them; communication cost, rather than the server enclosure, determines the useful partition.
The hierarchy also explains why pipeline parallelism occupies an intermediate position in the bandwidth requirements. In pipeline parallelism, the model is divided into sequential stages, with each stage assigned to a different group of accelerators. The communication between stages consists of activations flowing forward during the forward pass and gradients flowing backward during the backward pass, with a volume proportional to the batch size times the hidden dimension.
For our 175B model with hidden dimension 12,288 and a microbatch of 4 sequences at 2,048, the activation tensor at each stage boundary is approximately \(4 \times 2,048 \times 12,288 \times 2 B\) bytes (FP16) \(\approx\) 201 MB. This is far smaller than the 350 GB gradient AllReduce required by data parallelism, which is why pipeline parallelism places less demanding requirements on the inter-node network.
Activation transfers occur once per microbatch per stage boundary. That is far less often than tensor parallelism’s AllReduce inside every layer, yet more often than data parallelism’s gradient exchange, which happens once per step. Small messages at an intermediate frequency let pipeline parallelism tolerate the lower bandwidth of inter-node links, which makes it the natural way to split a model whose layers do not fit in one node.
Both pipeline and data parallelism therefore cross node boundaries, for different reasons (table 10). Pipeline traffic is small per message and sits between the other two in frequency. The data-parallel gradient exchange is the largest transfer, but it occurs once per step and can overlap the backward pass. That overlap makes it the most latency-tolerant of the three, although any unfinished exchange still delays the update. For the example topology, the resulting mapping places tensor parallelism within the node, pipeline stages across nodes, and data-parallel groups across the cluster. This de facto pattern is a starting point for the capacity and timing calculation; a different scale-up domain, message size, or overlap opportunity can justify a different placement.



Table 10: Traffic Shape by Parallelism Strategy: The placement rule follows from size and frequency together. Frequent exchanges on the critical path need the fastest tier, while the largest exchange can cross the slowest tier because it happens once per step and overlaps the backward pass.

The mapping constrains how the scheduler assigns devices and nodes. Members of a tensor-parallel group belong inside one fast domain (on this topology, one chassis joined by NVLink), because their dependent exchanges recur inside every layer. Adjacent pipeline stages belong in the same rack or neighboring racks, where their activation and gradient traffic crosses the fewest InfiniBand switch hops. Data-parallel groups can span the whole cluster. Physical adjacency helps only when it corresponds to better connectivity. The node’s PCIe hierarchy adds another placement constraint by connecting accelerators to host CPUs, network interface cards (NICs), and storage, including the path used to reach host DRAM.


While NVLink carries GPU-to-GPU traffic, PCIe Gen5 connects accelerators, host CPUs, network adapters, and storage through the node’s peripheral hierarchy. Host DRAM attaches to the CPU’s memory controllers; a GPU transfer to that memory also traverses its host-facing PCIe path. PCIe bandwidth, approximately 64 GB/s per direction (128 GB/s bidirectional) per x16 link, can therefore constrain data loading, checkpointing, or GPU-to-network transfers. Which traffic competes depends on the actual links and switches those paths share.
A standard DGX H100 node features two host CPUs, each managing a PCIe root complex, and PCIe switches fan those lanes out. Each of the 8 GPUs and each of the 8 InfiniBand host channel adapters (HCAs, the network interface cards of an InfiniBand fabric) has its own x16 link (figure 10). This configuration provides an aggregate theoretical bandwidth of about 2 TB/s within the chassis. However, this bandwidth is shared among competing traffic streams. During a single training step, the PCIe bus simultaneously carries host-to-GPU data batches, GPU-to-HCA gradient shards for inter-node AllReduce (via GPUDirect remote direct memory access (RDMA)), and periodic CPU-to-NVMe checkpoint writes. Contention between these streams can cause unexpected pipeline stalls, particularly when gradient synchronization saturates the links typically used for data loading.
The dual-CPU architecture introduces significant non-uniform memory access (NUMA) effects. The 8 GPUs are physically partitioned, with 4 connected to CPU 0’s root complex and 4 to CPU 1’s. A GPU connected to CPU 0 can reach CPU 0’s DRAM through its local PCIe root complex, whereas access to CPU 1’s DRAM also traverses the inter-socket link. The latency and bandwidth penalty depends on the processor, socket interconnect, PCIe topology, transfer size, and concurrent traffic, so no fixed percentage applies across nodes. Data-loading pipelines should measure this topology and place worker processes, pinned buffers, NICs, and target GPUs within the same NUMA domain when the local path improves sustained ingestion. Placement is therefore part of the parallelism strategy, because a scheduler that ignores PCIe roots, NIC locality, and NUMA domains can turn an otherwise valid tensor- or pipeline-parallel plan into a host-bound bottleneck.






Figure 10: Two Fabrics inside One Eight-GPU Node: NVSwitch joins all eight GPUs for GPU-to-GPU traffic, but every path to host memory, storage, or the network runs through a PCIe tree rooted at one of two CPU sockets. A GPU, its InfiniBand host channel adapter (HCA), and the host DRAM it reaches most cheaply therefore sit in one non-uniform memory access (NUMA) domain, and a transfer to the other socket’s DRAM also crosses the socket link. The two PCIe switches per socket are schematic; switch count and lane routing vary by server design.





↪ Mapping data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism onto intra-node and inter-node bandwidth tiers is developed in Hybrid Parallelism.




Given the bandwidth hierarchy, the node must connect 8 accelerators with enough bandwidth for tensor-parallel operations across their private memories. A switched fabric can provide full bisection bandwidth, enough capacity across any equal division of the endpoints to carry their full injection rate. Comparing a ring, a mesh, and a switched design shows what connectivity costs and which communication patterns it supports.
Eight GPUs in one chassis can be wired as a ring, a full mesh, or a switched fabric (figure 11). A ring is inexpensive, needing only \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) links for \(\AcceleratorsPerNode\) GPUs, and suits ring-AllReduce, in which each GPU sends to one neighbor while receiving from the other so that every link stays busy. Tensor parallelism, however, issues frequent collectives after sharded matrix operations. These include ReduceScatter, which leaves each participant with one shard of a combined result, and AllGather, which assembles shards at every participant. A ring’s fixed multi-hop paths (up to four hops between distant GPUs) constrain those patterns. A full mesh reaches every peer in one hop but needs \(\AcceleratorsPerNode(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1) / 2 = 28\) links for 8 GPUs, a count that grows quadratically and soon becomes impractical to route. The NVSwitch crossbar puts every pair one switch hop apart and provides full-bisection switched connectivity with a manageable number of switch chips.






Figure 11: Intra-node GPU Topology Comparison: Three ways to wire eight GPUs inside one node. Left: a ring gives each GPU only two links, so traffic between distant GPUs passes through up to four hops. Center: a full mesh reaches every peer in one hop but needs \(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1\) links per GPU and \(\AcceleratorsPerNode(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1)/2\) links in total, which becomes impractical to route beyond about eight GPUs. Right: an NVSwitch fabric gives each GPU one set of links to the switch and puts every pair one switch hop apart, with up to 450 GB/s per direction per H100 SXM GPU (900 GB/s bidirectional); that per-GPU injection bandwidth is not the aggregate bisection bandwidth of the switch fabric.



Consider the NVIDIA DGX H100 architecture. Eight H100 GPUs sit on a single baseboard, each connected to four NVSwitch chips via 18 NVLink 4.0 lanes. The NVSwitch chips form a non-blocking crossbar5 through which any GPU can reach any other GPU. Each GPU’s port budget is 900 GB/s bidirectional, or 450 GB/s in one direction, shared across that GPU’s simultaneous transfers; it is not a separate full-bandwidth link for every GPU pair.
5 Crossbar switch: A topology providing a dedicated path between every input-output pair simultaneously. An \(\SwitchRadix{\times}\SwitchRadix\) crossbar needs \(\SwitchRadix^2\) crosspoints, so its cost grows quadratically with port count; that growth is why a full crossbar stays inside a node and larger systems switch to multi-stage fabrics. Within that bound, the crossbar buys the all-to-all bandwidth that tensor parallelism demands.The result is a node with 640 GB of aggregate HBM capacity and a combined peak compute throughput of 8 \(\times\) 1,979 TFLOP/s, while each GPU retains private HBM. Training frameworks partition tensors explicitly across those devices, and NVSwitch reduces the communication cost between shards without making placement or collective synchronization transparent. The NVSwitch chips themselves consume approximately 200 W each (800 W total for the NVSwitch fabric), a nontrivial power overhead justified by the bisection bandwidth it provides. In physical terms, the NVSwitch fabric alone consumes more power than an entire previous-generation GPU (the V100 drew 300 W).
Tracing one tensor-parallel step of the running model shows what that NVSwitch power budget buys. Assume a schedule with one activation-sized AllReduce per layer in each forward and backward pass; the partition and collective schedule are scenario inputs, not a universal Transformer schedule. During the modeled tensor-parallel forward pass, each GPU holds one shard of each weight matrix and computes its portion of the matrix multiplication. For a Transformer layer with hidden dimension 12,288 (typical for a 175B model), each of the 8 GPUs holds a \(12{,}288{\times}1{,}536\) slice of the weight matrix at the projection that reduces the split inner dimension back to the full hidden width. Because that slice keeps the full output width while covering only one eighth of the inner sum, each GPU produces a full-width vector of partial sums for every token, and an AllReduce operation sums those partial results across all 8 GPUs over NVLink.
The logical output tensor for one AllReduce contains \(4 \times 2{,}048 \times 12{,}288 \times 2\) bytes (FP16). For a microbatch of 4 sequences at 2,048 tokens, that payload is roughly 201 MB. An ideal ring AllReduce with 8 participants moves \(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount=\) 1.75 times the payload per GPU (Collective Communication derives this factor), or about 352 MB. At 450 GB/s of one-direction bandwidth, the transfer-time lower bound is approximately 0.783 ms.
Across 96 forward layers and 96 backward layers, the 192 transfers sum to about 150.3 ms per step before overlap. NVSwitch provides the paths needed for the collective, but this value remains an ideal bandwidth-only lower bound that excludes startup latency, software overhead, and competing traffic.


↪ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model, which adds the fixed per-message startup latency this bound omits to the bytes-over-bandwidth transfer time, is developed in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth Communication Model.
Judging that bound needs a compute time to compare it with. This scenario assumes 200 ms of computation per step for the tensor-parallel group, a stated input rather than a derived value; the fractions below scale with it, so a longer compute time makes the same communication matter less. Against that assumption, the unoverlapped NVLink lower bound leaves computation at 57.1 percent of combined compute-plus-communication time. Actual tensor-parallel efficiency can be higher when collectives overlap useful computation or lower when latency, contention, load imbalance, and nonparallel work add delay, so it must be measured rather than inferred from peak link bandwidth alone.

Example 2.3: The NVLink bandwidth surpriseScenario: A team evaluates tensor parallelism over a hypothetical PCIe Gen5 path with 64 GB/s bandwidth, using the payload and the assumed 200 ms per-step compute time stated with the NVLink estimate above.
Diagnosis: The modeled tensor-parallel schedule executes 192 AllReduce events per step across 96 layers. Its PCIe bandwidth-only transfer times sum to 1057 ms per step. Without overlap, communication accounts for 84.1 percent of the combined compute and transfer estimate; this is not a measured stall fraction.
Systems lesson: Under the same assumptions, NVLink lowers the transfer bound to 0.783 ms per AllReduce and raises computation to 57.1 percent of the combined time. The comparison explains why this partition favors a fast local fabric. Real collective performance must also include startup, topology, contention, and overlap.


The DGX H100 pairs each GPU with its own InfiniBand ConnectX-7 HCA, which reads and writes GPU memory directly over PCIe through GPUDirect RDMA, so inter-node gradient exchange avoids staging copies in host DRAM while still consuming PCIe and network bandwidth. The host CPU prepares and loads batches, submits kernels, and coordinates the training framework. Sufficient CPU capacity and I/O bandwidth let that work overlap the accelerator fabric’s computation and communication; otherwise, slow preprocessing or submission can starve the GPUs even when their local memory and interconnect are fast enough.


↪ The RDMA and GPUDirect data path that bypasses host memory is developed in RDMA and GPUDirect.

Kanev, Svilen, Juan Pablo Darago, Kim Hazelwood, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, Tipp Moseley, Gu-Yeon Wei, and David Brooks. 2015. “Profiling a Warehouse-Scale Computer.” Proceedings of the 42nd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 158–69. https://doi.org/10.1145/2749469.2750392.
Host CPUs also pay a “data center tax” of shared infrastructure work. A profile of Google’s fleet found that such common building blocks consumed nearly 30 percent of cycles across jobs (Kanev et al. 2015), and network protocol processing, storage virtualization, and security functions add to that load on cloud hosts. ML nodes can therefore incorporate data processing units (DPUs) or SmartNICs. Devices like the NVIDIA BlueField DPU offload these infrastructure tasks to dedicated ARM cores and hardware accelerators integrated into the network adapter itself. Moving the control plane for RDMA, firewall rules, and storage protocols to the DPU recovers cycles for the ML pipeline: data loading, tokenization, and kernel orchestration on the host CPU. The DPU also acts as an isolated security domain, allowing cloud providers to maintain control over the network and storage layer via the DPU while granting customers full access to the host CPU and GPUs. For our 175B model training, DPU offload can keep RDMA protocol processing outside the host CPU critical path for gradient synchronization, which flows from GPU HBM toward the network fabric without host CPU involvement.


Spending board area, power, and cost on four NVSwitch chips makes sense when tensor-parallel collectives sit inside every layer, but workloads dominated by embedding capacity, data parallelism, or cost-sensitive serving hit different limits first. Alternative node designs reallocate that budget. An AMD MI300X server emphasizes large HBM capacity on each package, Google TPU pods wire chips directly into a mesh without a central baseboard switch, and Intel/Habana Gaudi nodes integrate Ethernet RDMA ports directly onto the accelerator die. Comparing them against a DGX H100 node reveals where each architecture spends its scarce budget.
In a switch-rich node like the DGX H100, universal any-to-any local exchange is the priority because each Transformer layer places intra-node collectives inside the model’s inner loop. The 900 GB/s H100 NVLink fabric therefore buys a software abstraction, in which the training framework can treat eight accelerators as one tightly coupled tensor-parallel group for the layers that must be split across chips.
Other systems move that boundary. TPU pods use the inter-chip interconnect and a mesh-oriented topology instead of making a central switch the defining component of the node; a TPU v5p chip’s vendor-specified ICI bandwidth is 1,200 GB/s. The mesh can reduce switch cost and expose a regular structure to the compiler, but it also makes placement more visible, because the runtime must respect neighbor relationships rather than assuming that every chip pair has the same communication path. That is a reasonable trade when the workload is regular enough for the compiler and collective libraries to map communication onto the topology.
The MI300X shifts the pressure point from local switching toward memory capacity. Its package exposes 192 GB of HBM at 5.3 TB/s, compared with 80 GB on an H100-class accelerator. An eight-accelerator MI300X node would therefore provide 1,536 GB of aggregate HBM, enough to hold the 350 GB FP16 weight tensor for our 175B running model. That does not eliminate the optimizer, gradient, activation, and fragmentation problem that section 2.5.3 quantifies, but it changes how often the system must spill state into slower memory tiers and how much microbatch headroom remains before offload becomes mandatory.
Gaudi takes a different route by integrating RDMA-capable Ethernet into the accelerator and using a more network-centric design for communication. A Gaudi 2 accelerator’s 24 integrated 100 GbE ports supply 300 GB/s of aggregate RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) bandwidth, against the 900 GB/s of local exchange per GPU in an H100-class NVLink node. The newer Gaudi 3 keeps that Ethernet-centric design while carrying 128 GB of HBM per accelerator, so capacity is not the trade being made. The question is whether simplifying the fabric and using Ethernet consistently across node and pod is worth giving up the high local exchange bandwidth of a switch-rich NVLink design. That trade can be attractive when data parallelism, inference serving, or cluster cost dominates, and less attractive when tensor-parallel collectives sit inside every layer.
These alternatives are not a ranking of vendors. They are different placements of scarce resources: switching bandwidth in the node, regular topology in the pod, HBM capacity in the package, or network attachment on the accelerator. For the 175B model used throughout this chapter, the tensor-parallel portion of training makes local accelerator communication unusually important, so the DGX-style answer is natural. In other regimes, especially memory-heavy recommenders, topology-regular training, or cost-sensitive serving fleets, a different boundary can become the one that matters most. Software ecosystem maturity, supply availability, and total cost of ownership then decide whether the theoretical architectural fit becomes a deployable system.




The node’s aggregate HBM must hold far more than the weights, and how that state divides across the node’s memory tiers decides which parallelism strategies are possible. Consider the memory budget for training our 175B model. The model weights in FP16 require 350 GB. The Adam optimizer maintains two additional values for every parameter (first and second moments) in FP32 precision, adding 175 \(\times 10^9 \times 2 \times 4\) bytes = 1,400 GB. Gradients require another 350 GB. This subtotal is approximately 2.1 TB, far exceeding both a single accelerator’s 80 GB HBM and an 8-H100 node’s 640 GB aggregate HBM, and it still omits two terms. Activations are the intermediate results the backward pass needs. The FP32 master weights are a full-precision copy of the parameters that the optimizer updates, kept because an update far smaller than a weight would be lost to FP16 rounding; this is the mixed-precision copy introduced with the precision formats in section 2.4.
A common misconception is that a model’s memory footprint equals its weight storage. With those two terms included, the FP32 master weights, optimizer moments, gradients, and activations collectively consume about 7–8\(\times\) more memory than the FP16 parameters alone. These components reside in different tiers of the node’s memory hierarchy. For our 175B model, training memory partitions across six distinct components (table 11).



Table 11: Training Memory Breakdown for a 175B-Parameter Frontier Model: The optimizer state alone (first and second moments in FP32) consumes 4\(\times\) the memory of the model weights, making optimizer memory the dominant component of training memory. This is why memory optimization techniques focus heavily on optimizer state sharding and offloading.
