title: 4 Data Storage
text:
If a multi-week training run suffers a sudden loss spike or a deployed model regresses, an engineering team that did not record which shard versions, preprocessing code, and shuffle seeds fed each step cannot tell a model bug from a silent change in the input data. A checkpoint manifest provides one commit boundary per save. The data pipeline that built the training corpus has many, one at every stage that turns raw inputs into processed shards. The storage system must record both the exact bytes read and the preprocessing code, shuffle seed, schema, and integrity checks that produced them before the run began.

Lighthouse 4.1: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Feature store latencyWhile Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) trains on static, versioned shards, Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) trains on live feature streams that change every second as users click and interact. Replaying an exact batch then becomes a point-in-time problem, which a feature store answers by keeping a retained, versioned feature log.




↪ Point-in-time correctness, the leakage it prevents, and the storage cost of retained feature history are developed in Point-in-time correctness.
13 Hash cost (SHA-256): Verifying the integrity of a 100 TB dataset using SHA-256 consumes approximately 55.6 CPU-core hours at a per-core hashing rate of 500 MB/s. The work parallelizes across shards, but it still competes with decoding for host cores and must read every byte, so the validation step is best pipelined with ingestion rather than run as a separate pass before the fleet starts.Even when the underlying shard files are immutable, a distributed loader produces a stream of consumed samples whose versions and order can shift across epochs during a 30-day run. Dataset versioning provides a “Git for data” record by snapshotting the cryptographic hashes13 of every data shard, the exact preprocessing code used for tokenization, and the random seeds governing the global shuffle. With that snapshot in place, engineers investigating a mid-run divergence can replay the exact batch that triggered the loss spike and test whether the culprit was a corrupted sample or numerical instability in the optimizer.
At petabyte scale, the data pipeline has to make every transformation reproducible. Raw documents are cleaned, tokenized, packed into training examples, and sharded across storage tiers. Each stage writes an immutable artifact, and each artifact records the input version, code version, schema, and statistical checks it satisfied. Once those dependencies are explicit, the pipeline forms a directed acyclic graph: later artifacts depend on earlier artifacts, and no stage is allowed to rewrite its own history. When a training job starts, the cluster manager verifies that each worker’s local NVMe shards match the data snapshot declared for the run. Treating the data pipeline as a graph of versioned artifacts rather than a simple file transfer makes silent data drift detectable and attributable to a specific stage, code version, or input snapshot. Immutability also pays a storage dividend. Because an artifact never changes once written, a manifest can name it by content identifier, and many experiments can reference the same unchanged shards without copying entire datasets.


When a tokenization worker crashes halfway through building a shard of the running example’s corpus, its replacement must decide which raw documents to process again without silently dropping records or writing duplicates. Versioned artifacts identify what a pipeline produced, while commit and replay rules determine whether mid-stage failures can alter that result. The storage system’s part in that decision is the commit boundary, the point at which a stage’s output becomes durable and visible downstream, the same contract that section 4.6 applied to checkpoint generations. That shared contract is why a storage chapter owns these semantics, because whether a replay loses or duplicates data is decided by what the store has committed. The restarted worker compares its input position with the last committed output and replays everything after it, so the work at risk is whatever accumulated past the last commit. Two service-rate effects govern how much accumulates. Records are assigned to workers by a partition key, such as a document’s source or a user identifier, and partition skew arises when one key owns disproportionate work and holds its stage open while the rest of the fleet idles. Backpressure propagates a slow downstream stage’s limit upstream by slowing admission or bounding in-flight data, a control response to overload rather than another name for slow processing.
Failures near that boundary raise a correctness question, and three guarantees answer it differently. At-most-once processing never replays uncertain work, so a document that was read but whose output was never confirmed is lost. At-least-once processing replays everything after the last confirmed commit, so a document whose output was written but not yet confirmed is written twice. An effectively exactly-once outcome combines replayable inputs with idempotent writes, writes that leave the same result however many times they repeat, or with transactional output keyed by a stable event or transaction identifier (Akidau et al. 2015). Reliable message delivery between workers cannot provide this guarantee on its own, because the duplicate arises from the worker’s own replay.

Example 4.2: The acknowledgment gapFailure trace: A feature-pipeline worker writes the output row for click event e42, then crashes before it records that the write succeeded. Its replacement cannot tell whether e42 was committed. Skipping the event risks losing it. Replaying it with an append writes the feature row a second time, so that click counts twice in every training set built from the table. Writing the row under the stable key (feature_version, e42) turns the replay into an overwrite of the same row, so the uncertain event can be reprocessed safely.
Systems lesson: Exactly-once belongs at the output commit boundary, whose record must bind the input position, transformation version, stable identifier, and commit state.


The two replays differ only in how the output is addressed. An append gives every attempt its own row, while a write under a stable key sends every attempt to the same row, so reprocessing uncertain work leaves the stored result unchanged (figure 9).






Figure 9: The Acknowledgment Gap at a Commit Boundary: A worker stores the output row for event e42 and crashes before it records the commit, so its replacement cannot tell whether the row exists and must replay the event. (a) Appending the replayed row duplicates it, and the click counts twice in every training set built from the table. (b) Writing under the stable key (feature_version, e42) makes the replay an overwrite of the same row, so at-least-once replay produces an effectively exactly-once result.



Streaming adds a time boundary to the contract. Event time records when an event occurred; processing time records when a worker handled it. A pipeline that aggregates clicks per hour must decide when an hour is finished, even though events can arrive late. A watermark is its running estimate that every event up to some event time has arrived, which lets it close that window and emit the result; a late-data policy determines whether later arrivals update, retract, quarantine, or drop the result (Akidau et al. 2015). Watermarks therefore trade freshness against completeness rather than prove that no older event remains.

Akidau, Tyler, Robert Bradshaw, Craig Chambers, Slava Chernyak, Rafael J. Fernández-Moctezuma, Reuven Lax, Sam McVeety, et al. 2015. “The Dataflow Model: A Practical Approach to Balancing Correctness, Latency, and Cost in Massive-Scale, Unbounded, Out-of-Order Data Processing.” Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment 8 (12): 1792–803. https://doi.org/10.14778/2824032.2824076.
Each of these mechanisms buys one property at the cost of another. Buffering absorbs finite bursts or temporary slowdowns but increases recovery state and freshness lag; sustained overload still requires backpressure or more service capacity. Aggressive watermarks reduce delay but exclude more late data, while retries help only when writes are safe to repeat. These choices change the stored result, because a feature table closed under an aggressive watermark holds different rows from one closed under a lenient watermark. A reproducible training snapshot must therefore record source and code versions alongside partitioning, replay policy, stable identifiers, watermark state, and late-data decisions. That record is what lets a later feature backfill, a replay of history under new code, rejoin features at the correct points in time without mixing old and new histories.


↪ Feature backfills that replay history under this snapshot contract are developed in Backfill procedures.



The versioned-artifact contract applies to generated training samples as well as collected ones. When a fleet generates candidate samples, filters them, and verifies the survivors, each stage adds storage traffic and records that must remain linked to the accepted payload. The pressure to generate comes from the compute-optimal allocation of AI Scaling Laws, which grows the token budget with the parameter count. As high-quality human-generated text becomes harder to expand, the fleet encounters the data wall: the point where additional training samples must increasingly come from synthesis, simulation, curation, or expensive human collection (Villalobos et al. 2024). This shift from simple collection to managed data generation sends more than payload bytes through the hierarchy. A “synthetic fuel line” must also store the provenance chain of every sample: which model generated it, which filters accepted or rejected it, which judge or verifier models scored it, and which downstream run consumed it. That lineage makes repeated reuse of generated material traceable. It supports investigation of model collapse, where recursive training on generated data can degrade the learned distribution (Shumailov et al. 2024); retaining provenance alone does not prevent the degradation. The storage design must separately budget retained artifacts and the repeated scans used to assess them.

Villalobos, Pablo, Anson Ho, Jaime Sevilla, Tamay Besiroglu, Lennart Heim, and Marius Hobbhahn. 2024. “Position: Will We Run Out of Data? Limits of LLM Scaling Based on Human-Generated Data.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 235: 49523–44.

Shumailov, Ilia, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, and Yarin Gal. 2024. “AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data.” Nature 631 (8022): 755–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y.

Napkin Math 4.8: The storage cost of synthetic dataProblem: A 1 TB synthetic dataset retains provenance metadata and undergoes three independent verification scans. How much persistent capacity and pipeline traffic does it require if judge outputs are not retained as full dataset copies?

Raw Payload: 1 TB.
Provenance Overhead: 40 percent extra for lineage hashes, generation logs, and reward-model scores.
Verification Traffic: 3 judge passes each read the payload, producing 3 TB of read traffic. Their scores reside in the provenance metadata rather than in three retained payload copies.
Capacity Result: Persistent capacity is 1 TB \(\times\) 1.4 = 1.4 TB, a 1.4× capacity factor.
Traffic Result: Writing the payload and metadata once and reading the payload three times moves 4.4 TB, a 4.4× traffic factor before generation and judge-model compute are counted.

Systems insight: Verification primarily draws on service rate and compute, while retained provenance consumes capacity. The two costs coincide only when the pipeline materializes each judge output as another full dataset. Synthetic storage must therefore budget bytes at rest separately from bytes moved and record which generator, filters, judges, and downstream runs produced each accepted sample.


Generated data therefore makes lineage part of the payload, so the store must budget retained provenance and verification traffic alongside the samples themselves. Every tier that holds those samples, checkpoints, or provenance records also carries a distinct price tag, turning placement across the hierarchy into an economic optimization problem.

Self-Check: Question

A feature-pipeline worker writes the output row for click event e42, then crashes before it records that the write succeeded. Its replacement cannot tell whether the row was committed. Which design lets the replacement reprocess e42 without losing the event or counting it twice?

Write each output row under a stable key such as (feature_version, e42), so a replay overwrites the same row instead of appending a second one.

Lengthen the watermark delay, so late events have more time to arrive before the window closes.

A team generates a \(1\text{ TB}\) synthetic text dataset. Retained provenance adds \(40\%\) metadata overhead, and 3 verifier models each read the payload once without materializing another full copy. What persistent capacity and total pipeline traffic are required?

\(1.4\text{ TB}\) of persistent capacity and \(4.4\text{ TB}\) of traffic: \(1\text{ TB}\) payload write, \(0.4\text{ TB}\) metadata write, and \(3\text{ TB}\) of verifier reads.
Exactly \(1.0\text{ TB}\), because verifier models run entirely in GPU registers without generating persistent storage artifacts.
Roughly \(0.4\text{ TB}\), because synthetic data compresses more efficiently than natural language text.
Roughly \(14\text{ TB}\), because every verifier model stores a full \(350\text{ GB}\) copy of its internal neural activations for every sample.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Checkpoints, training shards, and the lineage that binds them now each have a place in the hierarchy, and every placement carries a price set by the tier that holds the bytes and by how often they cross a billing boundary. ML storage economics is therefore not simply about choosing the cheapest capacity tier; the design objective is to minimize total cost of data delivery, which combines recurring storage charges, cross-boundary transfer fees, and the opportunity cost of idle accelerators.
Applied to one 100 TB training dataset, the per-gigabyte rates quoted earlier for each tier diverge by orders of magnitude: object storage (S3 Standard) costs $24,000 per year, provisioned local NVMe costs $120,000 per year, and archival storage (such as Glacier) drops to $4,800 per year. By contrast, hypothetically provisioning the same capacity as GPU memory at $15/GB would require $1,500,000 in upfront acquisition cost alone, before factoring in amortization, power, or server housing.
The 5× cost difference between local NVMe and object storage motivates placing data on the least expensive tier that meets its delivery and recovery requirements. Device technology contributes to the gradient: HBM uses 3D-stacked silicon with through-silicon vias, and accelerator-adjacent capacity is constrained by packaging and node design. Shared storage pools capacity across clients but introduces network and service dependencies. The cost comparison must include those dependencies rather than infer the cheapest usable path from capacity price alone.



Repeated cross-boundary egress, not storage, dominates cloud cost.
Storage cost, however, is only part of the equation. Data transfer costs can dominate, especially in cloud environments. When compute runs in a different region or cloud from the bucket, as assumed here, reading the 100 TB dataset from object storage to compute instances incurs a transfer charge of $9,000. For multi-epoch training that reads the dataset 10 times, the egress cost alone reaches $90,000, more than the annual storage cost. This inversion, where reading data costs more than storing it, drives the architecture decision to cache data on local NVMe rather than streaming from object storage each epoch.
The economic analysis changes further when accounting for the opportunity cost of accelerator idle time. The book’s reference cluster of 1,024 GPUs, half the chapter’s running cluster, at $2/GPU-hour costs $49,152 per day. If input stalls reduce its compute-active fraction from 90 percent to 70 percent, the lost compute time is valued at $9,830 per day. Over a 30 days training run, this amounts to $294,912. That value sets a budget for evaluating a storage upgrade, but the recoverable benefit depends on how much exposed wait the upgrade removes. Capacity that does not relieve the limiting stage yields no corresponding compute-time saving.

Systems Perspective 4.3: The storage cost icebergThe visible cost of storage ($/GB/month) is the tip of the iceberg. Below the surface lie costs that often exceed the storage cost itself:

Egress fees: The ten-epoch egress charge of $90,000 computed above already exceeds a year of storage.
IOPS charges: Object storage charges per-request fees. S3 Standard GET requests cost about $0.0004 per 1,000 requests, so a dataset of 100M individual files, read once, costs about $40 in GET request fees before data transfer or retrieval charges, even though the storage cost is $2,000/month.
Idle accelerator cost: The $9,830 per day of lost compute computed above dwarfs any storage saving.
Retrieval fees: Archive storage charges retrieval fees ($0.02/GB for Glacier) in addition to egress. Restoring a 100 TB dataset from Glacier costs $2,000 in retrieval fees plus $9,000 in egress.

The economically rational strategy often invests more in storage (local NVMe caching, parallel file system capacity) to reduce transfer costs and prevent accelerator stalls.


The cost iceberg reveals that raw storage capacity can account for less than half of the total expenditure; replication, metadata operations, API calls, and cross-region transfers can collectively dominate the bill at scale. Among those hidden line items, egress is the one that often flips the architecture decision. Unlike capacity charges, which scale with the volume of data stored, egress charges scale with the volume of data read, and ML training reads the full dataset on every epoch.

Napkin Math 4.9: The cost of egressProblem: A team trains a vision model on a 50 TB image dataset stored in S3. Training runs for 20 epochs. The decision is whether to stream from S3 each epoch or stage to local NVMe.
Option A: Stream from S3

Storage: 50 TB \(\times\) $0.02/GB/month \(\times\) 12 months = $12,000/year
Egress: 50 TB \(\times\) 20 epochs \(\times\) $0.09/GB = $90,000 per training run
Total for 4 training runs/year: $12,000 + $360,000 = $372,000/year

Option B: Stage to local NVMe

Storage (S3 source of truth): $12,000/year
NVMe capacity (50 TB across cluster): 50 TB \(\times\) $0.10/GB/month \(\times\) 12 = $60,000/year
Egress (stage once per training run): 50 TB \(\times\) 4 runs \(\times\) $0.09/GB = $18,000/year
Total: $12,000 + $60,000 + $18,000 = $90,000/year

Systems insight: Local NVMe caching saves $282,000/year at 20 epochs per run, enough to fund 9 additional H100 GPUs at list price. Including the $60,000/year provisioned NVMe cost and the once-per-run staging egress, the break-even point is just over 4 epochs per run; by the fifth epoch, local caching is cheaper than streaming from S3 every epoch.


The notebook turns the iceberg into a decision rule: the cheapest storage tier is not always the cheapest delivery path. Object storage can remain the source of truth, but repeated reads make egress, request overhead, and idle-accelerator cost part of the storage design. Multi-epoch vision training may justify staging on local NVMe by the fifth epoch, while single-epoch language-model pretraining may leave the corpus in object storage and optimize the streaming path instead. The running example stages anyway, although it reads its corpus only once, because egress is not what decides it. Each node’s share of the shards fits easily on local NVMe, the staging copy happens once before the clock starts, and local reads keep object-store latency tails out of every training step. When compute and bucket share a region, transfer fees largely disappear and the same comparison turns on request charges, latency, and idle accelerators instead. The architecture is therefore chosen from access pattern, read count, and latency sensitivity rather than from $/GB/month alone.
The cost analysis extends to the parallel file system tier, which occupies a middle ground between NVMe and object storage in both performance and price. A parallel file system capable of delivering 1 TB/s aggregate bandwidth requires roughly 100 OSS nodes, each with multiple NVMe drives and high-bandwidth network connections. Because the throughput target, not the stored capacity, sets that server count, a bandwidth-sized system costs far more than its stored bytes alone would suggest. This expense is justified only if the alternative, streaming from object storage and paying egress fees, is even more expensive, or if the latency requirements of checkpoint writes cannot be met by object storage alone. The break-even analysis depends on the organization’s workload mix. A team running a single long training job may find that staging data on local NVMe and bypassing the parallel file system entirely is the cheapest option, while a team running many concurrent short jobs benefits from the shared namespace that a parallel file system provides.
The decision to build vs. buy storage infrastructure hinges on the trade-off between the high capital expenditure of an on-premises parallel file system and the recurring operational expenditure of cloud object storage. A 1-petabyte Lustre deployment, sized for capacity rather than for the 1 TB/s target above, costs roughly $3–5 million in hardware, plus an additional $500,000 per year in operational overhead for power, cooling, and engineering support. Storing 1 PB in a cloud object store at $0.02/GB/month costs $240,000 per year for storage alone. Egress fees for accessing the data, however, dominate the total cost. Reading that petabyte at 10 reads/year adds $900,000 in data transfer fees. Under these assumptions, annual cloud delivery costs $1,140,000; after subtracting $500,000 of on-premises operations, the net savings are $640,000 per year. The resulting hardware break-even is roughly 4.7–7.8 years, and a payback within two years would require a hotter workload with many more full-dataset reads per year, lower capital expense, or non-egress drivers such as checkpoint latency and shared-namespace requirements. For the running example, the 6 TB serialized corpus is much smaller than 1 PB, so the local-storage case is driven more by latency, repeated experiments, and checkpoint staging than by one-year egress savings alone. Read-heavy training fleets also rarely wear out their drives under the DWPD budget of section 4.3.4, so a storage refresh cycle is usually driven by density rather than wear, and its timing belongs to the lifecycle cost analysis of Depreciation and lifecycle.


The cost structure laid out above turns tiering into a placement policy: keep data only as close to the accelerator as its access frequency and latency requirement justify. A tiering strategy encodes that policy across the hierarchy. Its hot, warm, cold, and archive labels name placement roles for a dataset rather than devices, and they follow the scope brackets of figure 1. The node-local pair is the hot tier, and the three shared services become the warm, cold, and archive tiers. The tier sections called local NVMe a warm cache because it sat in front of shared storage; in this placement vocabulary the same drives belong to the hot tier, because they hold the data the running job consumes.
The fastest and most expensive layer is the hot tier (local NVMe + host DRAM), which holds data being actively consumed by the running training job. Datasets are staged from shared storage to local NVMe at job start. This tier is provisioned per-node and is not shared across the cluster, so data that multiple jobs or teams need simultaneously cannot live here alone.
That shared-access requirement is what justifies the warm tier (parallel file system), which holds datasets accessed by multiple jobs or teams, shared checkpoints for fault recovery, and model artifacts under active development. The parallel file system provides the shared namespace necessary for multi-tenant access with strong consistency.
Below the warm tier sits the cold tier (object storage), which serves as the canonical repository for all organizational training data. Datasets are authored and versioned in object storage, then promoted to warmer tiers when needed for training. Object storage also serves as the durable backup for checkpoints after they are staged from local NVMe through the parallel file system.
Data that must be retained for compliance or reproducibility but is not expected to be accessed during normal operations drops to the archive tier (Glacier or equivalent). Lifecycle policies of the kind shown for the archive tier in section 4.3.8 automate both directions of movement. They promote data from cold to warm when a job requests it, demote it when no job has read it for a configured period, and transition cold data to archive after 90 to 365 days since last access.
In the running example, the 3 TB source corpus and 6 TB serialized shards live permanently in object storage (cold tier), and the staging and cleanup lifecycle of section 4.5.1 moves each node’s shards through local NVMe (hot tier) for the life of the job. The parallel file system holds only the job’s recent checkpoints, which the retention policy of section 4.6.2 governs.
The economic benefit of automated tiering compounds over time. An organization retaining 50 training datasets of 10 TB each would need 500 TB of parallel file system capacity if all data were left in place. If ten datasets are active concurrently and the other forty can be demoted after their jobs finish, automated tiering reduces the dataset capacity required on the parallel file system to 100 TB, saving $144,000 per year at the parallel file system’s per-TB rate. These savings are invisible in any single experiment but substantial when accumulated across the fleet. Tiering and staging thus settle where training data and checkpoints live and what each placement costs; serving reuses the same hierarchy for a different objective, governed by the time to bring a model into HBM and the latency of serving-time state rather than epoch throughput.

Self-Check: Question

A team trains a vision model on a \(50\text{ TB}\) dataset stored in cloud object storage (\(\$0.02/\text{GB-month}\)) for 20 epochs across 4 training runs per year. Reading from object storage across a network boundary incurs a \(\$0.09/\text{GB}\) data egress fee. Staging the dataset onto local NVMe caches costs \(\$0.10/\text{GB-month}\). What does the economic analysis reveal about streaming vs. staging?

Streaming directly from object storage every epoch is cheaper because local NVMe drives add unnecessary provisioned storage overhead.
Egress fees are negligible compared to monthly storage costs, making tier selection purely a matter of operational convenience.
Staging data once to local NVMe per run saves roughly \(\$282,000\) per year compared to streaming from object storage every epoch, breaking even after just 5 epochs per run.
The team should migrate the dataset to cold tape archive to eliminate both egress fees and provisioned storage costs.

In a 1,000-GPU cluster where compute time is billed at \(\$2.00\) per GPU-hour, an undersized storage system introduces an additional 20 percentage points of input stalls (reducing the active compute fraction from \(90\%\) to \(70\%\)). Calculate the daily cost of this lost compute capacity and explain why investing in high-performance storage is economically rational.
An enterprise evaluates building an on-premises 1 PB parallel file system (\(\$3\text{M to } \$5\text{M}\) capex plus \(\$500\text{k/year}\) opex) versus storing the 1 PB corpus in cloud object storage (\(\$240\text{k/year}\) storage) and paying \(\$0.09/\text{GB}\) egress fees for 10 full-dataset reads per year (\(\$900\text{k/year}\) egress). What is the realistic financial payback horizon for building the on-premises system under these parameters?

Between 4.7 and 7.8 years, because net annual cloud delivery savings (\(\$640\text{k/year}\)) require multiple years to amortize the multi-million dollar initial hardware expenditure.
Less than 6 months, because cloud egress fees make any on-premises storage investment instantly profitable.
Exactly 20 years, because on-premises operational overhead exceeds all cloud storage and egress fees combined.
There is no payback horizon because cloud object storage is perpetually free for research and training workloads.

In cloud-based ML infrastructure, the recurring fee charged by providers per gigabyte of data transferred out of an object storage bucket across region or internet boundaries is called an ____ fee.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Where full-corpus training streams datasets for weeks and writes checkpoints in bursts, the weight-resident serving baseline of section 4.2 reads the model weights once when a replica starts or recovers and then answers requests out of HBM, before KV-cache offload and retrieval indexes add serving-time I/O of their own.
That startup read makes model loading latency, often called cold-start time, the primary storage metric for weight-resident inference: the duration required to load a model from storage into the accelerator’s HBM. For the 175B parameter language model, the weights alone occupy 350 GB in FP16 format; loading that footprint sequentially from a single high-performance NVMe drive at 14 GB/s takes 25 seconds, an unacceptable delay for a user-facing application. Loading from a shared PFS at a per-node rate of 4 GB/s takes 87.5 seconds. Reading from object storage at 1 GB/s stretches the delay to 5.8 minutes.
To reduce cold-start time, the model is sharded and loaded in parallel. If the 350 GB model is striped across 8 NVMe drives, each loading a 43.75 GB shard at 7 GB/s, the total load time drops to roughly 6.2 seconds. When using tensor parallelism across 8 GPUs, each GPU loads only its 43.75 GB shard. If the weights already sit in host DRAM, each GPU’s own PCIe link could move its shard in about 0.7 seconds, but the 8 transfers share the node’s 200 GB/s of host-memory bandwidth, so the full load takes about 1.8 seconds. For the most latency-sensitive applications, organizations maintain warm replicas: one or more copies of the model weights kept preloaded in host DRAM, ready for that host-memory-bound transfer. This trades DRAM capacity for a load of about 1.8 seconds instead of the 6.2 seconds striped NVMe read.


↪ How cold-start time limits autoscaling, and how warm pools trade idle capacity for scaling response, is developed in Autoscaling and Capacity Control.
These load times describe one replica. The model rollout previewed in section 4.2 asks all 100 replicas to load a new version at once, 35 TB of weights in one burst. If every replica reads from object storage at the 1 GB/s single-client rate, the fleet asks the store for 100 GB/s. A store whose aggregate service matches that figure, the 100 GB/s of table 2, finishes the rollout in about 5.8 minutes, no slower than one replica’s cold start; any smaller aggregate share stretches the rollout in proportion. Reading from the 1 TB/s parallel file system instead would take about 35 seconds, but only by claiming the whole file system and starving every training job that shares it, the read-side mirror of a checkpoint storm. Serving fleets therefore stage the new version on local NVMe before switching traffic, roll the update across groups of replicas so that the old version keeps serving, or let replicas that have finished loading supply the rest.
During autoregressive generation, the server keeps a per-request record of the attention keys and values produced by earlier tokens so it can generate the next token without recomputing the entire prefix. This record, called the key-value cache (KV cache), grows with sequence length and can consume significant HBM. For long sequences (128K tokens or more), KV cache offloading to host DRAM or NVMe extends the effective context window at the cost of increased latency per generated token, because cache blocks must be moved back into HBM before attention can use them. The storage lesson is that inference maintains an active working set rather than presenting solely a model-loading demand. When serving must also retrieve external context to ground that generation, the storage pipeline faces an entirely different access pattern: low-latency random queries into high-dimensional vector indexes.


↪ KV-cache growth and the HBM capacity wall it creates for serving are developed in The KV cache wall and memory capacity.


An inference request that needs supporting documents cannot wait for a sequential scan of the training corpus. A retrieval system first converts documents into vectors that represent semantic meaning, then finds nearby vectors and returns their source documents as context. The same storage analysis still applies, but the unit of demand becomes a query and its index accesses, and the deadline becomes the serving latency budget. With a graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) index, the storage system traverses a high-dimensional vector graph instead of streaming sequential blobs via formats such as TFRecord or Parquet. Other index families shift the storage demand elsewhere. Exact flat search scans every stored vector and is bound by scan bandwidth, inverted-file (IVF) partitioning probes only the few clusters nearest the query, and product quantization (PQ) compresses each vector into short codes so that more of the index fits in memory, at some cost in accuracy.

Systems Perspective 4.4: The IOPS bottleneck in high-dimensional searchFor graph-based ANN, this architectural pattern shifts the primary storage bottleneck from sequential read bandwidth to random-access IOPS. The search traverses a high-dimensional graph to find approximate nearest neighbors across billions of embeddings. Its performance is governed by the trade-off among recall, latency, and capacity, where recall is the fraction of the true nearest neighbors that the approximate search returns. Raising recall requires traversing a larger portion of the index, driving up IOPS and latency. The arithmetic of a disk-resident traversal shows why IOPS, not bytes, binds. Each hop that misses DRAM costs one dependent SSD read of roughly 100 μs (table 2), and the next hop cannot start until that read returns, so ten such hops already spend a millisecond of the serving budget in storage alone. Throughput is bounded separately. A drive whose 4 KB random reads run near 0.5 GB/s (section 4.2) completes on the order of \(10^5\) such reads per second, and every concurrent query draws on that same budget, while each read moves only a few kilobytes. A 1,536-dimension embedding in FP32 (4 bytes per value) consumes approximately 6.1 KB, so a billion-document corpus requires roughly 6.1 TB before graph adjacency lists. If those lists add 50 to 100 bytes per node, they add 50 GB to 100 GB, making raw vectors plus minimal graph metadata about 6.2 TB at the high end. Production indexes can be larger once identifiers, graph levels, allocator overhead, deleted-entry slack, and replication are included. In-memory hierarchical navigable small world graph indexes make graph navigation fast when the index fits in DRAM (Malkov and Yashunin 2020). Disk-backed graph indexes such as DiskANN trade DRAM footprint against SSD traversal while targeting high recall and low query latency (Subramanya et al. 2019).



Subramanya, Suhas Jayaram, Fnu Devvrit, Harsha Vardhan Simhadri, Ravishankar Krishnawamy, and Rohan Kadekodi. 2019. “DiskANN: Fast Accurate Billion-Point Nearest Neighbor Search on a Single Node.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 32.

Malkov, Yury A., and Dmitry A. Yashunin. 2020. “Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs.” IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 42 (4): 824–36. https://doi.org/10.1109/TPAMI.2018.2889473.
Graph-based retrieval therefore spends storage budget on index levels that keep random traversal inside the serving latency service-level objective. A disk-backed graph is economical only if the extra SSD accesses do not erase the quality gain from searching a larger corpus. Flat, IVF, and PQ designs move that budget toward scan bandwidth, partition probes, or decompression and approximation error. The same hierarchy now supports bulk model loading, request-scoped KV state, and retrieval, each with a distinct service-rate contract. Every design so far also assumes today’s six tiers, and the boundaries between those tiers are themselves moving.

Self-Check: Question

A serving node must load the \(350\text{ GB}\) of FP16 weights of a 175B-parameter model into accelerator memory. Which source gives the shortest cold start under the chapter’s stated rates?

Eight Gen4 NVMe drives read in parallel, each supplying one \(43.75\text{ GB}\) shard at \(7\text{ GB/s}\), for about 6.2 seconds.
A single Gen5 NVMe drive at \(14\text{ GB/s}\), for about 25 seconds.
The node’s \(4\text{ GB/s}\) share of the parallel file system, for about 87.5 seconds.
A single object-storage client at \(1\text{ GB/s}\), for about 5.8 minutes.

A warm replica keeps the \(350\text{ GB}\) of weights in host DRAM. Each GPU’s own host link could move its \(43.75\text{ GB}\) shard in about 0.7 seconds, yet the full load takes about 1.8 seconds. Explain why.
A serving fleet of 100 replicas of a 175B-parameter model deploys a new version, so all replicas must read \(35\text{ TB}\) of FP16 weights at once. Which statement correctly evaluates the shared sources?

A \(100\text{ GB/s}\) object store finishes in about 5.8 minutes, while the \(1\text{ TB/s}\) parallel file system would take about 35 seconds but only by claiming the whole file system from co-tenant training jobs.
The parallel file system is always the right source because 35 seconds is shorter, and serving reads cannot interfere with training jobs.
The object store finishes in about 35 seconds because each replica reads only its own share of the weights.
Rollout time is independent of the source tier because each replica’s load is limited by its own PCIe link.

How does the storage performance bottleneck for a graph-based vector retrieval index at billion-vector scale contrast with the primary bottleneck of an ML training data loader?

Vector retrieval is bottlenecked by sequential streaming bandwidth (GB/s), whereas training data loaders are bottlenecked by random \(4\text{ KB}\) read IOPS.
Vector retrieval requires continuous multi-terabyte burst writes, whereas training data loaders perform purely read-only operations.
Vector retrieval is strictly compute-bound on matrix multiplication units and generates zero storage device interaction.
Vector retrieval traverses high-dimensional graph structures requiring high random-access IOPS and low point-lookup latency, whereas training data loaders require sustained high-bandwidth sequential streaming.

True or False: In graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search such as HNSW or DiskANN, increasing target recall from \(90\%\) to \(99\%\) generally requires exploring more graph nodes, increasing random storage accesses and query latency.
A billion-entry vector index of 1536-dimensional FP32 embeddings consumes roughly \(6.1\text{ TB}\) of raw vector data plus graph adjacency overhead. Explain why systems migrate from pure in-memory indexes (HNSW) to disk-backed graph indexes (DiskANN), and identify the primary hardware trade-off involved.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Today’s six-tier hierarchy leaves a 1,000× latency cliff between host DRAM (~100 ns) and local NVMe (~100 μs), forces the host CPU to spend cycles decompressing bytes that GPUDirect Storage could otherwise DMA directly, and pauses training while synchronous checkpoints reach flash. Compute Express Link (CXL), the coherent capacity tier of Compute express link (CXL), targets the DRAM-to-NVMe gap first. Seen from storage, CXL-attached memory is a “Tier 1.5,” slower than host DRAM but byte-addressable, with access latencies of roughly 200 to 500 ns against the roughly 100 μs of an NVMe read. It offers a capacity pool for the structures that the Tier 1 discussion showed competing for host DRAM. For the running example, CXL-attached memory could expand the effective host memory tier from 512 GB to over 4 TB per node. That pool could hold deeper prefetch queues, embedding-table spillover, or a local shard cache as large as the 3 TB compressed source corpus without paying NVMe access latency on every read, though it still falls short of the full 6 TB tokenized training copy on one node.
A different bottleneck appears when CPU-side decoding, not storage bandwidth, throttles the pipeline. The computational storage drive closes that gap by embedding processing elements (field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) or simple CPU cores) directly on the SSD controller, enabling decompression, filtering, or format conversion to happen at the storage device rather than consuming host CPU cycles. For ML pipelines where CPU-side decoding is the bottleneck, computational storage could eliminate the CPU from the data path entirely, complementing GDS by offloading work that direct DMA cannot address.
Checkpoint writes impose the pause \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) while a consistent snapshot reaches the first storage tier, and shrinking it makes frequent saves less costly. Persistent memory, despite market shifts such as Intel’s 2022 wind-down of its Optane memory business (Intel Corporation 2022), remains the architectural idea that attacks that term directly. Byte-addressable non-volatile memory could lower the destination-device latency, but the checkpoint pause still includes snapshot creation, byte transfer, and coordination. A lower device-access latency reduces \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) only to the extent that this device lies on the pause’s critical path.

Intel Corporation. 2022. Form 10-q for the Quarterly Period Ended July 2, 2022.
These technologies are not yet broadly deployed at the scale of the largest ML clusters, but they illustrate the direction of the storage hierarchy’s evolution. The fundamental principle remains unchanged, with faster, more expensive storage closer to the accelerator and slower, cheaper storage at the periphery. What changes is the granularity of the tiers and the size of the gaps between them.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Storage design errors are among the most expensive mistakes in ML infrastructure because they are discovered late, when training begins, and remediation requires either expensive hardware upgrades or time-consuming data reformatting. The following fallacies and pitfalls capture the most common errors that experienced storage engineers make when first encountering ML workloads.

Fallacy: NVMe is fast enough to feed GPUs directly without pipelining.
A single NVMe drive delivers 7 GB/s, while an H100 consumes 3.35 TB/s from HBM. The gap is roughly 479×. Even four drives in RAID-0 only close this gap to about 120× before overhead. Without pipelining and prefetching to hide the latency of loading from NVMe to host DRAM to HBM, every batch transfer introduces a stall equal to the transfer time. The HBM ratio measures tier disparity rather than the required input rate, because model state is reused many times for each batch loaded from storage. The relevant test compares measured input delivery with batch bytes divided by compute time, then checks whether buffering hides transfer latency and jitter. A device can have enough sustained bandwidth and still expose stalls when transfers are serialized with computation.


Pitfall: Relying on prefetching to hide object storage latency.
Prefetching hides latency only within the time covered by ready batches; it cannot hide an arbitrarily long interruption. With \(\PrefetchBufferCount\) batches ready and constant compute time, a complete interruption of supply exhausts the queue after \(\PrefetchBufferCount \times \IronLawComputeTime\). A slow request need not stall computation if other completed work remains available, but correlated delays can deplete many workers’ queues together. Provision buffer depth from measured delivery tails, test correlated interruptions, and verify that the sustained refill rate meets consumption. Local staging can reduce remote exposure when the required shards fit and remain valid.


Fallacy: Millions of small training files are harmless at scale.
Storing each training sample as an individual file (one JPEG per image, one JSON per text sample) creates repeated per-file work through operations such as open(), stat(), and close(). Metadata becomes the bottleneck when the resulting request rate exceeds the service’s capacity, even if byte bandwidth remains available. Aggregating samples into sequential shards amortizes that work (section 4.3.5). Packaging 10,000 to 100,000 samples per shard can reduce file-level operations by a corresponding 10,000 to 100,000\(\times\) when readers consume whole shards. The loader must still implement the intended sampling policy and avoid repeated enumeration.


Pitfall: Ignoring egress costs when designing the storage architecture.
Cloud egress costs are invisible during development but can dominate at scale. Under a representative $0.09/GB cross-boundary egress fee, a training job that reads a 100 TB dataset from object storage 10 times incurs $90,000 in egress fees, far exceeding the annual storage cost of $24,000 under the object-storage price assumption in section 4.3.7. These fees apply when reads cross a region, provider, or internet boundary; same-region reads may be free or discounted, which is exactly why the cost stays hidden until a cross-region or multi-cloud topology makes it unavoidable. Teams that prototype with small datasets on object storage and then scale up discover that their storage architecture is economically unsustainable. The fix is to budget egress costs explicitly and to design the data pipeline to minimize cross-tier transfers, typically by staging data on local NVMe at job start rather than streaming from object storage each epoch.


Fallacy: Average write bandwidth is enough for checkpoint design.
Checkpoints are written by all nodes simultaneously, creating bursts that can exceed steady-state bandwidth by 10\(\times\) or more. When the PFS write lies on the training critical path, sizing it only for average write load extends \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) during bursts and reduces effective training throughput. A synchronous PFS-direct design must provision enough burst bandwidth to meet its pause budget. With local staging, the first tier absorbs the burst and the PFS drains it in the background; the shared tier must then meet the durability deadline and keep up with repeated saves without an unbounded backlog.


Pitfall: Assuming faster accelerators automatically improve training throughput.
When an organization upgrades from A100 to H100 GPUs, they expect training time to decrease proportionally to the compute improvement. If the storage pipeline was already marginal on A100s, delivering data just fast enough to avoid stalls, the faster H100 compute hits the I/O wall sooner. The accelerator upgrade reduces \(\IronLawComputeTime\) without reducing \(\StepIoTime\), which means the data stall ratio increases. Every accelerator upgrade must be accompanied by a storage pipeline audit to ensure that the faster compute does not expose a previously hidden storage bottleneck.


Fallacy: RAID configurations optimized for databases are suitable for ML training.
RAID selection follows the tier’s failure contract. A disposable local cache can use RAID 0 to aggregate drives without parity, provided a durable source remains available and the fleet can tolerate restaging after a drive failure. Redundant layouts can still reduce disruption when restaging is slow or the cache supports an availability objective. A local checkpoint awaiting durable replication is not yet disposable merely because it lives on the same NVMe drives. Treating all ML storage as replaceable input data confuses capacity placement with recovery policy.


Pitfall: Creating full copies for each dataset snapshot.
Copying an entire dataset for every version duplicates unchanged content. For a 10 TB dataset with 5 percent of its bytes changed, a full copy retains 9.5 TB of redundant data. Content-addressable storage or delta encoding can reuse unchanged objects or blocks. If the storage granularity isolates the changed bytes, the new payload is roughly 500 GB, a 20× reduction before metadata and redundancy overhead. Rewriting large compressed shards can reduce that saving because a small sample change may replace a much larger stored object. Versioning must therefore preserve lineage while choosing a reuse granularity compatible with the dataset format.


Fallacy: Compression always helps because it reduces the amount of data to read.
Compression reduces stored and transferred bytes but adds decoding work. If decoding further saturates an already limiting host processor, it makes that bottleneck worse, not better. If transfer is limiting and decoding has headroom, compression can improve delivery until another stage becomes the limit. Compare candidate representations using output-equivalent stage rates, including CPU or GPU decoding, rather than select the strongest codec from an I/O-bound label alone. The same choice can reduce capacity cost without improving training throughput. These fallacies all return to the same accounting exercise: where each byte lives, how often it moves, and which tier pays the cost.


Self-Check: Question

A team selects RAID 5 for a disposable local training-data cache whose immutable source is durably stored elsewhere. The fleet can tolerate restaging after drive failure. Why might RAID 0 be a better throughput-and-capacity trade-off under this failure contract?

RAID 5 cannot be formatted with modern Linux filesystems such as ext4 or XFS.
RAID 5 disables hardware DMA transfers, preventing the GPU from accessing host DRAM.
The cache can be reconstructed from its durable source, so RAID 0 can aggregate drives without parity overhead when restaging disruption is acceptable.
RAID 5 increases drive endurance wear by \(10\times\) compared to single-drive configurations.

A training team upgrades its cluster from A100 to H100 GPUs, expecting a \(3\times\) end-to-end training speedup. However, wall-clock epoch time barely improves, and GPU utilization drops from \(85\%\) to \(35\%\). Traces show shorter uninterrupted compute time, unchanged measured input-delivery rate, and increased time waiting for ready input batches, while communication and checkpoint pauses remain unchanged. Diagnose the measured bottleneck and explain why faster compute exposed it.
A team replaces a lighter codec with a denser codec on local-NVMe training shards. On this corpus, illustrative measurements give the lighter codec a 3:1 ratio and 1.5 GB/s decoded output per core, versus 4:1 and 0.5 GB/s for the denser codec. Before the change, worker profiles show decoding and augmentation saturating the host CPU and the ready-batch queue repeatedly draining. Afterward, decompression consumes more CPU time, the queue drains more often, and training step time increases although stored bytes decrease. What caused this measured regression?

Compressed shards cannot be read by NVMe controllers because flash drives require raw uncompressed binary blocks.
The pipeline was already CPU-bound on data decoding and augmentation, so adding heavy decompression work saturated the host CPU, starving the GPU of assembled batches.
The denser codec introduces non-deterministic bit flips that cause stochastic gradient descent to diverge.
The parallel file system rejects compressed shards larger than 1 GB due to POSIX file locking constraints.

True or False: Sizing a data loader’s prefetch buffer depth based on average storage read latency ensures that training runs will not experience data stalls during multi-week training jobs on shared object storage.
A team creates full \(10\text{ TB}\) copies of a pretraining dataset for every snapshot version, creating 20 versions over six months (\(200\text{ TB}\) total storage). Explain how content-addressable storage or delta encoding optimizes this workflow when successive versions differ by only \(5\%\).

See Answers →

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Storage in ML systems is an active, multi-tiered pipeline that supplies accelerator inputs, preserves restorable state, and records the lineage of training and serving artifacts. The hierarchy exists because workloads need different combinations of bandwidth, capacity, latency, durability, and cost, and the demand on it grows with the scaling laws that drive the fleet. Larger models call for more training tokens and carry larger checkpoints, so storage pressure rises at every step up the model-size curve. The data pipeline throughput equation, \(\RequiredInputBandwidth = \InputConsumerAcceleratorCount \times \TargetComputeTimeFraction\times \BatchDataVolume / \IronLawComputeTime\), sizes delivery for a chosen training rate when applied to the representation and distinct input consumers at each tier. Measured against the Fleet Law, storage succeeds when it contributes no exposed time. Prefetching preserves the Fleet Law’s assumption that the next batch is already resident. Tiered checkpoint staging shrinks the save pause that surfaces in \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) to the local write and takes the slow shared-storage copy off the step entirely, so that copy costs step time only when it contends with collectives or input reads. Both spend communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) and coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) capacity to protect compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)).
Treating the hierarchy as a cache makes that sizing workload-specific. The hit rate and the service times of the hot and cold paths determine mean effective throughput, while the tail and correlation of misses determine whether a finite prefetch buffer drains. At the durable tiers, reliability also separates into three contracts: data survival, service response, and the version a reader may observe. These are durability, availability, and consistency, respectively; improving one does not automatically establish the others.
The diagnostic task is to identify which service contract fails before changing the storage tier. Low accelerator utilization can arise from metadata-intensive loading, a depleted prefetch queue, an exposed checkpoint write, or host-memory traffic crossing a contended NUMA link. Measure input wait separately from communication and synchronization before attributing it to storage. Full-corpus scans favor aggregated shards, while graph retrieval and live features require random access and explicit consistency. A depleted input queue can reflect slow storage, metadata contention, or insufficient decoding capacity; GDS helps when host payload copying is the limiting stage while retaining CPU control. Compare remedies by total delivery cost, including transfers and idle accelerators. For checkpoint writes, evaluate the shorter training pause together with the time until a complete generation becomes durable and publishable.

Key Takeaways: Feed the accelerators or waste them

Workload demand sizes the delivery path: Use \(\RequiredInputBandwidth = \InputConsumerAcceleratorCount \times \TargetComputeTimeFraction\times \BatchDataVolume / \IronLawComputeTime\) for the chosen training rate, then check each tier’s service rate and buffering (principle \(\ref{pri-storage-hierarchy}\)).
Workload determines the storage contract: Full-corpus scans favor sequential throughput and aggregated shards, and metadata operations can bind before byte bandwidth does (principle \(\ref{pri-io-wall}\)). Disk-backed graph retrieval must fit its random I/O within a serving deadline, and synthetic-data pipelines must budget verification traffic separately from retained capacity while keeping the versioned lineage of every accepted sample.
Tail latency sets the cache budget: A high hot-tier hit rate is insufficient when cold misses are orders of magnitude slower. Use equation 1 as a mean baseline, then size prefetch buffers from p99 I/O latency and test correlated miss bursts against the compute window.
Direct storage removes host payload copies: GDS retains CPU submission and coordination while bypassing host bounce buffers. The illustrative example assumes 75 percent less active CPU time per request; the benefit depends on whether payload copying limits the workload.
Checkpoint recovery is a storage protocol: Local NVMe staging can shorten pause time, but a restorable checkpoint also needs durable publication, a committed manifest, and verified shards; durability, availability, and consistency remain distinct contracts.
Pipeline correctness lives at commit boundaries: Replay preserves processing completeness only when stable identifiers and idempotent or transactional writes prevent duplicate effects. Event-time watermarks then make the separate freshness-completeness trade-off explicit.
Economics drive tiering: The 5× local-NVMe/object-storage price ratio illustrates the incentive to keep data on cheaper tiers under the stated pricing assumptions (principle \(\ref{pri-storage-hierarchy}\)). Compare total delivery cost, including transfer charges and idle accelerators, before deciding where to stage it.



Checkpoint staging shows the C\(^3\) trade-off in one design decision. Writing first to local NVMe shortens the compute pause, but asynchronous replication adds communication traffic and requires coordination to publish only complete generations. Once the shared-file-system write leaves the critical path, the bottleneck can move to local flash endurance, peer-replication bandwidth, or manifest commit latency. Measuring only the shorter training pause would miss the new recovery boundary.

What’s Next: From storage to communicationCompute silicon, network fabrics, and storage hierarchies establish the physical resources of the machine learning fleet. Coordinating those resources into one training computation remains a separate problem. This chapter’s 175B running model already exceeds, in its FP16 weights alone, the 80 GB device of the HBM placement example, so its state and work must span devices, and every division of that work obliges workers to exchange gradients, activations, or parameters across the fabric. Part II moves from physical infrastructure to distributed execution. It begins with the collective operations that carry those exchanges and the cost of each, then partitions neural networks across data, tensor, pipeline, and sequence dimensions, before turning to the hardware failures that a fleet must survive.





↪ The collective operations that carry gradient and activation exchanges, and the cost models that price them, are developed in Collective Communication.

title: 4 Data Storage
text:
Self-Check: Answer

An H100 accelerator consumes data from its HBM at roughly \(3.35\text{ TB/s}\), while a single local NVMe drive delivers sequential reads at roughly \(7\text{ GB/s}\). A team is designing the storage infrastructure for a 1,000-accelerator training fleet. Which conclusion follows directly from this bandwidth ratio?

The gap is easily bridged by standard NVMe RAID arrays because sequential read throughput scales without bound across drives.
The roughly \(479\times\) device-bandwidth gap motivates tiered staging, but required input bandwidth must be calculated from batch bytes and compute time rather than equated with HBM traffic.
The bandwidth gap is negligible because large-scale training is entirely compute-bound and rarely exercises HBM bandwidth.
The bandwidth gap disappears when high-speed InfiniBand fabrics deliver data directly into HBM from remote storage endpoints without local staging.

Answer: The correct answer is B. HBM and NVMe serve different traffic: model state and intermediate tensors can be reused many times for each input batch. The roughly \(479\times\) ratio illustrates tier disparity, not a storage-rate requirement. Batch bytes, compute time, concurrency, and buffering determine whether inputs arrive in time; neither RAID aggregation nor a faster network alone establishes that condition.
Learning Objective: Distinguish storage input demand from internal HBM traffic when interpreting the bandwidth gap
A 175B-parameter model trains for 30 days on 256 nodes, writing resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoints of roughly \(2.45\text{ TB}\) (\(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights, \(700\text{ GB}\) FP32 master weights, and \(1.4\text{ TB}\) of Adam moments) every 10 minutes. Explain why ML storage design is fundamentally a joint physics-and-economics optimization problem.
Answer: HBM supplies high local bandwidth for active tensors but cannot economically retain the corpus and checkpoint history. Shared durable storage pools capacity at lower cost, while interfaces, contention, and client allocation determine the rate and latency a consumer receives. Tier placement must satisfy input-delivery and checkpoint-recovery budgets at the lowest total delivery cost. Remote input reads can suffice when their sustained rate and buffered latency meet demand; local staging is useful when they do not. Compare capacity cost, transfers, and exposed accelerator wait rather than infer a stall from remote placement alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze why ML storage architecture requires tiered placement that simultaneously satisfies bandwidth physics and capacity economics
True or False: A cluster benchmark demonstrating that compute hardware achieves advertised peak TFLOP/s and network fabric achieves advertised bisection bandwidth is sufficient evidence that end-to-end training throughput will scale linearly with accelerator count.
Answer: False. Isolated compute and fabric benchmarks evaluate floating-point throughput and inter-node communication in synthetic conditions without exercising the end-to-end data pipeline. Real training throughput requires continuously streaming input batches, loading model weights, and absorbing periodic checkpoint write storms; if the storage hierarchy cannot deliver input samples within the compute window (\(\IronLawComputeTime\)), accelerators sit idle regardless of peak compute capability.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why compute and network benchmarks in isolation fail to guarantee scalable end-to-end training throughput without storage pipeline validation
An accelerator upgrade reduces compute time per batch while the input representation and storage delivery time remain fixed. What is the primary systems consequence for training cluster design?

Training pipelines automatically increase data compression ratios to prevent accelerator starvation without requiring architectural adjustments.
Storage hierarchies can eliminate intermediate DRAM and NVMe caching tiers because modern network fabrics directly absorb the difference.
Checkpoint intervals must be decreased proportionally to the compute growth to keep local NVMe buffers from overflowing.
The compute window available to deliver each batch shrinks, so input I/O can become the bottleneck unless the measured delivery path keeps pace.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Faster computation leaves less time to fetch the next batch. Overlap and prefetching hide latency within their buffering window, but cannot fix a sustained service-rate deficit. Automatic compression is not guaranteed, removing staging does not improve a slow source, and checkpoint frequency does not set input delivery throughput.
Learning Objective: Explain the systems consequences of compute throughput scaling significantly faster than persistent storage bandwidth
In large-scale distributed training, when hundreds of nodes simultaneously pause computation to write gigabytes of model weights and optimizer states to persistent storage, the resulting synchronized burst of write traffic is called a ____.
Answer: The correct term is checkpoint storm. A checkpoint storm occurs when all data-parallel or model-parallel workers simultaneously flush their memory shards to local or remote storage, creating extreme write contention that must be absorbed via tiered staging (such as writing to local NVMe before asynchronously copying to a parallel file system).
Learning Objective: Explain the technical term for synchronized cluster-wide write bursts generated during distributed training state saves

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A storage procurement team is sizing storage hardware for a cluster dedicated to pretraining foundation models on a \(200\text{ TB}\) immutable text corpus. Which purchasing decision represents the most severe misallocation of budget based on ML workload characteristics?

Paying a premium for enterprise SSDs optimized for high \(4\text{ KB}\) random-read IOPS while under-provisioning sustained sequential read bandwidth (GB/s).
Aggregating raw text samples into \(256\text{ MB}\) to \(4\text{ GB}\) contiguous binary shards prior to training to amortize file-system metadata operations.
Provisioning local NVMe drives on compute nodes to serve as a warm read cache for multi-epoch training passes.
Sizing the parallel file system write tier to absorb synchronized multi-terabyte checkpoint write bursts from hundreds of nodes.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Paying a premium for enterprise SSDs optimized for high \(4\text{ KB}\) random-read IOPS while under-provisioning sustained sequential read bandwidth (GB/s). ML pretraining streams large contiguous batches sequentially, where a drive delivers \(7\text{-}14\text{ GB/s}\), whereas \(4\text{ KB}\) random reads drop throughput to \(\approx 0.5\text{ GB/s}\); optimizing for random IOPS buys capabilities the workload never utilizes while starving the pipeline of raw gigabytes-per-second throughput. Shard aggregation is the standard mitigation against metadata serialization, local NVMe caching prevents repeated network egress, and sizing for checkpoint bursts directly addresses the bursty write inversion.
Learning Objective: Evaluate storage procurement decisions against the sequential-streaming and bursty-write inversions of ML workloads
True or False: An in-memory LRU cache sized to \(300\text{ GB}\) placed in front of a \(3\text{ TB}\) uniformly shuffled pretraining dataset will achieve roughly a \(90\%\) hit rate after the first epoch warms the cache because all samples are reused across epochs.
Answer: False. A cache holding one-tenth of a uniformly shuffled corpus does not gain a 90 percent hit rate merely because samples recur in later epochs. Most cached samples are evicted before reuse. A fixed cyclic scan larger than the cache can approach zero hits; independently reshuffled epochs allow low but nonzero cross-epoch hits that depend on cache fraction and sample order.
Learning Objective: Analyze why temporal-locality caching strategies such as LRU fail on uniformly streamed ML pretraining datasets
Explain why ML data loaders implement shard-level shuffling combined with within-shard buffer mixing rather than true global per-sample random shuffling across petabyte-scale training corpora.
Answer: Shard-level shuffling and within-shard buffer mixing preserve sequential I/O while introducing sample-order variation. Adequate mixing depends on shard composition and buffer size: homogeneous shards may require finer shards or larger mixing buffers. Validate the layout against the loss curve of a fully shuffled baseline on a subset before committing the run.
Learning Objective: Justify shard-level shuffling under explicit mixing and convergence checks
When an inference platform deploys a new version of a 175B-parameter model (\(350\text{ GB}\) FP16 weights) across 100 serving replicas, how does the storage access profile contrast with a training checkpoint save?

It generates continuous small random writes to update parameter journals on each replica node.
It streams an incremental delta of only modified parameters over hours to minimize bandwidth utilization.
It creates a synchronized fan-out read burst of roughly \(35\text{ TB}\) (\(100 \times 350\text{ GB}\)) that must complete within the deployment latency budget while serving traffic continues.
It requires sustained multi-gigabyte-per-second sequential write bandwidth to central durable object storage.

Answer: The correct answer is C. It creates a synchronized fan-out read burst of roughly \(35\text{ TB}\) (\(100 \times 350\text{ GB}\)) that must complete within the deployment latency budget while serving traffic continues. A model rollout is the architectural mirror image of a checkpoint storm: instead of many nodes simultaneously writing state to storage (fan-in burst), many replica nodes simultaneously read the same large model weights from storage (fan-out burst). The small-random-writes option describes OLTP database journaling. The delta-streaming option assumes parameter-level differential rollouts that production serving frameworks avoid in favor of immutable weight images. The central-write option confuses read distribution to serving nodes with training checkpoint writes.
Learning Objective: Classify model rollout storage traffic as a synchronized fan-out read burst and quantify its cluster-wide volume
A team plans one storage configuration for the whole life of a language-model project: tokenizing and deduplicating a \(3\text{ TB}\) compressed corpus into \(6\text{ TB}\) of shards, then training on those shards with periodic checkpoints. Why does the chapter conclude that no single configuration optimizes every phase?

Preprocessing reads and writes large sequential artifacts in MapReduce-like passes, while training reads immutable shards between bursty checkpoint writes, so the read/write balance and access pattern change by phase.
Training reads are dominated by small random lookups that only a database-style random-IOPS tier can serve, while preprocessing is purely sequential.
The tokenized corpus is smaller than the compressed source, so preprocessing frees capacity that the training phase cannot use.
Checkpoint writes are continuous and small, so they require a different write-ahead log configuration than preprocessing.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The fourth inversion is that the read/write ratio shifts by lifecycle phase: preprocessing scans and rewrites large artifacts, while training streams read-only shards between synchronized checkpoint bursts. Each phase loads the tiers differently, which is why ML systems use a multi-tier hierarchy rather than one storage technology. Training reads are not small random lookups, the tokenized corpus is larger than the compressed source, and checkpoints are bursty large writes, not continuous small ones.
Learning Objective: Explain why phase-dependent read/write behavior requires a multi-tier storage hierarchy

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Order the six tiers from Tier 0 through Tier 5 in the chapter’s placement hierarchy, moving outward from accelerator-resident memory through node-local resources to shared storage and archive: (1) Local NVMe SSD, (2) Object Storage, (3) Host DRAM, (4) GPU HBM, (5) Parallel File System, (6) Archive / Cold Storage.
Answer: The correct order is: (4) GPU HBM, (3) Host DRAM, (1) Local NVMe SSD, (5) Parallel File System, (2) Object Storage, (6) Archive / Cold Storage. HBM is accelerator-resident; host DRAM and local NVMe serve the node; the parallel file system provides shared access; object storage retains durable organizational data; and archive preserves rarely accessed history. This is the chapter’s placement order, not a universal bandwidth ranking. HBM rates are per accelerator, DRAM and local NVMe rates are per node, and shared-service rates must be allocated among clients and checked against the actual delivery path.
Learning Objective: Order the six storage tiers by placement and distinguish that order from a bandwidth comparison
Host DRAM (Tier 1) executes a four-stage data loader pipeline: Read, Decode, Augment, and Collate. Why place the final collated batch in page-locked (‘pinned’) host memory for direct asynchronous DMA to GPU HBM without an intermediate staging copy?

Pinned memory automatically compresses tensors using host CPU vector units before PCIe transmission.
Pinned memory locks physical pages in host RAM so the PCIe DMA controller can copy data directly to GPU memory without an intermediate pinned staging copy.
Pinned memory replicates the batch across all NUMA nodes to ensure uniform memory access for parallel data loader threads.
Pinned memory guarantees transactional ACID durability on host storage in case the worker process crashes during transfer.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Pinned memory locks physical pages in host RAM so the PCIe DMA controller can copy data directly to GPU memory without an intermediate pinned staging copy. Standard virtual memory pages can be paged out or relocated by the operating system, forcing the GPU driver to copy data into an intermediate pinned staging buffer before initiating DMA; allocating pinned memory directly (pin_memory=True in PyTorch) eliminates this extra CPU memory copy and allows direct DMA across PCIe. The compression option is incorrect as pinned memory is an OS page-locking mechanism, not a compression algorithm. The NUMA replication claim is false because pinning prevents paging rather than replicating data or choosing NUMA placement. The ACID durability option confuses volatile host DRAM staging with persistent transaction logging.
Learning Objective: Explain the architectural function of pinned host memory in accelerating CPU-to-GPU DMA data transfers
A vision training cluster migrating to a high-performance parallel file system (PFS) with \(500\text{ GB/s}\) rated aggregate bandwidth reports that throughput during ImageNet training is capped at under \(5\text{ GB/s}\), with storage data disks showing negligible I/O activity. The dataset consists of millions of individual JPEG files. A worker trace shows repeated waits for file opens, and the MDS reports a sustained operation queue with rising lookup latency while its service rate is saturated. What bottleneck do these additional measurements establish, and which fix addresses it?

The network fabric is dropping packets due to congestion; enable flow control on top-of-rack switches.
The parallel file system is bottlenecked on drive endurance wear-leveling; replace SSDs with high-DWPD enterprise drives.
The dataset is stored as millions of individual image files, saturating the Metadata Server (MDS) with per-file POSIX lookups; repackage images into large sequential shards (such as WebDataset tar archives).
The GPUs are compute-bound and cannot consume data faster; decrease the batch size to increase I/O request frequency.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The saturated MDS service rate, rising lookup latency, and worker file-open waits establish a metadata bottleneck in this case. Repackaging images into sequential shards amortizes per-file operations across many samples. Idle data disks and low throughput alone would not establish this cause; the supplied metadata measurements distinguish it from a slow decoder or another blocked pipeline stage.
Learning Objective: Analyze parallel file system metadata saturation from telemetry signatures and prescribe shard-aggregation remediation
A training node uses four local NVMe drives configured in RAID-0 as a warm cache for \(25\text{ TB}\) of pre-shuffled training shards. Explain why RAID-0 is an appropriate engineering trade-off for this specific tier, and identify what workload change would make RAID-0 catastrophic.
Answer: RAID-0 aggregates drive bandwidth without parity capacity overhead, making it appropriate for a disposable warm cache when a durable source remains available and the fleet can tolerate restaging after a drive failure. It does not protect availability: losing one drive can invalidate the array. If the array holds the only copy of an unrecoverable artifact or a checkpoint not yet durably replicated, a drive failure can permanently lose that state; the cache placement policy cannot substitute for a recovery contract.
Learning Objective: Justify RAID-0 storage configurations for warm cache tiers and identify failure boundaries where lack of redundancy causes unrecoverable data loss
