A warm replica therefore trades DRAM capacity for a host-memory-bound load that is still several times faster than a striped NVMe read.
Learning Objective: Identify the shared resource that bounds a parallel weight load from host memory
A serving fleet of 100 replicas of a 175B-parameter model deploys a new version, so all replicas must read \(35\text{ TB}\) of FP16 weights at once. Which statement correctly evaluates the shared sources?

A \(100\text{ GB/s}\) object store finishes in about 5.8 minutes, while the \(1\text{ TB/s}\) parallel file system would take about 35 seconds but only by claiming the whole file system from co-tenant training jobs.
The parallel file system is always the right source because 35 seconds is shorter, and serving reads cannot interfere with training jobs.
The object store finishes in about 35 seconds because each replica reads only its own share of the weights.
Rollout time is independent of the source tier because each replica’s load is limited by its own PCIe link.

Answer: The correct answer is A. The rollout reads \(35\text{ TB}\) in one burst, so time is volume divided by the aggregate rate the source can give the fleet: \(35\text{ TB} / 100\text{ GB/s} \approx 5.8\) minutes, or \(35\text{ TB} / 1\text{ TB/s} = 35\) seconds. The faster option starves every training job sharing the file system, the read-side mirror of a checkpoint storm, which is why fleets stage new versions locally, roll updates across replica groups, or let loaded replicas supply the rest.
Learning Objective: Size a fleet-wide model rollout against shared storage tiers and identify its interference with co-tenant training
How does the storage performance bottleneck for a graph-based vector retrieval index at billion-vector scale contrast with the primary bottleneck of an ML training data loader?

Vector retrieval is bottlenecked by sequential streaming bandwidth (GB/s), whereas training data loaders are bottlenecked by random \(4\text{ KB}\) read IOPS.
Vector retrieval requires continuous multi-terabyte burst writes, whereas training data loaders perform purely read-only operations.
Vector retrieval is strictly compute-bound on matrix multiplication units and generates zero storage device interaction.
Vector retrieval traverses high-dimensional graph structures requiring high random-access IOPS and low point-lookup latency, whereas training data loaders require sustained high-bandwidth sequential streaming.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Vector retrieval traverses high-dimensional graph structures requiring high random-access IOPS and low point-lookup latency, whereas training data loaders require sustained high-bandwidth sequential streaming. Retrieval-augmented generation inverts the training access pattern: instead of streaming large contiguous shards sequentially, vector search algorithms (like HNSW or DiskANN) navigate sparse high-dimensional graph adjacency lists, issuing thousands of small, non-sequential pointer lookups where latency and random IOPS govern query response time. The sequential-streaming option inverts the two workloads. The burst-write claim confuses retrieval query serving with training checkpointing. The zero-storage claim ignores that billion-scale vector indexes span terabytes of storage.
Learning Objective: Compare the storage performance bottlenecks of vector retrieval graph traversal against training data streaming
True or False: In graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search such as HNSW or DiskANN, increasing target recall from \(90\%\) to \(99\%\) generally requires exploring more graph nodes, increasing random storage accesses and query latency.
Answer: True for graph-based ANN under otherwise comparable settings. Raising recall generally expands the search beam or visits more candidate nodes, increasing vector-distance computations and random DRAM or SSD accesses and therefore latency. This mechanism is specific to graph traversal; flat scans, IVF indexes, and PQ-based designs expose different controls and bottlenecks.
Learning Objective: Analyze the recall-latency-IOPS trade-off in graph-based high-dimensional vector search
A billion-entry vector index of 1536-dimensional FP32 embeddings consumes roughly \(6.1\text{ TB}\) of raw vector data plus graph adjacency overhead. Explain why systems migrate from pure in-memory indexes (HNSW) to disk-backed graph indexes (DiskANN), and identify the primary hardware trade-off involved.
Answer: The raw vectors alone occupy about \(6.1\text{ TB}\). At 50 to 100 adjacency bytes per entry, minimal graph links add only \(50\) to \(100\text{ GB}\); identifiers, allocator overhead, slack, and replication can add more. A disk-backed graph index keeps compact navigation representations in DRAM and fetches other data from SSD, trading lower DRAM capacity for random SSD access latency. The actual memory reduction and latency penalty depend on the representation, cache, and search settings.
Learning Objective: Compare in-memory (HNSW) and disk-backed (DiskANN) vector indexing architectures in terms of capacity cost and query latency trade-offs

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A team selects RAID 5 for a disposable local training-data cache whose immutable source is durably stored elsewhere. The fleet can tolerate restaging after drive failure. Why might RAID 0 be a better throughput-and-capacity trade-off under this failure contract?

RAID 5 cannot be formatted with modern Linux filesystems such as ext4 or XFS.
RAID 5 disables hardware DMA transfers, preventing the GPU from accessing host DRAM.
The cache can be reconstructed from its durable source, so RAID 0 can aggregate drives without parity overhead when restaging disruption is acceptable.
RAID 5 increases drive endurance wear by \(10\times\) compared to single-drive configurations.

Answer: The correct answer is C. A disposable cache need not own durability when its source remains available. RAID 0 removes parity overhead but increases exposure to cache loss and restaging. RAID 5 can still be justified by availability requirements; checkpoints awaiting durable replication are not disposable. Filesystem support and DMA are not disabled by RAID 5, and the stated endurance multiplier is unsupported.
Learning Objective: Evaluate RAID parity and striping trade-offs for disposable ML caches under explicit durability and availability requirements
A training team upgrades its cluster from A100 to H100 GPUs, expecting a \(3\times\) end-to-end training speedup. However, wall-clock epoch time barely improves, and GPU utilization drops from \(85\%\) to \(35\%\). Traces show shorter uninterrupted compute time, unchanged measured input-delivery rate, and increased time waiting for ready input batches, while communication and checkpoint pauses remain unchanged. Diagnose the measured bottleneck and explain why faster compute exposed it.
Answer: The traces establish an input-delivery limit: compute finishes sooner, but the unchanged pipeline does not supply ready batches at the new consumption rate. More of the iteration is therefore exposed input wait. Prefetching can hide delays within its queue window but cannot overcome a sustained delivery-rate deficit. The utilization and epoch-time figures alone would not identify this cause; the supplied timing measurements distinguish it from communication or checkpoint pauses. Profile individual read, decode, and transfer stages before selecting a remedy.
Learning Objective: Analyze training throughput regressions following accelerator compute upgrades using the I/O wall framework
A team replaces a lighter codec with a denser codec on local-NVMe training shards. On this corpus, illustrative measurements give the lighter codec a 3:1 ratio and 1.5 GB/s decoded output per core, versus 4:1 and 0.5 GB/s for the denser codec. Before the change, worker profiles show decoding and augmentation saturating the host CPU and the ready-batch queue repeatedly draining. Afterward, decompression consumes more CPU time, the queue drains more often, and training step time increases although stored bytes decrease. What caused this measured regression?

Compressed shards cannot be read by NVMe controllers because flash drives require raw uncompressed binary blocks.
The pipeline was already CPU-bound on data decoding and augmentation, so adding heavy decompression work saturated the host CPU, starving the GPU of assembled batches.
The denser codec introduces non-deterministic bit flips that cause stochastic gradient descent to diverge.
The parallel file system rejects compressed shards larger than 1 GB due to POSIX file locking constraints.

Answer: The correct answer is B. The supplied worker profiles and ready-batch queues establish a host-processing limit before the change; additional decompression work further reduces completed-batch delivery. The denser codec saves stored bytes but requires more CPU work for the same decoded output under these corpus-specific measurements. These illustrative rates are not fixed properties of named compression levels. Compare output-equivalent stage rates and input wait when choosing a representation.
Learning Objective: Analyze the CPU-versus-I/O trade-offs of data compression and identify when decompression overhead degrades pipeline throughput
True or False: Sizing a data loader’s prefetch buffer depth based on average storage read latency ensures that training runs will not experience data stalls during multi-week training jobs on shared object storage.
Answer: False. Average latency does not bound tail stalls. A starting buffer budget is \(Q_{\text{prefetch}} = \lceil T_{\text{I/O,p99}} / T_{\text{compute}} \rceil\) plus margin, but longer or correlated delays can still drain it; sustained delivery bandwidth must also keep pace with consumption.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why prefetch queues sized to average latency fail to prevent accelerator stalls under tail-latency variance
A team creates full \(10\text{ TB}\) copies of a pretraining dataset for every snapshot version, creating 20 versions over six months (\(200\text{ TB}\) total storage). Explain how content-addressable storage or delta encoding optimizes this workflow when successive versions differ by only \(5\%\).
Answer: The first version requires \(10\text{ TB}\). Nineteen subsequent versions with \(5\%\) new content each add \(0.5\text{ TB}\), for \(19.5\text{ TB}\) total before metadata and replication, saving \(180.5\text{ TB}\) against 20 full copies. Content-addressable storage references unchanged blocks rather than copying them; the reduction assumes changes remain localized at the stored block or shard granularity.
Learning Objective: Compare naive full-copy dataset versioning against delta-encoded content-addressable snapshotting in terms of storage efficiency

← Back to Questions

title: 5 Collective Communication
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why does communication between machines constrain large-scale machine learning systems?
Computation scales by adding processors; communication scales by moving data between them. These scale differently. Adding processors increases available arithmetic capacity, but useful work stalls when the required data does not arrive in time. Exchanging gradients, activations, and parameters can then consume more time than computing them. On one machine, shortening the dominant calculation often shortens the job. Across a fleet, that same improvement may simply make each processor reach its next dependency sooner and wait longer for the others. The cost of that wait includes every reserved accelerator, so a small delay repeated throughout training can consume a substantial budget without advancing the model. Faster links help when transfer capacity is the constraint, but the benefit depends on which physical paths the traffic shares. More bandwidth cannot remove a dependency. Sending less data introduces its own choices about numerical accuracy, memory use, and when the next computation can begin. An exchange must also deliver the correct result to every participant that needs it. A fast transfer that combines the wrong contributions does not preserve a valid training run. The engineering decision is therefore how to organize communication so that its cost remains compatible with the work it enables. Light-speed delays, bandwidth limits, and the energy cost of movement make that decision as physical as processor design. In C³ terms, collective communication connects distributed compute through coordinated exchanges whose correctness and exposed cost determine whether the fleet delivers useful scale.

Learning Objectives

Apply communication cost models to estimate collective duration and message-size crossover points
Match collective communication primitives and AllToAll schedules to parallelism strategies, topology, message granularity, and skew
Compare ring, tree, butterfly, double-tree, and hierarchical reduction algorithms using scale-dependent cost models
Evaluate topology-aware collective schedules under link-bandwidth, rank-placement, and shared-capacity constraints
Evaluate compression, sparsification, and error feedback by balancing communication savings against convergence risk
Design overlap strategies with bucket fusion, asynchronous operations, and layer-by-layer gradient scheduling
Specify matched measurements for calibrating collective cost models across algorithms, process groups, and topologies



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



When 10,000 GPUs cooperate on one training update, the splits created by data, tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism determine which results must cross device boundaries. Workers execute collective operations within participating groups and point-to-point transfers between pipeline stages. In the multi-tier fleet stack of The Fleet Stack, these exchanges occupy the Distributed Execution row of the Distribution band, where logical parallelism becomes physical traffic.
Every such split assumes that replicas, shards, stages, and experts can exchange gradients, activations, parameters, and tokens quickly enough for the optimizer to see one coherent training run. In data parallelism, each worker holds a full copy of the model and processes its own slice of the batch, so the copies must agree on one combined gradient before every update. Tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism divide the model itself, so partial results must cross device boundaries within each step. Each of these exchanges is charged to the Fleet Law’s communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\), and the part of it not hidden behind computation counts against program goodput, the ratio of a step’s ideal execution time to its actual time (The iron law and the Fleet Law terms). Every way of splitting the model relocates work onto the network, and this chapter turns those exchanges into schedules whose latency, bandwidth, and topology costs can be computed.


↪ The partitioning strategies themselves, and the 3D parallelism cube that composes data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism into one configuration space, are developed in The Parallelism Design Space.
The gap between that assumption and the wire reveals an asymmetry in how computation and communication scale. Computation is local because each GPU works on its own data, so aggregate compute grows with the number of GPUs. Communication is global because keeping the fleet synchronized requires information to cross physical links with finite latency, bandwidth, interconnect topology, and energy. Gradient synchronization is the central case, because every synchronous data-parallel step repeats it on the full gradient. Scaling laws (principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\)) make that case harder over time, because the capability they reward comes from more parameters trained on more accelerators, so the gradient to be reduced and the group that must agree on it grow together.
Managing that global traffic begins by separating an operation’s result from the schedule that produces it. The Synchronization Backbone named AllReduce, AllGather, and AllToAll as the traffic the fabric must carry; here they become contracts on results. AllReduce1 combines corresponding tensor elements across participating workers and returns the reduced tensor to every worker. AllGather instead concatenates their shards, ReduceScatter combines contributions but leaves each worker with only a shard of the result, and AllToAll sends different data to different destinations. The parallel decomposition determines which contract each exchange needs; ring, tree, and hierarchical algorithms are alternative schedules for carrying that contract out.
1 AllReduce: The name comes from MPI and describes the result, not the schedule: a Reduce (combining every rank’s data at one root) followed by a Broadcast (returning the combined value to all ranks). A direct gather to the root concentrates raw input traffic there, but a tree can aggregate contributions along the way. The algorithms in section 5.6.3 distribute the reduction without a root.For the initial gradient budget, consider a ring schedule: each worker passes tensor chunks to a neighbor, first accumulating their sums and then circulating the completed chunks. Each phase moves nearly one tensor’s worth of data per worker, so the bandwidth budget is approximately twice the gradient size divided by link bandwidth. The detailed round count follows once the transfer model is established.

Definition 5.1: Gradient synchronization
Gradient synchronization is the collective communication step in synchronous data-parallel training in which every worker contributes its locally computed gradient tensor to an aggregate reduction, then receives the same reduced result so all model replicas apply an identical update.

Significance: Communicating all gradients of a 70B-parameter model in BF16 gives a 140 GB logical payload per replica per step. As a communication-only baseline, suppose every rank reduces that complete buffer. A ring across 1,000 GPUs at 50 GB/s per link has a bandwidth budget of approximately \(2 \times 140/50\) \(\approx\) 5.6 s of transfer per step. Model partitioning shrinks each rank’s share of that buffer, and only the portion of \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) left exposed after overlap adds to step time in the Fleet Law (equation 1.3).
Distinction: Unlike a parameter server, which concentrates every worker’s gradient at a central aggregator, ring AllReduce spreads the exchange so that each worker sends \(2 \times (\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes per step, approaching \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) however large the cluster grows (section 5.6.1 develops the comparison).
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that ring AllReduce makes every worker exchange data with every other worker. In ring AllReduce, each worker communicates with neighbors according to a schedule, and the per-node communication volume is approximately constant as the cluster grows. The scaling pressure comes from latency steps, topology, and the gradient volume per step, not from every worker opening a distinct stream to every other worker.



For standard synchronous data-parallel stochastic gradient descent (SGD), gradient synchronization supplies the shared gradient needed for one optimization trajectory. Replicas that apply different local gradients can diverge. To reproduce the intended global-batch update, they must also start from matching parameters and optimizer state, weight local contributions correctly, and apply the same update rule. The AllReduce primitive provides the reduction; convergence follows from the optimization assumptions, not from communication alone. Floating-point reduction order can still change low-order bits.
In general, a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters contributes \(2\Parameters\) bytes per data-parallel replica when all gradients are communicated in BF16 (2 bytes per parameter); stored weight precision alone does not determine that choice. For the 70-billion-parameter model in the definition above (a mid-sized dense model smaller than the 175B-parameter running instance of Archetype A, GPT-4/Llama-3), that complete logical gradient is 140 GB, and a ring moves nearly twice its input buffer size per rank.2 If a replica spans multiple ranks through model parallelism, each corresponding-shard group reduces its own portion rather than this full buffer.
2 Ring AllReduce: The algorithm dates to the HPC collective-communication literature; Patarasuk and Yuan analyzed bandwidth-optimal AllReduce algorithms for workstation clusters, Baidu’s Andrew Gibiansky popularized ring AllReduce for deep learning in February 2017, and Horovod plus NVIDIA NCCL helped make it a common distributed-training primitive (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009; Gibiansky 2017; Sergeev and Balso 2018; Jeaugey 2017).
Patarasuk, Pitch, and Xin Yuan. 2009. “Bandwidth Optimal All-Reduce Algorithms for Clusters of Workstations.” Journal of Parallel and Distributed Computing 69 (2): 117–24. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2008.09.002.

Gibiansky, A. 2017. Bringing HPC Techniques to Deep Learning. Baidu Research Technical Blog.

Sergeev, Alexander, and Mike Del Balso. 2018. “Horovod: Fast and Easy Distributed Deep Learning in TensorFlow.” CoRR abs/1802.05799.

Jeaugey, Sylvain. 2017. NCCL 2.0. GPU Technology Conference presentation.
Because every bandwidth term in this chapter scales linearly with payload size, the worked derivations use this compact 70B gradient (or the chapter’s reference gradient buffer first priced in the energy estimate of section 5.2) and vary rank count to isolate how each schedule scales, before section 5.7.1 prices the full 175B Archetype A model on this book’s reference cluster.
At large scale (hundreds of billions of parameters across thousands of GPUs), gradient synchronization can dominate training step time unless collective communication is systematically optimized. Understanding how to manage that overhead requires modeling data movement as physics rather than as an abstract API call.



Exposed gradient synchronization can dominate step time at scale.

Self-Check: Question

A dense-model training run triples its GPU count from 64 to 192 while holding the global work per update fixed. Step time drops by only 30%, and per-GPU compute utilization falls. Which scaling mechanism should the team investigate, without treating these aggregates as proof of the cause?

Backpropagation stops functioning correctly across multiple nodes because gradients cannot be computed concurrently across independent data batches.
Floating-point accumulation during gradient reduction becomes numerically unstable when more than 64 GPUs participate in the collective.
Host CPU memory bandwidth saturates because all optimizer states must be shuffled through host DRAM on every multi-node step.
Local compute can shrink while global synchronization and shared-link transfers remain exposed; rank-aligned traces are needed to determine whether communication actually limits the step.

A logical Ring AllReduce cost model uses a 140 GB input per rank, corresponding to the model-wide BF16 gradient size of a 70B-parameter model. Holding that input fixed, a team expects per-rank sent volume to grow over 100 times when the group grows from 8 to 1,000 ranks. Explain why the expectation is false and why time can still increase. Treat this as transfer arithmetic, not a claim that a full replicated training state fits on one GPU.
True or False: In synchronous data-parallel distributed training, using Ring AllReduce causes each GPU network bandwidth requirement to scale quadratically with the number of GPUs \(N\) because every worker must open a direct communication socket to every other worker in the cluster.

See Answers →





Whenever a gradient shard leaves an accelerator, three hardware limits bound its trip before any collective algorithm runs. The speed of light sets a propagation floor3 of roughly 5 \(\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) per kilometer in fiber. High-frequency signal loss limits how far copper traces can reach before the link must convert to optics (the bandwidth-distance product of Reach and medium for copper and optics). Host-kernel networking stacks add tens of microseconds of software copy overhead, unless kernel-bypass transports such as remote direct memory access (RDMA) and GPUDirect RDMA strip per-message initiation down to a few microseconds. Collective communication also pays an energy price for every bit moved across those links, which the schedule must respect as firmly as latency and bandwidth.
3 The speed-of-light constraint: Light travels through optical fiber at approximately 200,000 km/s, or 200 meters per microsecond. For a rack-to-rack fiber path of 100 meters, propagation alone contributes approximately 500 ns in one direction. Faster switches can reduce other latency components, but reducing this propagation delay requires a shorter path or a different propagation medium.
↩︎ Kernel-bypass RDMA, which strips the per-message software overhead, and GPUDirect RDMA, which removes the host-memory bounce, are established in RDMA and GPUDirect.

Moving data consumes energy across storage arrays, interfaces, serializers, transceivers, and switches. A transfer that starts in local SRAM can stay on-package in high-bandwidth memory (HBM), cross to an intra-node peer GPU, or traverse intermediate switches to a remote node. Each step widens the physical accounting boundary that an energy estimate must include (figure 1). Each boundary activates distinct physical components: on-package links, intra-node crossbars, serializers, optical transceivers, and switch fabrics. Distance alone does not determine energy per bit, and an endpoint-only estimate cannot be compared directly with a complete fabric-path estimate. Locality remains useful because it can avoid transfers and active interfaces; the energy saving must be evaluated under the same workload, utilization, and accounting boundary.







Figure 1: Data-Movement Accounting Boundaries: Successively broader paths involve different storage and communication components. The schematic identifies what an energy estimate must include; it assigns no universal distance law or fixed energy multiplier. Compare energy per transferred byte only after specifying endpoints, interfaces, switches, and utilization.



The chapter’s reference gradient buffer of 1 GB stands for one large fused reduction, far smaller than a full model gradient but large enough that per-byte transfer, not per-message startup, governs its cost; later examples return to it by name. Reducing it around an illustrative 10,000-rank ring sends approximately twice the payload from every rank. At a fabric-path transfer cost of 35 pJ/bit, a representative midpoint of the range typical of switched fabrics rather than a measurement of any particular one, this gives about 5.6 kJ per reduction, paid again at every synchronous step. The usable rule is that communication energy is the bytes an algorithm sends multiplied by the energy per bit of every boundary those bytes cross. An algorithm that moves fewer bytes, or a placement that keeps more of them inside the node, therefore saves energy as directly as it saves time. The share of the step’s total energy that communication represents must be measured at the same accounting boundary as the compute it accompanies. The fabric-path figure charges the serializers, transceivers, and switches between two endpoints. A whole-system estimate that also charges endpoint memory reads, host software, and idle network power assigns each byte crossing the network a much larger cost, so two per-byte figures can be compared only after their boundaries match.


↪ The energy cost of moving a byte across memory, storage, and network boundaries, and why movement can outweigh arithmetic, is developed in Energy per byte.
4 Zero-copy communication: GPUDirect RDMA lets the NIC read gradients directly from accelerator memory, so a 140 GB gradient never passes through host DRAM, whereas a staged path writes and then rereads it there (280 GB of host-memory traffic per send).These constraints govern different parts of a communication budget. Propagation latency sets a floor for every message regardless of size. Link bandwidth caps throughput once a transfer is large enough to fill the pipe. Protocol overhead adds a fixed per-message cost that penalizes fine-grained exchanges unless a kernel-bypass transport removes it. RDMA’s zero-copy path4 avoids staging each transfer through host memory and the kernel’s socket buffers, keeping that per-message cost low. Because the physical fabric fixes these limits, the collective schedule determines how many times the job pays them.
Across this section, the \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) cost model, the LogP processor-overhead extension, and the bisection-bandwidth ceiling have priced single transfers in isolation and exposed the 5,512.7 ms physical floor for a 140 GB gradient synchronization. Which collective operations a training step actually invokes, and how often they hit that latency-or-bandwidth wall, depends on how the workload partitions its parameters, activations, and tokens across devices.

Self-Check: Question

On the same fabric, one collective exchanges thousands of 4 KB messages per step while another moves a single 1 GB fused buffer. Which term governs each cost, and which lever addresses it?

Both are bandwidth-bound, so a faster link shortens both by the same factor.
The small messages pay per-message latency and protocol overhead on every send, so fusing messages or using a kernel-bypass transport helps; the 1 GB buffer is governed by per-byte transfer, so moving fewer bytes or adding bandwidth helps.
The small messages are bandwidth-bound because there are many of them, while the 1 GB buffer is latency-bound because a large transfer takes the longest path.
Both are latency-bound, because the speed of light sets a floor on every message regardless of its size.

A 10,000-rank ring AllReduce reduces a 1 GB gradient buffer over a fabric path that costs about 35 pJ per bit. Set up the energy of one reduction and explain what the result implies for algorithm and placement choices.
True or False: Energy per transferred bit grows in proportion to physical distance, so a transfer that travels twice as far costs about twice the energy.

See Answers →





Once a training job splits its batch, layers, or parameters across devices, no rank holds all the state needed to finish a step on its own. A synchronous data-parallel worker computes gradients from its local batch slice, but its optimizer cannot update the weights until every replica’s gradients have been combined. Some of those reductions can start as backward layers finish, while earlier layers are still computing. Tensor ownership determines where each tensor must go, and gradient or activation readiness determines when each transfer can start.
How the model is partitioned dictates which tensors cross device boundaries and which ranks must exchange them. For Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), dense gradient contributions are combined within each data-parallel group; in a hybrid layout, that group contains the matching parameter shard from each replica. AllReduce serves the replicated-gradient baseline. For Archetype B (DLRM at Scale),5 lookup requests travel to embedding-shard owners and the resulting vectors return to the workers that need them. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing similarly sends activations to the ranks hosting selected experts and returns their outputs. These destination-specific exchanges motivate AllToAll.
5 DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model): Meta’s 2019 architecture for click-through rate prediction uses sharded embedding tables and exchanges the resulting sparse lookups across workers, an AllToAll whose limiting term section 5.8 develops.
↩︎ The three lighthouse archetypes and the C³ regimes each one stresses are established in Three systems archetypes.

At large scale, these parallelism strategies can be combined. A 3D parallelism layout combines data parallelism, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism, creating distinct communication groups whose exchanges may overlap in time. In a node-local tensor-parallel example, layer reductions use NVLink, pipeline stages exchange activations and their gradients point-to-point across nodes, and data-parallel groups reduce matching parameter shards over InfiniBand. Other placements change those physical paths while retaining the logical communication requirements.
Each primitive operates on a different process group, a subset of the total GPU population that participates in that particular collective. Classical Message Passing Interface (MPI) uses a communicator as the object that names such a participating set; its communicator size is the number of ranks in that set. MPI libraries already selected collective algorithms based on communicator size and message size (Thakur et al. 2005). GPU communication libraries inherit that algorithm-selection problem and add the further challenge of coordinating overlapping process groups without creating contention between concurrent collectives.
Each parallelism strategy fixes the data it must move, the collective primitive that moves it, and the term most likely to bind (table 1), and with them which participants must exchange data. The collective primitives that follow make each exchange’s contract precise, the pricing model then charges it per round, and the collective algorithms provide its execution schedule.



Table 1: Parallelism-to-Collective Mapping: How each parallelism strategy becomes a traffic pattern. Pipeline parallelism alone relies on point-to-point transfers rather than a collective.

In this table, expert parallelism refers to the mixture-of-experts architecture pattern, in which each token activates only a few experts. Data parallelism and fully sharded data parallel (FSDP), which divides each replica’s parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across the data-parallel ranks, generate large reductions and gathers that reward byte-efficient rings and hierarchical schedules. Tensor and pipeline parallelism, by contrast, generate smaller, more frequent messages directly on the critical path, so low software overhead and fast node-local links dominate their cost. Expert parallelism and sharded embedding tables, in contrast, produce destination-specific traffic whose bottleneck shifts among message granularity, endpoint injection and reception, fabric bisection, oversubscription, routing, and skew.
The table’s rows describe data center parallelism, so they leave out the federated Archetype C. Across all three lighthouse archetypes, the dominant exchange and its bottleneck differ.

Lighthouse 5.1: Communication archetype patternsA gradient’s communication pattern depends on the system’s objective function and constraint regime. Each lighthouse archetype faces a distinct communication challenge, and the techniques developed in this chapter map to those challenges differently, as table 2 summarizes.



Table 2: Archetype-to-Collective Mapping: Each lighthouse archetype produces a characteristic traffic pattern, but the limiting term depends on message shape, placement, and the physical fabric.

The table separates traffic pattern from limiting resource. A dense reduction, a destination-specific exchange, and an intermittent device update require different interventions even though all three serve a training workload. Hierarchical AllReduce, AllToAll schedule selection, and compression with error feedback each receive their own treatment later in the chapter.


A traffic map names which pattern a workload generates, but it does not specify what each rank must hold when the call completes. Before any of those interventions can be priced, each exchange needs a precise contract that states which ranks contribute and what each holds afterward.

Self-Check: Question

A machine learning engineer evaluates the communication traffic induced by different model parallelism strategies. According to the chapter’s parallelism-to-collective mapping, which mapping correctly pairs a parallelism strategy with its primary collective primitive and primary physical constraint?

Sending a gradient tensor to a peer does not specify which workers must contribute or where the final result belongs. Collective operations supply that group-level contract, using a vocabulary standardized by MPI and inherited by modern ML communication libraries (Message Passing Interface Forum 2015). The four contracts sketched at the start of the chapter differ in what each rank holds afterward (figure 2). AllReduce leaves an identical sum (\(\Glyph{\Sigma}\)) on every rank. AllGather leaves every rank with the concatenation of all shards. ReduceScatter sums across ranks but leaves each rank one reduced shard (\(\Glyph{\Sigma}_i\)). AllToAll performs a distributed matrix transpose, routing each rank’s \(\DestinationRankIndex\)-th chunk to rank \(\DestinationRankIndex\). Two further primitives complete the set and serve as building blocks for these four: Broadcast, in which rank 0 sends its data to all ranks, and Reduce, in which all ranks aggregate into rank 0.

Definition 5.2: Collective operation
Collective operation is a distributed communication pattern in which every rank in a process group invokes a matching operation to aggregate, broadcast, or redistribute data. The operation’s contract specifies the output at each rank; it does not require simultaneous entry and does not, by itself, impose a general-purpose barrier before or after the call (Message Passing Interface Forum 2015).

Significance: Because the contract names only each rank’s result, the schedule that carries it decides how communication demand spreads as the group grows. A schedule that funnels every contribution through one endpoint makes the communication term \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3) grow with \(\DeviceCount\), while a balanced schedule keeps each rank’s bytes nearly constant; section 5.6.1 quantifies the gap.
Distinction: Unlike point-to-point communication, a collective defines one operation over a process group. Ranks may enter at different times, and some algorithms allow one rank to complete before another has entered; correctness depends on matching the operation sequence and argument contract across ranks, not on barrier semantics.
Common pitfall: Treating a non-blocking collective as complete when its initiation call returns. The returned request or stream event represents work in flight. A dependent consumer must wait for completion, and a late rank can extend that dependency even though the collective is not a barrier.










Figure 2: Four Central Collective Primitives: Standardized patterns for group communication in distributed systems. In each panel the four rows are ranks 0 to 3, read left to right from each rank’s input, through the collective, to what each rank holds afterward. (1) AllReduce: all aggregate and all receive the result. (2) AllGather: all send to all and concatenate. (3) ReduceScatter: all aggregate and results are distributed in shards. (4) AllToAll: every process sends unique data to every other process. The two foundational primitives Broadcast (rank 0 sends to all) and Reduce (all aggregate to rank 0) compose the patterns shown here and are defined in the surrounding prose.



The primitive choice is the first scaling decision because it fixes which ranks must coordinate and which result each must obtain. Once that contract is chosen, the algorithm and placement determine how the resulting traffic crosses the fabric.


Calling a full AllReduce when each rank’s optimizer updates only a \(1/\DeviceCount\) parameter shard moves twice as many bytes as the step needs, because half the work goes into assembling full tensors that every rank immediately discards. Choosing the right primitive therefore means matching the contract in table 3 to the exact slice the next computation consumes. The table’s rows run from the root-centered patterns (Broadcast and Reduce), through the three in which every rank contributes to and receives part or all of one shared tensor (AllReduce, AllGather, and ReduceScatter), to AllToAll, in which every pair of ranks exchanges distinct data. That order describes routing rather than cost: ReduceScatter and AllGather each move half of AllReduce’s bytes because each is one phase of it. The cost column previews the algorithms derived in section 5.6, using \(\DeviceCount\) for the participating rank count, \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) for the full tensor, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) for the per-rank AllToAll input payload. For AllReduce, the full tensor has the same byte size as each rank’s input payload, the convention used in the following algorithm models. Two schedules appear there: a ring passes chunks between neighbors, whereas a simple full-message tree reduces up a binary tree and broadcasts back down it, forwarding the whole tensor at each of its \(2\log_2 \DeviceCount\) levels. For Broadcast and Reduce, the table counts startup rounds and bytes per tree edge separately. Each traverses one tree depth, so the elapsed transfer cost accumulates across its levels. The Tree AllReduce derivation combines those two traversals.

Ring achieves AllReduce’s bandwidth-optimal cost while the simple full-message Tree model trades bandwidth for logarithmic latency (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009; Thakur et al. 2005). AllReduce itself also decomposes into ReduceScatter followed by AllGather. The decomposition is operational as well as mathematical, since Ring AllReduce’s first phase is a ReduceScatter and its second phase is an AllGather. ReduceScatter performs arithmetic, so it does not invert AllGather despite reversing the direction of shard expansion. Full ZeRO-style sharding and PyTorch FSDP use the pair the same way, gathering parameter shards with AllGather before a module needs them and reducing gradients with ReduceScatter after backward so each rank retains only its shard for the optimizer step (Rajbhandari et al. 2020). Sharding parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across workers reduces persistent model-state memory roughly by \(\DeviceCount\times\), while temporary full-parameter buffers and prefetching determine peak memory. That memory saving is developed in Memory-efficient data parallelism with ZeRO and FSDP; the communication it adds is priced in section 5.4.2.
The same AllGather/ReduceScatter pair also appears in sequence parallelism, where an AllGather reconstructs the activation view needed for a local operation and a later ReduceScatter redistributes the result along the sequence dimension. A primitive’s semantics stay fixed even when the tensor dimension being sharded changes, so every schedule developed for the pair applies to both uses.
Beyond defining data-movement dependencies, collective operations carry explicit interface and numerical contracts. At the interface level, every rank in a process group must issue collectives in a compatible sequence; mismatched operation orders can deadlock or pair unrelated buffers. Operations also enforce shape and type contracts. AllReduce requires matching element counts and datatypes across all ranks, whereas variable-size exchanges require explicit per-destination counts and displacements. These invariants form the contract between the parallel decomposition and the communication runtime: the model decides which tensor slices each rank owns, and the collective contract guarantees that those slices can be recombined deterministically.
Reduction order introduces a second, numerical contract. Floating-point addition is not associative, so ring, tree, and switch-assisted reductions may accumulate the same values in different orders and produce different low-order bits (Goldberg 1991). A correct AllReduce therefore guarantees the specified reduction over all contributions, not bitwise identity across algorithms, rank counts, or hardware. Reproducibility-sensitive workloads must fix the algorithm and process-group configuration or use a reproducible accumulation scheme; ordinary training should treat small order-dependent differences as numerical behavior while still checking for larger rank disagreement.

Goldberg, David. 1991. “What Every Computer Scientist Should Know about Floating-Point Arithmetic.” ACM Computing Surveys 23 (1): 5–48. https://doi.org/10.1145/103162.103163.
AllToAll scales differently from AllReduce with cluster size, and section 5.8 develops the bound that governs it. With the six contracts defined, every row of table 1 now names a primitive whose output and traffic pattern are precise. The sharded data-parallel row repays closer study, because sharding changes how often those primitives run rather than which ones run.



Sharding every parameter, gradient, and optimizer-state tensor across \(\DeviceCount\) data-parallel ranks saves memory, but it replaces one end-of-step reduction with a stream of collective calls inside the forward and backward passes. Under fully sharded data parallelism (Rajbhandari et al. 2020), each rank holds only \(1/\DeviceCount\) of a layer’s weights. It must call AllGather before the layer’s forward pass to assemble the full weights. After the backward pass, it calls ReduceScatter to leave each rank the gradient for its own shard, and then frees the temporary full weights.

Rajbhandari, Samyam, Jeff Rasley, Olatunji Ruwase, and Yuxiong He. 2020. “ZeRO: Memory Optimizations Toward Training Trillion Parameter Models.” SC20: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1109/sc41405.2020.00024.
Trading resident memory for on-demand assembly multiplies the collective call count. With one communication group per layer, a schedule that holds each layer’s gathered weights until its backward pass finishes issues \(2\LayerCount\) collective calls per step (one forward AllGather and one backward ReduceScatter per layer) where unbucketed data parallelism issues one AllReduce. To save peak activation memory, full-resharding FSDP instead frees the full weights right after each layer’s forward pass and runs a second AllGather before that layer’s backward pass, raising the count to about \(3\LayerCount\) calls per step. The byte volume changes far less. Because each AllGather and ReduceScatter over a large group moves nearly \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) bytes per rank across all layers combined, where \(\CollectiveTensorSize\) is the model-sized payload without optimizer state, the \(2\LayerCount\)-call schedule sends roughly the AllReduce’s \(2\CollectiveTensorSize\) per rank and the resharded \(3\LayerCount\)-call schedule sends about \(3\CollectiveTensorSize\) (\(1.5\times\)) when parameters and gradients travel at the same width. Different parameter and reduction datatypes shift that ratio. The call count carries its own price, because every call pays a startup cost. An effective startup cost \(\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) contributes approximately \(2\LayerCount\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) per step before overlap, or \(3\LayerCount\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) with resharding. FSDP is therefore more sensitive to \(\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) than an unbucketed data-parallel reduction even though its bytes barely change. The counts describe one grouping policy, since FSDP units need not coincide with layers and bucketed data parallelism also splits its reduction to enable overlap. FSDP implementations mitigate the startup cost through prefetching and communication-stream pipelining, but the relevant \(\CollectiveCallStartupLatency\) must come from a matched collective benchmark rather than a wire-latency specification.

Selecting the right collective algorithm at each invocation requires distinguishing transfer cost from dependency exposure. An FSDP AllGather is latency-sensitive in the scheduling sense, because a layer cannot compute until its full parameters arrive. Its transfer can nevertheless be bandwidth-bound when the parameter tensor is large. Prefetching can hide part of that gather, while a ReduceScatter can overlap with the remaining backward computation. Neither dependency alone selects Ring or Tree; message size, group size, topology, and the available overlap window jointly determine the useful schedule.
The primitives specify what must be communicated, and sharding shows how often a training step invokes them. Choosing a schedule for each invocation first requires a price for every round of an exchange.

A gradient bucket of tens of megabytes is large enough to saturate a single network link. Yet when a thousand-GPU ring divides that bucket into a thousand shards, each hop moves only tens of kilobytes and can spend more time starting the transfer than sending its bytes. Pricing a collective therefore requires separating the fixed time to initiate each message from the rate at which bytes move once in transit.
The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model \(\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) prices a transfer over a single link (principle \(\ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}\)), separating a fixed startup cost (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) from a per-byte transfer cost (\(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\)) (Hockney 1994). A collective pays that price at every step of its schedule, so the two terms, multiplied by the schedule’s round count and traffic factor, determine algorithm selection across the fleet.

For collectives, the parameters must describe the effective path. Latency (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) is the startup cost paid at every step of a schedule, so it includes recurring software overhead, PCIe traversal, and network switching time; one-time communicator initialization is a separate setup cost. Bandwidth (\(\LinkBandwidth\)) is the sustained per-direction transfer rate. The critical message size \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\), where the two terms are equal, carries over unchanged. It must, however, be compared against each step’s chunk (\(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) in an \(\DeviceCount\)-rank ring) rather than the whole tensor \(\CollectivePayloadSize\). That is why a large bucket can still fall below the inter-node crossovers in table 4. Below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), a step is latency-bound; above it, bandwidth-bound.
The crossover explains two recurring optimizations. For InfiniBand NDR at \(\MessageStartupLatency\approx\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth\approx\) 50 GB/s, the knee sits at \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize \approx\) 75 KB, the value The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model computed for a single transfer. A 4 KB routing message is far below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so the startup cost dominates. If 100 ready messages have compatible destinations and can share one transfer, fusing them into a 400 KB message reduces the modeled cost from approximately \(100\MessageStartupLatency=\) 150 μs to \(\MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\approx\) 9.5 μs. That is roughly a 16× improvement before packing costs. More generally, \(\SplitMessageCount\) serialized messages of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\SplitMessageCount\) can cost up to \(\SplitMessageCount\times\) as much as one message of size \(\PointToPointMessageSize\) when \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\SplitMessageCount\ll \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\). Fusion is the first optimization, and it motivates framework gradient buckets and destination-aware token coalescing.
Compression is the second, and the crossover tells where it pays. A 140 GB gradient tensor sits far above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so shrinking its bytes shrinks the dominant \(\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth\) term directly, provided encoding and aggregation costs are counted. Even keeping only the largest 1 percent of values (Top-k sparsification, developed in section 5.9) leaves 1.4 GB of values before their indices are added, still far above \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so the saving remains a byte saving. Compressing a 4 KB routing message, by contrast, offers little, because its unchanged \(\MessageStartupLatency\) term already dominates.
Across the typical data center interconnects tabulated in table 4, the critical-size column carries the load-bearing pattern: intra-node NVLink stays latency-bound up to several hundred kilobytes, whereas the inter-node fabrics cross over below roughly 100 KB. A message between those crossover sizes can therefore be latency-bound inside a node but bandwidth-bound once it travels between nodes.

Napkin Math 5.1: The critical message sizeProblem: A data-parallel job reduces a 25 MB gradient bucket with Ring AllReduce over InfiniBand NDR, with \(\MessageStartupLatency=\) 1.5 μs and \(\LinkBandwidth=\) 50 GB/s. The bucket is hundreds of times larger than the single-transfer knee. Does each step of the ring run in the bandwidth-bound regime on 64 GPUs, and on the 1,024-GPU reference cluster?
Math:

Knee: \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth=\) \(1.5 \times 10^{-6}\) s \(\times\) \(5 \times 10^{10}\) B/s \(=\) 75 KB.
Chunk per step: A ring sends \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) per step, 390.6 KB on 64 ranks (above the knee) but only 24.4 KB on 1,024 ranks (below it).
Ring time \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\left(\MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\DeviceCount\LinkBandwidth}\right)\): about 1.2 ms on 64 ranks, of which the byte term is 1.0 ms; about 4.1 ms on 1,024 ranks, where the byte term is still only 1.0 ms.

Systems insight: The regime belongs to the chunk, not to the tensor. The byte term barely moves as the group grows, but at 1,024 ranks each step carries a chunk below \(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize\), so startup dominates and the same bucket takes several times longer. Large language model (LLM) gradients are bandwidth-bound as tensors, yet a flat ring over a large group can still carry them in latency-bound steps. The levers then shift to larger buckets, fewer rounds, and hierarchy, which is why the algorithms of section 5.6 compete on round count as well as bytes.


For collectives, the two regimes map onto different levers. In the latency-bound regime \((\PointToPointMessageSize< \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize)\), where MoE routing tokens, scalar reductions, and the small chunks of a large-group schedule sit, the levers are fusion, fewer schedule rounds, fewer hops, and a leaner software stack. In the bandwidth-bound regime \((\PointToPointMessageSize\gg \LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize)\), where LLM gradients and optimizer states sit, they are compression, a byte-efficient algorithm, and link aggregation across multiple network interface cards (NICs). Classifying each exchange, and each chunk within it, into one regime is the diagnostic skill the rest of the chapter applies.

A correct AllReduce must give each of 1,000 GPUs the reduced sum of all 1,000 gradient contributions, subject to the floating-point reduction contract, and the algorithm that delivers it sets the cluster’s scaling ceiling. The naive answer, in which every GPU sends to one central server whose single network link must carry every worker’s gradient, fails first, which makes it the right place to start.


Consider a naive implementation using a parameter server (a star topology), with a dedicated server in addition to the workers. All \(\DeviceCount\) workers send their gradients to that server; it sums them and sends the result back. The server must receive \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes and send \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes, so its bandwidth budget grows as \(\CommunicationTime \propto \DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize/ \LinkBandwidth\). At 1,000 GPUs, concentrating those transfers at one server creates a scaling bottleneck even if the arithmetic is fast.
This naive approach captures the pressure that early distributed ML frameworks had to manage. Parameter-server systems receive, aggregate, and redistribute model updates through a server tier, and practical implementations shard the parameter space to spread that load (Dean et al. 2012; Li et al. 2014). Sharding reduces the per-server traffic from \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize\) to \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize/\ParameterServerCount\) (where \(\ParameterServerCount\) is the number of servers). The server tier still grows as workers and model state grow, and it introduces additional complexity in parameter partitioning and consistency management.

The bottleneck comes from concentration, not from total traffic. Every AllReduce algorithm moves more total data as workers are added, because every worker’s contribution must be combined and every worker must receive the result. A star, however, routes all of that traffic through one endpoint, so the server’s time grows as \(\DeviceCount\times \CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\). A ring spreads the same work so that each rank sends about \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) and its time stays near \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\) however large \(\DeviceCount\) becomes. The ratio of the two is about \(\DeviceCount/2\), so at 1,024 workers the server’s byte time is roughly 500× the ring’s, before startup, arithmetic, or contention are counted. Bandwidth optimality makes that comparison precise by measuring an algorithm’s required byte movement against a lower bound under a stated communication model, which the next derivation supplies for AllReduce.

War Story 5.1: When the parameter server became the bottleneck (2017)Context: In 2017, Alexander Sergeev and Mike Del Balso’s team at Uber open-sourced Horovod as part of Uber’s Michelangelo ML platform, where TensorFlow training jobs needed to scale across many GPUs without forcing every model author to rewrite large portions of training code (Sergeev and Balso 2018).
Mechanism: TensorFlow’s stock distributed training relied on a parameter-server pattern that concentrated gradient traffic through a central tier. As worker count \(\DeviceCount\) grew, the central server link saturated, degrading scaling efficiency.
Impact: Scaling training beyond a single node resulted in severe throughput bottlenecks and required complex, model-specific parameter partitioning.
Fix: Uber adopted Baidu’s ring AllReduce algorithm (Gibiansky 2017), wrapping bandwidth-optimal collective reduction behind a lightweight API that replaced parameter servers with ring communication.
Systems lesson: A collective algorithm is also a developer interface. Scaling improves when the communication primitive is both bandwidth efficient and easy enough that teams actually use it correctly.





Before choosing a schedule to replace the parameter server, we need to know the minimum byte volume any point-to-point AllReduce must move when \(\DeviceCount\) ranks each start with an \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte gradient and neither compression nor in-network switch reduction is used. Reducing one independent data item across \(\DeviceCount\) ranks and distributing its result requires at least \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) item transfers in aggregate (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009). The count has two halves. Combining \(\DeviceCount\) contributions that start on \(\DeviceCount\) different ranks takes at least \(\DeviceCount-1\) transfers, because each transfer combines at most two partial sums and so reduces the number of separate partial sums by at most one. Delivering the finished value to the other \(\DeviceCount-1\) ranks then takes at least one transfer each. For an \(\CollectivePayloadSize\)-byte tensor, the minimum aggregate sent volume is therefore \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes. At least one rank must send the average share, \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes; a balanced algorithm assigns that share to every rank.
Take \(\LinkBandwidth\) as each rank’s available send bandwidth, with equal receive bandwidth that can operate simultaneously. Dividing the required sent volume by \(\LinkBandwidth\) gives the full-duplex bandwidth lower bound:
\[\AllReduceMinimumBandwidthTime= \frac{2(\DeviceCount-1)}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}\]
As \(\DeviceCount\) grows large, the bandwidth lower bound approaches \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\), independent of \(\DeviceCount\) (principle \(\ref{pri-allreduce-bandwidth-bound}\)). Ring AllReduce matches the required byte volume under this model; startup and local reduction still add time (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009; Thakur et al. 2005). On a 64-GPU cluster synchronizing the chapter’s 1 GB reference buffer over 50 GB/s links, the ring’s byte term is about 39.4 ms, establishing the physical floor against which every concrete AllReduce schedule that follows must be judged.



To hit that \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) byte floor without funneling traffic through a central server, Ring AllReduce arranges nodes in a logical loop (\(0 \to 1 \to \dots \to \DeviceCount-1 \to 0\)) where each node sends to its successor while receiving from its predecessor at the same time. That even chunk schedule spreads the required byte volume across every rank and reaches the bandwidth lower bound in the ideal endpoint model (Patarasuk and Yuan 2009).
The algorithm splits the vector of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) into \(\DeviceCount\) chunks and then alternates communication and local reduction in two phases, a ReduceScatter phase (often called scatter-reduce) followed by an AllGather phase. Algorithm 1 states the mechanics before the figure and trace make the same dataflow concrete.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Ring AllReduce}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require $N$ ranks in a logical ring; each rank $i$ starts with tensor $\mathbf{g}_i$ of $M$ bytes, split into $N$ chunks
\Ensure every rank holds $\mathbf{g} = \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \mathbf{g}_i$
\State assign the ring order $0\to 1\to\dots\to N{-}1\to 0$
\For{$N-1$ ReduceScatter steps}
    \State each rank sends one chunk (or partial sum) right, receives one from the left, and adds it into the matching local sum
\EndFor
\State each rank now owns one fully reduced chunk of $\mathbf{g}$
\For{$N-1$ AllGather steps}
    \State each rank forwards a reduced chunk around the ring and stores the chunks it receives
\EndFor
\State \Return the complete reduced tensor $\mathbf{g}$, held on every rank
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(N\)

Across the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) send/receive rounds each rank moves \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes per round, for \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\) bytes sent and the same received. The bandwidth term therefore reaches the information-theoretic lower bound, while the latency term grows as \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency\). On a four-GPU ring with wrap-around links, the state progresses in two phases (figure 3). In row (a), \(\DeviceCount-1 = 3\) ReduceScatter steps circulate gradient chunks A through D until each GPU holds exactly one fully reduced partition (green \(\Glyph{\Sigma} \Glyph{A}\) through \(\Glyph{\Sigma} \Glyph{D}\)). In row (b), \(\DeviceCount-1 = 3\) subsequent AllGather steps forward those finished shards around the ring until every device holds the complete sum.

Every link carries data in every step, so each GPU sends \(2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes in total, while the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) steps each pay one startup latency \(\MessageStartupLatency\).



Logical ring edges may share physical links, and startup, local reduction, or contention can leave transfer capacity unused, so byte optimality does not guarantee peak physical-link utilization. To see how the logical schedule itself reaches that byte lower bound, consider 4 GPUs reducing a vector of 4 elements by summation. Generalizing the six-step trace of example 5.1 to \(\DeviceCount\) ranks yields the closed-form cost model for those checkpoint questions: each node sends and receives \(\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\DeviceCount}\) bytes in each of the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\) steps. \[
\RingAllReduceCompletionTime = \underbrace{2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency}_{\text{Latency Term}} + \underbrace{2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount} \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}}_{\text{Bandwidth Term}}
\]
The bandwidth term approaches \(2\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\) as \(\DeviceCount\to \infty\), reaching the full-duplex lower bound: each rank sends nearly \(2\CollectivePayloadSize\) bytes across the two phases and receives the same amount concurrently. In contrast, the latency term scales linearly with \(\DeviceCount\). Across 10,000 nodes, 19,998 sequential startup rounds accumulate substantial latency, which explains why Ring AllReduce becomes uncompetitive for small payloads. For a multi-gigabyte gradient buffer at moderate rank count, however, the bandwidth term dominates completely, as the 70B calculation in notebook 5.2 confirms.

The bandwidth term barely depends on rank count, so this smaller group reproduces the bandwidth-only estimate from the opening definition while keeping the latency term visible. Each rank contributes a complete logical gradient buffer communicated in BF16 (2 bytes per parameter). This calculation isolates collective cost without establishing that the training state fits on each GPU. How long does one AllReduce take?
Step 1: Size the gradient payload. Each rank in this baseline contributes the complete logical gradient tensor of \(7 \times 10^{10} \times 2\ \text{bytes}\) \(=\) 140 GB. Substituting: \(\RingAllReduceBandwidthTime\) = 1.96875 \(\times\) 140 GB / 50 GB/s \(\approx\) 5,512.5 ms.

Systems insight: The modeled full-buffer AllReduce takes over five seconds under the stated link and rank assumptions, and almost all of it is the bandwidth term. Its effect on step time depends on how much remains exposed relative to useful computation. When it is fully exposed, halving it saves about 2.8 s per step; across a 100,000-step campaign on these 64 GPUs, that is roughly 4,900 GPU-hours of reserved accelerator time. Large-scale training systems can launch reductions for output-side gradients while input-side layers are still computing. Partitioned training also changes each rank’s payload and participating group, so this complete-gradient budget must be recomputed for the actual layout.





Ring AllReduce’s byte efficiency comes with many startup rounds. As the group grows, the \(2(\DeviceCount-1)\MessageStartupLatency\) term can exceed the byte-transfer term for a fixed payload; the crossover depends on the measured path parameters. Tree AllReduce reduces the number of dependent rounds. In the simple reduce phase, pairs combine contributions and forward partial sums toward a root, taking \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) steps for a balanced power-of-two group. The broadcast phase distributes the result in another \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) steps. This shorter dependency chain motivates the comparison before bandwidth costs are counted.



Ring latency grows with N; tree stays logarithmic.
The simple full-message tree loses parallel activity as contributions converge. A ring activates all \(\DeviceCount\) logical edges in each round. In a pairwise tree reduction, the first round has \(\DeviceCount/2\) senders and \(\DeviceCount/2\) receivers; receiving is useful work, not idleness. The next round has \(\DeviceCount/4\) senders and \(\DeviceCount/4\) receivers, and the final reduction exchange involves two ranks while the remaining \((\DeviceCount-2)\) have completed their upstream contribution. Sending the full message through successive levels adds byte-transfer time along the dependency path. This is a limitation of the illustrated schedule, not every tree-based implementation or every physical link mapping.
The resulting time complexity depends on the specific tree variant. A simple reduce-then-broadcast tree has logarithmic latency but nonuniform traffic and root/interior bottlenecks. Recursive doubling, in which partners at doubling distances exchange the entire tensor in each of \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds, has the same logarithmic round count and incurs \(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\) full-message bandwidth per rank. The following simplified model captures the latency advantage and the potential bandwidth penalty of tree-like collectives: \[ \TreeLikeAllReduceTime\approx \underbrace{2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency}_{\text{Latency}} + \underbrace{2 \log_2 \DeviceCount\frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth}}_{\text{Bandwidth penalty in full-message exchange variants}} \]
The latency term is logarithmic (\(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\)). For 1,024 nodes, Ring needs 2,046 steps while Tree needs only 20. That roughly 100× reduction in steps makes Tree attractive for small, frequent collectives across large process groups, such as scalar reductions, control messages, or small-batch activation reductions. The bandwidth term carries the penalty, because tree-like algorithms can underutilize links or concentrate traffic on interior links, and recursive-doubling-style full-message exchanges add a \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) bandwidth factor. These penalties make naive tree variants a poor choice for data parallelism’s large gradient AllReduce, where bandwidth efficiency determines whether the network is saturated or partially idle.
For large-scale data parallelism, this bandwidth penalty decides the comparison whenever the implementation repeatedly exchanges full messages or creates root/interior bottlenecks. On the 64-GPU cluster of section 5.6.2, the simple tree forwards the whole tensor once per level on the way up and once per level on the way down, \(2\log_2 64 = 12\) full-message transfers. Its byte time is about 240 ms against the ring’s 39.4 ms, or 6.1× the ring’s byte time. The difference of roughly 200 ms per step would accumulate to about 5.6 hours over a 100,000-step run if fully exposed, although actual wall-clock savings also depend on startup, placement, and overlap. For a 70B-parameter model’s 140 GB gradient AllReduce across 1,000 GPUs, a bandwidth-inefficient tree-like variant can erase the latency advantage that motivated it. Optimized double-tree algorithms exist precisely to keep logarithmic latency without imposing that naive bandwidth penalty.
Small activation reductions provide a useful case for fewer startup rounds. For an eight-GPU group communicating a 1 MB tensor, the simple model reduces Ring’s \(2(8-1)\MessageStartupLatency= 14\MessageStartupLatency\) to Tree’s \(2\log_2(8)\MessageStartupLatency= 6\MessageStartupLatency\), but Tree’s byte term remains about 3.4× Ring’s. Whether the saved startups outweigh those extra byte transfers depends on the measured latency and bandwidth. Tensor-parallel collectives also have a scheduling constraint independent of this comparison: a layer that needs the reduced activation must wait for it. A critical-path dependency does not by itself imply a latency-dominated transfer or select a tree algorithm.



The simple full-message Tree reduces startup rounds but repeats more byte-transfer work than Ring. Recursive halving-doubling, sometimes called the Butterfly algorithm, combines logarithmic rounds with the optimal byte volume under the flat-network model. It pairs ranks exactly as recursive doubling does, but where recursive doubling exchanges the whole tensor in every round, halving-doubling halves the exchanged region in each ReduceScatter round and doubles it in each AllGather round. That difference removes the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) byte penalty. For a power-of-two group, it uses \(2\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds: \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) ReduceScatter rounds followed by \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) AllGather rounds. A partner-bit index \(\PartnerBitIndex\) selects the XOR pairing with mask \(2^\PartnerBitIndex\). The ReduceScatter trace below visits those bits in increasing order as messages shrink; the matching AllGather reverses that order as the assembled result grows.
In the ReduceScatter phase (first \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds), GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 2^\PartnerBitIndex\) (XOR of indices). Because the two partners made identical retention choices in all earlier rounds, both enter round \(\PartnerBitIndex\) holding partial sums for the exact same \(\CollectivePayloadSize/2^\PartnerBitIndex\)-byte region of the tensor. They split that active region in half, retain complementary halves of size \(\CollectivePayloadSize/2^{\PartnerBitIndex+1}\), and send the other half to each other to add into the half each retained. Across the \(\log_2 \DeviceCount\) rounds, the bytes each GPU sends form a geometric series \(\CollectivePayloadSize/2 + \CollectivePayloadSize/4 + \dots + \CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount = \frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\CollectivePayloadSize\), leaving each GPU with a distinct \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount\)-byte slice of the fully reduced result. AllGather traverses the partner bits in reverse, exchanging completed regions of doubling size \(\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount, 2\CollectivePayloadSize/\DeviceCount, \dots, \CollectivePayloadSize/2\) until every rank holds the full result.
Summing the \(2\log_2 \DeviceCount\) startups and the two symmetric geometric byte series gives the recursive halving-doubling cost: \[ \ButterflyAllReduceTime= 2\log_2 \DeviceCount\cdot \MessageStartupLatency+ 2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount} \cdot \frac{\CollectivePayloadSize}{\LinkBandwidth} \]
The schedule combines logarithmic latency (\(\mathcal{O}(\log \DeviceCount)\), like Tree) with bandwidth-optimal data movement (\(2(\DeviceCount-1)/\DeviceCount\cdot \CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth\), like Ring). The catch is that it requires nonneighbor communication (GPU \(\RankIndex\) must communicate with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 2^\PartnerBitIndex\), which may be physically distant), and it requires \(\DeviceCount\) to be a power of two. For clusters where \(\DeviceCount\) is not a power of two, additional complexity is needed to handle the irregular cases.
Recursive halving-doubling is used in MPI-style collective implementations and is useful as a theoretical point in the latency-bandwidth trade-off (Thakur et al. 2005). NVIDIA’s GPU collective backend, the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL), offers implementation families that include ring, tree-derived, hierarchical, NVLink/NVSwitch-aware, and pattern-aware choices, with exact names and availability changing by version and topology (Jeaugey 2017; NVIDIA 2026). Whatever a particular release calls them, practical communication libraries select algorithms through a topology-aware cost model because nonlocal communication patterns can create contention on shared network links that erodes theoretical advantages.

Thakur, Rajeev, Rolf Rabenseifner, and William Gropp. 2005. “Optimization of Collective Communication Operations in MPICH.” The International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications 19 (1): 49–66. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094342005051521.
The partner distance is where topology enters. Consider the ReduceScatter phase for 8 GPUs placed four per node on two nodes, GPUs 0–3 on the first and GPUs 4–7 on the second, which proceeds in \(\log_2(8) = 3\) rounds. In round \(\PartnerBitIndex=0\), each GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 1\), pairing neighbors: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7). They exchange half their data and reduce. In round \(\PartnerBitIndex=1\), the distance doubles: GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 2\), creating pairs (0,2), (1,3), (4,6), (5,7). In round \(\PartnerBitIndex=2\), the distance doubles again: GPU \(\RankIndex\) partners with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 4\), creating pairs (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7).
Physical placement determines the cost of these logical pairings (figure 4). Rounds \(\PartnerBitIndex=0\) and \(\PartnerBitIndex=1\) pair GPUs within a node, but in round \(\PartnerBitIndex=2\) every GPU on the first node exchanges with one on the second, so that round crosses the node boundary. On eight-GPU nodes the same crossing would appear one round later, at \(\PartnerBitIndex=3\) in a 16-rank group. In a separate 1,024-rank example, the final ReduceScatter round pairs GPU \(\RankIndex\) with GPU \(\RankIndex\oplus 512\). If the two rank halves occupy different racks, those exchanges share the inter-rack fabric. The algorithm’s logarithmic rounds and optimal byte volume therefore do not establish its runtime advantage; placement, shared paths, and the changing chunk size in each round must enter the comparison.
