title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
A cosmic ray that flips one bit in a GPU’s high-bandwidth memory and a solder joint that cracks under thermal cycling are physical events, but the recovery system never observes them directly. It observes symptoms: a gradient spike with no process crash, a rank that disappears from the collective, or a node that fails only after it heats under sustained load. The failure taxonomy of section 7.3 already classifies such events by persistence, manifestation, and scope. For hardware, persistence carries most of the operational weight because it decides whether the fleet should retry, quarantine, or replace a component, while manifestation decides whether the fleet notices the fault at all.
ML workloads raise the stakes of each fault. A training step performs trillions of arithmetic operations on state that persists into later steps, so a wrong value can survive beyond the computation that produced it. The damage depends on the affected value and its later use. Under the IEEE 754 format,6 a sign-bit flip inverts a weight, while an exponent-bit flip can move a small gradient by many orders of magnitude. Fault-injection studies show that network resilience varies with model, layer, and bit position, so a few faults in vulnerable locations can cost disproportionate accuracy (Reagen et al. 2018). A valid-looking corrupted value can enter learned state without triggering the process failure that would otherwise initiate recovery.
6 IEEE 754: The IEEE 754 floating-point standard defines the binary32 format with 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits (IEEE Standards Association 2019). Because bit positions differ so much in consequence, resilience mechanisms often prioritize the sign and exponent bits rather than treating all bits as equally important.
IEEE Standards Association. 2019. IEEE 754-2019: Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic. https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229.

Reagen, B., U. Gupta, L. Pentecost, P. Whatmough, S. K. Lee, N. Mulholland, D. Brooks, and G.-Y. Wei. 2018. “Ares: A Framework for Quantifying the Resilience of Deep Neural Networks.” 2018 55th ACM/ESDA/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/dac.2018.8465834.

↪ How an FP16 exponent-bit flip rescales a value by \(2^{16}\) and can saturate an attention softmax is developed in Silent Data Corruption in Attention.

Fleet scale turns these rare device events into routine operating conditions. Smaller geometries and lower operating voltages can reduce the charge needed to disturb a stored value (Baumann 2005). Fleet studies at Google and Meta found that a small but persistent population of processors, on the order of a few per several thousand machines, computes wrong results without raising any error (Hochschild et al. 2021; Dixit et al. 2021). Studies of accelerator training fleets reach the same conclusion: rare hardware faults appear often enough that software-level detection and recovery become part of the training system design (He et al. 2023). ML system architects must therefore treat hardware as an unreliable substrate and budget for end-to-end integrity checks, replayed computation on high-value paths, and periodic consistency checks as system requirements rather than high-performance computing specialties.


Each persistence class from the taxonomy maps to a different fleet action, from retry for a fault that leaves nothing to repair, through quarantine for one that returns under load, to replacement for one that repeats on every attempt (figure 5). A transient fault, as section 7.3.1 established, leaves no lasting defect from that event, so the fleet’s question is only whether its effect escaped. A single-event upset, a voltage droop on an unstable power path (Reddi and Gupta 2013), a timing violation, or a soft error in combinational logic (Mukherjee et al. 2005) can corrupt a tensor, packet, or instruction. Detection and correction can prevent propagation; affected state may otherwise require rollback. During training, an undetected error in weights or gradients can compromise convergence and contaminate subsequent checkpoints (He et al. 2023). During stateless inference, an activation error can remain confined to one request (Mahmoud et al. 2020). If that activation enters retained state such as a KV cache, later outputs can also depend on it.

Reddi, Vijay Janapa, and Meeta Sharma Gupta. 2013. Resilient Architecture Design for Voltage Variation. Synthesis Lectures on Computer Architecture. Springer International Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-01739-1.

Mukherjee, S. S., J. Emer, and S. K. Reinhardt. 2005. “The Soft Error Problem: An Architectural Perspective.” 11th International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture, 243–47. https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca.2005.37.






Figure 5: The ML Failure Spectrum: Hardware faults ordered by how long they persist. A transient fault leaves nothing to repair, an intermittent fault returns under the load that exposed it, and a permanent fault repeats on every retry. Persistence decides the fleet response, from retry through quarantine to replacement, and fault tolerance engineering must handle all three to keep a fleet making progress.



A permanent fault announces itself through repeatability. The same accelerator, memory cell, or link fails again after retry, often at the same address or in the same workload phase. Manufacturing defects and wear-out mechanisms such as electromigration7 and oxide breakdown produce this signature, and the stuck-at fault, in which a signal remains fixed at 0 or 1 regardless of input, is its standard abstract model (Seong et al. 2010). Repeatability helps locate the defect but does not make the result trustworthy. A permanent datapath fault keeps producing wrong gradients until the device is drained from the cluster (He et al. 2023), and rerunning the computation on the same device reproduces the error instead of exposing it. The fleet must stop trusting the component, quarantine it, and restore from a checkpoint that predates its first bad write.
7 Electromigration: Gradual displacement of metal atoms in conductors by electron momentum transfer, first characterized in early electromigration studies and later modeled in Black’s reliability equation (Black 1969). Mean time to failure decreases with higher current density and higher temperature, so sustained high-power accelerator workloads make thermal management a direct determinant of fleet lifespan.
Black, James R. 1969. “Electromigration–a Brief Survey and Some Recent Results.” IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices 16 (4): 338–47. https://doi.org/10.1109/T-ED.1969.16754.

Seong, N. H., D. H. Woo, V. Srinivasan, J. A. Rivers, and H.-H. S. Lee. 2010. “SAFER: Stuck-at-Fault Error Recovery for Memories.” 2010 43rd Annual IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture, 115–24. https://doi.org/10.1109/micro.2010.46.

He, Yi, Mike Hutton, Steven Chan, Robert De Gruijl, Rama Govindaraju, Nishant Patil, and Yanjing Li. 2023. “Understanding and Mitigating Hardware Failures in Deep Learning Training Systems.” Proceedings of the 50th Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1–16. https://doi.org/10.1145/3579371.3589105.

Rashid, Layali, Karthik Pattabiraman, and Sathish Gopalakrishnan. 2015. “Characterizing the Impact of Intermittent Hardware Faults on Programs.” IEEE Transactions on Reliability 64 (1): 297–310. https://doi.org/10.1109/tr.2014.2363152.

Zhang, Jeff, Kartheek Rangineni, Zahra Ghodsi, and Siddharth Garg. 2018. “ThUnderVolt: Enabling Aggressive Voltage Underscaling and Timing Error Resilience for Energy Efficient Deep Learning Accelerators.” 2018 55th ACM/ESDA/IEEE Design Automation Conference (DAC), 1–6. https://doi.org/10.1109/dac.2018.8465918.
Intermittent faults create the most operational ambiguity because they produce evidence and then disappear. A node may pass a reboot test, rejoin the fleet, and fail again only when the next job drives the package into the same thermal, voltage, or communication regime. Cracked solder joints, aging packages, and contamination between contacts create these load-dependent conditions (Constantinescu 2008; Rashid et al. 2015), and reduced voltage margins cause timing errors that are hard to reproduce (Zhang et al. 2018). Sporadic errors of this kind can accumulate across iterations and degrade convergence without any explicit failure (Rashid et al. 2015). An intermittent node should therefore remain suspect until evidence clears it. The fleet drains it from long jobs, correlates its error logs, and readmits it only after it passes stress tests under the load that exposed the fault. Otherwise one marginal component can make validation and recovery untrustworthy for every job that lands on it. Across the three persistence classes, the evidence that exposes a fault also determines the fleet’s response (table 3).



Table 3: Hardware Fault Persistence and Fleet Response: The persistence class of a hardware fault determines the evidence that exposes it and the action the fleet takes. Manifestation is a separate axis: any of the three classes can surface as a crash or as silent corruption (Constantinescu 2008).


Constantinescu, C. 2008. “Intermittent Faults and Effects on Reliability of Integrated Circuits.” 2008 Annual Reliability and Maintainability Symposium, 370–74. https://doi.org/10.1109/rams.2008.4925824.










Persistence
Fleet signature
Detection evidence
Fleet response




Transient
One-time wrong value or lost message; retry succeeds
Corrected-error counters, checksum mismatches, gradient spikes
Correct or retry; roll back if durable state was contaminated


Intermittent
Recurring errors under specific load, heat, or voltage
Correlated error logs and repeated anomalies on one node
Drain and quarantine; readmit only after screening under load


Permanent
Reproducible failure at the same device, address, or link
Failed self-test or replay mismatch on the same device
Replace the component; restore from a checkpoint before the fault









A newly unboxed accelerator rack is far more likely to fail in its first week of service than in its sixth month, and a multi-year-old rack that has endured thousands of thermal cycles becomes fragile again as packages and solder joints fatigue. While persistence classifies a fault after it strikes, the hazard function \(\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)\) describes when over a component’s operating lifespan faults are most likely to occur, partitioning hardware longevity into three reliability regimes (figure 6). The first phase, infant mortality, brings elevated failure rates from manufacturing defects, improper installation, and early-life failure of marginal components. For electronic components it typically lasts days to weeks, which is why burn-in testing8 stresses hardware before deployment to precipitate those early failures prior to production use.
8 Burn-in testing: A controlled screening procedure stresses components before deployment to expose early-life defects. Temperature, voltage, duration, and acceptance criteria depend on the component and its qualified test procedure; a generic semiconductor screening recipe is not an operating specification for an assembled accelerator. Screening reduces the defective population entering service but does not certify every later workload or fault mode.
Birolini, A. 2017. Reliability Engineering: Theory and Practice. 8th ed. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-54209-5.

Klutke, G., P. C. Kiessler, and M. A. Wortman. 2003. “A Critical Look at the Bathtub Curve.” IEEE Transactions on Reliability 52 (1): 125–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/tr.2002.804492.
After surviving infant mortality, components enter the useful-life phase, where failure rates remain relatively constant under the standard reliability-engineering model (Birolini 2017; Klutke et al. 2003). This phase spans the longest portion of a component’s lifetime and is the regime where the exponential reliability model in equation 1 applies most accurately. For data center GPUs, the useful-life window is an operational planning concept shaped by refresh cycles, cooling, utilization, and observed fleet health rather than a fixed physical duration.
As components age, they enter the wear-out phase, where failure rates increase due to accumulated wear. For GPUs, wear mechanisms include electromigration in circuits, thermal cycling stress on solder joints, and degradation of thermal interface materials. The onset of wear-out depends heavily on operating conditions; components operated at high temperatures or with frequent thermal cycling enter wear-out earlier.
The practical implication for ML systems is that fleet-wide failure rates can depend on age distribution. Under the bathtub model, a new cohort passes through elevated early-life risk, a relatively stable period, and eventual wear-out. Screening, operating conditions, and replacement policy determine how much of that pattern appears in field data. Mixed-age fleets combine cohorts at different stages, so their aggregate hazard need not follow the curve of a single cohort.














Figure 6: The Bathtub Curve: Hardware failure rates \(\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)\) vary over time. (1) Infant mortality: high failure rate initially due to manufacturing defects. (2) Useful life: constant, low failure rate where random failures dominate. (3) Wear-out: increasing failure rate as components age. Burn-in testing aims to filter out infant mortality failures before deployment.



These three hazard regimes in figure 6 translate directly into admission control and maintenance policies. Before assigning new or repaired nodes to a long training run, operators use matrix-multiply, memory, and communication stress tests to expose marginal components. During service, temperature trends, error counts, and performance degradation help identify devices for scheduled replacement. Screening moves failures out of expensive production runs. An infant-mortality failure caught during a few hours of stress testing costs only idle time, while the same failure weeks into a pretraining run forces a checkpoint rollback. For that reason operators often route fresh or repaired nodes to short jobs first. Monitoring then checks whether the constant-rate model remains appropriate as the fleet ages.



Burn-in screening and lifecycle replacement keep the most failure-prone hardware out of long training runs, but even healthy mid-life devices still suffer random faults that compound across a fleet just as the interruption rates of section 7.2 do. Field studies of DRAM in large data centers found memory errors frequent enough that error-correcting memory, background scrubbing, and error-rate monitoring are standard fleet practice rather than optional hardening (Schroeder et al. 2009; Sridharan et al. 2015). Protection consumes some capacity and bandwidth for check bits and scrubbing, but that cost is small compared with a corrupted multi-week run.

Schroeder, Bianca, Eduardo Pinheiro, and Wolf-Dietrich Weber. 2009. “DRAM Errors in the Wild: A Large-Scale Field Study.” ACM SIGMETRICS Performance Evaluation Review 37 (1): 193–204. https://doi.org/10.1145/2492101.1555372.
9 Hamming codes (1950): Richard Hamming developed error-correcting codes at Bell Labs after relay computers repeatedly detected errors in his unattended weekend jobs and abandoned them rather than repairing them. A Hamming code uses parity checks to locate a single-bit error with \(\mathcal{O}(\log \HammingDataBitCount)\) check-bit overhead; adding an overall parity bit yields the extended single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting form. Memory ECC implementations vary in code and coverage, so the system must account for both corrected errors and residual faults outside that coverage.
Hamming, R. W. 1950. “Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes.” Bell System Technical Journal 29 (2): 147–60. https://doi.org/10.1002/j.1538-7305.1950.tb00463.x.
10 CRC (cyclic redundancy check): Polynomial checksum family introduced by Peterson and Brown (1961). CRC coverage depends on the polynomial, frame length, and error model; it is best understood as a low-cost detection layer rather than a universal guarantee. In distributed ML training, checksums or hashes can validate gradient payloads exchanged during collectives; without a verification layer, a corrupted gradient packet can silently poison the parameter update for every worker in the collective.
Peterson, W. W., and D. T. Brown. 1961. “Cyclic Codes for Error Detection.” Proceedings of the IRE 49 (1): 228–35. https://doi.org/10.1109/jrproc.1961.287814.

Bushnell, Michael L, and Vishwani D Agrawal. 2002. “Built-in Self-Test.” Essentials of Electronic Testing for Digital, Memory and Mixed-Signal VLSI Circuits 1: 489–548. https://doi.org/10.1007/0-306-47040-3_15.

Hochschild, Peter H., Paul Turner, Jeffrey C. Mogul, Rama Govindaraju, Parthasarathy Ranganathan, David E. Culler, and Amin Vahdat. 2021. “Cores That Don’t Count.” Proceedings of the Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems, 9–16. https://doi.org/10.1145/3458336.3465297.
Detection works in layers with different coverage and cost. At the hardware layer, error-correcting codes9 (Hamming 1950) correct and detect the memory-error patterns covered by the implemented code, and link-level CRCs10 check corruption in transit. These protections operate within their enabled storage and transport boundaries; they do not validate an incorrect arithmetic result merely because its bytes arrive intact. Before deployment, built-in self-test and the burn-in screening of the hardware lifecycle expose manufacturing defects and permanent faults (Bushnell and Agrawal 2002). During service, operators periodically pull nodes from production and run known-answer stress tests on arithmetic, memory, and interconnect, because defective processors often fail only on particular instruction mixes, data patterns, or operating points (Hochschild et al. 2021; Dixit et al. 2021).
The software layer draws its cheapest evidence from metrics the training loop already emits. Statistical checks on loss, gradient norms, and activations flag silent drift (Chandola et al. 2009), missed heartbeats identify suspected failures (Kawazoe Aguilera et al. 1997), and watchdog timers catch tasks that stall without crashing (Pont and Ong 2002). A node that stays alive but runs slowly or erratically, the gray failure of the failure taxonomy, can degrade progress while still meeting a liveness timeout, so section 7.9.5 treats it through straggler detection. Redundant computation adds stronger evidence on selected paths, either periodically or in response to an anomaly, by replaying a step on another device or comparing independently computed results. Its frequency depends on the residual corruption risk, the value of the protected state, and the cost of detecting an error late.

Chandola, Varun, Arindam Banerjee, and Vipin Kumar. 2009. “Anomaly Detection: A Survey.” ACM Computing Surveys 41 (3): 1–58. https://doi.org/10.1145/1541880.1541882.

Kawazoe Aguilera, Marcos, Wei Chen, and Sam Toueg. 1997. “Heartbeat: A Timeout-Free Failure Detector for Quiescent Reliable Communication.” In Lect. Notes Comput. Sci. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/bfb0030680.

Pont, Michael J, and Royan HL Ong. 2002. “Using Watchdog Timers to Improve the Reliability of Single-Processor Embedded Systems: Seven New Patterns and a Case Study.” Proceedings of the First Nordic Conference on Pattern Languages of Programs, 159–200.

Checkpoint 7.2: Classifying a hardware fault
Verify your understanding of the transient, permanent, and intermittent fault categories and the fault, error, failure progression:

Transient fault: classify a GPU that produces a wrong result once after a cosmic-ray strike and then computes correctly for the rest of the run, and justify why detection and rollback to a known-good checkpoint, not node replacement, match that fault.

Silent corruption: explain why silent corruption sits apart from the other fault manifestations even when its underlying fault is an ordinary transient bit flip.




Self-Check: Question

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Of the hardware faults just classified, the costliest are the ones whose manifestation is silent. A corrupted value that raises no error passes every liveness check the fleet runs, and training keeps building on it. Defending against silent data corruption therefore requires checks that establish a correct result, not merely a live process, and choosing those checks starts with where the corruption comes from and how it surfaces in training.


An accelerator executes deterministic logic gates, yet the silicon carrying those gates operates under narrow physical margins where both random particle strikes and load-dependent defects can flip bits without halting the processor. Single-event upsets (SEUs), the particle strikes introduced with transient failures, create fleet exposure that grows with device count and operating time even when the per-device rate is low. Manufacturing variances can instead leave “marginal” chips that pass initial QA but fail under particular inputs or operating conditions. Voltage and temperature margins matter, including supply disturbances during rapid current changes (\(d\AcceleratorSupplyCurrent/d\TimeInstant\)). Because these margin defects produce repeatable errors under specific workloads while particle strikes arrive at random, fleet reliability requires a probabilistic exposure model even when individual hardware faults are deterministic.
Facebook documented a pervasive SDC issue where a hardware fault caused a valid file to be reported as “size zero” during decompression (Dixit et al. 2021); the system “worked” without crashing, but data was silently deleted. In ML, the same failure manifests as valid-looking but numerically corrupted gradients. The pipeline trace in figure 7 follows a single ALU or memory bit flip as it corrupts an individual tensor entry, taints gradient reduction during the backward pass, commits into weights, and finally surfaces as degraded quality at evaluation. The comparative timelines beneath contrast this silent latency with a standard detected error. A hardware trap halts within milliseconds to restart cleanly from the last checkpoint, whereas silent corruption commits contaminated state into checkpoints over hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a costly rollback.






Figure 7: Silent Data Corruption Propagation: A hardware bit flip moves left to right from one wrong tensor value through the backward pass and the weight update, surfacing only at the final stage as degraded model quality. The two timelines below contrast a detected error, which traps within milliseconds and restarts from the last checkpoint, with silent corruption, which is saved into checkpoints for hours or days before an evaluation alert forces a rollback; the gap between the two is the cost of silence.



Telemetry from production training fleets shows this corruption is routine rather than anomalous. At modern training scales, hardware bit flips occur regularly, and erroneous computations from a single malfunctioning accelerator can propagate into the global model state, as Jeff Dean documented in his MLSys 2024 keynote on silent data corruption (Dean 2024) (figure 8).






Figure 8: Silent Data Corruption at Scale: Jeff Dean presents on silent data corruption (SDC) at MLSys 2024, arguing that at the scale of large ML training jobs hardware errors occur routinely, and that incorrect computations from one buggy chip can propagate and infect an entire training run. Source: Jeff Dean, MLSys 2024 keynote (Google).



In the Google training telemetry presented by Dean (2024), figure 9 identifies an abrupt gradient-norm anomaly as an SDC event. The plot shows the symptom without identifying the damaged bit or circuit. Corrupting a floating-point exponent is one mechanism that can greatly change a tensor value and subsequent updates. Gradient clipping can limit update magnitude, but it does not reconstruct the correct gradient; an anomaly detector must trigger validation or recovery before suspect state is accepted.






Figure 9: Gradient Norm Deviation: Transient hardware faults, such as silent data corruption (SDC), can disrupt optimization by causing abrupt changes in gradient norms. Google’s production examples show SDC anomalies surfacing as visible gradient-norm spikes. Source: (Dean 2024).









Cumulative SDC probability nears certainty over a long run.
Even a small per-GPU SDC rate accumulates across repeated collective operations, and the accumulation grows with fleet size. Any single collective is unlikely to contain an SDC event. Under the illustrative rate used in the analysis that follows, the per-step probability remains small while the cumulative probability grows over a long training run, reaching \(1 - e^{-1} \approx 63\) percent once the expected number of events reaches one. On the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster, that rate gives one expected event roughly every 100 hours, or about 22 over the three-month run of the chapter opening. The notebook below scales the same estimate to a fleet ten times larger to show where the trend leads, since the expected interval shrinks in proportion to fleet size. Standard AllReduce reduces the supplied contributions; it does not establish that an alive worker computed a correct gradient. The fleet therefore needs validation appropriate to its fault model in addition to liveness checks.
Check-and-verify methods test data-path invariants, subject to the boundary drawn for transient failures in section 7.3.1. Digests test byte integrity and agreement within their error-detection limits; they cannot establish that the original computation was correct. Independent computation, an algorithmic invariant, or replay tests that additional claim under a declared fault model. A quick estimate shows how much exposure those checks must cover.

Napkin Math 7.1: SDC risk accumulationProblem: Under an illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption, calculate the probability that at least one GPU in a 100,000-GPU fleet experiences an SDC event during a single 2 s training step.

Fleet size: 100,000 accelerators.
Individual risk: \(10^{-6}\) per GPU-hour (an illustrative generic SDC-rate assumption).
The exposure: In a 2-second window, the fleet has \(100{,}000 \times (2/3600) \approx 56\) “GPU-hours” of exposure.
The probability: \(\Pr(\text{at least one SDC}) \approx\) 0.0056 percent.

Systems insight: Under this illustrative constant-rate assumption, a 100k-GPU fleet expects one SDC event every 18,000 steps (roughly every 10 hours), even though the per-step probability is only 0.0056 percent. A CRC or hash can protect each shard or reduced buffer against corruption in transit or storage, while a redundant reduction can test the arithmetic path independently. Robustness moves from being a restart problem to a verification problem only when the verification covers the failure mechanism being claimed.


Full replication protects a broader computation path at a correspondingly high resource cost. Dual modular redundancy runs every computation twice and compares the results, and triple modular redundancy runs it three times and takes a majority vote. These schemes pay 100 and 200 percent hardware overhead, respectively, to detect or mask a fault within a single control deadline (Sheaffer et al. 2007; Arifeen et al. 2020). These guarantees depend on the replicas avoiding a shared fault. The price is justified in safety-critical embedded control, such as a vehicle’s onboard computers, where one wrong output can endanger people and the replicated hardware is a small computer. For fleet training, duplicating every step of a run on 10,000 GPUs doubles the compute devoted to those steps, before comparison and coordination costs. When corruption is rare and rollback can recover valid state, selective redundancy can protect useful progress at lower cost. Screening removes suspect devices, statistical checks run continuously, standby pools absorb drained nodes, and periodic or triggered recomputation checks selected execution paths.

Sheaffer, J. W., D. P. Luebke, and K. Skadron. 2007. “A Hardware Redundancy and Recovery Mechanism for Reliable Scientific Computation on Graphics Processors.” Graphics Hardware 2007: 55–64. https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh07/055-064.

Arifeen, Tooba, Abdus Sami Hassan, and Jeong-A Lee. 2020. “Approximate Triple Modular Redundancy: A Survey.” IEEE Access 8: 139851–67. https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2020.3012673.
Google’s reactive hot-spare protocol shows how those pieces combine in three stages (figure 10). When runtime monitors flag an anomalous gradient and replay implicates a suspect accelerator (G2), the scheduler isolates that device and promotes a standby hot spare (S) into the active ring. It then provisions a replacement spare (S’) while the suspect unit undergoes hardware diagnostics (Dean 2024). The fleet pays in advance for one idle device per pool rather than for a duplicate of every computation, and the protocol shifts the burden of correctness from unverified hardware to system-level auditing. Even so, these hardware checks reduce only the risk of an unreliable physical substrate; they do not protect against faults that the software stack introduces itself, bugs that look like valid computation while corrupting the ML pipeline.






Figure 10: Hot-Spare Failover: An \(\DeviceCount+1\) pool of four active GPUs and one standby spare. When loss or gradient sanity checks flag a suspect GPU and replay implicates it, the job drains that device and resumes on the spare from the last known-good state; the device goes to repair and a healthy unit refills the spare slot. Google’s data-center examples use this reactive pattern to keep training moving despite hardware faults, in contrast to running every computation on two or three redundant units and comparing results (Dean 2024). The standing cost is the idle spare.


Dean, Jeff. 2024. Exciting Directions in Systems for Machine Learning. MLSys 2024 invited talk.



Checkpoint 7.3: Detecting silent corruption
Verify your understanding of Byzantine failures and SDC:

SDC danger: explain why silent data corruption is more dangerous for ML training than a simple node crash.
Hot spare vs. restart: compare a hot spare redundancy strategy with traditional checkpoint-restart in terms of recovery latency.
Sanity checker: identify the metric used as a “sanity checker” to identify potential hardware faults: GPU temperature or gradient norm.
Byzantine scope: assess the True or False claim that Byzantine failures only occur when a malicious actor intentionally sabotages the training cluster.




Self-Check: Question

In a 100,000-GPU training cluster where each device has an illustrative SDC probability of \(10^{-6}\) per GPU-hour, what is the expected SDC exposure and failure cadence during continuous AllReduce training with 2-second step times?

The cluster experiences roughly 55.6 GPU-hours of exposure per 2-second step, resulting in an expected SDC event approximately every 18,000 steps (every ~10 hours).
The cluster experiences an SDC event on every single step because 100,000 GPUs exceed the reliability threshold.
The cluster experiences an SDC event once every 1,000 days because \(10^{-6}\) is negligible for 2-second steps.
The cluster experiences an SDC event exactly every 50,000 hours regardless of cluster size.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
A team spends three months testing a large language model (LLM) against complex prompt-level failure cases, only to realize that its preprocessing script kept only the last 512 tokens of each input, silently discarding the system prompt on long requests. The example exposes an ordinary source of ML failure that algorithmic testing can miss. A logic error in a data loader or prompt assembler can preserve valid tensor shapes while changing the computation’s meaning, allowing the pipeline to continue without a crash.
Software faults require a different recovery lens from hardware failures. Hardware faults enter from silicon, electrons, and physical wear; software faults enter through design choices, dependency versions, and pipeline glue. The fault-tolerance problem shifts from replacing a failed component to identifying which valid-looking transformation corrupted data, gradients, or predictions. Every boundary between framework, library, runtime, and distributed system is a place where such a transformation can hide.


A single tensor reference leaked on every training iteration lets a correctly sized job drift toward the device memory limit over hundreds of steps and then crash with an out-of-memory error far from the code that leaked it. Across ML frameworks, software faults of this kind span logic errors, resource leaks, concurrency bugs, and integration mismatches that propagate across system boundaries. Race conditions in asynchronous updates can lose or overwrite parameter updates, and deadlocks11 leave workers waiting on messages that never arrive. Because many of these faults surface only under high load, on particular hardware, or with a specific pairing of a high-level framework and a low-level numerical library such as cuDNN, root-cause analysis must treat the model code, the runtime, and its dependencies as one versioned artifact.
11 Pipeline deadlock: In pipelined training, a deadlock can form when stage 1 waits for a free buffer to send activations to stage 2 while stage 2 waits for stage 1 to accept its backward gradients. Neither stage can proceed, and because every other stage depends on them, the whole job stalls with no error raised, which a collective timeout eventually converts into a detectable failure.


The prompt-truncation bug from the opening example and the memory or synchronization bugs above should never survive unchallenged into a multi-week run. Because many software faults leave the pipeline running while corrupting inputs or gradients, each verification gate must establish which invariant holds and which recovery action is safe when it fails. A unit test catches the tokenizer boundary before launch, an integration replay verifies that a recorded batch reproduces the expected shapes and state on known-good hardware, and a fault-injection test verifies that a corrupted buffer or lost worker triggers rollback before tainting committed state.
Several of these gates also test the recovery machinery itself before an incident relies on it. A restore drill verifies a checkpoint manifest, the record that names every saved shard and the training step they share (section 7.8.5.2). A membership fault-injection test kills or partitions a worker and checks that, once replaced, the stale process can no longer write state the job will trust under the epoch, lease, and fencing rules of section 7.9.2. Every recovery drill is judged against two bounds formalized in section 7.8: how much completed work a failure may lose and how long recovery may take before useful execution resumes. Across all six gates, each test earns its place through the operational decision it authorizes (table 4).



Table 4: Reliability Evidence and Recovery Decisions: Tests earn operational value when each one establishes an invariant and authorizes a specific rejection, rollback, isolation, or restore decision.










Reliability evidence
Invariant exercised
Decision enabled




Boundary unit test
Tokenizer limits, tensor shapes, masks, and step metadata remain valid
Reject the change before distributed execution


Deterministic replay
A recorded batch produces equivalent state on known-good hardware
Separate input or software defects from suspect hardware


Checkpoint restore drill
A committed manifest restores every shard and resumes at its named step
Accept the generation as satisfying the recovery contract


Membership fault injection
A killed or partitioned worker loses ownership and cannot write after replacement
Validate ownership handoff and communicator rebuild


Corruption injection
A changed shard, reduced buffer, or checkpoint fails the intended verifier
Block the optimizer step or roll back before propagation


Dependency rollback test
A versioned runtime and artifact set can return to the last known-good combination
Authorize automated rollback instead of manual repair






These safeguards matter only when each gate targets a concrete corruption path. A test that checks only whether the tokenizer runs is too weak; it must assert that system prompts, labels, masks, and sequence-length metadata survive preprocessing with the intended semantics. Integration replay then follows one recorded batch through loading, sharding, collation, and model input construction. Fault injection tests whether the detector fires before the protected commit and whether recovery stays within the named bounds on lost work and recovery time for the injected fault. Restore drills, stale-writer rejection, and corrupted-shard rejection therefore provide evidence that generic build success cannot supply, and section 7.14 exercises those claims directly once the recovery paths themselves have been built. Before building those paths, however, a fleet must decide how much protection each workload is worth.

Self-Check: Question

Why are GPU memory leaks in 70B+ parameter distributed training pipelines particularly destructive and difficult to diagnose compared to standard CPU memory leaks?

GPU memory is dynamically swapped to NVMe disk automatically, causing unpredictable I/O thrashing rather than out-of-memory errors.
GPU allocators immediately throw segmentation faults upon the first unreleased tensor, preventing any batch execution.
Accelerator memory is scarce (40–80 GB per device) and shared across weights, optimizer state, and activations; a small leak per batch gradually builds over hundreds of steps until triggering an un-checkpointed OOM crash mid-run.
GPU memory leaks only occur when using mixed-precision BF16 formats and disappear entirely when switching to FP32 weights.

Contrast a pipeline deadlock with a data race condition in distributed parallel training in terms of their system symptoms and impact on model convergence.
Justify why a silent data preprocessing defect (such as unintended prompt truncation or incorrect token masking) presents a much higher compute and financial risk than a syntax error that crashes on the first batch.
A preprocessing change silently truncates prompts and discards the system prompt. Sequence the reliability gates in the order that should catch the defect, from earliest and cheapest to the final proof that recovery works:


A fault-injection test showing that the resulting alert blocks publication or rolls back to a known-good state
A boundary unit test asserting that tokenizer limits, system prompts, and masks survive preprocessing
An integration replay that follows one recorded batch through loading, sharding, collation, and model input construction

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Losing an uncheckpointed day on a 10,000-GPU foundation-model run burns hundreds of thousands of dollars in accelerator time, whereas losing an hour on a small vision job costs a few hundred dollars and a failed update in an online recommender costs live revenue rather than batch rework. Hardware, silent corruption, and software together set how often a fleet fails, but the work a failure destroys determines what each incident costs. A defense is worth buying only where it removes more of that expected loss than it adds in standing overhead.


Three workload properties set the price of a training interruption: the burn rate of the cluster running the job, the footprint of state that must be saved and reloaded, and how sensitive model quality is to lost or reordered updates. Those three factors separate multi-terabyte foundation models and continuous recommenders from smaller vision, speech, and scientific workloads (table 5).



Table 5: Failure Impact by Model Type: The cost of training failures varies dramatically by model type, driven by training duration, checkpoint overhead, and the value of accumulated training state. The Archetype A cost is one lost day on the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster; the vision, speech, and scientific rows give illustrative ranges rather than measured values. These differences demand model-specific fault tolerance strategies.

Large language model training illustrates how a costly allocation magnifies each hour of lost progress. The chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster at approximately $2/GPU-hour incurs $0.5M in compute costs per day. A job checkpointed only once a day can lose up to a full day of progress to one failure, which costs $0.5M in wasted compute plus schedule delay. At the checkpoint interval derived in section 7.8.1, the same failure costs minutes of rework instead of a day. The checkpoint overhead is correspondingly large. At the 14-byte-per-parameter resumable format that the checkpointing analysis uses (BF16 weights, FP32 master weights, and two FP32 Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) moments), the 175B-parameter running example writes 2.45 TB at every save.



Every GPU cycle, network byte, and storage drive dedicated to checkpointing, standby nodes, or verification is a resource that is not training the model, yet skimping on protection leaves a multi-million-dollar run exposed to day-long rollbacks. Rational investment in fault tolerance therefore weighs what a failure destroys against what the defense costs to run.
When a failure strikes, its bill extends well beyond the GPU-hours burned on steps that must be replayed. Repeating lost work delays the delivery of the trained model, ties up accelerators that could have run other jobs, and pulls engineers away from research to diagnose faults and nurse manual restarts. On the other side of the cost account, prevention carries a continuous overhead even when the cluster is healthy. Checkpoint storage scales with model size and save frequency, and checkpoint writes compete for memory and network bandwidth. Hot spares and automated recovery controllers consume standing infrastructure, and fault-tolerant coordination adds software complexity that must be maintained and debugged.
Optimal investment balances these two curves against cluster scale. For a small job on a few GPUs where hardware failures are weeks apart, infrequent checkpoints and manual restarts are cheaper than standing recovery infrastructure. On thousands of GPUs where failures arrive several times a day, frequent checkpoints, automated failover, and elastic resizing pay back their overhead many times over. The checkpoint interval derived in section 7.8.1 applies this exact marginal balance to a single decision variable, choosing the cadence where the cost of one more save equals the expected rework it prevents.
Equation 5 presents a simplified economic model for expected cost per training run:
\[ \TotalTrainingRunCost= \BaseTrainingComputeCost+ \mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount] \times \FailureEventCost+ \FaultToleranceCost \tag{5}\]
where \(\BaseTrainingComputeCost\) is the base compute cost, \(\mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount]\) is the expected number of failures during training, \(\FailureEventCost\) is the cost per failure, and \(\FaultToleranceCost\) is the cost of fault tolerance mechanisms. The cost per failure includes wasted compute plus overhead.
Equation 6 formalizes when fault tolerance investment is justified:
\[ \frac{\partial \FaultToleranceCost}{\partial \FaultToleranceInvestment} < -\frac{\partial (\mathbb{E}[\TrainingFailureCount] \times \FailureEventCost)}{\partial \FaultToleranceInvestment}  \tag{6}\]
where \(\FaultToleranceInvestment\) represents investment in fault tolerance mechanisms and the base compute cost is held fixed. The negative derivative on the right is the marginal reduction in expected failure cost. Additional protection reduces total expected cost while this reduction exceeds its marginal cost; an interior optimum equates the two when the cost functions have a suitable minimum.
One investment worked through the criterion shows what it decides. Let \(\FaultToleranceInvestment\) be a hot-spare node held idle beside the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster, so that a failed node’s replacement no longer waits for the scheduler to find capacity. Its marginal cost is 8 GPUs idling all day, about $384 per day. Its marginal benefit is the recovery time it removes from each failure while every other GPU waits. At the cascade’s 6.2 failures/day, each minute removed from every recovery is worth about $2,100 per day, so the spare pays for itself once it shortens each recovery by about 11 seconds, provided it is refilled before the next failure arrives some 3.9 hours later. The same node beside an eight-GPU job, whose GPU-only MTBF in table 1 is 6,250 hours (260 days), would sit idle far longer than it could ever save. Scale reverses the verdict on the same hardware, and three foundational principles distill how that shift guides design across the rest of this chapter.

Systems Perspective 7.2: Three rules of failure at scale

At scale, failures are continuous, not exceptional. A 10,000-GPU cluster experiences a failure every 3.9 hours on average. Systems must be designed expecting failure as normal operation.
Checkpoint intervals have an optimum. The Young-Daly interval (developed in section 7.8.1) sets checkpoint frequency from write time and system MTBF under its stated assumptions, and it shrinks only with the square root of a falling MTBF.
Training and serving have fundamentally different fault tolerance requirements. A long training job can budget minutes for recovery while preserving accumulated progress; an interactive serving request may have only milliseconds left before its deadline. Those budgets motivate checkpoint recovery for training and ready alternate capacity for serving.



These three rules organize the rest of the chapter: rules 1 and 2 govern long-running training jobs that must protect accumulated progress, rule 3 governs low-latency serving fleets that must protect live requests, and observability and fault injection verify that both recovery paths work under fire. Training resilience begins with the durable state that every restart or resize falls back on.

Self-Check: Question

The expected cost of a training run is modeled as base compute, plus expected failures times the cost per failure, plus the cost of fault-tolerance mechanisms. Under this model, when does one more unit of fault-tolerance investment lower the total expected cost?

Whenever it reduces the expected number of failures, regardless of what it costs.
Whenever the cluster is large enough to fail several times per day.
While the reduction in expected failure cost it buys exceeds its own marginal cost.
Whenever total fault-tolerance spending stays below the base compute cost of the run.

A 175B-parameter language model trains on 10,000 GPUs at about $2 per GPU-hour, and a ViT-Large model trains for two days on a much smaller allocation. Both checkpoint once a day. Why can one failure cost the language model run roughly $0.5M of compute but the vision run only tens of thousands of dollars?

Each GPU in the language model run fails more often, so every failure destroys more work.
Lost progress is priced by what the allocation costs per hour and how much state must be recovered, so up to a day of rework on a 10,000-GPU allocation costs about $0.5M while a smaller allocation loses far less per day.
Vision checkpoints are larger than language model checkpoints, which shortens vision recovery.
Vision runs carry no state beyond their weights, so they can resume from any data position at no cost.

On the 10,000-GPU cluster, about 6.2 failures per day each stall every GPU during recovery, at about $2 per GPU-hour. An idle eight-GPU hot-spare node costs about $384 per day. Estimate how much recovery time the spare must save per failure to pay for itself, and state the condition attached to that estimate.
True or False: A hot-spare node that pays for itself beside a 10,000-GPU training cluster is also a sound investment beside an eight-GPU job, because the node and its daily cost are identical.

See Answers →

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
When a top-of-rack switch dies two weeks into the training run of a 175-billion-parameter model, the cluster loses 64 GPUs instantly. Because a large cluster experiences such interruptions routinely (section 7.1), it cannot restart multi-week jobs from scratch; training fault tolerance must preserve state, detect and classify the failure, and resume or resize the worker group. Checkpointing supplies the first of those three obligations, and every detection, restart, and elastic-resizing path later in the chapter depends on the durable snapshot it produces. The first design question is what that snapshot must contain to make a restart valid.

Definition 7.1: Checkpointing
Checkpointing is the periodic serialization of the complete training state (parameters, optimizer state, data loader position, and random state) to persistent storage at a recorded training step.

Significance: It minimizes lost work after a system failure by trading checkpoint I/O against rework. Writing too often wastes accelerator time on storage traffic; writing too rarely risks replaying many completed steps after a failure. The Young-Daly interval developed in this section chooses the cadence that balances write cost against expected lost work.
Distinction: A resumable checkpoint captures a consistent execution state, including optimizer state, random-number generator state, data position, and learning rate schedules. It can use full or incremental storage; bitwise replay additionally requires compatible deterministic execution.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that checkpointing is “just writing to disk.” For large models it is a storage-system stress test, because the simultaneous write from thousands of GPUs can trigger a checkpoint storm (definition \(\ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}\)) that saturates the shared network and storage bandwidth \((\Bandwidth)\).



A checkpoint is useful only if it resumes the recorded step consistently. In distributed training, every shard must belong to the same recoverable state; a collection of files from different steps does not preserve progress. For the interval model, assume that writing a checkpoint completes durably before it becomes available for recovery and that a failure discards the work performed since the last completed checkpoint.
Two recovery objectives turn those obligations into a contract. The recovery point objective (RPO) bounds acceptable lost progress, so checkpoint age and replication lag must fit within it. The recovery time objective (RTO) bounds the delay until useful work resumes, which covers detection, resource replacement, restore, and warmup. A 20-minute checkpoint interval cannot promise an RPO below 20 minutes without a more frequent durable log or replica, and asynchronous flushing can leave the last durable generation older still. A five-minute RTO is impossible if checkpoint reload alone takes eight minutes. These objectives apply to a stated fault model. Corruption discovered after several saves can require rollback beyond the newest durable checkpoint. The Young-Daly interval derived next minimizes expected waste; RPO and RTO impose service constraints that the expected-value optimum must still satisfy (Beyer et al. 2016).


When failures are expected during a job, the key engineering decision is how often to write that state, because every save costs I/O time and every unsaved step is work a failure can erase. The Young-Daly formula12 (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)) gives a first-order estimate of that balance through a square-root rule:
12 Young-Daly formula: Young (1974) derived the first-order optimal checkpoint interval, and Daly (2006) independently refined it with tighter second-order bounds.
Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.
\[ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{7}\]
\(\CheckpointWriteTime\) in distributed ML training is not the time to flush a small process state; it includes transferring model weights and optimizer state to durable storage. The reference format here stores BF16 weights, separate FP32 master weights, and two FP32 moment tensors per parameter for Adam. A single resumable checkpoint for a 70B-parameter model therefore approaches a terabyte at 14 bytes per parameter; for the later 175B-parameter running example, it exceeds two terabytes. Of those 14 bytes per parameter, the optimizer state13 dominates the payload, exactly as in the storage sizing of the same resumable checkpoint in Checkpoint Storage. The optimizer state rather than the model weights therefore sets most of \(\CheckpointWriteTime\). Reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) requires a smaller payload or higher sustained write bandwidth, and \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is the central constraint that determines how tightly the checkpoint interval can be set before I/O overhead displaces productive training compute.
13 Adam optimizer state: Adam’s per-parameter first-moment (\(\AdamFirstMoment\)) and second-moment (\(\AdamSecondMoment\)) estimates are two FP32 values, 8 of the 14 bytes per parameter in the resumable checkpoint; with the FP32 master weights, optimizer-side state accounts for all but the 2 bytes of BF16 weights. For a 175B parameter model, the two moments alone reach 1.4 TB, which typically dominates checkpoint size and recovery time, making optimizer state the primary bottleneck in checkpoint I/O design.

Optimizer state, not weights, dominates checkpoint size.

To see the balance, consider an interval between saves. Doubling that interval approximately halves the checkpoint writes per unit of training, but a failure then loses twice as much work on average. Under the constant-rate, rare-failure approximation, failure occurs approximately uniformly within an interval, so the average lost work is half the interval. When write time is small relative to the interval, the wasted fraction from saving and replaying work is approximately the sum below. Detection, allocation, and restoration time require a separate recovery budget.
\[ \CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointInterval}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{8}\]
Setting the first derivative to zero (\(\frac{d\CheckpointWasteFraction}{d\CheckpointInterval} = -\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf} = 0\)) directly yields the square-root minimum of equation 7. As clusters grow, system MTBF drops, so the optimal interval shrinks, demanding higher-bandwidth storage to keep \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) small before checkpoint overhead consumes the cluster’s compute capacity. Because the relationship is a square root, halving MTBF tightens the interval by only \(\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4\times\), so doubling cluster size does not demand doubling checkpoint I/O bandwidth when checkpoint size and the other assumptions stay fixed. Substituting the optimum back into equation 8 gives a minimum waste of \(\sqrt{2\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf}\). Because \(\SystemMtbf\) falls as \(1/\DeviceCount\) under independent failures, that optimized overhead grows as \(\sqrt{\DeviceCount}\), and doubling the cluster raises it by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\) even though the interval itself adapts.


↩︎ The per-tier storage bandwidths that bound how quickly a checkpoint can be written are established in The ML Storage Hierarchy.



The Young-Daly interval of equation 7 needs two inputs, the system MTBF and the write time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\), and the chapter’s 10,000-GPU cluster supplies both as computed values. The worked cascade (section 7.2.2) put full-system MTBF, including PCIe and network failures (the redundant power supplies add no term), at 3.87 hours. For the write time, the 175B running example’s 2.45 TB resumable checkpoint drains to shared storage at the sustained aggregate write bandwidth this chapter assumes for the cluster, 100 GB/s, which takes 24.5 s. Substituting these into the Young-Daly formula gives a candidate interval for this cluster, which must still satisfy its RPO and RTO.

Napkin Math 7.2: The Young-Daly optimal intervalProblem: A 10,000-GPU cluster has an MTBF of 3.87 hours. A full model checkpoint takes 24.5 s to write. What is the optimal checkpoint frequency?
Math: Apply the Young-Daly interval of equation 7 (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)).

Convert to common units: \(\SystemMtbf =\) 3.87 hours \(\times\) 3600 s/hour = 13932 s.
Substitute and solve: With \(\CheckpointWriteTime =\) 24.5 s and \(\SystemMtbf =\) 13932 s, the formula gives \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx\) 826.2 s, or about 13.8 min.

Systems insight: At this interval, the checkpoint overhead (time spent saving plus time spent recomputing) is minimized to approximately 5.9 percent. Checkpointing every hour instead would lengthen the expected rework after each failure, wasting about 13.6 percent of the cluster’s capacity.


The result connects measured or estimated interruption rates to checkpoint policy. At this interval, saving and expected replay together consume approximately 5.9 percent of training time in the first-order model, half from writes and half from replay, because at the square-root optimum the two terms of equation 8 are equal. Plotting those two terms for this cluster shows how forgiving the optimum is (figure 11). Write overhead falls hyperbolically and expected rework climbs linearly, so their sum has a shallow floor around 14 min. An interval slightly off the optimum costs little, while one several times too short or too long costs far more, which is why a rough MTBF estimate still yields a usable schedule. How far the estimate itself can be trusted depends on the simplifying assumptions behind it.














Figure 11: The Checkpoint Trade-Off: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter’s 175B running example on its 10,000-GPU cluster, with a 24.5 s checkpoint write and a 3.9 h full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near 14 min. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal.




Systems Perspective 7.3: Young-Daly formula assumptionsThe first-order Young-Daly formula provides valuable intuition but rests on assumptions that may not hold when write times are non-negligible relative to MTBF; the renewal model derived in Checkpoint Intervals Beyond the First-Order Approximation shows how finite checkpoint time changes the optimum. The assumptions are:

Exponentially distributed failures: Assumes a constant failure rate. Real hardware follows the bathtub curve, with higher rates during burn-in and wear-out phases.
Deterministic checkpoint time: Assumes \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is constant. In practice, checkpoint time varies from save to save with storage contention, network congestion, and memory pressure.
Recovery cost is independent of the chosen interval: A fixed per-failure recovery cost does not change the first-order minimizing interval. Recovery can take longer than checkpoint writing because it also includes job scheduling delays, topology reconstruction, and warmup; it still belongs in the total-waste budget.
Aggregate interruption process: Independent constant-rate failure sources can contribute to one job-interruption rate. Shared power, cooling, or switch failures require a model of incident frequency and recovery cost; adding per-device rates alone misses those common causes.
Infinite timeline: Optimizes for long training runs. Short runs, where total time is comparable to MTBF, require different analysis.

When assumptions are violated, the optimal interval may shift significantly, but restart overhead should not be treated as if it were paid at every checkpoint. In the first-order lost-time model, restart time adds a per-failure recovery term to total expected waste; it does not replace \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) inside equation 7 unless a recovery-aware Daly-style model is explicitly derived and calibrated.


Along an execution timeline, a training run alternates productive compute intervals (\(\CheckpointInterval\)) with synchronous save barriers (\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)), and a failure charges two distinct penalties (figure 12). Uncheckpointed progress is discarded as lost rework, and the restart latency (\(\FailureRecoveryTime\)) of job scheduling, checkpoint loading, and pipeline warmup follows before useful work resumes. Recovery latency therefore matters as much as write duration. Restart adds scheduling and warmup to reading the saved state back, so total restart time can exceed the checkpoint write time. It belongs in the total-waste and service-level objective (SLO) budgets as a per-failure term (perspective 7.3) rather than inside the per-checkpoint write term.






Figure 12: Checkpoint-Recovery Timeline: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.






The interval calculation chooses when the system preserves state; the write path decides what each save costs while training waits. Equation 9 generalizes the save-side term of equation 8 to include any pause beyond the write itself:
\[ \CheckpointOverheadFraction= \frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval} + \frac{\CheckpointExtraPauseTime}{\CheckpointInterval}  \tag{9}\]
Here, \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) is the dimensionless fraction of time lost to checkpointing, \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is checkpoint write time, \(\CheckpointInterval\) is the checkpoint interval, and \(\CheckpointExtraPauseTime\) is any training pause beyond the checkpoint write itself. This includes memory allocation, coordination, and serialization. Total first-order waste is then \(\CheckpointWasteFraction(\CheckpointInterval) \approx \CheckpointOverheadFraction+ \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)\), so checkpoint overhead in this section means the save side alone, with expected rework counted separately. How large \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) becomes depends first on whether training waits for durable storage.


Synchronous checkpointing resumes training only after every worker’s portion reaches durable storage. Asynchronous checkpointing instead pauses the accelerators only long enough to copy the weights and optimizer tensors from GPU memory into host memory or local staging, then flushes that staged copy to remote storage in the background while training continues. The brief device-to-host copy is necessary because the next optimizer step updates the live GPU tensors in place, which would otherwise overwrite state that is still being serialized. Synchronous and asynchronous checkpoint writes develops the write path behind both approaches. For recovery, blocking alone does not establish consistency, so the protocol must ensure that every shard belongs to the same recoverable training state. Recovery can use an asynchronous generation only after all required shards reach the storage tier that survives the modeled failure and the coordinator publishes completion. If a failure strikes while the background flush is still in flight, recovery must fall back to the previous committed generation.
A synchronous save pauses every accelerator in the job for the full remote write, and Checkpoint Storage prices that exposed pause on a slow shared tier. Asynchronous capture shrinks the exposed pause to the local staging copy and moves the remote flush off the critical path, which is why production systems stage checkpoints rather than block on shared storage. Write time also varies widely across model types, because larger models require longer writes but also earn longer optimal intervals (table 6).
The Archetype A row in table 6 uses the same 14-byte-per-parameter resumable checkpoint (2.45 TB) as the rest of the chapter. Its interval calculation uses the GPU-only cluster MTBF rather than the shorter full-system MTBF of the worked cascade, so the square-root rule gives a longer interval than the Young-Daly notebook. The table keeps the GPU-only basis because its purpose is comparison across model types. Switching every row to the full-system MTBF would shorten each interval, and raise each overhead, by the same square-root factor, leaving the ranking across rows unchanged. The ResNet-50 and BERT-Large rows count only FP32 weights, so their write times and resulting intervals are lower bounds for a resumable checkpoint. Their intervals of seconds describe the balance for that smaller payload; selecting a recovery cadence requires including optimizer, schedule, and input-stream state. Small-state jobs rarely run on a cluster this large, and their actual storage bandwidth and complete recovery state determine whether saves every few minutes or every epoch have negligible overhead. The large-state rows show why interval selection becomes consequential when each save moves hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes.



Table 6: Checkpoint Overhead by Model Type: The Archetype A row is the 175B running example at 14 bytes per parameter (weights, FP32 master weights, and Adam moments); the 20B, recommender, and vision transformer rows are representative scenario sizes, and the 4 TB embedding-heavy recommender is a smaller scenario than the 10 TB+ embedding tables of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) in table 5; the BERT-Large and ResNet-50 rows count FP32 weights only and omit optimizer state, so their write times understate a full resumable checkpoint. Larger models require longer save times but also benefit from longer optimal checkpoint intervals. The percentage column reports the save-side overhead \(\CheckpointOverheadFraction\) of equation 9 with no extra pause, not total Young-Daly waste; at the optimum, expected rework adds a comparable term.
