title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Fault tolerance turns the statistical expectation of hardware failure into a manageable operational routine. Individual component reliability compounds across thousands of devices, driving system-level MTBF from years down to hours. At fleet scale, systems must bound lost work and recovery delay through recovery that is automatic, fast, and minimally disruptive to training or serving.
In training, progress is only as safe as the last state the fleet can prove it can restore. Checkpointing bounds lost work, and the Young-Daly interval (equation 7) prices that bound against write cost, shrinking only with the square root of a falling MTBF. RPO and RTO turn the expected-value optimum into a service contract. A manifest published last defines which generation exists, and fencing at the resource boundary decides who may still write to it. The retries that recovery triggers stay safe only when each operation is idempotent, inherits its caller’s deadline, and draws on one shared retry budget, so the response cannot amplify the incident. Elastic recovery then trades capacity for continuity, valid only while the data, batch-size, and optimizer invariants survive the resize.
Serving inverts the budget. Training can spend minutes restoring state that satisfies its optimization contract; an interactive request has milliseconds, so serving buys availability with ready replicas and decides in advance which state it will rebuild, replicate, or abandon. The KV cache is the clearest case, derived state that can be reconstructed from retained history only when the latency budget allows. When neither redundancy nor reconstruction fits that budget, graceful degradation keeps the service useful by sacrificing a named property that was validated before the incident.
Recovery depends on evidence about both the failure and the state being restored. A loss spike can originate in hardware, data, numerical behavior, or synchronization. Suspect state can justify a pause or rollback while investigation continues; attributing the cause to a device requires corroborating telemetry, replay, or integrity evidence. Restore drills and fault injection then test whether the selected response actually preserves valid state and meets its recovery budget. Passing those tests establishes evidence for the exercised fault model, rather than a guarantee against every failure.

Key Takeaways: Failure is normal operation

Scale makes failure routine: A 10,000-GPU cluster encounters hardware failures every few hours under the chapter’s component-rate assumptions; software must treat failure as a normal state.
Liveness is not correctness: A gray failure keeps answering heartbeats while every peer waits on it, and silent data corruption passes ECC while feeding wrong gradients into a correct AllReduce, so detection needs progress measurements and check-and-verify evidence beside liveness checks.
Recovery is a contract: RPO bounds lost progress, RTO bounds recovery delay, MTTR combines with MTBF to determine steady-state availability, a manifest identifies committed state, and fencing prevents an expired worker epoch from writing after replacement.
Checkpoint cadence balances two costs: Under the first-order assumptions, \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\) balances checkpoint write overhead against expected rework; for the 175B running example on a 10,000-GPU cluster it lands near 13.8 min. The selected interval must also meet limits on lost progress; recovery delay needs its own budget.
Elasticity enables persistence: Designing training jobs to be “elastic” (rebuilding communication groups and rebalancing data shards as traced in figure 16) can reduce waiting for replacement capacity. The runtime must preserve valid state and data coverage, and either preserve batch size or validate the changed optimization policy. Checkpoint cadence still determines how much work must be replayed.
Serving recovery follows the state budget: Preserve authoritative history, then choose reconstruction, checkpointing, or replication for derived state according to the latency contract (table 13). A ready replacement provides useful service only when it can also recover the context the request needs.
Degradation is a designed mode: When recovery cannot finish inside the latency budget, a fallback validated in advance (a smaller model, cached results, default features, or shed low-priority load) keeps the service useful, provided monitoring exposes how much quality was traded away.



Fault tolerance makes the cost of coordination a deliberate part of the execution budget. Case 3 on coordination overhead works a complete coordination-bound diagnosis, attributing a large run’s lost wall time to checkpoints, failures, pipeline bubbles, and scheduling. In the Fleet Law (equation 1.3), checkpoint pauses, detection timeouts, and restarts all land in the synchronization term \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\), and in goodput accounting they are runtime losses. The chapter’s mechanisms spend Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) so that a failure does not erase completed Compute, and asynchronous checkpointing and warm restart earn their complexity by moving part of that synchronization cost into \(\OverlappedTime\) or shrinking it outright. The useful comparison is between time spent preserving and validating state during normal operation and time lost reconstructing trustworthy execution after a failure. A cheaper recovery mechanism is valuable only when it still meets the workload’s limits on lost progress, response delay, and degraded quality.

What’s Next: From resilience to resource managementKeeping the fleet running despite inevitable hardware failures requires three layers: checkpointing preserves progress, elasticity absorbs node losses, and redundancy protects stateful serving sessions. Each layer also assumed a decision made elsewhere: a spare pool deep enough to replace a drained node, a hot spare held idle, spot capacity that may vanish, and replicas placed across independent failure domains. Those are allocation decisions, made while many jobs compete for the same fleet, from month-long training runs to hour-long experiments. A fault-tolerant cluster therefore still needs orchestration to decide which jobs run where, when to preempt, and how to share capacity fairly among them.

title: 7 Fault Tolerance
text:
Self-Check: Answer

A production cluster operates 10,000 GPUs, where each individual GPU exhibits an independent MTTF of 50,000 hours and an availability of 99.99%. What is the resulting GPU-only cluster MTBF, and what is the probability that all 10,000 GPUs are simultaneously operational at any random instant?

Cluster MTBF is 50 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 90.5%.
Cluster MTBF is 500 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 99.0%.
Cluster MTBF is 5.0 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 36.8%.
Cluster MTBF is 0.5 hours; simultaneous cluster availability is approximately 1.0%.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The cluster MTBF scales inversely with component count: \(\text{MTBF}_{\text{cluster}} = \text{MTBF}_{\text{component}} / N = 50{,}000 / 10{,}000 = 5.0\) hours. The simultaneous availability follows the product of individual reliabilities: \(R_{\text{cluster}} = (0.9999)^{10{,}000} \approx e^{-1} \approx 0.368\) (36.8%). The 50-hour option incorrectly divides 50,000 by 1,000 instead of 10,000 and overestimates availability. The 500-hour and 0.5-hour options miscalculate the linear \(1/N\) scaling by one or two orders of magnitude.
Learning Objective: Calculate the system-level MTBF and availability scaling for large accelerator clusters.
Using an illustrative unprotected-memory soft-error rate of 250 FIT/Mbit and 80 GiB of HBM per device, explain why a 1,024-GPU training cluster needs ECC protection.
Answer: Using the chapter’s 80 GiB device capacity gives about \(7.04\times10^8\) Mbit across 1,024 GPUs. Multiplying by 250 FIT/Mbit yields about \(1.76\times10^{11}\) FIT. Since 1 FIT is one event per billion hours, this is about 176 raw memory errors per hour, approximately one every 20 seconds. ECC corrects covered error patterns before they become application-visible; the residual job-interrupting and silent-corruption rates depend on the protection scheme, not the raw rate alone.
Learning Objective: Analyze why high-density memory subsystems dominate the soft-error failure budget in distributed ML clusters.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

**Sequence the following failure domains in ascending order of their physical containment hierarchy and typical blast radius (from smallest number of affected GPUs to largest):


Top-of-rack (ToR) switch failure isolating 32–64 GPUs
Single GPU hardware lockup affecting 1 GPU
Multi-rack Power Distribution Unit (PDU) failure affecting 100–500 GPUs
Node-level power loss (a fault that exhausts a node’s redundant PSUs) affecting 8 GPUs
Regional power grid disruption affecting all GPUs in a data center**

Answer: The correct sequence is (2) -> (4) -> (1) -> (3) -> (5). - (2) Single GPU hardware lockup: Affects 1 GPU. - (4) Node-level power loss (redundant PSUs exhausted): Affects 8 GPUs. - (1) Top-of-rack (ToR) switch failure: Affects 32–64 GPUs. - (3) Multi-rack Power Distribution Unit (PDU) failure: Affects 100–500 GPUs. - (5) Regional power grid disruption: Affects all GPUs across the data center region.
Learning Objective: Classify infrastructure failure domains by hierarchical containment and blast radius.

During a distributed AllReduce operation, a single GPU rank experiences a silent bit flip in an exponent calculation. The rank does not crash, passes network timeouts, and contributes an anomalously large gradient to the collective average. How is this failure categorized, and what is its primary danger to the training run?

Byzantine failure; it silently poisons model weights and gradients while bypassing standard process-liveness and timeout detection.
Fail-stop failure; it immediately halts the AllReduce collective and triggers an automated container restart.
Transient network failure; it is automatically corrected by underlying InfiniBand packet retransmission protocols.
Benign gray failure; it is absorbed by stochastic gradient descent with zero impact on final convergence.

Answer: The correct answer is A. This is a Byzantine failure because the defective component continues participating in collective communication while transmitting mathematically corrupted data, silently poisoning global model parameters without triggering fail-stop crash handlers. Categorizing this as a fail-stop failure is incorrect because fail-stop components cease operation and are caught by timeout mechanisms. Categorizing this as a transient packet loss error confuses network transport retries with silent arithmetic corruption. Categorizing this as a benign gray failure that self-corrects through stochastic gradient descent is incorrect because exponent bit flips can scale gradients by orders of magnitude, causing divergence or NaN collapse.
Learning Objective: Compare Byzantine failures and silent data corruption against fail-stop failures in synchronous distributed training.

Learning Objective: Analyze the latency and state preservation challenges of transformer KV caches in stateful inference serving.
What is the primary operational trade-off between Active-Active and Active-Passive replication strategies in ML inference serving clusters?

Active-Active replication requires \(100\%\) manual failover by human operators, whereas Active-Passive replication is fully automated.
Active-Active distributes traffic across all live replicas to maximize resource utilization but requires reserve headroom to absorb traffic when a replica fails; Active-Passive maintains synchronized standby replicas that sit idle during normal operation, simplifying failover at higher resource cost.
Active-Active replication can only be deployed on CPU clusters, whereas Active-Passive replication is exclusive to GPUs.
Active-Active replication guarantees zero latency during network partitions, whereas Active-Passive replication triples inference compute requirements.

Answer: The correct answer is B. In Active-Active serving, all replicas actively process incoming requests, maximizing infrastructure efficiency, but the cluster must operate below peak capacity (with headroom) so surviving replicas are not overwhelmed when one fails. In Active-Passive serving, dedicated standby replicas remain idle while tracking state or heartbeats, ensuring clean failover capacity at the cost of paying for idle hardware. The other choices mischaracterize automation, hardware support, and network partition physics.
Learning Objective: Compare active-active and active-passive replication strategies for model inference workloads.
In stateless model serving (such as single-image classification), a crashed GPU replica requires complex distributed state synchronization and session rollback before a client’s request can be retried on another node.
Answer: False. A stateless request supplies the input needed by another compatible, ready replica, so no session-state restoration is required. A retry still needs surviving capacity, safe operation semantics, the original deadline and a bounded retry budget. Routing or detection delays can remain; statelessness does not guarantee immediate successful completion.
Learning Objective: Compare request failover mechanisms between stateless and stateful model serving systems.
After a serving replica suffers a GPU fault, what dependencies must hold before requests can safely use alternate replicas, and which recovery work can proceed concurrently?
Answer: Health evidence must remove the failed replica from routing. Alternate replicas must be ready and have capacity; stateful requests also need their required context restored or reconstructed. Retried work must be safe, remain within its original deadline and retry budget, and pass admission control. Provisioning a replacement can proceed concurrently with rerouting to existing ready replicas. Detection, routing propagation and state recovery can add delay; failover is not necessarily seamless.
Learning Objective: Analyze the automated health detection and traffic rerouting stages during inference replica failover.
Compare session affinity with external distributed state stores (such as Redis) for managing stateful conversational inference sessions in terms of failover speed and infrastructure complexity.
Answer: Session affinity keeps a conversation on the replica holding its KV cache, avoiding remote state access but exposing that session to cache loss when the replica fails. An external store can preserve conversation context so another replica can recover it. Unless KV state was also preserved, the replacement still recomputes the cache. The trade-off includes state-transfer latency and another storage dependency.
Learning Objective: Compare session affinity against distributed state stores for stateful inference fault tolerance.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A serving system under overload must drop some requests. Why does priority-based load shedding generally serve the product better than random shedding?

Random shedding drops more total requests than priority-based shedding at the same load.
Priority-based shedding eliminates the need for admission control at the system entry point.
Random shedding treats every request as equally valuable, while priority-based shedding degrades according to a predeclared contract, serving interactive and revenue-generating requests before background or analytics work.
Priority-based shedding guarantees that no request misses its latency target during overload.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Both policies preserve capacity by dropping a fraction of demand, so neither inherently drops fewer requests. Random shedding ignores request value, whereas priority-based shedding turns degradation into an explicit policy that protects the most valuable traffic first. Admission control is still needed to reject work at entry, and no shedding policy guarantees every surviving request meets its target.
Learning Objective: Compare load-shedding policies by how they allocate unavoidable service loss across request classes.
Explain the four-tier feature degradation strategy (Critical, Important, Useful, Optional) and describe how it maintains service availability when feature store dependencies degrade.
Answer: The example policy blocks requests missing Critical features, substitutes validated defaults for Important features, uses cached values for Useful features, and omits Optional features. Its 5–10%, 2–5%, and less-than-2% quality-loss ranges are illustrative policy budgets, not inherent effects of those categories. Defaults and cached representations must be compatible with the model, and measured fallback quality must satisfy the chosen budget before deployment.
Learning Objective: Design tiered feature degradation policies to maintain inference service availability during feature store outages.
An image classification service deploys a model cascade: ViT-Large (307M params, primary, 88% acc), EfficientNet-B4 (19M params, secondary, 83% acc), and MobileNet-V3 (5.4M params, tertiary, 75% acc). How should the serving tier execute model fallback during severe traffic spikes or partial accelerator outages?

It dynamically routes incoming requests to lighter secondary and tertiary models based on queue depth and p99 latency triggers with hysteresis, maintaining low latency and high availability at measured accuracy cost.
It executes all three models simultaneously on every request and votes on the majority class.
It drops all incoming traffic until additional ViT-Large GPU replicas finish provisioning.
It converts the ViT-Large model into a text-only classifier to save memory.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Model fallback ladders dynamically shift traffic to lighter, lower-compute models when queue depths or tail latency violate SLAs, preserving response availability while sacrificing a bounded percentage of accuracy. Hysteresis ensures the system does not oscillate rapidly between tiers. Executing all three adds their unequal compute costs rather than reducing load. Dropping traffic violates availability goals. Converting vision models to text-only is nonsensical.
Learning Objective: Evaluate multi-tier model fallback cascades for graceful quality-latency trade-offs.
Graceful degradation is an automatic emergent property of standard microservice architectures that requires no explicit pre-engineering or offline fallback validation.
Answer: False. Graceful degradation requires extensive pre-engineering: fallback models must be pre-deployed or precomputed, default feature stores populated, degradation triggers (latency, error rate) instrumented, fallback accuracy validated against reduced SLOs, and hysteresis policies implemented to prevent oscillation.
Learning Objective: Justify the requirement for proactive architectural design and validation in graceful degradation systems.
The fault-tolerance strategy of selectively dropping lower-priority background requests during severe load spikes to protect latency SLAs for high-priority interactive requests is known as load ____.
Answer: The correct answer is shedding (or load shedding / priority load shedding). Load shedding protects system stability by proactively dropping a portion of demand before saturation causes cascading timeouts.
Learning Objective: Explain load shedding strategies used to protect serving availability under extreme resource saturation.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Explain why Heisenbugs are particularly pervasive and challenging to diagnose in distributed collective communication (e.g., NCCL AllReduce) libraries.
Answer: Heisenbugs occur when the act of observing or instrumenting a software system alters its timing and masks the underlying defect. In distributed collective communication, inserting detailed logging, tracing hooks, or debug barriers alters packet transmission timing and synchronization barriers across ranks, inadvertently resolving the precise race condition, thread interleaving, or network jitter that triggered the deadlock or corruption in production.
Learning Objective: Analyze the diagnostic challenges posed by Heisenbugs and timing perturbations in distributed collective libraries.
In a production ML recommendation service, p99 latency suddenly jumps from 45 ms to 800 ms with a 15% error rate. How do the three pillars of observability (Metrics, Traces, Logs) work together to diagnose the root cause?

Metrics reveal that GPU utilization is 100%; Traces show that all requests are identical; Logs show that user passwords were typed incorrectly.
Metrics reveal the exact timing and scope of the latency spike; distributed Traces isolate the feature-service span consuming 700 ms (instead of normal 12 ms); structured Logs reveal repeated connection timeouts to the embedding cache followed by a database miss storm.
Traces generate automatic pull requests to fix the bug; Metrics execute the rollback; Logs alert the end users.
The three pillars cannot be correlated because each uses completely incompatible timestamp formats.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Metrics identify the symptom’s timing and scope; traces locate the excessive delay in the feature-service span; logs connect cache timeouts with increased direct database requests. Together they narrow the failure path and support containment through a circuit breaker and validated fallback. They do not yet distinguish a failed cache process from a network or resource problem, so targeted repair requires corroborating evidence. The other choices misstate the functions of observability or deny the shared identifiers that allow correlation.
Learning Objective: Analyze metrics, distributed traces, and structured logs to diagnose cascade failures in ML pipelines.
Explain the numerical mechanism of NaN propagation during backward gradient computation in FP16 mixed-precision training, and describe how loss scaling prevents gradient underflow.
Answer: Invalid operations such as zero divided by zero can produce NaN, which propagates through most arithmetic into gradients and optimizer state. Overflow can first produce infinity and later cause NaN through an invalid combination. Loss scaling raises small FP16 gradients above the underflow range, then unscales them before the update. Dynamic scaling must also detect nonfinite gradients and skip invalid updates; scaling alone does not cure arbitrary NaNs.
Learning Objective: Analyze numerical debugging techniques and loss scaling mechanisms in mixed-precision training.
In distributed tracing systems utilizing OpenTelemetry, capturing execution time across microservices is sufficient for incident triage without recording structured trace and span correlation identifiers in service logs.
Answer: False as a general sufficiency claim. Trace timing helps locate delayed spans, while trace and span identifiers in structured logs link those spans to local events and exceptions. Other evidence may still support initial triage without that linkage, but missing correlation makes exact request-level diagnosis harder.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the role of trace and span context propagation in distributed log correlation.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why might a software-based fault injection framework (such as PyTorchFI) overestimate a neural network’s vulnerability to radiation-induced soft errors when compared against physical beam testing on real silicon?

Software-based tools only inject faults into 8-bit integer quantized models, whereas physical radiation only affects 64-bit floating point registers.
Physical radiation only damages power delivery networks and never alters logic gate states in operational GPUs.
Software injection tools can only simulate permanent stuck-at faults and cannot model transient bit flips.
Software injection mutates high-level tensor variables directly, completely bypassing microarchitectural and circuit-level masking (such as ECC correction, speculative instruction discarding, and dead registers) that absorb soft errors in hardware.

Answer: The correct answer is D. In physical hardware, many single-event upsets are masked by circuit-level defenses (ECC, parity checks) or microarchitectural factors (errors on unused registers, speculative instructions that get squashed, or overwritten memory addresses before reads occur). Software-level fault injection bypasses these hardware filtering stages and directly perturbs active software tensors, leading to higher observed failure rates than physical beam experiments. The other options misstate data types, radiation physics, and the capabilities of software tools.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the abstraction gap between software-based fault injection and physical hardware fault mechanisms.
Explain why killing a rank mid-collective, partitioning a node from the rendezvous service, and corrupting one checkpoint shard are more valuable fleet-recovery experiments than tensor bit flips alone.
Answer: Each experiment exercises a recovery decision rather than only a corrupted value. Killing a rank or delaying its heartbeat tests whether detection timeouts fire and the worker group is rebuilt; partitioning a node from rendezvous tests whether membership and fencing stop the old owner from writing; corrupting a shard tests whether restore rejects a generation whose manifest digests do not match. A tensor bit flip tests how software responds to a wrong value, but it does not show that the detector fires before the protected commit or that recovery stays within its lost-work and recovery-time bounds.
Learning Objective: Design fault-injection experiments that exercise recovery decisions at the level where they are made.
Software-based fault injection frameworks are universally preferred over FPGA-based injection for production resilience certification because software tools capture register-level gate timing violations and physical alpha-particle strikes with higher fidelity.
Answer: False. Software injection trades physical fidelity for scale and controllable experiments. FPGA-based injection can expose lower-level state in the implemented design, while beam testing probes the actual device under physical radiation. Neither an FPGA implementation nor a tensor-level simulation automatically reproduces every timing, packaging, or fault-propagation behavior of production silicon.
Learning Objective: Compare the fidelity and scalability trade-offs between hardware-based and software-based fault injection methodologies.
Explain how fault-injection frameworks such as Fidelity bridge the abstraction gap between low-level hardware faults and high-level software models.
Answer: Such frameworks model how lower-level faults in registers, memory and numerical units become software-visible errors, then use that mapping to guide scalable software injection. The mapping narrows the abstraction gap; its fidelity depends on the modeled hardware, fault distribution and calibration. It does not automatically establish coverage of every production fault.
Learning Objective: Analyze how bridging frameworks map microarchitectural hardware faults to software-level tensor perturbations.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why does Google’s TPUv4 recovery design combine OCS-based replacement of unhealthy cubes with fault-tolerant routing for supported link-outage patterns?

Because TPU chips have zero local memory and cannot execute software routing algorithms.
Because optical circuit switches are cheaper than standard copper Ethernet cables for intra-rack links.
A machine outage can remove a required job participant, requiring a healthy replacement cube; a link outage can instead require a supported alternate communication path. The response must preserve the job’s communication topology.
Because OCS switches completely eliminate the need for checkpointing during multi-month training jobs.

Answer: The correct answer is C. OCS allows the recovery system to assemble job-sized slices from healthy spare cubes after machine outages. Fault-tolerant routing handles supported OCS outage patterns when alternate paths remain available. Replacing a participant and repairing a communication path are distinct responses; neither follows from the failed-device count alone. The other choices misrepresent memory architecture or economics, or incorrectly eliminate checkpointing.
Learning Objective: Analyze how optical circuit switching enables topology-preserving fault tolerance in tightly coupled accelerator pods.
During the training of Meta’s OPT-175B model on 992 A100 GPUs, describe how the team addressed both physical hardware failures and mathematical loss spikes.
Answer: For physical hardware failures (at least 35 manual and an estimated 70+ automatic restarts over two months from ECC memory errors, network issues, and lost GPUs), the team relied on restart from the latest checkpoint, with train-log freshness monitoring (a 15-minute threshold, later relaxed to one hour) contributing to detection delay; polling and response could extend the idle window. For mathematical loss spikes (numerical divergence and gradient overflow), the team rolled back to an earlier clean checkpoint and resumed with a reduced learning rate (ultimately roughly two-thirds of GPT-3’s rate). The two remedies differ, which is why the run had to retain checkpoint history rather than only its newest snapshot.
Learning Objective: Compare physical hardware fault recovery and algorithmic numerical divergence recovery in large-scale LLM training.
What fundamental principle of ML serving resilience is demonstrated by Netflix’s chaos engineering practice?

Resilience is an active practice of continuous verification: intentionally injecting latency, terminating feature caches, and simulating dependency outages under controlled conditions to empirically verify that fallback hierarchies function before real outages occur.
Fault tolerance code should only be executed during unplanned production disasters to minimize server load.
Machine learning models should never rely on external feature stores or databases.
Chaos testing is only applicable to CPU-based web servers and cannot be used in GPU inference clusters.

Answer: The correct answer is A. Netflix’s chaos engineering principles establish that fault tolerance mechanisms (such as model fallbacks, circuit breakers, and feature defaults) rot if left unexercised. Regularly injecting synthetic faults in production and staging verifies that fallback paths actually satisfy latency and availability SLOs when real dependencies fail. The other options contradict chaos engineering principles or assert false restrictions on ML systems.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the role of chaos engineering and active failure injection in validating ML serving fallback paths.
Google’s TPUv4 study reports daily failure rates of 0.08 percent of TPU machines, 0.005 percent of ICI cables, and 0.04 percent of OCS units. Explain why such small daily fractions still require an automated reconfiguration control plane rather than manual repair.
Answer: Small daily fractions multiply across thousands of machines, cables, and switches, so the pod meets a steady stream of failures rather than an occasional emergency. Each failure can interrupt a job that needs its slice’s full communication topology, so the response must assemble a healthy slice from spare cubes or route around a failed link quickly and repeatedly. Health monitoring and topology software that run this loop automatically keep availability high; a manual repair process would leave jobs waiting for every routine event.
Learning Objective: Analyze how fleet-scale failure statistics justify automated topology reconfiguration.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

An engineering team operates a 1,000-GPU training cluster with a system MTBF of 50 hours (\(3{,}000\text{ minutes}\)) and a checkpoint write time of 5 minutes. The team intuitively chooses to checkpoint ‘every 15 minutes to stay safe.’ According to the Young-Daly formula, what is the mathematically optimal interval, and what is the consequence of the team’s intuitive choice?

Optimal interval is 15 minutes; the intuitive choice is mathematically perfect.
The first-order optimum is approximately 173 minutes (~2.9 hours); writing every 15 minutes adds more checkpoint overhead than it saves in expected rework under this model.
Optimal interval is 50 hours; checkpointing every 15 minutes causes disk sectors to wear out in days.
Optimal interval is 1 minute; checkpointing every 15 minutes risks losing 100% of the training dataset.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Applying the Young-Daly formula: \(\tau_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot T_{\text{write}} \cdot \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}} = \sqrt{2 \times 5 \times 3000} = \sqrt{30{,}000} \approx 173.2\text{ minutes}\) (approx. 2.9 hours). Setting an interval of 15 minutes deviates by more than an order of magnitude, spending massive cluster time on unnecessary storage writes. The 15-minute, 50-hour, and 1-minute options misapply the square-root law or make exaggerated failure claims. A stricter recovery point objective can justify a shorter interval even when it increases expected waste.
Learning Objective: Calculate Young-Daly optimal intervals to demonstrate why intuition-based checkpoint scheduling causes excessive I/O overhead.
Explain what a GPU-only independent-failure estimate, \(\mathrm{MTBF}_{\mathrm{system}}=\mathrm{MTBF}_{\mathrm{component}}/N\), omits about shared failure domains and their recovery consequences.
Answer: The independent-component formula omits separate shared failure modes such as power or switch outages, and it says nothing about their blast radius. Add those fault domains and their recovery consequences explicitly. Correlation alone does not necessarily increase the count of distinct incidents for fixed marginal component rates; a shared outage can group many component failures into one large event.
Learning Objective: Justify why independent component reliability models fail to capture the risk and blast radius of correlated infrastructure failures.
Why does adding more GPUs (\(N\)) to a distributed training job eventually encounter a ‘reliability ceiling’ where total wall-clock training time increases rather than decreases?

Because GPUs consume more electrical power than data center transformers can supply.
Because floating-point numbers lose precision when divided across more than 1,000 workers.
Because the Python interpreter cannot spawn more than 512 concurrent threads.
Because aggregate cluster failure rate scales linearly (\(N\lambda\)), shrinking system MTBF until the cumulative time lost to failure detection, job restarts, checkpoint loading, and rework exceeds the marginal compute speedup of additional parallelism.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Under independent failures, adding workers increases the aggregate failure rate. Recovery and replay can eventually cost more than the marginal compute speedup, and this reliability ceiling applies on top of the Amdahl ceiling. Whole-run useful goodput must count only retained progress and include recovery time in the denominator, so its reliability penalty grows with the number of workers.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the reliability ceiling where aggregate cluster failure overhead outpaces parallel compute scaling.
Because modern accelerator hardware incorporates hardware ECC on High Bandwidth Memory and CRC on interconnects, application-level gradient checksums and loss validation checks are redundant and unnecessary in 10,000-GPU clusters.
Answer: False. ECC and CRC protect the error patterns covered by their implementations within storage and transport boundaries. They do not validate arbitrary arithmetic or software transformations. Checksums test byte integrity or agreement, while replay, independent computation, invariants and statistical checks provide different evidence about computed results. Coverage must match the declared fault model; no single check establishes end-to-end correctness.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the limitations of hardware ECC and justify the necessity of end-to-end software verification against silent data corruption.

← Back to Questions

title: Fleet-in-Production Principles
text:
Fleet-in-Production Principles
Parts I and II built the fleet, coordinated its distributed state, and executed the training run. Training, however, opens a model’s lifecycle rather than completing it, and production deployment is where the model must repay its cost under real demand. Part III shifts the focus from the single, large training run orchestrated across a dedicated cluster to the deployed fleet. That fleet comprises the thousands of geographically distributed servers that answer requests in real time, the billions of edge devices that run and adapt models locally, and the operational machinery that keeps every deployed version accountable. The transition changes the engineering constraints. A training run must finish a coordinated workload. A deployed fleet must sustain useful throughput on a dynamic request stream while meeting latency targets, keep models current as data and devices change, and govern how each change reaches production.
A serving fleet depends on the runtime behavior of each replica (one deployed copy of the model, potentially spread across devices), whose execution time and memory footprint determine how many requests it can accept and how much capacity the fleet must provision. Part III therefore begins with fleet efficiency, which follows the fleet’s capacity through scheduling, runtime, and execution to measure how much of it becomes useful work. Serving at scale uses that measured capacity to coordinate request queues, batching, serving precision, and distributed model state. Edge intelligence extends the argument to fleets of varied client devices with intermittent connectivity, including federated learning that coordinates training while data remains on participating devices. Production operations then governs rollout, monitoring, and recovery across the deployed fleet.
The principles below preview the constraints that each chapter of Part III makes quantitative, turning replica-level mechanisms into fleet-wide capacity and latency models rather than assuming that local efficiency alone guarantees an efficient fleet. Before optimizing any serving mechanism, the part establishes a measure of how much of a fleet’s capacity becomes useful work. Without an end-to-end accounting rule, losses in cluster scheduling, runtime recovery, and kernel execution hide behind separate team metrics.

Principle 1: The ML goodput decompositionInvariant: A fleet’s ML productivity goodput, the fraction of its capacity-time that becomes useful work, is the product of three factors, each counted at a stated boundary so that every loss belongs to exactly one. Scheduling goodput \(\SchedulingGoodput\) is the share of capacity held by complete allocations. Runtime goodput \(\RuntimeGoodput\) is the share of allocated time retained as progress after startup, input stalls, checkpoint pauses, restarts, and rework. Program goodput \(\ProgramGoodput\) is the fraction of the ideal rate that retained steps achieve, measured as MFU. \[ \MlProductivityGoodput = \SchedulingGoodput \times \RuntimeGoodput \times \ProgramGoodput \]
Implication: Lost capacity must be located before it is recovered, because each factor has a different owner. A faster kernel recovers nothing that a job loses waiting for a complete gang, and a better scheduler recovers nothing that a job loses running below its hardware’s rate. A change that moves a loss from one factor to another helps only if the product rises. The decomposition applies to a training step and to a serving replica alike; serving adds the latency targets that each completed request must meet.


Over a deployed model’s lifetime, serving can consume more of that capacity than training did, and serving also carries the book’s scaling thesis into the request path. When quality is bought with test-time compute, by spending more computation on each query, the scaling curve that drove the training fleet moves into serving, and its cost recurs with every request.

Principle 2: Serving cost dominanceInvariant: For high-traffic production models, cumulative inference cost can exceed the one-time training cost over the model’s lifetime.
Implication: Inference efficiency often becomes the dominant lifecycle optimization target. When traffic volume, product lifetime, and retraining cadence make serving cost dominate, engineers should focus quantization, distillation, and sparsity on the inference path. The quantity to reduce is the cost per completed request at a fixed quality and latency target, not the cost of an individual operation.


Within each request, the mechanics of generation impose the first limit. Autoregressive generation produces each new token from the preceding tokens while a key-value cache retains intermediate attention state for reuse, so a single serving replica can saturate either memory bandwidth or memory capacity long before its arithmetic units are full.

Principle 3: The autoregressive bottleneckInvariant: In low-batch dense transformer decode, weight streaming often makes throughput memory-bandwidth bound because every decode step must stream the model weights from device memory to the compute units. Higher batch sizes amortize weight streaming, and key-value (KV) cache traffic shifts the binding constraint at long context.
Implication: Throughput initially improves with batch size by amortizing weight reads across requests, until per-device latency budgets, KV cache capacity, or sustained compute become the binding ceiling. Serving systems therefore need batching, cache-management, and memory-layout policies that keep bandwidth useful without violating latency SLOs.


At scale, routing policy becomes another lever for protecting latency. Even well-tuned replicas develop long queues if incoming queries land on busy servers while neighboring replicas have spare capacity.

Principle 4: The power of two choices (P2C)Invariant: In the idealized process that sequentially places \(\ReplicaCount\) independent requests into \(\ReplicaCount\) replicas, with each request sampling replicas independently and uniformly at random, querying two replicas and selecting the least-loaded one reduces the maximum load from the one-choice bound \(\AsymptoticTightBound(\log \ReplicaCount/ \log \log \ReplicaCount)\) to \(\AsymptoticTightBound(\log \log \ReplicaCount)\) with high probability.
Implication: Simple randomized load-balancing algorithms produce dramatically lower maximum-load bounds with \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) coordination overhead. Under serving queueing assumptions, the lower maximum load translates into reduced tail latency at scale. Serving requests differ widely in remaining work and load probes go stale, so the two probes must read a work signal, such as active tokens or KV-cache pressure, rather than a request count.


Moving learning onto phones and other battery-powered devices adds a constraint that no data-center scheduler faces. The device belongs to its user, so background learning runs only when the device can spare it.

Principle 5: The participation selection principleInvariant: An edge device contributes to on-device or federated learning only in windows its admission policy accepts, when the predicted update energy fits the remaining energy slack, the added power stays within the thermal limit, and foreground latency still meets its deadline (equation 11.2). Those conditions correlate with hardware class, charging habits, and connectivity, so the population a shared model learns from is the admitted population, not the deployed one.
Implication: The admission policy that protects each device also selects the training population, which makes admission a fairness decision as well as a resource decision. A fleet must measure participation and completion rates per device and user cohort against the deployed population and correct the skew through stratified selection, participation quotas, or reweighting. Loosening admission is not a remedy, because it spends the energy, thermal, and latency budgets the policy exists to protect.


Whether a model is trained in the data center or across a population of devices, every change must eventually be released to the deployed fleet, and at fleet scale that release needs a single standard of evidence. Shipping a candidate on scattered benchmarks or informal spot checks leaves operators unable to tell whether a production incident reflects a bad release or an unmeasured shift in traffic.

Principle 6: The evaluation contract principleInvariant: At fleet scale, a release decision is valid only when all of its evidence refers to one versioned evaluation contract that pins the model and its dependencies, the workload, the metrics and statistical design, the acceptance thresholds, the rollback conditions, and the accountable owners. Reliability under that contract is a vector of budgets over availability, latency, freshness, and quality. With \(\ErrorBudgetConsumption_{\ReliabilityTargetIndex}\) denoting the fraction of observations that violate target \(\ReliabilityTargetIndex\) divided by the violating fraction that target allows, the service is inside its reliability envelope only when \[ \max_{\ReliabilityTargetIndex} \ErrorBudgetConsumption_{\ReliabilityTargetIndex} \le 1 . \]
Implication: No single accuracy number can authorize a release. Averaging the dimensions would hide a quality regression behind perfect uptime, and evidence gathered on different datasets, load profiles, or configurations certifies no single candidate. Thresholds and rollback conditions are fixed before exposure, an exhausted budget in any dimension stops promotion, and a change that leaves the contract’s validated envelope reopens the decision.


Part III takes the trained model from the cluster to the world. The path begins with fleet efficiency, which charges every lost hour of capacity to scheduling, runtime, or the program and so determines how much of the fleet’s capacity becomes useful work. It then moves to serving at scale, where request batching, cache management, serving precision, routing, and sharding turn single-device efficiency into fleet-level latency control. Edge intelligence extends this discipline to phone-class devices that adapt models locally and coordinate through federated learning under unequal memory, power, and connectivity budgets. Operations at scale closes the loop by monitoring the deployed fleet, coordinating platform ownership, and responding when production behavior diverges from design assumptions. Measured against the Fleet Law, these chapters shift from the training step to the serving request. Fleet efficiency charges each term of a step to the factor that loses it and shrinks the exposed ones. Serving at scale trades batching against the queueing and routing delays that play the role of \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\). Edge intelligence faces communication costs set by intermittent wireless links rather than a data-center fabric. Operations bounds the coordination cost of every rollout and rollback. Together, these chapters develop the operational discipline that turns a trained model into a durable production system.




 Back to top

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can lifetime inference cost dwarf training cost?
Training is paid for each model version; serving continues throughout that version’s operational lifetime. A model trained for millions of dollars may serve billions of requests, each consuming compute, memory, network, and energy. At high traffic, recurring inference expense can exceed the original training cost by orders of magnitude. Milliseconds of latency and small differences in accelerator utilization then compound across the service’s lifetime. A fast prediction measured on an otherwise idle machine does not reveal how the same model behaves when requests arrive together, vary in length, and compete for memory. Work can spend longer waiting than executing, while an apparently busy fleet produces responses that arrive too late to be useful. Keeping extra machines ready protects response time but incurs cost during quiet periods; admitting more work improves utilization only while the service can still meet its promises. Failures sharpen this tension because displaced requests consume the spare capacity intended to absorb demand changes. Continuing to accept work during overload can worsen the shortage when delayed requests trigger retries that compete for capacity. The engineering decision is therefore how much useful work the fleet can sustain at an acceptable cost while preserving response quality and timeliness. The answer depends on the request mix and service requirements, so a gain for one workload may become a loss for another. In C³ terms, compute reuse must pay for communication and coordination without exhausting the user’s latency budget.

Learning Objectives

Estimate lifetime serving cost from traffic volume, deployment duration, and measured cost per SLO-compliant request
Select batching, scheduling, and per-request compute-budget policies for vision, LLM, recommender, and streaming workloads
Analyze attention-cache capacity, fragmentation, and prefill-decode interference under workload-dependent serving constraints
Compare sharding, disaggregation, and quantized serving designs using communication, memory, and quality constraints
Evaluate routing, overload-control, and isolation policies against tail latency, retry amplification, and noisy-neighbor risks
Design autoscaling and multi-region routing policies that balance cold starts, cost, and SLO compliance
Synthesize serving architectures that manage C³ trade-offs across request, replica, service, and platform layers



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



A language model that costs millions of dollars to train over two months can, once deployed to a global user base at thousands of queries per second, consume a comparable sum in inference compute every week. Inference is then no longer a temporary batch job. It is a continuous, latency-sensitive service.
Running that continuous service takes more than an efficient steady-state replica. Fleet efficiency characterizes a replica by how close its decode steps come to the bandwidth floor, how long it takes to become ready, and how much of its held time runs at the ideal rate, each averaged over windows of hours to weeks. Serving policy determines how that capacity is shared when requests arrive unevenly and each carries a latency target. A faster decode step supplies a better service rate, but it does not determine how long requests wait to join a batch, which replica receives them, which requests receive scarce cache space, or when the fleet needs another replica. These decisions connect the local execution toolkit to user-visible performance under load.


↩︎ The serving replica’s program and runtime goodput, its bandwidth floor, and the fusion, graph replay, and compilation levers that shape it are established in Fleet Efficiency.
The service contract makes that distinction measurable. Offered load is the work arriving at the endpoint, including requests the service may reject; admitted load is the work it accepts. A service-level objective (SLO) specifies the required outcome over a measurement window, such as a latency percentile or successful-request fraction. For language models, request rate alone is insufficient because prompt and output lengths determine different amounts of work. Capacity comparisons must therefore hold the request mix and SLO fixed while measuring how much offered work completes successfully within the targets.
An admitted request passes through routing, preprocessing, queueing, batch formation, model execution, and response delivery, crossing between the host CPU and the accelerator twice on the way (figure 1). The host manages admission, tokenization, and detokenization, while the GPU executes the prompt prefill pass and iterative KV-cache decode loop. The figure maps noncompute serving overhead against the time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT, the average gap between streamed tokens) latency budgets. For an autoregressive model, prefill processes the prompt and builds cached attention keys and values; decode extends that KV cache as it generates subsequent tokens. Waiting before prefill delays the first token, while competition during decode delays the stream. The scheduler must budget both delays alongside execution time. Batching and cache management govern work within a replica, sharding changes the replica’s capacity, and routing and autoscaling distribute demand across replicas.


↩︎ Prefill’s arithmetic-bound regime and decode’s bandwidth floor, measured as MBU, are established in Program goodput and its measure.







Figure 1: End-to-End Inference Pipeline: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request’s latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute.



Distribution adds placement and coordination decisions to the local serving problem. Load balancing1 must distribute requests across replicas with different amounts of unfinished work and available memory. Request routing must also account for model-specific characteristics: recommendation systems with large sharded embedding tables require different placement strategies than language models that generate responses token by token. When demand changes faster than new replicas can become ready, routing alone cannot restore capacity. Autoscaling, spare capacity, and admission limits must work together to protect the service’s latency targets.
1 Load balancing for inference: Request service times can span milliseconds to tens of seconds as models, prompt lengths, and generated outputs vary. Queue-aware routing exposes that remaining work more directly than assignment counts alone.Training and serving place costs on different timelines. A model version’s training expense can be amortized over its deployment, while serving capacity must follow recurring demand. An e-commerce recommendation service, for example, must accommodate peak shopping traffic without paying for an unnecessarily large idle fleet during quiet periods. Both training efficiency and serving efficiency matter, but the serving decision must also account for when requests arrive and how long they can wait. Building such a service requires three linked decisions: when distribution becomes necessary, how the architecture meets latency targets under varying load, and how resource utilization stays high enough that serving cost does not erode the value the model creates. The worked scenarios that follow size these decisions using registry values for real hardware and models alongside labeled scenario assumptions for traffic, prices, and latency budgets, starting with the physical limits that force a service beyond a single machine.

A single accelerator fails a production endpoint in three ways: its memory fills before the model weights or caches fit, its throughput saturates below the arriving query rate, or its forward pass runs longer than a request’s latency budget. Overcoming those limits requires distributing work across several devices within one machine or across machines over the network. Table 1 categorizes these three triggers and their matching distribution strategies, whose necessity depends on the permitted precision, placement, and service contract.
The first signal is memory exhaustion, which occurs when model parameters, key-value caches, or embedding tables exceed single-device capacity. A single NVIDIA H100 GPU provides 80 GB of HBM32 memory, whereas an illustrative mixture-of-experts model with ~1.8T parameters requires ~3.5 TB for FP16 weights alone. Keeping all those weights resident on accelerators requires multiple devices regardless of request volume; quantization and offloading change that placement constraint. Recommendation systems with trillion-parameter embedding tables face similar constraints. Meta’s DLRM architecture3 stores embedding tables that require multiple terabytes of memory (Assumption Provenance records the provenance of the hardware and model constants used throughout this chapter).
2 HBM3 capacity and bandwidth: The H100 combines 80 GB of 3D-stacked DRAM with 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, compared with 2.04 TB/s for HBM2e on the A100. Capacity determines whether model and cache state fit; bandwidth bounds memory-bound decode throughput.3 DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model): Meta’s 2019 reference architecture combines dense features processed by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) with sparse features represented by embedding lookups (Naumov et al. 2019). This separation permits different placement strategies; it does not require embeddings on CPUs and MLPs on GPUs. Production recommendation characterizations show why this structure matters for serving: embedding-heavy recommendation models create memory-access and capacity constraints that differ from dense convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), or large language model (LLM) inference (Gupta et al. 2020).

Beyond memory constraints, throughput limitations emerge when request volume exceeds single-machine capacity even with optimal batching. Consider a recommendation system serving 100,000 queries per second with a 10 ms latency budget. If single-machine throughput peaks at 10,000 QPS, no amount of optimization on that machine can satisfy demand. Horizontal scaling across multiple replicas becomes mandatory.
Finally, latency requirements can motivate distribution even when memory is sufficient. A 70-billion parameter model requires approximately 140 GB of weight memory in FP16, exceeding a single 80 GB H100-class GPU before KV cache is considered. Quantization or larger-memory hardware can make a single-device configuration feasible, yet its execution time may still exceed the request budget. Sharding the model across multiple GPUs can divide computation and weight traffic, but it adds communication and synchronization. Because sharding shortens compute-bound prefill and bandwidth-bound decode by different amounts, the latency benefit must be measured for each phase against its own target.

Memory, throughput, and latency triggers all become user-visible once an interactive endpoint starts streaming. Time to first token (TTFT) determines when the user sees a response begin, while time per output token (TPOT) determines whether the rest of the response arrives at a readable pace. TPOT is the average of the time between tokens (TBT), the gap between successive streamed tokens, which many serving systems report as inter-token latency (ITL). A stream can meet its TPOT target while a single long TBT gap still stalls the reader, so average cadence is stated here as TPOT and per-gap tail targets as TBT. Protecting both first-token delay and stream cadence is why inference reverses many of the optimization priorities from training.

A replica that runs near its hardware limit still wastes its capacity if requests wait so long in queues, network hops, and host processing that responses arrive after the user’s deadline. Because a served request counts as useful work only when it meets its latency and quality targets, every stage it crosses spends part of that contract’s budget.


A training iteration that takes 2 seconds instead of the usual 1 second slows a run slightly, and faster steps later can still keep the job on schedule. An interactive request that takes 2 seconds against a 100 ms target fails its contract immediately, even if every subsequent request finishes on time. This contrast between training and inference centers on the unit of useful progress. Training evaluates throughput together with convergence over a run; interactive serving evaluates completed requests against quality and latency targets. Offline inference can also prioritize throughput, while training still loses progress to stragglers and stalls. The distinction is therefore which delays violate the workload’s contract, not whether one activity cares about time and the other does not. That difference reorders priorities across six system aspects, from the primary metric onward (table 2).

Failure handling follows those different contracts. Training restores a checkpoint and repeats lost work, charging recovery time to the run. Interactive serving has far less time per request, so redirecting work needs spare capacity and recoverable request state, and substituting a smaller model needs an acceptable quality fallback. SLOs define which failures and delays the service may tolerate, and a recovery mechanism helps only when its added work fits within that contract.
The same targets also define the serving system’s capacity metric. SLO goodput is the rate of completed requests that meet the stated TTFT and TPOT targets for a fixed request mix. It is the serving counterpart of the useful-progress goodput that coordination protects in training (Orchestration coordination layer), and it applies after ML goodput, which measures how much of a replica’s held capacity runs at its ideal rate. SLO goodput then counts how much of that capacity completes requests within their targets. A request that misses its contract counts for nothing, however busy the accelerators were while serving it, so increasing arrivals without completing more requests within those targets does not increase useful capacity.


↩︎ ML goodput, the fraction of fleet capacity that becomes useful work at the ideal rate, and its three factors are established in ML Goodput.



If an interactive request carries a 100 ms latency target and model execution takes 70 ms on an idle replica, routing, network transfers, serialization, coordination, and queueing must all fit inside the remaining 30 ms. Distributing inference adds transfers and coordination to a request that already spends time in host processing and queues. This “serving tax” is the exposed work outside model execution that consumes the request’s latency budget, and its size depends on which components the request crosses and which costs can overlap.
Network communication contributes setup and transfer time at each cross-machine dependency. Synchronization between GPUs can expose that cost when the next operation needs a remote result. For an illustrative path with four sequential exchanges taking 50–500 microseconds each, the exposed contribution is 200 microseconds to 2 milliseconds. Actual collective time also depends on payload, topology, contention, and the number of communication rounds; a generic network round-trip time cannot be charged once per collective without checking its implementation.


↩︎ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model, which splits each transfer into a fixed startup latency plus a bandwidth-dependent term, is established in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model.
Before and after those network hops, serialization adds host work whenever a service converts structured data into a wire representation and reconstructs it at the receiver. Protocol Buffers, JSON, and Python’s pickle provide different representations and implementation paths, so their cost must be measured for the actual payload and runtime. Tensor transfers within a sharded model need not pass through the same object-serialization path as a service request. Formats such as FlatBuffers and Cap’n Proto permit access to wire-format data in place, avoiding a separate unpacking step when the consumer supports that representation, though they do not eliminate network transfer or every downstream copy.
Once the payload is on the wire, load balancing adds a routing decision and sometimes another forwarding hop: examining request metadata, consulting replica state, and forwarding to the selected backend all consume time before execution begins. The measurement must separate decision time from waiting and transport so that a slow routing path is not mistaken for a slow model.
When a request fans out across several backend services—such as feature stores, retrieval indexes, and ranking models—coordination overhead emerges as the gateway joins their results. Independent feature or model calls can run concurrently, but a dependent ranking stage must wait for the inputs it needs, so the critical path includes exposed coordination and the slowest required branch rather than the sum of every branch’s runtime. Finally, queuing delay (\(\QueueingLatency\)) adds waiting time whenever work arrives while the required resources are busy, even when the average arrival rate remains below average service capacity.
The serving tax must be measured on the same request boundary as model execution. Equation 1 decomposes that latency, with each term counting an exposed contribution so concurrent work is not counted twice:
\[\EndToEndRequestLatency= \InferenceLatency+ \NetworkLatency+ \SerializationLatency+ \CoordinationLatency+ \QueueingLatency \tag{1}\]
In the 100 ms request budget above, the four sequential exchanges alone can claim up to 2 ms of the 30 ms non-compute slack before any request waits for a busy replica. The measured contribution determines the intervention: co-location removes a network hop, fewer dependent exchanges reduce startup costs, and a faster link shortens large transfers, whereas queueing requires controlling admitted work or increasing usable capacity. Each choice spends resources to recover latency budget, connecting the request-level diagnosis to lifetime serving cost.

At this traffic, one year of serving costs about nine times the training run.
A team that budgets millions of dollars to train a model can find within weeks of launch that serving traffic is spending more compute per month than the entire training run cost. While the serving tax in equation 1 consumes a fraction of each request’s latency budget, those per-request costs compound across every query over the model’s operational lifetime. By the serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)), recurring serving expense can dwarf upfront training expense by orders of magnitude because a model version incurs training cost once before deployment while serving cost recurs with traffic. Both activities can consume purchased or rented infrastructure; the distinction here is expense timing, not financial capitalization. In a high-volume deployment, that recurring traffic bill rapidly overtakes the one-time training investment (notebook 10.1).

Napkin Math 10.1: The serving cost multiplierProblem: A team has spent $2,000,000 training a 70B parameter model and now serves it to 1,000,000 daily active users, each making 50 requests/day. Is training or serving the dominant cost over 1 year?
Math:

Training cost: $2,000,000 (one-time).
Metric: Annual inference volume is \(10^{6}\,\text{users} \times 50\,\text{reqs} \times 365\,\text{days} \approx\) 18.25B requests/year.
Cost per request: Assume a 70B model on H100 costs \(\approx\) $0.001/request (input + output).
Annual serving cost: 18.25B requests \(\times\) $0.001/request = $18,250,000.

Systems insight: Serving costs 9.1× more than training in the first year alone. A 10 percent reduction in cost per request, at unchanged request volume and service quality, saves about $1.8M in the first year, nearly paying for the original training run.


For one model version at a fixed query rate and average cost per served query, equation 2 combines training expense with recurring serving expense:
\[\ModelLifetimeCost= \TrainingCost + \ServingCostPerQuery\times \DeploymentDuration\times \ArrivalRate \tag{2}\]
where \(\TrainingCost\) is the one-time cost to train the model, \(\ServingCostPerQuery\) is the cost per query served, \(\DeploymentDuration\) is the deployment duration in appropriate time units, and \(\ArrivalRate\) is the query rate. The rate must count the same served queries used to estimate unit cost. That cost must include the chosen serving boundary, including idle or reserved capacity when it is billed. Changing traffic mix, fleet size, or price requires evaluating separate intervals rather than treating one unit cost as constant throughout deployment.

An optimization tuned for one model family or one layer of the stack can miss the active bottleneck when applied to another. Paging a key-value cache does nothing for an embedding-heavy recommendation model, and fusing a GPU kernel cannot rescue a service whose requests stall in a load balancer. Controlling serving cost therefore requires separating the workload mix from the system layer that owns each bottleneck.


Designing a serving platform around autoregressive token generation alone leaves a fleet unprepared for the workloads that dominate consumer request volume. In large consumer platforms, recommendation and ranking workloads can consume the majority of AI inference cycles and capacity (Gupta et al. 2020; Hazelwood et al. 2018), stalling on terabyte-scale sparse embedding lookups under sub-10 ms deadlines rather than sequential weight reads. Vision and image processing, NLP and LLM workloads, fraud detection, ads, and other classification tasks create additional serving demands. Table 4 compares representative pressures: sparse lookup for recommendation, batch efficiency for fixed-shape vision, weight and cache traffic for LLM decode, and incremental deadlines for speech. These are starting points for diagnosis; the active bottleneck still depends on the model, input shape, and deployment.
Recommendation traffic illustrates why request volume must be derived from application behavior. A page load, scroll, or click can trigger ranking or retrieval, so one browsing session can produce many inference requests. A language-model application may likewise issue several model calls for one user action or run background tasks without an explicit query. Capacity planning therefore counts the model work triggered by each interaction rather than treating user count as request rate.
Workload structure also determines which techniques can help. Embedding sharding and lookup locality address large recommendation models (Naumov et al. 2019; Gupta et al. 2020), and feature store architectures must deliver the inputs a model expects within its latency budget, while continuous batching and KV cache management address variable-length autoregressive work. Text-to-image systems such as DALL-E add multimodal serving demands (Ramesh et al. 2021) whose volume and latency targets remain product-specific.

Tuning a replica’s kernels or cache allocator cannot fix tail latency when requests are waiting inside a router or starving behind a noisy neighbor on a shared cluster. To locate the right control, serving optimizations organize into a four-level serving hierarchy ordered by scope, where each level owns a distinct bottleneck and measurement boundary. The request level follows one request through preprocessing, batch-formation waiting, response caching, and model execution, where the target is the latency a user sees. The replica level looks inside one model instance, where utilization, KV-cache memory management, and kernel efficiency set the throughput it can deliver before it saturates. The service level turns many replicas of the same model into aggregate capacity through load balancing, request routing, and autoscaling. The platform level decides, across services and tenants, whether a shared serving fleet stays efficient without allowing one workload to degrade another.
Each level supplies a different measurement boundary. Table 5 associates request latency, replica throughput, aggregate service capacity, and cross-tenant efficiency with the controls most directly responsible for them. Their effects still cross boundaries: batching can increase replica throughput while adding request delay, and replica placement can change both communication cost and service capacity. The hierarchy helps locate the decision without treating its metric in isolation. In C³ terms, batching and cache management improve compute reuse, sharding introduces communication, and routing, isolation, and autoscaling coordinate the resources that make those gains usable.

The serving decisions that follow climb the hierarchy from the request level to the platform level. Batching sets how long each request waits to share execution. KV-cache layout, decode-time policies, and adapter state decide how many requests a replica can hold. The split between prefill and decode decides whether a new prompt and the streams already decoding share a worker or separate pools. Weight quantization and model sharding change the replica’s memory and compute budget. Routing, isolation, autoscaling, and global placement then turn replicas into a service and a platform. Precision enters every capacity calculation that follows through two separate budgets: reducing weight precision frees resident memory, whereas reducing KV precision lowers the memory required per active sequence. Section 10.9 compares the serving trade-offs of these representation choices before sharding divides a replica across devices.
