A stream of hundreds of disparate chat requests arrives at an inference server every second. Processing them one by one leaves much of the GPU idle, starved for work between small decode steps. Waiting to gather a large static batch forces the first request in line to endure unacceptable latency. Batching at scale therefore needs policies that group requests as they arrive without violating tail-latency deadlines.
Processing multiple requests together shares weight reads and kernel launch overhead across more useful work. The resulting service-rate gain can reduce queueing, but waiting to form a batch adds delay; the net effect on request latency depends on load. Single-machine serving applies this insight through dynamic batching, which collects requests within a time window before processing them together.
At scale, batching must also account for workload structure. A policy suited to uniform vision inputs can leave slots unused during variable-length generation, while grouping sparse embedding lookups solves a different problem from batching dense execution. The unit of reusable work determines which policy is worth evaluating. The strategies below proceed in order of mechanism rather than traffic share: vision (request batching), LLMs (iteration-level batching with KV state), and recommendation (feature-parallel batching over distributed embeddings), even though recommendation often dominates consumer inference volume (section 10.5.1).


Holding arriving requests until a fixed batch fills forces early arrivals to wait and pads shorter inputs with wasted work, whereas running every request immediately leaves later arrivals queued behind one-request passes that underuse the GPU. Batching efficiency depends on how computation scales with batch size relative to memory and communication constraints, and the execution timeline in figure 4 separates waiting to form a batch from waiting for the accelerator to become available. Unbatched serving adds no batch-formation delay, but later requests can still queue behind earlier forward passes. Static batching consolidates all four illustrated requests into one pass, adding formation delay and padding to accommodate different input lengths. Dynamic batching closes formation windows at fixed time intervals (\(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\)), producing two passes with two requests each in this example. The window limits intentional formation delay; it does not bound total queueing when ready batches arrive faster than the server can execute them.







Figure 4: Batching Strategies Compared: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay.



In vision models processing fixed-size images, arithmetic work grows roughly in proportion to batch size while requests share the weights, so larger batches improve weight reuse until compute, memory, or the latency budget binds. The largest feasible batch is not necessarily the best interactive operating point. By contrast, in LLMs during the decode phase, small batches perform little computation per byte of active weights loaded, so memory bandwidth binds. Larger batches raise arithmetic intensity until compute, KV-cache traffic, or the latency budget limits further gains. Small-batch decode therefore does not inherit a new accelerator generation’s headline compute improvement. From Volta to Blackwell, peak compute climbs 18× while memory bandwidth expands by only 8.9×, and figure 5 shows generation throughput tracking the slower curve whenever weight streaming dominates at small batch sizes.


↩︎ The accelerator trajectory behind this divergence, with compute outpacing memory bandwidth from one generation to the next, is established in Evolution of GPU architectures.
Recommendation systems shift the bottleneck again: sparse embedding lookup can limit throughput before dense computation does. Grouping sparse accesses improves locality and distributes lookup work across shards, while batching the dense stages improves matrix multiplication throughput. The serving policy must therefore account for both stages and the communication between them rather than infer the bottleneck from the model category alone.














Figure 5: Decode Inherits the Bandwidth Deficit: Peak compute and memory bandwidth for four accelerator generations, normalized to the V100. Compute rises 18× against bandwidth’s 8.9×. In weight-bandwidth-bound decode, each iteration loads the active weights and reuses them across its output tokens; at fixed batch size, bandwidth growth constrains the gain. These hardware ratios are not measured workload speedups. Specifications are dense peak rates and bandwidths from the vendor datasheets recorded in the chapter’s data file.






Raising batch size to maximize a replica’s throughput stretches each batch’s execution time and holds arriving requests in a formation queue until the service violates its latency SLO. Batch size is the single-replica control knob that moves a workload along the roofline by reusing each weight read across more requests, which raises arithmetic intensity. At fleet scale, the same knob also sets how long arriving work waits and how much request state the replica must hold. A model relating batch size \((\BatchSize)\), batch service time \((\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize))\), and batched service rate \((\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize))\) exposes that trade-off; selecting an operating point also requires the arrival pattern, memory budget, and latency target.


↪ The roofline bound, and why batch-one decode sits far below the ridge point, are collected for reference in The roofline bound.
The first model isolates batch execution. Here \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) is the service time once a batch begins execution; it excludes queueing and batch formation. Keeping the measurement boundary explicit prevents an execution-time improvement from being mistaken for an end-to-end SLO guarantee.
The service-time equation decomposes batch execution time into fixed overheads (kernel launch, memory loading) and variable costs (compute per sample):
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = \BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime\]
In this formulation, \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) captures costs paid once per batch, such as loading weights from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and kernel launch latency, while \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) denotes the marginal cost of adding one request, such as the compute time for that sample. Treating these terms as constants is a local approximation for a fixed workload and execution regime. Kernel changes, cache traffic, and resource saturation can alter the measured curve as batch size grows.
The throughput equation describes the system’s capacity:
\[\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)} = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime}\]
The resulting batching efficiency curve shows diminishing returns from amortizing overhead. For small batch sizes (\(\BatchSize\)), \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) dominates service time, so increasing \(\BatchSize\) shares that cost and raises throughput substantially. As \(\BatchSize\) grows, the relative contribution of \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) shrinks and the model approaches its asymptotic rate \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\). This limit alone does not identify whether compute or bandwidth binds on the actual device. The knee of the curve, where fixed and variable costs become comparable, is a useful candidate operating point. It is not an optimum independent of the service contract; a tight latency budget may require a smaller batch, while a throughput-oriented workload may benefit from a larger one.



Throughput saturates toward \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\); past the knee, each larger batch buys less.
The execution-only feasibility condition is \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) \le \text{SLO}\). In a live service, execution receives only the budget remaining after routing, queueing, batch formation, and response delivery. The batch-size decision must therefore use that remaining budget rather than consume the full SLO. Comparing a vision workload with a relatively high \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) against an LLM decode workload with a high \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) from weight loading shows how those measured costs shift the efficiency knee (notebook 10.2).

Napkin Math 10.2: The batching efficiency curveProblem: An engineer optimizes two services: a vision model (ResNet) and an LLM (70B). At what batch size does each hit the “knee” of its efficiency curve?
Math: The knee occurs where the variable compute cost \((\BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime)\) starts to exceed the fixed overhead \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime)\).

Vision Model \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime= 2\text{ ms}, \MarginalRequestServiceTime= 1\text{ ms})\):

Knee: \(\BatchSize\approx 2\text{ ms}/1\text{ ms} =\) 2.
Result: This simplified latency model reaches its first overhead-amortization knee at a small batch. It does not locate hardware saturation; measuring throughput at larger batches tests whether additional concurrency still helps.

LLM Decode \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime= 40\text{ ms}, \MarginalRequestServiceTime= 0.5\text{ ms})\):

Knee: \(\BatchSize\approx 40\text{ ms}/0.5\text{ ms} =\) 80.
Result: The larger fixed cost in this decode example moves the overhead-amortization knee to a larger batch.
Where 0.5 ms comes from: It is an assumed marginal cost per added sequence, dominated by reading that sequence’s own KV state at a moderate context length. Unlike the weight stream, that read is private to each sequence, so it grows with batch size instead of being shared.
Where 40 ms comes from: It is roughly the time to stream the model’s 140 GB of FP16 weights through one H100’s 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, the aggregate weight traffic of one decode step expressed in single-device time. No single H100 holds those weights. The reference replica of Where Fleet Capacity Goes spreads them over eight GPUs, which divides both \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) and \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) by the tensor-parallel degree and leaves their ratio, and therefore the knee, unchanged.


Systems insight: Because streaming the weights is the dominant per-step cost of decode, the system has not reached the efficiency knee until batch size 80. The knee depends on the ratio of fixed to per-request cost, not on how many devices share them, which is why sharing weight reads across concurrent requests matters at every replica size. The batch a service actually runs also depends on context length, cache capacity, kernel efficiency, and the latency target; continuous batching and paged allocation are the mechanisms that let a replica reach it.


While the analytical batching model locates the knee from each model class’s ratio of fixed to per-request cost (table 9), production serving stacks measure the resulting throughput-latency frontier directly. The open InferenceX benchmark serves DeepSeek-R1, a mixture-of-experts reasoning model, with 1,024-token prompts and 1,024-token responses on each accelerator across many combinations of serving framework, parallelism, and concurrency (SemiAnalysis 2026). For every configuration it records the output tokens per second each user receives, called interactivity (the reciprocal of TPOT), and the output tokens per second each GPU delivers across all users. Figure 6 plots 325 such configurations at FP8 precision and traces, for each accelerator, the frontier of configurations that no other configuration beats on both rates. Every frontier falls as interactivity rises, because a faster stream per user permits fewer concurrent sequences per decode step. The best B200 configuration delivers about 6,300 output tokens per second per GPU when each user receives about 13 tokens per second. It delivers about 210 when each user must receive at least 100, a 30× difference in per-GPU output paid for faster streams. The interactivity target alone moves per-GPU output by that much, so it must be fixed before any two throughput figures can be compared.
The same frontiers separate hardware generations by more than their datasheets do. At 50 tokens per second per user, the best measured H100 configuration delivers about 80 output tokens per second per GPU and the best GB200 NVL72 configuration about 3,650, a 44× difference. Yet the peak dense FP8 rate of a GB200 GPU is only about 2.3× that of an H100. The benchmark does not apportion the gap, but the candidates lie mostly beyond peak arithmetic, in memory bandwidth and capacity per GPU, a 72-GPU NVLink domain that keeps experts and KV state off slower networks, and platform-tuned serving software. A throughput figure quoted without its latency target therefore says little about either system.

Translating the batch-level equations into system-wide capacity planning requires Little’s law,4 a classical result from queuing theory that relates concurrency, throughput, and latency in any stable system. Whereas \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) prices one replica’s execution batch, Little’s law connects the external arrival rate and mean request time in system to the total number of requests concurrently in flight across the fleet.
4 Little’s law: The identity holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival or service distribution, which is why it survives the bursty, variable-length traffic of inference. Because it relates averages, it bounds neither maximum service capacity nor tail latency.
↩︎ The M/G/1 waiting-time model, in which utilization and service-time variability multiply queueing delay, is established in Scheduling Objectives and Their Conflicts.


Theorem 10.1: Little's law for inferenceConcept: In any stable queuing system, the average number of requests in the system \((\RequestConcurrency)\) equals the arrival rate \((\ArrivalRate)\) multiplied by the average time a request spends in the system \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\).
\[ \RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \]
Application: Concurrency planning. This idealized service counts only batch formation, queueing, and execution in its end-to-end latency; routing and response delivery add no delay. Assume the mean latency given below and full execution batches of the stated size. A percentile SLO cannot generally be substituted for the mean in Little’s law.

Target Throughput \((\ArrivalRate)\): 1,000 requests/sec
Assumed mean latency \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\): 100 ms (0.1 s)

Mean in-flight work \((\RequestConcurrency)\): \(1000 \times 0.1 =\) 100 concurrent requests
Capacity planning: If a single GPU replica executes batches of 8 in 80 ms, and the fleet targets at most 80 percent mean service utilization:

Replica throughput \(=\) \(8/0.08 =\) 100 req/s
Throughput-only lower bound \(=\) \(\lceil 1000/100\rceil =\) 10 replicas
Illustrative headroom-sized replica count \(=\) \(\lceil 1000/(0.8 \times 100)\rceil =\) 13 replicas

Verification: Maximum executing positions \(=\) \(13\text{ replicas} \times 8\text{ batch positions} =\) 104. These positions do not include requests waiting for execution or batch formation. Under the assumed fixed batch service time, Little’s law on the execution boundary gives 80 requests executing on average; the remaining 20 of the assumed mean in-flight population are waiting or accumulating. The throughput-only lower bound would run at the stability boundary; the utilization-sized candidate runs at about 76.9 percent service utilization. The assumed mean latency still needs validation, and this arithmetic does not prove a percentile latency SLO; that requires an arrival/service model or a measured load test.


This stability boundary can be measured faithfully only when the load generator preserves the workload claim. The measurement contract of The measurement contract guards against load that eases off while the replica stalls. A serving measurement therefore holds a fixed external arrival process rather than a fixed concurrency, because response-paced generation can reduce arrivals during a stall and make the system appear to have more headroom than it does. The distinction between throughput capacity and latency capacity is exactly what queuing theory formalizes.


↪ The mean queuing delay under a batched M/G/1 surrogate, and how utilization headroom and batch size trade against latency, is developed in Queuing theory for batched inference.



Static batching, which waits until exactly \(\BatchSize\) requests arrive before launching a forward pass, leaves early requests stranded during traffic lulls until their latency budgets expire. Vision models otherwise present the simplest batching case: preprocessed inputs share a fixed tensor shape and execute in a predictable time, so single-machine batching applies directly and fleet scale adds only the question of where batches form.
Dynamic batching collects requests for a maximum time window \(\BatchingWindow\) or until reaching maximum batch size \(\MaxBatchSize\), whichever occurs first. For Poisson arrivals with rate \(\ArrivalRate\), equation 3 organizes expected request latency into queueing, formation, and execution contributions:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestTimeInSystem] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueingLatency] + \BatchFormationDelay + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) \tag{3}\]
where \(\mathbb{E}[\QueueingLatency]\) is the expected queuing delay, \(\BatchFormationDelay\) represents mean batch formation delay (up to \(\BatchingWindow\)), and \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) represents mean inference time over the realized batch sizes \(\BatchSize\). Queueing here excludes time already counted as batch formation. The two waiting terms respond differently to load. Under Poisson arrivals the mean inter-arrival gap is \(1/\ArrivalRate\), so a higher arrival rate fills a batch faster and reduces formation delay. Queueing for a busy replica can nevertheless grow as arrival rate approaches service capacity; the batching timeout does not cap that queueing delay. Spending a small slice of the latency budget on batch formation can multiply per-GPU capacity while keeping end-to-end latency within target (example 10.1).

Example 10.1: Dynamic batching for ResNet-50Scenario: A vision classification service receives requests at 5,000 QPS with a 50 ms p99 latency SLO across 10 replicas, so each replica sees 500 QPS. One image served alone takes 5 ms. The scenario assumes that a batch of about 5 images executes in 8 ms and a batch of about 10 in 12 ms, because a batch shares weight reads and kernel launches across its images.
Diagnosis: Each utilization below is the per-replica arrival rate multiplied by the service time one request consumes. Option A serves every image alone, which overloads the replica (\(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate \times \BatchServiceTime = 500 \times 0.005 = 2.5\) utilization). Option B holds a 10 ms batching window, which collects about 5 requests (arrival rate \(\times\) window). Their batch runs in 8 ms, so each request consumes 1.6 ms of execution, and utilization falls to \(\ServingUtilization = 500 \times 0.0016 = 0.8\). The wider 20 ms window of Option C collects about 10 requests whose batch runs in 12 ms, or 1.2 ms each, reaching \(\ServingUtilization = 500 \times 0.0012 = 0.6\) and a further 33 percent of per-replica capacity. Both options leave service headroom. Whether they also meet the p99 SLO depends on the window plus the queueing delay each utilization implies under the service’s real arrival pattern, which utilization alone does not determine.
Systems lesson: Dynamic batching is effective when the latency budget has unused slack. The serving policy converts latency headroom into throughput, but requires careful tuning to prevent SLO violations.




↪ A procedure for this tuning, from fitting the service-time model to checking the p99 target, is developed in Batch size selection framework given an SLO.
At scale with multiple replicas, batch formation can occur either at individual replicas or at a centralized batching layer. Replica-local batching has each replica independently form batches from its assigned traffic. This avoids a shared batching stage, but splitting a light arrival stream among many replicas can leave each waiting to fill its batch. Centralized batching pools arrivals before dispatching formed batches, potentially shortening formation waits, at the cost of an additional network hop and a shared scheduling bottleneck. Load balancing helps local batching, but equal request counts do not guarantee equal work or reproduce the formation benefit of pooling arrivals. The choice depends on arrival density, request compatibility, and replica service times.



When a request-level batch locks its membership until the longest sequence finishes, a short reply that ends after 10 tokens leaves its slot stranded for the remaining 90 steps of a 100-token neighbor. Queued requests starve while the GPU still streams the full model weights on every step. The autoregressive bottleneck (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)) makes that wasted slot expensive: at small batch sizes, decode is typically bandwidth-bound because each iteration streams active model weights while generating only one token per sequence. Batching shares those weight reads across concurrent requests, and as the batch grows, compute or KV-cache traffic can become the binding constraint, so bandwidth-bound decode is an operating regime rather than a property of every serving configuration.

Definition 10.1: Continuous batching
Continuous batching is a serving strategy that updates batch membership at iteration boundaries, allowing new requests to enter without waiting for every request in the original batch to finish.

Significance: It reduces padding waste by refilling completed slots at iteration boundaries. Throughput gains require waiting requests, available KV-cache capacity, and scheduling overhead small enough to preserve the benefit.
Distinction: Unlike static or dynamic batching (which group requests at the request level), continuous batching operates at the iteration level, reshaping the active batch between decode iterations.
Common pitfall: Continuous admission must coordinate scheduling with KV-state ownership and lifetime. A Dynamic Memory Manager such as PagedAttention improves space utilization, but paging is not required: an implementation can recycle fixed-capacity request slots, at the cost of unused reserved space.



The Orca system (Yu et al. 2022) removed the request-level barrier by updating membership at iteration boundaries to enable slot reuse. Once a request completes, another can enter if its prompt has been processed and sufficient cache capacity is available. The scheduler must account for that preparation rather than treat every replacement as a decode-only operation.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Consider a fixed-width batch of 8 sequences. If one sequence completes after 10 tokens while others require 100 tokens, its slot contributes no useful output for 90 iterations. If the kernel continues executing padded work for that slot, the fraction of wasted compute attributable to it is:
\[\text{Wasted compute} = \frac{(100 - 10) \times 1}{100 \times 8} = 11.25\%\]
The waste grows with the spread of output lengths, a dependence that section 10.6.5 turns into a formula. A kernel that skips completed sequences avoids their padded arithmetic, but a fixed-membership policy still prevents waiting requests from using the vacated capacity. Algorithm 1 states the continuous-batching scheduler as a decode loop with a prefilled waiting queue. Completed requests release their pages in this simplified policy, eligible waiting requests enter freed slots, and the next kernel runs over the updated active set. For Archetype A workloads (GPT-4/Llama-3), refilling slots lets more useful tokens share each weight read. The gain comes from reusing transferred weights, not merely from saturating bandwidth, which a smaller batch may already do.


↩︎ Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the autoregressive transformer whose serving must stream billions of weights for every generated token, is established in Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3).

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Continuous batching decode scheduler}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require prefilled waiting queue $Q$; active set $A$; KV-cache page allocator; active-token capacity $C_{\text{tok}}$; batched decode kernel
\Ensure generated tokens for completed requests; a continually refreshed active batch
\While{the service is running}
    \State admit requests from $Q$ while capacity and free KV-cache pages remain; allocate state, append to $A$
    \State reserve pages for the next decode step; preempt requests that do not fit
    \State run one batched decode kernel over the remaining sequences in $A$
    \State append each sampled token; extend its KV-cache pages
    \State remove completed or length-limited sequences from $A$; return their pages to the allocator
    \If{HBM pressure exceeds the policy threshold}
        \State move low-priority sequences from $A$ to the paused set; page their KV-cache to CPU DRAM
    \EndIf
    \State fill freed capacity from $Q$, or resume paused sequences whose pages now fit
\EndWhile
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(Q\)

Admitting, completing, and refilling slots on every iteration lets waiting work use capacity released before the longest sequence finishes. The illustrated preemption path adds HBM-to-CPU-DRAM transfers under memory pressure, so recovered capacity must repay both scheduling and state-movement costs. Counted in slot-iterations (figure 7), fixed membership leaves only 20 of 32 productive, while continuous admission fills all 32 under the illustrated arrival and capacity assumptions. Prefill and decode cells do not necessarily take equal time. Slot occupancy therefore measures the opportunity; the realized throughput gain depends on how much longer the inserted prefill cells take than the decode steps they share an iteration with.







Figure 7: Static vs. Continuous Batching: In static batching (a), completed slots cannot be reused until the longest request finishes, although completed responses may already be released. Continuous batching (b) admits waiting requests into freed slots at iteration boundaries, starting each with a prefill step. Over the eight iterations shown, 20 of 32 slot-iterations do useful work under static batching and all 32 under continuous batching; the hatched idle slots are the capacity recovered when arrivals and cache capacity permit.






In a static batch whose output lengths vary widely, a single long response holds every completed slot idle until its final token, wasting a growing share of the batch’s sequence-iterations as length variance rises. Continuous batching recovers that stranded capacity by refilling vacated slots at iteration boundaries (figure 7). Counting useful and unused sequence-iterations in a fixed batch bounds the recoverable opportunity; arrivals, KV-cache admission, prefill scheduling, and scheduler overhead determine how much of that ceiling a live replica actually captures.


The 11.25 percent example of one early-finishing sequence generalizes to any mix of output lengths. For this waste model, traditional batching (also called static batching) retains a fixed batch width through all decode iterations until the longest sequence completes. Assume equal compute cost per sequence-iteration, including padded work for completed requests. For batch size \(\BatchSize\) with output lengths \(\{\RequestOutputLength_1, \RequestOutputLength_2, ..., \RequestOutputLength_{\BatchSize}\}\), the total compute performed under those assumptions is:
\[\StaticBatchingOperations= \BatchSize\times \BatchMaxOutputLength\times \SequenceIterationOperations\]
where \(\BatchMaxOutputLength= \max_i(\RequestOutputLength_i)\) and \(\SequenceIterationOperations\) is the compute cost per decode iteration per sequence. However, the useful compute is only:
\[\UsefulModelFlops = \sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \RequestOutputLength_i \times \SequenceIterationOperations\]
Equation 4 defines the waste ratio that quantifies the inefficiency:
\[\PaddingWasteFraction= 1 - \frac{\UsefulModelFlops}{\StaticBatchingOperations} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \RequestOutputLength_i}{\BatchSize\times \BatchMaxOutputLength} = 1 - \frac{\BatchMeanOutputLength}{\BatchMaxOutputLength} \tag{4}\]
where \(\BatchMeanOutputLength\) is the mean output sequence length. Waste therefore depends entirely on the ratio of mean to maximum output length within the batch. For uniform output lengths \((\BatchMeanOutputLength= \BatchMaxOutputLength)\), waste is zero. For highly variable lengths, waste can exceed 50 percent.

Result: Under fixed membership, only 500 of the 800 sequence-iterations do useful work. Continuous admission hands the rest to R5, R6, and R7, which start generating at iterations 50, 100, and 150 instead of waiting for a new batch, so the same 200 iterations now advance seven requests rather than four. Releasing each response on completion separately reduces the original requests’ average latency by 37.5 percent, numerically matching the unused-slot ratio, and static batching that released responses on completion would obtain the same original-request latencies.
Systems insight: Response release and slot reuse are separate decisions. Removing a response barrier helps the requests already in the batch; only continuous admission recovers the stranded iteration capacity shown in figure 7, and that recovered capacity is what raises a replica’s throughput.





The continuous-batching analysis relates recoverable slot capacity to the gap between a batch’s longest and average output lengths. Let \(\text{CV} = \OutputLengthStandardDeviation/ \WorkloadMeanOutputLength\) be the coefficient of variation of output lengths. For the idealized fixed-width schedule, suppose the longest request in a batch is roughly \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) standard deviations above the mean. The factor \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) is an assumption about the batch rather than a property of the workload, because a larger batch draws more samples and pushes its maximum further into the tail. With immediate refill and unchanged iteration time, the corresponding capacity ratio is:
\[\text{Improvement} \approx \frac{\BatchMaxOutputLength}{\BatchMeanOutputLength} = \frac{\WorkloadMeanOutputLength+ \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\OutputLengthStandardDeviation}{\WorkloadMeanOutputLength} = 1 + \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\cdot \text{CV}\]
where \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) specifies how far the batch maximum lies above the mean, so the expression is a scenario ceiling on the opportunity from filling otherwise unused slots; scheduler overhead, KV-cache pressure, and refill gaps reduce the recovered fraction. In the table that follows, the CV and \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) columns are inputs, the speedup column is an assumed realized fraction held below the \(1 + \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\cdot \text{CV}\) ceiling, and the waste column restates that speedup through \(\text{speedup} \approx 1/(1 - \EffectiveWasteFraction)\). Neither column is a measurement. Together they show how much of the ceiling a scheduler must recover to reach a given gain, which is the quantity a load test should measure. Continuous batching is most valuable when output lengths are unpredictable, mixed workload types share the same cluster, request volume is high enough to refill vacated slots, and latency SLOs make early completion valuable. It provides minimal benefit when output lengths are uniform, as in classification or embedding generation, when batch sizes are too small for slot reuse to matter, or when request volume is too low to refill vacated slots.
Because arrivals, KV-cache admission, prefill scheduling, and scheduler overhead decide how much vacated capacity is actually recovered, serving teams must compare policies under the same arrival trace, latency objective, and memory budget. The published vLLM system, which pairs iteration-level admission with paged KV allocation, reports 2–4\(\times\) higher throughput at comparable latency than FasterTransformer and Orca on its evaluated workloads (Kwon et al. 2023). That figure compares whole systems rather than isolating slot reuse, because paged allocation also permits larger active batches.



The same variability that makes continuous batching valuable also makes it harder to operate. Memory management must support overlapping request lifetimes. Fixed-membership batching can reserve cache regions when a batch forms and release them together, whereas continuous admission must track which request owns each region and when it becomes reusable, either through fixed-capacity slots that retain unused reservations or through paging with its block tables. Kernels must also handle variable-length sequences and changing batch membership, often by packing short sequences under shared attention masks.
Scheduler work moves into the decode loop as well. A fixed-membership policy checks once per batch whether it is full or its timeout has expired, while continuous admission tracks completions, free cache capacity, and eligible waiting requests at every iteration boundary. That work must stay small relative to a decode step or it erodes the throughput that slot reuse recovers, so engines keep the per-iteration path short and prepare the next iteration’s batch on the host while the accelerator executes the current one. Continuous batching therefore buys its throughput gain with implementation and operating cost, weighed dimension by dimension in table 8.

Even with continuous batching available, diagnosing tail latency anomalies requires systematic investigation across the system stack. A constructed p99 regression shows how to investigate infrastructure, execution, and serving layers. Its latency observations and mitigation outcome are scenario assumptions; only the transfer-time estimates are computed from payload and bandwidth.

Example 10.2: Debugging high p99 latencyScenario: An LLM serving system shows high tail latency: p50 = 100 ms and p95 = 180 ms maintain SLO, but p99 spikes to \(\TailRequestLatency =\) 500 ms against a 200 ms target despite a monitored GPU utilization of 85 percent.
Diagnosis: The system runs across 4 A100 GPUs linked via PCIe Gen4 (32 GB/s per GPU) rather than NVLink. For a 100 MB payload, the bandwidth-only transfer estimate is \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) \approx\) 3.1 ms over PCIe versus 0.17 ms over NVLink. Collective startup, topology, and contention can add time. The service still runs an older request-level batching server rather than an iteration-level engine, with max batch size 32 and timeout 50 ms, so a batch holds its members until its longest generation finishes. The scenario assumes that 5 percent of batches experience head-of-line queuing delay \(\QueueingLatency\) as short requests wait behind long generations.
Systems lesson: The latency distribution motivates tracing both candidates, because a transfer paid by every request also amplifies tail queueing near saturation. In this scenario, traces showing stable transfer times too small to explain the additional delay, together with short requests waiting behind long generations, identify the fixed-membership barrier as the immediate cause. Continuous admission removes that barrier; prefill scheduling, cache capacity, and other waits still require measurement. Until the server can be replaced, the following policy reduces output-length variation within request-level batches:

Request classification: Classify requests by expected output length (short: under 50 tokens, medium: 50 to 200 tokens, long: over 200 tokens)
Differentiated batching: Limit short batches to 8, medium to 16, long to 32

Grouping requests by expected length shrinks the spread of output lengths inside each batch, which is the quantity equation 4 says drives both waste and waiting. The scenario assumes a post-mitigation p99 latency of \(\TailRequestLatency =\) 185 ms; a real service confirms it by replaying the same arrival workload and measuring the tail.






A single recommendation request may issue thousands of sparse lookups across embedding tables holding billions of entries before the dense ranking head can score a candidate. Grouping requests solely at the dense MLP therefore leaves the service bottlenecked on scattered memory reads and cross-server transfers. While fixed-shape vision inputs allow simple request grouping and autoregressive generation pairs iteration-level admission with KV-cache management (and with prefill-decode scheduling in section 10.8), recommendation systems must also batch around the placement of sparse state. Sparse embedding lookups can dominate memory access and communication in an embedding-heavy workload even when dense matrix multiplications account for much of the arithmetic. Grouping those accesses by feature type and destination—feature-parallel batching—improves lookup locality at each shard, complementing request batching in the dense stages.
Recommendation batching starts by grouping work around embedding locality rather than request shape. An incoming request splits across user, item, and context feature types to query sharded embedding tables concurrently, after which a gather barrier concatenates the retrieved representations for the dense MLP ranking head (figure 8).







Figure 8: Feature-Parallel Batching Pipeline: Requests are batched by feature type (Users, Items, Context) and dispatched to specialized embedding servers in parallel. The retrieved embeddings are then concatenated and processed by the dense ranking head. This architecture enables scaling to trillions of parameters by decoupling embedding storage from dense compute.



The sparse lookup path and the dense feature path can execute concurrently before feature interaction combines their representations and a ranking head produces final scores. The interaction stage must wait for its required inputs, which puts the slowest embedding shard on the request’s critical path.
When sparse embedding access dominates latency, feature-parallel batching groups lookups by feature type and destination across requests. Each embedding server then handles the lookups for its shard across the whole batch. This turns feature sharding into a serving strategy rather than a storage detail, while preserving the association needed to reconstruct each request for ranking:
Request 1: [user_id_1, item_ids_1, context_1]
Request 2: [user_id_2, item_ids_2, context_2]
Request 3: [user_id_3, item_ids_3, context_3]

Feature-parallel view:
User embeddings:  [lookup(user_1), lookup(user_2), lookup(user_3)]  → parallel
Item embeddings:  [lookup(items_1), lookup(items_2), lookup(items_3)]  → parallel
Context features: [process(ctx_1), process(ctx_2), process(ctx_3)]  → parallel

Then: Combine features per request for ranking

Example 10.3: RecSys batching at hyperscaleScenario: A hyperscale recommendation service handles 10 million QPS, querying 5,000 embedding lookups per request across 1,000 shards.
Diagnosis: The assumed distribution of requests requires 50 million lookups/sec per shard. That rate is the capacity target each shard’s lookup service must sustain. Accumulating requests over a 1 ms window forms batches of 50K lookups per shard, creating an opportunity to deduplicate, reorder, or coalesce lookups. Batching alone does not make random addresses sequential.
Systems lesson: Shard-level batching exploits sparse feature locality, but its benefit depends on cache hits, access distribution, and the amount of work each shard receives. The formation window spends part of the 5.2 ms end-to-end latency budget; measured lookup and communication times must fit in what remains alongside the dense stages.





Holding a live audio chunk or robot control frame in a batching queue until a large batch fills stalls transcription and breaks closed-loop control. Speech recognition, video analysis, and robotics process an ongoing sequence of observations under tight per-frame deadlines, so batching across ready streams helps only while the added waiting time fits each frame’s slack.
Streaming inference processes inputs incrementally rather than waiting for the complete recording or interaction. Illustrative input cadences include 10–20 ms audio chunks for speech recognition, 30–60 FPS video, and 100–1000 Hz sensor or control updates in robotics. These rates specify how often work arrives, not a universal inference deadline. Buffering, frame selection, and batching must follow the application’s latency and freshness requirements.
A streaming service must sustain the arrival rate while meeting the latency budget for each accepted input. The end-to-end processing path includes:
\[\StreamingEndToEndLatency= \InputCaptureTime+ \TransferTimeForPayload+ \InferenceLatency + \ResultActionTime\]
where the sum must fit the end-to-end latency budget. A pipelined implementation must also sustain the input arrival rate; its slowest stage must process frames at least as quickly as they arrive. The end-to-end budget may span several frame intervals. A speech pipeline with 20 ms frames and a 100 ms budget can hold at most five frames of delay, so batching ready frames from independent streams helps only while the added waiting and service time fit that slack.



A batching window and maximum batch size tuned for daytime peak traffic either hold requests waiting too long when traffic drops at night or cap throughput too early when a flash crowd arrives. Because fixed batching parameters break as arrival rates and request mixes shift, production systems adapt their batching windows and size limits to live conditions.
Traffic-adaptive batching adjusts the batch window based on arrival rate:
\[\BatchingWindow= \min\left(\MaxBatchingWindow, \frac{\TargetBatchSize}{\ArrivalRate}\right)\]
When traffic is high, the window shrinks because the target batch size fills quickly. When traffic is low, the window extends but is capped to bound batch-formation delay. This cap does not bound the separate wait for a busy replica.
SLO-adaptive batching takes a complementary approach, monitoring latency percentiles and adjusting parameters aggressively:
if P99_latency > 0.9 * SLO:
    reduce B_max by 20%
    reduce T_window by 20%
elif P99_latency < 0.5 * SLO:
    increase B_max by 10%
    increase T_window by 10%
The feedback loop is a tuning heuristic, not a guarantee of latency headroom. Reducing batch size can shorten execution while also reducing service capacity and increasing queueing under heavy load. Feedback delay and noisy percentile estimates can cause oscillation, so the controller must be evaluated with the intended arrival trace and overload policy. Request-aware batching adds another dimension by considering request characteristics. For LLMs, prompt length can guide padding and prefill budgets, while estimated output length can guide grouping. Prediction errors and priority choices must be included when evaluating tail latency.
Production runtimes expose these controls directly. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server, for example, caps batches with max_batch_size, bounds formation waiting with max_queue_delay_microseconds, and accepts preferred_batch_size values for particularly efficient execution profiles; priority queues and overload policy remain separate controls. Under a load test, larger batches absorb rising traffic until offered load approaches execution capacity, after which completions fall below arrivals and the growing queue needs an admission or scaling response rather than a larger batch.
The batching strategies to this point focus on scheduling work under a chosen request budget. Output length remains uncertain, but the service can already cap generation. Reasoning-heavy inference makes that budget an explicit quality-cost decision. The service may allocate additional tokens or candidate evaluations when the expected benefit justifies their latency and capacity costs. This extends the scheduling question from when requests run to how much work they may consume.






Reasoning through 128 serial tokens turns a 100 ms answer into 12.8 s.

Schaeffer, Rylan, Brando Miranda, and Sanmi Koyejo. 2023. “Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 55565–81. https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-2425.
Letting a model emit hundreds of serial chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens or sample dozens of candidate solutions per query can turn a 100 ms interactive reply into a multi-second job that pins KV-cache memory and drains replica capacity. Test-time scaling buys answer quality by spending more compute on each query at inference time, which moves the scaling curve out of the training cluster and into the request path. Every increment of quality bought this way is paid on every request for the lifetime of the deployment, the recurring cost that the serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)) already prices. Whether extra generated tokens, internal CoT steps, or search branches actually improve quality on a given task is an empirical question. Capability studies describe abilities that appear abruptly with scale (Wei et al. 2022), while later analysis finds some apparent jumps to be artifacts of the metric chosen (Schaeffer et al. 2023). A serving budget should therefore rest on measured quality gains for the workload.
From a serving-systems perspective, the relevant shift is the work issued per request. Additional reasoning consumes accelerator time and can extend both latency and KV-cache residency. Increasing test-time work does not necessarily change the bottleneck of each decode step. It instead requires a per-request compute budget, a limit on the generated tokens, candidate solutions, or search steps a request may consume, stated in both latency and capacity. The budget binds when serial reasoning tokens exhaust a request’s latency target, or its share of fleet capacity, before additional reasoning stops improving the answer. A harder task may justify more work, but additional work does not guarantee a correct answer. Adaptive batching decides when requests run together; test-time compute allocation decides how much work each request is allowed to issue.


↩︎ Test-time scaling, the lifecycle regime that spends compute per request rather than per training run, is established alongside the empirical scaling laws in Resource-constrained scaling regimes.

Napkin Math 10.4: Scaling reasoning depthProblem: Calculate the latency impact of a model that uses 128 “Thinking Tokens” to solve a complex math proof vs. a standard answer.

Standard response: 1 token answer = 100 ms.
Reasoning response: 128 of internal search/CoT before the answer.
The latency: 128 \(\times\) 100 ms = 12.8 seconds.

Systems insight: The per-token time is a round figure chosen for easy arithmetic, more than ten times the batch-one decode step of the reference 70B replica in Drilling into the step. What the calculation teaches does not depend on it. Serial reasoning tokens multiply latency by the ratio of reasoning tokens to answer tokens, whatever each token costs, so a faster replica shortens both responses in proportion and leaves the 128-fold expansion intact. Against a direct answer of many tokens rather than one, the ratio shrinks accordingly; against a one-token answer it is largest. A search step that evaluates several candidates in parallel adds compute and KV residency without adding the same serial latency, which is why reasoning budgets must be stated in both time and capacity. At fleet scale, compute allocation weighs the measured quality gain against both the request deadline and the capacity the additional work consumes.


Variable work per request closes the batching story: continuous and adaptive batching handle variation the system observes, while test-time compute is variation the system chooses. A serving policy therefore sets each request’s budget from task difficulty, latency tolerance, and fleet load rather than applying a fixed decode budget to every prompt. With the batching mechanism and the per-request compute budget both defined, the remaining decision is which combination a given workload should run.



Each batching mechanism trades scheduler overhead against slot utilization, so a fixed-shape vision classifier needs a different policy than an autoregressive chat endpoint or a sparse recommendation ranker. Selecting a batching strategy starts by matching the mechanism to the model’s work shape, traffic variance, and where the request path spends its latency budget.

As a full-attention LLM generates a 2,000-word essay, each new token attends to representations of earlier tokens. The KV cache retains the keys and values needed for that attention, with a per-request footprint that grows as generation proceeds. Large contiguous reservations can leave HBM reserved but unused or create gaps too small for another reservation. Admission can then fail even though the stored attention state occupies less than the available capacity.

Definition 10.2: KV cache
KV cache is a per-request LLM inference memory buffer that stores key and value attention tensors for processed prompt and generated tokens. It avoids recomputing those tensors for the prefix; each new query still performs attention against the cached state.

Significance: Compared with recomputing full-prefix attention for each new token, caching changes the attention work from \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength)\) in sequence length for full attention with fixed model dimensions. Retaining that state costs memory proportional to context length and the number of active sequences, potentially exceeding the weight footprint. Section 10.7.1 sizes it per token and per replica.
Distinction: Model weights are shared across requests using the same model, while each sequence has its own logical KV state. Physical storage can still be shared for compatible common prefixes. The scheduler must budget for distinct retained state and its growth, rather than assume every request needs a wholly separate copy or that sharing removes the capacity limit.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that reducing model size proportionally reduces serving memory. In practice, the KV cache dominates HBM at long contexts, so a quantized 70B model can still be capacity-bound at batch sizes the weights alone would easily admit.



Two classes of techniques meet at this boundary. KV-state capacity techniques, such as PagedAttention and prefix caching, decide where attention state lives and how much fragmentation the memory manager tolerates. Decode-time latency techniques, such as speculative decoding, change how much target-model work is needed per emitted token. Speculative decoding is not KV-cache compression; it trades extra draft-model state, target-model verification, and scheduler complexity for lower TPOT under the same memory budget. Capacity accounting and adapter locality then determine how retained KV state and task-specific weights share the remaining memory budget.
Wherever they can, the calculations that follow share one reference replica, the 70B model on one eight-GPU H100 node that fleet efficiency measured as its serving replica, with FP16 weights split eight ways. A few calculations leave it on purpose and say so. The attention layout matters even more, because it sets the bytes cached per token. Grouped-query attention (GQA) with eight KV heads, the layout of the Llama-family 70B models, caches one eighth the state of a 64-head multi-head attention baseline. Each calculation therefore names its hardware and attention layout, and numbers from different calculations compare only after conversion to the same configuration.


↩︎ The reference serving replica, a 70B model on one eight-GPU H100 node, is established in Where Fleet Capacity Goes.


Even when a 4-bit quantized 70B model occupies only 35 GB of an 80 GB H100, admitting a second 128K-token request pushes the combined weight and KV-cache footprint past 80 GB and exhausts HBM before execution resources saturate. Increasing batch size in LLM serving therefore hits the KV cache wall long before compute binds. Figure 9 leaves the reference replica to show the wall on a single H100. It combines an idealized 35 GB weight payload for a quantized 70B model with its full-attention, eight-KV-head GQA state. The budget is a conservative decimal capacity that matches the nameplate label, unlike the registered byte capacity of the node estimator below. A batch of 8 reaches the memory boundary at roughly 17K tokens per sequence; quantization metadata, runtime buffers, and other allocations make the plotted boundary an optimistic sizing limit.














Figure 9: The KV Cache Wall: Total GPU memory usage for a 4-bit quantized 70B model (35 GB weights) on an 80 GB H100. While the model fits easily at small context lengths, the KV cache (sloped lines) eventually consumes all remaining HBM. At 128K context, a batch size of 2 is physically impossible on a single GPU (35 GB + 84 GB exceeds 80 GB), forcing the system to either reduce batch size, change the state representation, or distribute the state across devices.



The visualization explains why weight fit alone does not establish serving capacity. A long-context request can consume nearly all remaining memory in the illustrated configuration, leaving little space for other active sequences. Sharding can add headroom, but its communication cost must be weighed against alternatives such as lower concurrency or a smaller cache representation. The effect of a 128K context depends on the model’s cache dimensions and precision, not on context length alone.
The capacity model behind the figure starts from the cost of one cached token. Every layer stores a key vector and a value vector for each KV head, so with \(\LayerCount\) layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) KV heads, head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), and \(\ElementStorageSize\) bytes per element, equation 5 gives the bytes cached per token:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \times \LayerCount \times \KvHeadCount \times \AttentionHeadDimension \times \ElementStorageSize \tag{5}\]
A replica’s KV footprint is that cost multiplied by every token it holds, \(\KvCacheMemory = \BatchSize \times \SequenceLength \times \KvCacheBytesPerToken\), so the largest admissible batch at context \(\SequenceLength\) is the HBM left after weights and runtime allocations divided by \(\SequenceLength \times \KvCacheBytesPerToken\). Each serving lever acts on a different factor. Grouped-query attention lowers \(\KvHeadCount\), KV quantization lowers \(\ElementStorageSize\), a shorter admitted context lowers \(\SequenceLength\), and paging returns HBM lost to fragmentation without changing the per-token cost. The notebook below turns this budget into an explicit batch-size limit for a production node.

Systems insight: Even with GQA, whose shared key-value heads the 8-head count in this calculation already reflects, each 128K-context request consumes tens of gigabytes of KV state. This configuration therefore admits only a limited number of concurrent long-context requests. PagedAttention can recover allocation waste, but cannot shrink the attention tensors counted here. Increasing concurrency beyond that limit requires changing the memory budget, cache representation, or placement of state.





Preallocating a contiguous HBM slab for every sequence’s maximum permitted length—such as reserving 4,096 tokens for a reply that finishes after 100—strands 60 to 80 percent of KV-cache memory in unused reservations and noncontiguous gaps (Kwon et al. 2023). Traditional contiguous allocation creates two distinct forms of this waste.
Internal fragmentation wastes memory within each allocation. Preallocated memory management reserves room at admission for the prompt plus the permitted output, so a request allowed 4,096 output tokens holds that room even if generation stops after 50. The unused reservation cannot serve another request until it is released. If the output reservation holds 4,096 tokens but the average output uses 100 tokens, 97.6 percent of that output reservation goes unused. Prompt state consumes additional space; this calculation does not give the unused fraction of the combined prompt-and-output allocation.
External fragmentation compounds this problem across allocations. As sequences complete and new ones start, memory becomes fragmented into noncontiguous free blocks. Even with sufficient total free memory, no single block may be large enough for a new maximum-length allocation.
Consider a simplified example with 8 memory slots and maximum sequence length of 4. Fixed-size reservations first create internal fragmentation:
Time 0: Allocate Seq A (slots 0-3), Seq B (slots 4-7)
        [A][A][a][a][B][B][B][b]
        lowercase = reserved but unused
External fragmentation can arise when the allocator also permits smaller contiguous reservations. In a later state, two sequences occupy two slots each, leaving separated gaps:
Time 1: Active Seq C and Seq D leave two 2-slot gaps
        [ ][ ][C][C][ ][ ][D][D]

Time 2: Try to allocate Seq E (needs 4 contiguous slots)
        [ ][ ][C][C][ ][ ][D][D]  <- Total free slots = 4, largest block = 2

Result: enough total free capacity exists, but no contiguous block is large enough.
Under variable sequence lengths, the two effects compound. The vLLM authors measured roughly 60 to 80 percent of reserved KV-cache memory going unused in the prior serving systems they studied, capacity that could otherwise have admitted more sequences (Kwon et al. 2023).



The fragmentation example exposes the allocator failure: enough KV-cache capacity can exist in aggregate while no contiguous block is available for the next sequence. PagedAttention fixes that serving problem by treating KV-cache storage like virtual memory rather than a single preallocated slab (perspective 10.1 and definition 10.3).

Systems Perspective 10.1: Analogy: The inefficient hotelConsider a hotel storage room with 100 lockers. Each guest may bring up to 10 suitcases, but currently every guest has only one suitcase.
Under maximum-size reservation, the manager reserves 10 lockers for each guest. Ten guests exhaust the 100-locker budget while occupying only 10 lockers; the other 90 remain reserved but unused.
With on-demand allocation, each suitcase receives any free locker, and a directory records which lockers belong to each guest. At the current one-suitcase occupancy, the room can accommodate 100 guests. Additional suitcases still consume real capacity; allocation does not remove the storage limit.



Definition 10.3: PagedAttention
PagedAttention is an LLM serving memory management technique that applies virtual memory principles to KV cache allocation, storing attention states in noncontiguous, fixed-size physical blocks.

Significance: It eliminates external fragmentation within the fixed-block pool and bounds internal waste to the unused portion of each sequence’s final block. Recovering capacity from contiguous preallocation permits larger concurrent batches; the throughput gain depends on sequence lengths, demand, and the serving bottleneck.
Distinction: A contiguous allocation must find a sufficiently large free region; supporting later growth may require reserving extra space or relocating the allocation. PagedAttention uses a block table to map logical sequence indices to physical memory pages, allocating blocks as the sequence grows without requiring adjacent free space.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that PagedAttention speeds up individual token math. In reality, it is a capacity optimization: it improves system-level efficiency by allowing larger batch sizes, though it adds a small indirection overhead for the block-table lookups.



In vLLM (Kwon et al. 2023), this paged memory layout divides the KV cache into fixed-size pages, using 16-token blocks in the original paper’s default configuration, and allocates them on demand. Whereas contiguous reservation strands non-adjacent free slots when earlier sequences finish, each sequence’s block table maps logical token pages to scattered physical HBM slots as generation proceeds (figure 10). The block size fixes how many tokens each page holds, so a sequence’s pages need not form one contiguous allocation run.

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.







Figure 10: KV Cache Fragmentation and the PagedAttention Solution: The panels replay the eight-slot example from the text. (a) Contiguous reservation holds the maximum length of four slots per sequence, so the slots Seq A and Seq B never fill sit idle (internal fragmentation). (b) After sequences finish, four slots are free but the largest contiguous gap is two, so Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, cannot be admitted (external fragmentation). (c) PagedAttention maps Seq E’s logical pages through a block table onto any free physical blocks, so the same memory now holds it; only the unfilled tail of its final block remains unused.



Beyond the fragmentation bounds in the definition, paging gives two further capacity advantages. Sequences grow page by page without worst-case preallocation, and common prefixes across requests can share physical pages directly in memory. Together, these properties turn KV cache capacity into a schedulable resource rather than a fixed per-request reservation. The price is indirection, because custom attention kernels must gather keys and values from noncontiguous blocks through each sequence’s block table. Recovered capacity also raises throughput only when demand fills it. Allocator occupancy is not a throughput measurement, since throughput still depends on decode work, prefill interference, and the latency budget.



Recomputing the same 2,000-token system prompt, few-shot example block, or shared document on every arriving request burns prefill compute and fills HBM with identical copies of the same key-value tensors. Because many LLM workloads prepend those shared prefixes across thousands of concurrent queries, prefix caching stores the prefix’s KV-cache blocks once and shares them across compatible requests. Reuse requires the same token prefix and the same model computation, including any task-specific weight adapter and other inputs that affect the cached state. The cache key must distinguish those conditions, and the service must restrict sharing to the permitted users or tenants; matching visible text alone is insufficient. In valid block-level sharing (figure 11), logical tables for independent requests map common prefix tokens to physical blocks B0–B5, skipping their repeated prefill work while storing request-specific suffix state separately.






Figure 11: Prefix Caching via Block Sharing: PagedAttention enables efficient prefix caching by allowing multiple sequences’ block tables to point to the same physical blocks for shared content. In this example, the system prompt is stored in blocks 0–5. Request A and Request B map their first six logical pages to these same physical blocks, storing only their unique suffixes in new blocks. Sharing reduces KV memory and repeated prefill computation for workloads with a common context.



With PagedAttention, prefix caching uses copy-on-write semantics, in which shared blocks stay shared until a request must write into one, and that request then receives a private copy. Three requests that share a system prompt map their first six logical pages to the same physical blocks:
System prompt → Physical blocks [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Request A page table: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 11]  <- shares prefix blocks
Request B page table: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 12, 13, 14]  <- shares prefix blocks
Request C page table: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 15]  <- shares prefix blocks
All three requests reference the same physical blocks for the system prompt, and their distinct suffixes occupy new blocks. If a shared prefix ends partway through a block, appending a different suffix writes into a shared block, which is the copy-on-write case. In a chatbot deployment where thousands of concurrent users share a long system prompt, sharing those prefix blocks cuts total KV-cache memory by roughly four-fifths (notebook 10.6).

Without prefix caching:
