Self-Check: Answer

A team upgrades a cluster serving a 13B LLM from 80 GB GPUs to 140 GB GPUs with identical HBM3 memory bandwidth (3.35 TB/s). At an unchanged small batch and context length, with resident weights and weight-read-dominated decode, why does extra capacity alone not raise the bandwidth-limited throughput ceiling?

Autoregressive decode is strictly compute-bound; increasing memory without adding Tensor Cores leaves execution time unchanged.
Autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound (\(D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}\)); once model weights fit resident in memory, token generation speed is constrained by memory bandwidth, not total memory capacity.
140 GB GPUs automatically disable CUDA graph compilation, adding driver launch latency to every iteration.
The larger memory capacity forces PagedAttention block sizes to shrink from 16 tokens to 2 tokens.

Answer: The correct answer is B. At the same small batch and context length, when weight reads dominate decode and the resident model already fits, extra memory capacity does not increase the bandwidth ceiling. A larger admitted batch can nevertheless raise aggregate token throughput by sharing weight reads across more sequences while execution remains bandwidth-bound. The gain stops when KV traffic, compute, or the latency budget binds; crossing into a compute-bound regime is not required for batching to help.
Learning Objective: Analyze why memory bandwidth, rather than memory capacity, bounds autoregressive decode throughput.
A capacity planner provisions an inference serving fleet for 80% average utilization based on mean daily traffic. Why can traffic spikes exhaust headroom before reactive scaling helps, and what determines whether the P99 SLO is missed?
Answer: Waiting grows sharply as utilization approaches one. At an 80% baseline, a 25% traffic increase reaches exactly 100% utilization, leaving no spare capacity to absorb arrival or service-time variation; a larger sustained increase exceeds capacity. Cold starts can take minutes, so reactive scaling may arrive after latency failures begin. Whether a spike misses the P99 SLO depends on its duration, the arrival and service-time distributions, the waiting budget, and admission policy. Capacity planning therefore needs measured peak behavior and ready headroom alongside average traffic.
Learning Objective: Explain the queuing theory and autoscaling risks of provisioning inference fleets based on average rather than peak-plus-headroom demand.
True or False: Deploying continuous batching alone completely solves all throughput and latency bottlenecks in LLM serving.
Answer: False. Continuous batching reuses slots at iteration boundaries. It does not remove the quadratic attention work of long full-attention prefills, shrink the KV tensors needed by admitted requests, or eliminate communication within sharded replicas. Additional mechanisms are selected for the binding constraint: chunking can limit prefill interference, paging can recover allocation waste, compatible prefix reuse can avoid repeated work, and sharding or replication can supply needed capacity. No fixed combination establishes the service contract without workload measurements.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the scope and limitations of continuous batching within the end-to-end LLM serving pipeline.
True or False: Because each token activates only a small fixed number of experts, raising an MoE model’s expert count from 8 to 256 adds serving capacity at essentially no cost.
Answer: False. Every expert occupies memory whether or not a token selects it, so more experts mean more devices or less KV headroom, and a distributed placement adds dispatch, combine, and imbalance costs. The design is justified only when a matched-quality comparison shows active-compute savings exceeding routing, imbalance, memory, and communication costs.
Learning Objective: Analyze the system-level memory, communication, and load balancing costs of scaling expert counts in MoE models
A team moves its endpoint from INT8 to INT4 weights and INT4 KV cache, doubling tokens per second while held-out perplexity changes by less than 1 percent. What should it conclude before rollout?

The change doubles useful capacity, because perplexity confirms quality is unchanged
The change is safe only if the KV cache returns to FP16, because weight precision never affects quality
Useful capacity has not been established: low-bit formats can degrade rare languages, edge cases, or reasoning while perplexity barely moves, so quality must be evaluated per layer and per task and reported beside throughput
The change should be rejected, because INT4 always reduces quality below an acceptable level

Answer: The correct answer is C. Throughput and quality form a frontier, and a precision choice is a point on it. Perplexity can stay nearly flat while users see worse answers on hard or rare inputs, so targeted quantization measures per-layer sensitivity, keeps sensitive tensors at higher precision, and evaluates diverse quality benchmarks alongside latency and throughput. Neither blanket acceptance nor blanket rejection follows from bit width alone.
Learning Objective: Evaluate quantized serving changes on the throughput-quality frontier rather than throughput alone

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can lifetime inference cost dwarf training cost?
Training is paid for each model version; serving continues throughout that version’s operational lifetime. A model trained for millions of dollars may serve billions of requests, each consuming compute, memory, network, and energy. At high traffic, recurring inference expense can exceed the original training cost by orders of magnitude. Milliseconds of latency and small differences in accelerator utilization then compound across the service’s lifetime. A fast prediction measured on an otherwise idle machine does not reveal how the same model behaves when requests arrive together, vary in length, and compete for memory. Work can spend longer waiting than executing, while an apparently busy fleet produces responses that arrive too late to be useful. Keeping extra machines ready protects response time but incurs cost during quiet periods; admitting more work improves utilization only while the service can still meet its promises. Failures sharpen this tension because displaced requests consume the spare capacity intended to absorb demand changes. Continuing to accept work during overload can worsen the shortage when delayed requests trigger retries that compete for capacity. The engineering decision is therefore how much useful work the fleet can sustain at an acceptable cost while preserving response quality and timeliness. The answer depends on the request mix and service requirements, so a gain for one workload may become a loss for another. In C³ terms, compute reuse must pay for communication and coordination without exhausting the user’s latency budget.

Learning Objectives

Estimate lifetime serving cost from traffic volume, deployment duration, and measured cost per SLO-compliant request
Select batching, scheduling, and per-request compute-budget policies for vision, LLM, recommender, and streaming workloads
Analyze attention-cache capacity, fragmentation, and prefill-decode interference under workload-dependent serving constraints
Compare sharding, disaggregation, and quantized serving designs using communication, memory, and quality constraints
Evaluate routing, overload-control, and isolation policies against tail latency, retry amplification, and noisy-neighbor risks
Design autoscaling and multi-region routing policies that balance cold starts, cost, and SLO compliance
Synthesize serving architectures that manage C³ trade-offs across request, replica, service, and platform layers

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A language model that costs millions of dollars to train over two months can, once deployed to a global user base at thousands of queries per second, consume a comparable sum in inference compute every week. Inference is then no longer a temporary batch job. It is a continuous, latency-sensitive service.
Running that continuous service takes more than an efficient steady-state replica. Fleet efficiency characterizes a replica by how close its decode steps come to the bandwidth floor, how long it takes to become ready, and how much of its held time runs at the ideal rate, each averaged over windows of hours to weeks. Serving policy determines how that capacity is shared when requests arrive unevenly and each carries a latency target. A faster decode step supplies a better service rate, but it does not determine how long requests wait to join a batch, which replica receives them, which requests receive scarce cache space, or when the fleet needs another replica. These decisions connect the local execution toolkit to user-visible performance under load.


↩︎ The serving replica’s program and runtime goodput, its bandwidth floor, and the fusion, graph replay, and compilation levers that shape it are established in Fleet Efficiency.
The service contract makes that distinction measurable. Offered load is the work arriving at the endpoint, including requests the service may reject; admitted load is the work it accepts. A service-level objective (SLO) specifies the required outcome over a measurement window, such as a latency percentile or successful-request fraction. For language models, request rate alone is insufficient because prompt and output lengths determine different amounts of work. Capacity comparisons must therefore hold the request mix and SLO fixed while measuring how much offered work completes successfully within the targets.
An admitted request passes through routing, preprocessing, queueing, batch formation, model execution, and response delivery, crossing between the host CPU and the accelerator twice on the way (figure 1). The host manages admission, tokenization, and detokenization, while the GPU executes the prompt prefill pass and iterative KV-cache decode loop. The figure maps noncompute serving overhead against the time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT, the average gap between streamed tokens) latency budgets. For an autoregressive model, prefill processes the prompt and builds cached attention keys and values; decode extends that KV cache as it generates subsequent tokens. Waiting before prefill delays the first token, while competition during decode delays the stream. The scheduler must budget both delays alongside execution time. Batching and cache management govern work within a replica, sharding changes the replica’s capacity, and routing and autoscaling distribute demand across replicas.


↩︎ Prefill’s arithmetic-bound regime and decode’s bandwidth floor, measured as MBU, are established in Program goodput and its measure.







Figure 1: End-to-End Inference Pipeline: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request’s latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute.



Distribution adds placement and coordination decisions to the local serving problem. Load balancing1 must distribute requests across replicas with different amounts of unfinished work and available memory. Request routing must also account for model-specific characteristics: recommendation systems with large sharded embedding tables require different placement strategies than language models that generate responses token by token. When demand changes faster than new replicas can become ready, routing alone cannot restore capacity. Autoscaling, spare capacity, and admission limits must work together to protect the service’s latency targets.
1 Load balancing for inference: Request service times can span milliseconds to tens of seconds as models, prompt lengths, and generated outputs vary. Queue-aware routing exposes that remaining work more directly than assignment counts alone.Training and serving place costs on different timelines. A model version’s training expense can be amortized over its deployment, while serving capacity must follow recurring demand. An e-commerce recommendation service, for example, must accommodate peak shopping traffic without paying for an unnecessarily large idle fleet during quiet periods. Both training efficiency and serving efficiency matter, but the serving decision must also account for when requests arrive and how long they can wait. Building such a service requires three linked decisions: when distribution becomes necessary, how the architecture meets latency targets under varying load, and how resource utilization stays high enough that serving cost does not erode the value the model creates. The worked scenarios that follow size these decisions using registry values for real hardware and models alongside labeled scenario assumptions for traffic, prices, and latency budgets, starting with the physical limits that force a service beyond a single machine.

Self-Check: Question

True or False: A service that meets its latency SLO on every admitted request is serving all of its offered load.
Configuration X reports 900 requests per second on a benchmark of short prompts, and configuration Y reports 700 requests per second on the production prompt and output mix, both at the same TTFT and TPOT targets. Which conclusion is justified?

X has more capacity, because request rate is the capacity metric for a serving system.
Neither can be ranked yet, because prompt and output lengths change the work per request, so capacity must be compared at the same request mix and SLO by counting offered work that completes within the targets.
Y has more capacity, because production traffic always contains longer requests than a benchmark.
The two are equivalent, because both meet the same latency targets.

In a streaming language-model service, explain which latency budget is consumed by waiting before prefill and which by contention during decode, and why a faster decode kernel alone cannot settle either problem.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A single accelerator fails a production endpoint in three ways: its memory fills before the model weights or caches fit, its throughput saturates below the arriving query rate, or its forward pass runs longer than a request’s latency budget. Overcoming those limits requires distributing work across several devices within one machine or across machines over the network. Table 1 categorizes these three triggers and their matching distribution strategies, whose necessity depends on the permitted precision, placement, and service contract.
The first signal is memory exhaustion, which occurs when model parameters, key-value caches, or embedding tables exceed single-device capacity. A single NVIDIA H100 GPU provides 80 GB of HBM32 memory, whereas an illustrative mixture-of-experts model with ~1.8T parameters requires ~3.5 TB for FP16 weights alone. Keeping all those weights resident on accelerators requires multiple devices regardless of request volume; quantization and offloading change that placement constraint. Recommendation systems with trillion-parameter embedding tables face similar constraints. Meta’s DLRM architecture3 stores embedding tables that require multiple terabytes of memory (Assumption Provenance records the provenance of the hardware and model constants used throughout this chapter).
2 HBM3 capacity and bandwidth: The H100 combines 80 GB of 3D-stacked DRAM with 3.35 TB/s of bandwidth, compared with 2.04 TB/s for HBM2e on the A100. Capacity determines whether model and cache state fit; bandwidth bounds memory-bound decode throughput.3 DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model): Meta’s 2019 reference architecture combines dense features processed by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) with sparse features represented by embedding lookups (Naumov et al. 2019). This separation permits different placement strategies; it does not require embeddings on CPUs and MLPs on GPUs. Production recommendation characterizations show why this structure matters for serving: embedding-heavy recommendation models create memory-access and capacity constraints that differ from dense convolutional neural network (CNN), recurrent neural network (RNN), or large language model (LLM) inference (Gupta et al. 2020).
Naumov, Maxim, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Hao-Jun Michael Shi, Jianyu Huang, Narayanan Sundaraman, Jongsoo Park, Xiaodong Wang, et al. 2019. “Deep Learning Recommendation Model for Personalization and Recommendation Systems.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1906.00091.

Gupta, Udit, Carole-Jean Wu, Xiaodong Wang, Maxim Naumov, Brandon Reagen, David Brooks, Bradford Cottel, et al. 2020. “The Architectural Implications of Facebook’s DNN-Based Personalized Recommendation.” 2020 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 488–501. https://doi.org/10.1109/HPCA47549.2020.00047.
Beyond memory constraints, throughput limitations emerge when request volume exceeds single-machine capacity even with optimal batching. Consider a recommendation system serving 100,000 queries per second with a 10 ms latency budget. If single-machine throughput peaks at 10,000 QPS, no amount of optimization on that machine can satisfy demand. Horizontal scaling across multiple replicas becomes mandatory.
Finally, latency requirements can motivate distribution even when memory is sufficient. A 70-billion parameter model requires approximately 140 GB of weight memory in FP16, exceeding a single 80 GB H100-class GPU before KV cache is considered. Quantization or larger-memory hardware can make a single-device configuration feasible, yet its execution time may still exceed the request budget. Sharding the model across multiple GPUs can divide computation and weight traffic, but it adds communication and synchronization. Because sharding shortens compute-bound prefill and bandwidth-bound decode by different amounts, the latency benefit must be measured for each phase against its own target.



Table 1: Triggers for Distributed Inference: Each constraint type indicates different distribution strategies. Memory constraints require model sharding; throughput constraints require replication; latency constraints may require either depending on whether the bottleneck is compute or memory bandwidth.

Memory, throughput, and latency triggers all become user-visible once an interactive endpoint starts streaming. Time to first token (TTFT) determines when the user sees a response begin, while time per output token (TPOT) determines whether the rest of the response arrives at a readable pace. TPOT is the average of the time between tokens (TBT), the gap between successive streamed tokens, which many serving systems report as inter-token latency (ITL). A stream can meet its TPOT target while a single long TBT gap still stalls the reader, so average cadence is stated here as TPOT and per-gap tail targets as TBT. Protecting both first-token delay and stream cadence is why inference reverses many of the optimization priorities from training.

Checkpoint 10.1: Distribution strategy selection
Verify your understanding of when to move from single-machine to distributed inference:

Shard vs. replicate: for a 13B model (26 GB weights) that fits on a single A100, select model sharding or horizontal replication when throughput requirements double.
Latency floor: for a real-time speech-to-text service where TBT is the primary bottleneck, determine whether data-parallel replication reduces this latency.
Mandatory sharding: explain why a 175B model requires multiple 80 GB GPUs when all FP16 weights must remain accelerator-resident, regardless of request volume.
Latency trigger: identify when a latency target forces distribution and when added network, serialization, coordination, or queuing overhead can erase the benefit.

A recommendation service must answer 100,000 queries per second within 10 ms. Its model fits comfortably on one machine, which peaks at 10,000 queries per second with optimal batching. Which strategy addresses the binding constraint?

Shard the model with tensor parallelism across machines, because sharding is the general remedy whenever one machine is insufficient.
Quantize the weights so a single machine runs ten times faster.
Replicate the full model across at least ten machines and route requests among them, because the binding constraint is throughput rather than memory or per-request latency.
Raise the batch size on one machine until it reaches 100,000 queries per second.

A 70B-parameter model needs roughly 140 GB of FP16 weights, more than one 80 GB accelerator holds, and quantization can make it fit on one device. Explain why the team might still shard it, and how they should decide.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A replica that runs near its hardware limit still wastes its capacity if requests wait so long in queues, network hops, and host processing that responses arrive after the user’s deadline. Because a served request counts as useful work only when it meets its latency and quality targets, every stage it crosses spends part of that contract’s budget.


A training iteration that takes 2 seconds instead of the usual 1 second slows a run slightly, and faster steps later can still keep the job on schedule. An interactive request that takes 2 seconds against a 100 ms target fails its contract immediately, even if every subsequent request finishes on time. This contrast between training and inference centers on the unit of useful progress. Training evaluates throughput together with convergence over a run; interactive serving evaluates completed requests against quality and latency targets. Offline inference can also prioritize throughput, while training still loses progress to stragglers and stalls. The distinction is therefore which delays violate the workload’s contract, not whether one activity cares about time and the other does not. That difference reorders priorities across six system aspects, from the primary metric onward (table 2).



Table 2: Training vs. Inference System Requirements: The fundamental inversion from throughput to latency optimization ripples through system design, state management, batch formation, and failure recovery.










Aspect
Distributed training
Distributed inference




Primary metric
Throughput (samples/hour)
Latency (p99 ms)


Acceptable variance
Hours
Milliseconds


State management

Session state (continuous)


Batch formation
Large, controlled
Request-driven, variable


Failure tolerance

Redirect if capacity and state allow


Cost structure
Fixed duration, variable rate
Variable duration, fixed SLO






Failure handling follows those different contracts. Training restores a checkpoint and repeats lost work, charging recovery time to the run. Interactive serving has far less time per request, so redirecting work needs spare capacity and recoverable request state, and substituting a smaller model needs an acceptable quality fallback. SLOs define which failures and delays the service may tolerate, and a recovery mechanism helps only when its added work fits within that contract.
The same targets also define the serving system’s capacity metric. SLO goodput is the rate of completed requests that meet the stated TTFT and TPOT targets for a fixed request mix. It is the serving counterpart of the useful-progress goodput that coordination protects in training (Orchestration coordination layer), and it applies after ML goodput, which measures how much of a replica’s held capacity runs at its ideal rate. SLO goodput then counts how much of that capacity completes requests within their targets. A request that misses its contract counts for nothing, however busy the accelerators were while serving it, so increasing arrivals without completing more requests within those targets does not increase useful capacity.


↩︎ ML goodput, the fraction of fleet capacity that becomes useful work at the ideal rate, and its three factors are established in ML Goodput.



If an interactive request carries a 100 ms latency target and model execution takes 70 ms on an idle replica, routing, network transfers, serialization, coordination, and queueing must all fit inside the remaining 30 ms. Distributing inference adds transfers and coordination to a request that already spends time in host processing and queues. This “serving tax” is the exposed work outside model execution that consumes the request’s latency budget, and its size depends on which components the request crosses and which costs can overlap.
Network communication contributes setup and transfer time at each cross-machine dependency. Synchronization between GPUs can expose that cost when the next operation needs a remote result. For an illustrative path with four sequential exchanges taking 50–500 microseconds each, the exposed contribution is 200 microseconds to 2 milliseconds. Actual collective time also depends on payload, topology, contention, and the number of communication rounds; a generic network round-trip time cannot be charged once per collective without checking its implementation.


↩︎ The \(\MessageStartupLatency\)-\(\LinkBandwidth\) model, which splits each transfer into a fixed startup latency plus a bandwidth-dependent term, is established in The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model.
Before and after those network hops, serialization adds host work whenever a service converts structured data into a wire representation and reconstructs it at the receiver. Protocol Buffers, JSON, and Python’s pickle provide different representations and implementation paths, so their cost must be measured for the actual payload and runtime. Tensor transfers within a sharded model need not pass through the same object-serialization path as a service request. Formats such as FlatBuffers and Cap’n Proto permit access to wire-format data in place, avoiding a separate unpacking step when the consumer supports that representation, though they do not eliminate network transfer or every downstream copy.
Once the payload is on the wire, load balancing adds a routing decision and sometimes another forwarding hop: examining request metadata, consulting replica state, and forwarding to the selected backend all consume time before execution begins. The measurement must separate decision time from waiting and transport so that a slow routing path is not mistaken for a slow model.
When a request fans out across several backend services—such as feature stores, retrieval indexes, and ranking models—coordination overhead emerges as the gateway joins their results. Independent feature or model calls can run concurrently, but a dependent ranking stage must wait for the inputs it needs, so the critical path includes exposed coordination and the slowest required branch rather than the sum of every branch’s runtime. Finally, queuing delay (\(\QueueingLatency\)) adds waiting time whenever work arrives while the required resources are busy, even when the average arrival rate remains below average service capacity.
The serving tax must be measured on the same request boundary as model execution. Equation 1 decomposes that latency, with each term counting an exposed contribution so concurrent work is not counted twice:
\[\EndToEndRequestLatency= \InferenceLatency+ \NetworkLatency+ \SerializationLatency+ \CoordinationLatency+ \QueueingLatency \tag{1}\]
In the 100 ms request budget above, the four sequential exchanges alone can claim up to 2 ms of the 30 ms non-compute slack before any request waits for a busy replica. The measured contribution determines the intervention: co-location removes a network hop, fewer dependent exchanges reduce startup costs, and a faster link shortens large transfers, whereas queueing requires controlling admitted work or increasing usable capacity. Each choice spends resources to recover latency budget, connecting the request-level diagnosis to lifetime serving cost.

Self-Check: Question

The two are equal, because both process the same request mix.
X, because requests that miss their targets still return results to users.
Y, because SLO goodput counts only requests that meet their targets, about 950 per second against about 840 for X.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
At this traffic, one year of serving costs about nine times the training run.
A team that budgets millions of dollars to train a model can find within weeks of launch that serving traffic is spending more compute per month than the entire training run cost. While the serving tax in equation 1 consumes a fraction of each request’s latency budget, those per-request costs compound across every query over the model’s operational lifetime. By the serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)), recurring serving expense can dwarf upfront training expense by orders of magnitude because a model version incurs training cost once before deployment while serving cost recurs with traffic. Both activities can consume purchased or rented infrastructure; the distinction here is expense timing, not financial capitalization. In a high-volume deployment, that recurring traffic bill rapidly overtakes the one-time training investment (notebook 10.1).

Napkin Math 10.1: The serving cost multiplierProblem: A team has spent $2,000,000 training a 70B parameter model and now serves it to 1,000,000 daily active users, each making 50 requests/day. Is training or serving the dominant cost over 1 year?
Math:

Training cost: $2,000,000 (one-time).
Metric: Annual inference volume is \(10^{6}\,\text{users} \times 50\,\text{reqs} \times 365\,\text{days} \approx\) 18.25B requests/year.
Cost per request: Assume a 70B model on H100 costs \(\approx\) $0.001/request (input + output).
Annual serving cost: 18.25B requests \(\times\) $0.001/request = $18,250,000.

Systems insight: Serving costs 9.1× more than training in the first year alone. A 10 percent reduction in cost per request, at unchanged request volume and service quality, saves about $1.8M in the first year, nearly paying for the original training run.


For one model version at a fixed query rate and average cost per served query, equation 2 combines training expense with recurring serving expense:
\[\ModelLifetimeCost= \TrainingCost + \ServingCostPerQuery\times \DeploymentDuration\times \ArrivalRate \tag{2}\]
where \(\TrainingCost\) is the one-time cost to train the model, \(\ServingCostPerQuery\) is the cost per query served, \(\DeploymentDuration\) is the deployment duration in appropriate time units, and \(\ArrivalRate\) is the query rate. The rate must count the same served queries used to estimate unit cost. That cost must include the chosen serving boundary, including idle or reserved capacity when it is billed. Changing traffic mix, fleet size, or price requires evaluating separate intervals rather than treating one unit cost as constant throughout deployment.
The same leverage can hold across application categories with different cost structures. In the chapter’s illustrative recommendation scenario, a DLRM trained for $8,000 ($2,000 hardware for 1,000 GPU-hours at $2/GPU-hour, plus 3× additional engineering cost for data and experimentation) and served at 10,000 QPS for 730 days accumulates \(6.31 \times 10^{11}\) lifetime queries. At the assumed $10/million queries, those queries cost $6,307,200 to serve, producing a 788.4× ratio in this scenario. Other workload envelopes span orders of magnitude in both terms, and the sensitivity ranges in table 3 are illustrative envelopes rather than market-price estimates.

A reduction in cost per completed request yields recurring savings only if workload volume and service quality stay fixed; lower latency alone does not reduce billed capacity. Unit cost also changes with daily request volume, as the constructed cost curves of figure 2 illustrate. Against its assumed price of $0.05 per 1,000 tokens, the optimized curve crosses near \(2 \times 10^{5}\) requests per day and the unbatched single-GPU curve near \(4 \times 10^{7}\) requests. These crossings follow from the assumed curves, not measured profitability, so a deployment needs its own token mix, occupied capacity, and cost boundary to locate its break-even point.

The cost ranges in table 3 give a static comparison. Figure 3 instead accumulates assumed monthly serving expense over a 36-month deployment and marks when the serving portion equals the initial training expense, within days in the plotted recommendation scenario and roughly six weeks in the 70B LLM scenario. These timings follow from the specified expenses, not from model size or user count, and a larger training expense, lower traffic, or shorter deployment can reverse which activity dominates. When recurring traffic makes inference the dominant expense, serving-specific designs can substantially reduce cost and power per query (Patel et al. 2024), provided each optimization targets the workload’s actual bottleneck and the right level of the serving stack.

These differences follow from the specified training costs, traffic, and unit serving prices.

Nothing more, because idle replicas do no work and therefore add no cost per query.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
An optimization tuned for one model family or one layer of the stack can miss the active bottleneck when applied to another. Paging a key-value cache does nothing for an embedding-heavy recommendation model, and fusing a GPU kernel cannot rescue a service whose requests stall in a load balancer. Controlling serving cost therefore requires separating the workload mix from the system layer that owns each bottleneck.


Designing a serving platform around autoregressive token generation alone leaves a fleet unprepared for the workloads that dominate consumer request volume. In large consumer platforms, recommendation and ranking workloads can consume the majority of AI inference cycles and capacity (Gupta et al. 2020; Hazelwood et al. 2018), stalling on terabyte-scale sparse embedding lookups under sub-10 ms deadlines rather than sequential weight reads. Vision and image processing, NLP and LLM workloads, fraud detection, ads, and other classification tasks create additional serving demands. Table 4 compares representative pressures: sparse lookup for recommendation, batch efficiency for fixed-shape vision, weight and cache traffic for LLM decode, and incremental deadlines for speech. These are starting points for diagnosis; the active bottleneck still depends on the model, input shape, and deployment.
Recommendation traffic illustrates why request volume must be derived from application behavior. A page load, scroll, or click can trigger ranking or retrieval, so one browsing session can produce many inference requests. A language-model application may likewise issue several model calls for one user action or run background tasks without an explicit query. Capacity planning therefore counts the model work triggered by each interaction rather than treating user count as request rate.
Workload structure also determines which techniques can help. Embedding sharding and lookup locality address large recommendation models (Naumov et al. 2019; Gupta et al. 2020), and feature store architectures must deliver the inputs a model expects within its latency budget, while continuous batching and KV cache management address variable-length autoregressive work. Text-to-image systems such as DALL-E add multimodal serving demands (Ramesh et al. 2021) whose volume and latency targets remain product-specific.

Tuning a replica’s kernels or cache allocator cannot fix tail latency when requests are waiting inside a router or starving behind a noisy neighbor on a shared cluster. To locate the right control, serving optimizations organize into a four-level serving hierarchy ordered by scope, where each level owns a distinct bottleneck and measurement boundary. The request level follows one request through preprocessing, batch-formation waiting, response caching, and model execution, where the target is the latency a user sees. The replica level looks inside one model instance, where utilization, KV-cache memory management, and kernel efficiency set the throughput it can deliver before it saturates. The service level turns many replicas of the same model into aggregate capacity through load balancing, request routing, and autoscaling. The platform level decides, across services and tenants, whether a shared serving fleet stays efficient without allowing one workload to degrade another.
Each level supplies a different measurement boundary. Table 5 associates request latency, replica throughput, aggregate service capacity, and cross-tenant efficiency with the controls most directly responsible for them. Their effects still cross boundaries: batching can increase replica throughput while adding request delay, and replica placement can change both communication cost and service capacity. The hierarchy helps locate the decision without treating its metric in isolation. In C³ terms, batching and cache management improve compute reuse, sharding introduces communication, and routing, isolation, and autoscaling coordinate the resources that make those gains usable.

Checkpoint 10.2: The serving hierarchy
Verify your understanding of where specific optimizations sit within the serving hierarchy:

Replica level: identify the hierarchy level at which KV-cache paging reduces GPU memory waste, and explain why that raises concurrent request capacity rather than single-request latency.
Caching level: distinguish response caching, which shortens one request’s path, from KV-cache paging, which raises a replica’s capacity, and place each in the hierarchy.
Load balancing: identify why load balancing belongs at the service level and explain how its choice of replica can affect both aggregate goodput and a request’s queueing delay.
Isolation level: evaluate the claim that multi-tenancy and resource isolation are primarily request-level concerns.



The serving decisions that follow climb the hierarchy from the request level to the platform level. Batching sets how long each request waits to share execution. KV-cache layout, decode-time policies, and adapter state decide how many requests a replica can hold. The split between prefill and decode decides whether a new prompt and the streams already decoding share a worker or separate pools. Weight quantization and model sharding change the replica’s memory and compute budget. Routing, isolation, autoscaling, and global placement then turn replicas into a service and a platform. Precision enters every capacity calculation that follows through two separate budgets: reducing weight precision frees resident memory, whereas reducing KV precision lowers the memory required per active sequence. Section 10.9 compares the serving trade-offs of these representation choices before sharding divides a replica across devices.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A stream of hundreds of disparate chat requests arrives at an inference server every second. Processing them one by one leaves much of the GPU idle, starved for work between small decode steps. Waiting to gather a large static batch forces the first request in line to endure unacceptable latency. Batching at scale therefore needs policies that group requests as they arrive without violating tail-latency deadlines.
Processing multiple requests together shares weight reads and kernel launch overhead across more useful work. The resulting service-rate gain can reduce queueing, but waiting to form a batch adds delay; the net effect on request latency depends on load. Single-machine serving applies this insight through dynamic batching, which collects requests within a time window before processing them together.
At scale, batching must also account for workload structure. A policy suited to uniform vision inputs can leave slots unused during variable-length generation, while grouping sparse embedding lookups solves a different problem from batching dense execution. The unit of reusable work determines which policy is worth evaluating. The strategies below proceed in order of mechanism rather than traffic share: vision (request batching), LLMs (iteration-level batching with KV state), and recommendation (feature-parallel batching over distributed embeddings), even though recommendation often dominates consumer inference volume (section 10.5.1).


Holding arriving requests until a fixed batch fills forces early arrivals to wait and pads shorter inputs with wasted work, whereas running every request immediately leaves later arrivals queued behind one-request passes that underuse the GPU. Batching efficiency depends on how computation scales with batch size relative to memory and communication constraints, and the execution timeline in figure 4 separates waiting to form a batch from waiting for the accelerator to become available. Unbatched serving adds no batch-formation delay, but later requests can still queue behind earlier forward passes. Static batching consolidates all four illustrated requests into one pass, adding formation delay and padding to accommodate different input lengths. Dynamic batching closes formation windows at fixed time intervals (\(\FiniteChange \TimeInstant\)), producing two passes with two requests each in this example. The window limits intentional formation delay; it does not bound total queueing when ready batches arrive faster than the server can execute them.







Figure 4: Batching Strategies Compared: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay.



In vision models processing fixed-size images, arithmetic work grows roughly in proportion to batch size while requests share the weights, so larger batches improve weight reuse until compute, memory, or the latency budget binds. The largest feasible batch is not necessarily the best interactive operating point. By contrast, in LLMs during the decode phase, small batches perform little computation per byte of active weights loaded, so memory bandwidth binds. Larger batches raise arithmetic intensity until compute, KV-cache traffic, or the latency budget limits further gains. Small-batch decode therefore does not inherit a new accelerator generation’s headline compute improvement. From Volta to Blackwell, peak compute climbs 18× while memory bandwidth expands by only 8.9×, and figure 5 shows generation throughput tracking the slower curve whenever weight streaming dominates at small batch sizes.


↩︎ The accelerator trajectory behind this divergence, with compute outpacing memory bandwidth from one generation to the next, is established in Evolution of GPU architectures.
Recommendation systems shift the bottleneck again: sparse embedding lookup can limit throughput before dense computation does. Grouping sparse accesses improves locality and distributes lookup work across shards, while batching the dense stages improves matrix multiplication throughput. The serving policy must therefore account for both stages and the communication between them rather than infer the bottleneck from the model category alone.














Figure 5: Decode Inherits the Bandwidth Deficit: Peak compute and memory bandwidth for four accelerator generations, normalized to the V100. Compute rises 18× against bandwidth’s 8.9×. In weight-bandwidth-bound decode, each iteration loads the active weights and reuses them across its output tokens; at fixed batch size, bandwidth growth constrains the gain. These hardware ratios are not measured workload speedups. Specifications are dense peak rates and bandwidths from the vendor datasheets recorded in the chapter’s data file.






Raising batch size to maximize a replica’s throughput stretches each batch’s execution time and holds arriving requests in a formation queue until the service violates its latency SLO. Batch size is the single-replica control knob that moves a workload along the roofline by reusing each weight read across more requests, which raises arithmetic intensity. At fleet scale, the same knob also sets how long arriving work waits and how much request state the replica must hold. A model relating batch size \((\BatchSize)\), batch service time \((\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize))\), and batched service rate \((\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize))\) exposes that trade-off; selecting an operating point also requires the arrival pattern, memory budget, and latency target.


↪ The roofline bound, and why batch-one decode sits far below the ridge point, are collected for reference in The roofline bound.
The first model isolates batch execution. Here \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) is the service time once a batch begins execution; it excludes queueing and batch formation. Keeping the measurement boundary explicit prevents an execution-time improvement from being mistaken for an end-to-end SLO guarantee.
The service-time equation decomposes batch execution time into fixed overheads (kernel launch, memory loading) and variable costs (compute per sample):
\[\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) = \BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime\]
In this formulation, \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) captures costs paid once per batch, such as loading weights from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and kernel launch latency, while \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) denotes the marginal cost of adding one request, such as the compute time for that sample. Treating these terms as constants is a local approximation for a fixed workload and execution regime. Kernel changes, cache traffic, and resource saturation can alter the measured curve as batch size grows.
The throughput equation describes the system’s capacity:
\[\EffectiveServiceRate(\BatchSize) = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)} = \frac{\BatchSize}{\BatchFixedOverheadTime+ \BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime}\]
The resulting batching efficiency curve shows diminishing returns from amortizing overhead. For small batch sizes (\(\BatchSize\)), \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) dominates service time, so increasing \(\BatchSize\) shares that cost and raises throughput substantially. As \(\BatchSize\) grows, the relative contribution of \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) shrinks and the model approaches its asymptotic rate \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\). This limit alone does not identify whether compute or bandwidth binds on the actual device. The knee of the curve, where fixed and variable costs become comparable, is a useful candidate operating point. It is not an optimum independent of the service contract; a tight latency budget may require a smaller batch, while a throughput-oriented workload may benefit from a larger one.



Throughput saturates toward \(1/\MarginalRequestServiceTime\); past the knee, each larger batch buys less.
The execution-only feasibility condition is \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) \le \text{SLO}\). In a live service, execution receives only the budget remaining after routing, queueing, batch formation, and response delivery. The batch-size decision must therefore use that remaining budget rather than consume the full SLO. Comparing a vision workload with a relatively high \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) against an LLM decode workload with a high \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) from weight loading shows how those measured costs shift the efficiency knee (notebook 10.2).

Napkin Math 10.2: The batching efficiency curveProblem: An engineer optimizes two services: a vision model (ResNet) and an LLM (70B). At what batch size does each hit the “knee” of its efficiency curve?
Math: The knee occurs where the variable compute cost \((\BatchSize\times \MarginalRequestServiceTime)\) starts to exceed the fixed overhead \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime)\).

Vision Model \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime= 2\text{ ms}, \MarginalRequestServiceTime= 1\text{ ms})\):

Knee: \(\BatchSize\approx 2\text{ ms}/1\text{ ms} =\) 2.
Result: This simplified latency model reaches its first overhead-amortization knee at a small batch. It does not locate hardware saturation; measuring throughput at larger batches tests whether additional concurrency still helps.

LLM Decode \((\BatchFixedOverheadTime= 40\text{ ms}, \MarginalRequestServiceTime= 0.5\text{ ms})\):

Knee: \(\BatchSize\approx 40\text{ ms}/0.5\text{ ms} =\) 80.
Result: The larger fixed cost in this decode example moves the overhead-amortization knee to a larger batch.
Where 0.5 ms comes from: It is an assumed marginal cost per added sequence, dominated by reading that sequence’s own KV state at a moderate context length. Unlike the weight stream, that read is private to each sequence, so it grows with batch size instead of being shared.
Where 40 ms comes from: It is roughly the time to stream the model’s 140 GB of FP16 weights through one H100’s 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, the aggregate weight traffic of one decode step expressed in single-device time. No single H100 holds those weights. The reference replica of Where Fleet Capacity Goes spreads them over eight GPUs, which divides both \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\) and \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime\) by the tensor-parallel degree and leaves their ratio, and therefore the knee, unchanged.


Systems insight: Because streaming the weights is the dominant per-step cost of decode, the system has not reached the efficiency knee until batch size 80. The knee depends on the ratio of fixed to per-request cost, not on how many devices share them, which is why sharing weight reads across concurrent requests matters at every replica size. The batch a service actually runs also depends on context length, cache capacity, kernel efficiency, and the latency target; continuous batching and paged allocation are the mechanisms that let a replica reach it.


While the analytical batching model locates the knee from each model class’s ratio of fixed to per-request cost (table 9), production serving stacks measure the resulting throughput-latency frontier directly. The open InferenceX benchmark serves DeepSeek-R1, a mixture-of-experts reasoning model, with 1,024-token prompts and 1,024-token responses on each accelerator across many combinations of serving framework, parallelism, and concurrency (SemiAnalysis 2026). For every configuration it records the output tokens per second each user receives, called interactivity (the reciprocal of TPOT), and the output tokens per second each GPU delivers across all users. Figure 6 plots 325 such configurations at FP8 precision and traces, for each accelerator, the frontier of configurations that no other configuration beats on both rates. Every frontier falls as interactivity rises, because a faster stream per user permits fewer concurrent sequences per decode step. The best B200 configuration delivers about 6,300 output tokens per second per GPU when each user receives about 13 tokens per second. It delivers about 210 when each user must receive at least 100, a 30× difference in per-GPU output paid for faster streams. The interactivity target alone moves per-GPU output by that much, so it must be fixed before any two throughput figures can be compared.
The same frontiers separate hardware generations by more than their datasheets do. At 50 tokens per second per user, the best measured H100 configuration delivers about 80 output tokens per second per GPU and the best GB200 NVL72 configuration about 3,650, a 44× difference. Yet the peak dense FP8 rate of a GB200 GPU is only about 2.3× that of an H100. The benchmark does not apportion the gap, but the candidates lie mostly beyond peak arithmetic, in memory bandwidth and capacity per GPU, a 72-GPU NVLink domain that keeps experts and KV state off slower networks, and platform-tuned serving software. A throughput figure quoted without its latency target therefore says little about either system.














Figure 6: Throughput versus Interactivity in Measured LLM Serving: Output tokens per second per GPU against output tokens per second per user for DeepSeek-R1 at FP8 with 1,024-token prompts and responses. Faint points are individual serving configurations (framework, parallelism, and concurrency); each line is the frontier of configurations that no other configuration on the same accelerator beats on both axes. The dashed line marks 50 tokens per second per user. Data from SemiAnalysis (2026), latest published result per configuration as of October 2026.


SemiAnalysis. 2026. InferenceX: Open Source Continuous Inference Benchmark.


Translating the batch-level equations into system-wide capacity planning requires Little’s law,4 a classical result from queuing theory that relates concurrency, throughput, and latency in any stable system. Whereas \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) prices one replica’s execution batch, Little’s law connects the external arrival rate and mean request time in system to the total number of requests concurrently in flight across the fleet.
4 Little’s law: The identity holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival or service distribution, which is why it survives the bursty, variable-length traffic of inference. Because it relates averages, it bounds neither maximum service capacity nor tail latency.
↩︎ The M/G/1 waiting-time model, in which utilization and service-time variability multiply queueing delay, is established in Scheduling Objectives and Their Conflicts.


Theorem 10.1: Little's law for inferenceConcept: In any stable queuing system, the average number of requests in the system \((\RequestConcurrency)\) equals the arrival rate \((\ArrivalRate)\) multiplied by the average time a request spends in the system \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\).
\[ \RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \]
Application: Concurrency planning. This idealized service counts only batch formation, queueing, and execution in its end-to-end latency; routing and response delivery add no delay. Assume the mean latency given below and full execution batches of the stated size. A percentile SLO cannot generally be substituted for the mean in Little’s law.

Target Throughput \((\ArrivalRate)\): 1,000 requests/sec
Assumed mean latency \((\RequestTimeInSystem)\): 100 ms (0.1 s)

Mean in-flight work \((\RequestConcurrency)\): \(1000 \times 0.1 =\) 100 concurrent requests
Capacity planning: If a single GPU replica executes batches of 8 in 80 ms, and the fleet targets at most 80 percent mean service utilization:

Replica throughput \(=\) \(8/0.08 =\) 100 req/s
Throughput-only lower bound \(=\) \(\lceil 1000/100\rceil =\) 10 replicas
Illustrative headroom-sized replica count \(=\) \(\lceil 1000/(0.8 \times 100)\rceil =\) 13 replicas

Verification: Maximum executing positions \(=\) \(13\text{ replicas} \times 8\text{ batch positions} =\) 104. These positions do not include requests waiting for execution or batch formation. Under the assumed fixed batch service time, Little’s law on the execution boundary gives 80 requests executing on average; the remaining 20 of the assumed mean in-flight population are waiting or accumulating. The throughput-only lower bound would run at the stability boundary; the utilization-sized candidate runs at about 76.9 percent service utilization. The assumed mean latency still needs validation, and this arithmetic does not prove a percentile latency SLO; that requires an arrival/service model or a measured load test.


This stability boundary can be measured faithfully only when the load generator preserves the workload claim. The measurement contract of The measurement contract guards against load that eases off while the replica stalls. A serving measurement therefore holds a fixed external arrival process rather than a fixed concurrency, because response-paced generation can reduce arrivals during a stall and make the system appear to have more headroom than it does. The distinction between throughput capacity and latency capacity is exactly what queuing theory formalizes.


↪ The mean queuing delay under a batched M/G/1 surrogate, and how utilization headroom and batch size trade against latency, is developed in Queuing theory for batched inference.



Static batching, which waits until exactly \(\BatchSize\) requests arrive before launching a forward pass, leaves early requests stranded during traffic lulls until their latency budgets expire. Vision models otherwise present the simplest batching case: preprocessed inputs share a fixed tensor shape and execute in a predictable time, so single-machine batching applies directly and fleet scale adds only the question of where batches form.
Dynamic batching collects requests for a maximum time window \(\BatchingWindow\) or until reaching maximum batch size \(\MaxBatchSize\), whichever occurs first. For Poisson arrivals with rate \(\ArrivalRate\), equation 3 organizes expected request latency into queueing, formation, and execution contributions:
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestTimeInSystem] = \mathbb{E}[\QueueingLatency] + \BatchFormationDelay + \BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize) \tag{3}\]
where \(\mathbb{E}[\QueueingLatency]\) is the expected queuing delay, \(\BatchFormationDelay\) represents mean batch formation delay (up to \(\BatchingWindow\)), and \(\BatchServiceTime(\BatchSize)\) represents mean inference time over the realized batch sizes \(\BatchSize\). Queueing here excludes time already counted as batch formation. The two waiting terms respond differently to load. Under Poisson arrivals the mean inter-arrival gap is \(1/\ArrivalRate\), so a higher arrival rate fills a batch faster and reduces formation delay. Queueing for a busy replica can nevertheless grow as arrival rate approaches service capacity; the batching timeout does not cap that queueing delay. Spending a small slice of the latency budget on batch formation can multiply per-GPU capacity while keeping end-to-end latency within target (example 10.1).

Example 10.1: Dynamic batching for ResNet-50Scenario: A vision classification service receives requests at 5,000 QPS with a 50 ms p99 latency SLO across 10 replicas, so each replica sees 500 QPS. One image served alone takes 5 ms. The scenario assumes that a batch of about 5 images executes in 8 ms and a batch of about 10 in 12 ms, because a batch shares weight reads and kernel launches across its images.
Diagnosis: Each utilization below is the per-replica arrival rate multiplied by the service time one request consumes. Option A serves every image alone, which overloads the replica (\(\ServingUtilization = \ArrivalRate \times \BatchServiceTime = 500 \times 0.005 = 2.5\) utilization). Option B holds a 10 ms batching window, which collects about 5 requests (arrival rate \(\times\) window). Their batch runs in 8 ms, so each request consumes 1.6 ms of execution, and utilization falls to \(\ServingUtilization = 500 \times 0.0016 = 0.8\). The wider 20 ms window of Option C collects about 10 requests whose batch runs in 12 ms, or 1.2 ms each, reaching \(\ServingUtilization = 500 \times 0.0012 = 0.6\) and a further 33 percent of per-replica capacity. Both options leave service headroom. Whether they also meet the p99 SLO depends on the window plus the queueing delay each utilization implies under the service’s real arrival pattern, which utilization alone does not determine.
Systems lesson: Dynamic batching is effective when the latency budget has unused slack. The serving policy converts latency headroom into throughput, but requires careful tuning to prevent SLO violations.




↪ A procedure for this tuning, from fitting the service-time model to checking the p99 target, is developed in Batch size selection framework given an SLO.
At scale with multiple replicas, batch formation can occur either at individual replicas or at a centralized batching layer. Replica-local batching has each replica independently form batches from its assigned traffic. This avoids a shared batching stage, but splitting a light arrival stream among many replicas can leave each waiting to fill its batch. Centralized batching pools arrivals before dispatching formed batches, potentially shortening formation waits, at the cost of an additional network hop and a shared scheduling bottleneck. Load balancing helps local batching, but equal request counts do not guarantee equal work or reproduce the formation benefit of pooling arrivals. The choice depends on arrival density, request compatibility, and replica service times.



When a request-level batch locks its membership until the longest sequence finishes, a short reply that ends after 10 tokens leaves its slot stranded for the remaining 90 steps of a 100-token neighbor. Queued requests starve while the GPU still streams the full model weights on every step. The autoregressive bottleneck (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)) makes that wasted slot expensive: at small batch sizes, decode is typically bandwidth-bound because each iteration streams active model weights while generating only one token per sequence. Batching shares those weight reads across concurrent requests, and as the batch grows, compute or KV-cache traffic can become the binding constraint, so bandwidth-bound decode is an operating regime rather than a property of every serving configuration.

Definition 10.1: Continuous batching
Continuous batching is a serving strategy that updates batch membership at iteration boundaries, allowing new requests to enter without waiting for every request in the original batch to finish.

Significance: It reduces padding waste by refilling completed slots at iteration boundaries. Throughput gains require waiting requests, available KV-cache capacity, and scheduling overhead small enough to preserve the benefit.
Distinction: Unlike static or dynamic batching (which group requests at the request level), continuous batching operates at the iteration level, reshaping the active batch between decode iterations.
Common pitfall: Continuous admission must coordinate scheduling with KV-state ownership and lifetime. A Dynamic Memory Manager such as PagedAttention improves space utilization, but paging is not required: an implementation can recycle fixed-capacity request slots, at the cost of unused reserved space.



The Orca system (Yu et al. 2022) removed the request-level barrier by updating membership at iteration boundaries to enable slot reuse. Once a request completes, another can enter if its prompt has been processed and sufficient cache capacity is available. The scheduler must account for that preparation rather than treat every replacement as a decode-only operation.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Consider a fixed-width batch of 8 sequences. If one sequence completes after 10 tokens while others require 100 tokens, its slot contributes no useful output for 90 iterations. If the kernel continues executing padded work for that slot, the fraction of wasted compute attributable to it is:
\[\text{Wasted compute} = \frac{(100 - 10) \times 1}{100 \times 8} = 11.25\%\]
The waste grows with the spread of output lengths, a dependence that section 10.6.5 turns into a formula. A kernel that skips completed sequences avoids their padded arithmetic, but a fixed-membership policy still prevents waiting requests from using the vacated capacity. Algorithm 1 states the continuous-batching scheduler as a decode loop with a prefilled waiting queue. Completed requests release their pages in this simplified policy, eligible waiting requests enter freed slots, and the next kernel runs over the updated active set. For Archetype A workloads (GPT-4/Llama-3), refilling slots lets more useful tokens share each weight read. The gain comes from reusing transferred weights, not merely from saturating bandwidth, which a smaller batch may already do.


↩︎ Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), the autoregressive transformer whose serving must stream billions of weights for every generated token, is established in Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3).

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Continuous batching decode scheduler}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require prefilled waiting queue $Q$; active set $A$; KV-cache page allocator; active-token capacity $C_{\text{tok}}$; batched decode kernel
\Ensure generated tokens for completed requests; a continually refreshed active batch
\While{the service is running}
    \State admit requests from $Q$ while capacity and free KV-cache pages remain; allocate state, append to $A$
    \State reserve pages for the next decode step; preempt requests that do not fit
    \State run one batched decode kernel over the remaining sequences in $A$
    \State append each sampled token; extend its KV-cache pages
    \State remove completed or length-limited sequences from $A$; return their pages to the allocator
    \If{HBM pressure exceeds the policy threshold}
        \State move low-priority sequences from $A$ to the paused set; page their KV-cache to CPU DRAM
    \EndIf
    \State fill freed capacity from $Q$, or resume paused sequences whose pages now fit
\EndWhile
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(Q\)

Admitting, completing, and refilling slots on every iteration lets waiting work use capacity released before the longest sequence finishes. The illustrated preemption path adds HBM-to-CPU-DRAM transfers under memory pressure, so recovered capacity must repay both scheduling and state-movement costs. Counted in slot-iterations (figure 7), fixed membership leaves only 20 of 32 productive, while continuous admission fills all 32 under the illustrated arrival and capacity assumptions. Prefill and decode cells do not necessarily take equal time. Slot occupancy therefore measures the opportunity; the realized throughput gain depends on how much longer the inserted prefill cells take than the decode steps they share an iteration with.







Figure 7: Static vs. Continuous Batching: In static batching (a), completed slots cannot be reused until the longest request finishes, although completed responses may already be released. Continuous batching (b) admits waiting requests into freed slots at iteration boundaries, starting each with a prefill step. Over the eight iterations shown, 20 of 32 slot-iterations do useful work under static batching and all 32 under continuous batching; the hatched idle slots are the capacity recovered when arrivals and cache capacity permit.






In a static batch whose output lengths vary widely, a single long response holds every completed slot idle until its final token, wasting a growing share of the batch’s sequence-iterations as length variance rises. Continuous batching recovers that stranded capacity by refilling vacated slots at iteration boundaries (figure 7). Counting useful and unused sequence-iterations in a fixed batch bounds the recoverable opportunity; arrivals, KV-cache admission, prefill scheduling, and scheduler overhead determine how much of that ceiling a live replica actually captures.


The 11.25 percent example of one early-finishing sequence generalizes to any mix of output lengths. For this waste model, traditional batching (also called static batching) retains a fixed batch width through all decode iterations until the longest sequence completes. Assume equal compute cost per sequence-iteration, including padded work for completed requests. For batch size \(\BatchSize\) with output lengths \(\{\RequestOutputLength_1, \RequestOutputLength_2, ..., \RequestOutputLength_{\BatchSize}\}\), the total compute performed under those assumptions is:
\[\StaticBatchingOperations= \BatchSize\times \BatchMaxOutputLength\times \SequenceIterationOperations\]
where \(\BatchMaxOutputLength= \max_i(\RequestOutputLength_i)\) and \(\SequenceIterationOperations\) is the compute cost per decode iteration per sequence. However, the useful compute is only:
\[\UsefulModelFlops = \sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \RequestOutputLength_i \times \SequenceIterationOperations\]
Equation 4 defines the waste ratio that quantifies the inefficiency:
\[\PaddingWasteFraction= 1 - \frac{\UsefulModelFlops}{\StaticBatchingOperations} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{\BatchSize} \RequestOutputLength_i}{\BatchSize\times \BatchMaxOutputLength} = 1 - \frac{\BatchMeanOutputLength}{\BatchMaxOutputLength} \tag{4}\]
where \(\BatchMeanOutputLength\) is the mean output sequence length. Waste therefore depends entirely on the ratio of mean to maximum output length within the batch. For uniform output lengths \((\BatchMeanOutputLength= \BatchMaxOutputLength)\), waste is zero. For highly variable lengths, waste can exceed 50 percent.

Result: Under fixed membership, only 500 of the 800 sequence-iterations do useful work. Continuous admission hands the rest to R5, R6, and R7, which start generating at iterations 50, 100, and 150 instead of waiting for a new batch, so the same 200 iterations now advance seven requests rather than four. Releasing each response on completion separately reduces the original requests’ average latency by 37.5 percent, numerically matching the unused-slot ratio, and static batching that released responses on completion would obtain the same original-request latencies.
Systems insight: Response release and slot reuse are separate decisions. Removing a response barrier helps the requests already in the batch; only continuous admission recovers the stranded iteration capacity shown in figure 7, and that recovered capacity is what raises a replica’s throughput.





The continuous-batching analysis relates recoverable slot capacity to the gap between a batch’s longest and average output lengths. Let \(\text{CV} = \OutputLengthStandardDeviation/ \WorkloadMeanOutputLength\) be the coefficient of variation of output lengths. For the idealized fixed-width schedule, suppose the longest request in a batch is roughly \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) standard deviations above the mean. The factor \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) is an assumption about the batch rather than a property of the workload, because a larger batch draws more samples and pushes its maximum further into the tail. With immediate refill and unchanged iteration time, the corresponding capacity ratio is:
\[\text{Improvement} \approx \frac{\BatchMaxOutputLength}{\BatchMeanOutputLength} = \frac{\WorkloadMeanOutputLength+ \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\OutputLengthStandardDeviation}{\WorkloadMeanOutputLength} = 1 + \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\cdot \text{CV}\]
where \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) specifies how far the batch maximum lies above the mean, so the expression is a scenario ceiling on the opportunity from filling otherwise unused slots; scheduler overhead, KV-cache pressure, and refill gaps reduce the recovered fraction. In the table that follows, the CV and \(\BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\) columns are inputs, the speedup column is an assumed realized fraction held below the \(1 + \BatchMaximumDeviationMultiple\cdot \text{CV}\) ceiling, and the waste column restates that speedup through \(\text{speedup} \approx 1/(1 - \EffectiveWasteFraction)\). Neither column is a measurement. Together they show how much of the ceiling a scheduler must recover to reach a given gain, which is the quantity a load test should measure. Across workload types, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al. 2020), this accounting yields the scenario rows of table 7.

Continuous batching is most valuable when output lengths are unpredictable, mixed workload types share the same cluster, request volume is high enough to refill vacated slots, and latency SLOs make early completion valuable. It provides minimal benefit when output lengths are uniform, as in classification or embedding generation, when batch sizes are too small for slot reuse to matter, or when request volume is too low to refill vacated slots.
Because arrivals, KV-cache admission, prefill scheduling, and scheduler overhead decide how much vacated capacity is actually recovered, serving teams must compare policies under the same arrival trace, latency objective, and memory budget. The published vLLM system, which pairs iteration-level admission with paged KV allocation, reports 2–4\(\times\) higher throughput at comparable latency than FasterTransformer and Orca on its evaluated workloads (Kwon et al. 2023). That figure compares whole systems rather than isolating slot reuse, because paged allocation also permits larger active batches.



The same variability that makes continuous batching valuable also makes it harder to operate. Memory management must support overlapping request lifetimes. Fixed-membership batching can reserve cache regions when a batch forms and release them together, whereas continuous admission must track which request owns each region and when it becomes reusable, either through fixed-capacity slots that retain unused reservations or through paging with its block tables. Kernels must also handle variable-length sequences and changing batch membership, often by packing short sequences under shared attention masks.
Scheduler work moves into the decode loop as well. A fixed-membership policy checks once per batch whether it is full or its timeout has expired, while continuous admission tracks completions, free cache capacity, and eligible waiting requests at every iteration boundary. That work must stay small relative to a decode step or it erodes the throughput that slot reuse recovers, so engines keep the per-iteration path short and prepare the next iteration’s batch on the host while the accelerator executes the current one. Continuous batching therefore buys its throughput gain with implementation and operating cost, weighed dimension by dimension in table 8.
