title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Admitting a 4,096-token prompt onto a worker that is already streaming replies to thirty users saturates the GPU’s Tensor Cores for hundreds of milliseconds and freezes every active token stream until the prompt finishes. A language-model request is two workloads in sequence. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one forward pass and writes its keys and values into the cache sized in section 10.7.1, while decode extends that cache one token per step until the response ends. Because the two phases run the same weights on opposite sides of the roofline ridge, their asymmetry decides which optimization helps which phase, how a replica schedules them when they share a worker, and whether they should share one at all.


That roofline split comes directly from how many tokens each phase feeds through a linear projection at once. During the prefill phase, the engine computes key-value representations across all prompt tokens (\(\PromptLength\)) concurrently. Because all prompt tokens are processed in parallel, the linear projection GEMM operations operate on large sequence dimensions (\(\GemmRowDimension= \PromptLength\)). For a projection layer with hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), arithmetic intensity scales with prompt length: \[\PrefillArithmeticIntensity\approx \frac{2 \cdot \PromptLength\cdot \HiddenDimension^2}{2 \cdot \HiddenDimension^2} = \PromptLength\quad \left[\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{byte of weights loaded}}\right]\] A 1,024-token prompt therefore performs about 1,024 FLOPs per byte of FP16 weights, well past an H100’s FP16 ridge. Under this weight-traffic-only approximation, increasing \(\PromptLength\) beyond the accelerator’s ridge point moves the projection’s roofline ceiling to the compute limit. Reaching that ceiling still depends on kernel efficiency; short prompts, attention, other memory traffic, and communication can limit the complete prefill phase, so prefill as a whole still requires profiling.


↩︎ The ridge point that separates compute-bound from bandwidth-bound execution is established in Roofline model.
In contrast, the subsequent decode phase generates a single token per sequence sequentially, so the GEMM’s row dimension is the number of sequences decoding together, not the prompt length. At batch one the intensity is about 1 FLOP per byte of FP16 weights. At the decode batch sizes this chapter considers, from tens of sequences up to the knee near 80 in notebook 10.2, the arithmetic intensity \(\DecodeArithmeticIntensity\approx \DecodeBatchSize\) stays below the ridge point. This places the weight projections in a memory-bandwidth-bound regime under this approximation. Each decode iteration streams the active weights from HBM and reuses them across the batch, which is why batch size is the decode phase’s control knob. The approximation omits KV-cache reads, which grow with every sequence’s context, so larger batches and longer contexts add bytes to every step and hold decode on the bandwidth slope short of the ridge.



Long-prompt prefill reaches the compute ceiling; decode stays on the bandwidth slope.
The asymmetry also sorts the optimizations by phase. Tiled, IO-aware attention reduces attention’s memory traffic mainly during prefill, because only prefill forms the full prompt-by-prompt score matrix that a tiled kernel avoids writing to HBM (Tiling and IO-aware attention). A decode step has a single query row and no quadratic intermediate; it benefits instead from a fused kernel that reads each cached key and value once and computes scores, softmax, and the weighted sum in one pass. Speculative decoding (section 10.7.6) targets decode alone, and KV-cache quantization reduces decode’s storage and read traffic while its encoding cost begins when prefill writes the cache. Precision helps both phases through different mechanisms. A weight-activation format raises the compute ceiling that long-prompt prefill reaches, while low-bit weights shrink the bytes that weight-dominated decode streams (section 10.9). Each gain depends on format and kernel support, conversion overhead, and the costs the change leaves untouched, and each must preserve output quality.
These are properties of each phase in isolation. Once continuous batching admits new prompts onto a worker that is decoding other streams, the asymmetry becomes a scheduling conflict between them, and a replica has two ways to resolve it: interleave the phases on one worker, or give each phase its own pool.



Continuous batching admits work at iteration boundaries, yet production requests arrive with widely disparate prompt lengths. Admitting a long prompt in one piece holds the worker for its entire compute-bound prefill while the bandwidth-bound decode streams beside it wait.

Definition 10.5: Chunked prefill
Chunked prefill is an LLM serving mechanism that divides long prompt evaluations into discrete token chunks of size at most \(\PrefillChunkSize\), interleaving prefill computation with ongoing decode iterations within a shared token budget.

Significance: It limits the prompt-decode interference problem where monolithic prefills stall active decode streams for hundreds of milliseconds, giving the scheduler control over how much prefill work can lengthen the TBT of active streams. Meeting interactive streaming service-level objectives (SLOs) still requires measuring the resulting tail latency.
Distinction: Unlike continuous batching with monolithic prefill (which prefills each prompt in one uninterrupted pass before the worker returns to decoding), chunked prefill treats prefill as a multi-step iterative process co-scheduled alongside memory-bound decode tokens.
Common pitfall: Sizing the chunk budget \(\PrefillChunkSize\) too small incurs kernel launch and attention mask overheads, degrading overall prefill throughput. Sizing it too large allows prefill compute to monopolize execution time, causing TBT tail spikes.



With an unchunked prefill policy, the scheduler runs an incoming prompt through the whole model before returning to decode work. The interference comes from scheduling that whole operation without interleaving other requests’ decode steps, and the delay lands in the TBT of requests already decoding on the same worker. A long response can dilute an isolated stall in its average TPOT even though the user sees a conspicuous gap, so prioritizing the new prompt’s time to first token can consume the streaming-latency budget of requests already decoding. The measured prefill duration and the endpoint’s TBT target determine whether interleaving is necessary.


To limit this interference, chunked prefill (definition 10.5, used by Sarathi-Serve (Agrawal et al. 2024)) partitions prompts into chunks of at most \(\PrefillChunkSize\) tokens. A candidate range such as \(256\text{--}512\) tokens must be tested against the model, hardware, and streaming deadline rather than treated as a universal setting. A prompt of length \(\PromptLength\) requires at least \(\lceil \PromptLength/ \PrefillChunkSize\rceil\) scheduling iterations; a smaller residual token budget can require more.
The two schedules in figure 13 hand the same long prompt to the same worker. Run whole, its prefill sits between two decode steps of every active stream, so each stream’s token gap stretches to the full prefill time. Split into chunks, the prompt advances one chunk per hybrid iteration beside the streams’ decode tokens, so each stream waits at most one hybrid iteration, while the prompt’s own first token arrives later than it would have under the monolithic schedule.






Figure 13: Chunked Prefill Trades One Prompt’s TTFT for Every Stream’s TBT: Three streams decode while a long prompt P arrives; the timing is illustrative. (a) A monolithic prefill runs P’s whole prompt in one pass, and every active stream stalls for its full duration. (b) Chunked prefill gives P one chunk per hybrid iteration beside the streams’ decode tokens, so each stream’s gap shrinks to one hybrid iteration, and P’s first token arrives later. Chunking changes when the prefill work runs, not how much of it there is.



In each iteration, the scheduler constructs a hybrid batch combining active decode requests with prefill chunks under a global iteration token budget \(\IterationTokenBudget\), a count of tokens rather than a time, as formulated in equation 8:
\[\DecodeBatchSize+ \sum_{\PrefillRequestIndex \in \ActivePrefillRequestSet} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex} \le \IterationTokenBudget \tag{8}\]
where \(\DecodeBatchSize\) is the number of active decode tokens and \(\PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex}\) is the number of prompt tokens allocated to waiting prefill request \(\PrefillRequestIndex\), so every term counts tokens. The simplified loop assumes admission control reserves sufficient KV-cache capacity and a future decode slot for each admitted request, keeping the decode count within the iteration budget even after prefills are promoted. Each waiting request contributes at most one chunk per iteration, with its committed prompt offset unchanged until execution completes. Algorithm 3 formalizes this iteration-level hybrid scheduling loop.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Chunked prefill and hybrid batch scheduler}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require waiting prefill queue $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}$; active decode set $\mathcal{D}$; iteration token budget $N_{\text{budget}}$; maximum chunk size $C_{\text{chunk}}$
\Ensure generated tokens for decode requests; incremental KV-cache construction for prefills
\While{serving engine is active}
    \State $B_{\text{dec}} \gets |\mathcal{D}|$
    \State $N_{\text{rem}} \gets N_{\text{budget}} - B_{\text{dec}}$
    \State $\mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}} \gets \emptyset$
    \For{each $R_i$ in a snapshot of $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}$, in queue order}
        \If{$N_{\text{rem}} > 0$}
            \State $o_i \gets R_i.\text{offset}$
            \State $C_i \gets \min(C_{\text{chunk}}, N_{\text{rem}}, R_i.\text{prompt\_length} - o_i)$
            \State $\mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}} \gets \mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}} \cup \{(R_i, o_i, C_i)\}$
            \State $N_{\text{rem}} \gets N_{\text{rem}} - C_i$
        \EndIf
    \EndFor
    \State run hybrid forward pass using each prefill slice $R_i[o_i:o_i+C_i]$ and the decode set $\mathcal{D}$
    \State append newly generated tokens for all $R \in \mathcal{D}$
    \State remove completed decode requests from $\mathcal{D}$ and release their KV blocks
    \For{$(R_i, o_i, C_i) \in \mathcal{B}_{\text{prefill}}$}
        \State update prompt offset: $R_i.\text{offset} \gets o_i + C_i$
        \If{$R_i.\text{offset} = R_i.\text{prompt\_length}$}
            \State promote $R_i$ from $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}$ to $\mathcal{D}$
        \EndIf
    \EndFor
\EndWhile
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(\mathcal{Q}_{\text{prefill}}\)




Executing prefill and decode tokens together in shared projection operations amortizes weight loading across both phases, an effect termed decode piggybacking. Alternating separate prefill and decode operations limits scheduling interference but does not by itself establish this weight reuse.
In a small-batch isolated decode step, streaming the model parameters (\(\WeightMemory\) bytes) from HBM to registers achieves low arithmetic intensity because only \(\DecodeBatchSize\) tokens share the weight reads. Memory bandwidth then limits how much work the compute units can sustain, leaving arithmetic capacity available for a larger shared projection.
In a hybrid iteration, the model weights loaded from HBM into on-chip cache and registers are simultaneously reused for both the compute-dense prefill chunks (\(\sum_{\PrefillRequestIndex} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex}\) tokens in total) and the memory-bound decode tokens (\(\DecodeBatchSize\) tokens). Ignoring attention-state traffic, communication, and scheduling overhead gives the projection-only lower-bound estimate in equation 9:
\[\HybridIterationTime\gtrsim \max\left(\frac{\WeightMemory}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}, \frac{2 \cdot (\DecodeBatchSize+ \sum_{\PrefillRequestIndex} \PrefillAllocatedTokenCount_{\PrefillRequestIndex}) \cdot \ActiveParameterCount}{\PeakRate}\right) \tag{9}\]
where \(\ActiveParameterCount\) is the active parameter count, \(\SustainedMemoryBandwidth\) is HBM memory bandwidth, and \(\PeakRate\) is peak accelerator compute throughput. These quantities must describe the same device or shard. Balancing the total prefill token allocation against weight streaming can amortize weight-loading cost across both phases, but this lower bound cannot guarantee \(\HybridIterationTime\le \text{SLO}_{\text{TBT}}\). Chunk sizing must leave room for the omitted costs and be validated against measured tail latency under the intended workload.

Example 10.5: Sarathi: Chunked prefill implementationScenario: An LLM inference server receives a mix of long input prompts (\(10{,}000+\) tokens) and interactive short decode requests (Agrawal et al. 2024).
Diagnosis: When the worker schedules a full long-prompt prefill before returning to decode, that prefill can occupy execution for hundreds of milliseconds and create a TBT spike for active streams.
Systems lesson: Chunking moves the cost of a long prompt rather than removing it. At \(512\) tokens per chunk, a \(10{,}000\)-token prompt needs at least \(\lceil 10{,}000/512 \rceil = 20\) iterations to finish its prefill. With this prompt as the only prefill request, active streams share each decode iteration with at most one of its chunks, while the prompt’s own time to first token stretches across those 20 iterations. Multiple waiting prompts can contribute additional chunks within the total iteration budget. The chunk budget sets that exchange between other streams’ TBT and the long prompt’s TTFT, so it must be tuned against both measured tails.



Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.




Even with chunked prefill, every hybrid step still forces active decode streams to wait while prompt chunks execute on the same GPU, and a single worker pool must compromise between prefill’s compute-heavy parallelism and decode’s bandwidth- and capacity-heavy layout. Disaggregation removes that compromise by giving each phase its own hardware pool, while the KV-cache sizing of section 10.7.1 sets the price of separating them. The cache that prefill builds is the exact payload that the network must hand off to the decode pool.
Disaggregation partitions the serving pipeline into specialized physical tiers (figure 14). In the illustrated long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime, the compute-bound prefill pool and the bandwidth-bound decode pool are joined by a remote direct memory access (RDMA) KV-cache transfer (Zhong et al. 2024). This keeps the phases from competing on one accelerator and permits independent parallelism and capacity plans. The phase asymmetry tells each pool what to buy. The prefill pool wants arithmetic throughput for its compute-bound GEMMs, while the decode pool wants memory bandwidth and capacity for weight streaming and KV cache, which also makes it the natural home for aggressive weight quantization. The transfer and queueing at each pool still add to request latency, and other batch or context sizes can change which resources bind.

Zhong, Yinmin, Shengyu Liu, Junda Chen, Jianbo Hu, Yibo Zhu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin, and Hao Zhang. 2024. “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-Optimized Large Language Model Serving.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), July, 193–210.







Figure 14: Disaggregated Serving Architecture: A long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime separates compute-bound prefill instances from memory-bandwidth-bound decode instances, mediated by RDMA KV-cache transfer. Because prefill sets time to first token and decode sets time per output token, each pool is sized for its own token rate. Other batch and context sizes can change the binding resources.



The disaggregation decision therefore depends on a quantitative contract, not on the phase labels alone. If prefill produces \(\KvCacheMemory\) bytes of attention state and the usable inter-pool bandwidth is \(\LinkBandwidth\), then the handoff consumes at least
\[\KvCacheHandoffTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \frac{\KvCacheMemory}{\LinkBandwidth}, \tag{10}\]
where \(\MessageStartupLatency\) includes transfer setup and queueing for the operating point being evaluated; it is not a fixed network latency once load changes. The payload term sets the scale. A 128K-token request on the GQA model of notebook 10.5 carries tens of gigabytes of KV state, so moving it over a single 450 GB/s NVLink direction takes on the order of a hundred milliseconds, and an inter-node link takes longer still. Spreading the transfer across a tensor-parallel group divides that time only when each device has its own path to its counterpart in the decode pool. Because \(\KvCacheMemory\) grows linearly with prompt length, the long prompts that make disaggregation attractive are also the prompts whose handoff costs most, and that cost lands on TTFT.
Equation 10 therefore makes placement part of the service contract. The prefill pool must sustain the admitted prompt-token rate, the decode pool must sustain the admitted output-token rate, and both pools need headroom for the request-length distribution. Disaggregation justifies its KV-cache transfer cost only when eliminating phase interference and balancing the two pools raises SLO goodput. Otherwise, colocated chunked prefill avoids the additional handoff and pool coordination.
Whether the phases share a worker or split into pools, the base weights remain the largest fixed claim on each device’s memory and, for decode, the largest share of the bytes streamed per step. Weight quantization addresses that part of the budget, with numerical quality and execution cost determining how much of the storage saving becomes useful serving capacity.

Self-Check: Question

Why do the prompt prefill phase and the token decode phase of LLM serving exhibit different performance bottlenecks on the same accelerator?

Prefill generates tokens sequentially one by one, making it memory-bound by weight reads, whereas decode processes all prompt tokens in parallel, making it compute-bound by Tensor Cores
Prefill relies exclusively on integer arithmetic units, whereas decode requires floating-point matrix multiplication units
Long-prompt prefill GEMMs reuse weights across prompt tokens and can have a compute ceiling, whereas weight-dominated single-request decode has low intensity and a bandwidth ceiling
Prefill requires continuous network AllToAll collective exchanges between GPUs, whereas decode requires no inter-GPU communication

How can an un-chunked long prompt prefill delay active decode streams on the same worker, and what trade-off does chunked prefill introduce?
The architectural pattern that decouples LLM inference by executing the compute-bound prompt prefill phase and the bandwidth-bound autoregressive token decode phase on separate, specialized hardware pools is known as ____ serving.
True or False: Because disaggregation removes prefill-decode interference, moving a deployment to separate prefill and decode pools lowers time to first token most for the longest prompts.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
INT4 turns a two-GPU model into a one-GPU candidate.
Keeping a 70B model’s 140 GB of FP16 weights intact forces every replica across at least two 80 GB GPUs and makes every decode step wait on streaming 140 GB from HBM. Weight quantization for serving is therefore a bottleneck-selection decision: reducing precision turns that 140 GB FP16 weight payload into a 35 GB INT4 payload, allowing a model that previously required multiple GPUs to fit on one (perspective 10.3). The ideal payload reduction is 4\(\times\), although metadata, runtime buffers, and KV state still enter the deployment’s memory budget. Because neither quality loss nor speedup is fixed by nominal bit width, both must be measured for the deployed representation and workload.

Systems Perspective 10.3: Quantization as a serving constraintIn serving systems, quantization changes the binding resource as well as the model’s size. Post-training quantization (PTQ) can shrink a deployed model without retraining, while quantization-aware training (QAT) spends training effort to preserve accuracy at lower precision. QAT simulates low-precision rounding in the forward pass and passes gradients through the rounding step as if it were absent, the straight-through estimator (Bengio et al. 2013), so the weights adapt to the error they will carry. It earns that cost only after a PTQ recipe misses the quality budget at the target precision, and a recipe that passes at INT8 says nothing about INT4. The practical order is to deploy with PTQ when it meets quality and reach for QAT, or adapter-based fine-tuning of a quantized base, when it does not, rechecking quality after the final deployment conversion. The systems question is which constraint the lower-precision representation relaxes: GPU memory capacity, HBM bandwidth during decode, accelerator instruction support, or cost per served token.



Bengio, Yoshua, Nicholas Léonard, and Aaron Courville. 2013. “Estimating or Propagating Gradients Through Stochastic Neurons for Conditional Computation.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1308.3432.
Choosing a quantized representation starts with deciding which quantity should shrink: resident weights for fit, bytes moved per decode step for bandwidth, activations for prefill throughput, or the precision path supported by target hardware. Serving at scale also introduces distinct operational constraints: a deployment team may need post-training quantization without the original training corpus, quality must be preserved across diverse inputs, and hardware deployment targets vary from data center GPUs to edge accelerators. Lack of the original corpus does not imply data-free calibration; the methods that follow may still require representative deployment inputs. Production inference therefore starts from a decision model rather than from the methods. Table 11 ties each method family to the serving constraint it relaxes; what changes for each when it is deployed is its calibration cost, kernel path, and the evaluation a serving team must run.



Table 11: Serving Quantization Decision Model: Quantization methods are useful only when they relax the resource that binds the serving system. The method family follows from the bottleneck: fit, bandwidth, prefill compute, or outlier robustness.











Binding serving constraint
Representation change

Risk to test before rollout

When a single weight or activation channel is ten times larger than its neighbors, uniform per-tensor quantization must either clip that extreme value or stretch its step size across the entire range, collapsing the surrounding small values to zero. Large language models produce such outlier features routinely: in the models studied by Dettmers et al. (2022), about 0.1 percent of hidden dimensions carried activation magnitudes roughly 3–20\(\times\) larger than the rest. Weight tensors face the same damage when a few large weights set the scale for the whole matrix. Block-wise quantization contains that weight-side damage inside the stored format.

Definition 10.6: Block-wise quantization
Block-wise quantization is an ML quantization scheme that partitions a weight tensor into nonoverlapping groups of \(\QuantizationBlockSize\) elements and assigns each group its own scale. An affine scheme uses \(\QuantizationScale_i = (\BlockRangeMaximum- \BlockRangeMinimum) / (2^\NumericBitWidth- 1)\) together with an offset or zero point; a symmetric scheme centers the range at zero and needs only scale metadata. The metadata examples below assume symmetric scale-only quantization.

Significance: With block size \(\QuantizationBlockSize = 64\) and \(\NumericBitWidth= 4\) bits, weights compress from 16 bits to 4 bits (a 4\(\times\) memory reduction) while each FP16 scale adds \(16/64 = 0.25\) bits per weight. This yields an effective bit-width of \(4.25\) bits per weight: 6.25 percent overhead relative to the INT4 payload, or about 1.6 percent of the original FP16 weight size.
Distinction: Unlike per-tensor quantization, which applies a single scale across the entire weight matrix, block-wise quantization contains outlier damage within individual blocks. Per-tensor scaling forces that scale to accommodate outlier values, which wastes precision on the majority of near-zero weights. A single extreme value therefore cannot degrade quantization fidelity for the whole tensor.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that block size is a free hyperparameter. Smaller blocks (\(\QuantizationBlockSize = 32\)) can improve local range resolution but double the scale metadata overhead vs. \(\QuantizationBlockSize = 64\). At \(\QuantizationBlockSize = 16\), the scale adds 1 bit per weight: 25 percent overhead relative to the INT4 payload, or 6.25 percent of the original FP16 weight size. The effect on model quality and kernel speed must be evaluated rather than inferred from block size alone.



The metadata price stays small across formats. An INT8 scheme with one FP32 scale per 128 weights adds \(32/128 = 0.25\) bits per weight, about 3 percent of its payload. Block-wise scaling therefore isolates outliers without the bandwidth penalty of a higher-precision format, which keeps the decode traffic saving of a low-bit format intact. Figure 15 isolates this dynamic-range protection across an eight-weight sample containing a single outlier (\(58.7\)). Under per-tensor scaling (left), the outlier dictates a coarse scale factor (\(\QuantizationScale\approx 0.462\)) that forces six of the seven small weights to round to zero. Partitioning the tensor into four-element blocks (right) confines that coarse scale to the second block, allowing the uncorrupted first block to adopt a fine scale (\(\QuantizationScale_1 \approx 0.00165\)) that preserves full INT8 resolution.






Figure 15: Block-Wise versus Per-Tensor Quantization: Under per-tensor scaling (left), one outlier weight sets the scale for the whole tensor, so six of the seven small weights round to zero and the seventh rounds to one. Under block-wise quantization (right), each group of weights gets its own scale: the block without the outlier keeps full INT8 resolution, while the small weights that share the outlier’s block are still crushed. Smaller blocks confine the damage further at the cost of more scale metadata.






Block-wise scaling handles weight outliers inside the stored format. The outlier activation problem is harder, because activations arrive at run time and their extreme channels cannot be rescaled offline block by block. A coarse scale loses resolution for smaller values, while a narrow range clips large ones. This trade-off is not unique to language models, but its channel structure motivates the methods below.
For a serving deployment the consequence is that no single INT8 scale suits both the outlier channels and the typical values. The method families therefore differ in which part of the serving contract they protect, at which stage they pay for it, and what they cost to deploy. LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al. 2022) pays at run time. It detects outlier dimensions against a magnitude threshold, multiplies them in FP16 and the rest in INT8, and sums the two products. This preserves quality at the cost of outlier detection and a second execution path on every step.

Dettmers, Tim, Mike Lewis, Younes Belkada, and Luke Zettlemoyer. 2022. “LLM.int8(): 8-Bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 30318–32. https://doi.org/10.52202/068431-2198.

Frantar, Elias, Saleh Ashkboos, Torsten Hoefler, and Dan Alistarh. 2023. “GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-Trained Transformers.” In CoRR, abs/2210.17323. https://doi.org/10.48550/ARXIV.2210.17323.

Lin, Ji, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, Wei-Ming Chen, Wei-Chen Wang, Guangxuan Xiao, Xingyu Dang, Chuang Gan, and Song Han. 2024. “AWQ: Activation-Aware Weight Quantization for on-Device LLM Compression and Acceleration.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 6: 87–100.
GPTQ (Frantar et al. 2023) and AWQ (Lin et al. 2024) pay offline and both produce 4-bit weight-only artifacts. GPTQ quantizes a layer’s weights in sequence and adjusts the still-unquantized weights to compensate for the error already introduced, guided by a second-order estimate from calibration activations of how sensitive the layer’s output is to each weight. AWQ instead protects the salient weights, those that multiply large activations, because a small rounding error on a weight channel that multiplies a large activation produces a large output error. Multiplying those salient weight channels by a scale factor greater than one before group quantization forces them to span a larger portion of the shared 4-bit integer grid, reducing their relative rounding error while an inverse scale is applied to the corresponding input activations. Both methods need representative calibration inputs and supported packing kernels, a reconstruction objective that is only a proxy for task quality, and a comparison at the same model, bit budget, and held-out evaluation. AWQ also needs its inverse scales fused into the preceding layer of the deployed graph, or it spends part of the latency saving on an extra runtime operation.
SmoothQuant (Xiao et al. 2023) targets low-precision matrix multiplication rather than weight-only storage and pays in a preprocessing transform. It divides each activation channel by a smoothing factor and multiplies the matching weights by the same factor. This leaves the product unchanged before rounding and migrates part of the extreme activation range into the weights, so that both tensors can fit inside INT8 for W8A8 execution. That matters for compute-bound prefill, although shrinking the activation range stretches the weight range and makes the weights harder to quantize. The smoothing factor therefore balances the two quantization errors, and production activation extremes can still differ from the calibration ranges. Rotation-based methods such as QuaRot (Ashkboos et al. 2024) apply orthogonal Hadamard transforms that spread large coordinates across channels, which makes W4A4 a serving candidate at the price of some online rotation work.

Xiao, Guangxuan, Ji Lin, Mickaël Seznec, Hao Wu, Julien Demouth, and Song Han. 2023. “SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models.” International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 38087–99.

Ashkboos, Saleh, Amirkeivan Mohtashami, Maximilian L. Croci, Bo Li, Pashmina Cameron, Martin Jaggi, Dan Alistarh, Torsten Hoefler, and James Hensman. 2024. “QuaRot: Outlier-Free 4-Bit Inference in Rotated LLMs.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 100213–40. https://doi.org/10.52202/079017-3180.
None of these properties fixes quality. Each artifact must be compared with the FP16 baseline on the same model, evaluation data, and runtime, reporting its calibration set, group size, kernel path, and any online-transform overhead. Its serving benefit must also be measured as SLO-compliant throughput on the target workload rather than inferred from nominal bit width.



Quantizing only the weights (W8A16 or W4A16) cuts weight traffic during decode but leaves compute-bound prefill executing on FP16 Tensor Cores at unchanged arithmetic speed, whereas quantizing both weights and activations (W8A8) risks accuracy loss from activation outliers without further shrinking weight bytes. The prefill-decode split therefore decides which path can pay: both schemes shrink the weights, but only W8A8 changes the arithmetic ceiling. Table 12 bounds what each 8-bit path can buy relative to the FP16 baseline.



Table 12: W8A8 SmoothQuant vs. Weight-Only Quantization: Ceilings derived from bytes per weight and the H100’s INT8-to-FP16 peak ratio, not measured speedups. Both schemes halve weight bytes, so both can at most halve weight traffic in bandwidth-bound decode. Only W8A8 moves prefill onto INT8 Tensor Cores. Realized gains and quality loss depend on kernels, calibration, and the request mix.

The distinction is which ceiling binds. Among these configurations, W8A8 enables INT8 matrix multiplication, with the illustrated 2× peak ratio providing a compute ceiling rather than a measured prefill speedup. Both quantized schemes halve the weight payload. If weight reads dominate decode, activation quantization does not further reduce that traffic, although it can change other memory and compute costs. Quantization and dequantization also add work. The end-to-end benefit therefore depends on the prompt/output mix, batch sizes, and measured execution path.
Hardware and software support decide which of these savings reach the serving workload, because the arithmetic format and the resident storage format need not be identical. A common INT4 weight-only kernel reads packed weights and dequantizes them to FP16 on chip during the GEMM, so it cuts weight capacity and read traffic without any INT4 arithmetic. For batch-one decode dominated by weight reads, throughput then scales roughly as memory bandwidth divided by the model’s weight bytes, omitting KV-cache traffic and execution overhead, and leaving the arithmetic in FP16 costs little because arithmetic is not the binding term. At large batch or in prefill, where execution approaches the compute ceiling, the gain comes instead from a weight-activation format, W8A8 or FP8 on hardware with FP8 Tensor Cores, which raises the ceiling that weight-only formats cannot move. In the ideal memory-bound case, 4-bit weights cut weight traffic by 4\(\times\), but realized decode throughput depends on kernel support, dequantization overhead, KV-cache precision, batch shape, and whether HBM bandwidth is truly the bottleneck. A serving system can therefore run different formats at different operating points, with each configuration evaluated against the same quality criterion and its own latency targets, and the value of 4-bit serving is strongest when it increases model residency or batch capacity.



Loading a 4-bit checkpoint into a serving runtime that expands the weights back into resident FP16 tensors at startup or falls back to unoptimized kernels forfeits both the memory capacity and the HBM bandwidth savings before a single request arrives. Production serving frameworks determine whether a quantized artifact retains its intended advantages by converting packed weights inside the execution kernel rather than in HBM. The serving stack must therefore report the resident representation and kernel path, budget KV state around actual allocations, and expose quality and latency regressions (table 13).



Table 13: Quantized Serving Runtime Contract: Framework-specific APIs differ, but every production path has to preserve representation, choose supported kernels, plan memory, and validate quality under the deployed traffic mix.









Runtime responsibility
Why it matters




Preserve the quantized artifact
Full-model expansion into resident FP16 forfeits the reduced weight storage and traffic.


Select compatible low-precision kernels
Unsupported operators fall back to slower or higher-precision execution.


Plan memory around weights and KV cache
The capacity gain matters only if the freed memory becomes useful batch headroom.


Validate quality and latency together
A lower-bit path that meets latency but fails task quality is not a serving win.






Weight quantization reduces the weight allocation, while PagedAttention reduces waste in allocating KV state. Both feed the same admission budget as the capacity estimator of notebook 10.5, with quantized weights in place of FP16 ones. That estimate is optimistic, because a usable integer limit must round down after reserving runtime buffers, quantization metadata, and safety headroom, and sharded deployments must satisfy the budget on every device.
This comparison uses a conservative decimal HBM budget matching the A100 nameplate label, rather than the registered byte capacity used by the node estimator. A 70B model with 4-bit weights requires approximately 35 GB, leaving 45 GB on an 80 GB A100 for KV cache. With FP16 KV cache at about 2.6 GB per 1K-token sequence for the MHA baseline, this supports about 17 concurrent 1K-token sequences before other runtime overheads. With FP16 weights, the same 70B model would not fit on one A100 at all, so weight-only quantization changes both feasibility and batch capacity.



Choosing a quantization format from datasheet TFLOPS or nominal bit width alone fails when a 4-bit checkpoint degrades task accuracy on production prompts or when a smaller replica completes fewer SLO-compliant tokens per GPU. The final selection must satisfy memory, quality, and latency requirements together. Native support makes a precision path a candidate without establishing the model’s quality at that precision, and no universal quality ordering separates 4-bit weight-only from 8-bit weight-and-activation quantization, so both are evaluated against the same task baseline. For compute-bound prefill, W8A8 offers the illustrated 2× INT8 compute ceiling; for decode dominated by weight reads, W4A16 can cut the weight payload by up to 4\(\times\), provided conversion and other costs leave a useful saving.
These precision choices affect cost per million useful tokens. The A100 residency calculation explains why fewer GPUs become possible at all, because INT4 weights shrink the resident payload enough for a 70B replica to fit on fewer devices. Table 14 isolates the effect of GPU count by assuming equal per-GPU prices and the same completed token rate across three configurations. Under that contract, reducing the number of billed GPUs reduces cost proportionally. The calculation does not establish that the smaller replicas sustain the same rate or meet the same quality and latency targets.



Table 14: Quantization Impact on Serving Cost: Estimated cost per million tokens at three configurations. At equal unit prices and unchanged useful token throughput, halving the GPU count halves the cost; halving it again brings the per-million-token cost to one quarter of the FP16 baseline. The cost savings come almost entirely from fewer GPUs rather than from per-GPU throughput gains.

The illustrated 2–4\(\times\) cost reduction follows from the assumed device-count reduction at unchanged useful throughput. If the smaller replica completes fewer qualifying tokens per second, cost per token falls by less and can increase. A deployment comparison must therefore combine billed replica cost with measured SLO-compliant output under the same quality contract.
Precision moves the capacity wall without removing it. A 175-billion-parameter model still needs about 87.5 GB for its 4-bit weight payload alone, more than one 80 GB H100 holds before KV state and runtime allocations. Keeping that representation accelerator-resident requires distributing it across devices. Offloading to host memory is another placement choice, but introduces transfers that must fit the latency budget. Sharding addresses the capacity problem while adding communication and coordination to each replica.

Self-Check: Question

How does SmoothQuant enable efficient 8-bit weight and 8-bit activation (W8A8) inference, and why is its speedup significantly higher during prefill than during decode?

It prunes 50% of model weights using structured sparsity, accelerating decode but having no effect on prefill.
It divides activations by a per-channel scale \(s\) and multiplies weights by \(s\), moving quantization difficulty toward weights; compute-bound prefill can benefit from native INT8 arithmetic while decode remains sensitive to memory traffic
It rotates the coordinate basis using randomized Walsh-Hadamard matrices, eliminating memory bandwidth bottlenecks during decode.
It converts floating-point weights into binary spikes, enabling single-cycle bitwise operations during token generation.

True or False: In block-wise INT4 quantization with one FP16 scale per block, reducing the block size from 64 to 16 weights can improve local range resolution but quadruples the scale metadata, from 0.25 bits per weight (6.25 percent overhead on the INT4 payload) to 1.0 bit per weight (25 percent overhead).
GPTQ and AWQ both produce 4-bit weight-only artifacts offline. How do they differ, and what extra deployment step does AWQ need?

GPTQ quantizes activations while AWQ quantizes weights; AWQ needs no calibration data.
GPTQ compensates rounding error with approximate second-order information, while AWQ scales salient channels chosen from activation statistics; AWQ’s scales must be fused into the deployed graph or they cost an extra runtime operation.
GPTQ requires full retraining while AWQ is applied at runtime; AWQ needs a second GPU to hold its scales.
Both methods are identical except for bit width; AWQ needs its weights stored in FP32.

Explain what a rotation-based method such as QuaRot changes before quantization, what that makes possible for serving, and what it costs at run time.

Test the method family’s specific risk (calibration mismatch, kernel support, activation outliers, or transform overhead) before rollout
Identify which resource binds the serving system: memory fit, decode bandwidth, prefill compute, or outlier robustness
Choose the method family that makes that change
Choose the representation change that relaxes that resource

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
When a deployment must retain a 70B model’s 140 GB of FP16 weights in accelerator memory, or when a 175B model’s 87.5 GB INT4 weight payload still exceeds a single 80 GB GPU, no single accelerator can hold the replica. Where quantization shrinks the representation, sharding keeps it intact and divides it across multiple GPUs that execute together as one logical replica. The resulting design adapts tensor and pipeline parallelism from training, but must evaluate their communication and scheduling costs against per-request inference deadlines.


A single-GPU replica fails when model weights overflow its HBM capacity or when its serial forward pass takes too long to meet the endpoint’s TTFT and TPOT targets. Model sharding addresses the memory and latency rows of table 1 through different mechanisms, and the timing analysis below determines whether parallel execution repays its communication cost.
The first driver is memory capacity. If the selected representation must remain in accelerator memory but does not fit on one device, the replica needs multiple devices. For a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters at precision \(\NumericBitWidth\) bits, equation 11 gives the weight payload before metadata and runtime state:
\[\WeightMemory = \Parameters\times \frac{\NumericBitWidth}{8} \text{ bytes} \tag{11}\]
Applied to the 70B model in FP16 (16 bits), equation 11 recovers the payload quoted since section 10.2. Each parameter occupies two bytes, so the unquantized checkpoint alone requires:
\[M_{\text{weights}} = 7 \times 10^{10} \times \frac{16}{8} = 140 \text{ GB}\]
The result exceeds the 80 GB capacity of an H100 GPU, establishing a weight-only lower bound of 2 shards for an accelerator-resident replica. KV state, buffers, replication within the chosen partition, and uneven placement can require a larger degree.
The second driver is latency. Even when a model fits in memory, sharding can reduce latency by parallelizing computation. Equation 12 is the Fleet Law (equation 1.3) applied to a single inference request, separating the compute term that sharding divides from the communication and synchronization terms it adds:
\[\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount) = \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\DeviceCount} + \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) + \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime \tag{12}\]
where \(\DeviceCount\) is the number of devices in the sharding group, \(\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\) is the communication overhead, \(\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)\) is synchronization overhead, and \(\OverlappedTime\) is communication hidden behind useful compute. In the common no-overlap simplification with negligible extra synchronization, this reduces to \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount+ \CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)\). Sharding provides latency benefit only when the nonoverlapped overhead is smaller than the time saved through parallelization.



Splitting every linear projection independently across GPUs would force an AllReduce synchronization after every matrix multiplication, stalling decode on interconnect latency. Tensor parallelism (Shoeybi et al. 2019) avoids half of those collectives by splitting each layer with the column-row partitioning developed for training. This keeps the activation between paired linear layers local and costs two AllReduce operations per transformer block, one after attention and one after the feed-forward sublayer.

Shoeybi, Mohammad, Mostofa Patwary, Raul Puri, Patrick LeGresley, Jared Casper, and Bryan Catanzaro. 2019. “Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1909.08053.

↩︎ Column-row tensor partitioning and its two AllReduce operations per transformer block are established in Tensor parallelism.

The attention computation partitions across heads, so with \(\AttentionHeadCount\) heads and tensor-parallel degree \(\TensorParallelDegree\) each device computes attention for \(\AttentionHeadCount/\TensorParallelDegree\) of them when the head count divides evenly. The KV cache is sharded with the heads, so each device stores cache only for its own heads. A multi-head attention layout spreads many KV heads across the group, while grouped-query attention with eight KV heads leaves one per device in an eight-way group.
8-way tensor parallelism, 64 KV heads (MHA):
Device 0: KV cache for heads 0-7
Device 1: KV cache for heads 8-15
...
Device 7: KV cache for heads 56-63
Cross-device reuse requires compatible cache content and placement. Matching tensor-parallel configurations can align the head partitions, but the receiver must also use the same model state, prefix inputs, cache representation, and logical token positions. A different partition requires redistribution rather than direct shard reuse. Equal parallelism degree alone does not establish cache validity.
Each device applies its shard of the attention output projection to its local heads, and an AllReduce sums the projected partial outputs; its latency includes collective startup and coordination as well as payload transfer. Figure 16 traces the resulting two synchronization points per layer across two GPU ranks.






Figure 16: Tensor Parallelism for Inference: Computation is distributed across devices by splitting tensor operations. Attention heads are partitioned across GPUs, requiring an AllReduce operation to synchronize results. Feed-forward networks use a column-row splitting strategy that requires only one AllReduce synchronization per block. This partition can reduce latency when saved compute exceeds communication cost, which is why the two collectives run over a fast local interconnect.



The inference time with tensor parallelism follows equation 13:
\[\TensorParallelLayerTime= \frac{\IronLawComputeTime}{\TensorParallelDegree} + 2 \times \AllReduceCompletionTime(\CollectivePayloadSize) \tag{13}\]
Equation 13 is the per-layer instance of equation 12. Here \(\IronLawComputeTime\) is now the sequential compute time of one layer, and \(\CollectivePayloadSize\) is the full activation payload each rank contributes to each AllReduce, priced by the ring cost model of Ring AllReduce. Compute divides ideally across ranks, but the reduced activation keeps its full shape, (tokens in the step) \(\times\) (hidden width) \(\times\) (bytes per element), and the factor of 2 counts the attention and feed-forward collectives (example 10.6). When a model spans multiple nodes without high-bandwidth NVLink across every rank, those two per-layer collectives become prohibitively expensive, motivating inter-layer pipeline partitioning instead.


↩︎ Hiding tensor-parallel collectives behind compute on one node, and what that overlap can and cannot recover, is established in Tensor-parallel collectives under contention.

Example 10.6: Tensor parallelism for Llama-70BScenario: An engineering team deploys Llama-70B (70B parameters, FP16 footprint 140 GB) across an 8-GPU H100 node with NVLink (Touvron et al. 2023).
Diagnosis: The calculation assumes 30 ms of serial layer compute as a reference, independent of the devices required to hold the weights: 12 ms for attention and 18 ms for the feed-forward block. That reference describes a long-prompt prefill, in which every prompt token passes through the layer in one step, so it is far larger than one layer’s share of a decode step on the reference replica. Ideal eight-way division gives 1.5 ms and 2.25 ms, and the two AllReduce operations of equation 13 add an assumed 0.3 ms each, for 4.35 ms per layer.
Systems lesson: The illustrative eight-way model gives a 6.9× reduction relative to its serial-compute reference (prefill time reduced from 2,400 ms to 348 ms). The entire shortfall from the ideal 8\(\times\) is the two collectives, a fixed cost per layer that dividing compute cannot shrink. Their share of the layer therefore grows as per-device compute falls, which is why a decode step, with far less compute per layer than this prefill reference, feels the collective cost most.



Touvron, Hugo, Louis Martin, Kevin Stone, Peter Albert, Amjad Almahairi, Yasmine Babaei, Nikolay Bashlykov, et al. 2023. “Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.09288.



Splitting an 80-layer model sequentially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle during an isolated request and does nothing to shorten its forward pass. Pipeline parallelism distributes layers across devices so each stage runs a contiguous subset of layers and passes activations to the next stage without intra-layer synchronization.
For inference, pipeline parallelism creates bubbles differently than in training. Executing an isolated request serially across four GPU stages leaves three accelerators idle at every step, whereas maintaining multiple in-flight requests fills the pipeline and amortizes the initial bubble across steady-state token delivery (figure 17).







Figure 17: Pipeline Parallelism Bubbles: (a) An 80-layer model split into four stages passes one request’s activations from stage to stage, so splitting the layers alone does not shorten its sequential computation; it must still traverse all four stages. (b) With many requests in flight, later stages idle during the fill bubble, and from slot t4 onward every stage is busy and one request leaves the pipeline per slot. Pipeline parallelism therefore suits throughput-oriented serving better than latency-critical interactive serving.



For a single request, pipeline staging does not parallelize the dependent layers. If stage execution times are unchanged, the request still pays their sum plus transfers, so staging alone provides no execution-latency reduction. A comparison against a memory-constrained implementation that offloads weights can differ because keeping stages resident changes those execution costs.
Pipeline parallelism instead scales throughput by sustaining multiple concurrent requests across execution stages, as tracked in the steady-state schedule of figure 17(b). Once the pipeline reaches saturation, throughput is limited by the slowest stage. For \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) balanced stages with negligible transfer overhead, this is \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) times the throughput of executing the whole model sequentially on one device, not \(\PipelineParallelDegree\) times a single stage’s throughput. An individual request still traverses every stage, so its execution latency remains approximately the sum of the stage times.
Pipeline parallelism therefore suits inference when memory forces sharding but latency targets are relaxed, when aggregate throughput matters more than individual request latency, or when the interconnect handles point-to-point transfers better than fast AllReduce. The two sharding approaches differ in single-request latency, throughput, communication pattern, activation memory, and implementation complexity (table 15).



Table 15: Pipeline vs. Tensor Parallelism: Key trade-offs between layer-internal tensor splitting (can reduce single-request latency when compute savings exceed collective cost) and inter-layer pipeline staging (overlaps concurrent requests but introduces pipeline bubbles). Throughput is relative to sequential execution of the whole model on one device; per-layer AllReduces keep tensor parallelism below the \(\TensorParallelDegree\times\) ideal, and balanced, full pipelines approach \(\PipelineParallelDegree\times\).

The decision starts with capacity feasibility and then compares latency and throughput on the available topology. Neither a fast interconnect nor a relaxed deadline alone establishes the best choice; the request mix and measured execution costs determine the useful partition.



An MoE model activates only a small fraction of its parameters per token, yet replicating the entire expert pool on every GPU quickly exhausts device memory. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models such as DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI 2025) and Mixtral (Jiang et al. 2024) replace each feed-forward network with parallel expert sub-networks and a lightweight router that selects a few experts per token, growing parameter capacity without proportionally growing expert arithmetic per token. Routing, shared layers, and communication still add work. Expert parallelism places different experts on different GPUs to distribute their storage and execution when the model and workload exceed a single device.

DeepSeek-AI. 2025. “Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures.” Proceedings of the 52nd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture, 1731–45. https://doi.org/10.1145/3695053.3731412.

Jiang, A. Q., A. Sablayrolles, A. Roux, A. Mensch, B. Savary, C. Bamford, D. S. Chaplot, et al. 2024. “Mixtral of Experts.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2401.04088.


MoE serving separates two capacity measures. The total parameter count sets the weight-storage requirement at the chosen precision, while the active parameter count estimates the weight-related arithmetic and traffic for each token. Neither count includes all runtime costs. An accelerator-resident deployment must accommodate inactive experts as well as active ones, even though each token uses only a subset.
The following comparison isolates weight-related costs at batch size 1. Streaming all weights of a dense 400B FP16 model moves 800 GB per step. Counting only DeepSeek-V3’s 37B active parameters gives approximately 74 GB in FP16, a 10.8× reduction in weight bytes per token. The proportional estimate of weight-related arithmetic is 10.8× lower. These are payload and arithmetic comparisons, not equivalent-quality model comparisons or measured speedups; cache traffic, expert placement, routing, and communication affect realized latency.



MoE keeps every expert resident but activates few per token.
The trade-off is resident capacity: keeping all experts on accelerators avoids fetching inactive experts when routing changes. Offloading can reduce that resident footprint but adds transfer and scheduling costs. DeepSeek-V3’s full model in FP16 requires approximately 1342 GB, requiring many devices if the entire FP16 weight set remains accelerator-resident.

Napkin Math 10.8: MoE capacity planningThis comparison uses a conservative decimal budget of 80 GB per GPU, matching the H100 nameplate label rather than the registered byte capacity used by the node estimator.
Problem: A team deploys DeepSeek-V3 (671B total parameters, 37B active per token) for a chatbot application. The model uses FP8 weights (1 byte per parameter). The cluster has 8-GPU nodes, each with 8\(\times\) H100 GPUs (80 GB HBM per GPU, 640 GB per node). How many nodes are needed, and what is the per-token decode latency?
Math:

Memory: Total weight memory = 671 GB. A single node (640 GB) is insufficient. 2 provide 1,280 GB in aggregate. The remaining capacity must still accommodate KV state, metadata, buffers, and any replicated weights on each device.
Latency: Count 37B active parameters (37 GB) per decode step. If their reads were evenly distributed across 16 GPUs, each would read about 2.3 GB. At the stated 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth, \(\PerDeviceWeightReadTime\approx\) 0.69 ms. The scenario adds 0.3 ms for routing. Expert placement and token routing do not guarantee this balance, especially at batch size 1.
Floor: The simplified sum is \(\approx\) 1.0 ms/token, corresponding to 1,000 tokens/s at batch size 1 under these assumptions. It is an optimistic estimate, not a measured rate or a rigorous latency bound; compute, KV traffic, synchronization, and imbalance remain unmodeled.

Systems insight: Sparse activation separates resident parameter capacity from the work selected for one token. Planning an accelerator-resident 671B model therefore requires both a per-device memory budget and a timing model for the actual expert placement. Dividing total active bytes by device count does not establish that every device can contribute bandwidth equally.





Expert parallelism carries over from training unchanged in mechanism. Each GPU holds a subset of experts, and each token travels to the devices holding the experts its gate selects. What changes in serving is who pays for imbalance, because an overloaded expert now delays live requests rather than a training step. In an MoE layer, a gating network selects \(\RoutedExpertCount\) of the \(\ExpertCount\) experts for each token and sums their outputs weighted by its gate probabilities. An even expert placement assigns each device \(\ExpertCount/\DeviceCount\) experts, where \(\DeviceCount\) is the number of expert-parallel devices, and each token then makes the round trip of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) AllToAll Routing. One AllToAll dispatches its representation to the ranks hosting its experts, and a second returns their outputs for the weighted sum.
The communication pattern differs from tensor parallelism. AllReduce delivers one combined result to every device, so per-link traffic is fixed by the message size. Expert parallelism uses AllToAll to deliver different routed tokens to different devices, so link and receiver load depend on the router’s choices, and the host of a popular expert becomes an incast point whose completion time the other hosts wait on. Balancing the number of stored experts does not balance token traffic.
Serving inherits training’s balance controls without their guarantees. The auxiliary balancing loss shapes routing on training data, not on future traffic. The expert capacity factor caps accepted tokens per expert (1.25\(\times\) is an illustrative setting), leaving the server to decide what happens to the excess. Dropping or rerouting it changes the model computation and needs quality validation, while expert buffering retains it at the cost of latency and queue capacity.


↩︎ The capacity factor, the auxiliary load-balancing loss, and the hot-expert skew they bound during training are established in Expert parallelism (mixture of experts).



Router behavior affects both system performance and model quality. Expert collapse during training concentrates traffic on a few experts, and at serving time a shifted input distribution can create hotspots without any change to the stored model. Token dropping under a capacity limit makes the computation differ from the uncapped model, so its quality impact must be evaluated together with any throughput gain. Because routing selects experts dynamically,5 the routing pattern becomes a systems workload rather than only a model-internal choice.
5 MoE (mixture-of-experts) serving trade-off: Only a subset of experts activates per token (2 of 8 in Mixtral, 8 of 256 routed experts in DeepSeek-V3). Keeping all weights accelerator-resident gives a total-to-active weight ratio of roughly 3.6× (Mixtral) to 18× (DeepSeek-V3). Expert parallelism distributes that storage while adding token-routing communication; offloading is an alternative that trades resident capacity for weight transfers.
Example 10.7: Expert parallelism for Mixtral-8x7BScenario: Mixtral-8x7B (46.7B total parameters, ~12.9B active per token) is served across a 4-GPU group using top-2 routing.
Diagnosis: Replicating all 8 experts on every GPU requires the full 93.4 GB FP16 weight set per device, more than one 80 GB H100 holds. Placing 2 experts on each GPU (4-way expert parallelism) cuts each device’s share to about 25.8 GB, the shared attention layers plus its local experts. Every MoE layer, however, now needs an AllToAll dispatch and gather to move tokens to the devices that hold their selected experts.
Systems lesson: Expert parallelism trades AllToAll communication for per-GPU parameter memory. The trade pays only when the collective, repeated at every MoE layer, fits inside the decode budget that the smaller resident footprint makes possible.


Expert parallelism couples state placement to input-dependent access. Embedding-heavy recommendation models face a related problem: entity popularity determines which stored vectors receive traffic. Their sharding strategy must therefore balance storage and lookup load, just as expert placement must account for both resident weights and routed tokens.




Production recommendation models carry multi-terabyte embedding tables that cannot fit on any single server and would stall every ranking query if fetched over thousands of serial network hops. Meta’s DLRM reference architecture applies model parallelism to those tables while scaling dense layers separately (Naumov et al. 2019), and serving inherits the row-wise, column-wise, and hybrid layouts that training uses to shard them (Sparse embedding sharding).
What changes at serving time is the constraint the layout answers to. Training shards tables for sparse update throughput, while serving must finish every lookup within a per-request deadline. Popularity skew concentrates lookups on the shards that own hot keys, and under a latency SLO the slowest of those shards sets the tail of every request that touches it. Serving layouts therefore replicate or column-partition hot entries even at extra storage cost, keep the cold tail row-sharded, and batch lookups by destination shard so that one request does not wait on thousands of sequential round trips.
The following Archetype B scenario combines row-wise, column-wise, and hybrid sharding. The 100 TB platform-wide resident budget deliberately sits well above the 10 TB-plus embedding tables of a single Archetype B model, so that the sharding arithmetic is stressed at the upper end of the regime.

Lighthouse 10.1: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): Embedding sharding budgetConsider an Archetype B recommendation workload with a large entity catalog and a smaller resident embedding tier:
Scale:

Resident embedding budget (platform-wide): 100 TB
Entity catalog: 10 trillion identifiers
Embedding dimension: 128–256
Shards: 1,000+ servers

The arithmetic of these bullets is the design constraint. A dense INT8 table with 10 trillion entities and 128 dimensions would require at least 1,280 TB, while 100 TB across the same entity count averages only 10 bytes per entity, a fraction of one 128-byte vector. Most entities therefore cannot hold a resident vector at all. The resident tier keeps the frequently accessed subset, and the long tail lives in another tier or a compressed representation, which is exactly the split the sharding strategy below is built around.
Sharding strategy:
The tier percentages below describe the admitted resident population, not the full entity catalog. Replica bytes count against the platform-wide resident budget, so the admitted population and replication scope must be chosen together.

Hot embeddings (top 1 percent by access frequency): Replicated within selected shard groups
Warm embeddings (next 10 percent): Column-sharded with 8-way parallelism
Cold embeddings (remaining 89 percent): Row-sharded with consistent hashing

Each inference request requires approximately 5,000 embedding lookups. Instead of one RPC per lookup, the batched design accumulates lookups for 1 ms, deduplicates entities across requests, groups lookups by destination shard, dispatches to all shards in parallel, and assembles embeddings as responses arrive.
Illustrative before-and-after assumptions for sequential dispatch versus parallel shard batching appear in table 16.

The lighthouse lesson is that sparse embedding placement and lookup coordination can dominate DLRM-scale serving even when dense arithmetic has spare capacity. The illustrated workload motivates measuring shard traffic and lookup latency before adding dense compute.





Extending tensor parallelism across node boundaries stalls decode on slow inter-node AllReduces, while using pipeline parallelism alone leaves single-request latency untouched. Production systems therefore combine sharding strategies into hybrid sharding, using one axis to cut per-token latency inside a node, another to fit weights across nodes, and a third to route sparse components without forcing dense layers onto the wrong device. Joint placement across these axes is established in Hybrid Parallelism, so the serving question is which axis buys latency. Tensor and pipeline parallelism combine when a model needs both memory distribution and latency reduction:
8 GPUs organized as 2 by 4 (pipeline stages by tensor parallel):

Stage 0 (Layers 1-40):  TP across GPUs 0,1,2,3
Stage 1 (Layers 41-80): TP across GPUs 4,5,6,7
The four-way tensor split can cut per-layer compute time by up to 4\(\times\), while the two pipeline stages complete the eight-way memory distribution; pipelining adds no per-request latency benefit of its own. Expert-parallel MoE layers and recommendation models that keep embeddings on CPU servers beside a tensor-parallel dense model follow the same rule, and the recommendation split reappears in the case study of section 10.15.2.
Hybrid sharding buys fit or latency by adding new communication patterns at every boundary between shards. The next question is whether that added communication time stays inside the latency and throughput budget.



Sharding a model across more GPUs can make inference slower rather than faster when collective synchronization takes longer than the compute time it saves. Each sharding strategy has a characteristic communication pattern, and each pattern carries a cost model developed earlier in this book. Pipeline parallelism passes activations point to point between stages and pays one startup latency plus a bandwidth term per transfer (The \MessageStartupLatency-\LinkBandwidth performance model). Tensor parallelism pays a ring AllReduce per collective, whose startup term grows linearly with the number of devices while its bandwidth term approaches twice the payload divided by link bandwidth (Ring AllReduce). Expert parallelism pays an AllToAll, whose completion time is set by the largest of per-message startup, endpoint injection or reception, and traffic across the fabric bisection (AllToAll Exchanges at Scale).
These models give an initial communication budget, not a complete prediction of request latency. Skewed expert traffic, network contention, or a different collective algorithm can change the realized timing, so the chosen topology and collective implementation must sustain that budget under the intended concurrent load.
Communication overhead depends heavily on the interconnect technology, because each candidate link fixes the physical bandwidth, latency, and scope available to the sharded model (table 17).

For tensor parallelism the latency column, not the bandwidth column, decides placement. Decode divides a small per-layer compute time across the group while still paying two collectives per layer for every generated token, so the fixed per-collective latency in table 17 sets the overhead share. The 0.3 ms per collective assumed in example 10.6 already lies an order of magnitude above the bandwidth-only transfer time on NVLink, so startup, synchronization, and launch costs dominate it. An inter-node link with higher per-message latency would multiply that cost on every token. That decode regime is why tensor-parallel groups are normally kept inside one NVLink domain.



Choosing the wrong sharding axis either burns interconnect bandwidth on per-layer collectives that the link cannot support or leaves single-request latency above the SLO. No approach wins on latency priority, throughput priority, interconnect limits, and implementation effort at once (table 18).

Strategy selection starts from the deployment bottleneck. Tensor parallelism is a candidate when reduced layer execution can repay frequent collectives; pipeline parallelism distributes layers and can sustain throughput when enough concurrent work fills the stages. Expert and embedding sharding distribute sparse state while adding routed communication. These choices can be combined, but each must fit the per-device memory budget and the measured latency contract.
Once a replica’s memory footprint and execution capacity are established, demand determines how many replicas the service needs. The next decision is where to send each arriving request. Routing must account for work already in progress and reusable state, so that replica capacity becomes useful fleet capacity.

An illustrative recommendation service has a resident embedding tier smaller than its full entity catalog. Within that admitted resident population, 1% of embeddings are hot, 10% warm, and 89% cold. Which hybrid placement matches the chapter’s scenario while counting replicas against the resident memory budget?

Order the sequence of operations that occurs during token execution in an Expert-Parallel (MoE) transformer layer:


AllToAll dispatch transmits token activation vectors to the specific GPUs hosting the selected experts
Gating network evaluates input representations and computes top-\(k\) routing probabilities
AllToAll gather routes expert output activations back to the originating host devices
Selected expert sub-networks compute local feed-forward transformations on assigned tokens
Weighted sum combines expert outputs with gating coefficients and adds residual connections
