title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Suppose ten model replicas are serving traffic when a request for a 5,000-word document summary arrives. Assigning it to an overloaded replica adds waiting and can increase interference for work already admitted there. The effect depends on admission, batching, and priority policies. Round-robin assignment does not inspect those differences in remaining work. A state-aware router uses memory and queue information to choose a feasible destination, while limiting the cost and staleness of its observations.

Lighthouse 10.2: Archetype B (DLRM at Scale): The tail at scaleArchetype B (DLRM at Scale) uses \(\text{p99} \le 100\text{ ms}\) as its illustrative latency target. At \(10^{7}\) QPS, an event probability of \(10^{-4}\) implies an expected 1,000 such events per second. This count motivates examining the tail, but does not identify its cause. Two-choice routing can reduce imbalanced queuing delay \(\QueueingLatency\); traces must establish whether queueing, inference time \(\InferenceLatency\), or another component drives the misses.


Load balancing serves two goals that can conflict: sending each request to the replica that can serve it fastest, and spreading load so that no replica idles or saturates. Latency-optimal routing can concentrate load on fast replicas until they slow down. Evaluation therefore needs signals for both goals, queue length and estimated remaining work per replica for latency and utilization spread for balance. It also needs the decision overhead of the routing choice. All signals are judged against completed-request tail latency and admission outcomes rather than balanced request counts.


When a serving request fans out to 100 backend shards that each meet their own p99 latency target independently, the assembled response misses that threshold about 63 percent of the time. Many serving requests are not one call but a set of parallel sub-requests whose results must all return before the response can be assembled. Examples are a ranking query that scores candidates on many shards, a recommendation that looks up embeddings across tables, and a sharded model whose replicas must all finish a step. Because the request completes only when its slowest leaf returns, it inherits the tail of every leaf it touches, the way a series system fails when any one component fails. If each of \(\SeriesComponentCount\) leaves independently exceeds its own latency threshold with probability \(\IndependentEventProbability\), the request exceeds it with probability \(1 - (1 - \IndependentEventProbability)^{\SeriesComponentCount}\).
Reading the same expression backward turns it into a budgeting rule. To keep the whole request within its p99 target, each of the 100 leaves may be slow only about 0.01 percent of the time, so the leaf target moves from p99 to roughly p99.99. Fan-out width is therefore a tail-latency cost that the service pays per request, and the levers act on different terms. Fewer, larger shards lower \(\SeriesComponentCount\). Queue-aware routing and isolation lower \(\IndependentEventProbability\) by keeping leaves out of their own queueing tails. A deadline with a partial or default result, as in the search cascade of section 10.15.4, caps the damage when a leaf still misses. Hedged requests lower \(\IndependentEventProbability\) further at the price of duplicated work. The independence assumption is optimistic, because a shared switch, host, or hot key slows many leaves together, so the measured composed tail is the quantity to budget, not the formula alone.


↩︎ The same independence model applied to storage reads, and hedged reads with their failure-domain placement, are established in Tier 3 parallel file systems.



Routing requests in a fixed cycle or at random works when every call costs the same, but in an inference fleet where one request generates 10 tokens and the next generates 2,000, stateless assignment piles long queues onto unlucky replicas while others sit idle. Round-robin cycles through the servers in order, which distributes work evenly only when servers are homogeneous and processing times identical, while random assignment picks a server uniformly, converging to an even mean with higher variance. Both are reasonable baselines for identical servers, but heterogeneous GPU generations, variable request sizes, warmup behavior, and replicas nearing memory limits make the state of the server fleet matter in production.
A static placement model isolates the imbalance caused by random choice: place \(\ReplicaCount\) equal-size jobs sequentially into \(\ReplicaCount\) initially empty bins, without departures. With uniform independent choices, the expected maximum bin occupancy follows the classical balls-into-bins result (Mitzenmacher 2001) in equation 14:


Two-choice routing flattens the tail imbalance of random placement.

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{max bin occupancy}] =\AsymptoticTightBound\left(\frac{\log \ReplicaCount}{\log \log \ReplicaCount}\right) \tag{14}\]
Here \(\ReplicaCount\) counts both jobs and bins. The asymptotic expression does not predict a finite serving queue at a given fleet size, because arrivals, departures, job sizes, and service rates are absent from this model. The power of two choices (principle \(\ref{pri-power-two-choices}\)) changes the occupancy tail using one additional probe.



Polling every replica in a large fleet on every arrival turns the load balancer into a coordination bottleneck, yet picking one replica blindly leaves hot queues unchecked. A foundational result in load-balancing theory (Mitzenmacher 2001) shows that querying only two random servers before making a routing decision provides exponentially better load distribution than random assignment in the static balls-into-bins model. The procedure is deliberately small, but the load signal must match the serving workload. The destination must atomically admit or reject the request because probe results can become stale; a rejection requires bounded retry or overload handling. For a homogeneous vision fleet, current queue length may be enough. For an LLM fleet, active tokens, estimated remaining decode work, and KV-cache pressure better approximate the work a replica has already accepted. Algorithm 4 states a representative routing loop: probe two replicas, compare normalized work, and route without polling the whole fleet.

Mitzenmacher, M. 2001. “The Power of Two Choices in Randomized Load Balancing.” IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems 12 (10): 1094–104. https://doi.org/10.1109/71.963420.

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Power-of-two choices request routing}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require eligible replica set $\mathcal{S}$; request $r$; positive capacity weights $w_s$; per-replica work signal $W_s$ (queue length, active tokens, predicted work, or KV-cache occupancy); finite attempt budget
\Ensure an admitting replica for $r$, or an overload rejection
\For{each allowed attempt}
    \If{$\mathcal{S}$ is empty}
        \State \Return overload rejection
    \EndIf
    \State sample two candidate replicas $s_a, s_b$ from $\mathcal{S}$ with replacement \Comment{capacity-weighted}
    \State query $W_{s_a}, W_{s_b}$; estimate incremental work $\hat{c}(r)$ (expected output tokens or KV pages)
    \State $u_s \gets (W_s + \hat{c}(r)) / w_s$ for $s \in \{s_a, s_b\}$ \Comment{post-admission load}
    \State $s^\star \gets$ candidate with smaller $u_s$ \Comment{ties: cache affinity}
    \If{$s^\star$ atomically admits $r$ and reserves its local capacity}
        \State \Return $s^\star$
    \EndIf
\EndFor
\State \Return overload rejection
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
\(\mathcal{S}\)

Two probes avoid an all-replica scan. The practical algorithm uses predicted work and capacity weights; it is a serving heuristic, not the uniform static placement process. For the latter process, choosing the less occupied of two independently sampled bins gives equation 15:
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{max bin occupancy}]_{\text{two choices}} = \AsymptoticTightBound(\log \log \ReplicaCount) \tag{15}\]

Theorem 10.2: Power-of-two choices load-balancing boundFor \(\ReplicaCount\) equal-size jobs placed sequentially into \(\ReplicaCount\) initially empty bins, without departures, uniform random placement has maximum occupancy \(\mathcal{O}(\log \ReplicaCount/ \log \log \ReplicaCount)\) with high probability. Choosing the less occupied of two independent uniform candidates reduces this to \(\mathcal{O}(\log \log \ReplicaCount)\).
The bound shows that limited probing substantially improves maximum occupancy in this static model. Two probes avoid the \(\ReplicaCount\)-probe cost of examining every bin. Applying the idea to serving requires a load signal that reflects remaining work and available capacity; the theorem does not establish near-optimal latency for changing queues, heterogeneous replicas, or stale measurements.


The mechanism is the suppression of repeated unlucky placement. If \(\HighOccupancyBinCount\) of \(\ReplicaCount\) bins have occupancy at least \(\OccupancyThreshold\), one uniform probe hits that set with probability \(\HighOccupancyBinCount/\ReplicaCount\), whereas two independent probes both hit it with probability \((\HighOccupancyBinCount/\ReplicaCount)^2\).



Sending equal request rates to replicas with different hardware capacities saturates the slower tier while leaving the faster tier underutilized. In a mixed A100 and T4 fleet, the lower-capacity replicas reach saturation first as demand increases; equal routing does not imply overload at every arrival rate. Weighted assignment accounts for measured capacity by allocating the following long-run request share to each server:
\[\Pr(\text{route to server } \ServerIndex) = \frac{\ServerRoutingWeight_i}{\sum_j \ServerRoutingWeight_j}\]
where \(\ServerRoutingWeight_i\) is the weight, or capacity, of server \(\ServerIndex\). Weighted two-choices applies the same idea to tail control: sample two servers with probability proportional to their weights, compare current load relative to capacity, and route to the lower relative load. The weighted-routing example makes this policy concrete for mixed GPU hardware.

Example 10.8: Heterogeneous GPU clusterScenario: A serving cluster mixes 10 H100 GPUs (1000 QPS each) and 20 A100 GPUs (600 QPS each), processing 15,000 QPS target traffic.
Diagnosis: Unweighted round-robin routes equal request counts (500 QPS) to all nodes, leaving H100s underutilized (50 percent) while leaving less latency headroom on A100s (83.3 percent). Weighted routing assigns H100s a weight of 4.5 percent and A100s a weight of 2.7 percent, balancing utilization across tiers (68.2 percent vs. 68.2 percent).
Systems lesson: Heterogeneous inference clusters require capacity-weighted routing. Equal request volumes produce unbalanced load when hardware tiers have different service rates.


Static weights handle known capacity differences, but production replicas also change over time. Adaptive load balancing adjusts weights dynamically based on observed performance:
For each server i:
    latency[i] = exponential_moving_average(observed_latency)
    weight[i] = 1 / latency[i]  # Inverse latency weighting
Inverse latency weighting reduces traffic to replicas whose observed latency rises. That observation mixes server condition with request cost: a replica receiving longer generations can appear slow even when its hardware is healthy. Delayed measurements can also make weights oscillate as traffic shifts. The heuristic therefore needs evaluation against comparable request classes, measurement lag, and overload behavior before its weights can be treated as capacity estimates.



Even capacity-weighted routing can overload a replica that draws several long-running generations in a row while neighboring servers finish short replies. Least-connections routes to the server with the fewest active requests, incrementing a counter on dispatch and decrementing it on completion. This accounts for unfinished requests that round-robin does not inspect, though a connection carrying multiple requests needs different bookkeeping. The policy improves routing only to the extent that the count represents the work and capacity competing at each replica.
The challenge is maintaining accurate connection counts in a distributed system. A centralized counter gives a single source of truth but can become a bottleneck. Distributed counters with gossip scale better but may route using stale information. Sampled least-connections combines the idea with two choices by probing only a subset of servers and choosing the minimum. Connection counts are themselves a proxy. Two in-flight LLM requests can differ fiftyfold in remaining decode work, from a 10-token reply to a 500-token essay, so active tokens or estimated remaining work track load more faithfully than the count of open requests.
No routing policy wins on every axis. Random and round-robin assignment have low decision overhead but ignore work in progress. Two-choice routing samples load state, while least-connections tracks outstanding requests at the cost of maintaining current counts. Neither counts nor limited probes fully describe remaining work when request costs vary widely. Which policy meets a tail target is an empirical question, evaluated with the same arrival trace, request-length mix, and replica capacities.



Routing each turn of a multi-turn conversation to a different replica forces the receiving server to recompute or fetch the entire conversation’s KV cache before generating a single new token. How much state a serving system retains across requests determines what must be preserved when traffic moves between replicas. Vision inference and individual embedding lookups can expose stateless interfaces because they need no session history from an earlier request. A ready replica with the required model and data can then accept a rerouted request. Adding replicas still requires loading that state, distributing traffic, and checking downstream capacity; failure recovery also requires spare capacity and a policy for retrying interrupted work. Statelessness removes session-state migration from these operations, but does not remove their resource costs.


↩︎ Stateless and stateful failure recovery mechanics are established in Stateless vs. stateful serving.
An autoregressive request is stateful while it is generating because its KV cache belongs to that in-flight sequence. Cross-request statefulness is optional. An API may send the full conversation history with every turn and rebuild KV state during prefill, making any replica eligible for the next request. A serving platform may instead retain a completed turn’s KV state as a session cache, reducing repeated prefill at the cost of replica affinity, cache lifetime management, and recovery complexity. Sticky routing is an optimization for that retained cache, not a correctness requirement of autoregressive models.
The scaling divide is therefore an interface and cache-policy decision. Every live generation needs request-scoped state, but the service decides whether state survives the request boundary. Session-cached service saves prefill work but must drain, migrate, or rebuild cached state during scaling and failure, so affinity earns its place only when measured cache-reuse value exceeds the resulting imbalance and recovery costs. Recommendation sessions that carry user context and streaming inference that depends on state from earlier frames benefit from the same routing affinity, while a stateless LLM API may still use prefix-aware routing when a reusable prefix happens to be cached.
Consistent hashing6 (Karger et al. 1997) maps requests to servers based on a hash of the routing key (user ID, session ID):
6 Consistent hashing: The ring-based algorithm was introduced for distributed caching (Karger et al. 1997) and then used in large-scale content delivery. Its limited-remapping property made it useful wherever membership changes should preserve cache locality.
Karger, D., E. Lehman, T. Leighton, R. Panigrahy, M. Levine, and D. Lewin. 1997. “Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web.” Proceedings of the Twenty-Ninth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing - STOC ’97, 654–63. https://doi.org/10.1145/258533.258660.
\[\text{server}(\text{request}) = \operatorname{arg\,min}_{\HashRingServer\in \HashRingServerSet} \text{distance}(\text{hash}(\text{key}), \text{hash}(\HashRingServer))\]
where \(\HashRingServerSet\) is the set of servers mapped onto the ring, and each request routes to the nearest server clockwise.
For fixed ring membership, consistent hashing sends the same key to the same server. Membership changes affect only part of the ring. With balanced equal-capacity assignments and uniformly distributed keys, adding a server moves an expected \(1/(\HashRingServerCount+1)\) fraction of keys, while removing one affects its expected \(1/\HashRingServerCount\) share. Virtual nodes help smooth uneven ranges, but popular keys can still concentrate traffic even when key counts are balanced. For session-cached LLM serving, affinity increases the chance of reaching reusable state. That benefit must outweigh additional waiting; overload routing, failure, eviction, and remapping can still require repeated prefill. The same stateful routing machinery becomes a correctness boundary when cached state is user-specific.

War Story 10.1: When cache state crossed users (2023)Context: ChatGPT used Redis Cluster through the redis-py client to cache user information and conversation titles in a high-volume serving system (OpenAI 2023).
Mechanism: Under an Asyncio connection-pooling race condition, canceled requests left unread responses in recycled connection buffers, causing subsequent requests to receive cache data belonging to previous users.
Impact: On March 20, 2023, OpenAI took ChatGPT offline after a bug allowed some users to see another active user’s conversation titles. Further investigation found possible exposure of payment-related information for a subset of active Plus subscribers during a nine-hour window; full credit card numbers were not exposed.
Fix: OpenAI sent the Redis maintainers a patch for the redis-py cancellation path and added redundant checks that the data returned from the cache belongs to the requesting user.
Systems lesson: Stateful inference infrastructure needs isolation guarantees around caches, connection pools, and routing keys. A cache is part of the serving correctness boundary, not merely an optimization.



OpenAI. 2023. March 20 ChatGPT Outage: Here’s What Happened. OpenAI incident report.

↪ Shared prefix caches as a cross-tenant leakage channel, and the tenant-scoped caches that close it, are developed in Shared accelerators and caches.




Treating individual GPUs inside a sharded model as independent routing targets breaks execution: a tensor-parallel group must run every layer in lockstep across all its ranks, and a pipeline group can admit new requests only at its first stage. A sharded replica is therefore one routing destination even though several devices execute the request. A tensor-parallel group presents one destination whose latency already includes its per-layer collectives (figure 16). A pipeline group admits requests at its first stage (figure 17), so the router must account for the group’s service capacity rather than treat each stage as a replica. In expert-parallel architectures, the gating network (section 10.10.4.2) routes tokens across internal expert destinations after the external router has chosen the replica, so expert imbalance and replica imbalance require different controls. The result is a two-tier topology (figure 18) in which the external load balancer sees each shard group as one destination and the group’s NVLink collectives stay inside it.







Figure 18: Horizontal Scaling with Shard Groups: The load balancer treats each shard group as a single logical inference server and chooses among groups by round-robin, two-choice, or session-affinity routing. Within a group, eight GPUs hold the tensor-parallel weight shards and join partial results with an NVLink AllReduce inside every layer, which the router never sees. Adding ready groups raises aggregate capacity; the group’s internal parallelism affects per-request latency.






When a replica fails or consistent hashing remaps a session to a new shard group, the new group cannot generate the next token until it either receives the conversation’s gigabyte-scale KV cache over the network or reruns prefill across the entire history. Routing a request to a shard group fixes where its KV state lives (section 10.10.2), so moving an active session between groups forces a choice between network transfer and recomputation (section 10.11.6). Transfer requires a reachable source or a saved copy; after an unrecoverable replica failure, the service rebuilds from authoritative conversation history:
Migration options:
1. Rebuild: Re-run prefill on new replica (cost grows with context length)
2. Transfer: Send KV cache over network (cache bytes / link bandwidth)
3. Hybrid: Transfer if small, rebuild if large

Decision threshold:
if cache_size_bytes/network_bandwidth < prefill_time:
    transfer()
else:
    rebuild()
For Llama 3 70B with GQA and a 4,096-token context, KV cache is about 1.3 GB total per sequence, or about 168 MB per device under 8-way tensor parallelism. At 100 Gb/s (12.5 GB/s), the bandwidth-only estimate for one shard is roughly 13 ms, while sending the full cache over one such link takes about 107 ms. The prefill approximation counts \(5.8 \times 10^{14}\) FLOPs (\(2 \times 7.1 \times 10^{10}\) parameters \(\times\) 4,096 tokens), giving roughly 180 ms on the tensor-parallel group at the assumed 40 percent utilization. Transfer is faster in this comparison, but achieving the per-shard time for the whole group requires concurrent links with sufficient aggregate bandwidth. Shared network bottlenecks, source availability, cache conversion, and destination queueing can change the decision. Long-context attention adds rebuild work omitted from this approximation, so measured transfer and prefill times should determine the policy.
The shard group boundary also defines readiness. A group can accept work only when the devices, model state, and cache capacity required for its execution plan are available, so the load balancer needs a health signal for the serving replica as a whole.



An inference worker whose HTTP server responds 200 OK to a shallow ping can still time out every real query if its weights are still loading, its KV pool is exhausted, or its CUDA context is wedged. Load balancers can route around failure only if the health signal matches the failure mode across three probe tiers (liveness, readiness, and inference correctness) that escalate from cheapest to most realistic. On an accelerator replica, each tier must test a different part of the serving state: readiness includes admission capacity as well as loaded weights and completed warmup, while an inference probe compares a fixed prompt’s output or logits against expected bounds. Passing that probe does not establish correctness or capacity for every request shape, so production errors and latency remain necessary health signals. Failover then depends on the detected failure, available replacement capacity, and whether affected KV state can be transferred or must be reconstructed.


↩︎ Liveness, readiness, and inference-correctness probes, the failover time their settings bound, and stateful failover are established in Failover mechanisms.



When a GPU inference server slows down, routing more requests to it can turn a local problem into a fleet-wide failure. Consider an illustrative rise in service time from 50 ms to 500 ms. Queues accumulate, client timeouts generate retries, and rerouted work consumes neighboring replicas’ headroom. The cause might be a stalled dependency, device degradation, or resource contention. The load balancer needs a policy for withdrawing an unhealthy replica while controlling the displaced load.
The circuit breaker pattern (Nygard 2007) limits repeated work sent to an unhealthy destination. In the closed state, the server receives normal traffic. When the configured error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded, the breaker opens and requests fail fast or become candidates for rerouting. After a recovery interval, a half-open state admits limited probes, closing on recovery or reopening on failure (figure 19). Opening a breaker does not create replacement capacity, so rerouting must respect admission limits and retry budgets or it can overload the surviving replicas.






Figure 19: Circuit Breaker States: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency’s health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open.



Backpressure propagation complements the breaker by making overload visible upstream. When queue depth crosses a threshold, the server returns a signal such as 503 Service Unavailable; the load balancer marks the replica as degraded and routes fewer requests to it. If all replicas become degraded, the system shifts from routing control to admission control, rejecting some requests at the edge rather than accepting work it cannot serve within the latency SLO. Load-shedding policies decide which requests to reject first. Circuit breakers isolate unhealthy replicas; backpressure tells the rest of the system to slow down before retries amplify the failure.


↩︎ Load shedding, model fallback, and the other strategies that trade quality for availability are established in Graceful degradation strategies.
Backpressure works only when the request contract propagates through the whole serving graph. The gateway converts the client timeout into an absolute deadline and every downstream stage subtracts elapsed time before admitting more work. If the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancellation must reach queued CPU work, accelerator batches, retrieval calls, and streamed output. A canceled request that remains in a continuous batch is zombie work: it consumes KV pages and decode bandwidth while producing no useful response. Some kernels cannot be interrupted mid-launch, so cancellation commonly takes effect at the next batch or token boundary; the scheduler must measure that cancellation lag rather than promise instantaneous preemption.
The same request identifier must connect routing, queueing, prefill, decode, cache allocation, and response streaming. A useful serving trace records admitted and rejected requests, queue delay, TTFT, TPOT, input and output tokens, cache pages, batch membership, preemptions, cancellations, and fallback decisions. Aggregate accelerator utilization cannot distinguish useful work from late or canceled work. SLO goodput and the wasted-token rate close that gap. SLO goodput reports how much completed work met its contract. The wasted-token rate is the fraction of generated tokens spent on requests that were canceled, timed out, or delivered after their deadline, the execution the system performed after the result had lost value.
A saturated LLM fleet operating under severe KV cache pressure has three workload-specific relief options. Engines can apply context eviction through an explicitly supported sliding-window or approximate policy with a quality check, or truncate retained history and recompute its state. Silently dropping old KV entries is not equivalent to recomputing a shorter conversation, because later cached states already depend on the earlier context. Disabling speculative execution reduces draft work, but reclaiming its memory also requires unloading draft weights and releasing the associated cache state. Finally, fallback routing can send eligible requests to a smaller model with available capacity, provided that model meets the application’s fallback quality contract.
These options change latency, resource use, or model behavior in different ways. The application must specify which changes are acceptable at each pressure tier. Context truncation can remove information essential to an answer, and a smaller model can fail the task’s quality requirement. In those cases, an explicit rejection can be preferable to an apparently successful but unacceptable response.
Routing relies on estimates of replica capacity, but shared hardware can make that capacity change when another workload becomes active. Critical production models may share a cluster or device with experimental models and developer endpoints. Protecting the serving contract under that interference requires multi-tenant isolation in addition to routing.

Self-Check: Question

Why does the power-of-two-choices result motivate probing two replicas, and what limitation applies when using the classical balls-into-bins bounds to predict a 1,000-server serving fleet?

It eliminates all network packet headers by broadcasting requests to all 1,000 servers simultaneously.
Two probes improve static occupancy scaling from \(\Theta(\log R/\log\log R)\) to \(\Theta(\log\log R)\), but do not determine production queue depths or P99 latency
It guarantees zero queuing delay by dynamically compiling new CUDA kernels on the fly for each request.
It forces all requests to execute on CPU fallback nodes whenever GPU utilization exceeds 50%.

Explain why Consistent Hashing is critical for routing multi-turn LLM conversations, and describe what happens to KV cache state when an autoscaling event adds a new replica.
True or False: Standard HTTP 200 process liveness checks are sufficient to detect GPU inference degradation caused by thermal throttling or silent HBM memory pool exhaustion.
A heterogeneous inference cluster contains 10 H100 servers (delivering 1,000 QPS capacity each) and 20 A100 servers (delivering 600 QPS capacity each), serving a total target load of 15,000 QPS. What weighted routing ratio should be applied to achieve equal utilization across all hardware tiers?

Route 500 QPS equally to every server regardless of type, producing 50% utilization on H100 and 83.3% on A100.
Assign weight 1.0 to H100 and 1.0 to A100 so all servers receive equal traffic shares.
Assign capacity-proportional weights (H100 weight \(= 1000/22000 \approx 4.55\%\) per server; A100 weight \(= 600/22000 \approx 2.73\%\) per server), achieving uniform 68.2% utilization across all nodes.
Route 100% of traffic to A100 servers first and overflow remaining traffic to H100 servers.

The three-state resilience pattern that fails fast and stops routing traffic to a degraded or thermally throttled GPU replica before retries cascade across the fleet is called a ____.
True or False: An autoregressive LLM must retain state during active decoding, but a serving API can still be stateless across completed requests if each new request supplies the required conversation history.

crumbs: Part III: The Fleet in Production

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Consider a critical customer-support chatbot running on the same GPU server as an experimental computer vision script. If the experimental workload monopolizes the PCIe bus or memory bandwidth, the chatbot can miss its latency target. Sharing saves capacity only when the resulting interference remains within each service’s contract. Fleet quotas, fair-share hierarchies, and priority preemption decide how much of the cluster a serving system receives; the problem here is controlling contention among the tenants who share that allocation, request by request.


↩︎ Fleet quotas, hierarchical fair-share, and the priority classes that govern preemption are established in Multi-Tenancy and Quotas.
Sharing a serving pool can raise utilization and reduce separately provisioned capacity when tenant demand peaks occur at different times. This statistical-multiplexing gain weakens when bursts are correlated, and shared resources introduce interference even when aggregate demand fits. Pooling therefore needs both a demand model and enforceable isolation.



One tenant’s burst can degrade every workload sharing the pool.
A burst from one tenant can delay others through shared KV-cache capacity, network bandwidth, and accelerator time. The pool must preserve each tenant’s data boundary and service contract; different SLOs can require different admission limits, reservations, or placements. Noisy-neighbor interference comes first because it connects shared-resource contention directly to those latency contracts.


A noisy neighbor, the tenant whose consumption of a shared resource slows the others on the same hardware, interferes inside a serving pool through three resources at once, and each is denominated in units a request-level scheduler can meter. Unchecked demand for KV-cache capacity, network egress bandwidth, or accelerator execution time lets one bursty workload erode the headroom of every co-located tenant.
GPU memory contention can limit admission before compute capacity is exhausted. Consider three tenants sharing a 60 GB KV pool with nominal 20 GB shares. Without enforced limits, one tenant’s long-context requests can raise its allocation to 45 GB. In the scenario, the others lose capacity from 200 concurrent sequences each to 75, a 62.5 percent reduction. That is a concurrency loss, not a proportional throughput prediction; the effect depends on their execution regime and preemption costs. Egress bandwidth and accelerator time are additional shared resources whose contention must be measured alongside memory occupancy.


↩︎ Noisy-neighbor contention and the device-level interference channels of shared accelerators (memory bandwidth, cache hierarchy, host-device interconnect, and thermal dissipation) are established in Resource isolation.

Example 10.9: Quantifying noisy neighbor impactScenario: An inference platform serves 10 tenants on shared H100 GPUs at 100 QPS each under a 50 ms p99 SLO. Tenant 3 bursts to 500 QPS, 5× its baseline.
Diagnosis: Without quotas, contention raises pool-wide p99 into the 22 ms to 45 ms range in this scenario, eroding every tenant’s headroom while remaining within the stated target. With quotas, Tenant 3 is limited to 120 QPS and the other tenants retain 15 ms p99. Throttling turns Tenant 3’s excess into rejected or delayed requests, which are judged against Tenant 3’s own contract rather than spread across the pool.
Systems lesson: Shared capacity raises utilization only when it is coupled with isolation. Quotas turn pool-wide erosion of latency headroom into an admission decision confined to the tenant that caused it; without them, a larger burst or a tighter SLO turns the same erosion into violations across the pool.





Limiting tenants by request count alone fails when one request carries a 20-token query and the next submits a 100,000-token document that monopolizes KV-cache pages and prefill compute. Resource quotas limit what each tenant can consume across every scarce resource, preventing any single tenant from monopolizing shared hardware. Hard quotas turn shared serving into admission control: request rate and concurrency bound arrival pressure, while input tokens, output tokens, KV-cache pages, accelerator time, and egress bytes bound the work performed after admission. Listing 1 shows representative gates so a tenant can be throttled at the scarce resource boundary instead of degrading the whole batch.



Listing 1: Multidimensional Resource Quotas: A snapshot check compares prospective resource use with tenant limits. Atomic reservation and scheduler enforcement are separate requirements.


class TenantQuota:
    max_concurrent_requests: int  # e.g., 100
    max_kv_cache_mb: int  # e.g., 20,000
    max_qps: int  # e.g., 1,000
    max_input_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_output_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_batch_tokens: int  # e.g., 50,000


def check_quota_snapshot(tenant_id, request):
    quota = get_quota(tenant_id)
    usage = get_usage(tenant_id)

    if usage.concurrent + 1 > quota.max_concurrent_requests:
        return RateLimitError("concurrent request limit")
    if usage.kv_cache_mb + request.reserved_kv_mb > quota.max_kv_cache_mb:
        return RateLimitError("memory limit")
    if usage.requests_last_second + 1 > quota.max_qps:
        return RateLimitError("rate limit")
    if usage.input_tokens + request.input_tokens > quota.max_input_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("input-token limit")
    if usage.output_tokens + request.max_output_tokens > quota.max_output_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("output-token limit")

    if request.prefill_chunk_tokens > quota.max_batch_tokens:
        return RateLimitError("prefill chunk exceeds batch-token limit")

    return None  # Snapshot is eligible; no resources have been reserved.



This listing assumes that reserved_kv_mb includes the requested prompt and output-token budget, and that usage counters include outstanding reservations in their stated time windows. A passing snapshot is not an admission guarantee: simultaneous callers can observe the same free capacity. Production admission must check and reserve resources atomically, roll back failed admissions, and release reservations on completion or cancellation. The batch scheduler separately enforces the aggregate batch-token limit. Quotas protect the resources they account for; shared compute, networking, and control-plane contention still require isolation and measurement.
Soft quotas permit borrowing unused capacity while preserving an enforceable share when demand rises. The unit of account matters: equal request counts can hide large differences in prefill work, output length, and retained state. Input and output tokens therefore need separate accounting, with memory and concurrency limits alongside them. The progressive-filling approach in Dominant-resource fairness allocation reduces to max-min fairness when only one divisible resource constrains the allocation. For three tenants demanding 30,000, 20,000, and 80,000 output tokens/sec from an idealized 100,000-token/sec pool with equal token costs, the allocation is 30,000, 20,000, and 50,000. Coupled prefill, decode, and memory constraints require joint feasibility checks; independent fair allocations do not automatically compose into a feasible service.



First-come, first-served scheduling treats a paid interactive query and a background batch job identically, letting a surge of free-tier or offline traffic delay revenue-critical requests past their SLO. Priority-aware scheduling gives eligible high-priority requests precedence at scheduling boundaries: a production API might classify revenue-generating customer requests as critical, internal batch processing as standard, and free-tier traffic as best-effort. Already-running kernels and shared resources can still delay critical work, so admission limits and reserved capacity must complement priority ordering. Priority becomes an isolation tool once its classes map to tenants and service tiers. Fleet priority classes govern preemption across allocations; request priority applies inside a serving allocation. Table 19 illustrates a policy that combines precedence with reservations. Those reservations must be provisioned and enforced separately: priority alone cannot create capacity, interrupt every running kernel, or guarantee a deadline under unbounded critical traffic.



Table 19: Priority Scheduling Classes: Three-tier priority hierarchy for multi-tenant inference. Critical traffic gets 100 percent reserved capacity and can preempt any lower class; standard traffic shares capacity proportionally and can preempt best-effort; best-effort runs on leftover capacity with no guarantees.











Class
Use case
Preemption
Resource guarantee




Critical
Revenue-generating
Can preempt lower
100% reserved


Standard
General traffic
Can preempt best-effort
Weighted share


Best-effort
Background, batch
Cannot preempt
No guarantee






Preemption extends priority to requests already in flight, but priority does not make state movement free. The retain, swap, recompute, or reject choice of section 10.7.7 still decides how a displaced request’s KV state is handled; priority adds an input to that choice rather than replacing it. A priority class determines who may be displaced, while remaining service time, state size, and deadline slack determine which victim is cheapest. Ignoring those costs lets aggressive preemption consume more capacity than it releases.



Quotas and priority queues inside a single shared serving process cannot stop a malformed request or out-of-memory fault from crashing the worker and dropping every tenant’s in-flight generations at once. The bulkhead pattern7 (Nygard 2007), named after ship compartments intended to contain flooding, partitions resources across separate concurrency pools, processes, or dedicated hardware so exhaustion or failure in one allocation stays contained.
7 Bulkhead limits: A divider isolates failure only if it closes the relevant boundary. The Titanic’s incomplete bulkheads allowed water to cascade between compartments; similarly, a soft quota cannot isolate shared memory or bandwidth that remains globally exhaustible.
Nygard, Michael T. 2007. Release It!: Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software. Pragmatic Bookshelf.
Dedicated replicas separate more resources than request limits inside one process. Figure 20 assigns distinct compute and memory pools to tenant groups, so an engine crash or exhausted local allocation in the standard tier need not stop the gold-tier engines. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane services can still carry interference across that boundary.






Figure 20: Bulkhead Isolation Patterns: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. Deployment-level bulkheads (shown) assign dedicated physical replicas to high-priority tenants, separating their compute and memory pools. Request-level bulkheads enforce strict concurrency limits within shared processes. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane dependencies remain possible paths for interference.



Deployment-level bulkheads cost pooling efficiency and the operational overhead of dedicated infrastructure. Request-level bulkheads are cheaper but weaker. Caps such as 8,000 input tokens, 2,000 output tokens, and 30 seconds of execution bound request size and duration when the scheduler enforces them, but they still need concurrency limits, reservations, and cancellation handling, and they cannot contain a crash. A malformed request that crashes a shared worker interrupts every tenant on that worker, so service tiers that require stronger fault isolation need placement boundaries to match.

Example 10.10: Bulkhead configuration for API tiersScenario: An LLM API platform serves Enterprise, Professional, and Free service tiers across shared and dedicated hardware.
Diagnosis: Unpartitioned pools allow Free-tier bursts or shared-worker failures to affect Enterprise requests. The example assigns Enterprise to dedicated GPU pools with a 99.9 percent availability target, allocates 70 percent of the remaining shared capacity to Professional, and caps Free at 30 percent best-effort capacity. Meeting that target still requires reliability evidence for the dedicated pools themselves.
Systems lesson: Bulkheads concentrate isolation overhead where business requirements dictate. Hardware partitioning reduces cross-tenant compute and memory contention. SLO compliance still depends on sufficient capacity, admission policy, shared dependencies, and failure handling.


Multi-tenant isolation limits the blast radius of excess demand, but it does not create capacity. Once protected queues approach their latency budgets, the service needs a control loop that can add replicas before admission begins to fail.

Self-Check: Question

Which statement best distinguishes deployment-level bulkheads from request-level bulkheads in a multi-tenant inference platform?

Deployment-level bulkheads enforce rate limits using software counters; request-level bulkheads isolate GPU power supplies.
Deployment-level bulkheads apply only to batch inference; request-level bulkheads apply only to interactive chat.
Deployment-level bulkheads dynamically quantize weights to INT4; request-level bulkheads dynamically compile CUDA graphs.
Deployment-level bulkheads physically isolate tenant tiers onto dedicated GPU replicas, while request-level bulkheads cap input/output token lengths and execution time within shared processes.

Why is pure First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling problematic for multi-tenant LLM serving, and what mechanism does preemptive scheduling use to resolve it?

FCFS requires excessive GPU memory for block tables; preemptive scheduling replaces block tables with static pointers.
FCFS causes extreme AllReduce communication overhead; preemptive scheduling converts tensor parallelism to pipeline parallelism.
FCFS forces all requests to run at INT4 precision; preemptive scheduling dynamically promotes high-priority requests to FP16.
FCFS can let long requests occupy scarce slots while short requests wait; preemption pauses selected requests and manages their KV state to admit other work

When multiple tenants with unequal demand compete for a shared GPU pool, the fair-allocation algorithm that maximizes the minimum allocation by bounding per-tenant consumption using token generation rate (tokens/sec) is called ____ fairness.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A serving autoscaler that reacts only to average accelerator utilization can scale in the wrong direction. Decode can saturate memory bandwidth while arithmetic units appear idle, long prompts can consume prefill capacity before request count rises, and queued work can violate an SLO while fleet-wide utilization remains moderate. The control signal must represent outstanding work relative to phase-specific service capacity. Every replica the controller adds is also a claim on accelerators that training jobs may hold, so fleet-level arbitration with training bounds how quickly and how far serving can grow.


↩︎ The arbitration between serving replicas and training jobs for shared accelerators, including the minutes-long cost of switching a device between them, is established in The training-serving resource boundary.
For a conventional fixed-cost model, queueing delay and request rate per ready replica can guide scaling. Autoregressive serving also needs prompt-token and output-token rates, KV occupancy, and measured phase service rates. A colocated replica must satisfy all phase requirements; disaggregated prefill and decode pools need separate counts and a feasible transfer budget. SLO goodput measures useful supply, but rejected work and backlog must remain visible as unmet demand. A latency threshold can detect deterioration after a model change, yet controller timing and headroom still need validation. Adding replicas also depends on their startup delay. Changing an existing accelerator allocation may require a restart or state migration, depending on the runtime and execution plan.
Scale-up and scale-down require asymmetric evidence. Scale-up acts on sustained queue growth, forecast demand, or declining deadline slack because cold-start delay makes late reactions expensive. Scale-down requires low demand over a longer window, enough spare capacity to survive one replica failure, and a drain plan for in-flight requests and any optional session cache. This hysteresis prevents oscillation in which replicas repeatedly load large weights, accept work, and terminate before amortizing startup cost.
The controller also needs observability that distinguishes demand from impaired supply: the per-request serving trace of section 10.11.10, plus ready replicas, model-load failures, and per-phase service rate. Without readiness and service-rate measurements, an autoscaler can respond to a sick replica by adding cold replicas indefinitely while the original failure remains hidden.


If a traffic spike hits a serving pool in 10 seconds but acquiring a GPU node and loading 140 GB of weights takes five minutes, the autoscaler cannot prevent the queue from overflowing during the gap. The scaling response budget is the sum of the control loop’s detection, decision, provisioning, and warmup delays, as equation 16 makes explicit:
\[\AutoscalingResponseTime= \AutoscalingDetectionTime+ \AutoscalingDecisionTime+ \ReplicaProvisioningTime+ \ReplicaWarmupTime \tag{16}\]
Each term has its own typical duration and its own primary lever, from a shorter metrics interval for detection to warm pools for provisioning and precompilation for warmup (table 20).



Table 20: Scaling Response Time Components: The four phases of a scaling event with illustrative durations and their primary optimization lever. Provisioning dominates this example; a deployment must measure its own critical path, which may instead be dominated by artifact loading.





Component
Duration
Optimization

Reduce metrics interval

Faster autoscaler


Provisioning

Warmup
5–30s
Precompilation






Provisioning can dominate the illustrated budget, making already allocated capacity valuable. The large-model example that follows shows that artifact loading can instead dominate startup; the relevant term is the one measured on the deployment’s critical path. Finer-grained metrics can reduce detection delay but increase noise, while prepared scaling decisions and precompiled engines reduce other costs. A warm pool removes only the phases already completed at its stated readiness level.



When a 70B replica takes nearly seven minutes to boot and stream its weights from object storage, waiting for a morning traffic ramp to appear in queue metrics guarantees several minutes of overloaded replicas. A cold start for a 70B replica shows the scale of that delay, and a demand forecast shows how a controller can begin the wait before the traffic arrives.

Example 10.11: Cold start timeline for Llama-70BScenario: An autoscaling engine provisions a Llama-70B replica during a traffic surge, using an H100-based allocation large enough for its FP16 weights, cache, and runtime state.
Diagnosis: The scenario’s sequential startup estimate is 6.7 minutes (\(\ReplicaColdStartTime= \ReplicaProvisioningTime+ \ReplicaModelLoadTime+ \ReplicaWarmupTime\)): 1 minute for provisioning, 4.7 minutes to fetch 140 GB of artifacts at the assumed 0.5 GB/s, and 1 minute for device loading and warmup. Cached artifacts or overlapping phases can shorten this path; scarce capacity and shared storage can lengthen it. If existing headroom cannot absorb the surge, newly requested replicas arrive too late to protect short deadlines.
Systems lesson: Cold-start latency depends on artifact size, effective storage bandwidth, provisioning delay, compilation, and warmup. The controller must measure this distribution and begin provisioning far enough ahead that its high percentile fits inside the forecast horizon.



Example 10.12: Predictive scaling for trafficScenario: A commercial chatbot service faces predictable diurnal traffic patterns, ramping from 500 QPS at night to 3,000 QPS at peak.
Diagnosis: A controller that waits for the morning ramps at 06:00 and 09:00 UTC before requesting capacity must cover the assumed 7-minute startup interval with existing headroom or admission limits. Without enough ready capacity, queues grow while replicas start. Forecasting can shift that wait ahead of the expected demand.
Systems lesson: Predictive autoscaling converts demand forecasts into planned pre-warming windows (table 21). Starting 30 minutes ahead of the expected ramps exceeds the modeled startup time. Readiness still depends on actual provisioning and warmup, and forecast errors can leave the fleet short or idle. Reactive correction and an overload policy remain necessary.

Systems insight: Against an assumed reactive peak of 45 replicas, the forecast-based peak of 30 is a 33 percent reduction in peak replica count at equal unit cost. The reactive controller over-provisions because it reacts to a queue that has already formed and must add capacity for the backlog as well as the demand. Peak count is only part of the bill. Total spending counts replica-hours, including the pre-warming window, so the forecast pays only when the replica-hours spent warming ahead of demand are fewer than those the reactive overshoot would consume.


Example 10.12 shows how capacity can be prepared before demand arrives. Figure 21 depicts a forecast that anticipates the surge, while the reactive curve starts later and temporarily lacks capacity. Whether that deficit produces queueing, rejection, or missed deadlines depends on admission and existing headroom. The predictive curve illustrates a successful forecast, not a guarantee that future demand or startup time will match it.














Figure 21: Predictive vs. Reactive Scaling: Reactive scaling (gray line) responds to traffic spikes after they occur, leaving a capacity deficit (red region) during cold start in this scenario. Predictive scaling (green line) anticipates traffic and begins provisioning before the spike peaks, shrinking that deficit to a brief, small shortfall at onset in the illustrated forecast. Its early ramp does not eliminate every interval when demand exceeds capacity.






Demand forecasts still miss unscheduled traffic spikes, and cold-starting a large model from scratch takes minutes that an interactive SLO cannot spare. Maintaining prewarmed replicas in a warm pool buys readiness before unexpected demand arrives. Sizing that pool begins with the total capacity needed during the provisioning delay, then subtracts capacity already ready to serve. If peak demand doubles and the chosen headroom factor is 1.5, the target is three times baseline capacity, assuming unchanged per-replica throughput. Partly prepared replicas count only if they can become ready before that capacity is needed. The expression \(\text{Pool size} \times \text{GPU cost/hour} \times \text{Idle fraction}\) estimates the hourly cost attributed to idle GPU capacity; it excludes busy capacity and non-GPU resources. Readiness comes in tiers, each trading activation delay against the cost of waiting (table 22).



Table 22: Tiered Warm Pool Readiness Levels: Readiness trades activation delay against idle resource cost. Actual delay and billing depend on the deployment. Cold capacity is subject to quotas and physical availability.

Warm

Artifact storage; no allocated GPU






When a traffic spike hits, the controller routes work to ready replicas, activates prepared capacity, and requests additional instances if needed. Pool sizing must cover the measured provisioning delay and include an overload policy for capacity that cannot be acquired in time.



Revoking a spot GPU replica mid-generation destroys every in-flight sequence’s KV cache unless the worker can drain or migrate its active requests inside the cloud provider’s two-minute warning window. Discounted interruptible capacity enters serving through the same purchasing tiers that fleet capacity planning uses (Cloud Capacity Reservation Tiers): reserved capacity for the steady baseline, on-demand capacity for bursts, and spot capacity for work that tolerates revocation. equation 8.3 derives the effective cost of preemptible capacity from its productive fraction. Serving adds a loss that training checkpoints do not cover, because the productive fraction must also pay for draining, rerouting, and rebuilding in-flight KV state without violating the affected requests’ SLO. Listing 2 orders the shutdown path so new work stops first, in-flight work drains while time remains, recoverable state is persisted, and the load balancer stops sending traffic before the instance disappears.


↩︎ Capacity purchasing tiers and the effective cost of interruptible capacity are established in Cost Optimization.



Listing 2: Spot Termination Handling: Graceful shutdown sequence that stops admission, deregisters from the load balancer, drains in-flight requests, and persists recoverable state.


async def handle_spot_termination():
    # Received 2-minute warning
    # 1. Stop admission and remove the replica from routing
    stop_accepting_requests()
    deregister_from_loadbalancer()

    # 2. Complete in-flight requests (if possible)
    await complete_inflight(timeout=90)

    # 3. Save state for resumption elsewhere
    save_kv_cache_to_storage()

    # 4. Terminate gracefully
    shutdown()



Replica-level draining protects in-flight requests only if the upstream router avoids placing strict-SLO traffic on interruptible capacity in the first place. The gateway in figure 22 separates traffic by its tolerance for capacity revocation, and an eviction notice triggers draining when time permits; requests that cannot finish need a permitted retry, reconstruction, or rejection path.







Figure 22: Spot-Aware Traffic Distribution: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. The traffic split is illustrative; cost savings depend on provisioned capacity, discounts, retries, and idle headroom.



Savings under this split depend on provisioned GPU-hours, discounts, retries, and reserve capacity rather than on the traffic share, and spot capacity changes none of the fault-tolerance requirements of the SLO-critical path. Even a well-scaled single-region fleet, however, remains bounded by wide-area network latency to distant users and by the blast radius of a regional outage.

Self-Check: Question

In an illustrative fresh-replica startup, fetching 140 GB of model artifacts takes five minutes while detection and controller decisions take seconds. Why are pre-warmed pools or predictive scaling useful?

Artifact loading dominates this scenario, so pre-warmed pools or advance provisioning can make capacity ready before the surge
\(\AutoscalingDecisionTime\) dominates (10–15 minutes evaluating autoscaling PID loops); mitigated by switching to manual scaling.
\(\AutoscalingDetectionTime\) dominates (30 minutes gathering Prometheus metrics); mitigated by removing metric telemetry entirely.
\(\ReplicaWarmupTime\) dominates (1–2 hours running CUDA kernel JIT compilation); mitigated by disabling Tensor Cores.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A fleet confined to one region can batch, shard, route, isolate, and autoscale well, yet a user in Sydney still pays roughly a 200 ms round trip to a US-East deployment before any of that machinery acts. A regional outage also removes every replica at once. Extending resource isolation and failure boundaries beyond one data center introduces placement decisions at geographic scale. Distance, regional failures, and data-placement requirements can motivate regional replicas, caches, or a centralized service with an explicit network budget. Figure 23 illustrates three tiers: edge points of presence for reusable responses, regional gateways for authentication and routing, and GPU clusters for model execution. Its 10 ms, 50 ms, and 2 s budgets are scenario targets, not measured performance or universal deadlines. The application must define whether its execution budget governs first response, individual tokens, or completion of the entire request.







Figure 23: Serving Deployment Stack: A cache miss crosses three tiers before reaching a model replica. Tier 1 edge points of presence (PoPs) enforce authorization and reuse eligibility before answering repeated requests from cache; a miss passes to Tier 2, where the gateway applies rate limits and authentication and the router picks a destination; Tier 3 GPU workers run prefill and decode while an autoscaler sizes the fleet from queue depth and KV cache use. Tokens stream back up through the tiers to the client. The per-tier latency budgets on the right, drawn on a log scale, are illustrative.





Serving all global traffic from a single US-East cluster forces European, Asian, and Australian users to pay a 75 to 200 ms wide-area network round trip on every request and leaves the entire service vulnerable to a single regional outage. Single-region deployment couples every user to the same geographic site and regional failure domain. Network round-trip time (RTT) adds a latency floor for distant users, and illustrative regional timings show that floor rising with distance from the serving region (table 23). Actual paths, access networks, and congestion require measurement.



Table 23: Network RTT by User Location: A single US-East deployment imposes a 75 to 200 ms RTT on European, Asian, and Australian users, an order of magnitude above the local-region floor. Sequential calls that cross this boundary can add repeated wide-area delay. Regional replicas can reduce that exposed delay when placement policy, workload volume, and available capacity justify them.

RTT to local region

Network delays compound when a request makes sequential calls across the distant boundary; multiple model calls inside one backend region do not each pay another client-to-region RTT. Regional replication can shorten that path and separate failure domains. Data-placement policies also constrain eligible destinations. The General Data Protection Regulation permits international transfers under specified conditions rather than requiring blanket EU-only processing; applicable law and contractual commitments must be translated into explicit placement rules. Regional replicas, edge caches, and cross-region sharding then trade capacity, communication, and coordination within those rules.



Deploying replicas in multiple regions cuts wide-area latency only if the global router avoids sending users to a nearby region whose GPU queues are already saturated or whose data-residency rules forbid the request. In figure 24, a global load balancer selects among regions that satisfy placement policy, readiness, and capacity requirements. Measured network latency helps choose among those eligible destinations, because geographic proximity alone does not determine completion time, while a shared registry supplies versioned artifacts to the independent regional replicas.







Figure 24: Global Load Balancing across Inference Regions: A global load balancer routes each user to an eligible region with suitable latency and ready capacity (table 23 gives the round-trip times this avoids). Each region (US-East, EU-West, Asia-Pacific) runs independent replicas of the same model, and EU requests can stay in the EU to meet data-residency rules. A shared model registry supplies versioned weights to every region. If a region fails, the load balancer reroutes its users only to destinations that still satisfy placement, readiness, and capacity requirements.



Replication also creates a version-management obligation. Push-based synchronization sends artifacts to each region, while pull-based synchronization lets regions fetch them after notification or polling. Neither mechanism alone guarantees consistent serving versions. Artifact verification, readiness gates, and coordinated activation determine when a region may serve the new version; hybrid synchronization combines push notification with pull verification.
During a rollout, regions may serve different versions. The application must decide whether that is acceptable and whether a request or session needs version pinning. A region-by-region canary deployment exposes the new version to one region’s traffic share at a time, and each expansion passes its own error-rate, latency, and quality gate with compatible prior artifacts retained for rollback.


↪ Staged rollout and the canary observation window, sized from the required sample count and the canary’s traffic share, are developed in Canary deployment (equation 12.7).



Standing up a full GPU cluster in every continent is an expensive way to reduce round-trip latency when a large fraction of distant requests ask repeated FAQ or autocomplete questions. Caching responses at the edge avoids both the wide-area round trip and repeated central inference whenever a stored response remains valid for the incoming request. Before returning a hit, the edge must enforce authorization and match the relevant model version, conversation or retrieval context, generation policy, and freshness requirements. Identical visible queries do not necessarily permit the same answer, and fresh-sample semantics may prohibit reuse. A hit returns within an illustrative 10 ms budget, while a miss reaches the central cluster (figure 25); only responses eligible for reuse should enter the edge store.







Figure 25: Cache Hit and Cache Miss Paths at the Edge: A query first reaches the nearest edge point of presence (PoP). After enforcing authorization and reuse eligibility, the edge targets a cache-hit response in under 10 ms without touching a GPU. On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and a response eligible for reuse can be stored at the edge for later queries. The saving depends on the rate of requests eligible for reuse; open-ended generation may offer few such requests.



On the two paths of figure 25, cache hits avoid the backend round trip, while misses incur it. Effectiveness depends on request repeatability across workloads such as autocomplete, FAQ chatbots, open-ended chat, and code generation. Table 24 supplies illustrative hit-rate envelopes for sensitivity analysis; an actual design must derive hit rate and correctness from production traces.



Table 24: Illustrative Edge-Cache Hit-Rate Envelopes: Assumed cache-hit ranges for four workload shapes. These values are scenario inputs, not universal workload statistics. Trace-derived repeatability, response validity, and latency saved determine whether caching is worthwhile.

Semantic caching8 (caching based on embedding similarity rather than exact match) can improve hit rates for open-ended workloads. Any cache miss still requires full model execution, raising the question of whether a large model can be split across regions or must run inside a single data center.
8 Semantic caching: A similarity lookup can reuse responses beyond exact string matches, but it adds retrieval work and can return an invalid answer when superficially similar queries require different responses. The similarity threshold therefore trades cache coverage against correctness.


Splitting a single model replica across data centers puts wide-area network latency directly on the request’s execution path: when pipeline stages reside in separate regions, every stage crossing pays a 75–150 ms inter-region transfer against only 1–5 ms of local stage computation. That illustrative gap can slow inference by 10–100\(\times\), though the exact penalty depends on the model’s stage layout. Such placement needs a reason strong enough to justify that cost, such as unavailable colocated capacity, and must be evaluated against the actual stage layout and deadline. Because cross-region sharding is so costly on the steady-state path, most production designs keep inference co-located and use other regions for resilience. The cross-region question therefore shifts from splitting one request across regions to deciding how quickly traffic can move when a region fails.



When a region becomes unavailable, failover must choose a healthy destination permitted to process the request and able to absorb its work. A simplified fallback tries the nearest eligible region first and, on timeout or rejection, the next one (listing 3). A production policy must also preserve the request’s remaining deadline, version requirements, and data-placement constraints when selecting the secondary region.



Listing 3: Active-Active Failover: A bounded retry policy selects eligible regions and limits each attempt to the remaining request deadline.


# Eligibility includes placement, version, readiness, and capacity.
def route_request(user_region, request):
    attempted = set()
    for attempt_budget in (2.0, 5.0):
        remaining = request.deadline - monotonic_time()
        regions = eligible_regions(request, excluding=attempted)
        if remaining <= 0 or not regions:
            break
        region = nearest_region(user_region, regions)
        attempted.add(region)
        try:
            # The endpoint atomically admits work and enforces the deadline.
            return call_region(region, request,
                               timeout=min(attempt_budget, remaining))
        except (Timeout, RegionUnavailable, AdmissionRejected):
            # Cancel abandoned work; retries require replay-safe semantics.
            cancel_attempt(region, request)
    return unavailable_or_deadline_exceeded(request)



Rerouting is only part of regional failover. The destination needs accessible, authoritative conversation history to reconstruct lost KV state and enough headroom for both reconstruction and continuing traffic. If the required history is unavailable or cannot be processed there under the placement policy, a healthy replica alone cannot restore the session.


↩︎ Regional headroom, session rebuilding, and the gradual return of traffic to a recovered region are established in Replication strategies.



Running every batch job and latency-tolerant query in the primary interactive region overpays whenever another compliant region has cheaper spot or off-peak GPU capacity. Because GPU pricing varies by provider, contract, region, and time, table 25 uses a hypothetical price snapshot to show how placement can balance cost against latency requirements; it must not be used for procurement.



Table 25: Hypothetical Regional Price and Latency Snapshot: Scenario prices and RTTs illustrate a placement calculation. Both inputs are time- and provider-specific; a deployment must refresh them from its contract and measured network paths before making a routing decision.

Cost-aware routing compares eligible regions for latency-tolerant work (listing 4). GPU price alone is insufficient: transfer charges, startup and idle capacity, retries, and achieved useful throughput determine the cost of completing the workload. Deadline and data-placement constraints must filter destinations before that comparison.



Listing 4: Cost-Aware Routing: The router filters eligible destinations before comparing completion cost for low-priority work or proximity for interactive work.


def route_batch_request(request):
    # Filter by placement, version, readiness, capacity, and deadline.
    regions = eligible_regions(request)
    if not regions:
        return no_feasible_destination(request)
    if request.priority == "low":
        return lowest_completion_cost_region(request, regions)
    return nearest_region(request.user_location, regions)



Time-of-day routing can reduce batch cost when regional price differences exceed data-transfer and coordination costs. Savings require a workload-specific calculation, and interactive traffic must retain its own latency budget. Regional placement completes the serving hierarchy, from one request’s batch slot to a fleet that spans continents. The design cases that follow show how these techniques combine when a service must meet specific cost and latency targets.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Individual serving optimizations—quantization, continuous batching, sharding, or caching—can look decisive in isolation yet still leave a production endpoint missing its latency, memory, or cost contract when combined under real traffic. The five design cases below are illustrative composites rather than descriptions of named companies’ internal deployments, and their request rates, latency budgets, hardware allocations, and update cadences follow the chapter’s scenario convention. Each case binds on a different constraint: one replica’s decode step, embedding scale, variable-length generation, cascade cost, or multimodal freshness. Orca and vLLM supply the previously cited scheduling and memory-management mechanisms; the scenarios combine those ideas with precision, routing, sharding, and admission control.


Even before a serving cluster worries about routing or multi-region failover, a single replica can fail its per-token latency target on a batch of one—leaving zero headroom to batch additional requests. The first case stays inside one replica, the reference 70B model on eight NVLink-connected H100s with FP16 weights split eight ways, serving an interactive endpoint whose illustrative TPOT target is 50 ms. A batching policy can only spend the headroom that a batch-one decode step leaves, because every admitted sequence lengthens the step (section 10.6.2), so the first question is whether one batch-one step fits inside the target at all. This constructed example illustrates budget accounting, not benchmark results. Every interval is an exposed, nonoverlapping contribution to the same request’s critical path, and time to first token, output quality, and throughput under load each need their own measurements.
The deployment’s FP16 weights occupy 140 GB, about 17.5 GB per GPU. The assumed baseline decode step is 85 ms, about 16× the 5.2 ms that streaming each shard at full HBM bandwidth would take, so the replica runs at an MBU of about 6.1 percent (Program goodput and its measure). That gap, not the weight-streaming floor, is what eager dispatch, unfused kernels, and exposed synchronization must explain, and table 26 apportions the whole step among those causes on one absolute-time boundary. In an actual trace, overlapping work must not be counted twice when constructing such a budget.

The first experiment targets weight-read traffic with INT4 weight-only quantization, the bandwidth-bound decode row of table 11. Assume that quality validation succeeds and that exposed GEMM time falls by 45 percent, with every other interval unchanged. The step takes 69.7 ms, still above the 50 ms target, because a large cut to one interval removes only that interval’s share of the step. INT8 KV-cache compression is a separate candidate whose benefit is capacity, as notebook 10.7 computes; it needs its own quality check and a new profile, so this column grants it no latency benefit.
The second experiment targets exposed attention, element-wise work, and launch gaps, using the single-replica levers of Kernel-level levers. Assume a validated fused decode-attention kernel, the single-pass kernel over the KV cache of section 10.8.1, reduces attention by 25 percent, fusion reduces element-wise work to 3.4 ms, and graph replay reduces launch and runtime overhead to 2 ms. These are scenario assumptions, and each intervention would be tested separately before the combination is retained. The step becomes 49.6 ms, inside the target with almost no slack and still about 9× above the bandwidth floor. Communication remains 10.2 ms, unchanged in absolute time even as its share of the shorter step grows. Spread across the 160 AllReduces of an 80-layer step, that interval implies about 64 μs per collective, against roughly 5 μs of launch and transfer, or about 0.8 ms per step. The difference is the protocol and synchronization cost of small collectives that Tensor-parallel collectives under contention flags for measurement, and a trace that attributed it would make communication the next experiment.
The third experiment changes how much output each step yields. Assume a draft model proposes \(\SpeculativeDraftLength=\) 5 tokens in 4 ms, verification costs one round-two step, and each candidate is accepted independently with probability \(\DraftTokenAcceptanceProbability=\) 0.78. Equation 6 gives 3.52 tokens per round, so a 53.6 ms round yields 15.2 ms per emitted token, an amortized 3.26-fold improvement in TPOT. The tokens, however, arrive in blocks. The gap between blocks is a whole round, 53.6 ms, which exceeds the same 50 ms if the endpoint also states it as a per-gap TBT target. Speculation thus meets an average-cadence contract with room to spare while missing a per-gap one on every round, which is why the TPOT and TBT targets of section 10.2 are stated separately. The gain also belongs to batch one; as the speculative-decoding policy in section 10.7.6 warns, larger batches consume the spare compute that made verification cheap.
The budget exposes bottleneck displacement without crediting a system improvement to an isolated kernel speedup. Precision changes one interval, fusion and replay change others, and speculation changes the output per round; their benefits compose only on a shared accounting boundary, with quality preserved. What the sequence produces is a set of candidate replica configurations, not a serving result. Accepting one for production means replacing the illustrative intervals with measurements, preserving the request-length distribution and offered load, and measuring SLO goodput (section 10.3) at the batch the scheduler will actually admit. Memory freed by INT4 weights can permit that larger batch, but neither the freed capacity nor a faster batch-one step shows that the service meets every target at once. Where this first case stays inside one dense LLM replica fighting per-token latency, the next case shifts to a fleet where sparse embedding lookups across terabytes of state dominate the budget before dense GPU execution even begins.



An embedding-heavy recommendation service binds on sparse lookup rather than dense forward-pass compute. Modeled on feeds, advertising, and content ranking, it processes billions of requests per day under a p99 budget below \(10\text{ ms}\) for the ranking service, nested inside the roughly 100 ms end-to-end tail target of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale). The service spans hundreds of model variants and trillions of unique sparse features. The serving stack separates sparse lookup from dense ranking:
User request → Feature collection → Embedding lookup → Model inference → Response

                    |                     |                  |
                    v                     v                  v
             Feature Store        Embedding Servers      GPU Inference
             (CPU, DRAM)         (CPU + SSD, 1000s)     (GPU, 100s)
The hybrid sharding strategy in lighthouse 10.1 supplies the sparse path: replication protects hot entries, column sharding spreads warm-entry access, and row sharding places the cold tail. Feature-level batching then combines lookups across requests. The remaining design decision is where each stage runs. In the GPU-CPU hybrid architecture, memory-rich CPU servers serve sparse embeddings while GPUs execute dense ranking. Table 27 connects that placement to the end-to-end latency budget.



Table 27: Illustrative Hybrid CPU/GPU Architecture: Illustrative hardware-workload mapping for the recommendation scenario. CPU + SSD handles the bandwidth-bound sparse path; CPU handles low-arithmetic-intensity feature processing; GPU handles the compute-dense ranking forward pass. The component budgets exclude queueing and response delivery; their sum alone does not establish the p99 target.
