The serving lesson is that recommendation latency is often dominated by embedding lookup rather than dense model inference. Feature-parallel batching and a hybrid CPU-GPU architecture match the hardware to the sparse and dense halves of the workload, which sets up a contrast with GPT-style API serving where request variance and autoregressive state dominate.



A multi-model generation API binds on request variance, because short prompts, long-context requests, and different model sizes share capacity while users expect predictable TTFT. The platform serves millions of requests per hour under a time-to-first-token target below \(2\text{ s}\), with models from billions to hundreds of billions of parameters and contexts up to 128K tokens. The serving stack separates routing, scheduling, cache management, and shard groups:
API Gateway → Rate Limiting → Request Router → Model Cluster → Response Streaming

                                     |
                                     v
                              +-------------+
                              | Model Pool  |
                              | +---------+ |
                              | | Large   | |
                              | | 8×H100  | |
                              | +---------+ |
                              | +---------+ |
                              | | Smaller | |
                              | | 4×A100  | |
                              | +---------+ |
                              +-------------+
The main design decision is to prevent long prompts from blocking decode service for everyone else. An Orca-style design uses continuous batching to refill completed slots. Chunked prefill limits interference from long prompts by interleaving prompt chunks with ongoing generation. The TTFT target must be validated across prompt lengths; admitting a 128K-token prompt does not imply that it meets the short-request latency target. Slot reuse and long-prompt interference are separate concerns. Continuous batching addresses the first and chunking bounds the second, so neither mechanism alone establishes the utilization or tail latency the API will see.
The tensor-parallel degree must satisfy weight and KV-cache capacity while leaving enough latency budget for communication. This scenario allocates eight H100 GPUs per large-model shard group connected via high-speed NVLink for intra-node communication, with consistent hashing at the gateway to maintain session affinity and enable compatible cross-turn KV cache reuse. The eight-device allocation is a design choice to validate against the model, precision, and admitted context lengths, not a requirement of GPT-class models in general.
To prevent noisy neighbors from exhausting capacity, the illustrative API applies hierarchical rate limiting across multiple granularities: per-API-key request arrival limits, per-API-key token-per-minute consumption limits, organization-level capacity quotas, and global model capacity ceilings. Within those ceilings, capacity can also shift between models on queue depth, subject to model-loading delay and each service’s minimum allocation, using the autoscaling signals of section 10.13.
LLM APIs are governed by variance control. Continuous batching reuses execution slots, prefix caching avoids compatible repeated work, and multi-tier rate limiting bounds admitted demand. Their combined effect on latency still depends on prompt scheduling and available capacity. Search ranking faces a different shape of the same problem. Many cheaper models must cooperate under one strict deadline.



The search-ranking scenario binds on cascade cost, because each query coordinates many smaller models for query understanding, document relevance, and result ranking under one end-to-end budget rather than serving one large model. The system processes billions of searches per day under a target below \(200\text{ ms}\) while evaluating thousands of candidate documents per query, so screening candidates with cheaper models reserves the expensive ranking budget for a smaller set.
To meet this latency budget while evaluating thousands of documents, the ranking cascade in figure 26 screens candidate pools across four progressively expressive tiers. Early lexical and approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) embedding retrievers discard 99 percent of candidates within a 10 ms budget, reserving compute-intensive cross-attention transformers for the final top 100 items. This saving creates a recall constraint. A relevant document discarded upstream cannot be recovered by a more accurate downstream ranker, so each stage’s candidate budget must be evaluated for retained relevant items as well as latency.


↩︎ The vector indexes behind the L0 retrieval stage, and the storage cost of keeping them fast enough for a serving deadline, are established in Retrieval indexes.






Figure 26: Ranking Cascade Architecture: To optimize latency and cost, search and recommendation systems use a cascade of increasingly complex models. Early stages (Retrieval) filter millions of candidates down to thousands using fast, cheap heuristics. Later stages use expensive, high-precision models only on the most promising candidates.



The central design decision is progressive refinement through a ranking cascade rather than one expensive model applied to every candidate. Each stage of the cascade spends a larger latency budget on a smaller candidate set (table 28), so the expensive L3 transformer is affordable only because L0 through L2 have already cut the candidates by four orders of magnitude.



Table 28: Illustrative Ranking Cascade: Each stage evaluates fewer candidates with a more expensive model. The final stage has the largest latency allocation in this scenario; candidate reduction makes that expense affordable.

The cascade reduces final L3 evaluations by 10,000× compared to running L3 on all candidates. If the stage budgets are treated as additive model work and L3 cost scales linearly with candidate count, the L3 allocation implies 1 ms per candidate. Applying L3 to the full million-candidate set would then consume about 1000 s of model work, while the cascade budget sums to 180 ms. The resulting reduction is roughly 5,600× under these assumptions. This accounting estimate is not a measured latency speedup; batching and parallel execution can change elapsed time without changing the candidate count.
A deadline-constrained ranking ensemble can use speculative execution when it has a validated fallback-quality policy. Here, speculation means launching candidate ranking work in parallel under a deadline, not draft-token verification for LLM decoding:
# Instead of sequential:
#   q1 = model1(query)
#   q2 = model2(query)
#   q3 = model3(query, q1, q2)

# Speculative parallel:
async_q1 = async model1(query)
async_q2 = async model2(query)
async_q3 = async model3(query, predicted_q1, predicted_q2)

# Use actual results if they arrive in time, otherwise use speculative
Each sub-request carries an explicit remaining-time budget, and workers order their local queues by deadline proximity rather than arrival order. When a queued sub-request cannot complete before its budget expires, the worker returns a cached or default score immediately instead of timing out the parent query:
Worker queue: [Doc1: 50 ms left] [Doc2: 30 ms left] [Doc3: 80 ms left]
                                      ↑ Process first

If deadline will be missed:
  Return cached/default result rather than timing out
The serving lesson is that ranking cascades reduce cost by spending expensive models only on a shrinking candidate set, at the risk of losing relevant items upstream. Deadline propagation and priority scheduling expose the remaining time budget; meeting it also requires sufficient capacity and a validated fallback when work cannot finish. The next case adds a freshness constraint that deadline scheduling alone cannot solve.



The multimodal recommendation scenario binds on freshness under a tight ranking SLO: video understanding is expensive, new content arrives continuously, and user modeling remains online. The system ranks millions of videos per second under a p99 target below \(50\text{ ms}\) while ingesting millions of new videos daily across video, audio, text, and interaction signals, which is why online and offline work must separate. The serving stack separates content and user paths:
User request → User embedding → Candidate videos → Video understanding → Ranking

                    |                  |                    |
                    v                  v                    v
             User Tower          Video Cache          Vision Models
           (Transformer)        (Pre-computed)        (On-demand)
The scenario separates user understanding (online) from content understanding (offline) through a two-tower architecture with caching.9 The user tower runs online on every request, while the video tower refreshes in hourly offline batches (table 29).
9 Two-tower architecture: Encodes user features and item features through separate neural networks (“towers”) into embeddings, then scores via dot product. Its serving advantage is that item embeddings can be precomputed offline and cached, reducing online candidate generation to the user tower forward pass and vector similarity search. Search latency depends on index size, placement, and the required recall. The trade-off is reduced model expressiveness from late interaction, since the towers cannot attend to each other’s features during encoding.


Table 29: Illustrative Two-Tower Update Cadence: User and video towers run on different cadences: user features change second-to-second and must run inference online; video features change much more slowly and are precomputed in hourly batches. This asymmetric scheduling is the design that takes vision inference out of the critical path for almost every request.

Video embeddings are precomputed and cached, eliminating vision inference from the critical path for most requests. A newly uploaded video without a cached embedding needs an explicit policy: process it before admitting it to recommendations, serve a validated fallback, or run vision inference on demand if the request budget permits. The hourly refresh cadence alone does not meet the shorter ingestion targets below; those targets require a separate path for new content.
The online path below separates candidate generation from a later dense reranker. Its user-tower budget is distinct from the reranker budget:
User features → CPU preprocessing (1 ms)
             → Embedding lookup (2 ms, CPU+DRAM)
             → User tower (5 ms, GPU)
             → Dense reranking (10 ms, GPU)
             → Response formatting (1 ms)
New uploads enter an ingestion queue with priority tiers, so time-sensitive content is embedded within minutes and bulk imports absorb hours of slack, although priority only changes who waits when ingestion capacity falls short. The modality embeddings (video, audio, text) are combined late by a small fusion model, so updating one modality’s encoder requires a compatibility check and, when its embedding contract changes, regeneration of the cached embeddings.
The serving lesson is that freshness requires separating online and offline work. Two-tower architectures make aggressive caching possible because item embeddings can be refreshed asynchronously, while priority-based processing spends the freshest compute where it has the largest user impact.



Trying to serve LLM token generation, sparse recommendation ranking, and multimodal retrieval through one generic model server forces every workload to pay for scheduling and memory abstractions it does not need. Across these cases, the common pattern is specialization rather than a universal serving stack. Embedding and retrieval stay separate from ranking and generation, hardware is matched to each stage, caches accept bounded staleness, candidate sets shrink before expensive work, and deadlines propagate so quality-latency trade-offs stay explicit under pressure. Table 30 distills the same choices along five design axes for the three workload families the cases cover. Its entries are candidate combinations for the illustrated constraint regimes, not prescriptions, because a model class alone does not fix a scheduler or topology, which also depend on model size, request mix, available hardware, and service targets.

The workload’s state, scheduling, and hardware constraints guide selection; the service contract determines whether a combination supplies useful capacity.

crumbs: Part III: The Fleet in Production

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
A DevOps team that applies its standard web-server load-balancing rules to a new fleet of GPU inference nodes can see tail latency climb sharply, because those rules ignore the extreme variance of autoregressive token generation. Web services also face variable work and queueing, but an inference fleet adds model residency, accelerator scheduling, and per-sequence state to those familiar concerns. The fallacies below arise when a serving design ignores these constraints or treats one optimization as a complete solution.

Fallacy: Serving at scale is synonymous with LLM serving.
The misconception leads to over-focus on LLM-specific techniques. As section 10.5.1 showed, recommendation and ranking models can consume most AI inference cycles on large consumer platforms (Gupta et al. 2020; Hazelwood et al. 2018). A practitioner who knows only continuous batching and KV cache management is unprepared for the feature-parallel batching and embedding sharding that dominate that traffic. Technique selection must match the actual workload.

Hazelwood, Kim, Sarah Bird, David Brooks, Soumith Chintala, Utku Diril, Dmytro Dzhulgakov, Mohamed Fawzy, et al. 2018. “Applied Machine Learning at Facebook: A Datacenter Infrastructure Perspective.” 2018 IEEE International Symposium on High Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA), 620–29. https://doi.org/10.1109/hpca.2018.00059.


Pitfall: Using training infrastructure for production serving.
Training and serving have different requirements, as table 2 summarized. Interactive serving must satisfy per-request latency targets under external arrivals, so its batch size depends on the workload and waiting budget, and its recovery policy must account for in-flight requests, retries, and the availability target rather than a checkpoint. Hardware can be shared or repurposed, but a training configuration does not establish serving readiness.


Fallacy: Continuous batching solves the whole LLM serving problem.
Continuous batching reuses slots released by completed requests, but it addresses only one dimension of the problem. Prefill can remain a bottleneck for long contexts because scheduling subsequent decode iterations does not remove the quadratic attention work of full-attention prefill. Section 10.7 demonstrates that KV cache memory, not compute, often limits batch size. Network bandwidth between sharded model components can dominate latency for large models. The value of continuous batching depends on the workload; slot reuse alone does not resolve these other constraints.


Pitfall: Sizing the fleet by average throughput.
Average throughput alone does not establish capacity for bursts. With unchanged work per request and service capacity, a 25 percent traffic increase from 80 percent utilization reaches 100 percent utilization, leaving no spare capacity to absorb variance. Whether the resulting queue violates an SLO depends on burst duration, the waiting budget, and admission policy. Cluster-level cold starts can delay relief for multiple minutes. Capacity planning must therefore account for peak load, burst duration, ready headroom, and the work the service can defer or reject.


Fallacy: Load balancing does not matter much for inference.
Simple load balancing strategies like round-robin can distribute request counts while leaving work uneven. The static placement analysis in section 10.11 motivates two probes, but its occupancy bounds do not predict production queue lengths. Serving comparisons must preserve arrivals, request lengths, cache affinity, and replica capacity. Work-aware routing earns its place when it improves measured tail latency without excessive coordination cost.


Pitfall: Ignoring the serving tax.
Distributed inference adds network round-trips and shard coordination to the serialization, routing, and queueing costs that can already surround a single-machine model. This serving tax depends on deployment topology and load. In the illustrative budget of section 10.3, 70 ms of model execution leaves only 30 ms for every other stage of a 100 ms request target, and queueing alone can consume that remainder as load rises. A kernel benchmark measures only the first term of equation 1; the serving latency is the measured sum along the complete request path.


Fallacy: More GPU memory always means larger batch size and higher throughput.
Larger GPU memory raises throughput only when the extra capacity supports useful work within the latency budget. Even when memory bandwidth is saturated, a larger decode batch can increase tokens per second by sharing weight reads across more sequences. That gain stops when compute, per-sequence KV-cache traffic, or the SLO becomes binding. The bottleneck hierarchy distinguishes these limits.
For an H100 with 80 GB memory and 3.35 TB/s HBM3 bandwidth, capacity and transfer rate are separate limits. More capacity may admit additional sequences, but the resulting batch must still meet compute, bandwidth, and latency budgets. Once extra sequences no longer improve useful throughput within those budgets, adding memory alone cannot help. Capacity planning therefore measures the bottleneck at the intended batch size and context length rather than assigning one permanent bottleneck to the model.


Pitfall: Neglecting multi-tenancy isolation until production.
In development and staging, single-tenant deployments work well. In production, noisy neighbors cause sudden, unpredictable performance degradation that is difficult to diagnose and resolve. A tenant bursting to 5\(\times\) normal traffic can degrade latency for all other tenants on shared infrastructure. As emphasized in section 10.12, resource quotas, priority scheduling, and bulkhead isolation must be designed into the system from the start, not retrofitted after production incidents.


Fallacy: The lowest supported precision is always the best precision.
Aggressive quantization (INT4 weights, INT4 KV cache, FP8 activations) can degrade model quality in ways that standard benchmarks miss but users see. Perplexity on a held-out dataset may change by less than 1 percent while responses degrade for edge cases, rare languages, or complex reasoning. A serving system that doubles its tokens per second with a format that lowers answer quality has not doubled its useful capacity, because throughput and quality form a frontier and a precision choice is a point on it. The disciplined approach is targeted quantization: measure per-layer sensitivity under representative workloads, restrict lower bit widths to the tensors that tolerate them, and evaluate KV caches, endpoint layers, and attention logits empirically rather than by a presumed sensitivity ranking. Calibration on representative data, followed by evaluation on diverse quality benchmarks reported beside the latency and throughput results, comes before any quantized model reaches production (section 10.9).


Pitfall: Treating MoE expert count as a free scaling knob.
Adding experts to an MoE model raises total parameters without proportionally raising active per-token arithmetic, which makes expert count look free. Every expert still occupies memory whether or not a token selects it, as section 10.10.4.1 prices for resident versus active parameters, so more experts mean more devices or less KV headroom. A distributed placement also adds dispatch and combine communication to every layer. The realized cost depends on experts selected per token, token-to-expert skew, expert capacity, topology, and batching, and no universal expert count marks where the design starts to lose. The change is justified only when a matched-quality comparison shows that active-compute savings exceed routing, imbalance, memory, and communication costs over the intended workload envelope.

These fallacies and pitfalls identify what a serving evaluation must test: traffic variance, cost per completed request within the SLO, output quality beside throughput, and interference across tenants. Correct technique selection must be followed by measurement under the intended load and failure conditions.

Self-Check: Question

A team upgrades a cluster serving a 13B LLM from 80 GB GPUs to 140 GB GPUs with identical HBM3 memory bandwidth (3.35 TB/s). At an unchanged small batch and context length, with resident weights and weight-read-dominated decode, why does extra capacity alone not raise the bandwidth-limited throughput ceiling?

Autoregressive decode is strictly compute-bound; increasing memory without adding Tensor Cores leaves execution time unchanged.
Autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth bound (\(D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}\)); once model weights fit resident in memory, token generation speed is constrained by memory bandwidth, not total memory capacity.
140 GB GPUs automatically disable CUDA graph compilation, adding driver launch latency to every iteration.
The larger memory capacity forces PagedAttention block sizes to shrink from 16 tokens to 2 tokens.

A capacity planner provisions an inference serving fleet for 80% average utilization based on mean daily traffic. Why can traffic spikes exhaust headroom before reactive scaling helps, and what determines whether the P99 SLO is missed?
True or False: Deploying continuous batching alone completely solves all throughput and latency bottlenecks in LLM serving.
True or False: Because each token activates only a small fixed number of experts, raising an MoE model’s expert count from 8 to 256 adds serving capacity at essentially no cost.
A team moves its endpoint from INT8 to INT4 weights and INT4 KV cache, doubling tokens per second while held-out perplexity changes by less than 1 percent. What should it conclude before rollout?

The change doubles useful capacity, because perplexity confirms quality is unchanged
The change is safe only if the KV cache returns to FP16, because weight precision never affects quality
Useful capacity has not been established: low-bit formats can degrade rare languages, edge cases, or reasoning while perplexity barely moves, so quality must be evaluated per layer and per task and reported beside throughput
The change should be rejected, because INT4 always reduces quality below an acceptable level


See Answers →

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Serving at scale turns trained models and distributed hardware into a service under continuously arriving work. Training optimizes aggregate progress over a run; serving must also meet user-visible latency targets while paying recurring operating costs. The useful capacity of the fleet is the work it completes within its service contract, not the work its accelerators execute in isolation. Test-time compute sharpens the point. When quality is bought by spending more compute per query, the scaling curve that drove the fleet’s growth moves into the request path, and every increment of quality is paid again on every request.
Serving performance depends on the balance between compute and memory bandwidth. In the terms of the single-machine iron law recalled in The Fleet Law, long-prompt prefill can be compute-bound (\(\Operations/\PeakRate\)), while small-batch decode is often bandwidth-bound (\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)). Each decode iteration reads active weights and the sequences’ KV state; batching shares weight reads across more tokens, whereas longer contexts increase KV traffic. Single-replica efficiency (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) therefore depends on phase, batch size, and context length. Variable output lengths make fixed batch membership waste capacity after shorter requests finish.
To maximize throughput under memory-bandwidth constraints, modern serving architectures co-design the memory hierarchy and the iteration scheduler. Continuous batching recovers idle slots by inserting new requests at token boundaries. PagedAttention reduces physical memory fragmentation through fixed-block allocation while retaining partial-page waste. Prefill/decode disaggregation assigns prompt processing and token generation to separate hardware pools sized around their measured compute, memory, and communication costs.
When model state exceeds device memory, sharding spreads a replica across accelerators; when demand exceeds a replica’s service capacity, additional replicas supply aggregate throughput. In Fleet Law terms, sharding divides the compute term \(\IronLawComputeTime/\DeviceCount\) of equation 12 but adds communication and synchronization \((\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount), \SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount))\) governed by interconnect latency floors (\(\MessageStartupLatency\)) and transfer bandwidth (\(\LinkBandwidth\)). Replication, routing, isolation, autoscaling, and multi-region placement add coordination costs and wide-area round trips to the same budget, and their tail control requires headroom. Across the serving hierarchy, the engineering objective is to increase useful completed work while preserving the latency and reliability contract under load.

Key Takeaways: Serving capacity is constrained by its contract

Serving cost recurs throughout deployment: Training is paid per model version, while inference expense accrues with traffic (principle \(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)). In the chapter’s high-volume recommendation scenario, lifetime serving cost reaches 788.4× the training cost, making efficiency a recurring economic lever.
SLO goodput is the capacity measure: A serving fleet’s capacity is the rate of completed requests that meet their TTFT and per-token targets for a fixed request mix, so batching, sharding, caching, and autoscaling help only when they raise that rate. Aggregate throughput overstates capacity whenever queueing, first-token delay, or slow token delivery makes completed work miss its contract.
Decode turns memory into capacity: Long-prompt prefill often binds on compute, while small-batch decode rereads active weights and expands private KV state token by token (principle \(\ref{pri-autoregressive-bottleneck}\)). Continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix reuse, and KV compression matter because they convert scarce HBM bandwidth and memory into admitted requests.
Prefill and decode compete for a shared worker: A monolithic long-prompt prefill lands in every active stream’s token gap. Chunked prefill bounds that gap by moving the cost into the long prompt’s own time to first token, while separate prefill and decode pools remove the interference only when their KV-cache transfer is repaid in SLO goodput.
Model class sets the primitive: Vision models benefit from predictable static or dynamic batches, recommenders from feature-parallel embedding sharding, and LLMs from iteration-level scheduling. A fleet scheduler must match the workload shape instead of applying one universal batch-size rule.
Distribution always sends a bill: Sharding, routing, isolation, and failover buy capacity or resilience while consuming communication and coordination budgets. Power-of-two choices (principle \(\ref{pri-power-two-choices}\)) illustrates the value of limiting coordination: routing can use a small number of probes rather than polling every replica.



The serving cost dominance principle (\(\ref{pri-serving-cost-dominance}\)) makes local efficiency valuable only when the service can turn it into useful capacity. Memory released by quantization may admit more sequences, but those sequences still compete for execution time and can push the endpoint beyond its latency budget. The economic comparison therefore holds the request mix, quality requirement, and service targets fixed before asking whether a change lowers the cost of completed work.

What’s Next: From data center to edgeThe serving designs developed here coordinate accelerator replicas under data-center memory, network, and availability assumptions; even the global stack’s edge points of presence only answer from cache and leave model execution in the clusters. Many applications also run models on smartphones and other personal devices, where sustained power is a few watts, memory is shared with foreground work, and connectivity is intermittent. When those devices must also adapt to local data, the fleet has to decide where learning happens, which device updates it accepts, and how a population improves a shared model without collecting raw examples.





↪ On-device adaptation under device resource budgets and federated learning across device populations are developed in Edge Intelligence.

title: 10 Serving at Scale
text:
Self-Check: Answer

True or False: A service that meets its latency SLO on every admitted request is serving all of its offered load.
Answer: False. Offered load counts all arriving work, including requests the service rejects or sheds, while admitted load counts only the work it accepts. A service can meet its latency target on admitted requests by refusing others, so capacity must be judged by how much offered work completes within the targets.
Learning Objective: Distinguish offered load from admitted load when judging whether a service meets its contract.
Configuration X reports 900 requests per second on a benchmark of short prompts, and configuration Y reports 700 requests per second on the production prompt and output mix, both at the same TTFT and TPOT targets. Which conclusion is justified?

X has more capacity, because request rate is the capacity metric for a serving system.
Neither can be ranked yet, because prompt and output lengths change the work per request, so capacity must be compared at the same request mix and SLO by counting offered work that completes within the targets.
Y has more capacity, because production traffic always contains longer requests than a benchmark.
The two are equivalent, because both meet the same latency targets.

Answer: The correct answer is B. For language models, request rate alone is insufficient because prompt and output lengths determine how much work each request carries, so a benchmark of short prompts inflates the rate. Ranking by raw rate repeats that error, and assuming production traffic is always longer replaces measurement with a guess. Meeting the same targets on different mixes does not make the configurations equivalent.
Learning Objective: Justify why serving capacity must be compared at a fixed request mix and SLO rather than by raw request rate.
In a streaming language-model service, explain which latency budget is consumed by waiting before prefill and which by contention during decode, and why a faster decode kernel alone cannot settle either problem.
Answer: Everything up to the end of prefill, including routing, admission, tokenization, queueing, and the prefill pass, counts against time to first token, while contention among sequences sharing decode steps stretches the gaps between streamed tokens and so consumes the TPOT budget. A faster decode step raises the service rate, but it does not decide how long a request waits to join a batch, which replica receives it, which requests get scarce KV-cache space, or when the fleet adds a replica. A request queued 400 ms behind a burst misses a 300 ms TTFT target however fast decode runs, so the scheduler must budget waiting and contention alongside execution time.
Learning Objective: Analyze how queueing before prefill and contention during decode consume the TTFT and TPOT budgets independently of kernel speed.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A recommendation service must answer 100,000 queries per second within 10 ms. Its model fits comfortably on one machine, which peaks at 10,000 queries per second with optimal batching. Which strategy addresses the binding constraint?

Shard the model with tensor parallelism across machines, because sharding is the general remedy whenever one machine is insufficient.
Quantize the weights so a single machine runs ten times faster.
Replicate the full model across at least ten machines and route requests among them, because the binding constraint is throughput rather than memory or per-request latency.
Raise the batch size on one machine until it reaches 100,000 queries per second.

Answer: The correct answer is C. The model fits and a single request meets its budget, so the shortfall is aggregate throughput, which horizontal replication solves by multiplying independent replicas. Sharding addresses memory or per-request latency and adds communication without multiplying throughput. Larger batches cannot help because the 10,000-query peak already assumes optimal batching, and quantization does not reliably deliver a tenfold gain.
Learning Objective: Classify a serving shortfall as a memory, throughput, or latency trigger and select replication or sharding accordingly.
A 70B-parameter model needs roughly 140 GB of FP16 weights, more than one 80 GB accelerator holds, and quantization can make it fit on one device. Explain why the team might still shard it, and how they should decide.
Answer: Fitting in memory removes the memory trigger, but the single-device execution time may still exceed the request latency budget. Sharding across several GPUs divides computation and weight traffic, yet it adds communication and synchronization, and it shortens compute-bound prefill and bandwidth-bound decode by different amounts. The team should measure the sharded configuration’s prefill latency against the TTFT target and its decode latency against the TPOT target separately, and shard only if both phases gain more than the added communication costs.
Learning Objective: Evaluate when a latency target justifies sharding a model that already fits on one device, measuring each phase against its own target.
True or False: A stream that meets its TPOT target cannot stall the reader, because TPOT bounds the gap between successive tokens.
Answer: False. TPOT is the average of the gaps between tokens, so one long gap can stall the reader while the average still meets its target. Per-gap tail targets are stated as time between tokens (TBT), which must be monitored separately from average cadence.
Learning Objective: Distinguish average token cadence (TPOT) from per-gap time between tokens (TBT) when setting streaming latency targets.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Two configurations serve the same request mix under the same TTFT and TPOT targets. Configuration X completes 1,200 requests per second, of which 70 percent meet both targets; configuration Y completes 1,000 requests per second, of which 95 percent meet both. Which has more serving capacity?

X, because it completes more requests per second and keeps its accelerators busier.
The two are equal, because both process the same request mix.
X, because requests that miss their targets still return results to users.
Y, because SLO goodput counts only requests that meet their targets, about 950 per second against about 840 for X.

Answer: The correct answer is D. SLO goodput is the rate of completed requests that meet the stated TTFT and TPOT targets for a fixed request mix, so X delivers about 840 useful requests per second and Y about 950. A request that misses its contract counts for nothing however busy the accelerators were, so higher raw throughput or a returned result does not add useful capacity.
Learning Objective: Calculate SLO goodput from completion rate and target attainment, and use it to compare serving configurations.
Explain the composition of the distributed ‘serving tax’ (\(\EndToEndRequestLatency = \InferenceLatency + \NetworkLatency + \SerializationLatency + \CoordinationLatency + \QueueingLatency\)) and describe how zero-copy serialization formats mitigate serialization overhead.
Answer: The serving tax comprises exposed network, serialization, coordination, and queueing delays beyond model execution. Zero-copy formats can expose compatible wire-format data without a separate parse-and-copy pass. They do not remove network transmission, all validation, or every memory copy: layout, ownership, device placement, and transport determine what can be avoided. Measure each contribution on the request critical path rather than adding overlapping intervals.
Learning Objective: Analyze the components of the distributed serving tax and the mechanism by which zero-copy serialization reduces latency.
True or False: Interactive inference recovery is judged against request latency and availability objectives, whereas long-running training recovery is usually judged against lost progress and time to completion.
Answer: True. Interactive serving may need rerouting, bounded retries, or a fallback before a request deadline. Training often restores a checkpoint and repeats lost work. Neither mode guarantees invisible recovery; the acceptable interruption follows the workload contract.
Learning Objective: Compare operational fault tolerance and state management requirements between distributed training and distributed inference.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A production recommendation model costs $50,000 to train (a one-time expense) and serves 10,000 QPS continuously for 2 years (730 days) at an operational cost of $10 per million queries. What is the ratio of lifetime serving cost to training cost?

Approximately \(1.3\times\)
Approximately \(126.1\times\)
Approximately \(12.6\times\)
Approximately \(630.7\times\)

Answer: The correct answer is B. The model serves \(10{,}000 \times 86{,}400 \times 730 = 6.3072 \times 10^{11}\) queries. At \(10^{-5}\) dollars per query, serving costs 6,307,200 dollars, or approximately 126.1 times the 50,000-dollar training cost. The other ratios miscount accumulated queries or unit cost. This result depends on the specified sustained traffic, lifetime, and price rather than a universal cost ratio.
Learning Objective: Calculate the lifetime economic leverage of recurring inference expense relative to one-time training expense.
True or False: Serving cost always exceeds training cost once a model is large enough, because larger models cost more per query.
Answer: False. Whether serving dominates depends on traffic, unit serving cost, deployment duration, and the training expense, not on model size alone. A low-traffic deployment or a short lifetime can leave training as the larger cost over the whole deployment.
Learning Objective: Identify the inputs that decide whether serving or training dominates a model’s lifetime cost.
A team estimates its cost per query from GPU time on fully loaded replicas, but its fleet also bills for reserved replicas that sit idle overnight to absorb the daytime peak. What does the lifetime cost model require?

Nothing more, because idle replicas do no work and therefore add no cost per query.
Doubling the query rate to account for the peak, because peaks set the cost.
Replacing cost per query with training cost, because idle capacity is a one-time expense.
Charging the billed idle and reserved capacity inside the unit cost, and counting the same served queries in the rate that was used to estimate that cost.

Answer: The correct answer is D. Unit serving cost must include the chosen serving boundary, including idle or reserved capacity whenever it is billed, and the query rate must count the same served queries. Treating idle replicas as free understates the bill, and inflating the query rate double-counts traffic rather than fixing the cost boundary. Reserved capacity recurs with every billing period, so it is not a one-time expense.
Learning Objective: Apply a consistent accounting boundary when estimating unit serving cost for the lifetime cost model.
A model costs $2M to train, and its first year of serving costs about $18M. Explain why a 10 percent reduction in cost per request can be worth nearly as much as the original training run, and state the conditions under which that saving is real.
Answer: Serving expense recurs with traffic, so a 10 percent reduction in cost per request saves about $1.8M in the first year alone and keeps saving every year after, while training was paid once. The saving is real only if request volume and service quality stay fixed, because the reduction must lower billed capacity for the same useful work. A change that only lowers latency does not reduce billed capacity, so engineering effort on a deployed model should target cost per completed request at the SLO.
Learning Objective: Justify why recurring serving savings can rival training cost, and identify the conditions under which a unit-cost reduction yields real savings.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

In the four-level Serving Hierarchy (Request, Replica, Service, Platform), which level and primary optimization lever are correctly matched to their target bottleneck?

Platform level: Minimizing single-forward-pass latency via kernel fusion and memory layout
Request level: Ensuring fair-share GPU quotas and tenant isolation across organizations
Service level: Managing aggregate capacity across multiple replicas via load balancing and autoscaling
Replica level: Reducing client-side network RTT via edge caching and CDN routing

Answer: The correct answer is C. The Service level coordinates multiple replicas of the same model to deliver aggregate capacity through load balancing, request routing, and autoscaling. The proposal linking the Platform level to kernel fusion confuses fleet-wide multi-tenancy with intra-device execution; the proposal placing fair-share tenant quotas at the Request level incorrectly attributes platform governance to per-request transformations; and the proposal placing edge CDN caching at the Replica level confuses single-device execution with edge routing infrastructure.
Learning Objective: Classify inference optimization levers according to their respective tiers in the Serving Hierarchy.
**Order the four levels of the Serving Hierarchy from the most granular execution tier to the highest fleet-wide governance tier:


Service level (fleet routing, load balancing, autoscaling)
Request level (per-request latency, tokenization, dynamic batching)
Platform level (multi-tenancy, cross-workload scheduling, placement)
Replica level (intra-instance utilization, GPU memory allocation, kernel fusion)**

Answer: The correct sequence is (2) -> (4) -> (1) -> (3). - (2) Request level operates on individual input tensors, handling preprocessing, dynamic batching, and per-request latency. - (4) Replica level optimizes single-instance execution, managing GPU memory, KV cache allocation, and fused kernels. - (1) Service level coordinates multiple identical replicas into aggregate capacity via load balancers and autoscaling. - (3) Platform level manages the global fleet across multiple models and tenants, enforcing fair sharing, resource quotas, and physical placement.
Learning Objective: Structure the hierarchy of inference optimization tiers from individual request processing to global platform management.
← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

A vision model has fixed latency overhead \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime = 2\text{ ms}\) and variable compute time \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime = 1\text{ ms/item}\). An LLM decode step has \(\BatchFixedOverheadTime = 40\text{ ms}\) (loading 140 GB weights from HBM) and \(\MarginalRequestServiceTime = 0.5\text{ ms/token}\). At what approximate batch size \(\BatchSize\) does each workload reach the ‘knee’ of its batching efficiency curve (\(\BatchSize \approx \BatchFixedOverheadTime / \MarginalRequestServiceTime\))?

Vision knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 10\); LLM decode knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 20\)
Vision knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 80\); LLM decode knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 2\)
Vision knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 4\); LLM decode knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 40\)
Vision knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 2\); LLM decode knee at \(\BatchSize \approx 80\)

Answer: The correct answer is D. The knee of the batching efficiency curve occurs where the variable compute cost (\(\BatchSize \times \MarginalRequestServiceTime\)) begins to exceed fixed overhead (\(\BatchFixedOverheadTime\)). For the vision model, \(\BatchSize \approx 2\text{ ms} / 1\text{ ms} = 2\). For LLM decode, \(\BatchSize \approx 40\text{ ms} / 0.5\text{ ms} = 80\). The larger LLM knee illustrates a stronger incentive to amortize weight reads across concurrent requests. The chosen batch can remain below that knee when arrivals, KV-cache capacity, or the latency budget limit useful concurrency; the knee is not a universal batch requirement. The inverted result swaps the two workloads; the intermediate configurations miscalculate the quotient of fixed and variable parameters.
Learning Objective: Calculate the knee point on the batching efficiency curve for compute-bound versus memory-bandwidth-bound inference workloads.
For a static LLM batch that retains all slots and pads completed sequences until the longest sequence finishes, define the waste ratio \(W=1-\bar{S}/S_{\max}\). How can continuous batching reduce this waste?
Answer: The stated implementation allocates \(B S_{\max}\) token-step slots but performs only \(B\bar{S}\) useful token steps, leaving a waste fraction \(1-\bar{S}/S_{\max}\). Continuous batching can replace completed sequences with waiting requests at each iteration. This reduces padded-slot waste when enough admissible work is queued; it does not guarantee a full batch under light arrivals or memory pressure. Holding responses until the batch finishes is a separate response-barrier policy, not an inherent consequence of fixed membership.
Learning Objective: Analyze the mathematical formulation of batching waste in static LLM execution and the mechanism of continuous batching.
For a recommendation pipeline that first retrieves sparse features and then processes dense features before combining them, order: (1) Feature Interaction, (2) Dense Feature Processing, (3) Sparse Feature Lookup, (4) Ranking Head.
Answer: The correct sequence is (3) Sparse Feature Lookup -> (2) Dense Feature Processing -> (1) Feature Interaction -> (4) Ranking Head for the stated pipeline. Interaction consumes both sparse and dense representations; ranking consumes their combined features. Sparse lookup and dense processing can run concurrently in other implementations when neither depends on the other, so their serial order is an explicit scenario assumption.
Learning Objective: Structure the sequential execution stages of a feature-parallel recommendation model pipeline.
A stable inference service completes 1,000 requests/sec with an assumed mean end-to-end latency of 100 ms. Each replica executes full batches of eight in 80 ms, giving 100 requests/sec of service capacity. With a separate target of at most 80% mean service utilization, what mean in-flight work and candidate fleet size follow, without claiming a P99 guarantee?

Mean in-flight work is 100 requests; sizing service capacity at the 80% utilization target gives 13 replicas
Required concurrency \(Q_{\text{req}} = 1{,}000\); minimum SLO-sized fleet \(= 125\) replicas
Required concurrency \(Q_{\text{req}} = 80\); minimum SLO-sized fleet \(= 10\) replicas
Required concurrency \(Q_{\text{req}} = 100\); minimum SLO-sized fleet \(= 10\) replicas

Answer: The correct answer is A. Little’s law gives 1,000 × 0.1 = 100 requests in flight on average, including waiting work. Fleet sizing instead uses the separate utilization target: ceil(1,000/(0.8 × 100)) = 13 replicas, running at about 76.9% utilization. Their 104 executing positions exclude queues. Under the idealized assumption that all other latency is waiting or batch formation, the fixed 80 ms service time gives 80 requests executing on average and leaves 20 waiting or accumulating. Ten replicas are the throughput-only saturation boundary. The assumed mean and tail SLO both require validation; dividing in-flight work by batch slots does not establish the fleet size.
Learning Objective: Separate mean in-flight occupancy from executing capacity and size a candidate fleet with an explicit service-utilization target.
What is a per-request compute budget for test-time compute, and how does additional reasoning change the serving cost of a request?
Answer: A per-request compute budget limits the generated tokens, candidate evaluations, or search steps a request may consume, stated in both latency and capacity. It binds when serial reasoning tokens exhaust a request’s latency budget or its share of fleet capacity before further reasoning stops improving the answer. Additional generated tokens, candidate evaluations, or search steps increase work per request and can extend KV-cache residency without changing the bottleneck of each decode step. A serving policy sets that budget from measured quality gains, request deadlines, and fleet load. Parallel candidate evaluations consume capacity without necessarily adding the same serial latency.
Learning Objective: Explain the serving cost of test-time compute and why a per-request compute budget is stated in both latency and capacity.
True or False: Increasing the batching timeout window during a high-traffic spike is always the optimal policy for reducing tail latency.
Answer: False. In the chapter’s traffic-adaptive rule, a fixed target batch fills sooner as arrival rate rises, permitting a shorter formation window. This reduces intentional formation delay, not the separate wait for a busy replica. Shrinking the maximum batch can also reduce service capacity and worsen queueing. The policy must be evaluated against arrival patterns, measured service rates, tail latency, and overload handling; neither a longer nor a shorter window is universally optimal.
Learning Objective: Evaluate adaptive batching control policies under varying traffic arrival intensities.

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

How does PagedAttention reduce memory waste in LLM KV cache management, and what system-level benefit can follow?

It compresses KV cache tensors using lossless entropy coding to reduce arithmetic intensity in attention kernels.
It replaces standard multi-head attention with grouped query attention by dynamically merging key-value heads.
It maps logical tokens to non-contiguous fixed-size physical blocks, reclaiming unused reservations so that more requests may fit
It offloads 100% of KV cache data to host CPU DRAM, eliminating GPU HBM usage entirely for active sequences.

Answer: The correct answer is C. Any free block can extend a sequence, removing external fragmentation within the fixed-block pool. Only the final partly filled block retains internal waste. Reclaimed capacity can support larger batches, but the gain depends on request lengths, available memory, and the latency contract. Paging changes allocation; it neither compresses tensor values nor changes the number of KV heads.
Learning Objective: Analyze the virtual memory mapping mechanism of PagedAttention and its impact on KV cache fragmentation and serving throughput.
What cost does a colocated draft model impose on a speculative decoding replica, and how does it influence whether speculative decoding should be enabled for a specific serving endpoint?

The latency penalty paid when draft models fail to generate valid UTF-8 token encodings.
The GPU memory allocated to draft model weights and draft KV cache, which reduces available HBM for batch concurrency.
The serialization overhead incurred when transmitting draft tokens across InfiniBand interconnects.
The loss in model generation accuracy caused by greedy sampling during draft token verification.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Draft weights and draft KV cache consume memory that could otherwise support target-model concurrency. Speculation is useful when lower latency or more accepted output per target pass outweighs that capacity cost and draft execution. The result depends on load, acceptance, and both models; a latency-oriented endpoint does not automatically benefit, nor is every throughput-oriented endpoint harmed.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the memory and throughput trade-offs of speculative decoding as an admission and scheduling policy under service-level agreements.
Why does speculative decoding accelerate autoregressive generation on modern GPUs without altering the target model’s output probability distribution?

It lets the draft model’s tokens through whenever the draft model’s own confidence exceeds a fixed threshold, so the target pass can be skipped for confident tokens
It runs the target model at lower precision during verification, so each verification pass streams fewer weight bytes than an ordinary decode step
It accepts each draft token with probability equal to the smaller of one and the ratio of the target model’s probability to the draft model’s probability, resamples a rejected position from the normalized positive difference between the two distributions, and verifies all drafts in one target pass for roughly the weight traffic of one token
It verifies only the first draft token and emits the remaining drafts unchecked, relying on the draft model’s training to match the target

Answer: The correct answer is C. The acceptance-and-resampling rule makes the emitted sequence follow the target model’s distribution exactly, and verifying every drafted position in one target pass streams the target’s weights once, the same reuse batching buys but drawn from one request’s future tokens. Confidence thresholds or partial verification are approximate rules that do not inherit the guarantee, and verification runs at the target’s own precision.
Learning Objective: Analyze how speculative decoding achieves latency speedups while preserving exact target model output distributions
A chatbot has 1,000 concurrent users sharing a 2,000-token prefix and retaining 500 private response tokens each. For a hypothetical MHA model with 80 layers, 64 KV heads, head width 128, and FP16 cache, explain the reduction from about 6.6 TB to 1.3 TB with prefix sharing.
Answer: Each cached token uses 2 × 80 × 64 × 128 × 2 = 2,621,440 bytes. Without sharing, 2,500,000 token positions consume 6.5536 TB; storing the shared prefix once leaves 2,000 + 1,000 × 500 = 502,000 positions, or 1.316 TB. The reduction is 79.92%. This is an MHA scenario, not the smaller eight-KV-head GQA cache of Llama-2-70B; saved memory alone does not prove a fivefold throughput gain.
Learning Objective: Calculate KV cache memory savings achieved through prefix caching in shared-context multi-tenant workloads.
True or False: When measured acceptance falls and the scheduler stops running the draft model, the memory that speculative decoding consumed returns immediately to the target model’s KV-cache admission budget.
Answer: False. Disabling draft execution stops the drafting and verification work, but the resident draft weights and any draft KV pages remain allocated. Recovering that memory for target requests requires unloading the draft weights and ending or migrating the speculative state, so the speculation policy and the admission controller must be evaluated together.
Learning Objective: Evaluate speculative decoding as a serving policy whose memory cost persists until the draft state is released.
In the precision dividend for the reference 70B replica, FP16 weights use 17.5 GB per GPU on eight 80 GB GPUs. Ignoring runtime reserves and quantization metadata, INT4 weights use about 4.4 GB per GPU and INT8 KV cache halves the per-request cache footprint. Why is the gain in maximum batch about 2.4 times rather than the fourfold weight reduction?

Because INT4 weights must be dequantized into a resident FP16 copy, so only part of the weight saving survives in HBM
Because the gain applies only to the eight-head GQA cache; the 64-head MHA baseline gains nothing from INT8 KV storage
Because the freed weight memory raises the KV budget from 62.5 GB to about 75.6 GB per GPU, a factor of about 1.21, and halving bytes per cached request doubles the count again, so the two effects multiply to about 2.4
Because quantizing the KV cache lengthens each decode step enough to cancel most of the extra capacity

Answer: The correct answer is C. Maximum batch is free memory divided by per-request cache. INT4 weights raise free memory by 75.6/62.5 ≈ 1.21, and INT8 cache halves per-request state, a factor of two, giving about 2.4 for either attention layout. The weight reduction is fourfold, but weights are only part of each GPU’s budget. Runtime reserves, metadata, and the latency target lower the deployable batch below this bound.
Learning Objective: Synthesize how weight and KV-cache quantization interact multiplicatively to expand serving batch capacity

← Back to Questions



Self-Check: Answer

Why do the prompt prefill phase and the token decode phase of LLM serving exhibit different performance bottlenecks on the same accelerator?

Prefill generates tokens sequentially one by one, making it memory-bound by weight reads, whereas decode processes all prompt tokens in parallel, making it compute-bound by Tensor Cores
Prefill relies exclusively on integer arithmetic units, whereas decode requires floating-point matrix multiplication units
Long-prompt prefill GEMMs reuse weights across prompt tokens and can have a compute ceiling, whereas weight-dominated single-request decode has low intensity and a bandwidth ceiling
Prefill requires continuous network AllToAll collective exchanges between GPUs, whereas decode requires no inter-GPU communication

Answer: The correct answer is C. Long-prompt prefill GEMMs can reuse weights across many prompt tokens, while single-request decode streams weights for one token. The simplified FP16 estimates place those components above and below the ridge, respectively. Neither estimate proves saturation or classifies every operator: actual traffic, kernel shapes, cache reads, dispatch, and communication require profiling. The phases use compatible arithmetic rather than exclusively different number types.
Learning Objective: Compare the computational characteristics and primary hardware bottlenecks of the prefill and decode serving phases
How can an un-chunked long prompt prefill delay active decode streams on the same worker, and what trade-off does chunked prefill introduce?
Answer: A policy that schedules a full long-prompt prefill before returning to decode can create a conspicuous gap in active streams’ time between tokens (TBT). An isolated stall can be diluted in a long response’s average time per output token (TPOT). Chunked prefill interleaves bounded prompt-token chunks with decode work, controlling how much prefill work enters each iteration. Smaller chunks can reduce interference while adding overhead and extending the incoming prompt’s TTFT. True or False: Deploying continuous batching alone completely solves all throughput and latency bottlenecks in LLM serving.
Answer: False. Continuous batching reuses slots at iteration boundaries. It does not remove the quadratic attention work of long full-attention prefills, shrink the KV tensors needed by admitted requests, or eliminate communication within sharded replicas. Additional mechanisms are selected for the binding constraint: chunking can limit prefill interference, paging can recover allocation waste, compatible prefix reuse can avoid repeated work, and sharding or replication can supply needed capacity. No fixed combination establishes the service contract without workload measurements.
Learning Objective: Evaluate the scope and limitations of continuous batching within the end-to-end LLM serving pipeline.
True or False: Because each token activates only a small fixed number of experts, raising an MoE model’s expert count from 8 to 256 adds serving capacity at essentially no cost.
Answer: False. Every expert occupies memory whether or not a token selects it, so more experts mean more devices or less KV headroom, and a distributed placement adds dispatch, combine, and imbalance costs. The design is justified only when a matched-quality comparison shows active-compute savings exceeding routing, imbalance, memory, and communication costs.
Learning Objective: Analyze the system-level memory, communication, and load balancing costs of scaling expert counts in MoE models
A team moves its endpoint from INT8 to INT4 weights and INT4 KV cache, doubling tokens per second while held-out perplexity changes by less than 1 percent. What should it conclude before rollout?

The change doubles useful capacity, because perplexity confirms quality is unchanged
The change is safe only if the KV cache returns to FP16, because weight precision never affects quality
Useful capacity has not been established: low-bit formats can degrade rare languages, edge cases, or reasoning while perplexity barely moves, so quality must be evaluated per layer and per task and reported beside throughput
The change should be rejected, because INT4 always reduces quality below an acceptable level

Answer: The correct answer is C. Throughput and quality form a frontier, and a precision choice is a point on it. Perplexity can stay nearly flat while users see worse answers on hard or rare inputs, so targeted quantization measures per-layer sensitivity, keeps sensitive tensors at higher precision, and evaluates diverse quality benchmarks alongside latency and throughput. Neither blanket acceptance nor blanket rejection follows from bit width alone.
Learning Objective: Evaluate quantized serving changes on the throughput-quality frontier rather than throughput alone

title: 12 ML Operations at Scale
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why do practices that work for managing one model collapse when organizations deploy hundreds?
One model is a project. A hundred models form a system of systems whose dependencies and failures cannot be managed one model at a time. A data-pipeline change may affect models built by several teams, while a deployment failure may require coordinated rollbacks across interconnected services. The team making a change may not know every consumer, and the team seeing a regression may not control its cause. Practices that work when one engineer knows the entire system become unreliable when ownership, data, and release schedules are distributed. Adding faster machines does not resolve that uncertainty. A fleet can have spare compute capacity and still be unable to ship safely because nobody can establish which models depend on a changed input or who may authorize recovery. Shared infrastructure can reduce this repeated coordination, but it also concentrates dependencies and introduces its own operating cost. Centralizing every decision can turn the platform team into a bottleneck; leaving every team to improvise makes compatibility and accountability difficult to sustain. The engineering task is to make routine changes repeatable while preserving evidence about their effects and clear authority over their consequences. Growth becomes manageable when adding a model does not require rebuilding the surrounding operational process, yet its owners remain responsible for acceptable behavior. In C³ terms, fleet operations makes coordination a designed system constraint alongside the compute and communication resources that models consume.

Learning Objectives

Explain why operational load grows with coupling through shared features, pipelines, and capacity rather than with model count
Design registries, release gates, and evaluation contracts that preserve lineage, dependency safety, and rollback confidence
Design feature-store operations that manage freshness, ownership, compatibility, and training-serving skew
Size staged rollouts and production experiments whose sample size, stopping rule, and interference assumptions bound user exposure
Diagnose production incidents using monitoring hierarchies and multidimensional reliability budgets across the fleet
Calculate platform return, utilization break-even, and lifecycle total cost, then attribute fleet spend to accountable owners
Evaluate platform organization and lifecycle choices using adoption, versioning, and retirement evidence



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



Consider a team of five engineers maintaining a single recommendation model. When the model drifts, they manually retrain it. When the API latency spikes, they manually scale the instances. Now, scale that same team to support five hundred models across dozens of product surfaces. The same engineering team cannot sustain that growth by performing machine learning operations (MLOps), the practices that version, deploy, monitor, and roll back production models, by hand for every model. Shared controls must preserve human accountability while automating routine coordination. The fleet becomes the unit of capacity planning and investment. Versioned model and feature state makes changes reviewable, release gates bound their exposure, and monitoring and incident review feed production evidence back into those controls.
In the fleet stack of The Fleet Stack, the Operations row sits directly above Runtime and Serving and directly below Assurance, the first row of the Governance band. It belongs to the Serving band because it operates models that are already deployed, whereas the Reliability and Control row two rows lower schedules and recovers individual jobs. The Operations row acts as the fleet’s control plane, the dashboard, steering, and maintenance system that keeps physical infrastructure, training systems, serving paths, edge deployments, and governance rules from drifting apart. Once models span data centers, serving platforms, and heterogeneous edge fleets of adaptive devices, reliability depends less on any single model and more on the operational machinery that keeps the whole fleet observable, coordinated, and recoverable. Adaptive edge fleets sharpen the requirement, because there the operator ships a versioned adaptation policy rather than fixed weights, and that policy stays safe only while telemetry keeps it observable and rollback keeps it recoverable. Those controls must operate as shared infrastructure for every model the fleet runs.


↩︎ Adaptive edge device populations and the constraints that shape them are established in Edge Intelligence.
Shared dependencies make local operational choices fleet-wide concerns. An upstream data change can affect several models, concurrent deployments can contend for the same capacity, and independent alerts can obscure a common failure. Training and serving also compete for expensive infrastructure whose idle capacity still incurs cost. The platform must coordinate those interactions while preserving each team’s responsibility for model behavior.
The organizational response is platform thinking. Rather than treating each model as an independent system with its own infrastructure, platforms provide shared services that amortize operational costs across the entire model portfolio. Feature stores1 share feature definitions and values across models. Their contract is that training and serving use compatible feature meanings, with historical training values restricted to information available at the prediction time. Unified deployment pipelines ensure consistent rollout practices. Centralized monitoring aggregates signals across models to detect system-wide issues and enable capacity planning. The challenge is designing, implementing, and operating these platforms so they scale with the portfolio rather than against it. This is the C³ coordination axis at its widest. The Fleet Law charges synchronization within one distributed step, while fleet operations pays the coordination cost of every release, rollback, and shared dependency across the whole portfolio.
1 Feature store: A centralized repository that manages the computation, storage, and serving of ML features. The core systems problem it solves is training-serving skew; section 12.4 develops that failure mode and the platform invariant that contains it.
Self-Check: Question

Why can manual, per-model operational maintenance become difficult to sustain as an organization expands to hundreds of models that share features, resources, and release dependencies?

Shared data dependencies, contested resources, and independent alert streams add coordination work that can exceed the capacity of manual per-model processes.
Modern deep learning framework compilers prohibit deploying more than one model graph per physical datacenter.
Single-model architectures run on asynchronous virtual memory subnets that cannot route traffic through standard TCP/IP gateways.
Network switches automatically drop telemetry packets when concurrent endpoint connections exceed ten.

What is the primary architectural purpose of the Control Plane in an enterprise ML platform spanning datacenters, cloud clusters, and edge fleets?
Treating each model in an enterprise as an isolated, independent entity with bespoke pipelines remains an economically sound strategy as long as each individual model achieves high predictive accuracy.

See Answers →





The five engineers of the opening example do not acquire five hundred models overnight, and the path from one model to many explains where a control plane becomes necessary. An organization’s first homepage recommender, search ranker, and fraud detector can each run on a bespoke, team-local pipeline for data processing, training, validation, and deployment that lets each group optimize for its immediate requirements. As the fleet grows, those independent pipelines begin sharing features, embeddings, and GPU pools, until one uncoordinated upstream change breaks five downstream models at once.
As the number of models grows, shared dependencies create operational complexity faster than model count alone suggests. Dense interactions produce superlinear coordination work unless strong ownership and interface boundaries contain them. Between one model and a hundred, deployment coordination moves from a team-local task to the critical path, and shared data dependencies grow from a single pipeline into a dense graph. Monitoring, on-call scope, utilization, debugging, and governance change with them (table 1).



Table 1: Operational Complexity Growth at Scale: Illustrative challenges across 1, 10, and 100 models. Even one model requires deployment coordination and depends on its data pipeline. Shared dependencies can make releases a fleet-wide critical path, dashboards require aggregation, and debugging span team boundaries; actual complexity depends on coupling and ownership.

Napkin Math 12.1: Shared versus dedicated accelerator poolsProblem: A platform team manages a fleet of 100 GPUs. Under dedicated per-team quotas, average idle time is 70 percent. Moving to a multi-tenant ML platform that shares resources across teams and uses idle training GPUs for inference reduces aggregate idle time to 30 percent. What hardware cost does the platform save?
Math: For a fixed active workload, required hardware is inverse to utilization, while useful work per GPU is proportional to utilization. The problem states idle time, so the calculation first converts it to utilization.

Utilization: Utilization is one minus the idle fraction, so dedicated quotas run at 0.30 and the shared platform at 0.70.
Efficiency Gain: 0.70 (shared utilization) / 0.30 (dedicated utilization) = 2.33× more work per GPU.
Hardware Reduction: 1 \(-\) (0.30 / 0.70) = 57.1 percent.
Annual Savings: 57 percent of $1.75M budget \(\approx\) $1,000,000/year.

Systems insight: Multi-tenancy acts as an infrastructure multiplier. Under the assumed utilization improvement, breaking down resource silos reduces required hardware by 57 percent for the same workload; with the same hardware budget, it raises useful work from 30 to 70 active GPU-equivalents. In the machine learning fleet, statistical multiplexing pools demands whose peaks do not fully coincide, allowing teams to share capacity that separate allocations would leave idle. Realizing these savings requires enough headroom for coincident peaks and failures, together with isolation that preserves each workload’s service contract.





One upstream embedding update can degrade every dependent model.
Per-model validation does not establish compatibility across a dependency chain. When Model A depends on features computed by Pipeline B, which uses embeddings from Model C, a change to one component can affect its downstream consumers. A seemingly innocuous update to Model C’s embedding layer might shift the feature distributions that Model A depends upon, degrading its performance even though Model A itself has not changed. This cascading interdependence makes the interfaces between models part of the operational contract.

Systems Perspective 12.1: The complexity explosionAs a fleet accumulates shared dependencies, system-level coordination can become the binding problem. A new model adds its own operating cost, but it can also change feature pipelines, release schedules, and contention for infrastructure used by existing models. The marginal cost therefore depends on how the new model couples to the portfolio rather than on how many models the fleet already contains.


A sketch of operational load across production model counts, drawn on logarithmic axes with one assumed growth shape per source of work, shows how coupling outruns a fixed team (figure 1). Alerts grow linearly because each model brings its own fixed set of monitored metrics. The sketch assigns deployment coordination an intermediate \(\ProductionModelCount \log \ProductionModelCount\) growth shape; this is an illustrative assumption rather than a release-scheduling complexity bound. A dense dependency graph motivates the quadratic conflict curve because \(\ProductionModelCount\) models form roughly \(\ProductionModelCount^2/2\) possible pairs; the recorded dependencies determine which pairs can actually conflict. Under these shapes the total crosses the team-capacity ceiling near 50 models. The shapes are a sketch, not measurements, so the crossing marks where repeated work outgrows a team rather than a threshold a real organization can read off the plot. Measured dependency density, engineering effort, and remediation cost decide when platform engineering pays.














Figure 1: The N-Models Complexity Explosion: The curves show monitoring alerts growing linearly with model count, deployment coordination growing as \(\mathcal{O}(\ProductionModelCount \log \ProductionModelCount)\), and dependency conflicts growing quadratically as models share features and data sources. Under these assumed shapes, the total operational load crosses team capacity around 50 models, sketching the transition from artisanal model management to platform-required operations.



Once operational load exceeds team capacity, continued portfolio growth requires reducing repeated work, simplifying dependencies, or expanding the team’s capacity. Shared platform engineering addresses the repeated work of deploying, monitoring, and debugging models. Its economic case begins with identifying which of those responsibilities can be shared and which must remain with model owners.


Separating shared platform duties from model-owner responsibilities starts with seeing where single-model habits fail in a coupled portfolio. A single-model team can promote a release through a canary (a small slice of live traffic served by the candidate) and roll back in isolation. In a shared fleet, pushing an updated upstream model can silently shift inputs for downstream rankers, exhaust shared GPU headroom during concurrent rollouts, or leave dependent services broken if one model rolls back alone. Platform-scale deployment must preserve compatibility with dependent models at every intermediate state. Compatible interfaces can permit independent updates; a changed feature representation may instead require a coordinated migration. Rollback follows the same dependency contract, because reverting one model may require restoring compatible features or dependent models. Concurrent deployments also compete for GPU memory and network bandwidth, making resource headroom part of the release decision.
For recommendation systems, this complexity appears along the request path. Candidate retrieval and ranking models execute alongside diversity filters and business rule layers, sometimes in sequence and sometimes in parallel. Updating a component requires identifying which consumers depend on its outputs and testing whether the complete path still meets its quality and latency targets.
Monitoring requirements evolve similarly. Model-specific metrics such as prediction accuracy, inference latency, and data drift remain necessary, but separate dashboards do not expose shared causes by themselves. When many models depend on the same feature pipeline, a single upstream failure can appear as many unrelated model alerts. Responders need a portfolio view that connects those symptoms before investigating individual models.
Platform monitoring must therefore aggregate across models while maintaining the ability to drill down into specifics. This requires hierarchical metrics that run from business outcomes through portfolio and model signals down to infrastructure health, the structure section 12.6.3 develops. The same contrast between one model and a portfolio also changes what each release must prove, because workloads differ in how fast they change and how much harm a bad version can do.



Applying a single release policy across a fleet either starves a fraud detector that needs hourly updates and second-scale rollback as attackers adapt, or rushes a \(70\text{B}\text{--}405\text{B}\) generalist large language model (LLM) into production before multi-domain evaluation catches a capability regression. Different deployment contexts impose different operational contracts, and the archetype taxonomy in Three systems archetypes helps interpret the illustrative policies in table 2. Release frequency follows data change and validation cost; rollback targets follow the harm and reversibility of a bad release. Model family alone determines neither: LLMs may need long observation windows while still requiring rapid traffic rollback, and fraud detection needs fast containment even when a new model takes longer to validate.

Rollback means routing to a validated version; the observation period needed to approve a new version can be much longer.
