title: 13 Security & Privacy
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Fleet stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a correctly functioning machine learning service still disclose sensitive information or enable an attack?
Many useful machine learning systems depend on personal data, institutional knowledge, or behavioral patterns, creating tension between utility and protection. Models can encode sensitive information and later reveal it through their outputs, extending risk beyond transient data processing. An authorized request can expose a private training example, while accepted training data can be manipulated to alter future behavior. In both cases, the software may execute as designed while the service violates its intended boundaries. Protecting a single server therefore leaves questions about what the model learned, who supplied it, and what callers can induce it to do. Scaling introduces more participants, copies, credentials, and handoffs, often across organizations with different responsibilities. A control applied at one boundary may leave another exposed, and a compromised participant can affect work shared across the fleet. The engineering decision is which actors to trust with which information and authority, then how to enforce those choices throughout training, release, and operation. Protection also consumes resources: restricting access can complicate coordination, checking requests adds work, and limiting information release can reduce model utility. Those costs must fit the service’s operating budget without making safeguards optional when demand rises. A high-performing model may still be undeployable if sensitive information or control escapes the intended boundary. In C³ terms, Compute, Communication, and Coordination must preserve confidentiality, integrity, and accountable control as well as throughput.

Learning Objectives

Distinguish security from privacy in ML systems through formal definitions, threat models, and quantitative trade-offs
Explain how a correctly executing model can disclose memorized training data through authorized outputs
Analyze ML-specific attack vectors across model theft, data poisoning, adversarial examples, fleet-internal gradient exchange, and hardware vulnerabilities
Apply lessons from historical breaches and a layered maturity model to prioritize controls for a deployment’s threat model
Design layered defenses across data, model, runtime, and hardware, weighing each control by the trust boundary it protects and the compute, communication, or coordination cost it imposes
Specify privacy-accounting inputs and assess reported budgets against sampling assumptions, composition, and measured utility
Select rollback and forensic responses for a suspect model by tracing its provenance through the release record



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



A serving fleet can meet its latency target while an authenticated client collects enough responses to copy model behavior. A federated training job can converge while a participating device submits poisoned updates. The release gates and hierarchical monitoring that govern the fleet can report both systems healthy, because a copied model and a planted backdoor need not move any availability, latency, or aggregate-quality signal. Operational health alone therefore cannot establish security. In the fleet stack (The Fleet Stack), the governance band begins with the Assurance row, which sits directly above Operations and which this chapter shares with Robust AI. That row must preserve the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the fleet across the same interfaces that make distributed training and serving possible.
Selecting a defense starts by identifying the protected asset, the actor who threatens it, the access that actor has, and the boundary that access must not cross. An API client can observe responses; a training participant can submit updates; a host administrator may inspect runtime state. Those capabilities call for different controls. The breach cases make these boundary failures concrete, the threat model turns them into explicit assumptions, and the later mechanisms enforce those assumptions at measurable compute, communication, and coordination cost.
An attacker can steal database records, alter them, or disrupt access to them. Machine learning adds a learned representation through which those failures can propagate. An adversary may probe a model for memorized training examples or poison its training data to introduce a backdoor that activates on a chosen trigger. Protecting the stored records therefore does not fully protect the behavior learned from them or the information exposed through predictions.
Operational platforms manage hundreds of models across distributed infrastructure, extending the attack surface across workers, devices, and administrative domains. In synchronous data-parallel training, one compromised worker contributes directly to the gradient that every replica applies, and the collective traffic carries that contribution across the training fabric. Its confidentiality depends on the fabric’s isolation and encryption controls. Federated aggregation creates another observation boundary because model updates can reveal information even when raw records remain on devices. Accelerators and caches shared among tenants introduce extraction and leakage risks that also exist on a single shared machine. Section 13.6 develops these fleet-internal boundaries. Scaling the system requires identifying which actors can observe or alter each exchange.


↩︎ Multi-tenant platforms and the isolation they require are established in Multi-tenancy and isolation.
Learned-information exposure follows from the difference between transient processing and persistent learning. Many applications process sensitive data without encoding it into learned parameters; machine learning systems can preserve patterns from training data in their model parameters. Sensitive information may then remain in a model after the original processing has ended and become accessible through outputs or systematic interrogation. Queries to a healthcare model may expose memorized patient information, while queries to a proprietary model may reveal enough behavior to train a substitute. The first threatens training-data privacy (section 13.5.2); the second threatens model confidentiality.
Architectural complexity compounds these challenges. A contemporary ML deployment spans data ingestion pipelines, distributed training infrastructure, model serving systems, and continuous monitoring frameworks, each introducing distinct vulnerabilities as figure 1 maps across the ML lifecycle. Continuous adaptation at edge nodes and federated coordination protocols add further entry points, each with its own trust assumptions.







Figure 1: ML System Attack Surface: Red arrows mark where an adversary enters the system: the training data, the training job and its dependencies, the stored weights, the serving API, and the infrastructure beneath all three layers. Each entry point calls for a different control, so defense spans data collection, training and weights, the serving interface, and the provenance of firmware and hardware.




Self-Check: Question

A security team deploys an enterprise ML inference service behind a web application firewall with strict mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication and rate limiting. Despite zero network-level intrusions, an external adversary reconstructs the model’s proprietary decision boundaries and extracts memorized training records. What fundamental characteristic of ML systems explains this vulnerability?

ML models act on and compress learned data, exposing an algorithmic attack surface through properly authenticated inputs and valid response signals.
mTLS certificates fail to encrypt floating-point tensors at the network transport layer.
Traditional firewalls cannot inspect JSON payloads formatted as numerical arrays.
Token-bucket rate limiting in standard firewalls is incapable of tracking HTTP/2 request streams.

An ML platform engineer must classify two distinct failure modes: (1) a malicious actor submits crafted audio noise to cause an emergency dispatch classifier to miss distress calls, and (2) an observer examines a public salary prediction model and infers whether a specific executive was included in the training set. How should these two issues be categorized according to threat model and objective?


is a privacy violation targeting confidentiality; (2) is a security breach targeting system availability.


is an adversarial security attack targeting model integrity; (2) is a privacy leakage issue targeting participation inference.

Both (1) and (2) are pure infrastructure security incidents requiring network-layer firewall rule updates.

is a stochastic robustness failure; (2) is an unauthorized access control violation requiring credential rotation.


An inference service encrypts its stored training records and authenticates every caller, yet an authorized caller extracts memorized records from its predictions. Explain what the two controls protect and which privacy question remains.

See Answers →





Defense starts by separating two concerns that often share the same vocabulary. Security asks how an adversary can steal, manipulate, or disable the fleet; privacy asks how sensitive information can leak or be inferred even when the system behaves as designed. Keeping those questions separate determines which controls belong at each layer: authentication and isolation around adversarial pathways, provenance and monitoring across the release chain, and privacy accounting wherever learned parameters carry traces of the data that produced them.


The first half of that separation is security, which defends model parameters, training pipelines, deployment infrastructure, and inference interfaces against intentional adversarial behavior. An attacker who crafts an adversarial patch on a stop sign, steals model weights from an unauthenticated bucket, or floods a generative endpoint with cost-maximizing queries compromises the system’s integrity, confidentiality, or availability.

Definition 13.1: Security
Security is the set of system properties (confidentiality, integrity, and availability) that protect an ML system’s data, model weights, and inference pipeline from intentional adversarial actions, spanning both the infrastructure layer (network intrusion, credential theft) and the algorithmic layer (model extraction, prompt injection, adversarial examples).

Significance: Security failures operate on both surfaces simultaneously. At the infrastructure layer, theft of a large proprietary model represents direct IP loss. At the algorithmic layer, model extraction via black-box queries can recover decision boundaries or distill a functional approximation of a deployed model at a small fraction of its training cost (section 13.5.1 quantifies the query budgets), bypassing the investment and competitive moat. Either failure transfers the value of the original training investment to the attacker without the attacker paying its compute cost.
Distinction: Security specifies an intentional adversary and the boundaries that actor can cross. Robustness evaluates how model behavior changes under specified perturbations, including both accidental shifts and adversarial inputs; the two concerns overlap when the perturbation comes from an attacker.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that traditional IT security (firewalls, access controls, encryption) adequately secures ML systems. ML introduces an algorithmic attack surface orthogonal to infrastructure: a properly authenticated API request containing an adversarial input or a prompt injection bypasses all network-layer defenses and manipulates model behavior through the model’s own learned functions.



A facial recognition system deployed in public transit infrastructure, for example, may be targeted with adversarial inputs that cause it to misidentify individuals or fail entirely, representing a runtime security vulnerability that threatens both accuracy and system availability. The confidentiality-integrity-availability triad matters because each property breaks a different system contract. Confidentiality protects data and model access. Integrity protects the correctness of training and inference behavior. Availability protects the service from being disabled or degraded when it is needed.



Whereas security addresses adversarial manipulation and unauthorized access, privacy limits the exposure and inference of sensitive information across training data, inference inputs, and model outputs. An authorized user querying a clinical classifier or a language model can extract a patient’s sensitive diagnosis or verbatim personal record without ever breaching a firewall or stealing a password. Privacy protections must therefore account for unintended disclosure during ordinary operation. They must also account for active adversaries who choose queries, combine outputs with auxiliary information, or exploit repeated releases to infer sensitive facts.

Definition 13.2: Privacy
Privacy is the protection of sensitive information from unauthorized disclosure, inference, and misuse across the ML lifecycle.

Significance: It limits the exposure risk of training data and user inputs. Differentially private training introduces a utility-privacy trade-off: tighter privacy bounds generally require more noise or data, which can increase the training compute, the \(\IronLawComputeTime\) term of the Fleet Law (equation 1.3), required to reach a target utility.
Distinction: Unlike confidentiality (which focuses on access control), privacy in ML focuses on inference risks: the ability of a user, operator, or adversary to infer sensitive facts or reconstruct training samples from model outputs, weights, or repeated releases.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that removing names (de-identification) is sufficient for privacy. In reality, neural networks are correlation engines that can inadvertently memorize and leak unique snippets of sensitive data through high-dimensional patterns.



Privacy failures are not limited to raw records or explicit identifiers. Aggregated behavioral traces can reveal sensitive routines when the surrounding geography makes individuals and sites easy to infer. Differential privacy (DP) bounds how much the distribution of released results can change when one protected contribution changes. Mechanisms can achieve this guarantee through calibrated randomization, such as adding noise to a query result. The protected contribution may be one record or all records from one person; the guarantee must specify which. Its utility cost depends on the task, data, mechanism, and training procedure.
Differential privacy provides one mechanism-level guarantee; it does not provide lifecycle privacy by itself. A system must still minimize collection, establish an appropriate basis for use, enforce access controls, limit retention, honor deletion obligations, and prevent raw inputs or sensitive outputs from leaking through logs and caches. These controls answer questions that a formal privacy bound does not: whether the data should have been collected, who may use them, how long derived artifacts remain, and which copies must be removed. Production privacy therefore composes formal accounting with data-governance controls across collection, training, serving, telemetry, and retirement.
Before the formal treatment of differential privacy, the chapter needs only one knob. A privacy budget \(\PrivacyBudget\) bounds how much the probabilities of released results may change when one protected contribution changes; smaller values give a tighter bound, and \(\PrivacyBudget\) is not an accuracy percentage. Because additional data-dependent DP releases about the same data spend more of that budget, the budget belongs to the history of releases rather than to any one server. Using a fixed DP-trained model does not spend additional training privacy budget. Section 13.9 states the formal definition, its additive slack term, and the accounting that tracks spending across releases, once the defense architectures that surround it are in place.



Security and privacy intersect in controls such as encrypted storage, yet they differ in their objectives, threat models, and mitigation strategies. Encrypting a hospital’s training bucket stops an external attacker from stealing files, whereas the model trained on that bucket can still reveal whether a specific patient was in the cohort through an ordinary, authorized prediction query. These security-privacy distinctions matter because the two domains optimize for different failure modes. Their distinct goals carry through to typical concerns, example attacks, the defenses practitioners must consider, and regulatory standing (table 1).



Table 1: Security-Privacy Distinctions: Machine learning systems require distinct approaches to security and privacy; security mitigates adversarial threats targeting system functionality, while privacy protects sensitive information from both intentional and unintentional exposure through data leakage or re-identification. This table clarifies how differing goals and threat models shape the specific concerns and mitigation strategies for each domain.










Aspect
Security
Privacy




Primary Goal
Prevent unauthorized access or disruption
Limit exposure of sensitive information


Threat Model
Adversarial actors (external or internal)
Passive exposure and active inference with auxiliary information


Typical Concerns
Model theft, poisoning, evasion attacks
Data leakage, re-identification, memorization


Example Attack
Adversarial inputs cause misclassification
Model inversion infers sensitive training-data properties


Representative Defenses
Access control, adversarial training
Differential privacy; federation with accounted privacy controls


Relevance to Regulation
Emphasized in cybersecurity standards
Central to data protection laws (for example, GDPR)







Systems Perspective 13.1: The privacy-utility trade-offSecurity and privacy are deeply interrelated but not interchangeable. A secure system helps maintain privacy by restricting unauthorized access to models and data. Privacy-preserving designs can improve security by reducing the attack surface; minimizing the retention of sensitive data reduces the risk of exposure if a system is compromised.
However, their controls can impose competing requirements. Differential privacy bounds information disclosed by a release but may lower model utility. Encryption restricts who can inspect protected data, so an audit that needs those data requires an authorized inspection path and appropriate key custody. The design must preserve useful evidence while limiting what that evidence reveals.


Security and privacy therefore constrain the same system through different boundaries. Access control, cryptography, trusted execution, and differential privacy address different failure modes; their combination must protect model assets, limit data exposure, and retain the evidence needed to investigate failures. The breach histories make those boundaries concrete by tracing how aggregate releases, compromised components, and excessive access can expose information or alter system behavior.




A public heatmap built for runners became a military-intelligence leak when sparse GPS traces outlined movement around sensitive sites. That privacy failure belongs beside three landmark security breaches because each case turns an abstract control objective into an operational constraint. Behavioral telemetry can identify people. Supply-chain compromise can alter physical systems. Weak isolation can expose safety-critical control paths. Default credentials can turn cheap devices into attack infrastructure. Although most of these incidents did not target ML systems directly, every failure mode they demonstrated has a direct analog in training pipelines, inference APIs, edge deployments, and privacy-preserving data products. Starting with the 2018 Strava heatmap shows how an aggregate data release can fail on privacy without a single security intrusion, before the three security breaches that follow trace supply-chain, isolation, and endpoint failures.

War Story 13.1: The heatmap that revealed routines (2018)Context: In late January 2018, public scrutiny of Strava’s global activity heatmap, an aggregate built from users’ uploaded GPS traces, revealed that it exposed activity at military bases (Russell 2018). The release showed patterns of movement without displaying a list of named participants.
Mechanism: Aggregation hides individuals only where many people contribute. In sparsely populated regions, the few bright tracks came largely from personnel exercising on and around bases, so the heatmap traced base perimeters and the routes people ran, even where a site’s location was already known.
Impact: The map exposed an operational-security risk in consumer telemetry. An aggregate intended to help people find exercise routes also told an observer where personnel moved routinely, prompting reviews of how fitness devices were used near sensitive facilities.
Design response: A system releasing location aggregates must assess what sparse regions reveal, limit sensitive contributions, and make participation controls understandable. These are design requirements suggested by the incident, not evidence that a particular product change eliminated the risk.
Systems lesson: Privacy failures can occur without names, passwords, or model weights leaking. Aggregation alone does not establish privacy when the released pattern and its surrounding context reveal sensitive behavior.



Russell, Jon. 2018. “Strava Says It Will Simplify Privacy Settings and Review App Features After Exposing Military Bases.” TechCrunch, January.


Discovered in 2010, the Stuxnet worm used four zero-day vulnerabilities among its infection and propagation mechanisms, including spread through infected USB media. It targeted Siemens Step7 software and the programmable logic controllers (PLCs) it managed in industrial systems, including the air-gapped1 environment at Iran’s Natanz nuclear facility (Farwell and Rohozinski 2011). Altered control behavior accompanied by apparently normal telemetry demonstrated that operational health signals can conceal a compromise. An analogous ML failure occurs when poisoned training data or a backdoored model changes selected predictions while the inference server continues to meet its latency and availability targets. The common mechanism is a violation of behavioral integrity that ordinary service-health monitoring need not detect.
1 Air-gapped: Physical network separation does not eliminate transfer paths through removable media or authorized personnel. An isolated ML training cluster still needs a controlled process for admitting frameworks, datasets, and pretrained weights; each transfer must preserve the intended trust boundary.
Farwell, J. P., and R. Rohozinski. 2011. “Stuxnet and the Future of Cyber War.” Survival 53 (1): 23–40. https://doi.org/10.1080/00396338.2011.555586.
ML supply chains that ingest public packages, datasets, model weights, or firmware face four analogous vectors: compromised dependencies (malicious packages in PyPI and conda repositories), poisoned datasets on public platforms, backdoored model weights in model repositories, and tampered accelerator firmware. Each can introduce behavior through an artifact the pipeline accepts. Because a model’s behavior depends on every contributor to its data, code, weights, and hardware, the model can be trusted only as far as a verifiable record of those contributors extends. That statement is the provenance bound on trust (principle \(\ref{pri-provenance-bounds-trust}\)), and it carries the Stuxnet lesson to every artifact an ML pipeline admits. Artifact signatures and immutable provenance logs establish origin and integrity evidence; controlled dependency admission limits which artifacts enter the pipeline. Behavioral testing addresses a different question, because an authentic, unchanged artifact can still contain a backdoor. Each stage of the Stuxnet attack chain has a counterpart in the ML supply chain (figure 2).







Figure 2: Stuxnet and the ML Supply Chain: The top row traces the Stuxnet chain from removable media through Windows hosts and Siemens Step7 software to altered PLC logic, which damaged centrifuges while operators saw normal readings. The bottom row places the ML analog under each stage: a compromised public artifact passes through trusted build and training steps into a model whose misbehavior monitoring does not reveal.






Security researchers remotely compromised a Jeep Cherokee’s engine, transmission, and braking systems by exploiting a vulnerability in the vehicle’s internet-connected Uconnect entertainment system, without physical access to the car (Miller and Valasek 2015; Miller 2019). Insufficient isolation allowed the compromised entertainment system to reach safety-critical controller area network bus controllers and manipulate vehicle functions.

Miller, Charlie, and Chris Valasek. 2015. Remote Exploitation of an Unaltered Passenger Vehicle. Black Hat USA 2015 Whitepaper.

Miller, C. 2019. “Lessons Learned from Hacking a Car.” IEEE Design & Test 36 (6): 7–9. https://doi.org/10.1109/mdat.2018.2863106.
The ML lesson concerns authority across a trust boundary. Perception or diagnostic models may need to communicate with actuator controllers, but compromise of an externally reachable inference component must not grant unrestricted control authority. Segmentation, authenticated narrow gateways, sandboxed model execution, and minimal privileges constrain that path. Controllers must validate permitted commands and apply a system-specific safe response when inputs are invalid or communication fails; a network path makes the attack possible only if the controller accepts what arrives over it.



In 2016, the Mirai botnet exploited weak credentials on Internet of Things (IoT) devices, including cameras, digital video recorders, and routers, to build infrastructure for distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. The longitudinal study of Mirai measured a peak of about 600,000 infections and documented attacks against services including Dyn, whose disruption affected other internet services (Antonakakis et al. 2017). The scaling lesson is that many individually limited devices can collectively threaten much larger services.

Antonakakis, M., T. April, M. Bailey, M. Bernhard, E. Bursztein, J. Cochran, Z. Durumeric, et al. 2017. “Understanding the Mirai Botnet.” 26th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 17) 16: 1093–110.
For ML edge deployments, a compromised endpoint may expose more than bandwidth. Its accessible records can include images or transcripts, and its enrolled federated-learning identity may let an attacker submit malicious updates. The defense must match those capabilities. Device-specific credentials limit shared-secret exposure, authenticated encrypted channels protect communication, and secure boot constrains which startup software is accepted. Hardware security modules (HSMs), tamper-resistant devices that hold keys and perform cryptographic operations without exposing those keys to host memory, can protect key custody where the platform supports them. Monitoring provides evidence of misuse, while update validation remains necessary because an authenticated device can still send harmful data.
Together, the Strava, Stuxnet, Jeep, and Mirai incidents expose failures at four different boundaries: an aggregate release, accepted components, paths to safety-critical control, and endpoint credentials. The engineering task is to identify the asset and attacker capability at each boundary before choosing a control. A threat model makes those assumptions explicit, so defenses can be evaluated against the failures they are intended to prevent and the resources they consume.

An authenticated request can still probe a model for memorized data, and an accepted training sample can still carry a backdoor. Network security and user authentication therefore need a threat model that includes learned behavior. Training data can be manipulated to embed backdoors, input perturbations can exploit learned decision boundaries, and systematic API queries can expose enough behavior to train a substitute. Each attack uses an interface the system needs for ordinary work.
Each of these vectors requires a formal threat model, written down as four fields: asset, boundary, adversary, and control. The asset defines what must remain confidential, intact, or available. The boundary defines where trust changes, such as between training data and model registry, user prompt and system instruction, or tenant workload and shared accelerator. The adversary field records the actor’s capability (what it can access, observe, or modify) and its goal (what it seeks to compromise). The control identifies a permission, isolation mechanism, or observable signal that constrains the attack or supports a response. Without those fields, a risk matrix cannot explain why a particular defense deserves resources. Attack cost and expected benefit help assess feasibility, but the model must also cover actors whose objective is disruption rather than financial return.
For a federated training round, suppose the coordinator may inspect messages but follows the aggregation protocol, while a compromised enrolled client may submit an arbitrary update. The same update crosses two boundaries. Hiding individual contributions from the coordinator addresses confidentiality; checking or limiting a client contribution addresses integrity. Authenticating the client establishes who sent an update, not whether the update is benign. A defense comparison is meaningful only after stating which of these actors, capabilities, and possible collusions it covers.


Systematic threat modeling identifies what must be protected and from whom. It is a structured approach to security analysis that characterizes the attack surface and guides defensive investments. For machine learning systems, threat modeling must account for dependence on training data, statistical decision boundaries, and distributed deployment patterns.


The attack surface of an ML system encompasses all points where an adversary can interact with or observe the system. It includes the lifecycle risks of ordinary software, such as compromised dependencies, as well as the data and learned state that determine model behavior. Decomposing this surface into data, model, interface, and infrastructure layers identifies where a control can constrain the attacker and what remains exposed beyond that control.
The training data pipeline lets an adversary influence behavior before the model exists. At collection endpoints, raw data enters through application logs, sensors, forms, APIs, or uploads. Training corpora then reside in object stores, warehouses, feature stores, or dataset registries. Preprocessing pipelines normalize, filter, augment, and join these inputs, while human annotation, weak-labeling rules, or model-assisted labeling supply the targets used for learning. Dataset manifests and lineage systems identify which snapshot enters a release. A compromised source can affect successive model versions if the pipeline continues to ingest its records, and a backdoor may persist when training reuses an affected checkpoint. Retraining alone therefore does not establish that the compromised contribution has been removed.
The model itself presents multiple attack surfaces spanning training infrastructure, model storage and versioning systems, model serialization and deserialization code, hyperparameter configuration management, and gradient computation and aggregation processes. Attacks at the model layer can compromise integrity by embedding trojans during training, extract intellectual property through parameter theft, or manipulate behavior through weight poisoning.
Deployed models expose additional attack surfaces through inference API endpoints and load balancers, authentication and authorization systems, input validation and preprocessing logic, output formatting and response generation, and monitoring and logging infrastructure. At this interface layer, input checks enforce the accepted request contract, query limits constrain collection, and output controls restrict the information returned. An adversarial input can satisfy the request contract, and a permitted response can still reveal useful model behavior, so these controls need evaluation against the specified attack.
The underlying computational infrastructure presents traditional attack surfaces amplified by ML-specific concerns, including accelerator firmware and drivers, container orchestration and scheduling systems, network communication between distributed training nodes, key management and secrets infrastructure, and supply chain for ML frameworks and dependencies. Infrastructure compromises can affect all systems running on shared resources, making this layer critical for multi-tenant ML platforms.



Threat-vector classification matters because the same model failure demands different defenses when the attacker has only API access, partial design knowledge, or full insider access. The three axes are access type, knowledge level, and attack timing.
Access type specifies how the adversary can inspect or interact with the model. Under black-box access, the available interface returns outputs for submitted inputs. It can support model extraction (Tramèr et al. 2016) and query- or transfer-based adversarial attacks (Papernot et al. 2016) without exposing the target’s parameters. Gray-box access adds partial internal information, such as the architecture or training procedure. White-box access supplies the model’s parameters and architecture, enabling direct gradient-based attacks (Goodfellow et al. 2015) and parameter copying when the files are accessible. These labels describe model visibility; they do not grant permission to alter training data, replace weights, or modify the runtime. Those write capabilities must be stated separately. Each access level has a typical attack it enables and a typical deployment where it arises (table 2).

Knowledge level adds the background information available beyond the exposed interface. A black-box client may know the application domain, public architecture documentation, or examples resembling the training distribution. An insider may know the deployment configuration without being able to read every training record. Model visibility and auxiliary knowledge therefore overlap, but neither replaces an explicit inventory of what the adversary knows. Claims of full knowledge must identify whether they include training records, preprocessing, and defense settings as well as model parameters.
Attack timing determines where the defense can still intervene across the system lifecycle. Training-time attacks, such as data poisoning or backdoor injection, manipulate the learning process before the model artifact is produced. Deployment-time attacks compromise model distribution, serialization, or container installation before serving begins. Once in production, inference-time attacks exploit the deployed model through adversarial inputs or extraction queries. Finally, postdeployment attacks target online model updates, monitoring telemetry, or operational feedback loops after the model is already in service. The defense surface therefore moves in lockstep with the model lifecycle, from data controls to artifact integrity to serving-time containment.
Combining these dimensions defines a testable threat scenario. A public API adversary might query a deployed classifier, know its task and output format, and lack access to its parameters or training records. A training insider might inspect the model and alter a specified subset of examples before fitting begins. The second scenario permits poisoning because it grants a write capability, not merely because the attacker knows more about the model.



Effective defense against the threat vectors identified by the threat model requires a layered strategy that addresses each attack surface while accounting for adversary capabilities. The defense framework operates on three principles: defense in depth, minimal attack surface, and fail-safe defaults.
No single defensive mechanism provides complete protection. The principle of defense in depth requires multiple independent layers such that compromising one layer does not grant full system access. For ML systems, this means combining data validation with model robustness techniques, access controls with output perturbation, and software defenses with hardware security mechanisms.
The principle of minimal attack surface treats every exposed interface, stored artifact, and network endpoint as a potential entry or observation point. An API should expose only the functionality and output precision its users need, because detailed scores provide additional observations of model behavior. Encryption at rest protects stored models and training corpora when the attacker cannot also obtain their keys. Separating training clusters from inference endpoints constrains lateral movement, while protected access logs support investigation of sensitive operations. Each control reduces a particular exposure; none removes the need to examine the paths that remain.
The principle of fail-safe defaults makes access depend on established permission rather than the absence of a detected threat. A request that cannot be authorized must not acquire privileges because a service failed. Behavioral anomalies require a separate response policy because they can also arise from legitimate traffic or distribution shift. Depending on the application, the system may reject a request, defer to a verified fallback, suspend a release, or isolate an affected component while preserving essential service. The safe response follows from the consequences of both continued operation and interruption; it cannot be inferred from an anomaly score alone.
Each layer of the attack surface calls for its own defensive mechanisms and detection methods (table 3). Data defenses validate provenance, model defenses protect learned behavior and weights, API defenses govern query exposure, and infrastructure defenses anchor runtime trust.

Attack surfaces, threat vectors, and the defense mapping together enumerate what could go wrong and which control addresses each failure. They do not say which failure to address first, and no deployment can fund every control at once.




A team that spends months hardening against physical laser fault injection while leaving a public inference API without query budgets or loading untrusted pickle checkpoints from a public hub leaves its highest-probability attack paths wide open. Prioritization ranks the enumerated threats by how likely each is in the deployment and how much damage it would cause. Impact is not purely technical. Regulatory obligations raise the cost of some failures, as when an erasure request under the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)2 obliges the operator to trace personal data through derived datasets, logs, and deployed artifacts. A prioritization matrix based on likelihood and impact turns the threat model into an allocation decision. Teams automate defenses for threats that are both likely and damaging, prepare for rare but severe failures, and avoid spending scarce engineering time on low-value controls.
2 GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): Article 17 establishes a right to erasure under specified grounds and exceptions. For an ML pipeline, responding to an applicable request requires tracing personal data through source records, derived datasets, logs, and deployed artifacts. Whether a trained model requires remediation depends on the data it retains and the applicable obligation; deleting a source row does not establish that every derived copy or learned disclosure has been removed. Retraining and machine unlearning are possible technical responses whose effectiveness requires separate validation.Penalties make the regulatory part of impact concrete. In healthcare, where ML systems routinely handle patient data, a breach can violate the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), with significant legal and ethical consequences. Similar regulatory risks apply globally. For personal data within its territorial and material scope, GDPR authorizes fines up to 2 percent of total worldwide annual turnover when an organization fails to implement appropriate security measures, and up to 4 percent for violations of its core processing principles or data-subject rights (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016).
The following placements illustrate a threat model rather than universal attack frequencies. High-likelihood/high-impact poisoning is plausible in a federated deployment that admits untrusted contributors and suffers severe consequences from manipulated predictions. Such a deployment needs controls on update integrity and a response path for suspected compromise. High-likelihood/low-impact extraction describes a different scenario in which public queries are accessible but behavioral copying creates limited competitive loss. Output restrictions and query budgets may then be proportionate controls, although their effectiveness still requires evaluation.
The lower-likelihood quadrants receive different treatment. Low-likelihood/high-impact hardware side-channel attacks describe a deployment in which obtaining the necessary observations is difficult but a successful attack could reveal valuable secrets. The required access depends on the channel; some attacks use a physical probe, while others exploit shared resources or remotely observable timing. In the public API scenario used for this matrix, membership inference attacks, which test whether a particular record was part of the training set (section 13.5.2.1), may sit in a lower-likelihood/lower-impact quadrant than direct integrity failures. That placement must be reassessed when the training data is sensitive or the exposed outputs make membership easier to infer. The matrix records those deployment assumptions rather than assigning a permanent rank to each attack family.
The framework guides resource allocation, as figure 3 summarizes. The example prioritizes accessible model and data threats before more specialized hardware attacks. A deployment with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware may require a different order. The allocation decision depends on the expected harm, the control’s effectiveness, and its engineering cost, not on the attack category alone.

A stop sign with strategically placed black and white stickers can remain recognizable to a human while an evaluated image classifier labels it as a speed limit sign. The attacker changes the observed input rather than the classifier’s code or stored weights. This adversarial example illustrates why the lifecycle entry point matters. Training data, model artifacts, and runtime inputs give an attacker different ways to influence the system and require controls at different boundaries.
The lifecycle entry point separates five objectives. Model theft targets confidentiality by obtaining artifacts or reproducing behavior from queries. Output leakage targets the training data, which the same queries can expose through the predictions the service is authorized to return. Poisoning targets training integrity by changing what the model learns. Adversarial examples target deployed behavior by changing the inputs a model receives. Availability abuse uses the same serving interface to exhaust the service’s compute and cost budget rather than to change any prediction. Data poisoning therefore requires an intervention in the learning pipeline, whereas adversarial inputs and availability abuse call for controls on the deployed service. Written as the four-field threat model of section 13.4, the objectives differ mainly in asset and adversary capability. Theft targets weights or behavior and needs either artifact access or query access, and output leakage targets the training data with nothing more than query access. Poisoning targets training integrity and needs write access to something the model learns from. Adversarial inputs target deployed decisions and need control over an input, while availability abuse targets the serving budget and needs nothing beyond an account. These objectives connect the attack surface analysis in section 13.4.1 to the controls available before training, during artifact handling, and at inference, while section 13.5.5 examines how token-stream architectures fuse instructions, untrusted content, and retrieved data across those objectives.
These entry points sit at different stages of the ML lifecycle (figure 4). Upstream, an attacker may inject samples or alter labels in a data source the pipeline accepts. A backdoor can then remain inactive on ordinary evaluation inputs and activate on a chosen trigger. Downstream, deployed files expose an artifact-access boundary, while prediction APIs expose a query boundary. An adversarial input crosses the latter without requiring the attacker to alter the training pipeline.
Controls must act at the relevant entry point and preserve their assumptions through later stages. Data validation limits what enters training, artifact controls authenticate what deployment loads, and serving controls constrain requests and returned information. None establishes behavioral correctness by itself; the threat model determines which attack each control must withstand.







Figure 4: ML Lifecycle Threats: Poisoning, backdoor insertion, model theft, and adversarial inputs enter at different lifecycle stages (red arrows), and each stage has its own first control (green gates). Dashed lines show a training-time compromise that passes its gate persisting into every later stage, so a control placed at a different stage cannot intercept the threat before it takes effect.





A competitor spending a few thousand dollars on public API queries to train a surrogate model, or an insider copying unencrypted weights from a bucket, can replicate a model that cost millions of dollars to train (Oliynyk et al. 2023). Model theft, the first of those five objectives, targets confidentiality by recovering a trained model’s parameters, architecture, or output behavior, undermining its economic value or exposing private information encoded in its weights.

Such threats arise across a range of deployment settings, including public APIs, cloud-hosted services, on-device inference engines, and shared model repositories. Prediction interfaces can leak enough signal to recover model functionality (Tramèr et al. 2016; Oliynyk et al. 2023), while classifier outputs can reveal meaningful information about training sets or learned structure (Ateniese et al. 2015). Artifact handling introduces separate risks. Unsafe deserialization3 can execute attacker-supplied code, while insufficient access controls can expose model files or deployment packages directly.
Model theft pursues two distinct objectives, and each requires different controls (figure 5). Exact artifact theft obtains the model file or deployment artifact through storage, registry, or device access. The attacker can reuse the recovered weights without repeating their training. Approximate behavioral theft uses API responses, such as labels, logits, embeddings, or confidence scores, to train a surrogate. It can exploit permitted queries without breaking authentication. The literature names this query-based branch in several ways. Model extraction and model stealing are synonyms for the attack, while knockoff modeling and model distillation name its usual training step, in which a surrogate learns from the victim’s outputs. Its usual product is a behavioral surrogate, but the same query access can also recover selected internal parameters, a third outcome that the OpenAI results below demonstrate. Encryption, access control, and protected deployment paths restrict artifact access; signatures separately authenticate artifact integrity. Output limits, query budgets, auditing, and pricing constrain behavioral extraction, while watermarking can support attribution after copying.

Approximate behavioral theft (right) uses black-box API queries, output signals, and surrogate training or distillation to clone the model’s behavior without direct access to weights.




Definition 13.3: Model extraction
Model extraction is the class of attacks in which an adversary, with only black-box query access to a deployed model’s prediction interface, recovers the model’s parameters, decision boundaries, or behavior by analyzing observable outputs.

Significance: Successful extraction often costs orders of magnitude less than the original training. Published demonstrations have recovered logistic regression, neural-network, and decision-tree models from public machine-learning APIs with high fidelity and modest query cost (Tramèr et al. 2016). Later work has reconstructed components of large language models, including OpenAI deployments studied by Carlini et al. (2024), using only public query access. The BERT extraction example below illustrates the same dynamic on a transformer model, using only synthetic queries to train the copy.
Distinction: Extraction differs from direct theft of model files (which requires intrusion into the storage layer) and from model inversion (which uses model outputs to infer training-data properties or reconstruct representative inputs rather than the model itself). Its attack surface is the model’s query interface, so every deployed ML service faces it by construction whenever the model is reachable.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that rate limiting alone is a sufficient defense. An attacker willing to issue queries slowly, distribute requests across accounts, or accept a multi-month attack window may still extract useful behavior. Reducing output information, detecting systematic probing, and pricing queries can raise the cost or expose the attempt, but their combination does not guarantee prevention.



Model theft can also enable attacks on information encoded by the model. Extraction studies demonstrate recovery of useful behavior or selected internal parameters, although those outcomes do not imply complete replication of a large model or its training pipeline (Tramèr et al. 2016; Carlini et al. 2024). A competitor holding a stolen Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) recommendation model obtains its embedding tables, which store a learned vector for each value of each categorical feature. In a recommender those features commonly include user and item IDs, so the stolen tables hand the competitor a per-user vector shaped by that user’s history, a natural starting point for inferring the user’s attributes. Whether this exposes particular customer attributes depends on the model, accessible features, and auxiliary information. Model inversion attacks investigate that boundary by attempting to infer sensitive input properties from the learned model (section 13.5.2.2). Even when the artifact itself remains secured, the approximate behavioral extraction path in figure 5 becomes practical because black-box query cost can be much lower than the cost of training the original model.

Example 13.1: The BERT model extractionScenario: Proprietary language models deployed behind public inference APIs return full probability vectors and confidence scores to client queries (Krishna et al. 2020).
Diagnosis: The attacker needed no real training data. Because both the victim and the copy were fine-tuned from the same publicly released pretrained BERT, queries made of random word sequences shaped by simple task-specific heuristics supplied enough labeled outputs to train a student. That student recovered much of the victim’s task performance on tasks including natural language inference and question answering (Krishna et al. 2020). With a shared public starting point, the API responses had to supply only the task-specific fine-tuning signal. Retaining task accuracy is distinct from agreeing with the target on each input; neither implies recovery of its exact parameters.
Systems lesson: API endpoints expose intellectual property when outputs carry raw decision-boundary logits. Serving platforms combine rate-limiting, query auditing, and confidence-score truncation to make model extraction more costly and detectable.

Exact artifact theft targets the model’s stored structure and learned parameters. The exposed path may be an artifact-download API, an on-device inference package, or a model repository. This differs from querying a prediction API: the attacker obtains the artifact itself. Weak access control or unprotected packaging can expose that artifact without requiring full control of the underlying infrastructure.
The value of a stolen artifact depends on what it contains and what the attacker wants to reproduce. Learned parameters and architecture details can support inference when the necessary preprocessing and runtime are available. Training hyperparameters, including learning rate schedules, batch sizes, and regularization settings, help reproduce or extend training, but are not required merely to execute an existing checkpoint. Side-channel attacks,4 reverse engineering, or analysis of observable outputs may reveal additional structure when the artifact is incomplete. The threat model should therefore distinguish running a copied model from rebuilding the pipeline that produced it.

System designers must account for these risks by separating artifact security from interface security. Artifact controls secure model files, registry entries, and deployment packages; interface controls restrict APIs, reduce output precision, audit query patterns, and price or rate-limit access so behavioral extraction becomes harder to perform economically (Tramèr et al. 2016; Oliynyk et al. 2023).



Insider access is often the shortest path to artifact theft, because an insider needs no exploit to reach files that the development environment already grants. The two cases below involve documents and source code rather than model weights, and that difference is their lesson. The protected asset extends beyond the serialized model to the code and data that produced it. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski was accused of taking proprietary Waymo materials before founding a competing startup (The New York Times 2017), a case about engineering intellectual property rather than demonstrated extraction of model weights. In March 2019, Tesla filed two trade-secret lawsuits involving former employees who left for autonomous-vehicle competitors (Korosec 2019). One complaint alleged that employees who joined Zoox copied proprietary warehousing, logistics, and inventory-control documents. A separate complaint alleged that former Autopilot engineer Guangzhi Cao copied Tesla Autopilot source-code repositories before joining XPeng/XMotors.

API-level extraction defenses do not reach this boundary. Restricting prediction queries cannot prevent a developer from copying repositories that the developer can already access. Development access, artifact handling, and release provenance therefore belong in the same threat model as inference interfaces, with controls matched to the sensitivity of each asset.

The service therefore has to limit accumulated observations while preserving the outputs legitimate users need.
Query access can also expose internal parameters rather than only supply examples for a surrogate. In their paper, Carlini et al. (2024) show how to reconstruct the final embedding projection matrix of OpenAI’s ada and babbage models, and to recover the hidden dimensionality (and estimate the cost of full matrix recovery) for gpt-3.5-turbo, using only public API access. That final projection maps a hidden state vector to a much larger token vocabulary, so every output logit vector lies in a linear subspace whose rank equals the model’s hidden dimension. Collecting logit vectors across enough varied prompts until new responses become linearly dependent on earlier ones reveals where the rank saturates and recovers the hidden dimensionality. For the smaller models, solving for a basis of that subspace replicates the weight matrix up to affine transformations. This partial parameter extraction is distinct from both copying a complete artifact and training a behavioral substitute. It stops short of recovering the full model, yet it shows that an API’s exposed scores and query controls can reveal internal structure that its operator intended to keep private.

Unlike data poisoning and adversarial perturbations, whose algorithmic defenses are developed in Robust AI, and training-data leakage, whose formal privacy bounds are developed in section 13.9, model extraction is countered directly at the serving API boundary. This subsection therefore develops the chapter’s complete quantitative treatment of API-level extraction defenses alongside the attack, leaving section 13.8.2 to cover artifact custody, cryptographic packaging, and endpoint authentication infrastructure. Model extraction defenses must account for what an adversary can accumulate through the API across four operational levers. Reducing output precision or returning fewer classes restricts the observations supplied by each response. Query quotas constrain collection per credential, and pricing increases its cost. Behavioral monitoring supplies evidence of systematic probing that can trigger investigation or enforcement. A daily rate limit only slows collection without bounding its lifetime total, and an attacker can combine observations from several accounts. The defense must therefore connect output design to cumulative budgets and the identities over which those budgets can actually be enforced.
Monitoring supplies evidence for adjusting those controls. High query volume is one possible signal, although legitimate batch jobs can produce it and an extractor can deliberately slow collection. A high-traffic, general-purpose prediction API might begin with an illustrative volume rule:
\[
\text{alert}(\text{user}) = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \DailyAccountQueryCount> 10{,}000 \text{ or } \HourlyAccountQueryCount> 2{,}000 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\DailyAccountQueryCount\) and \(\HourlyAccountQueryCount\) represent query counts. Such thresholds are only the first signal. They must be calibrated by service tier and by the shape of normal use, because batch customers and attackers can both generate high volume.
The next signal compares the inputs with expected use. Synthetic or systematically varied queries may reveal probing, but an extractor can also submit ordinary examples. A detector can compare the user’s query distribution with a baseline chosen for the service and customer workload:
\[
\KlDivergence(\AccountQueryDistribution\lVert \ExpectedQueryDistribution) > \ResponseThreshold
\]
where \(\KlDivergence\) is Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and \(\ResponseThreshold\) is an alert threshold. A practical detector needs a tractable representation of inputs and enough observations to estimate those distributions. For a language model API, unusual token distributions or repetitive prompt templates may provide useful features. Regular inter-query intervals can add evidence of automation, but legitimate applications also automate requests and attackers can vary their timing.
An anomaly detector combines these signals into a score that can drive enforcement:
\[
\text{score}_{\text{anomaly}}(\ApiAccount) = \ExtractionAnomalyClassifier(\text{qps}(\ApiAccount), \KlDivergence(\ApiAccount), \InterQueryIntervalDeviation(\ApiAccount), \ldots)
\]
where \(\ExtractionAnomalyClassifier\) is a trained classifier and the features capture query volume, distribution, and temporal regularity. The score supports a response policy rather than establishing that theft occurred. A service can tighten quotas, request additional verification, or refer activity for review, with thresholds calibrated against legitimate workload variation. Free, paid, and enterprise tiers can carry different limits, but account-level enforcement constrains an adversary only to the extent that collection across credentials is also controlled.
A concrete quota ladder for the same general-purpose API makes that information cap visible. A free tier might allow 1,000 queries/day with a 10 queries/s burst, a basic paid tier might allow 100,000 queries/day with 100 queries/s, and an enterprise tier might allow 10M queries/day with custom burst limits and contractual monitoring. The exact numbers depend on product needs, but the ladder matters because extraction cost scales with accumulated responses.
An illustrative adaptive policy connects the anomaly score to a request limit. Higher scores reduce the quota, so false positives translate directly into lost capacity for legitimate workloads:
\[
\text{limit}_{\text{effective}}(\ApiAccount) = \text{limit}_{\text{base}} \times \exp(-\QuotaReductionSensitivity\cdot \text{score}_{\text{anomaly}}(\ApiAccount))
\]
where \(\QuotaReductionSensitivity\) controls sensitivity. With \(\QuotaReductionSensitivity=1\), a user with anomaly score 0.8 keeps about 45 percent of the base quota, a 55 percent rate reduction. The calculation specifies enforcement strength, not detection accuracy. Its security effect also depends on the response: full logits, hidden states, or detailed confidence scores can make each permitted query more useful to an extractor. Quota design therefore needs an explicit output contract.
Output shaping reduces the leakage per response while preserving the part of the answer legitimate users usually need. Confidence rounding returns coarser probabilities instead of full-precision logits or probabilities:
\[
\RoundedClassProbability_i = \text{round}(\PredictedClassProbability_i, \RoundingDecimalCount)
\]
where \(\RoundingDecimalCount\) is the number of decimal places. For a 1000-class ImageNet classifier, rounding from 6 decimals to 2 decimals removes 4 decimal digits, about 13.3 bits per class. The count uses a decimal-bin model, which treats each decimal digit as selecting one of ten equally likely levels, so every dropped digit removes \(\log_2 10 \approx 3.3\) bits. This counts representational precision, not measured information about the model. Rounding can also create score ties, so the service must evaluate the effect on ranking and downstream decisions.
The top-\(\TopClassCount\) truncation defense returns only the top-\(\TopClassCount\) predicted classes rather than the full probability distribution:
\[
\text{output} = \{(\ReturnedClassLabel_i, \PredictedClassProbability_i) : \LabelCategoryIndex\in \text{top-}\TopClassCount\}
\]
For \(\TopClassCount=\) 5 on a 1000-class problem, the API returns only those top scores instead of the full softmax vector, eliminating 99.5 percent of the distribution entries an extractor could otherwise observe per query. Legitimate users often need only the top few predictions, while an extractor benefits from the full distribution.



Top-\(\TopClassCount\) truncation exposes far fewer scores per query than the full distribution.
When rounded or truncated outputs still leak too much, calibrated noise can make repeated measurements less useful. Adding Gaussian noise to the score vector \(\PredictedOutput\) of a \(\Glyph{K}\)-class model (uppercase \(\ClassCount\) for the class count, distinct from the \(\Glyph{k}\) of top-\(\TopClassCount\)) can push some scores below zero, so the noisy vector is projected back onto a valid probability distribution:
\[
\NoisyClassProbabilityVector=\SimplexProjection\!\left(\PredictedOutput+\ScoreNoiseVector\right),
\qquad \ScoreNoiseVector\sim\GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector,\ScoreNoiseStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)
\]
where \(\SimplexProjection\) returns the closest valid distribution to the noisy vector, one whose scores are all nonnegative and sum to one \((\NoisyClassProbability_i\geq 0,\ \sum_i\NoisyClassProbability_i=1)\). The set of such vectors is the probability simplex \(\ProbabilitySimplex^{\ClassCount-1}\). The noise scale \(\ScoreNoiseStandardDeviation\) must balance extraction defense with utility preservation. Too little noise leaves the confidence surface measurable; too much noise changes decisions for legitimate users. This randomized response shaping is not, by itself, a differential privacy guarantee: such a claim also requires an adjacency relation, a sensitivity bound, calibrated noise, and composition accounting.
Differential privacy addresses a different objective when a response is computed from sensitive records. It bounds the change in the released distribution under a specified change to the protected data. Section 13.9 develops the full \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) definition and the adjacent-dataset notation. Repeated interactive DP releases compose, but queries to a fixed DP-trained model are post-processing and do not consume additional training privacy budget. Such queries may still enable model extraction, so output shaping and rate limits remain security controls even when no additional DP loss is incurred.
The final lever is economics. Consider a simplified comparison in which extraction and independent training produce equally useful substitutes and query charges represent the extraction cost. If training from scratch costs \(\TrainingCost\) and extraction requires \(\ExtractionQueryCount\) queries at price \(\QueryPrice\) per query, extraction is the cheaper option when:
\[
\ExtractionQueryCount\cdot \QueryPrice< \TrainingCost
\]
Setting \(\QueryPrice\) so that \(\ExtractionQueryCount\cdot \QueryPrice> \TrainingCost\) makes extraction costlier than independent training in this simplified equal-quality comparison. It does not remove incentives based on unavailable training data, competitive value, or objectives other than acquiring a substitute cheaply. For example, if training a competitive large model costs $5M and extraction requires 100M queries, the break-even price is $0.05/query; pricing above that makes extraction more expensive than retraining under those assumptions. The comparison must include the attacker’s alternative costs of compute, data, and engineering. In practice, pricing, monitoring, quotas, and output shaping work together. Restricted outputs and coarse confidence bins reduce exposed detail, while quotas constrain access through the identities they cover. Neither control alone bounds all information an actor can accumulate across accounts, alternate endpoints, or other sources.

Napkin Math 13.1: Protecting a production APIProblem: For a production ResNet-50 image-classification API serving 1M daily queries from 10,000 users, how can the operator make model extraction economically unattractive without degrading normal service?
Scenario: The model costs about $5K to train in this scenario. An extractor needs about 5M queries for 90 percent fidelity, or 5,000 queries/class for a 1,000-class classifier. Without defenses, an attacker abusing a free tier can send 25K queries/day for 200 days and pay nothing, making extraction economically favorable. The service is far smaller than the general-purpose API above, so its tiers and alert thresholds are scaled to its own traffic, and its training cost sits three orders of magnitude below the large model of the break-even example.
Mechanism: The defense stack works as a sequence:

Cap collection: The free tier allows 100 queries/day, the paid tier costs $50/month for 10K queries/day, and enterprise access requires authentication plus monitoring.
Monitor probing: The monitoring path watches for systematic measurement behavior, including more than 5K queries/day from one user or median inter-query gaps below 100 ms; the lightweight detector adds 2 ms per query.
Shape outputs: Output shaping rounds confidences to 2 decimal places, retaining about 6.7 bits from each rounded scalar probability, and returns only the top-5 classes, eliminating 99.5 percent of distribution entries.
Price extraction: At pay-as-you-go $0.001/query (above tier caps), 5M extraction queries cost $5K, matching the training cost in this scenario. An attacker limited to the $50/month tier (10K queries/day) would need 500 days and about $833 total, which is cheaper under these assumptions. A daily quota slows collection but does not cap its lifetime total.
Cap cumulative collection: A per-principal lifetime budget closes that route. If each principal’s queries beyond an allowance well below 5M are billed at the pay-as-you-go $0.001/query, assembling the full extraction set costs close to $5K on any tier, the same as training the model.

Outcomes to measure: Whether the design works is decided by four measurements, namely the surrogate’s accuracy, the accuracy legitimate users still receive, the latency the controls add, and the share of users flagged by mistake. The values below are constructed inputs that show the shape of that measurement, not results derived from the controls above. Suppose the surrogate’s accuracy drops from 90 percent without defenses to 72 percent with defenses, an 18 percentage-point reduction, while legitimate top-5 accuracy remains 99.2 percent, close to the 99.3 percent baseline. Monitoring and output shaping add 2.5 ms on top of 100 ms inference, or 2.5 percent overhead, while flagging 0.3 percent of users for manual review.
Systems insight: Tier caps, monitoring, and output shaping slow an extractor; only the cumulative budget makes the full extraction set cost as much as retraining. Break-even is the design target rather than a weakness. At that price the query bill alone equals the cost of training an equivalent model. The extractor still pays for the surrogate’s own training run and engineering on top of it while receiving a copy that the shaped outputs leave less faithful. Under the assumed equal-quality comparison, a lifetime price at or above break-even therefore removes the cost advantage of extraction over training an equivalent model independently. The residual route is to spread queries across many accounts, which account issuance controls and cross-account detection must bound, because a per-principal budget constrains an adversary only as far as principals map to real actors. The accuracy, latency, and false-positive figures are assumptions that the operator must measure before the design ships.


Pay-as-you-go pricing alone would charge the full training cost, but an extractor can stay inside the flat-fee tier, and tracking the cumulative bill against the queries collected shows what that choice is worth (figure 6). A daily quota stretches collection over 500 days but leaves the total near $833. A lifetime budget that bills every query beyond an allowance of 100K queries at the pay-as-you-go price instead makes the bill climb with the extraction set itself, reaching about $4,917 when the set is complete, close to the cost of training the model.

Pay-as-you-go pricing and a lifetime per-principal budget both reach the training cost when the extraction set is complete; a daily quota on a flat-fee tier only slows collection, so the full set still costs a fraction of training. Whereas model theft copies the model, a second confidentiality failure needs no copy at all, because a model that executes correctly can disclose its training data through the outputs it is authorized to return. Persistent learning (section 13.1) carries sensitive information past the original processing, and the attacker reads nothing but permitted predictions, so storage encryption and caller authentication offer no protection. Three attacks exploit that leakage at increasing levels of detail. Membership inference learns a single bit indicating whether a given record was in the training set. Model inversion reconstructs properties of the training data, such as a representative input for a class or an identity. Training-data extraction recovers memorized records verbatim. All three need only query access or released weights, and all three grow more effective as the model fits its training data more closely than the population that data came from.


Membership inference tests whether a particular record was part of a model’s training set (Shokri et al. 2017). The attack exploits a gap that training creates. The model has fitted its training members, so it usually assigns them lower loss and higher confidence than records it has never seen. The simplest test thresholds that signal and declares a record a member when the model’s confidence on its true label exceeds a calibrated cutoff. A stronger test trains shadow models on data drawn from the same distribution with known membership. It learns from their outputs how member and nonmember responses differ, and it applies that classifier to the target model’s outputs (Shokri et al. 2017). Both tests succeed in proportion to the gap between training and held-out behavior, so the risk grows with overfitting and tends to concentrate on small datasets and on rare records that the model had to fit individually. A control added for another threat can widen that gap,5 so each one is rechecked against membership inference.

For threat modeling, the relevant variable is what the adversary observes: confidence scores, labels only, or individual client updates. Attack success depends on the target model, data, outputs, and adversary knowledge. Confirming that an individual’s data was in a training set can still create privacy and compliance risk. In healthcare or legal prediction, membership itself can disclose sensitive information about a person, such as a diagnosis or a case. Whether that disclosure violates GDPR, HIPAA, or another rule depends on the data, parties, and deployment context (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016; U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2003).
Membership inference is also the standard privacy audit, and the audit and differential privacy bound the same leakage from opposite sides. An audit runs the strongest available attack against the trained model and reports its success. It must state which attacker access it assumes, because some threat models permit only model queries while others grant parameters or auxiliary information. A successful attack proves leakage. A failed attack shows only that this attack, under these assumptions, found none, so an empirical audit is a lower bound on what the model reveals. Differential privacy (section 13.9) supplies the upper bound. A membership test is itself a computation on the released model, so the guarantee applies to its verdict directly and limits how much more often any test can flag a protected record when that record was in training than when it was absent. Under a guarantee with budget \(\PrivacyBudget\) and no additive slack, the rate at which a test flags true members can exceed the rate at which it falsely flags nonmembers by at most a factor of \(e^{\PrivacyBudget}\), which places a ceiling over every possible attack. The distance between the measured lower bound and the accounted upper bound is the uncertainty that a privacy claim carries, the band between the audit curve and the ceiling in figure 7.

A differential privacy guarantee with no additive slack at the illustrative budget \(\PrivacyBudget = 1\) confines every possible test below the dark ceiling, an upper bound on leakage. Model inversion infers sensitive properties of the training data, or a representative input for a class or identity, from the learned model (Fredrikson et al. 2015). It can use either query access or exposed model internals. Confidence scores, for example, can guide a search for inputs that the model associates with a target identity or attribute. A reconstructed face may reveal recognizable features without reproducing an exact training photograph; the privacy claim must distinguish those outcomes. Gradient inversion applies the same idea to the updates that a federated client sends (section 13.8.5.2).

Memorization is the strongest form of the leak, in which a model retains enough of a specific training record to reproduce it. It is not confined to language models. Under one published extraction protocol, a diffusion model reproduced a training-set photograph almost exactly (Carlini et al. 2023); figure 8 pairs the original with the reconstruction. Evidence of extraction concerns that specific training instance; a similar-looking output of the same subject would not establish memorization. The exposure matters most for assistants trained or adapted on user logs, where the memorized strings are the users’ own messages.
