Lighthouse 13.1: Archetype C (Federated MobileNet): Google Gboard federated learningFor the Archetype C mobile/federated workload, Google’s Gboard keyboard (whose on-device next-word suggestion and autocomplete inference interfaces appear in On-Device Prediction Strategies) provides a concrete production baseline for learning from data retained on edge devices. The original keyboard study demonstrates federated training, and the systems report describes the production orchestration challenges (Hard et al. 2018; Bonawitz et al. 2019). Those reports do not by themselves establish that every described model combines secure aggregation with a formal DP guarantee. The engineering pattern separates three contracts: FL keeps raw typing data local, secure aggregation can hide individual messages under its protocol assumptions, and an accounted DP mechanism can bound what the released model reveals. A deployment claim must identify which contracts its actual training run satisfies. For this archetype the threat model therefore starts after the raw data remain on the device, with what each device’s update reveals and who can observe it.



Bonawitz, K., H. Eichner, W. Grieskamp, D. Huba, A. Ingerman, V. Ivanov, C. Kiddon, et al. 2019. “Towards Federated Learning at Scale: System Design.” Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 3.

Hard, Andrew, Kanishka Rao, Rajiv Mathews, Swaroop Ramaswamy, Françoise Beaufays, Sean Augenstein, Hubert Eichner, Chloé Kiddon, and Daniel Ramage. 2018. “Federated Learning for Mobile Keyboard Prediction.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1811.03604.
18 Homomorphic encryption: Operations on ciphertexts correspond to operations on the underlying plaintexts. Gentry’s 2009 work supplied the first fully homomorphic construction; it did not make arbitrary ML workloads immediately practical. Inference cost depends on circuit depth, packing, rotations, numerical representation, and the chosen security parameters.
Gentry, C. 2009. “Fully Homomorphic Encryption Using Ideal Lattices.” Proceedings of the Forty-First Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, 169–78. https://doi.org/10.1145/1536414.1536440.

Yao, Andrew C. 1982. “Protocols for Secure Computations.” 23rd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (Sfcs 1982), 160–64. https://doi.org/10.1109/sfcs.1982.38.
Federated learning changes where raw data reside, while differential privacy bounds the effect of a protected contribution on released results. Cryptographic computation addresses a third boundary: who can observe inputs and intermediate values during execution. Homomorphic encryption (HE)18 and secure multiparty computation (SMPC) support computation over inputs represented as ciphertexts or protocol-specific shares (Gentry 2009; Yao 1982). Their costs depend on the chosen protocol and representation. Quantization can help some encrypted computations, but its effect must be assessed together with ciphertext packing, rotations, nonlinear-function approximations, and required accuracy. Hardware acceleration changes execution cost without removing those mathematical constraints.
In the case of HE, evaluating a supported function on a ciphertext produces a ciphertext that decrypts to the corresponding plaintext result: \[
\HomomorphicCiphertext\leftarrow \operatorname{Enc}(\HomomorphicPublicKey,\PlaintextInput), \qquad
\operatorname{Dec}\!\left(\HomomorphicSecretKey,\operatorname{Eval}(\HomomorphicPublicKey,\HomomorphicFunction,\HomomorphicCiphertext)\right)=\HomomorphicFunction(\PlaintextInput)
\]
This property supports inference over encrypted inputs in an untrusted computing environment. Its confidentiality guarantee depends on the scheme and key custody; it does not by itself prove that the server evaluated the intended function correctly. The deployment must also measure the cost of representing that function as supported encrypted operations, including any approximation that changes prediction quality.

Napkin Math 13.2: The cost of trusted compute
Problem: A team deploying a health-monitoring model compares three security levels:

Plaintext: Standard inference.
Encrypted transport (AES): Model and data are encrypted at rest and in transit.
Encrypted compute (fully homomorphic encryption [FHE]): Inference performed on encrypted data.

Treat the following overheads as assumed scenario inputs, not universal AES or FHE performance ratios. The comparison is whether these configurations satisfy the application’s latency budget.
Math: Inference latency scales by the complexity of the security protocol.

Plaintext: 20 ms.
AES-256: 20 ms + 0.5 ms = 20.5 ms (negligible overhead).
FHE: 20 ms \(\times\) 10,000× = 200 seconds.

Systems insight: Under the assumed overheads, protected computation takes longer than encryption around plaintext execution. Whether FHE fits an application depends on its latency budget and the measured encrypted circuit; the multiplier here does not generalize across models or implementations. Hardware isolation provides a different trust boundary in which computation uses protected plaintext. Comparing that option requires its own measured overhead and an explicit hardware trust assumption.





Under the assumed overheads, AES adds almost nothing; FHE adds four orders of magnitude.
Homomorphic computation costs depend on the supported operations, circuit depth, numerical representation, and chosen security parameters. Supporting arbitrary computation does not by itself determine the cost of a particular inference circuit. Feasibility requires measuring the protected workload against its latency, throughput, and utility requirements. The hardware-enforced isolation of section 13.8.1.1 offers a different trade-off: plaintext computation inside a trusted boundary, with security dependent on that boundary’s hardware and software assumptions.
SMPC,19 by contrast, distributes computation across parties while protecting their private inputs under the protocol’s stated corruption and collusion assumptions. The protocol specifies which parties receive the output; privacy hides additional information beyond what those outputs and a party’s own inputs reveal. This is particularly useful in joint training across institutions with strict data-use policies, such as hospitals or banks.
19 SMPC performance overhead: Cryptographic computation adds protocol-specific communication and local work. The bottleneck depends on round count, network latency, arithmetic representation, and the adversary model; a single slowdown factor does not characterize all deployments. Moving some layers outside protection changes the information exposed and therefore requires a new privacy analysis.


Removing names and account numbers is the oldest privacy technique for a released dataset, and on its own it fails. The fields that remain act as quasi-identifiers, which an attacker can join against auxiliary data to single out a person. Linkage of the Netflix Prize dataset20 showed the failure at scale. Researchers inferred individual movie preferences from records released without names by matching them to public ratings, not by querying a trained model (Narayanan and Shmatikov 2006). The Strava heatmap of section 13.3 showed the aggregate form of the same failure, in which sparse regions singled out the few people behind them.
20 Netflix deanonymization: As few as 8 movie ratings with approximate dates uniquely identified 99 percent of records in the anonymized Netflix Prize dataset, and correlation with public IMDb ratings re-identified users (Narayanan and Shmatikov 2008). For ML training data, removing direct identifiers does not establish privacy when retained records can be linked to auxiliary information.
Narayanan, Arvind, and Vitaly Shmatikov. 2008. “Robust de-Anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets.” 2008 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP 2008), 111–25. https://doi.org/10.1109/sp.2008.33.

Narayanan, Arvind, and Vitaly Shmatikov. 2006. “How to Break Anonymity of the Netflix Prize Dataset.” In CoRR, abs/cs/0610105.
21 \(\Glyph{k}\)-anonymity: A property of a released dataset (Sweeney 2002). Generalization, such as coarsening dates or postal codes, and suppression of rare rows can achieve the property at the cost of information loss. It does not bound inference from homogeneous sensitive attributes or auxiliary knowledge and is not a per-request privacy guarantee.
Sweeney, Latanya. 2002. “K-ANONYMITY: A MODEL for PROTECTING PRIVACY.” International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems 10 (05): 557–70. https://doi.org/10.1142/s0218488502001648.
A release satisfies \(\Glyph{k}\)-anonymity21 when every combination of its designated quasi-identifiers occurs in at least \(\AnonymitySetSize\) records, so no record can be singled out from fewer than \(\AnonymitySetSize\) candidates. The property belongs to a specified release; transforming one request without defining that reference dataset does not establish it. It also constrains only the shape of the released table. When every record in a group shares the same sensitive value, or the attacker holds auxiliary knowledge about a person, knowing which group holds that person still discloses the attribute. The property therefore excludes an observer of the release only from singling out a record, and it bounds nothing about what a model trained on the data reveals. Differential privacy (section 13.9) closes that gap by bounding how much one record changes what is released rather than how the released table looks.



Synthetic data generation changes the privacy decision from hiding raw records to replacing them with generated surrogates. Generated data can let downstream researchers train models without receiving the source records, but the generator and its outputs must still be evaluated for leakage.
Synthetic data generation works by training a generative model (such as a GAN, variational autoencoder (VAE), or diffusion model) on the original sensitive dataset, then using this trained generator to produce new artificial samples. The intended result preserves useful population patterns without reproducing individual records. Learning a distribution does not ensure that separation, however; a generator can memorize its training data, so synthetic sampling alone cannot establish privacy.
Synthetic data generation typically advances through three ordered stages. First, in distribution learning, a generative model \(\SyntheticDataGenerator\) trains on real data \(\RealDataset= \{\ModelInput_1, \ModelInput_2,\ldots, \ModelInput_n\}\) to approximate the underlying data distribution \(\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)\). Next, synthetic sampling produces new records \(\SyntheticDataset= \{\SyntheticDataGenerator(\GeneratorLatentVector_1), \SyntheticDataGenerator(\GeneratorLatentVector_2),\ldots, \SyntheticDataGenerator(\FinalGeneratorLatentVector)\}\) by sampling latent vectors from random noise \(\GeneratorLatentVector_i \sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector,\IdentityMatrix)\). Finally, empirical validation measures selected aspects of fidelity to \(\RealDataset\) and tests for memorization or linkage under the chosen attack model. Sampling can preserve useful statistical properties without distributing the source table (Goncalves et al. 2020), but passing those tests does not prove that every training record is protected. A formal release guarantee requires an additional mechanism, and validation that accesses sensitive source data must itself remain within the intended privacy boundary.

Goncalves, A., P. Ray, B. Soper, J. Stevens, L. Coyle, and A. P. Sales. 2020. “Generation and Evaluation of Synthetic Patient Data.” BMC Medical Research Methodology 20 (1): 1–40. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-020-00977-1.
While appealing, synthetic data generation faces important limitations. Generative models can suffer from mode collapse, failing to capture rare but important patterns in the original data. Adversaries can also extract information about the original training data through generative model inversion or membership inference attacks. The privacy protection depends heavily on the generative model architecture, training procedure, and hyperparameter choices, making it difficult to provide formal privacy guarantees without additional mechanisms like differential privacy.
Consider a hospital that wants to share synthetic data for ML research. It trains a GAN on 10,000 patient records containing demographics, lab results, and diagnoses, seeking to preserve useful relationships among those features. The hospital applies differential privacy during training and uses a tested accountant, specifying whether the protected contribution is one record or all records from one patient. Before release, it evaluates clinical fidelity and subgroup utility, since an acceptable overall score can hide poor performance for rare conditions. Memorization tests supply additional empirical evidence, while the formal guarantee comes from the accounted mechanism. DP limits the effect of a protected contribution; it does not prevent learning population patterns or all sensitive inferences based on them.
Across federated learning, differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, and synthetic data, the privacy-preserving approaches differ in the guarantees they offer and in their system-level implications. Production designs often combine them, for example by applying differential privacy inside a federated setup or by reserving homomorphic encryption for the few inference stages whose inputs justify its cost. The choice of mechanism therefore depends on computational constraints, deployment architecture, and regulatory requirements. Once the formal machinery of differential privacy is in place, these methods can be weighed on privacy guarantee, runtime overhead, operational maturity, and use case fit together rather than as independent properties (table 8).
The defense stack now covers each tier, from hardware roots of trust through deployment, runtime, and model-design controls to the data path, where federation, secure aggregation, encrypted computation, and synthetic data each move raw records or individual updates away from a particular observer. Data locality, message hiding, encrypted computation, and synthesis alone do not bound what the released model reveals. A secure training cluster and confidential links can still publish a model that exposes memorized examples, as the GPT-2 case showed, because the leak travels through an authorized output rather than an unauthorized access. Closing that gap requires a guarantee stated about the release itself, with the protected contribution, the randomization, and the accumulated loss across releases all made explicit.

Self-Check: Question

A team wants to run deep learning inference inside an Intel SGX enclave with a 128 MiB Enclave Page Cache (EPC). A ResNet-50 model with FP32 weights occupies approximately 102.2 MB of memory before accounting for intermediate activation tensors and runtime buffers. What happens if the combined memory footprint of the model and activations exceeds the available resident EPC capacity on a configuration that supports protected paging during inference?

Protected pages can be paged to untrusted memory with cryptographic protection, adding workload-dependent overhead that must be measured against the serving deadline.
The SGX hardware automatically quantizes all FP32 weights to 2-bit integers to force the model into the EPC.
The CPU halts immediately and burns an internal fuse, requiring physical motherboard replacement.
The inference pipeline automatically falls back to unencrypted peer-to-peer federated learning across local nodes.

In federated learning, raw data remains on client devices, but Deep Leakage from Gradients (Zhu et al., 2019) demonstrated that an adversary observing raw gradient updates can reconstruct original training images pixel-by-pixel. Explain how secure aggregation mitigates this attack and describe its operational boundary.
A production ML platform is replacing legacy PyTorch .pth checkpoint files with the SafeTensors format for its public model repository. What primary security vulnerability does this change eliminate?

It prevents black-box model extraction queries against the deployed HTTP API endpoint.
It eliminates arbitrary code execution during model deserialization by storing only tensor data buffers without executable Python object serialization.
It guarantees \((\epsilon, \delta)\) differential privacy for the training dataset encoded in the weights.
It reduces inference latency by replacing floating-point operations with optical matrix multiplication.

When designing privacy-preserving cloud inference for sensitive patient records, compare the systems trade-offs of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) versus Confidential Computing with hardware TEEs (such as NVIDIA H100 Confidential Computing) across latency overhead and trust assumptions.
To support an ownership claim for a proprietary neural network, developers may embed a model ____, such as a secret trigger-set response pattern, and test its effect on normal utility and its survival under model modification.
Arrange the steps of a hardware-anchored secure boot sequence in chronological order from initial device power-on to user application execution:


Verify and load Linux kernel and root filesystem by verifying signatures or hashes authenticated by the preceding trusted stage
Power up and initialize core hardware platform
Launch verified ML runtime and load signed model artifacts
Read immutable hardware Root of Trust (ROM) and verify bootloader digital signature
Execute authenticated bootloader to perform platform self-diagnosis

title: 13 Security & Privacy
text:
Suppose an adversary queries a medical diagnosis model using the exact attributes of a known patient and compares the answers with what a model trained without that patient would return. Encryption and access control cannot help here. The adversary is an authorized caller, and the query reaches only the trained model, never the stored records. A difference in one pair of predictions alone does not prove a privacy violation. The relevant question is how much the distribution of released outcomes permits an adversary to distinguish datasets with and without that patient, relative to a stated privacy bound.
Differential privacy constrains a randomized training or analysis mechanism so that its output distributions remain close on adjacent datasets. The adjacency definition specifies the protected contribution, such as one record or all records from one person. The information leakage invariant (principle \(\ref{pri-information-leakage}\)) holds that any observable output can carry information about a protected training record, so a privacy claim must name the protected unit and the observations available to an adversary. Differential privacy answers that requirement by bounding the additional evidence a release supplies about the named contribution. For a fixed mechanism and workload, tighter privacy bounds require more noise or fewer data-dependent releases, and the first cost appears as lost utility. Recovering that utility with more data or more training steps raises the training compute, the \(\IronLawComputeTime\) term the privacy definition flagged, and per-example clipping in DP-SGD lowers throughput on its own. Whether a tighter bound costs accuracy, compute, or both is therefore a design choice, which places DP in the deployment architecture rather than only in a legal checklist.

Definition 13.5: Differential privacy
Differential privacy is a mathematical guarantee that bounds changes in the output distribution of a randomized algorithm under a specified change to one protected contribution. The neighboring relation defines that contribution and the permitted change. Approximate differential privacy permits a multiplicative bound and additive slack, formalized by the \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) bound \(\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) \in \MechanismOutputSet] \leq e^{\PrivacyBudget} \Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) \in \MechanismOutputSet] + \PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) for adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset\) and \(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset\) and any measurable output set \(\MechanismOutputSet\) (Dwork et al. 2006; Dwork and Roth 2014).

Significance: The privacy budget \(\PrivacyBudget\) converts an algorithmic property into an engineering currency that can be allocated, composed, and depleted. Production reports and benchmark studies show that privacy budgets are deployment-specific: Apple describes local-DP telemetry deployments with per-event \(\PrivacyBudget\) values chosen by use case, while DP-SGD studies show accuracy and compute trade-offs across benchmark tasks (Apple Differential Privacy Team 2017; Abadi et al. 2016; Bu et al. 2020; De et al. 2022). Smaller \(\PrivacyBudget\) raises the noise floor and degrades classification accuracy along the empirical frontier plotted in figure 26, where CIFAR-10 suffers double-digit accuracy drops even at \(\PrivacyBudget= 8\). DP-SGD can also reduce training throughput because per-sample gradient clipping works against the batch-level parallelism that makes accelerator training efficient.
Distinction: Unlike de-identification, which removes identifiers from records and fails against re-identification through auxiliary data, and unlike statistical disclosure control, which depends on the attacker’s model, differential privacy is a property of the algorithm, not of the data. Its guarantee holds against any adversary, including one with arbitrary side information about other records in the dataset.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that an \(\PrivacyBudget\) label applies independently to every data access. Sequential composition of \(\ComposedMechanismCount\) DP mechanisms, each with privacy loss \(\PrivacyBudget_0\), yields total loss at most \(\ComposedMechanismCount\PrivacyBudget_0\) under basic composition, with tighter bounds available from mechanism-specific accountants (section 13.9.2). A system that runs DP-SGD steps or answers interactive DP queries against sensitive data must therefore track cumulative loss and stop or redesign the release when the allocated budget is exhausted. Rotating cryptographic keys does not reset privacy loss, while querying a fixed DP-trained model is post-processing and incurs no additional training privacy loss.




Apple Differential Privacy Team. 2017. Learning with Privacy at Scale. Apple Machine Learning Research.
The salary-average notebook in section 13.9.1.2 uses the central model of differential privacy. Each person supplies a bounded salary to a trusted analyst; the analyst computes the sum, adds one Laplace draw calibrated to the sum’s global sensitivity, and divides by the fixed, public group size. The example protects a salary replacement within a public roster. If participation itself is private, adjacency must be add/remove, meaning adjacent datasets differ by the presence or absence of one person’s records rather than by a change to one value. Under that relation the count becomes data dependent and needs its own privacy treatment, so division by that count is not automatically safe post-processing. This differs from local differential privacy, in which each person randomizes a value before submission and the analyst aggregates the randomized reports. Both models compare output distributions on adjacent inputs, but their mechanisms, trust assumptions, and utility are not interchangeable.
A randomized mechanism \(\RandomizedMechanism\) run on adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset\) and \(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset\) produces two output densities that overlap without coinciding (figure 25, blue and orange curves). Overlap means that either dataset can produce outcomes in the same region; it does not make the distributions identical. For a discrete outcome \(\MechanismOutcome\) in \(\text{Range}(\RandomizedMechanism)\), relative likelihood can be expressed as \(\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset)=\MechanismOutcome] / \Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)=\MechanismOutcome]\) when the denominator is positive. Continuous curves instead depict densities, whose ratio is not their vertical difference. The \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) guarantee applies to probabilities of measurable output sets: it bounds one probability by \(e^{\PrivacyBudget}\) times the other plus \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\). For a continuous output, those probabilities are areas under the curves over the selected set. The definition therefore constrains distributional change across all such sets, rather than declaring an overlapping region private or treating additive slack as a pointwise density-ratio allowance.














Figure 25: Differential Privacy and Output Distributions: These illustrative densities show how outputs can overlap without having identical likelihoods. Differential privacy bounds how much the output distribution can change between adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset\) and \(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset\). The privacy parameters limit, rather than eliminate, the information an observer can gain about any one individual’s inclusion.



A randomized algorithm \(\RandomizedMechanism\) is said to be \(\PrivacyBudget\)-differentially private if, for all adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset\) and \(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset\) differing in one record, and for all measurable output sets \(\MechanismOutputSet \subseteq \text{Range}(\RandomizedMechanism)\), the following holds (Dwork et al. 2006; Dwork and Roth 2014): \[
\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) \in \MechanismOutputSet] \leq e^{\PrivacyBudget} \Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) \in \MechanismOutputSet]
\]

Dwork, Cynthia, Frank McSherry, Kobbi Nissim, and Adam Smith. 2006. “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis.” In Theory of Cryptography Conference (TCC), edited by Shai Halevi and Tal Rabin, vol. 3876. Lecture Notes in Computer Science. Springer Berlin Heidelberg. https://doi.org/10.1007/11681878_14.
The parameter \(\PrivacyBudget\) quantifies the privacy budget. In the pure-DP definition above, smaller values of \(\PrivacyBudget\) impose a tighter likelihood-ratio bound; achieving that bound may require more noise or a different mechanism. No universal \(\PrivacyBudget\) value denotes “strong,” “moderate,” or acceptable privacy: interpretation depends on adjacency, the additive slack \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) in approximate DP, composition, and the consequences of inference. Under pure DP, the multiplicative factor \(e^{\PrivacyBudget}\) bounds ratios of probabilities for the same output event on adjacent datasets. Approximate DP relaxes that event-probability inequality with additive slack, as developed below.
This bound limits how distinguishable the output distributions can be when a protected contribution changes; it does not make them identical or prevent inference of population-level patterns. Common DP mechanisms add calibrated noise to model updates or query responses, using distributions such as Laplace or Gaussian. Training techniques like differentially private stochastic gradient descent22 combine contribution bounds with calibrated noise and composition accounting. Their guarantee applies to the specified contribution and release, which must be identified before selecting the mechanism.
22 DP-SGD (differentially private stochastic gradient descent): Introduced by Abadi et al. (2016), DP-SGD clips each per-sample gradient and adds calibrated Gaussian noise. Per-example clipping adds memory, recomputation, and reduction work that ordinary minibatch training avoids; vectorized clipping implementations recover much of the parallelism, so the throughput cost must be measured for the chosen model and implementation.
Abadi, M., A. Chu, I. Goodfellow, H. B. McMahan, I. Mironov, K. Talwar, and L. Zhang. 2016. “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy.” Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security, CCS ’16, 308–18. https://doi.org/10.1145/2976749.2978318.


Attaching an \(\PrivacyBudget\) label to a model without stating whether adjacency protects one record or one person, how many training steps composed, and what \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) slack was allowed makes the privacy claim meaningless. Repeated training steps, retraining runs, or queries that access protected data may compose, while post-processing a fixed DP release incurs no additional privacy loss for that data. The mathematical foundations specify the guarantee, noise calibration, and accounting for those data-dependent operations so teams can define a valid accounting boundary before attaching an \(\PrivacyBudget\) value to a deployed release.


The pure \(\PrivacyBudget\)-DP definition provides strong guarantees but can be overly restrictive for practical ML applications. The relaxed formulation already stated in the definition callout, \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-differential privacy, adds slack \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) to the probability bound controlled by \(\PrivacyBudget\), and it is restated here as the starting point for noise calibration. Approximate DP is widely used with Gaussian perturbations in deep learning. Its role follows from the probability bound and noise calibration, not from unbounded support alone; Laplace noise also has unbounded support.
Formally, a randomized algorithm \(\RandomizedMechanism\) satisfies \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-differential privacy if for all adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset, \AdjacentNeighboringDataset\) and all measurable output sets \(\MechanismOutputSet\): \[
\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) \in \MechanismOutputSet] \leq e^{\PrivacyBudget} \Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) \in \MechanismOutputSet] + \PrivacyAdditiveSlack\]
The parameter \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) is additive slack in this event-probability inequality, not generally the probability of a catastrophic disclosure. In practice, \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) is commonly chosen smaller than the inverse dataset size, often \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack< 1/\DatasetSize\) or smaller depending on policy and threat model; smaller \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) tightens the guarantee at additional utility cost. For a dataset with 1 million records, \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack= 10^{-12}\) specifies a small additive slack, but does not by itself assign a probability to every possible privacy failure.



ML systems implement differential privacy through carefully calibrated noise injection. The two primary mechanisms used in ML systems differ in their noise distributions and applicability. The first is the Laplace mechanism. For pure \(\PrivacyBudget\)-DP, it adds noise drawn from \(\text{Lap}(\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery/\PrivacyBudget)\), where \(\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery\) is the global sensitivity of the function (the maximum change in output when one record changes). For a query \(\DatasetQuery\), the privatized output is: \[
\PrivatizedQuery(\NeighboringDataset) = \DatasetQuery(\NeighboringDataset) + \text{Lap}\left(\frac{\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery}{\PrivacyBudget}\right)
\]
The Laplace distribution has density \(\ProbabilityFunction(\LaplaceNoiseSample) = \frac{\PrivacyBudget}{2\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery}\exp\left(-\frac{\PrivacyBudget|\LaplaceNoiseSample|}{\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery}\right)\), with scale parameter \(\LaplaceNoiseScale= \QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery/\PrivacyBudget\). For a fixed query and adjacency relation, tightening the bound from \(\PrivacyBudget= 1.0\) to \(\PrivacyBudget= 0.1\) increases the noise scale by 10\(\times\). Individual noise draws remain random; the scale controls their distribution rather than fixing their magnitude.
The Laplace derivation shows why the noise scale must match sensitivity. To prove that the Laplace mechanism achieves \(\PrivacyBudget\)-DP, consider the ratio of output densities on adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset\) and \(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset\). Let \(\DatasetQuery(\NeighboringDataset) = \DatasetQueryResult\) and \(\DatasetQuery(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) = \AdjacentQueryResult\), where \(|\DatasetQueryResult- \AdjacentQueryResult| \leq \QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery\) by the sensitivity bound. For any output \(\MechanismOutcome\), the density ratio is: \[
\frac{\ProbabilityFunction(\MechanismOutcome | \NeighboringDataset)}{\ProbabilityFunction(\MechanismOutcome | \AdjacentNeighboringDataset)} = \frac{\exp(-\PrivacyBudget|\MechanismOutcome - \DatasetQueryResult|/\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery)}{\exp(-\PrivacyBudget|\MechanismOutcome - \AdjacentQueryResult|/\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery)} = \exp\left(\frac{\PrivacyBudget(|\MechanismOutcome - \AdjacentQueryResult| - |\MechanismOutcome - \DatasetQueryResult|)}{\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery}\right)
\]
Using the triangle inequality, \(|\MechanismOutcome - \AdjacentQueryResult| - |\MechanismOutcome - \DatasetQueryResult| \leq |\DatasetQueryResult- \AdjacentQueryResult| \leq \QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery\). Therefore: \[
\frac{\ProbabilityFunction(\MechanismOutcome | \NeighboringDataset)}{\ProbabilityFunction(\MechanismOutcome | \AdjacentNeighboringDataset)} \leq \exp\left(\frac{\PrivacyBudget\cdot \QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery}{\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery}\right) = e^{\PrivacyBudget}
\]
This establishes that the Laplace mechanism satisfies \(\PrivacyBudget\)-differential privacy. The derivation reveals why sensitivity calibration is necessary, because the noise scale must match the maximum possible change in the query output to mask individual contributions.

Napkin Math 13.3: The cost of differential privacyProblem: Consider computing the average salary of 1000 employees while guaranteeing privacy budget \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 1. The salaries range from $0 to $200,000. Assume a fixed, public employee roster and neighboring datasets that differ in one employee’s salary, with both values inside these bounds. How much noise must the mechanism add?
Math:

Sensitivity \((\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery)\): The maximum one person can change the sum is $200,000.
Privacy Budget \((\PrivacyBudget)\): 1.
Laplace Noise Scale \((\LaplaceNoiseScale)\): the Laplace mechanism sets its noise scale to the sensitivity divided by the privacy budget, so \(\LaplaceNoiseScale= \QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery/ \PrivacyBudget=\) $200,000 / 1 = $200,000.
Impact on Mean: The mean-estimation noise comes from noise added to the sum with magnitude approximately $200,000.

Error in the mean = $200,000 / 1000 = $200. The mechanism draws noise once, for the sum; dividing by the group size spreads that single draw across the mean.


Systems insight: Under this fixed-roster contract, the published mean receives zero-mean Laplace noise with expected absolute magnitude $200; individual draws can be smaller or larger. For a dataset of \(\DatasetSize=\) 100, the expected absolute error grows to $2,000. The noise needed to hide one person is fixed by the sensitivity, while the signal grows with the number of people, so small groups pay the largest relative cost and large datasets dilute it through the factor \(1/\DatasetSize\).


The Gaussian mechanism serves the ML case where the relaxed \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) guarantee is acceptable. It adds noise with standard deviation \(\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation\) calibrated based on \(\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack\), and the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\QuerySensitivity_2 \DatasetQuery\): \[
\PrivatizedQuery(\NeighboringDataset) = \DatasetQuery(\NeighboringDataset) + \GaussianDistribution\left(\ZeroVector, \GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix\right)
\]
Unlike the Laplace mechanism, which achieves pure \(\PrivacyBudget\)-DP, the Gaussian mechanism generally requires the relaxed \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-DP formulation because shifted Gaussian densities can have arbitrarily large likelihood ratios in the tails. Bounding those tail events gives a sufficient way to establish the \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) slack. The derivation works with the privacy loss, the log of the ratio between the two output densities at the observed output. Because the output is random, so is this log ratio, which is why it is called the privacy loss random variable.
For adjacent datasets with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\QuerySensitivity_2 \DatasetQuery\), the privacy loss at output \(\MechanismOutputVector\) follows: \[
\PrivacyLossVariable(\MechanismOutputVector) = \ln\frac{\ProbabilityFunction(\MechanismOutputVector|\NeighboringDataset)}{\ProbabilityFunction(\MechanismOutputVector|\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)} = \frac{\|\MechanismOutputVector- \DatasetQuery(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)\|_2^2 - \|\MechanismOutputVector- \DatasetQuery(\NeighboringDataset)\|_2^2}{2\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2}
\]
When \(\MechanismOutputVector= \DatasetQuery(\NeighboringDataset) + \GaussianMechanismNoiseVector\) for noise \(\GaussianMechanismNoiseVector\sim \GaussianDistribution(\ZeroVector, \GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2 \IdentityMatrix)\), expanding the difference of squared norms cancels the quadratic term \(\|\GaussianMechanismNoiseVector\|_2^2\) and leaves a constant shift plus a linear inner product between \(\GaussianMechanismNoiseVector\) and the dataset difference \(\DatasetQuery(\NeighboringDataset) - \DatasetQuery(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)\). Unlike the Laplace log ratio, which the triangle inequality caps at a constant across the entire output space, this linear function of \(\GaussianMechanismNoiseVector\) grows without bound along the direction of the dataset difference. For an adjacent pair attaining the sensitivity bound, the privacy loss is therefore a shifted Gaussian random variable with mean \(\frac{\QuerySensitivity_2 \DatasetQuery^2}{2\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2}\) and variance \(\frac{\QuerySensitivity_2 \DatasetQuery^2}{\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2}\), and \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) bounds the probability that a noise draw lands far enough in the tail to push \(\PrivacyLossVariable(\MechanismOutputVector)\) above \(\PrivacyBudget\). For one application of the mechanism and \(0<\PrivacyBudget<1\), a classic sufficient calibration is: \[
\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation\geq \frac{\QuerySensitivity_2 \DatasetQuery}{\PrivacyBudget}\sqrt{2\ln\left(\frac{1.25}{\PrivacyAdditiveSlack}\right)}
\]
This sufficient bound is a one-shot Gaussian-mechanism result within that parameter domain. Neither it nor the one-shot Laplace ratio \(\QuerySensitivity \DatasetQuery/\PrivacyBudget\) of the salary example can set a DP-SGD noise multiplier by substituting the final training budget. DP-SGD clips sampled per-example gradients, adds Gaussian noise to their sum, and composes many such steps, so its budget requires a sampled-Gaussian accountant. Smaller \(\PrivacyBudget\) or \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\) generally requires more noise, but the resulting accuracy change must be measured for the specific task and training procedure.

Napkin Math 13.4: One-shot Gaussian mechanismProblem: Determine a sufficient noise standard deviation \(\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation\) for the Gaussian mechanism to achieve \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-differential privacy for a single vector-valued query.
Variables: \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\QuerySensitivity_2 \DatasetQuery=\) 1, target \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 0.5, \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack=\) \(10^{-5}\).
Math: Classic sufficient bound requires \(\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation\geq\) 9.7.
Systems insight: This calculation applies to a single Gaussian release. DP-SGD repeats a Gaussian release at every optimization step, so its budget must be composed across thousands of steps, and the accountants of section 13.9.2.1 bound that composed total more tightly than adding up the per-step bounds would.


Gaussian noise fits the clipped-gradient mechanism because clipping explicitly bounds gradient norms in \(\ell_2\) space, making sensitivity analysis tractable. Rényi differential privacy accounting can retain mechanism-specific information to improve on generic composition bounds; that advantage belongs to mechanisms like clipped-gradient training and makes no case for Gaussian noise in every private computation.




Releasing 10 models trained on the same patient cohort at \(\PrivacyBudget=1\) each does not maintain \(\PrivacyBudget=1\) protection; under basic composition the cumulative bound reaches \(\PrivacyBudget=10\). Because a full training run or a sequence of model releases applies a mechanism many times, privacy loss accumulates across every additional data-dependent DP release about the same protected population. Basic composition bounds the total by adding the per-release bounds, which is valid but often loose, while mechanism-specific accountants retain more information about each mechanism to obtain tighter bounds across noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) steps before expressing the result as an \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) budget. Repeated use of a fixed released DP model is post-processing and does not add to its training privacy loss.



Ten \(\PrivacyBudget=1\) releases add up to a basic bound of \(\PrivacyBudget=10\).
Privacy accounting depends on three primary composition tools. Simple composition bounds the cumulative privacy loss of \(\ComposedMechanismCount\) pure-DP mechanisms with bounds \(\PrivacyBudget_i\) by \(\sum \PrivacyBudget_i\); for approximate DP, their additive slack parameters also accumulate. In suitable parameter regimes, advanced composition improves the bound using square-root and linear terms while allocating additional slack in the probability inequality. For iterative mechanisms like DP-SGD, the moments accountant and Rényi differential privacy developed next track the loss across steps before converting it to an explicit \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) guarantee, and no accountant is uniformly tighter than every alternative. Organizations must maintain a privacy accounting log for the protected population and halt or redesign further data-dependent releases when the allocated bound would be exceeded.


A more refined approach to privacy analysis tracks the privacy loss random variable, which measures how strongly an observation favors one adjacent dataset over the other through a log-likelihood ratio. For adjacent datasets \(\NeighboringDataset, \AdjacentNeighboringDataset\) and algorithm output \(\MechanismOutcome\), the discrete-output expression is: \[
\OutcomePairPrivacyLoss = \ln\frac{\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) = \MechanismOutcome]}{\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) = \MechanismOutcome]}
\]
The privacy loss random variable characterizes the log-likelihood ratio between outputs on adjacent datasets; for continuous outputs, the ratio uses densities rather than point probabilities. A sufficient condition for \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-DP is that every ordered adjacent pair satisfies \(\Pr[\PrivacyLossVariable> \PrivacyBudget] \leq \PrivacyAdditiveSlack\), with the output sampled from the numerator distribution. This tail condition is stronger than the general definition, but it enables composition analysis through moment-generating functions.
The moments accountant technique, introduced for DP-SGD by Abadi et al. (2016), bounds exponential moments of the privacy loss distribution. It retains more information about the mechanism than a single per-step privacy bound while still taking the worst case over adjacent datasets. For mechanism \(\RandomizedMechanism\) with privacy loss \(\PrivacyLossVariable\), the moments accountant computes: \[
\MechanismLogMoment(\MomentOrder) = \max_{\NeighboringDataset,\AdjacentNeighboringDataset} \ln \mathbb{E}_{\MechanismOutcome\sim \RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset)}\left[\left(\frac{\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) = \MechanismOutcome]}{\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) = \MechanismOutcome]}\right)^{\MomentOrder}\right]
\]
for moment order \(\MomentOrder\). Because the total privacy loss across steps with fresh noise draws is the sum of the per-step privacy losses, its exponential moment factors into the product of the per-step moments, and its logarithm adds across steps. If each of \(\ComposedMechanismCount\) steps satisfies the same log-moment bound, composition gives an upper bound of \(\ComposedMechanismCount\cdot \MechanismLogMoment(\MomentOrder)\). Instead of converting every step into a separate tail cutoff and summing those cutoffs, the accountant accumulates the log-moments first and applies the Markov inequality once at the end to yield \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) bounds: \[
\PrivacyBudget(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack) = \min_{\MomentOrder>0} \left[\frac{\ComposedMechanismCount\cdot \MechanismLogMoment(\MomentOrder) + \ln(1/\PrivacyAdditiveSlack)}{\MomentOrder}\right]
\]
The numerical result depends on the sampling rule, sampling rate, noise multiplier, step count, adjacency relation, and accountant. In DP-SGD, random subsampling at rate \(\LotSamplingProbability\) also shrinks \(\MechanismLogMoment(\MomentOrder)\) at each step because a given record participates in only a \(\LotSamplingProbability\) fraction of lots on average. For example, Abadi et al. (2016) report that with sampling rate \(\LotSamplingProbability=0.01\), noise multiplier \(\PrivacyNoiseMultiplier=4\), and \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack=10^{-5}\), their moments accountant gives \(\PrivacyBudget=1.26\) after 100 epochs and \(\PrivacyBudget=2.55\) after 400 epochs, whereas the corresponding strong-composition bounds are 9.34 and 24.22. These values belong to that experiment and are not reusable constants for another DP-SGD run.



Rényi differential privacy (RDP), introduced by Mironov (2017), provides a convenient representation for composition by tracking Rényi divergence. A mechanism \(\RandomizedMechanism\) satisfies \((\RenyiOrder, \RenyiPrivacyBudget)\text{-RDP}\) if for all adjacent \(\NeighboringDataset, \AdjacentNeighboringDataset\): \[
\RenyiDivergence(\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) \lVert \RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)) = \frac{1}{\RenyiOrder-1}\ln \mathbb{E}_{\MechanismOutcome \sim \RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset)}\left[\left(\frac{\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\NeighboringDataset) = \MechanismOutcome]}{\Pr[\RandomizedMechanism(\AdjacentNeighboringDataset) = \MechanismOutcome]}\right)^{\RenyiOrder}\right] \leq \RenyiPrivacyBudget\]

Mironov, I. 2017. “Rényi Differential Privacy.” 2017 IEEE 30th Computer Security Foundations Symposium (CSF), 263–75. https://doi.org/10.1109/csf.2017.11.
where \(\RenyiOrder> 1\) is the Rényi order. RDP composition is simple. If mechanism \(\RandomizedMechanism_i\) satisfies \((\RenyiOrder, \MechanismRenyiPrivacyBudget)\text{-RDP}\), then their composition satisfies \((\RenyiOrder, \sum_i \MechanismRenyiPrivacyBudget)\text{-RDP}\). This representation avoids repeatedly applying a generic \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\) composition theorem to every training step.
For an unsampled Gaussian mechanism with unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity and noise standard deviation \(\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation\), the RDP guarantee is: \[
\RenyiPrivacyBudget(\RenyiOrder) = \frac{\RenyiOrder}{2\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2}
\]
Subsampling changes this mechanism. In particular, \(\LotSamplingProbability^2\RenyiOrder/(2\GaussianMechanismStandardDeviation^2)\) is only a leading-order approximation in restricted regimes, not a privacy guarantee that can certify a DP-SGD run. A sampled-Gaussian accountant must evaluate the specified sampling scheme and adjacency relation at multiple Rényi orders, compose the resulting per-step bounds across the actual number of steps, and then convert the result to \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-DP. Production implementations should use a tested accountant such as Google DP Accounting, TensorFlow Privacy, or Opacus and record its version and sampling convention with the released model.
This RDP guarantee supplies a valid \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)\)-DP bound using the following conversion; the result is an upper bound on privacy loss, not generally its exact value: \[
\PrivacyBudget= \RenyiPrivacyBudget+ \frac{\ln(1/\PrivacyAdditiveSlack)}{\RenyiOrder- 1}
\]
optimized over \(\RenyiOrder\). The moments-accountant and RDP views are closely related; which implementation gives the tightest reported bound depends on the mechanism, orders, and numerical accountant rather than a universal multiplier.



Consider training a CNN on 50,000 CIFAR-10 images with \((\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack) = (\) 3 \(, 10^{-5})\) target privacy. DP-SGD groups examples into lots, the randomly sampled sets whose clipped gradients are summed and share one noise draw per step; with Poisson sampling the lot size varies from step to step around its expected value. The run uses DP-SGD with:

Poisson sampling with expected lot size \(\BatchSize=\) 4,000 (inclusion probability \(\LotSamplingProbability= \BatchSize/\DatasetSize =\) 0.08)
Per-example gradient clipping norm \(\GradientClippingNorm=\) 1
Noise multiplier \(\PrivacyNoiseMultiplier=\) 1.3 (noise scale relative to clipping)
Training for \(\EpochCount=\) 60 epochs (\(\ComposedMechanismCount= \EpochCount\cdot \DatasetSize/\BatchSize=\) 750 steps)

These inputs do not determine a privacy guarantee through the shortcut \(\LotSamplingProbability^2\RenyiOrder/(2\PrivacyNoiseMultiplier^2)\). Before release, a tested sampled-Gaussian accountant must evaluate Poisson sampling with add/remove adjacency, compose all 750 steps, convert to the specified \(\PrivacyAdditiveSlack\), and verify whether the result meets target \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 3. The release record must pin the accountant library and version, sampling convention, adjacency relation, and evaluated Rényi orders.
The adjacency relation also decides what the bound protects. Per-example clipping bounds the contribution of one record, so when one person contributes many records, as a repeat customer does to a review corpus, a record-level guarantee does not protect that person as a unit. Person-level protection requires bounding each person’s total contribution and accounting under person-level adjacency.
Training for \(\EpochCount=\) 25 reduces the number of composed steps, while reducing the expected lot size to \(\BatchSize=\) 2,000 changes the Poisson inclusion probability to \(\LotSamplingProbability=\) 0.04. The accountant must be rerun for either change; neither direction should be assigned a numerical \(\PrivacyBudget\) through the leading-order shortcut. If the accountant reports a budget above the target, the operator raises the noise multiplier, trains for fewer epochs, or lowers the sampling rate, and then reruns it. Each change has a utility and compute cost that must be measured. The guarantee itself comes from clipping, calibrated noise, and the privacy accountant; listing 1 shows the mechanism sequence without implementing an accountant.



Listing 1: DP-SGD Training Step: Per-step clipping, noise addition, and accountant update that together enforce the privacy budget.


fix a public normalization B for the expected lot size under the sampling design
check prospectively that the accountant permits the next step within the budget
independently sample each record with probability q (Poisson sampling)
clip each sampled per-example gradient to norm C
sum clipped gradients; use the zero vector for an empty lot
add noise N(0, sigma^2 C^2 I), then divide by fixed B
take one optimizer step with the privatized gradient
record the step in the matching privacy accountant
stop before a step that would exceed the release budget
account for private-data-dependent selection; retuning does not erase prior releases







Tightening differential privacy to single-digit \(\PrivacyBudget\) keeps MNIST within 3.3 percentage points of its 98.3 percent nonprivate baseline, yet drops CIFAR-10 trained from scratch by roughly 14 to 22 percentage points even at \(\PrivacyBudget =\) 8 (Abadi et al. 2016; Bu et al. 2020; De et al. 2022). That gap shows how strongly the utility cost of differential privacy depends on task complexity, architecture, privacy accountant, pretraining, and whether extra public data are allowed.
Figure 26 collects those published MNIST and CIFAR-10 results on a logarithmic axis (Abadi et al. 2016; Bu et al. 2020; De et al. 2022). These comparisons show setting-specific utility costs; differences in architectures and training procedures prevent isolating task complexity alone. The plotted MNIST results stay within 3.3 percentage points of the 98.3 percent nonprivate baseline at every plotted single-digit budget, the smallest of which is \(\PrivacyBudget =\) 2. For CIFAR-10 without extra data, the plotted results reach 73 percent in Abadi et al. (2016) and 81.4 percent in De et al. (2022) at \(\PrivacyBudget=\) 8, roughly 14 to 22 points below the displayed 95.0 percent nonprivate reference. These CIFAR-10 settings therefore pay several times the MNIST accuracy cost at a budget four times looser. That reference is a comparison point, not a ceiling on achievable accuracy. Selecting a budget therefore requires the full training regime, adjacency relation, additive slack, accountant, and utility requirements rather than the horizontal coordinate alone.














Figure 26: Published Privacy-Utility Results: Accuracy at selected privacy budgets from (Abadi et al. 2016; Bu et al. 2020; De et al. 2022). MNIST stays comparatively accurate under single-digit epsilon budgets in these experiments, while CIFAR-10 trained from scratch without extra data remains harder, with De et al. reporting 81.4 percent at \(\PrivacyBudget = 8\). Comparisons require the full mechanism, accountant, adjacency relation, training regime, and data rather than epsilon alone.


Bu, Zhiqi, Jiawen Dong, Qi Long, and Weijie J. Su. 2020. “Deep Learning with Gaussian Differential Privacy.” Harvard Data Science Review 2. https://doi.org/10.1162/99608f92.cfc5dd25.


These empirical results show why a privacy budget alone does not predict utility. The original DP-SGD experiments achieved higher accuracy on MNIST than on CIFAR-10, while later training methods improved the CIFAR-10 result under the same budget. Public pretraining changes the learning problem again. With an NFNet-F3 pretrained on JFT-4B, De et al. (2022) report 86.7 percent ImageNet accuracy at \((8, 8 \times 10^{-7})\)-DP, so comparisons must state which data receive protection and which data support pretraining. The figure supplies selected operating points rather than a complete privacy-accuracy curve. A deployment needs its own sweep over \(\PrivacyBudget\) with the other privacy assumptions and acceptance criteria held explicit.

De, Soham, Leonard Berrada, Jamie Hayes, Samuel L. Smith, and Borja Balle. 2022. “Unlocking High-Accuracy Differentially Private Image Classification Through Scale.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2204.13650.



Committing to \(\PrivacyBudget = 1\) before checking rare-subgroup accuracy or 8-GPU training budgets can leave a clinical classifier too inaccurate or too expensive to ship. The quantified trade-offs turn differential privacy from a mathematical guarantee into a deployment decision: specify the required protection first, then test whether a mechanism can deliver it at acceptable utility and systems cost. A mandatory privacy bound is a feasibility constraint; an accuracy improvement does not by itself justify exceeding it.
Start with the regulatory and legal requirement. DP becomes especially valuable when policy, contracts, audits, or risk assessments require demonstrable privacy bounds. Regulations rarely mandate DP by name, but GDPR’s data-protection-by-design principle (European Parliament and Council of the European Union 2016) and privacy-by-design framing (Cavoukian 2012) motivate privacy-preserving system design. HIPAA’s technical safeguards, in turn, require controls such as access control, audit controls, integrity protections, authentication, and transmission security (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services 2005). DP can complement those controls by documenting a mathematical privacy-loss bound, but it does not replace HIPAA safeguard implementation. Organizations handling EU health data, US medical records, or California personal data subject to California state privacy laws (CCPA/CPRA) should evaluate DP as one possible compliance-supporting mechanism.

European Parliament, and Council of the European Union. 2016. Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016. Official Journal of the European Union.

Cavoukian, A. 2012. “Privacy by Design: Origins, Meaning, and Prospects for Assuring Privacy and Trust in the Information Era.” Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner 1: 170–208. https://doi.org/10.4018/978-1-61350-501-4.ch007.
Next, match the threat model to the mechanism. DP bounds how much any one record can change the released distribution, even when an adversary chooses queries adaptively and combines outputs with auxiliary information. This property can limit membership inference and record-level extraction, but only under the stated adjacency relation and composed budget. When the primary threats are data breaches of stored data rather than inference from a release, encryption and access controls address the relevant boundary; DP does not substitute for them.
The dataset and task then determine whether the guarantee is usable. Effective DP training depends on whether the clipped signal remains learnable after adding calibrated noise. Effective sample size captures why repeated observations, class imbalance, and subgroup rarity can limit learning even in a large table. Task complexity also matters, but class count alone does not determine noise tolerance; representation, label quality, and the training regime affect the result. The data sensitivity distribution raises a separate question about whose errors carry the greatest consequences. Rare subgroups may suffer disproportionate utility loss even when the same formal privacy bound covers every protected contribution. This unequal utility impact must not be confused with unequal privacy parameters or with the mathematical sensitivity used to calibrate noise.
The utility budget must also be explicit. Before deployment, the team must define task-specific acceptance criteria for overall performance, rare subgroups, calibration, and safety-relevant errors. An average accuracy change that appears small can still be unacceptable if DP noise concentrates errors on a protected subgroup or a high-cost clinical class. Published results supply comparison points on the privacy-utility frontier (figure 26), but the release decision requires an experiment on the actual model and data.
Finally, the computational budget decides whether the design can ship. DP-SGD adds clipping, noise generation, and accounting work, while attaining acceptable private utility can change the batch size and training duration. The resulting runtime and memory cost depends on the model and implementation. Deployment planning needs measured time to the required utility under the privacy budget, rather than a universal compute multiplier.


Use DP when a formal participation or contribution bound addresses the stated threat model, a tested accountant covers the relevant data-dependent releases, measured utility satisfies the task’s acceptance criteria, and the training system can afford the mechanism’s compute and memory cost. Use different controls when the primary boundary is unauthorized access to stored data. If a required DP bound cannot coexist with acceptable utility, redesign the mechanism, task, or data strategy, or withhold the release. Federated learning, encryption, access control, and audit logging do not substitute for a required release guarantee merely because they are easier to deploy.

Checkpoint 13.4: Applying the DP decision framework
A wearable cardiac monitor classifies arrhythmias from raw ECG signals collected on-device for 5,000 enrolled patients. The product is sold in the United States and is HIPAA-regulated; the training pipeline runs on a cloud cluster of 8 GPUs, and a competing vendor has incentive to extract the model. Apply each of the five decision criteria to determine whether DP-SGD belongs in the training pipeline.

Criterion 1 (regulatory): decide whether HIPAA supports a DP guarantee here and identify the documentation DP supplies that ad-hoc de-identification cannot.
Criterion 2 (threat model): identify the adversary populations that matter for a cardiac-monitor model and evaluate membership inference as a credible attack.
Criterion 3 (dataset characteristics): evaluate effective sample size, class imbalance, repeated measurements, and rare clinical subgroups before selecting a mechanism.
Criterion 4 (acceptable utility loss): define safety-critical error, calibration, and subgroup acceptance criteria, then measure whether the private model satisfies them.
Criterion 5 (compute): estimate the runtime and memory cost of private training on the stated cloud allocation, measure utility under the selected privacy budget, and identify the binding deployment constraint.



This framework treats DP as one tool in a privacy-preserving toolkit rather than a universal solution. Production deployments often combine an accounted DP mechanism with data minimization, federated execution where raw-data centralization is out of scope, secure aggregation for contribution confidentiality, and access controls for deployment security.
Returning to the data-layer techniques of section 13.8.5, differential privacy sits beside federated learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, and synthetic data generation, and each strikes its own balance among privacy strength, accuracy, and computational cost (table 8). The maturity labels are a deployment snapshot for the regimes discussed here, not a permanent ranking of the underlying techniques. Cryptographic guarantees depend on key custody and the stated adversary model; they do not prevent an authorized output from revealing sensitive information. Differential privacy instead bounds disclosure through the released result under a specified adjacency relation.



Table 8: Privacy-Preserving Technique Comparison: Data privacy techniques impose varying computational costs and offer different levels of formal privacy guarantees, requiring practitioners to balance privacy strength with model utility and deployment constraints. Weighing privacy guarantees, computational overhead, maturity, typical use cases, and trade-offs together guides the design of privacy-aware machine learning systems.

Increasing the noise to reduce \(\PrivacyBudget\) may degrade model accuracy, especially in low-data regimes or fine-grained classification tasks. Consequently, DP is often applied selectively (either during training on sensitive datasets or at inference when returning aggregate statistics) to balance privacy with performance goals (Dwork and Roth 2014).

Dwork, Cynthia, and Aaron Roth. 2014. “The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy.” Foundations and Trends® in Theoretical Computer Science, Foundations and trends in theoretical computer science, vol. 9 (3-4): 211–487. https://doi.org/10.1561/0400000042.
Differential privacy completes the data layer of the defense stack. With the mechanisms of every layer now in view, the remaining engineering questions are which of them a given deployment needs and in what order to adopt them.

Self-Check: Question

A data engineering team computes an aggregate query with global \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1 f = 2.0\) and \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f = 2.0\). title: 13 Security & Privacy
text:
Moving from mathematical guarantees to production controls requires more than setting an epsilon value. A common mistake is attempting to deploy every defense at once, including differential privacy, trusted execution environments, adversarial training, model watermarking, and red-team automation, while basic controls such as access boundaries and artifact signing remain weak. Two decisions prevent that mistake. The first selects the defenses a deployment context requires; the second sequences them so that each control rests on the ones beneath it.


A hospital training a federated diagnostic model on patient records and a public-facing customer chatbot face completely different attackers, latency budgets, and legal mandates. The hardware mechanisms of table 7, the deployment and runtime controls, and the cryptographic and statistical privacy techniques of the data layer therefore form a menu rather than a fixed recipe. The appropriate defense for any given deployment depends on three interacting factors: the threat model (who attacks and with what capabilities), the deployment context (what computational and latency budgets exist), and the regulatory environment (what legal mandates constrain design). A defense selection framework maps seven common deployment contexts to their primary threats, recommended defense combinations, and the trade-offs each combination requires evaluating (table 9). The rows that include differential privacy require an accounted mechanism, built from the sensitivity and composition machinery of section 13.9, rather than a universal privacy-budget value.



Table 9: Defense Selection Framework: Maps deployment contexts to threat-specific defensive strategies and deployment trade-offs. The framework provides starting points for security architecture design, highlighting primary threats, recommended defense combinations, and key implementation trade-offs across seven common ML system deployment scenarios.











Deployment context
Primary threats
Recommended defenses
Key trade-offs




Healthcare ML (federated diagnostic models)
Data leakage (HIPAA violation); membership inference; unauthorized access
Accounted differential privacy for training when the threat model requires it; federated learning across hospitals; TEE for inference on sensitive data; audit logging and RBAC
Privacy and TEE parameters require task-specific utility and latency measurement

Model theft (IP loss); adversarial evasion; data poisoning
Model encryption (AES-256) at rest; HSM for cryptographic key management; adversarial training on perturbed transactions; input validation and per-principal rate limiting; output confidence monitoring
HSM units cost roughly $20,000–$100,000 each before integration and certification; rate limiting may impact legitimate high-frequency users

Physical access; side-channel attacks; model extraction
Secure boot; a suitable TEE; authenticated encrypted model storage; PUF-backed device identity
Protected working set, paging support, power cost, and physical-attack resistance depend on the platform


Cloud ML Training (multi-tenant platform)

Secure data pipelines with provenance; accounted DP-SGD when participation leakage is in scope; gradient verification and anomaly detection; secure aggregation for federated training; model watermarking for IP protection
DP and verification overhead depend on implementation and workload; federated aggregation requires authenticated, confidential communication


Public-Facing LLM (chatbot/API)
Prompt injection; data extraction (training leakage); abuse/overuse
Instruction-data separation; input/output policy checks; isolated execution; authentication and rate budgets
Measure latency and false-positive cost; filtering and confidence scores do not guarantee resistance to injection


Multi-Party ML (cross-organizational training)
Data sharing restrictions; curious or malicious participants; regulatory duties
Federated learning (no raw data sharing); SMPC for secure aggregation; accounted differential privacy when participation leakage is in scope; homomorphic encryption for selected operations
Communication and cryptographic overhead depend on topology and protocol; utility must be measured for the selected privacy mechanism; requires agreements for liability


Critical Infrastructure (autonomous vehicles, power grids)
Supply chain compromise; real-time adversarial attacks; safety-critical failures
Hardware attestation (trusted platform module, or TPM, and PUF); Secure Boot and runtime integrity checks; redundant model validation; fault injection detection; fail-safe fallback mechanisms
Validate physical threat coverage, latency, fail-safe behavior, and the required assurance process







Checkpoint 13.5: Mapping hardware and deployment threats to defenses
The chapter introduced six hardware-level attack categories, four hardware-security primitives (table 7), and a framework mapping seven deployment contexts to full-stack defenses (table 9). Apply that combined mapping to the scenarios below.

Primitive matching: match fault injection on model weights and side-channel extraction from the inference pipeline to the most relevant hardware-security primitives and runtime controls across the critical-infrastructure and edge rows of table 9.
Edge defense stack: select a combination of hardware and deployment controls for an edge inference deployment facing physical access, side-channel attacks, and model extraction.
Supply-chain gap: identify which supply-chain compromises remain outside the four hardware primitives’ guarantees in the selected edge or cloud-training deployment, and specify the provenance or inspection evidence needed to assess those risks.
TEE vs. attestation: distinguish runtime isolation from cryptographic evidence about an execution environment, and identify which fault-injection, counterfeit-hardware, and output-leakage risks remain outside those guarantees.



A recurring theme across table 9 is the cost of privacy. Differential privacy appears in three of seven deployment contexts, and each such row exposes an accuracy or systems cost that must be weighed against regulatory mandates and risk tolerance. The table is therefore a deployment triage tool rather than a universal recipe, because serialization, artifact integrity, access control, runtime isolation, and privacy budgets each defend a different boundary. Selecting the right defenses for a context settles what to build; the maturity model settles the order in which to build it.



Deploying homomorphic encryption or a red-team harness while model checkpoints sit in an unauthenticated bucket and API keys lack per-principal budgets leaves the easiest attack paths wide open. A maturity model asks which system property is currently unprotected: access boundary, data privacy, model integrity, adversarial robustness, or governance evidence. The dependency structure in table 10 keeps that choice tied to the boundary being defended.



Table 10: ML Security and Privacy Maturity Model: Security controls should be added according to the threat model and deployment context. The order is not a calendar; it is a dependency structure from basic access boundaries to stronger privacy, integrity, adversarial, and governance controls.










Maturity layer
Primary question
Control family




Access and configuration boundary
Who can touch data, weights, deployments, and logs?
Least privilege, service identity, encrypted transport, audit logging


Data and privacy boundary
What can be learned from training, fine-tuning, or output?
Privacy accounting, output limiting, secure aggregation, sensitive-data isolation


Model integrity boundary
How is the validated model and data path authenticated?
Signed artifacts, registry controls, hash checks, release gates, rollback paths


Adversarial and abuse boundary
What can an adaptive attacker extract, infer, or induce?
Query monitoring, rate limiting, robustness evaluation, red-team exercises


Governance and evidence boundary
Which obligations must be proven after deployment?
Compliance mapping, incident records, retention policy, reproducible control checks






The maturity layers are cumulative. Access controls and encrypted channels close paths that model-interface defenses do not cover, such as an exposed registry. Privacy analysis begins with the original training data and continues through fine-tuning, personalization, and telemetry feedback loops. When DP is required, the release budget becomes a system resource covering the relevant training, selection, and evaluation mechanisms that access protected data. Model-integrity controls protect the artifact path: signed manifests, key management, hash checks, and release gates connect the loaded model to the approved version, subject to the enforcement boundary remaining intact.
Adversarial evaluation tests deliberate, adaptive behavior in addition to accidental failures. Query monitoring and output limiting constrain extraction attempts, while robustness evaluation and red-team exercises test whether an attacker can induce unsafe behavior. Trusted execution environments and certified robustness defenses protect different boundaries, so each needs a threat model that justifies its costs and assumptions. Governance defines obligations and evidence requirements from the start, rather than entering only after technical controls. Audit logs, compliance mappings, incident records, and reproducible checks then help assess whether those obligations remain satisfied as the model, data, and traffic change.
Different domains traverse the model differently. A healthcare deployment prioritizes privacy accounting and governance evidence before broad patient-facing use. A financial fraud system emphasizes access control, model integrity, and abuse monitoring because extraction and evasion directly change loss exposure. An autonomous system emphasizes adversarial robustness and incident evidence because safety depends on behavior under distribution shift and physical-world perturbations. The point is not to follow a universal implementation calendar; it is to make the threat model determine which control boundary must mature next.
The evidence produced by these controls supports a separate governance decision: which uses are permitted, who accepts residual risk, and who can require remediation. The Governance and Assurance Lifecycle develops those institutional responsibilities. Here the engineering obligation is to make access decisions, release budgets, and incident histories verifiable. By sequencing controls around those boundaries, the maturity model moves security from reactive patching toward proactive threat control, though even well-designed systems can still fail when teams mistake a local mechanism for a complete guarantee.

Self-Check: Question

An ML team wants to deploy automated red-teaming adversarial evaluations and differential privacy accounting on their newly deployed recommender service. However, their model registry permits unauthenticated write access and internal API calls lack TLS encryption. According to the ML Security and Privacy Maturity Model, why is this defensive plan structurally flawed?

The open registry permits artifact substitution and cleartext channels can expose payloads; those paths need controls even when a correctly released DP artifact retains its release-level guarantee.
Differential privacy cannot be mathematically calculated unless the model registry uses hardware security modules.
Adversarial red teaming is strictly illegal under GDPR without prior completion of ISO 27001 certification.
Red-teaming algorithms require unencrypted network channels to simulate black-box query traffic.

Compare how a healthcare diagnostic ML system and an autonomous vehicle perception system should prioritize their progression through the ML Security and Privacy Maturity Model based on their distinct threat models.
To enforce the Model Integrity Boundary in a continuous deployment ML pipeline, which set of controls connects the served checkpoint to the approved artifact, assuming the verification and enforcement boundary remains trusted?

Applying randomized output perturbation at the web proxy layer without checking checkpoint signatures.
Cryptographic signing of model packages, SHA-256 checksum verification against an authenticated registry manifest, and automated release gates with rollback paths.
Adding Laplace differential privacy noise to the model weights prior to saving checkpoints.
Storing model checkpoints in Python pickle format on public, unauthenticated object buckets.

At the foundational Access and Configuration layer of the maturity model, enforcing the principle of ____ ensures that data engineers, ML researchers, and inference services possess only the minimum permissions required for their specific lifecycle tasks.
