The environmental impact of AI systems spans the complete lifecycle: from semiconductor manufacturing and data center construction to model training, inference deployment, and electronic waste (Wynsberghe 2021; Gupta et al. 2022; Luccioni et al. 2023). Treating this full lifecycle as an engineering problem rather than a corporate responsibility exercise transforms sustainability from a vague objective into a measurable engineering requirement. Optimizing this footprint requires first grounding intuition in the raw physical energy of a single large-model training run.
Any such calculation first has to fix what the energy measurement includes. This is the accounting discipline that the energy accounting boundary (equation 1.5) imposes on fleet comparisons, applied here to a single run. Accelerator energy excludes host processors, host memory, networking, and storage. IT energy includes those supporting systems; facility energy additionally includes cooling and facility-side power losses. Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is the ratio of facility energy to IT energy over the same interval (equation 2); section 15.4.1.3 gives its formal definition and what it leaves out. Dividing useful training FLOPs by the run’s fleet energy productivity, its useful FLOPs per joule, gives energy at the boundary over which that productivity was measured. If that boundary is IT equipment, multiplying by PUE gives facility energy; if it already includes the facility, applying PUE again double counts overhead. The opening calculations use one completed training run as their unit of work and account for operational electricity. Manufacturing and other lifecycle terms enter separately.

A training run measured in megawatt-hours is hard to reason about, because few engineers carry an intuition for what a megawatt-hour of grid electricity costs the atmosphere. The same energy on a hydro-heavy grid would emit a small fraction as much, the placement lever that notebook 15.2 quantifies.


The same run’s emissions depend on where its electricity comes from. For a fixed workload, the grid emissions factor and the facility overhead together determine the attributed carbon, and the placement calculations separate those effects, starting with the grid factor alone.

A fleet decision must compare feasible sites and schedules using both workload energy and the emissions associated with supplying it.


The ratio holds only at equal facility electricity and these annual-average factors. A second gain from waiting for cleaner hours, the temporal lever of section 15.9.4, therefore cannot simply be multiplied onto it; the joint schedule must be evaluated as one decision.
The GPT-3 household-year calculation above anchors the workload scale. The fleet-scale consequence is larger. IEA projects global data-center electricity consumption to reach about 945 TWh by 2030, just under 3 percent of global electricity demand, with AI-accelerated servers driving much of the growth (International Energy Agency 2025).2 Historical studies document rapid growth in training compute (Sevilla et al. 2022), but a compute multiplier is not an energy multiplier without a matching efficiency measurement.
2 Data center industrial scale: The IEA projection is an electricity-demand metric, not directly comparable to aviation or cement shares of global emissions. Estimate disposal impacts from the actual equipment inventory, material composition, and end-of-life route. Extending useful service life can defer manufacturing and disposal, while certified handling limits exposure to hazardous materials in discarded electronics.Beyond direct energy consumption, AI systems drive environmental impact through hardware manufacturing and resource consumption. Producing processors and their supporting equipment requires materials and industrial processes whose impacts precede the first training run.3 At the other end of the hardware’s life, retired equipment joins the electronic-waste stream whose scale section 15.8.5 quantifies. Rising workload requirements can motivate accelerator replacement before physical failure; whether replacement creates waste depends on the equipment’s reuse and disposal path.4
These environmental challenges are part of the energy ceiling, not an add-on to it, because the communities that host land, water, grid capacity, and waste streams also carry part of the system cost. These scale calculations turn sustainability into an allocation problem. AI progress creates benefits in one part of the system while assigning electricity, water, land, and disposal costs to another, so environmental responsibility must be treated as part of systems design rather than as postdeployment reporting (section 15.10.4 examines how site selection distributes these burdens across communities). A static snapshot of today’s footprint still understates the engineering challenge, however, because the computational demand driving these electricity, water, and hardware budgets is compounding far faster than hardware efficiency can absorb it.

Between 2012 and 2023, the training compute of frontier models expanded from roughly \(4.7 \times 10^{17}\) FLOPs for AlexNet to \(2 \times 10^{25}\) for GPT-4-class systems, an increase of about 45 million in 11 years that outpaced hardware efficiency gains by orders of magnitude. Larger models, longer training runs, and rising serving volume each add to that total work through a different mechanism. Energy per operation can fall while total fleet energy rises; the outcome depends on how much useful work the fleet performs and how efficiently it performs that work.

Historically, semiconductor scaling combined greater transistor density with lower switching energy. Moore’s Law described the growth in transistor count, while Dennard scaling explained how reducing dimensions and voltage together could preserve power density. Transistor count alone did not guarantee better energy efficiency. Once voltage scaling encountered leakage and other device limits, a denser chip could no longer assume proportional power savings.5 Further efficiency gains require improvements in devices, architecture, and the work performed by the application.
5 Dennard scaling: Robert Dennard observed in 1974 that smaller transistors could operate at constant power density by reducing voltage proportionally. This scaling pattern ended around 2005 when leakage current made further voltage reduction impractical. The discussion of Dennard scaling in Power and thermal envelopes drew the facility consequence, that every refresh must fit installed power and cooling. The consequence for AI sustainability is equally direct: without Dennard scaling, each process node no longer delivers proportional power savings, which pushes efficiency work toward specialized accelerators, such as GPUs and the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU), that exploit architectural parallelism rather than transistor physics alone.At a fixed accounting boundary, energy depends on total work divided by realized work per joule. Improvements in execution efficiency reduce IT energy, and PUE then adds the facility overhead on top of that IT energy. Algorithmic changes can also reduce the work required to meet a quality target. These effects must be measured together rather than inferred from a historical compute curve.
Per-job efficiency and total demand can move in opposite directions. Fleet energy is the energy per completed job multiplied by the number of completed jobs, so a fleet forecast must state both factors, including the workload mix. Cheaper jobs can raise the job count faster than they lower the energy of each one. If energy per task falls tenfold while task volume rises a hundredfold, fleet energy rises tenfold. This rebound is a second way demand can outrun efficiency, distinct from the scaling-driven growth described at the start of the chapter. Scaling-driven growth concerns how much compute each frontier model requires as scaling laws push quality upward; rebound concerns how many tasks run once each task becomes cheaper. The mitigation strategies of section 15.9 treat rebound under its historical name, the Jevons paradox.


A short training burst can trip substation breakers or overwhelm chillers even when its cumulative megawatt-hour budget is modest, whereas a month-long job on a smaller cluster may consume far more total energy while staying safely inside its power envelope. The energy account divides work by realized work per joule and applies facility overhead at the boundary. Physical infrastructure, however, imposes a separate instantaneous power constraint: the grid connection, electrical distribution, and cooling system limit how much active fleet can operate safely at once.
The two limits obey different arithmetic (figure 2). The power limit is instantaneous. A facility cannot draw more than its grid feed (\(\FacilityPower\le \GridFeedCapacity\)), which caps the number of servers active at once (\(\PoweredServerCount\le \InformationTechnologyPower/ \ServerPower\)) regardless of how long a job runs. The energy account is cumulative, integrating average power over wall-clock time to give run energy (\(\TotalEnergy = \AveragePower\times \JobDuration\)). Exceeding electrical or thermal capacity can force power limiting, throttling, or protective shutdown. Cumulative energy instead enters the electricity and emissions accounts, which also depend on tariffs and the applicable grid emissions factors.






Figure 2: Power and Energy Boundaries: Substation grid feeds and facility cooling capacities impose instantaneous power caps on active accelerator concurrency. Integrating instantaneous power over wall-clock duration yields cumulative run energy; instantaneous power constraints and cumulative energy budgets represent distinct physical limits.



The energy wall is therefore a workload-specific feasibility problem, not a universal multiplier. Engineers must fit the required work, deadline, and quality target within available power and cooling, then calculate energy over the actual runtime. More efficient hardware helps only to the extent that the workload uses its efficiency and the resulting demand remains within those constraints. At frontier scale, the binding question is whether enough power can be delivered to the cluster at all.

Lighthouse 15.1: Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3): The energy wallTraining at the scale of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3) exposes the power problem most sharply. At frontier scale, a single 25,000-GPU cluster is roughly 24 times the 1,024-GPU reference cluster used throughout this book. At 700 W per chip, it requires 17.5 MW of accelerator power before server, network, and cooling overhead. The constraint is physical, not financial: it is a grid capacity problem. Organizations operating Archetype A workloads may need dedicated power infrastructure or regions with excess renewable energy. Carbon-aware scheduling (shifting nonurgent work toward cleaner grid hours) and geographic optimization (placing workloads where power, cooling, and carbon constraints fit the job) therefore become fleet decisions as consequential as capacity planning.


That accelerator draw alone, before server, network, and cooling overhead, makes grid capacity a condition of deployment. Even when the grid can supply that sustained average power, the synchronized execution of a training job swings the load up and down across the cluster in unison.



When thousands of accelerators enter a collective communication barrier simultaneously and then resume matrix multiplication together, their power draw steps down and up in lockstep across the data hall. Unlike conventional cloud workloads whose independent requests smooth out across racks, synchronized training phases correlate power swings and push those transients toward the electrical grid interface.

War Story 15.1: When the grid became the bottleneck (2022)Context: In July 2022, the Government of Ireland published its Government Statement on the Role of Data Centres in Ireland’s Enterprise Strategy, addressing electricity constraints on further development in a country where data centers had become a substantial source of demand (Government of Ireland 2022; International Energy Agency 2024).
Mechanism: Demand growth outpaced grid expansion. The statement reported that Dublin needed significant transmission reinforcement before it could accommodate new data-center power requests.
Impact: Grid connection capacity became the gating input for proposed Dublin facilities. New requests had to wait for transmission reinforcement or look to other regions, while contracted projects and existing sites continued to operate.
Fix: The statement prioritized network reinforcement, suitable regional locations, and development aligned with additional renewable supply. These were proposed responses to the constraint, not evidence that operators had already resolved it.
Systems lesson: Sustainable AI is constrained by interconnection, geography, and power-system adequacy. Efficient accelerators help, but the fleet cannot scale faster than the grid that feeds it, moving the binding constraint from the chip to the substation.

Training phases can change accelerator demand rapidly, but a device-side load step does not propagate unchanged to the utility connection. Its amplitude depends on per-device power, the number of coordinated workers, and computation-communication overlap. Local regulators, decoupling, power converters, and UPS controls shape the upstream response. Energy buffering supplies or absorbs energy during a load change; its location, capacity, and control response must match the electrical boundary being protected.



The grid and siting constraints become severe because large training campaigns concentrate energy demand into long, synchronized runs. The GPT-3 anchor established the total scale; the new systems concern is its temporal concentration and the additional energy from distributed-training communication.6
6 Training communication overhead: Distributed training adds network transfers, synchronization stalls, and checkpoint I/O to the energy account. The fraction is workload- and topology-dependent: parallelism strategy, tensor sizes, link technology, utilization loss, and any extra iterations determine whether communication is a secondary term or the binding energy cost. The measurement contract must therefore meter or model these terms for the actual run rather than apply a universal percentage.Concentration in time is what separates a training campaign from the same energy spread across a year of ordinary load. A frontier run holds the 17.5 MW accelerator draw of the Archetype A cluster, before servers, network, and cooling, for the weeks or months the run lasts. Its synchronized computation and communication phases swing that draw together across the cluster (section 15.3.2). The facility must therefore provision for the sustained peak rather than for the annual average, and the grid sees one large, correlated load rather than many small independent ones. That concentration makes efficiency improvements an engineering imperative. Large generative models intensify the problem when successive generations increase parameter counts, token budgets, or both.
The scaling laws introduced in AI Scaling Laws explain why that concentration keeps growing. Within the ranges studied by Kaplan et al. (2020), test loss falls along smooth power laws in compute, dataset tokens, and parameters (figure 3), and for an energy account the small compute exponent is the quantity of interest. It means each fixed fractional reduction in loss costs a multiplicative increase in the resource. Because required compute scales as the loss ratio raised to the power 20, lowering compute-limited loss by 10 percent takes 8.2× the compute, and the next 10 percent costs the same multiple again. The diminishing return in principle \(\ref{pri-universal-scaling}\) therefore arrives at the facility as a multiplicative increase in training energy unless realized FLOPs per joule improve at the same pace. Within these studied regimes, quality gains were purchasable with hardware and data, which is why compute demand has outrun hardware efficiency. Beyond training, high-volume deployed systems such as large-scale recommender systems and generative services require continuous inference at scale, consuming energy even after training completes. The cumulative energy burden therefore depends on both the one-time training run and the sustained query volume that follows deployment.

Building out the clusters required by this concentration adds emissions before an operator runs a single training step, so expanding the fleet increases manufacturing impact even when each new accelerator uses less energy per useful task. An operator’s inventory records that fabrication under Scope 3, the category for supply-chain emissions rather than on-site generation or purchased electricity (section 15.5.5 quantifies the manufacturing term, and section 15.5.2 assigns it to reporting scopes). Bounding any of these operational or embodied costs requires decomposing facility power into component-level models and direct telemetry under a consistent measurement contract.

A cluster drawing five megawatts during a large language model training run directs only a fraction of that power into matrix multiplications; host processors, memory, networking, power conversion, and cooling consume the rest. Engineers cannot optimize those losses from a single monthly utility bill: effective energy modeling requires decomposing facility power into granular, component-level metrics that engineers can target for optimization.
Power delivery networks and cooling systems establish hard physical constraints on data center compute capacity. Systematic measurement turns these constraints into numbers an engineer can act on, provided the measurement fixes what it records and which lifecycle phase it targets before any power model or instrument is applied. Just as performance engineering requires profiling before optimization, sustainable AI engineering requires measurement before mitigation.

The decision procedure is the same throughout the chapter: measure the dominant lifecycle term, identify the physical bottleneck behind it, choose the intervention that changes that term, and check whether rebound effects erase the gain. Operational electricity, embodied carbon, cooling overhead, water use, and e-waste each call for different levers. Moving a job changes its operational setting without undoing emissions already incurred in manufacturing. Keeping hardware longer changes future procurement needs but also extends its operating energy account. Sustainable design therefore traces each intervention through the terms it changes before comparing the full result.
A sustainability claim is comparable only when it satisfies a sustainability measurement contract, which extends the reproducible measurement contract of The measurement contract. That contract already fixes the workload and its quality gate, the system state, the timing boundary, and a statistical report with its window and spread. A sustainability claim adds five fields that progressively close the remaining accounting degrees of freedom. The functional unit names the work being charged, such as one completed training run or 1,000 served requests at a specified output quality. The system boundary states which compute, memory, network, facility, manufacturing, and end-of-life terms enter that account (International Organization for Standardization 2006a, 2006b). Because multiple workloads and hardware generations share a facility, an attribution rule must then allocate shared infrastructure and embodied emissions. A declared average or marginal carbon signal, recorded with its time and location, converts the resulting energy into emissions. Finally, the statistical report extends to the sensitivity of the conclusion to those consequential assumptions. A result that omits any of these fields may still diagnose one component, but it cannot support an end-to-end comparison.

Present, Elaina, Pieter Gagnon, Eric J. H. Wilson, Noel Merket, Philip R. White, and Scott Horowitz. 2024. Choosing the Best Carbon Factor for the Job: Exploring Available Carbon Emissions Factors and the Impact of Factor Selection. NREL/CP-5500-86682. National Renewable Energy Laboratory.
This contract separates two questions that otherwise become conflated. Attributional accounting allocates an inventory of observed emissions to workloads for reporting, typically using average grid intensity and an explicit share of common infrastructure. Consequential accounting estimates how a decision changes emissions, for example by modeling the generator affected when a scheduler moves one megawatt-hour of demand. The former answers what share of an existing footprint belongs to a workload; the latter answers whether changing the workload changes the footprint (Present et al. 2024). Carbon-aware scheduling therefore needs a signal appropriate for consequential analysis even when the organization’s retrospective inventory uses attributional averages. The available marginal factors may be historical estimates, forecasts, or unavailable at the workload’s required time and location. The contract must therefore record the source, resolution, and uncertainty rather than treat “marginal” as a universally observable datum.


Lowering numerical precision or pruning half the weights of a model does not automatically cut the data center’s electricity bill in half, because static leakage, memory traffic, and facility cooling each take their own share before power reaches the arithmetic units. Tracing where a watt goes requires a model that climbs three levels. The CMOS power equation at the chip level explains why voltage, precision, and switching activity matter. Physical optimization mechanisms show how algorithms change those variables. Facility-level metrics reveal whether chip-level savings survive cooling and power-delivery overhead.


Every digital circuit consumes power through two fundamental mechanisms. Dynamic power arises from switching transistors between states, while static power results from leakage current that flows even when transistors are nominally off. Equation 1 formalizes the total power consumption:
\[\TotalChipPower= \DynamicPower+ \LeakagePower = \SwitchingActivityFactor \SwitchedCapacitance \SupplyVoltage^2 \ClockFrequency+ \SupplyVoltage \LeakageCurrent \tag{1}\]
In the dynamic component \(\DynamicPower= \SwitchingActivityFactor \SwitchedCapacitance \SupplyVoltage^2 \ClockFrequency\), the switching activity factor \(\SwitchingActivityFactor\) summarizes capacitance-weighted switching per clock cycle and is not useful compute utilization. The term \(\SwitchedCapacitance\) is the effective load capacitance of the circuits and interconnect being switched. Supply voltage \(\SupplyVoltage\) enters quadratically, and clock frequency \(\ClockFrequency\) sets the rate of switching opportunities. Useful work per joule depends on how much productive computation those transitions accomplish.
The static power component \(\LeakagePower = \SupplyVoltage\cdot \LeakageCurrent\) depends on leakage current, whose temperature sensitivity varies with device technology, voltage, and operating point. Rising temperature can increase leakage, adding heat that further raises temperature. Cooling and power control must keep this feedback within a stable operating range. A leakage model therefore needs parameters appropriate to the device rather than a universal temperature-doubling rule (Dayarathna et al. 2016).

Dayarathna, Miyuru, Yonggang Wen, and Rui Fan. 2016. “Data Center Energy Consumption Modeling: A Survey.” IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials 18 (1): 732–94. https://doi.org/10.1109/comst.2015.2481183.
The quadratic voltage dependence means that reducing voltage from 1 V to 0.8 V decreases dynamic power by 36 percent when activity, capacitance, and frequency stay fixed. The circuit must still complete its transitions within each clock period. A lower voltage may therefore require a lower frequency, which further reduces dynamic power but can lengthen execution. The energy benefit depends on both the resulting runtime and the static power consumed during it.



The power equation illuminates why specific optimization techniques can improve efficiency. Quantization reduces numerical precision, which can shrink arithmetic units and reduce bytes moved through the memory hierarchy. The realized energy change depends on the implemented kernels, packing and conversion overhead, memory traffic, utilization, and the original bottleneck (Gholami et al. 2022). Lower precision does not by itself permit a lower supply voltage: voltage and frequency remain constrained by the physical implementation, process, and timing margins. Quantization therefore changes the operation and data-movement terms, but only measurement establishes the end-to-end reduction.

Pruning removes weights from neural networks, but it does not remove physical transistors from an existing accelerator. It saves dynamic energy when the resulting execution skips arithmetic or data movement. Structured pruning can map to smaller dense kernels; unstructured pruning needs an implementation that exploits the sparse pattern without spending the savings on indexing and irregular memory access. The power equation explains the benefit through reduced switching activity and powered execution time, not a change to the fabricated circuit capacitance \(\SwitchedCapacitance\).
Specialized accelerators can improve useful work per joule by reducing instruction-control overhead, reusing data locally, and mapping operations to suitable datapaths. Keeping arithmetic units productive can amortize static and support power, but raising switching activity without raising useful output only raises power.



The PUE ratio has carried every facility-energy estimate since the opening energy boundary. The chip-level model now explains what happens inside the IT term, so the ratio itself needs its precise definition and its blind spots. Equation 2 gives the ratio at this chapter’s facility boundary:
\[\text{PUE} = \frac{\FacilityPower}{\InformationTechnologyPower} \tag{2}\]

Definition 15.2: Power usage effectiveness (PUE)
Power usage effectiveness (PUE) is the data-center efficiency ratio ML system operators use to compare total facility power consumption against the power consumed specifically by IT equipment \((\FacilityPower/ \InformationTechnologyPower)\).

Significance: It measures the infrastructure overhead of the data center. A PUE of 1.0 is the theoretical ideal; a PUE of 1.10 means that for every 100 watts consumed by IT equipment, an additional 10 watts are required for non-IT facility overhead, including cooling and facility-side power distribution.
Distinction: Unlike computing efficiency (which focuses on FLOP/s per watt), PUE focuses on facility efficiency: it measures non-IT overhead relative to IT consumption. Idle equipment and power losses inside the IT measurement boundary remain in the denominator; PUE does not measure useful computation.
Common pitfall: A frequent misconception is that a low PUE means a “green” data center. PUE measures only overhead efficiency, not the carbon intensity of the energy source; a coal-powered data center can have a better PUE than a solar-powered one while having a much higher environmental impact.






PUE measures facility overhead on top of IT energy.

Napkin Math 15.3: PUE: The cost of cooling
Problem: A team operates a 2 MW cluster. If the facility can be optimized from a legacy air-cooled PUE (1.58) to state-of-the-art (1.10), how much energy and money does that save annually?
Math: Energy saved is the difference in infrastructure overhead \((\text{PUE}-1)\) across the IT load.

Overhead Reduction: 1.58 - 1.10 = 0.48.
Annual energy savings: 2 MW \(\times\) 0.48 \(\times\) 8760 h/year \(\approx\) 8,409.6 MWh.
Financial Savings: 8,409.6 MWh \(\times\) $70/MWh \(\approx\) $588,672. This facility-only saving leaves the model unchanged and scales with reducible non-IT overhead, so cooling optimization matters most in inefficient facilities.



A PUE of 1.0 would mean no measured non-IT overhead, not that all electricity produces useful computation. Idle servers and stalled accelerators remain inside the IT denominator. Surveyed data centers reported an average PUE near 1.55 in 2022, meaning that roughly 55 percent additional energy beyond IT consumption went to infrastructure, with older air-cooled sites higher still (Uptime Institute 2022). Leading hyperscale facilities achieve PUE between 1.1 and 1.2 through advanced cooling techniques including free-air cooling in cold climates, liquid cooling for high-density GPU clusters, and optimized power distribution.

Uptime Institute. 2022. Uptime Institute Global Data Center Survey 2022. Uptime Institute.
Equation 3 formalizes water usage effectiveness (WUE), capturing the water consumption that evaporative cooling and other processes require:
\[\text{WUE} = \frac{\FacilityWaterConsumption}{\InformationTechnologyEnergy} \tag{3}\]
The units are liters per kilowatt-hour, with typical values ranging from 0.5 to 2.0 L/kWh depending on climate and cooling technology. A data center with WUE of 1.8 L/kWh training a model requiring 10,000 MWh of IT energy would consume 18 million liters of water. That is equivalent to roughly 40–47 US household-years of water use under a 380,000–450,000 L/year household baseline. A facility-energy estimate must first be converted to the IT boundary before applying this WUE.
Serving has a water account too, and it is computed the same way. Google reports a fleet WUE of 1.15 L/kWh for the data centers that serve its Gemini assistant (Elsworth et al. 2025). Applied to the IT energy of the median prompt measured in section 15.7.3, which excludes facility overhead, that WUE gives the 0.26 mL of water per prompt that the study reports. A single prompt’s water is negligible. A service answering billions of prompts a day turns the same arithmetic into a facility-scale demand, which is why the cooling choice, and the watershed it draws on, belongs in the serving design rather than only in the training budget. Facility-level metrics therefore identify where engineering intervention yields the greatest returns, including in how a facility operates the cooling plant it already has.

Server load, weather, and interactions among pumps and chillers complicate fixed operating heuristics (Buyya et al. 2010). Building on earlier work predicting PUE (Gao 2014), DeepMind trained neural networks from facility telemetry to predict future PUE and recommend settings. Additional models predicted temperature and pressure to check those recommendations against operating constraints.

In the reported live-site test, the system reduced cooling energy consumption by 40 percent and overall PUE overhead by 15 percent (Barroso et al. 2019; Evans and Gao 2016). By equation 2, a 15 percent cut in overhead removes 15 percent of the non-IT term (PUE minus 1), not 15 percent of total facility energy. At equal IT energy, the same fractional overhead reduction saves more electricity where the initial overhead is larger. The reported result establishes a benefit for the tested facility, not an identical saving at every site.
The saving came from changing how the existing pumps, chillers, and cooling towers were operated rather than from installing new cooling equipment, which makes control software a lever available to a facility that cannot be rebuilt. The transferable lesson is to evaluate operating controls alongside equipment changes. Telemetry supports the prediction, operating limits constrain the recommendation, and metered energy establishes whether the change saves electricity.




Cutting a model’s FLOP count in half saves almost no energy when the workload spends nearly all of its joules shuttling weights between off-chip DRAM and the processor. Comparing hardware architectures and algorithmic changes therefore requires a systematic metric ladder that moves from energy per operation to energy per byte and then to the roofline relationship between arithmetic intensity and data movement.


A basic metric for computational energy efficiency is energy consumed per operation, typically measured in picojoules. State the operation type and precision: a floating-point multiply-accumulate (MAC) is conventionally two FLOPs, whereas an integer MAC is two integer arithmetic operations.
Hardware architecture changes which overheads can be reduced. Each architecture class carries an effective energy coefficient in this chapter’s models, paired with the measurement needed to test it (table 1). The coefficients span three orders of magnitude, from 100 pJ/FLOP for a general-purpose core, where instruction fetch and control dominate each operation, to 0.1 pJ/FLOP for a fixed-function datapath. They fold local operand delivery and control into each operation, which is why the GPU coefficient of 10 pJ/FLOP sits well above the roughly 3.7 pJ of a bare FP32 multiply at 45 nm (Horowitz 2014). They are order-of-magnitude modeling inputs, not a ranking of products.

Narrower formats can reduce circuit area, switched capacitance, and memory traffic, but bit width alone does not determine wall energy. The resulting design levers target data movement as well as arithmetic. On-chip SRAM and registers support operand reuse, while systolic arrays pass operands and partial sums between neighboring processing elements instead of repeatedly returning to off-chip memory. Compression and sparse representations can reduce transferred data when saved payload exceeds metadata and conversion overhead. The energy benefit therefore depends on the implemented memory traffic, rather than solely on nominal model size or arithmetic throughput.

Arithmetic intensity, the operations-per-byte ratio recalled in Arithmetic Intensity Boundary, connects the operation count to the data-movement volume. Combined with energy per operation and per byte, it identifies which contribution dominates this energy model; it does not by itself identify the resource limiting execution speed. Equation 4 defines the workload ratio. In these equations, \(\Operations\) is the operation count in FLOPs, \(\DataVolume\) is data volume in bytes, \(\EnergyPerOperation\) is energy per FLOP, and \(\EnergyPerByteMoved\) is energy per byte moved:
\[\ArithmeticIntensity= \frac{\Operations}{\DataVolume} \tag{4}\]
At fixed energy coefficients, arithmetic intensity measured in FLOP/byte determines the relative size of the compute and movement terms. Equation 5 expresses modeled energy \(\TotalEnergy\) at the chip-and-memory boundary as their sum (the facility total \(\FacilityEnergy\) appears later in equation 9), while equation 6 isolates the roofline-style dominant term. Static power and supporting systems require additional terms if the comparison includes them:
\[\TotalEnergy = \Operations\times \EnergyPerOperation + \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved \tag{5}\]
\[\DominantComponentEnergy= \max\left(\Operations\times \EnergyPerOperation, \DataVolume \times \EnergyPerByteMoved\right) \tag{6}\]
The maximum identifies the larger energy contribution, not the sum. Near balance, omitting the other term substantially understates the modeled energy. Equation 7 defines the crossover arithmetic intensity where compute and memory energy balance:
\[\EnergyCrossoverIntensity= \frac{\EnergyPerByteMoved}{\EnergyPerOperation} \tag{7}\]
For a GPU with \(\EnergyPerOperation\) of 10 pJ/FLOP and \(\EnergyPerByteMoved\) of 160 pJ/byte (DRAM access):
\[\EnergyCrossoverIntensity = \frac{160 \text{ pJ/byte}}{10 \text{ pJ/FLOP}} = 16 \text{ FLOP/byte}\]
The energy roofline model in figure 4 bounds energy efficiency (GFLOP/J) against arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte), with a 16 FLOP/byte crossover under the stated component costs. Below this point, the larger energy contribution is memory movement (160 pJ/byte). Above it, arithmetic sets the horizontal upper bound of 100 GFLOP/J (10 pJ/FLOP). The piecewise bound keeps only the larger contribution, whereas actual energy includes both and any omitted system overhead. Its crossover therefore answers a different question from the performance ridge, which equals peak arithmetic throughput divided by memory bandwidth and often sits well above 16 FLOP/byte on modern accelerators. A kernel whose arithmetic intensity falls between the energy crossover and the performance ridge is still paced in execution time by memory bandwidth even though arithmetic already accounts for more of its modeled dynamic energy. Applying this crossover to matrix multiplication shows how problem dimension alone flips the dominant energy term.

Systems insight: Energy optimization follows the same bottleneck logic as latency optimization. Dense matrix multiply rewards efficient arithmetic; element-wise work rewards reducing memory movement.


The energy roofline model reveals why different optimization strategies suit different workloads. When arithmetic dominates the energy account, large dense matrix operations benefit from lower energy per executed operation. When data movement dominates, element-wise kernels benefit from data layout optimization, kernel fusion to reduce memory round-trips, and on-chip memory utilization. Faster execution alone does not establish either saving; average power and execution time must be measured together. This framework guides architectural and algorithmic choices for sustainable AI system design.




Reading nvidia-smi during a training step misses host DRAM, NVMe storage, network switches, and chiller pumps, whereas reading the substation utility meter lumps every co-located job into a single total. Quantifying AI system energy consumption therefore requires choosing measurement instruments across multiple levels of the hardware stack. On-chip counters provide fine attribution, mobile profilers expose platform-specific subsystems, external edge instruments capture duty-cycle behavior, and system-level tools connect component measurements to the facility overhead that device counters miss.


Modern processors expose manufacturer-provided power telemetry that software can query through device interfaces. These counters provide workload-correlated estimates within the rails and sampling windows the device reports; they are not universal ground truth for wall-plug energy, and their update rate, calibration, and component coverage vary by platform. External instruments remain necessary when a comparison requires traceable total energy or finer temporal resolution.
Intel’s running average power limit (RAPL) interface exposes cumulative energy counters for supported power domains, with coverage depending on the processor. A controlled measurement samples the relevant counter before and after the workload and divides the energy delta by elapsed time to recover average power. This makes RAPL useful for host-side work, provided the account identifies the domains actually reported and handles counter rollover. Package and subdomain counters must not be added when their coverage overlaps. RAPL does not measure discrete GPU energy, and access can require elevated permissions.
NVIDIA GPUs expose power information through the NVIDIA Management Library, accessible via the nvidia-smi command-line tool or programmatic bindings. GPU power monitoring must distinguish an instantaneous reading from a sensor-averaged value; the reported behavior depends on the device and query. Integrating samples requires a cadence and workload interval appropriate to that averaging window. Sampling an averaged signal more frequently does not recover short power spikes. Supported accumulated-energy counters can simplify interval accounting, but their scope and resolution still need checking, and neither method supplies full facility energy by itself.
Edge devices and microcontrollers often lack built-in power counters and require external instrumentation. Select current range, voltage measurement, sampling rate, and analog bandwidth to capture the workload’s active and sleep intervals. Board-level monitors can integrate inference energy; resolving shorter events requires adequate instrument bandwidth and careful treatment of filtering and aliasing. A fast sample rate alone cannot attribute energy to individual operations.



On mobile platforms, measurement depends on how much subsystem attribution the host operating system exposes. Some platforms report per-rail or per-component power for the CPU, GPU, neural processing unit, and radio, which lets a developer see which subsystem dominates total draw. Others expose only relative energy-impact scores or thermal states, which are useful for spotting regressions during development but cannot support an absolute energy claim. Vendor profilers that correlate power traces with kernel execution sit between these extremes. The design question is whether the reported quantity covers the electrical boundary the comparison needs, not which tool to use. A relative score cannot be converted into joules per inference. When it cannot, external instrumentation is required. Edge power measurement instruments differ by measurement role, and each role requires its own checks (table 4).

Edge energy measurements are useful only when they reflect the deployed duty cycle rather than an idealized active-only inference burst, so reproducible evaluation requires experimental controls matched to that workload. Simultaneous current and voltage logging must span both the active and quiescent states being measured. It captures rail voltage fluctuations rather than inferring power from current alone. Thermal and frequency stabilization is necessary for sustained-load comparisons, whereas cold starts and periodic bursts must be measured across their actual state transitions. Because edge devices spend most of their deployment life waiting between events, realistic duty-cycle accounting records both peak inference draw and time-averaged power across typical idle intervals. Component attribution may isolate or subtract peripheral loads to expose accelerator consumption. A deployment estimate, however, must restore the radios, sensors, and other subsystems needed to deliver the service. For duty cycle accounting, equation 8 expresses this relationship between active and idle power:
\[\AveragePower= \ActiveInferencePower\times \InferenceDutyCycle + \StandbyPower\times (1 - \InferenceDutyCycle) \tag{8}\]
where \(\InferenceDutyCycle\) is the duty cycle (fraction of time performing inference).



Comprehensive energy accounting requires combining chip-level measurements with infrastructure overhead. The component terms must be disjoint: GPU-board telemetry that already includes device memory must not be added to another measurement of that same memory. They must also cover the IT boundary, with storage and server support loads included in the relevant measured terms. Equation 9 formalizes total energy as the sum of those component contributions scaled by facility overhead:
\[\FacilityEnergy= (\CpuEnergy+ \GpuEnergy+ \MemorySubsystemEnergy+ \NetworkEnergy) \times \text{PUE} \tag{9}\]
No single counter spans the full energy path, so system-level profilers like Intel VTune, NVIDIA Nsight Systems, and open-source tools such as PowerJoular aggregate measurements across components. On-chip counters estimate device power and may differ in sampling rate, coverage, and calibration; a rack power distribution unit (PDU) provides an independent measurement of the downstream IT load. A rack PDU does not measure central chillers, pumps, lighting, or upstream conversion losses, so facility energy must instead come from facility meters or from an explicitly time-matched PUE applied to the measured IT load. The same rule holds for power: facility power is the measured IT power, the sum of server, network, and storage equipment power, multiplied by the PUE of equation 2, so the overhead enters once at the facility boundary.
Development-time carbon tracking matters when it feeds placement and complexity decisions rather than becoming a report after the fact. Tools such as CarbonTracker (Anthony et al. 2020) and CodeCarbon (Schmidt et al. 2021) wrap the workload boundary, estimate energy from hardware counters or utilization models, attach the local grid intensity, and record the resulting emissions alongside the experiment metadata. The important systems pattern is not the API call but the timing of the measurement: the estimate must appear while model size, training duration, region, and schedule are still adjustable, before the run has already consumed its energy. Even then, facility energy is still not a complete footprint, because converting it to emissions requires a grid factor and the hardware that drew it carries manufacturing emissions that no power meter records.

Consider a data center supplied by a hydro-heavy grid. Its operational carbon intensity can be far below a fossil-heavy grid, but hydroelectric generation is not lifecycle-zero, and the AI system is not carbon-free. Reservoir construction and operation have impacts, while mining the silicon, manufacturing the GPUs, and pouring the concrete for the data center emitted carbon before the servers were turned on. A complete footprint calculation must account for operational electricity, embodied carbon, and the ecological effects excluded from a carbon-only metric.
Building that footprint term by term starts with which lifecycle phase dominates the workload and then with whose inventory each emission belongs to, because the same physical emission can appear in more than one organization’s report. The grid factor, operational carbon, embodied carbon, and their lifecycle sum then each take an equation that generalizes across workloads, grids, and amortization assumptions.


Published estimates of the energy of a single chat prompt vary by about an order of magnitude because different studies count different components of the serving stack (Elsworth et al. 2025), and best-effort estimates stripped of their assumptions quickly circulate as facts (Luccioni et al. 2025). Without a workload-level accounting model that fixes those boundaries, teams cannot audit whether choosing a smaller model, lower-power hardware, a cleaner region, or deferred training actually reduces environmental impact.

Carbon footprint analysis turns sustainability from a general obligation into an auditable design constraint by linking energy consumption, grid carbon intensity, and lifecycle resource demands to the same decisions that govern performance and efficiency (Schwartz et al. 2020; Patterson et al. 2021). Traceability is the technical bridge between measurement and accountability, and it is the engineering response to a transparency gap: the absence of per-model energy, carbon, and water records that would let anyone outside the team check a claim. A team should be able to connect a model version, training run, serving workload, region, energy source, and lifecycle estimate well enough that carbon and water claims can be verified.
For measurement to constrain design, reported metrics must expose workload-level cost rather than aggregate cloud-scale claims, which stay opaque when reporting holds at the company-total level. The production measurement in section 15.7.3 shows how far the boundary alone moves a reported figure. The practical standard is therefore accountability for resource usage across the full AI lifecycle. It requires the same evidence chain used for latency, accuracy, and reliability: a claim should connect to logs, meters, model versions, and deployment decisions rather than to aggregate sustainability pledges alone. The footprint calculation makes that evidence chain explicit by combining workload energy, facility PUE, grid carbon intensity, and embodied carbon, and it starts from the lifecycle phase that dominates.


The practical question is which lifecycle phase dominates a given workload, because the answer determines the optimization lever. Effective carbon footprint measurement therefore separates three phases that collectively determine environmental impact: training, inference, and the manufacturing of the hardware both run on. Two other groupings appear later in the chapter, the reporting scopes of section 15.5.2 and the lifecycle stages of section 15.8. Both regroup these same emissions, by reporting organization and by time, rather than adding new ones. Table 5 maps the three groupings onto one another.
For training-centric research workloads, the training phase often dominates operational emissions because mathematical optimization requires sustained parallel computation.7 Geographic placement then changes the operational result, because an identical workload can encounter very different grid intensities.8 For high-volume production services, by contrast, the inference phase can dominate lifetime emissions because serving repeats continuously after training ends, so its cumulative impact scales with deployment breadth and usage frequency.
7 Optimizer memory as energy cost: Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) stores per-parameter first and second moment estimates, unlike plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD). For a 70B model in FP32, these two moment buffers total about 560 GB, bringing parameters plus moments to about 840 GB (excluding gradients). The sustainability implication is direct: larger optimizer state means more off-chip memory traffic per training step, and at roughly 160 pJ/byte for a DRAM access, memory movement can dominate the energy budget of parameter updates.8 Carbon intensity variance: Regional averages and time-varying grid factors answer different questions. A generation technology’s lifecycle factor is neither a measured regional average nor the marginal emissions response to another job. Scheduling must choose the signal appropriate to its decision and retain the source, period, and boundary.9 Embodied carbon break-even: Embodied carbon covers manufacturing, transport, and end-of-life treatment rather than use. Allocating NVIDIA’s HGX H100 baseboard product carbon footprint evenly across its eight GPUs gives roughly 164 kg CO2e per H100 (NVIDIA Corporation 2025); assuming continuous accelerator power of 700 W on the average U.S. grid, the modeled operational emissions match that allocation in roughly three to four weeks. This comparison omits host and facility overhead and uses rated power rather than a measured workload trace. A cleaner grid lengthens the modeled interval, but this equality alone does not decide whether replacing hardware reduces future emissions.
NVIDIA Corporation. 2025. Product Carbon Footprint Summary for NVIDIA HGX H100. NVIDIA Datasheet.
The manufacturing phase contributes embodied carbon from hardware production, including material extraction, semiconductor fabrication, and supply chain logistics.9 For a fixed manufacturing footprint, longer operation on a carbon-intensive grid increases operational emissions and lowers the embodied share of the total. Cleaner electricity or less operating time raises that relative share without changing the manufacturing emissions already incurred. Operational efficiency does not undo those emissions; procurement, design, reuse, and service-life decisions determine future embodied costs.




When an AI organization rents a cloud GPU cluster, the electricity that powers the run appears on the cloud provider’s utility bill, the chip fabrication emissions appear in the foundry’s inventory, and neither registers as direct fuel or electricity on the renter’s own meters. Whereas the training, inference, and manufacturing account groups emissions by the physical activity that produces them, the three emission scopes defined by the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol (World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable Development 2023) classify that same footprint relative to a reporting organization. These are different views of the same emissions, not additional totals to add together. Connecting the workload account to an organizational inventory requires naming who owns the equipment, purchases the electricity, and buys the service.
Within an owned data-center facility boundary, Scope 1 emissions include direct combustion in owned generators and refrigerant leakage from cooling equipment, whereas purchased electricity used to run cooling or IT equipment belongs in Scope 2, not Scope 1. Scope 2 emissions represent indirect emissions from purchased electricity, steam, heat, and cooling consumed by the reporting organization. Purchased electricity is often the dominant category for an operator’s owned facility, and it varies dramatically by geographic location and grid energy mix. Electricity used by a cloud provider is Scope 2 for that provider, but a customer’s purchased cloud service is generally accounted for in the customer’s Scope 3 value chain. The physical electrons do not change; the reporting boundary does. The geography notebook in section 15.2 uses a declared pair of illustrative factors; actual accounting requires factors matched to the location, time, and method.
Scope 3 emissions constitute the most complex category, encompassing hardware manufacturing, cloud supply chains, transportation, disposal, and downstream use. Semiconductor manufacturing is carbon-intensive.10 The manufacturer reports the same fabrication emissions inside its own organizational boundary, so the two inventories describe one physical emission from two sides. How long operation takes to match that embodied term depends on how hard and on which grid the hardware runs. The H100 break-even worked with the lifecycle phases (section 15.5.1.1) stretches from a few weeks at rated power on the US-average grid to months or years at low utilization or on a clean grid. Under company-wide or value-chain AI accounting, Scope 3 can dominate even when Scope 2 dominates a single owned facility’s operational footprint.
10 Lithography and embodied energy: Advanced semiconductor fabrication can use energy-intensive lithography, including extreme ultraviolet (EUV) processes. Emissions per usable chip depend on the process sequence, facility energy mix, yield, die area, and allocation method. Neither transistor count nor a nominal process-node label alone determines the number of exposure steps or manufacturing footprint.11 Edge AI energy trade-off: Edge inference can reduce network transfers and response latency, while distributing computation across devices with different duty cycles and power states. It does not eliminate network or cloud work, and distributed consumption, although harder to attribute, remains part of the accounting boundary; section 15.7.4 works through the comparison.Downstream use can also enter Scope 3, including end-user smartphones, IoT devices, and edge computing.11 Companywide totals do not by themselves identify the footprint of a particular AI service; that attribution still requires workload-level accounting.
The operational emissions of a final training run and its deployed service omit the development that produced them, including failed experiments, hyperparameter searches, and the build and test infrastructure. Repeated experiments can exceed the cost of the final run. A search that trains \(\SweepCandidateCount\) candidates at a fraction \(\SweepCandidateCostFraction\) of the final run’s cost adds \(\SweepCandidateCount \SweepCandidateCostFraction\) final-run equivalents before the chosen model starts, so a sweep of 50 candidates at 10 percent of full scale costs 5× the run that gets reported. Continuous integration, compilation, and evaluation add further work whose contribution depends on run frequency and scale. The development boundary must record these activities before assigning their emissions to the reporting organization’s inventory; the phase of model development does not itself determine the emissions scope.
The GHG Protocol arranges these scopes as concentric reporting boundaries that widen outward from the operator’s direct control (figure 5). On-site diesel generators sit in Scope 1, purchased grid electricity for compute and cooling in Scope 2, and upstream semiconductor fabrication and end-of-life recycling in Scope 3.

Each type of factor must be identified before it enters the calculation (table 6).

For its 2024 data centers, Google reports a location-based grid factor of 345 g CO2e/kWh and a market-based factor of 94 g CO2e/kWh after crediting its purchases of carbon-free electricity, a 3.7× difference for the same electricity (Elsworth et al. 2025). The same median prompt therefore carries about 0.08 g CO2e or 0.023 g CO2e of electricity emissions depending on the factor, and only the second matches the figure the company publishes. Neither is wrong, but a comparison is meaningful only when both sides declare the same factor type, period, and boundary.
Applied to a fixed 10,000 MWh facility-energy account, regional electricity factors change operational carbon by nearly two orders of magnitude (figure 6). The assumed factors range from 10 g/kWh for Norway (100 t \(\text{CO}_2\) for the workload) to 820 g/kWh for Poland (8,200 t \(\text{CO}_2\)), producing a calculated 82× emissions ratio. These rounded annual-average factors (International Energy Agency 2023), the same ones notebook 15.2 used for Quebec and Poland, illustrate the effect of placement while holding facility energy constant. They are not measurements of the same job run at every site. Actual placement decisions require time-matched grid evidence and must include changes in facility overhead and the energy needed to move or resume the work.

Multiplying raw GPU thermal design power by runtime and a regional grid factor understates a job’s operational carbon when it omits host servers and chiller power, or overstates it if facility overhead is accidentally applied a second time. Equation 10 computes operational carbon from the facility-level energy \(\FacilityEnergy\) of equation 9, which already includes IT support and \(\text{PUE}\) once, scaled by the electricity grid’s carbon intensity \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{grid}}\):
\[\text{CO}_{2,\text{operational}} = \FacilityEnergy\times \text{CO}_{2,\text{grid}} \tag{10}\]
Applied to a mid-scale training run, the equation separates the facility energy from the grid factor that converts it into emissions. The worked account below builds that facility energy step by step from accelerator draw, rack support, and PUE before comparing the resulting emissions across two regional grids.

Napkin Math 15.5: Training emissions calculationProblem: Quantify the operational carbon footprint of training a 7B parameter model on 64 A100 GPUs for 14 days, assuming continuous accelerator draw at the rated power and the stated rack-support and facility overheads.
Math:

Compute energy: 64 GPUs \(\times\) 400 W \(\times\) 336 hours = 8,601.6 kWh.
Apply IT support and PUE: host processors, memory, and networking add to the accelerator load. This calculation borrows the ratio of IT power to accelerator power from the DGX H100 rack profile itemized later in table 7. That ratio is a modeling proxy for an A100 server’s support load rather than a measurement of it. It scales accelerator energy by 1.38 to 11,827.2 kWh, so total facility energy = 11,827.2 kWh \(\times\) 1.12 = 13,246.5 kWh.
Calculate emissions: On US average grid (429 g/kWh \(\text{CO}_2\)), emissions = 5.7 t. On Quebec hydro grid (20 g/kWh), emissions = 264.9 kg.

Systems insight: The grid factor alone produces a 21.4× difference in training emissions for this pairing, the same placement lever quantified in notebook 15.2. The model architecture is unchanged.





Moving the 64-A100 training run of the preceding section from the US-average grid to Quebec’s hydro-dominated grid cuts operational emissions by more than an order of magnitude, yet the carbon emitted to fabricate those 64 GPUs in the semiconductor foundry does not fall by a single gram. The training-emissions notebook priced electricity only, where a lower grid emissions factor reduces operational carbon and raises the amortized manufacturing share from about 1.6 percent of total emissions on the US-average grid to about 25.8 percent on Quebec’s grid. Whether embodied carbon remains a minor correction or becomes a major share depends on the manufacturing footprint, utilization, and service life, so those quantities must enter the comparison before an engineer can choose between reducing electricity use and extending hardware service.
Embodied carbon encompasses emissions from raw material extraction, semiconductor fabrication, assembly, transportation, and end-of-life disposal. For AI hardware, the energy-intensive nature of advanced semiconductor processes dominates manufacturing emissions, including wafer fabrication at advanced process nodes, high-bandwidth memory production, and packaging. An NVIDIA A100 GPU carries an embodied footprint of approximately 150 kg CO2e per unit (Luccioni et al. 2023). NVIDIA’s HGX H100 product carbon footprint implies roughly 164 kg CO2e per H100 when the baseboard footprint is allocated evenly across its eight GPUs (NVIDIA Corporation 2025). Equation 11 amortizes this embodied carbon over the hardware lifetime to compute per-use emissions:
\[\text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied,daily}} = \frac{\text{CO}_{2,\text{manufacturing}}}{\HardwareServiceLife\times 365} \tag{11}\] with \(\HardwareServiceLife\) in years.
The manufacturing emissions have already occurred when the hardware enters service. Amortization allocates that burden over time; it does not describe additional manufacturing emissions accumulating each day. Utilization and service life determine how much useful work shares the initial burden.

Systems Perspective 15.1: Embodied carbon amortizationRenting a GPU for an hour uses hardware whose manufacturing emissions have already occurred. The workload account allocates a share of those emissions to the rental interval, regardless of whether the monetary fee explicitly prices carbon.
Expressing equation 11 per hour and multiplying by the job’s duration makes that allocation explicit: \[\text{CO}_{2,\text{total}} = \text{CO}_{2,\text{operational}} + \left( \frac{\text{CO}_{2,\text{manufacturing}}}{\HardwareServiceLife \times 365 \times 24} \times \JobDuration \right)\] with \(\HardwareServiceLife\) in years and \(\JobDuration\) in hours.
Scenario: Training a model for 10 hours on 8 NVIDIA H100s. This accelerator-only illustration uses thermal design power (TDP) as a constant-power assumption and excludes host, network, and facility energy. Its embodied share uses the allocated baseboard footprint; it is not a complete fleet lifecycle inventory.

Operational: 8 \(\times\) 0.7 kW \(\times\) 10 hours = 56 kWh. At 0.429 kg/kWh (US-average grid) = 24 kg.
Embodied: 8 \(\times\) 164 kg = 1312 kg.
Amortization: Lifetime = 3 years, the standard service life (26280 hours).

Hourly “Rent” = 1312 kg / 26280 hours \(\approx\) 0.050 kg/h.
Job Cost = 0.050 kg/h \(\times\) 10 hours = 0.5 kg.


Systems insight: For long-lived hardware in dirty grids, electricity dominates (24 kg vs. 0.5 kg). However, in clean grids (hydro, 0.020 kg/kWh), operational drops to 1.1 kg, making embodied carbon a significant fraction (~30.8 percent) of the total footprint.


The perspective’s H100 job, like the lifecycle notebook later in this chapter, amortizes over the 3-year standard service life. The A100 recap that follows keeps its own setup’s 4-year extended life, which spreads the same manufacturing carbon over more service. For an accelerator with 150 kg embodied carbon (the A100 estimate cited earlier) and that 4-year data center lifetime, the first step is daily amortization: 150 kg / (4 years \(\times\) 365 d/year) \(\approx\) 0.103 kg/day. The second step assigns that daily share to the job: a training run lasting 14 days on 64 accelerators carries 64 \(\times\) 14 days \(\times\) 0.103 kg \(\approx\) 92.1 kg CO2 of amortized embodied carbon.
Adding that 92.1 kg embodied contribution to the 5,682.7 kg of operational emissions calculated earlier for the US-average grid yields the 1.6 percent manufacturing share noted at the start of this section, whereas pairing the same hardware burden with Quebec’s 264.9 kg of operational emissions raises the manufacturing share to 25.8 percent. The manufacturing term did not change; the cleaner grid shrank everything around it.



Reporting only the final training run’s electricity and the serving cluster’s power bill leaves out the failed architecture sweeps that preceded the run and the manufacturing emissions of the racks that host it. A complete workload account (equation 12) groups operational emissions into training and inference, adds embodied emissions, and requires that development experiments and supporting services enter the inventory rather than disappear when accounting starts at the final run:
\[\text{CO}_{2,\text{lifecycle}} = \text{CO}_{2,\text{training}} + \text{CO}_{2,\text{inference}} + \text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied}} \tag{12}\]
Each term has its own physical drivers (figure 7). The embodied term \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{embodied}}\) is fixed before the hardware runs, at roughly 150 kg to 164 kg CO2e per accelerator for the devices priced above. The training term \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{training}}\) is a one-time cost set by cluster scale, PUE, and checkpoint I/O, while the inference term \(\text{CO}_{2,\text{inference}}\) recurs for as long as request traffic and KV-cache residency keep serving replicas powered. Their relative proportions therefore shift over the deployment lifetime, as the worked account in notebook 15.6 and the serving crossover in section 15.7.3 show.

Block widths show timing, not magnitude. The relative size of each term is workload-specific: serving volume, grid factor, and hardware lifetime determine which one dominates.



The equations become a decision tool once each factor is measured or declared. A worked account for a large training run shows how the operational and embodied terms combine, and which of them dominates.

A complete footprint must extend the inventory to those boundaries.



Schneider, Ian, and Taylor Mattia. 2024. “Carbon Accounting in the Cloud: A Methodology for Allocating Emissions Across Data Center Users.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2406.09645.
Time is one defensible allocation basis, not a universal one. Shared fleets may instead allocate embodied emissions by accelerator-hours, reserved capacity, or a workload’s share of useful computation. Google’s cloud carbon reporting combines two of these bases, allocating the energy and emissions of shared machines by each customer’s resource reservations and hourly measured usage (Schneider and Mattia 2024). The chosen denominator must be reported and applied consistently; otherwise a low-utilization job can appear artificially inexpensive merely because another tenant absorbs the idle capacity. These workload shares support engineering comparisons; they do not determine the reporting year or category in a corporate emissions inventory. Procurement decisions need the unallocated fleet total as well as the workload-attributed share, because amortization changes ownership of an emission in the inventory but does not remove it from the atmosphere.
Every lifecycle estimate should therefore carry an uncertainty interval rather than a single authoritative total. Average workload power, PUE, grid intensity, hardware lifetime, utilization, and manufacturing footprint are measured or modeled with different errors. A sensitivity analysis varies the assumptions that could reverse the decision, including clean-grid versus carbon-intensive operation, three- versus five-year service life, and low versus high serving volume. It then reports whether the preferred design remains preferred. Precision in arithmetic cannot compensate for an unstable system boundary.
The balance among these terms changes with serving volume and duration. A high-volume service can exceed its entire training footprint within months, or within days at higher traffic, a crossover that section 15.7.3 works through for a deployed model.
The account becomes an engineering tool when it runs on every job rather than once after the fact. A partial lifecycle carbon calculator (listing 1) combines measured energy, the rack support multiplier, a declared facility PUE, an explicitly selected grid-intensity factor, and amortized embodied carbon. Its example reproduces the 64-A100 run, with each input drawn from the facility, grid, or hardware profile it describes; section 15.9.4.1 compares the sources of the grid factor.



Listing 1: Lifecycle Carbon Calculation: Computing total carbon footprint including operational and embodied emissions.


from mlsysim import Hardware, Infrastructure, ReferenceStats, Systems


def calculate_carbon_footprint(
    gpu_power_watts: float,
    num_gpus: int,
    training_hours: float,
    it_power_multiplier: float,
    pue: float,
    grid_intensity_gco2_kwh: float,
    gpu_embodied_kg: float,
    gpu_lifetime_years: float,
) -> dict:
    """Estimate operational emissions plus allocated GPU manufacturing emissions."""

    # Operational emissions (plain floats: watts, hours, kWh, grams)
    gpu_energy_kwh = gpu_power_watts * num_gpus * training_hours / 1000
    it_energy_kwh = gpu_energy_kwh * it_power_multiplier  # + host, net
    facility_energy_kwh = it_energy_kwh * pue  # overhead, applied once
    operational_kg = (
        facility_energy_kwh * grid_intensity_gco2_kwh / 1000
    )

    # Embodied emissions (amortized by time over the service life)
    daily_embodied = gpu_embodied_kg / (gpu_lifetime_years * 365)
    training_days = training_hours / 24
    embodied_kg = num_gpus * training_days * daily_embodied

    return {
        "energy_kwh": facility_energy_kwh,
        "operational_carbon_kg": operational_kg,
        "embodied_carbon_kg": embodied_kg,
        "total_carbon_kg": operational_kg + embodied_kg,
        "embodied_fraction": embodied_kg
        / (operational_kg + embodied_kg),
    }


# Example: 7B model training on a 64-GPU A100 cluster for 14 days.
# Each input names its source: PUE is a facility property, the
# grid factor a property of the electricity supply.
_rack = Systems.Racks.DGX_H100_4Node  # proxy support-load profile
_facility = Infrastructure.FacilityCooling.BestAir  # PUE 1.12
_grid = Infrastructure.Grids.US_Avg  # annual-average factor
_run = ReferenceStats.MidScaleTrainingCarbonProfile
result = calculate_carbon_footprint(
    gpu_power_watts=Hardware.Cloud.A100.tdp.m_as("W"),  # 400 W
    num_gpus=Systems.Clusters.Lab_64_A100.total_accelerators,  # 64
    training_hours=_run.TrainingDays.m_as("h"),  # 336 h
    it_power_multiplier=(
        _rack.it_power / _rack.accelerator_power
    ).m_as(""),
    pue=_facility.pue,
    grid_intensity_gco2_kwh=_grid.carbon_intensity_g_kwh,
    gpu_embodied_kg=Hardware.Cloud.A100.embodied_carbon_kg,

A training cluster can fit its accelerator power budget yet exceed its facility budget once support systems and cooling enter the account. Whether a facility can host the cluster at all is a feasibility question; the sustainability question is whether a change in power delivery or cooling reduces lifecycle cost while preserving that feasible operating envelope. The relevant comparison includes annual energy, local water use, equipment lifetime, and the energy wasted when cooling failures interrupt useful work.
Facility sustainability therefore has to be read as a chain of constraints rather than as a single PUE number. Persistent megawatt demand sets the grid and emissions exposure. Power delivery determines how much electricity becomes useful IT load. Cooling sets the facility overhead and the water drawn to remove heat. Water use then determines whether a technically efficient site is locally sustainable. The physical mechanisms below matter here because each assigns losses or resource use to a different accounting boundary.

At facility scale, the optimization target is no longer a single model in isolation but the aggregate demand, facility overhead, and grid context surrounding every watt of IT power. Every kilowatt-hour in those national totals begins as electricity delivered to a rack and leaves as heat that must be removed from it. Delivering 120 kW to a single cabinet (the rated draw of one GB200 NVL72 rack) starts at the substation, and every conversion stage between the grid and the chip takes its share along the way.



Capacity planning fails when engineers budget only accelerator TDP, because transformers, uninterruptible power supplies, rack distribution, and voltage regulators each dissipate part of the incoming grid power as heat before a single watt reaches the silicon. Power and thermal envelopes traced that electrical path from the utility feed to the voltage regulator, and equation 2 measures the facility overhead along it. For a sustainability account, the question is where along that path energy and reliability margin are lost, and which boundary carries each loss. The first constraint sits outside the building: large grid-supplied ML facilities need sufficient substation and utility-interconnection capacity. Internal distribution improvements cannot raise that import limit, and on-site generation or storage adds a separate supply whose capacity, duration, and reliability must enter the design.



Substation lead time can run 4× longer than GPU procurement.

Systems Perspective 15.2: The interconnection queueDeploying 10,000 GPUs and deploying the electrical substation required to power their IT load (9.6 MW, after the 7 MW GPU subtotal is expanded for rack support power) operate on different timelines. In this planning comparison, GPU procurement takes 6 months, while permitting, engineering, procurement, construction, and grid connection for a new 10+ MW substation take 24 months. The infrastructure path is therefore 4× longer than the accelerator path. Actual schedules depend on the site, utility, equipment availability, and approvals, so the ratio illustrates a dependency rather than a universal lead time.
Systems insight: In this comparison, power delivery determines when the fleet can begin useful work even if the accelerators arrive on schedule. The US generation-and-storage interconnection queue is distinct from a data center’s load-connection request; neither queue total directly measures available capacity for a new ML facility. Procurement must therefore follow a site-specific power-delivery schedule. Otherwise, delivered silicon can remain “electrically stranded” while the facility waits for its connection or transformer.


Inside the facility, every conversion stage turns part of the delivered power into heat. Along the path traced in Power and thermal envelopes (The Power Delivery Path), the utility transformer loses about 1–2 percent, an online double-conversion uninterruptible power supply (UPS) 3–5 percent (or 1–2 percent in eco mode), the power distribution unit (PDU) 2–3 percent, and baseboard voltage regulation 5–8 percent. Compounded, these stages dissipate roughly 9–17 percent of grid power before it reaches a transistor, and server power supplies add their own conversion loss on top. The accounting boundary decides where each loss appears. Losses upstream of the IT boundary, such as the transformer, UPS, and facility distribution, raise PUE. Server power supplies and baseboard voltage regulators sit inside the measured IT load, and their heat must be removed by the same cooling system that serves the accelerators. Higher-voltage distribution is one of the few design changes that shrinks this overhead directly, because the same power at a higher voltage needs less current, and resistive distribution losses \(\ConductorCurrent^2\ElectricalResistance\) fall with the square of that current. The 48 V rack distribution of Power delivery networks and transient dynamics applies that principle, and its realized saving depends on conductor design and the added conversion stages.
At ML rack power densities, the difference between 95 percent and 98 percent distribution efficiency is meaningful. Using 33 kW as a reference rack load, a first-order estimate applies the difference between those efficiencies as 3 percent of that load, yielding approximately 0.99 kW per rack. Across 300 racks, the estimated reduction is 297 kW, equivalent to roughly 36 GPU nodes or 9 four-node racks under this power mix. Sustaining that reduction over a 3-year lifecycle at $0.07/kWh gives estimated electricity savings of ~$546,361. An exact fixed-load comparison divides delivered power by each efficiency before subtracting input powers. The released capacity can support more work or lower consumption; spending it on additional nodes does not preserve the same electricity saving.

Synchronized training also changes the shape of the load. The correlated power swings introduced with grid dynamics (section 15.3.2) now appear inside the delivery chain, where coordinated computation and communication phases align across thousands of accelerators.
