title: 17 Conclusion
text:
When a reasoning model spends seconds of test-time compute on a single user prompt or an optical interconnect replaces copper across a switching tier, that test of transfer applies directly: the binding constraint shifts again without leaving the Fleet Law behind. The same six principles govern workloads and substrates that are only now emerging. Test-time compute, introduced among the scaling regimes in Resource-constrained scaling regimes, already moves part of the scaling curve from the training cluster into the serving path, where Test-time compute and the per-request budget prices it as a per-request compute budget. Beneath the fleet, new interconnect and packaging substrates change the rates that every Fleet Law term inherits. Each shift relocates cost without exempting it from the Fleet Law.
Gains from scheduling, placement, and overlap depend on a physical fabric, so software and substrate choices must be evaluated together. Once software has removed avoidable coordination, the remaining frontier is the substrate that moves tokens, activations, and power through the fleet. For Archetype A, the pressure on that substrate comes from specific collective patterns rather than from scale in general. Tensor parallelism issues frequent collectives across partitioned tensors, and mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing issues an AllToAll dispatch at each expert layer. Across thousands of accelerators, link energy accumulates with the volume of that collective traffic, which makes lower-energy interconnects a plausible fabric-efficiency lever.
Candidate substrates attack different factors of that physical account: energy per bit, path length, bandwidth density, or the distance between memory and compute. Optical I/O and co-packaged optics lower the energy required to move each bit across the fabric, while 3D integration extends the vertical stacking of HBM and advanced packaging to shorten interconnect paths. Neuromorphic event-driven substrates instead organize computation around sparse events such as spikes and keep state beside the compute units that use it. Automated architecture search and AI-for-systems optimization offer ways to explore candidate designs, but each proposal still needs a workload-specific comparison of useful work, data movement, power, and implementation cost. A lower energy per bit also reaches the fleet only in proportion to the links’ share of fleet power, the affected-share arithmetic of Amdahl’s law applied to energy. Its value is measured as that share, as the optical dividend of Optical interconnects does for a switch and a cluster. A lower link-energy measurement alone therefore does not establish a better fleet, and a new substrate still needs fault tolerance and responsible governance.


↩︎ Neuromorphic and other non-von Neumann directions are established in Future research directions.
Whatever the substrate, the discipline stays the same. An engineer chooses the unit of useful work, accounts for its full resource cost, and states which comparisons the evidence supports. Narrowing that boundary to a single component, layer, or benchmark in isolation produces the recurring failure modes of fleet design.

title: 17 Conclusion
text:
The closing mistakes all come from optimizing the wrong unit of design. A model can improve while the fleet becomes slower, less reliable, more expensive, or harder to govern.

Fallacy: A faster model is automatically a better system.
Raw model speed matters, but it is only one term in the Fleet Law. In the illustrative equal-work, barrier-dominated step, a worker running at 80 percent of peer speed reduces throughput by 20 percent relative to uniformly fast workers. A faster kernel on every worker but that one leaves the step bound by the straggler, because speeding the workers already waiting at the barrier does not shorten the limiting computation. A design that reduces kernel time while increasing checkpoint pressure, network contention, serving variance, or governance risk can make the total system worse. The systems question is whether the change improves useful throughput, the ML goodput of ML Goodput, under the actual constraints: data movement, synchronization, failure recovery, power, latency, and accountability.


Pitfall: Optimizing one layer while hiding the constraint it creates in another.
A local improvement becomes dangerous when it moves cost to a layer that no one is measuring. Larger batches may raise accelerator utilization while worsening tail latency, aggressive compression may reduce communication while increasing accuracy risk, and carbon-aware scheduling may lower emissions while requiring more slack in the service budget. Good engineering respects the displacement of overhead, keeping the transferred constraint visible so the system can choose deliberately rather than inheriting a hidden bottleneck.


Fallacy: Fleet-scale lessons are tied to today’s hardware and software stack.
Specific processors, frameworks, and serving engines will change, but the durable relationships remain. Data must reach compute at the required rate. Workers must communicate before synchronization stalls the job. Failures must be expected at large component counts. Serving systems must meet tail-latency budgets. Governance constraints must be engineered into the operating path. The technology names are examples; the rate, failure, and accountability relationships are the lesson.


Pitfall: Treating governance and sustainability as external reviews rather than system constraints.
Postponing security, fairness, privacy, and carbon accounting can create architectural debt. Retrofitting audit trails, demographic monitoring, access controls, deletion workflows, or carbon-aware placement may require reconstructing evidence or redesigning deployed components. Identifying these obligations during design lets teams budget the required paths and test whether they work before release; the actual cost still depends on the control and deployment.


Self-Check: Question

A performance engineering team rewrites an attention kernel to execute 40% faster on a microbenchmark by storing intermediate QK values in an uncompressed, custom shared-memory layout. When integrated into the full 2,048-GPU production serving fleet, however, end-to-end request throughput decreases by 15% and p99 tail latency doubles. Matched measurements show higher memory residency, lower feasible serving concurrency, and increased exposed tensor-parallel communication. Which closing fallacy from the chapter explains this outcome?

Pitfall: “Expecting the cluster to parallelize a kernel for free.” The 2,048-GPU cluster should have automatically vectorized the kernel across nodes without memory transfers.
Pitfall: “Treating governance as an external review.” The custom layout violated data privacy compliance rules, causing the GPU scheduler to pause execution.
Fallacy: “A faster model is automatically a better system.” The local kernel speedup increased memory footprint and communication serialization, degrading global serving throughput and tail latency under fleet constraints.
Fallacy: “Fleet-scale lessons are tied to today’s software stack.” The kernel failed solely because the team compiled it with an outdated version of CUDA.

An infrastructure team notices that inter-node network bandwidth is saturated during distributed training. To relieve network congestion, they introduce an aggressive gradient compression algorithm that achieves a 10x reduction in transmitted bytes. However, the compression and decompression routines add substantial CPU overhead, causing worker nodes to fall behind and increasing overall training step time by 25%. Which pitfall does this engineering failure illustrate?

Pitfall: “Optimizing one layer while hiding the constraint it creates in another.” Relieving network communication displaced the bottleneck into host CPU compute and synchronization, increasing end-to-end step time.
Fallacy: “Carbon budgets forbid lossy gradient encodings.” Compressing gradients violated data-center carbon budgeting policies.
Pitfall: “Treating governance as an external review.” The compression algorithm altered gradient numerical representations without legal consent.
Fallacy: “Network switches compress payloads in flight.” The network switch hardware should have automatically compressed the packets in flight at zero CPU cost.

True or False: Because deep learning frameworks, accelerator instruction sets, and interconnect standards change every few years, fundamental distributed systems principles (such as Amdahl’s law, Little’s law, MTBF scaling, and rate matching) must be completely reinvented with each new hardware generation.
The chapter cautions against the fallacy that fleet-scale lessons are tied to today’s hardware and software stack.

title: 17 Conclusion
text:
At fleet scale, improving a model or accelerator does not establish that the complete service improves. The engineering object is the coupled system that moves data, schedules work, survives failure, serves users, and satisfies governance obligations under physical and organizational constraints. Within their fitted regime, scaling laws set the demand for fleet growth, the Fleet Law sets its price, and the six principles locate where in the fleet that price is paid. The method that recurs across the book follows from all three. It identifies the binding constraint, quantifies its cost, and evaluates the proposed change across every affected operating path, so that the cost it displaces stays visible instead of resurfacing unmeasured in another layer.

Key Takeaways: The fleet is the unit of design

The fleet is the object: The six principles reduce to one habit, following the binding constraint across infrastructure, communication, coordination, serving, and governance. The fleet, not any single model or component, is the unit to build, measure, and optimize.
Growth must earn its price: Within a fitted regime, each doubling of compute buys a smaller absolute loss reduction, while interruption exposure and checkpoint overhead grow with the fleet and exposed communication can grow with it. Expansion is a decision justified by measurements and release evidence, not a default.
Scale changes the probability model: When server delays are independent, a request that touches 100 servers has a 63.4 percent chance that at least one responds beyond its 99th-percentile latency, and a job that needs every one of \(\RequiredComponentCount\) independent components sees its interval between interruptions shrink as \(1/\RequiredComponentCount\). Fleet behavior is not single-node behavior repeated.
Orchestration gains require system measurements: Scheduling, placement, and communication overlap improve useful throughput only when their gains survive recovery costs, serving deadlines, and resource budgets. Measure the complete operating path before accepting a local improvement as a fleet-wide gain.
Obligations belong in the path: Security, privacy, fairness, robustness, carbon, and auditability are production constraints, not external reviews. The discipline is to design them into data pipelines, schedulers, serving paths, and operating procedures before scale makes the trade-off irreversible.




Closing Distillation: The discipline of ML systemsThe Scale Moment traced the scale moment through a training run that stopped every few hours. Meta’s Llama 3 cluster of 16,384 GPUs recorded 419 unexpected interruptions in 54 days and still kept more than 90 percent of elapsed time as useful training (Dubey et al. 2024). Those numbers now read as engineering. An unexpected interruption every 3.1 hours is the reliability gap of a job that needs every one of its accelerators at once, and it measures the run’s recovery exposure. The effective training fraction, the run’s runtime goodput, measures how much progress the recovery machinery retained across elapsed time. The report credits faster startup, checkpointing, and diagnosis, including communication traces that made stalled collectives inspectable, for that retained fraction, so the fraction summarizes all of them together rather than measuring any single Fleet Law term. Each worker still computed, exchanged, and waited, as in the synchronous step with which the book began; Compute, Communication, and Coordination are those three activities, measured.
A proposed larger run can now be judged rather than presumed necessary. Under the expansion example’s independent, identical constant-rate failure model and unchanged checkpoint write time, doubling the fleet halves the expected interruption interval and raises optimized checkpoint-and-rework overhead by about 1.41×. It buys calendar time only by spending more accelerator-hours on the same work. Whether that run should be built depends on the shrinking quality gain its fitted scaling curve predicts for the doubling, the measured time and energy required to deliver it, and the evidence its release requires. The engineering achievement is a justified decision, including the decision to retain the current fleet when expansion cannot meet those conditions. The same discipline applies whether the work scales training compute across thousands of accelerators or serves a model to millions of users under a latency contract. The engineer follows the binding constraint across the fleet, accounts for every displaced cost, and accepts a design only when the evidence supports it.



Dubey, Abhimanyu, Abhinav Jauhri, Abhinav Pandey, Abhishek Kadian, et al. 2024. The Llama 3 Herd of Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2407.21783.
Prof. Vijay Janapa Reddi, Harvard University

title: 17 Conclusion
text:
Self-Check: Answer

A team transitions an ML model from single-node workstation experimentation to a multi-data-center production service handling 50,000 queries per second with high-availability and regulatory compliance requirements. According to the chapter’s synthesis, which shift in engineering focus best characterizes this transition?

Shifting from PyTorch tensor definitions to CUDA kernel compilation to maximize single-device arithmetic precision.
Extending single-node reasoning about models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment to coupled fleet infrastructure, data center fabrics, distributed protocols, automated fault recovery, and governance frameworks.
Shifting from empirical hyperparameter tuning to symbolic loss optimization across isolated server instances.
Shifting from self-supervised pre-training objectives to supervised fine-tuning loops to eliminate inter-node network synchronization.

Answer: The correct answer is B. Extending single-node reasoning about models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment to coupled fleet infrastructure, data center fabrics, distributed protocols, automated fault recovery, and governance frameworks. The section establishes that single-node ML engineering already couples models, data pipelines, execution, and deployment constraints. Distributed ML engineering extends that reasoning across shared infrastructure, distributed protocols, and fleet governance. The answer describing CUDA kernel compilation focuses on low-level single-device acceleration rather than fleet-scale infrastructure. The choice regarding symbolic loss optimization misidentifies training mathematics as a distributed systems shift. The option suggesting that fine-tuning eliminates network synchronization is false, as distributed fine-tuning across clusters still requires communication and collective synchronization.
Learning Objective: Distinguish the core focus of distributed ML systems engineering from foundational single-node model development.
**Order the four bands of the fleet stack from bottom (physical foundation) to top (governance and social constraints), reflecting how physical limits propagate upward to bound higher-level systems:


The Fleet (Facility & Accelerators; Fabric & Storage)
The Responsible Fleet (Assurance; Governance & Sustainability)
Distributed ML (Distributed Execution; Reliability & Control)
The Fleet in Production (Runtime & Serving; Operations)**

Answer: The correct sequence is (1) The Fleet (Facility & Accelerators; Fabric & Storage) -> (3) Distributed ML (Distributed Execution; Reliability & Control) -> (4) The Fleet in Production (Runtime & Serving; Operations) -> (2) The Responsible Fleet (Assurance; Governance & Sustainability). The Infrastructure band (The Fleet) establishes raw throughput, bandwidth, and thermal ceilings; the Distribution band (Distributed ML) turns those hardware limits into partitioning, synchronization, and recovery; the Serving band (The Fleet in Production) converts trained models into live services with latency, availability, and cost targets; and the Governance band (The Responsible Fleet) defines the normative boundaries on security, fairness, privacy, and carbon.
Learning Objective: Classify the four bands of the fleet stack and trace how physical limits propagate upward to bound serving and governance.

True or False: In a distributed ML system, optimizing individual layers in isolation (such as independently maximizing storage IOPS, network bandwidth, or serving concurrency) guarantees optimal end-to-end system throughput.
Answer: False. In distributed ML systems, the layers are coupled rates and constraints. A local optimization that improves one component can be completely negated if another layer binds the system (for example, high storage read bandwidth is wasted if collective communication saturates the network fabric). End-to-end system optimization requires cross-layer co-design and matching rates rather than isolated layer improvements.
Learning Objective: Evaluate why isolated component optimizations fail to guarantee end-to-end distributed system performance.
Explain why any single constraint in the fleet stack, such as a slow storage checkpoint or an unmeasured governance requirement, can bind the entire production pipeline, even when compute accelerators operate at peak utilization.
Answer: Distributed ML systems operate as a coupled chain of interdependent rates and operational obligations. A blocking synchronous checkpoint pauses the participating training workers while it completes. Asynchronous checkpointing can overlap writes with useful work, but exposed pauses, resource contention, and incomplete durable state still constrain progress and recovery. In serving, fabric congestion or queuing tail effects convert high raw FLOP throughput into unacceptable user-visible latency. At the governance layer, failing to establish data provenance, privacy bounds, or fairness auditing can legally or operationally block deployment regardless of technical performance. Thus, the system is bounded by its tightest operational constraint, not its fastest compute resource.
Learning Objective: Analyze how non-compute bottlenecks (storage, fabric, governance) bind end-to-end production ML pipelines.

When scaled to 8,000 GPUs on the same network fabric without changing hyperparameters, scaling efficiency plummets to 38%. Cluster telemetry reveals that per-device arithmetic execution speed remained constant, but workers spend over 55% of step time waiting at collective barriers. These implementations evolve and will be superseded over successive generations. - Durable Relationships: Mathematical and physical laws that govern distributed systems, including the single-machine iron law, the Fleet Law of distributed step time (\(\DistributedStepTime\)), Little’s law in serving queues (\(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \RequestTimeInSystem\)), and the Young-Daly optimal checkpoint cadence (\(\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \CheckpointWriteTime \SystemMtbf}\)).

Why Invariants Persist Across New Substrates:


Rate-Matching: Computation fundamentally requires data; whether processing is performed via electronic transistors, photonic circuits, or memristive crossbars, if memory and I/O channels cannot supply activations and weights at the rate compute consumes them, processing elements will stall.
Failure Scaling: Under the simplified identical independent failure-rate model where every accelerator failure interrupts the job, aggregate cluster mean time between failures scales inversely with accelerator count (\(\SystemMtbf = \ComponentMttf/\DeviceCount\)), requiring automated checkpointing and fault recovery.
Learning Objective: Evaluate how durable systems invariants persist across transitions in underlying physical hardware and software tools.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
Every fleet is built from single machines, and this book assumes that the reader already reasons fluently about one of them. This appendix restates that single-machine foundation in reference form so that a reader who meets the prerequisites only loosely can work every calculation in the book without another text. It collects the Data, Algorithm, and Machine (D·A·M) diagnostic framework and the iron law it rests on, arithmetic intensity and the roofline bound, the accelerator memory hierarchy, the kernel-level levers that shorten a single device’s step, the byte accounting of mixed-precision training, and the arithmetic of transformer training and inference. The chapters build the fleet-scale Compute, Communication, and Coordination (C\(^3\)) framework on this base.

Learning Objectives

Classify single-machine bottlenecks by dominant Data, Algorithm, or Machine axis while recognizing mixed causes
Map optimization techniques to their D·A·M intersection zone to understand which axes they span
Apply the iron law equation to quantitatively diagnose performance problems
Distinguish between memory-bound and compute-bound workloads using arithmetic intensity and the roofline bound
Calculate the per-parameter memory of mixed-precision training and the FLOPs of transformer training and decoding
Select appropriate profiling tools and optimization strategies for each Data, Algorithm, or Machine axis
Evaluate system health using D·A·M scorecard metrics (I/O overhead, active parameters, MFU)





This appendix is a reference for single-node performance and for the single-machine quantities that fleet-scale arguments take as given. Start from the symptom or the missing quantity:

When a single accelerator is slow: Use the iron law mapping (section 1.2) and the bottleneck diagnostic (section 1.3.2) to decide which term binds.
When deciding whether a kernel is memory bound or compute bound: Use the roofline bound (section 1.3.1).
When a byte must cross a memory boundary: Use the memory hierarchy (section 1.4) to see which tier sets its cost.
When a trace shows many short kernels, launch gaps, or attention intermediates written to device memory: Use the kernel-level levers (section 1.5).
When sizing model state: Use the training memory accounting (section 1.6) for bytes per parameter.
When estimating training compute or decode cost: Use transformer arithmetic (section 1.7).

When training is slow on a single GPU, check utilization, data wait time, and model FLOPs utilization (MFU), then map each to its Data, Algorithm, or Machine axis. When serving misses a latency target, identify whether the regime is latency-bound (overhead), memory-bound (weight/KV movement), or compute-bound. When cost is exploding, use the D·A·M rubric to ensure that effort targets the dominant term, not a nonbottleneck.
The Data · Algorithm · Machine (D·A·M) taxonomy is the diagnostic framework for single-node ML systems engineering: it formalizes how information flow, mathematical logic, and physical execution interact across three diagnostic axes,1 while recognizing that real systems can involve mixed causes or interactions between axes.
1 MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive): A classification principle from management consulting (popularized by McKinsey) requiring that categories do not overlap and together cover every possibility. Applied to systems engineering, it is useful as an idealized decomposition, but D·A·M bottlenecks often overlap in practice. A kernel can be simultaneously memory-bound, synchronization-heavy, and poorly matched to available hardware.


When performance stalls or behavior degrades on a single node, the first diagnostic question is whether the flow of work is blocked by memory movement, arithmetic volume, or hardware throughput. The D·A·M taxonomy maps these three failure modes directly to the iron law of ML systems, the single-machine equation that The Fleet Law restates before extending it to the Fleet Law. Each axis plays a distinct role, binds on a distinct physical quantity (bandwidth, operations, or peak throughput), and answers to its own high-leverage optimization (table 1).



Table 1: D·A·M Axis Reference: Each axis maps to a distinct physical constraint and a high-impact optimization strategy. Start diagnosis here: identify which constraint is binding, then follow the optimization lever.











Axis
Role
Physical constraint
High-leverage optimization




Data (D)
Information (The Fuel)
Bandwidth (\(\Bandwidth\))
I/O Pipeline Optimization


Algorithm (A)
Logic (The Blueprint)
Operations (\(\Operations\))
Model Compression


Machine (M)
Physics (The Engine)
Throughput (\(\PeakRate\))
Hardware Acceleration






The three axes seldom bind in isolation. Pruning weights to cut operations can fragment memory access, and a denser storage format that saves bytes can saturate the host CPUs that must decode it before the accelerator sees any data. Because an intervention on one axis shifts pressure onto the other two, diagnosis has to account for the regions where axes overlap. Figure 1 draws the three axes as overlapping sets. Each circle carries the factor its axis contributes to equation 1, and each pairwise overlap names the question its two axes must answer together. Data and Algorithm decide what the model learns from, Data and Machine decide how information moves, and Algorithm and Machine decide how computation executes efficiently. A bottleneck that sits in an overlap needs a fix that respects both of its axes, and the center, where all three meet, is the domain of ML systems engineering.






Figure 1: The D·A·M Intersection Landscape: Each circle is one diagnostic axis (Data, information; Algorithm, logic; Machine, physics), labeled with the factor it contributes to execution time in equation 1. Each pairwise overlap names the question its two axes must answer jointly (what to learn from, how to move information, and how to execute efficiently). At the center, where all three meet, is ML systems engineering.






When a training step or serving request runs slower than expected on a single GPU, the first question is whether the time went to moving bytes, executing arithmetic, or waiting on dispatch overhead. The iron law answers that question in two steps. The first step factors execution time along the three D·A·M axes. A task processes some number of samples (examples in vision or tabular workloads, tokens in language models), each sample costs some number of operations, and the machine takes some time to complete each operation. By dimensional cancellation, total execution time \(\Time\) (seconds) is the product of these three factors (equation 1):
\[ \Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data (D)}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm (A)}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine (M)}}  \tag{1}\]
The first two factors fix the total arithmetic work \(\Operations\). Training a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters on \(\DatasetSize\) tokens costs roughly \(6\Parameters\DatasetSize\) operations across the forward and backward passes (equation 4), and inference costs roughly \(2\Parameters\) operations per token in the forward pass. The third factor is the realized time per operation, and no real machine achieves its datasheet value of \(1/\PeakRate\).
The second step explains the gap. Executing an operation requires moving its operands through memory and interconnect, driving the arithmetic units at some realized utilization, and paying fixed control costs. Assuming these three costs occur in sequence, the iron law unpacks execution time into their sum (equation 2):
\[ \Time= \underbrace{ \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} }_{\text{Memory time}} + \underbrace{ \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} }_{\text{Compute time}} + \underbrace{ \Latency }_{\text{Overhead}}  \tag{2}\]
Data enters the two equations in different units. In equation 1, the Data factor counts logical samples or tokens. In equation 2, \(\DataVolume\) counts the physical bytes that cross a memory or interconnect bus, which include model weights, activations, cached sequence state, and gradients as well as the inputs themselves. Batch-1 decode of a language model shows how far apart the two can be. The task processes a single token, yet \(\DataVolume\) spans the gigabytes of weights streamed from high-bandwidth memory to produce it.
Algorithm and Machine share the compute term and are separated by which variable the engineer controls. Reducing the total operations (\(\Operations\)) is an algorithm lever, while improving the hardware’s peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)) or utilization (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) is a machine lever. The memory term belongs to no single axis. The Data axis sets how many inputs move, the Algorithm axis sets how many weights and activations move with them, and the Machine axis supplies the bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\) that carries them.


The additive iron law represents sequential execution, the worst case where Data, Algorithm, and Machine take turns. Overlap can move the sum toward a max, with perfect overlap defining the ideal lower bound:
\[ \SequentialExecutionTime= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency \quad \xrightarrow{\text{overlap}} \quad \PipelinedExecutionTime\geq \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth},\; \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\right) + \Latency \]
The systems engineer’s job is to make these components run in parallel, not in series. Prefetching, separate CUDA streams, asynchronous gradient synchronization, and double buffering each let one axis proceed while another is in flight (table 2).



Table 2: D·A·M Overlap Techniques: Each technique allows one D·A·M axis to execute while another is in flight, converting the iron law’s additive terms into overlapped terms.










Technique
D·A·M axes overlapped
Implementation

D overlaps M

Separate streams for H2D transfer and compute


Async Gradient Sync

Overlap gradient AllReduce with remaining backward computation as gradient buckets become ready

This overlap view still leaves one practical question: whether a workload is waiting on bytes or on FLOPs. The boundary between Data (memory bound) and Machine (compute bound) is not arbitrary; it is defined mathematically by the arithmetic intensity2 (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)) of the workload.
2 Arithmetic intensity: The ratio of floating-point operations to bytes transferred (FLOP/byte). It determines whether a workload is memory-bound or compute-bound by comparison against the hardware’s ridge point (\(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\)).The symptoms below are screening signals, not diagnoses. A workload whose arithmetic intensity sits left of \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) cannot keep the accelerator fed with enough useful work per byte. Raw utilization must still be read alongside memory-bandwidth utilization, data-loader wait, kernel occupancy, and trace gaps.

Low GPU utilization (\(<\) 80 percent): Screen for data, CPU, or launch starvation. Confirm with data-loader wait, host CPU saturation, memory-bandwidth counters, and timeline gaps.
High GPU utilization (\(>\) 95 percent): Treat this as machine bound only if compute units are busy and memory bandwidth is not saturated. If memory bandwidth is saturated, the bottleneck is still on the Data/Machine boundary.
If batch size is 1: Treat this as a warning that latency or launch overhead may matter. For large language model (LLM) decode, batch-1 execution is often memory-bandwidth bound unless traces show dispatch gaps.
If arithmetic intensity is below the ridge point (about 295.2 FLOP/byte on H100): The workload is likely memory bound (Data/Machine boundary).



Arithmetic intensity is a property of the workload and its implementation, not of the hardware. A large matrix multiply reuses each weight it loads across many multiply-accumulates and so has high intensity. An element-wise operation, or the generation of a single token, uses each loaded value only once or twice. The ridge point belongs to a simple upper bound on single-device throughput, the Roofline Model (Williams et al. 2009). A kernel with arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\), running on a device with peak compute rate \(\PeakRate\) and memory bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\), can attain at most

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[ \AttainableComputeRate(\ArithmeticIntensity) = \min\!\left(\PeakRate,\; \ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth\right)  \tag{3}\]
On log-log axes, the bound is a bandwidth roof of slope one (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth\)) that meets a flat compute roof (\(\PeakRate\)) at the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\). Left of the ridge, a kernel is memory bound, and only more bandwidth or fewer bytes per operation raises its ceiling. Right of the ridge, it is compute bound, and only a faster or better-used datapath helps. In D·A·M terms, the bandwidth roof belongs to the Data axis, the compute roof to the Machine axis, and the Algorithm axis decides where on the intensity axis the kernel sits. The roofline is a ceiling, not a prediction. A kernel far below both roofs is limited by something the model omits, such as launch overhead, synchronization, or low occupancy. The H100 Roofline Landscape draws both roofs for an H100 and places decode, prefill, and training workloads against them.
For an H100, the book’s hardware constants give a dense FP16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s and a high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s, which places the ridge at about 295.2 FLOP/byte. Batch-1 decode of a 7-billion-parameter language model stored in 16-bit precision performs about two operations per parameter for each generated token (one multiply and one add). It must read every two-byte weight once, so its intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte. Equation 3 then caps attainable throughput at 3.35 TFLOP/s, roughly 0.3 percent of peak, however well the kernels are written. Serving \(\BatchSize\) sequences in one decode step reuses each loaded weight \(\BatchSize\) times and raises the intensity to roughly \(\BatchSize\) FLOP/byte, until key-value cache traffic, which grows with batch size and context length, begins to dominate the bytes moved. That arithmetic is why batching is the first lever of every serving system. The communication-computation ratio carries the same reasoning to the network, where interconnect bandwidth takes the place of HBM bandwidth.



Each optimization shortens only one term of the iron law, so adding peak FLOP/s to a memory-bound kernel or adding memory bandwidth to a compute-bound kernel leaves step time unchanged while wasting engineering effort (table 3).



Table 3: What Works vs. What Is Wasted: Optimizing the wrong term yields limited improvement and poor cost efficiency. A memory-bound model will not speed up from more peak FLOP/s alone; it needs higher arithmetic intensity, less data movement, or a faster memory subsystem.











If the workload is…
Dominant term
Optimization that works
Optimization that is wasted




Memory-Bound
\(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth\)
Quantization, pruning, batching, kernel fusion, higher memory bandwidth
More peak FLOP/s alone


Compute-Bound
\(\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)\)
Better kernels, Tensor Cores, faster GPU, lower precision
More memory bandwidth (not binding)


Latency-Bound
\(\Latency\)
Batching requests, kernel fusion, async dispatch
Neither compute nor bandwidth (overhead dominates)










An accelerator is a fast arithmetic engine surrounded by memories that trade bandwidth for capacity, and most performance arguments in this book reduce to the question of which boundary a byte must cross. Nearest the compute units, registers and on-chip shared memory (SRAM) hold the operands of the kernel that is executing, backed by a shared on-chip L2 cache (50 MB on an H100). Beyond the die, HBM holds the model’s working state (80 GB at 3.35 TB/s on an H100). Host memory is reached over PCIe at 64 GB/s per direction, roughly 52× less than HBM, and local NVMe storage sits below host memory.
A kernel whose working set stays on chip runs near arithmetic speed; one that streams operands from HBM is bounded by the roofline above; one that must reach host memory or storage is slower still. The memory wall, the widening gap between arithmetic throughput and the bandwidth that feeds it, is the single-machine form of the constraint that reappears at fleet scale as the network wall. A multi-accelerator node adds a scale-up fabric between devices (NVLink, at 450 GB/s per direction on an H100), and the scale-out network adds tiers beyond the node. Numbers Every Fleet Engineer Should Know tabulates those tiers.



Four techniques shorten one device’s step without changing the model’s mathematics. Each removes a different cost in the iron law of section 1.2, and each counts as a gain only when a measured trace confirms it. The four differ in which term they remove, what limits them, and what evidence a trace shows (table 4).


Operator fusion combines consecutive operations into one kernel, so an intermediate result stays in registers or shared memory instead of being written to HBM and read back by the next kernel. It shrinks the data volume \(\DataVolume\) of the data term and removes one launch per fused operation from the overhead term \(\Latency\). The common kinds are chains of element-wise operations, an element-wise operation fused with a reduction such as a normalization, and operator-specific fusions such as a matrix multiply that applies its bias and activation before writing its output. Fusion stops paying when the live values of the combined kernel exceed the registers and shared memory available, which lowers occupancy or spills to memory, and when a reduction needs results from every thread block. A trace confirms it with fewer kernels and fewer HBM bytes before the step time falls.



Tiling sizes blocks of a computation to fit on-chip memory, so each operand fetched from HBM feeds many operations and arithmetic intensity rises. IO-aware attention such as FlashAttention applies the idea to attention. It computes the scores block by block, keeping a running maximum and sum for the softmax, so the full matrix of scores between every pair of positions is never written to HBM. The workspace grows linearly with sequence length rather than quadratically. The price is extra rescaling arithmetic and, in training, recomputing the scores in the backward pass. Decode processes one query row per step and has no quadratic intermediate, so its fused attention kernel is a single pass over the KV cache. Tiling reduces \(\DataVolume\) and frees HBM capacity for the KV cache and larger batches.



Graph replay, offered on NVIDIA GPUs as CUDA Graphs, records a stable sequence of kernels and memory copies once and then submits the whole sequence with one request in later steps. It removes the host-dispatch part of \(\Latency\), which matters when many short kernels leave launch gaps between them, as in batch-one decode. A captured graph replays only the shapes, memory addresses, and control flow it recorded, so a server keeps one graph per shape bucket, and decode captures more easily than prefill, whose shapes vary with prompt length. Replay fuses nothing. The same kernels run with the gaps between them removed, which a timeline shows directly.



Graph compilation automates the three levers above. A compiler captures the program as a graph, rewrites and decomposes its operations, fuses them, selects or generates a kernel for each fused group (often by timing candidates, which is called autotuning), and plans memory. Just-in-time compilers keep the eager programming model, ahead-of-time inference engines specialize the program to a declared range of shapes, and tile-level kernel languages let an engineer write a fusion the compiler missed. Compilation reduces both \(\DataVolume\) and \(\Latency\), at the cost of build and warmup time, regions split at graph breaks where the compiler cannot capture the program, and recompilation when a new shape arrives. Compilation builds prices that cost across a fleet and finds when it pays back.



Table 4: Kernel-Level Levers: Each lever shortens a different term of one device’s step, so a trace must show that term moving before a step-time gain counts.












Lever

Introduction to Machine Learning Systems develops these mechanisms in full, for a reader who wants more than this recap. Here, the four rows of table 4 serve as the checklist for verifying whether a local optimization has moved the intended iron-law term.




Whether a large model fits in an 80 GB H100 memory bank or must be partitioned across dozens of accelerators depends on how many bytes each parameter and optimizer state occupies. In the number formats listed in the notation conventions at the front of the book, FP32 occupies 4 bytes, BF16 and FP16 occupy 2, and FP8 and INT8 occupy one. Mixed-precision training runs the forward and backward passes in a 16-bit format for speed and memory, while it keeps an FP32 master copy of the weights so that small updates are not lost to rounding. The Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer adds two FP32 moment estimates per parameter. Table 5 totals the resulting bytes per parameter.



Table 5: Mixed-Precision Adam Memory per Parameter: Persistent training state before activations, framework metadata, and communication buffers. The checkpoint omits gradients because a resumed run recomputes them in its first step.

For Archetype A, the 175B-parameter dense model the chapters use as their running instance, the training state is 2.8 TB and a resumable checkpoint is 2.45 TB. A single H100 offers 80 GB of HBM (a binary nameplate, about 85.9 GB in decimal units), so the persistent state alone requires at least 33 devices before a single activation is stored. That floor is why the model state must be partitioned across devices, which Distributed Training develops. Serving the same model needs only the 16-bit weights, 350 GB, plus the key-value cache.
Activations are the other large consumer of training memory. The intermediate tensors that the backward pass needs grow with batch size, sequence length, hidden width, and depth, and for long sequences they can exceed the parameter state. Activation checkpointing stores only selected activations and recomputes the rest during the backward pass, trading additional compute for memory.



Most worked examples in this book use decoder-only transformers, and three counting rules cover nearly all of their arithmetic. The symbols follow the book’s deep learning notation, with \(\Parameters\) parameters, \(\DatasetSize\) training tokens, \(\LayerCount\) layers, hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), and sequence length \(\SequenceLength\).
Each transformer layer holds four \(\HiddenDimension\times \HiddenDimension\) attention projections and a feed-forward block that expands to \(4\HiddenDimension\) and back, about \(12\HiddenDimension^2\) weights in total. A model thus has roughly \(\Parameters\approx 12 \LayerCount \HiddenDimension^2\) parameters excluding embeddings. GPT-3 has \(\LayerCount =\) 96 and \(\HiddenDimension=\) 12,288, which gives 173.9B against its published 175B.
Every weight contributes one multiply and one add per token, so a forward pass costs about \(2\Parameters\) FLOPs per token. The backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights and costs about twice the forward pass, so training costs about \(6\Parameters\) FLOPs per token and
\[ \TrainingCompute \approx 6\Parameters \DatasetSize \tag{4}\]
in total. For GPT-3, trained on 300 billion tokens, equation 4 gives 3.15 × 10²³ FLOPs, within 1 percent of the reported 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs. The rule omits the attention-score products, which add at most about \(\SequenceLength/(6\HiddenDimension)\) to the weight FLOPs, or 2.8 percent for GPT-3 at \(\SequenceLength=\) 2,048. That fraction stays small while the context is short compared with the hidden width and grows with long contexts.
Serving an autoregressive model has two phases with different physics. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once as matrix-matrix products, so its arithmetic intensity is high and it tends to be compute bound. Decode generates one token per step for each sequence as matrix-vector products; at batch size 1 it reads every weight to perform two FLOPs per weight, the memory-bound regime that the roofline example above quantifies. To avoid recomputing attention over the whole prefix at every step, decode stores each layer’s keys and values in a key-value (KV) cache of \(2 \LayerCount \HiddenDimension\, \ElementStorageSize\) bytes per token for standard multihead attention, or 4.72 MB per token for GPT-3 in FP16. KV cache fundamentals sizes that cache against device memory.



Back-of-envelope byte and FLOP counts narrow the likely bottleneck, but hardware and runtime counters must confirm which iron-law term actually binds before an engineer rewrites a kernel or data pipeline. Each D·A·M axis is exposed by a distinct set of profiling utilities and primary metrics (table 6).

The efficiency ratios in table 7 grade a system’s performance against its theoretical limit. This report card is anchored by MFU,3 the ratio of achieved model FLOP/s to the hardware’s theoretical peak FLOP/s. The MFU grades are illustrative targets for compute-dominated training; memory-bound or latency-bound workloads must be judged against their attainable roofline and service-level objective (SLO) latency.
3 MFU (model FLOPs utilization): Counts only useful model computation in the numerator. Gradient synchronization, memory management, and other overhead within the measurement window remain in elapsed time and lower the reported ratio.

These single-node grades become most useful when they are carried forward into distributed design. The D·A·M taxonomy is the diagnostic baseline for a single machine, but as systems scale from a single node to the machine learning fleet, each axis undergoes a qualitative transformation.


Crossing the node boundary replaces local bus limits and single-device failure rates with cluster-wide fabric and power limits. Scaling from one node to a fleet changes the kind of constraint on every axis, not only its size (table 8).



Table 8: D·A·M Constraints from Node to Fleet: How each axis of the D·A·M taxonomy shifts when scaling from a single node to a multi-node fleet. The node-level focus (left) gives way to a qualitatively different fleet-scale constraint (right); the bottleneck migrates from local resource to global coordination cost.










Axis
Node-level focus (D·A·M)

The communication wall: the bottleneck shifts from local storage to the bisection bandwidth of the network fabric.

Machine (M)

The power and reliability wall: the constraint is no longer just silicon speed, but watts per rack and cluster-wide MTBF.









While D·A·M diagnoses the components of a single node, the C\(^3\) taxonomy (The C^3 Taxonomy) diagnoses the interactions of the fleet. Each of its three dimensions inherits a specific piece of the single-machine diagnostic model:

Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)) inherits the Algorithm and Machine axes, now evaluated per device after the work is partitioned across \(\DeviceCount\) devices.
Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) inherits the Data axis, but is governed by network bandwidth, topology, and, over long distances, the speed of light rather than by local I/O alone.
Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) makes coordination costs explicit at fleet scale. Synchronization, checkpoints, and failure recovery also occur on one node, but distribution expands their scope and couples them to other machines.

This progression exposes cases where higher single-node MFU comes at the expense of scaling efficiency, so the complete fleet outcome can determine the choice. The node is optimized to serve the fleet.




The D·A·M taxonomy provides the diagnostic baseline for every ML systems analysis. By isolating the bottleneck to Data, Algorithm, or Machine, practitioners ensure that optimization efforts target the binding constraint. The memory hierarchy, the byte accounting of mixed-precision training, and the transformer counting rules supply the quantities that fleet-scale arguments take as given. This single-node discipline is the prerequisite for the fleet-scale engineering addressed throughout this book.

Key Takeaways: Single-machine diagnostic heuristics

Identify the dominant axis: Decide whether Data, Algorithm, or Machine is the binding constraint before proposing any optimization.
Profile arithmetic intensity: Arithmetic intensity, read against the roofline’s ridge point, quantitatively distinguishes between Data-bound and Machine-bound regimes.
Use the iron law: The iron law transforms vague symptoms into specific term-based bottlenecks.
Count bytes and FLOPs per parameter: Mixed-precision Adam training holds 16 bytes per parameter (14 in a checkpoint), and dense transformer training costs about \(6\Parameters \DatasetSize\) FLOPs. These two rules size most memory and compute budgets in the chapters.
Grade with the scorecard: The Data-Algorithm-Machine scorecard standardizes “good” performance before moving to fleet scale.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
This appendix is a reference for single-node performance and for the single-machine quantities that fleet-scale arguments take as given. Start from the symptom or the missing quantity:

When a single accelerator is slow: Use the iron law mapping (section 1.2) and the bottleneck diagnostic (section 1.3.2) to decide which term binds.
When deciding whether a kernel is memory bound or compute bound: Use the roofline bound (section 1.3.1).
When a byte must cross a memory boundary: Use the memory hierarchy (section 1.4) to see which tier sets its cost.
When a trace shows many short kernels, launch gaps, or attention intermediates written to device memory: Use the kernel-level levers (section 1.5).
When sizing model state: Use the training memory accounting (section 1.6) for bytes per parameter.
When estimating training compute or decode cost: Use transformer arithmetic (section 1.7).

When training is slow on a single GPU, check utilization, data wait time, and model FLOPs utilization (MFU), then map each to its Data, Algorithm, or Machine axis. When serving misses a latency target, identify whether the regime is latency-bound (overhead), memory-bound (weight/KV movement), or compute-bound. When cost is exploding, use the D·A·M rubric to ensure that effort targets the dominant term, not a nonbottleneck.
The Data · Algorithm · Machine (D·A·M) taxonomy is the diagnostic framework for single-node ML systems engineering: it formalizes how information flow, mathematical logic, and physical execution interact across three diagnostic axes,1 while recognizing that real systems can involve mixed causes or interactions between axes.
1 MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive): A classification principle from management consulting (popularized by McKinsey) requiring that categories do not overlap and together cover every possibility. Applied to systems engineering, it is useful as an idealized decomposition, but D·A·M bottlenecks often overlap in practice. A kernel can be simultaneously memory-bound, synchronization-heavy, and poorly matched to available hardware.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
When performance stalls or behavior degrades on a single node, the first diagnostic question is whether the flow of work is blocked by memory movement, arithmetic volume, or hardware throughput. The D·A·M taxonomy maps these three failure modes directly to the iron law of ML systems, the single-machine equation that The Fleet Law restates before extending it to the Fleet Law. Each axis plays a distinct role, binds on a distinct physical quantity (bandwidth, operations, or peak throughput), and answers to its own high-leverage optimization (table 1).

The three axes seldom bind in isolation. Pruning weights to cut operations can fragment memory access, and a denser storage format that saves bytes can saturate the host CPUs that must decode it before the accelerator sees any data. Because an intervention on one axis shifts pressure onto the other two, diagnosis has to account for the regions where axes overlap. Figure 1 draws the three axes as overlapping sets. Each circle carries the factor its axis contributes to equation 1, and each pairwise overlap names the question its two axes must answer together. Data and Algorithm decide what the model learns from, Data and Machine decide how information moves, and Algorithm and Machine decide how computation executes efficiently. A bottleneck that sits in an overlap needs a fix that respects both of its axes, and the center, where all three meet, is the domain of ML systems engineering.






Figure 1: The D·A·M Intersection Landscape: Each circle is one diagnostic axis (Data, information; Algorithm, logic; Machine, physics), labeled with the factor it contributes to execution time in equation 1. Each pairwise overlap names the question its two axes must answer jointly (what to learn from, how to move information, and how to execute efficiently). At the center, where all three meet, is ML systems engineering.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
When a training step or serving request runs slower than expected on a single GPU, the first question is whether the time went to moving bytes, executing arithmetic, or waiting on dispatch overhead. The iron law answers that question in two steps. The first step factors execution time along the three D·A·M axes. A task processes some number of samples (examples in vision or tabular workloads, tokens in language models), each sample costs some number of operations, and the machine takes some time to complete each operation. By dimensional cancellation, total execution time \(\Time\) (seconds) is the product of these three factors (equation 1):
\[ \Time = \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Samples}}{\text{Task}}\right)}_{\text{Data (D)}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Sample}}\right)}_{\text{Algorithm (A)}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{\text{Seconds}}{\text{FLOP}}\right)}_{\text{Machine (M)}}  \tag{1}\]
The first two factors fix the total arithmetic work \(\Operations\). Training a model with \(\Parameters\) parameters on \(\DatasetSize\) tokens costs roughly \(6\Parameters\DatasetSize\) operations across the forward and backward passes (equation 4), and inference costs roughly \(2\Parameters\) operations per token in the forward pass. The third factor is the realized time per operation, and no real machine achieves its datasheet value of \(1/\PeakRate\).
The second step explains the gap. Executing an operation requires moving its operands through memory and interconnect, driving the arithmetic units at some realized utilization, and paying fixed control costs. Assuming these three costs occur in sequence, the iron law unpacks execution time into their sum (equation 2):
\[ \Time= \underbrace{ \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} }_{\text{Memory time}} + \underbrace{ \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} }_{\text{Compute time}} + \underbrace{ \Latency }_{\text{Overhead}}  \tag{2}\]
Data enters the two equations in different units. In equation 1, the Data factor counts logical samples or tokens. In equation 2, \(\DataVolume\) counts the physical bytes that cross a memory or interconnect bus, which include model weights, activations, cached sequence state, and gradients as well as the inputs themselves. Batch-1 decode of a language model shows how far apart the two can be. The task processes a single token, yet \(\DataVolume\) spans the gigabytes of weights streamed from high-bandwidth memory to produce it.
Algorithm and Machine share the compute term and are separated by which variable the engineer controls. Reducing the total operations (\(\Operations\)) is an algorithm lever, while improving the hardware’s peak throughput (\(\PeakRate\)) or utilization (\(\EfficiencyHw\)) is a machine lever. The memory term belongs to no single axis. The Data axis sets how many inputs move, the Algorithm axis sets how many weights and activations move with them, and the Machine axis supplies the bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\) that carries them.


The additive iron law represents sequential execution, the worst case where Data, Algorithm, and Machine take turns. Overlap can move the sum toward a max, with perfect overlap defining the ideal lower bound:
\[ \SequentialExecutionTime= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency \quad \xrightarrow{\text{overlap}} \quad \PipelinedExecutionTime\geq \max\left(\frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth},\; \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw}\right) + \Latency \]
The systems engineer’s job is to make these components run in parallel, not in series. Prefetching, separate CUDA streams, asynchronous gradient synchronization, and double buffering each let one axis proceed while another is in flight (table 2).

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
This overlap view still leaves one practical question: whether a workload is waiting on bytes or on FLOPs. The boundary between Data (memory bound) and Machine (compute bound) is not arbitrary; it is defined mathematically by the arithmetic intensity2 (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\)) of the workload.
2 Arithmetic intensity: The ratio of floating-point operations to bytes transferred (FLOP/byte). It determines whether a workload is memory-bound or compute-bound by comparison against the hardware’s ridge point (\(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\)).The symptoms below are screening signals, not diagnoses. A workload whose arithmetic intensity sits left of \(\PeakRate/\Bandwidth\) cannot keep the accelerator fed with enough useful work per byte. Raw utilization must still be read alongside memory-bandwidth utilization, data-loader wait, kernel occupancy, and trace gaps.

Low GPU utilization (\(<\) 80 percent): Screen for data, CPU, or launch starvation. Confirm with data-loader wait, host CPU saturation, memory-bandwidth counters, and timeline gaps.
High GPU utilization (\(>\) 95 percent): Treat this as machine bound only if compute units are busy and memory bandwidth is not saturated. If memory bandwidth is saturated, the bottleneck is still on the Data/Machine boundary.
If batch size is 1: Treat this as a warning that latency or launch overhead may matter. For large language model (LLM) decode, batch-1 execution is often memory-bandwidth bound unless traces show dispatch gaps.
If arithmetic intensity is below the ridge point (about 295.2 FLOP/byte on H100): The workload is likely memory bound (Data/Machine boundary).



Arithmetic intensity is a property of the workload and its implementation, not of the hardware. A large matrix multiply reuses each weight it loads across many multiply-accumulates and so has high intensity. An element-wise operation, or the generation of a single token, uses each loaded value only once or twice. The ridge point belongs to a simple upper bound on single-device throughput, the Roofline Model (Williams et al. 2009). A kernel with arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\), running on a device with peak compute rate \(\PeakRate\) and memory bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\), can attain at most

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[ \AttainableComputeRate(\ArithmeticIntensity) = \min\!\left(\PeakRate,\; \ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth\right)  \tag{3}\]
On log-log axes, the bound is a bandwidth roof of slope one (\(\ArithmeticIntensity\times \Bandwidth\)) that meets a flat compute roof (\(\PeakRate\)) at the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate/\Bandwidth\). Left of the ridge, a kernel is memory bound, and only more bandwidth or fewer bytes per operation raises its ceiling. Right of the ridge, it is compute bound, and only a faster or better-used datapath helps. In D·A·M terms, the bandwidth roof belongs to the Data axis, the compute roof to the Machine axis, and the Algorithm axis decides where on the intensity axis the kernel sits. The roofline is a ceiling, not a prediction. A kernel far below both roofs is limited by something the model omits, such as launch overhead, synchronization, or low occupancy. The H100 Roofline Landscape draws both roofs for an H100 and places decode, prefill, and training workloads against them.
For an H100, the book’s hardware constants give a dense FP16 peak of 989 TFLOP/s and a high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s, which places the ridge at about 295.2 FLOP/byte. Batch-1 decode of a 7-billion-parameter language model stored in 16-bit precision performs about two operations per parameter for each generated token (one multiply and one add). It must read every two-byte weight once, so its intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte. Equation 3 then caps attainable throughput at 3.35 TFLOP/s, roughly 0.3 percent of peak, however well the kernels are written. Serving \(\BatchSize\) sequences in one decode step reuses each loaded weight \(\BatchSize\) times and raises the intensity to roughly \(\BatchSize\) FLOP/byte, until key-value cache traffic, which grows with batch size and context length, begins to dominate the bytes moved. That arithmetic is why batching is the first lever of every serving system. The communication-computation ratio carries the same reasoning to the network, where interconnect bandwidth takes the place of HBM bandwidth.



Each optimization shortens only one term of the iron law, so adding peak FLOP/s to a memory-bound kernel or adding memory bandwidth to a compute-bound kernel leaves step time unchanged while wasting engineering effort (table 3).



Table 3: What Works vs. What Is Wasted: Optimizing the wrong term yields limited improvement and poor cost efficiency. A memory-bound model will not speed up from more peak FLOP/s alone; it needs higher arithmetic intensity, less data movement, or a faster memory subsystem.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
An accelerator is a fast arithmetic engine surrounded by memories that trade bandwidth for capacity, and most performance arguments in this book reduce to the question of which boundary a byte must cross. Nearest the compute units, registers and on-chip shared memory (SRAM) hold the operands of the kernel that is executing, backed by a shared on-chip L2 cache (50 MB on an H100). Beyond the die, HBM holds the model’s working state (80 GB at 3.35 TB/s on an H100). Host memory is reached over PCIe at 64 GB/s per direction, roughly 52× less than HBM, and local NVMe storage sits below host memory.
A kernel whose working set stays on chip runs near arithmetic speed; one that streams operands from HBM is bounded by the roofline above; one that must reach host memory or storage is slower still. The memory wall, the widening gap between arithmetic throughput and the bandwidth that feeds it, is the single-machine form of the constraint that reappears at fleet scale as the network wall. A multi-accelerator node adds a scale-up fabric between devices (NVLink, at 450 GB/s per direction on an H100), and the scale-out network adds tiers beyond the node. Numbers Every Fleet Engineer Should Know tabulates those tiers.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
Four techniques shorten one device’s step without changing the model’s mathematics. Each removes a different cost in the iron law of section 1.2, and each counts as a gain only when a measured trace confirms it. The four differ in which term they remove, what limits them, and what evidence a trace shows (table 4).


Operator fusion combines consecutive operations into one kernel, so an intermediate result stays in registers or shared memory instead of being written to HBM and read back by the next kernel. It shrinks the data volume \(\DataVolume\) of the data term and removes one launch per fused operation from the overhead term \(\Latency\). The common kinds are chains of element-wise operations, an element-wise operation fused with a reduction such as a normalization, and operator-specific fusions such as a matrix multiply that applies its bias and activation before writing its output. Fusion stops paying when the live values of the combined kernel exceed the registers and shared memory available, which lowers occupancy or spills to memory, and when a reduction needs results from every thread block. A trace confirms it with fewer kernels and fewer HBM bytes before the step time falls.



Tiling sizes blocks of a computation to fit on-chip memory, so each operand fetched from HBM feeds many operations and arithmetic intensity rises. IO-aware attention such as FlashAttention applies the idea to attention. It computes the scores block by block, keeping a running maximum and sum for the softmax, so the full matrix of scores between every pair of positions is never written to HBM. The workspace grows linearly with sequence length rather than quadratically. The price is extra rescaling arithmetic and, in training, recomputing the scores in the backward pass. Decode processes one query row per step and has no quadratic intermediate, so its fused attention kernel is a single pass over the KV cache. Tiling reduces \(\DataVolume\) and frees HBM capacity for the KV cache and larger batches.



Graph replay, offered on NVIDIA GPUs as CUDA Graphs, records a stable sequence of kernels and memory copies once and then submits the whole sequence with one request in later steps. It removes the host-dispatch part of \(\Latency\), which matters when many short kernels leave launch gaps between them, as in batch-one decode. A captured graph replays only the shapes, memory addresses, and control flow it recorded, so a server keeps one graph per shape bucket, and decode captures more easily than prefill, whose shapes vary with prompt length. Replay fuses nothing. The same kernels run with the gaps between them removed, which a timeline shows directly.



Graph compilation automates the three levers above. A compiler captures the program as a graph, rewrites and decomposes its operations, fuses them, selects or generates a kernel for each fused group (often by timing candidates, which is called autotuning), and plans memory. Just-in-time compilers keep the eager programming model, ahead-of-time inference engines specialize the program to a declared range of shapes, and tile-level kernel languages let an engineer write a fusion the compiler missed. Compilation reduces both \(\DataVolume\) and \(\Latency\), at the cost of build and warmup time, regions split at graph breaks where the compiler cannot capture the program, and recompilation when a new shape arrives. Compilation builds prices that cost across a fleet and finds when it pays back.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
Whether a large model fits in an 80 GB H100 memory bank or must be partitioned across dozens of accelerators depends on how many bytes each parameter and optimizer state occupies. In the number formats listed in the notation conventions at the front of the book, FP32 occupies 4 bytes, BF16 and FP16 occupy 2, and FP8 and INT8 occupy one. Mixed-precision training runs the forward and backward passes in a 16-bit format for speed and memory, while it keeps an FP32 master copy of the weights so that small updates are not lost to rounding. The Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer adds two FP32 moment estimates per parameter. Table 5 totals the resulting bytes per parameter.

For Archetype A, the 175B-parameter dense model the chapters use as their running instance, the training state is 2.8 TB and a resumable checkpoint is 2.45 TB. A single H100 offers 80 GB of HBM (a binary nameplate, about 85.9 GB in decimal units), so the persistent state alone requires at least 33 devices before a single activation is stored. That floor is why the model state must be partitioned across devices, which Distributed Training develops. Serving the same model needs only the 16-bit weights, 350 GB, plus the key-value cache.
Activations are the other large consumer of training memory. The intermediate tensors that the backward pass needs grow with batch size, sequence length, hidden width, and depth, and for long sequences they can exceed the parameter state. Activation checkpointing stores only selected activations and recomputes the rest during the backward pass, trading additional compute for memory.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
Most worked examples in this book use decoder-only transformers, and three counting rules cover nearly all of their arithmetic. The symbols follow the book’s deep learning notation, with \(\Parameters\) parameters, \(\DatasetSize\) training tokens, \(\LayerCount\) layers, hidden dimension \(\HiddenDimension\), and sequence length \(\SequenceLength\).
Each transformer layer holds four \(\HiddenDimension\times \HiddenDimension\) attention projections and a feed-forward block that expands to \(4\HiddenDimension\) and back, about \(12\HiddenDimension^2\) weights in total. A model thus has roughly \(\Parameters\approx 12 \LayerCount \HiddenDimension^2\) parameters excluding embeddings. GPT-3 has \(\LayerCount =\) 96 and \(\HiddenDimension=\) 12,288, which gives 173.9B against its published 175B.
Every weight contributes one multiply and one add per token, so a forward pass costs about \(2\Parameters\) FLOPs per token. The backward pass computes gradients with respect to both activations and weights and costs about twice the forward pass, so training costs about \(6\Parameters\) FLOPs per token and
\[ \TrainingCompute \approx 6\Parameters \DatasetSize \tag{4}\]
in total. For GPT-3, trained on 300 billion tokens, equation 4 gives 3.15 × 10²³ FLOPs, within 1 percent of the reported 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs. The rule omits the attention-score products, which add at most about \(\SequenceLength/(6\HiddenDimension)\) to the weight FLOPs, or 2.8 percent for GPT-3 at \(\SequenceLength=\) 2,048. That fraction stays small while the context is short compared with the hidden width and grows with long contexts.
Serving an autoregressive model has two phases with different physics. Prefill processes the whole prompt at once as matrix-matrix products, so its arithmetic intensity is high and it tends to be compute bound. Decode generates one token per step for each sequence as matrix-vector products; at batch size 1 it reads every weight to perform two FLOPs per weight, the memory-bound regime that the roofline example above quantifies. To avoid recomputing attention over the whole prefix at every step, decode stores each layer’s keys and values in a key-value (KV) cache of \(2 \LayerCount \HiddenDimension\, \ElementStorageSize\) bytes per token for standard multihead attention, or 4.72 MB per token for GPT-3 in FP16. KV cache fundamentals sizes that cache against device memory.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
These single-node grades become most useful when they are carried forward into distributed design. The D·A·M taxonomy is the diagnostic baseline for a single machine, but as systems scale from a single node to the machine learning fleet, each axis undergoes a qualitative transformation.


Crossing the node boundary replaces local bus limits and single-device failure rates with cluster-wide fabric and power limits. Scaling from one node to a fleet changes the kind of constraint on every axis, not only its size (table 8).

While D·A·M diagnoses the components of a single node, the C\(^3\) taxonomy (The C^3 Taxonomy) diagnoses the interactions of the fleet. Each of its three dimensions inherits a specific piece of the single-machine diagnostic model:

Compute (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_1\)) inherits the Algorithm and Machine axes, now evaluated per device after the work is partitioned across \(\DeviceCount\) devices.
Communication (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_2\)) inherits the Data axis, but is governed by network bandwidth, topology, and, over long distances, the speed of light rather than by local I/O alone.
Coordination (\(\OperationalTaxonomyDimension_3\)) makes coordination costs explicit at fleet scale. Synchronization, checkpoints, and failure recovery also occur on one node, but distribution expands their scope and couples them to other machines.

This progression exposes cases where higher single-node MFU comes at the expense of scaling efficiency, so the complete fleet outcome can determine the choice. The node is optimized to serve the fleet.

title: Single-Machine Foundations
text:
The D·A·M taxonomy provides the diagnostic baseline for every ML systems analysis. By isolating the bottleneck to Data, Algorithm, or Machine, practitioners ensure that optimization efforts target the binding constraint. The memory hierarchy, the byte accounting of mixed-precision training, and the transformer counting rules supply the quantities that fleet-scale arguments take as given. This single-node discipline is the prerequisite for the fleet-scale engineering addressed throughout this book.

Key Takeaways: Single-machine diagnostic heuristics

Identify the dominant axis: Decide whether Data, Algorithm, or Machine is the binding constraint before proposing any optimization.
Profile arithmetic intensity: Arithmetic intensity, read against the roofline’s ridge point, quantitatively distinguishes between Data-bound and Machine-bound regimes.
Use the iron law: The iron law transforms vague symptoms into specific term-based bottlenecks.
Count bytes and FLOPs per parameter: Mixed-precision Adam training holds 16 bytes per parameter (14 in a checkpoint), and dense transformer training costs about \(6\Parameters \DatasetSize\) FLOPs. These two rules size most memory and compute budgets in the chapters.
Grade with the scorecard: The Data-Algorithm-Machine scorecard standardizes “good” performance before moving to fleet scale.

title: Foundations recap
text:
How to Use This Appendix
This appendix is designed as a reference when translating fleet-scale design questions into specific physical constraints and identifying available optimization levers. The five routing bullets below map common engineering questions to the sections that follow.

When evaluating inter-node communication: Consult section 1.2 for the bandwidth and latency hierarchy.
When sizing GPU allocations: Consult section 1.3 to analyze why doubling accelerator counts does not halve training time.
When calculating cluster reliability: Check section 1.2 for mean time between failures (MTBF) tables and failure probability models.
When evaluating power and cooling limits: Consult section 1.4 for power density ceilings and cooling constraints.
When budgeting runtime overhead: Use section 1.2 for the four overhead categories that erode useful wall time.

title: Foundations recap
text:
The Three System Paradigms
Machine learning infrastructure at scale inherits design DNA from two distinct computing lineages and then breaks the assumptions of both. A designer must understand where ML systems borrow from high-performance computing (HPC) and where they borrow from warehouse-scale computing (WSC) to choose the right design trade-offs. A system architect who treats ML training as “just HPC” will build infrastructure that cannot tolerate failures. One who treats it as “just web services” will build infrastructure that cannot sustain the tight coupling that synchronous training demands.

High-performance computing
HPC systems descend from the supercomputer tradition, where the design goal is to maximize FLOP/s on tightly coupled simulations such as weather modeling, molecular dynamics, and nuclear physics. Because every node participates in lockstep, these clusters rely on specialized interconnects (InfiniBand), low-latency fabrics, and homogeneous hardware. Their fault tolerance follows the checkpoint/restart model: if one node fails, the entire job stops, rolls back to the last checkpoint, and resumes from that saved state. Batch schedulers such as Slurm allocate rigid resource shapes (“512 nodes for 24 hours”), treating nodes as individually tracked “pets.”


Warehouse-scale computing
WSC systems descend from the web services tradition, aiming instead to maximize queries per second across loosely coupled services such as search, email, and social media. Because requests are independent, these fleets mix hardware generations over commodity Ethernet and rely on redundancy for fault tolerance: when a node fails, a load balancer reroutes traffic to another replica without the user noticing. Dynamic schedulers such as Kubernetes and Borg bin-pack workloads elastically across interchangeable, expendable “cattle” nodes.


The ML fleet as hybrid architecture
ML systems require the computational throughput of HPC to train large models with synchronous gradient updates, yet they must operate at the scale and failure rates of WSC, where thousands of accelerators run for weeks. This tension produces a hybrid architecture that borrows selectively from both lineages.
Training workloads are synchronous and bandwidth-hungry like HPC jobs, whereas long-running fleet operations demand WSC-style fault tolerance, and inference workloads reverse the blend by pairing WSC latency sensitivity with HPC compute density. To serve both regimes, the network fuses TCP/IP control planes with InfiniBand or NVLink data planes. Fault tolerance combines checkpoint/restart with elastic training strategies where supported, which allow jobs to adjust resource allocations even when resharding, state restoration, or worker restarts remain necessary. Scheduling pairs all-or-nothing gang allocation for training with dynamic preemption and replacement. ML fleets therefore cannot adopt either HPC or WSC patterns wholesale; they combine elements from each according to the workload phase, as the design trade-offs across the three paradigms in table 1 show.



Table 1: Three System Paradigms: ML fleets inherit design DNA from both HPC and WSC but break assumptions of each. Training resembles HPC (tight coupling), inference resembles WSC (elastic serving), and fault tolerance is a hybrid of both.
