For any cluster above a few thousand GPUs running jobs longer than a day, the probability of experiencing at least one failure is effectively 100 percent. This is why Fault Tolerance treats fault tolerance as an architectural requirement rather than a defensive measure.
The exponential failure model assumes a constant failure rate, which holds during the steady-state useful-life phase. During burn-in (first few hundred hours) and wear-out (approaching end-of-life), failure rates are higher. In practice, fleet operators observe that newly deployed nodes show 2–3\(\times\) higher failure rates in their first week, making burn-in testing essential before admitting nodes to production clusters. Because failures will interrupt long training jobs, the practical question is how to minimize the lost progress.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
On a 10,000-GPU cluster that fails every few hours, pausing all 10,000 accelerators to flush a multi-terabyte state snapshot to shared storage stalls training, yet spacing snapshots hours apart sacrifices thousands of GPU-hours of progress whenever a node drops out. Choosing a checkpoint cadence therefore trades guaranteed write overhead against expected rework after a crash (Young 1974; Daly 2006).

Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.


During a synchronous checkpoint, writing state to storage takes time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (the checkpoint cost), during which no useful training occurs. Extending the interval between checkpoints amortizes that pause, but a failure that arrives at a random point inside the interval destroys on average half the interval’s work. Equation 7 states the Young-Daly formula that minimizes the sum of those two expected losses:
\[ \OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \times \CheckpointWriteTime \times \SystemMtbf}  \tag{7}\]
where \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is the checkpoint write time in seconds and \(\SystemMtbf\) is the cluster or job-level system MTBF in seconds.
The intuition behind equation 7 is geometric-mean-like. When checkpoints are cheap relative to the MTBF (\(\CheckpointWriteTime \ll \SystemMtbf\), the common case), the optimal interval sits between the two time scales. If checkpoints took zero time, the optimal cadence would be every step. If the system never failed, no checkpoints would be required. The square root interpolates between those extremes.
The formula assumes that failures follow an exponential distribution (memoryless property) and that checkpoint cost \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) is small compared to \(\SystemMtbf\). Correlated outages, changing hazard rates, long writes, and asynchronous persistence can require a more detailed model. Under the first-order assumptions, evaluating equation 7 for a concrete model requires only the cluster MTBF and the write duration \(\CheckpointWriteTime\), which is set by the serialized state volume and storage bandwidth.



Resuming a mixed-precision training run after a node failure requires restoring not only the low-precision weights used in the forward pass, but also the full-precision master weights and optimizer moments accumulated across prior steps, which multiplies the serialized footprint and sets the write time \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) in equation 7. For common mixed-precision training checkpoints with the adaptive moment estimation (Adam) optimizer, each parameter requires approximately 14 bytes of persistent state:

2 bytes for BF16 model weights
4 bytes for FP32 master weights
4 bytes for FP32 first moment (Adam \(\AdamFirstMoment\))
4 bytes for FP32 second moment (Adam \(\AdamSecondMoment\))

Equation 8 aggregates these per-parameter costs into the total checkpoint footprint. The resulting byte volume scales linearly with model parameter count:
\[ \text{Checkpoint Size} = \Parameters\times 14 \text{ bytes/parameter}  \tag{8}\]
Here, \(\Parameters\) is the number of trainable model parameters whose persistent optimizer and weight state must be serialized. Transient activation buffers and unsharded temporary workspaces are excluded because they are recomputed after restore.
Mixed-precision Adam checkpoint sizing (table 4) demonstrates how state scales from manageable gigabytes to frontier-scale terabytes. Even with high-bandwidth parallel storage, serializing these footprints requires tens of seconds to several minutes per snapshot:

At frontier scale (175B+ parameters), these sizes reach the terabyte range. This makes checkpoint write time a significant cost that directly affects the Young-Daly optimal interval. The checkpoint strategies in Fault Tolerance discuss techniques for reducing \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) (asynchronous checkpointing, incremental deltas, and distributed storage), all of which improve the Young-Daly result by shrinking the \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) factor under the square root.



Combining the checkpoint write time with the 10,000-GPU MTBF gives a concrete checkpoint cadence. The worked example below walks through the two-step calculation and shows how doubling the cluster size shifts the optimum.

Napkin Math 1.1: Young-Daly: 175B model on a 10,000-GPU clusterSetup: Consider training a 175B-parameter model on a 10,000-GPU cluster. The cluster MTBF is 3.75 hours (table 2). The checkpoint size is 2,450 GB, and the parallel storage system writes at 100 GB/s.
Step 1: Checkpoint write time (\(\CheckpointWriteTime\)). \[T_{\text{write}} = \frac{\text{Checkpoint Size}}{\text{Write Bandwidth}} = \frac{2,450 \text{ GB}}{100 \text{ GB/s}} = 24.5 \text{ s}\]
Step 2: Apply the Young-Daly formula (equation 7). \[T^\ast_{\text{ckpt}} = \sqrt{2 \times T_{\text{write}} \times \text{MTBF}_{\text{system}}} = \sqrt{2 \times 24.5 \text{ s} \times 3.75 \text{ h} \times 3{,}600 \text{ s/h}} = 13.6 \text{ min}\]
Interpretation: The optimal checkpoint interval is approximately 14 minutes. The overhead from checkpointing alone is \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\OptimalCheckpointInterval \approx\) 3.0 percent of training time.
Systems insight: If the cluster were doubled to 20,000 GPUs, the MTBF would halve and the optimal interval would shrink to 9.6 minutes. The system therefore checkpoints more frequently because failures happen more often. Larger clusters are faster but must interrupt themselves more often to protect progress, which is the tension at scale.


When \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) approaches \(\SystemMtbf\) (checkpoint cost approaches MTBF), checkpoint and rework overheads become so large that checkpoint/restart alone may fail to maintain useful forward progress, requiring the alternative strategies in section 1.4.1. Even when \(\CheckpointWriteTime \ll \SystemMtbf\), the Young-Daly cadence prices only the periodic write pause and the average step replay after a fault; a real cluster outage also stalls on failure detection, node replacement, and checkpoint reload before replay can begin.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
When a node drops out of a 10,000-GPU training step, every surviving accelerator idles while the control plane times out the dead heartbeat, allocates a replacement node, streams terabytes of checkpoint state back into GPU memory, and recomputes the steps lost since the last snapshot. Pricing how much wall-clock capacity those interruptions consume requires decomposing the outage into its constituent phases and translating the total stall time into runtime goodput.


A single hardware fault triggers four sequential recovery phases between the instant a worker stalls and the moment the job returns to new training steps. Equation 9 sums them into total recovery time:
\[ \TotalFailureRecoveryTime= \FailureDetectionTime+ \JobRestartTime + \CheckpointLoadTime + \LostWorkReplayTime \tag{9}\]
The terms are all durations: failure detection, replacement scheduling, checkpoint reload, and replay of lost training work since the last checkpoint. Their sum is the wall-clock time before the job returns to productive training.
Table 5 breaks recovery into the phases that determine how long the cluster remains below full productivity after a failure. Because detection, rescheduling, checkpoint reload, and replay appear as separate rows, the table shows which operational bottlenecks dominate total downtime.

In this sequence, replay time \(\LostWorkReplayTime\) typically dominates and is controlled directly by the checkpoint interval, since on average half the interval must be replayed. This creates a reinforcing loop with the Young-Daly formula. Shorter intervals mean less replay but more checkpoint overhead, and the formula finds the minimum of this sum. The other phases offer distinct engineering levers. More aggressive heartbeat intervals shorten \(\FailureDetectionTime\), at the cost of false positives. Preallocated hot spare nodes shorten \(\JobRestartTime\) through the fleet orchestration policies covered in Fleet Orchestration. Higher storage bandwidth or smaller checkpoints shorten \(\CheckpointLoadTime\), which motivates the compression and sharding techniques discussed in Fault Tolerance.



Every minute a cluster spends writing a periodic snapshot or executing the four-phase recovery pipeline of table 5 is billed wall-clock allocation that advances the final model by zero training steps. Comparing the committed step rate (the steps a checkpoint retains for the final model) against the fault-free step rate (the rate the configured cluster could sustain without checkpoint or recovery interruptions) defines the runtime goodput of a job whose only losses are checkpoints and failures:
\[ \RuntimeGoodput \approx \frac{\text{Committed Useful-Step Rate}}{\text{Fault-Free Step Rate}} \approx \frac{\UsefulTrainingTime}{\AllocatedWallTime} \]
Runtime Goodput defines runtime goodput as one factor of ML goodput and also charges startup and input stalls to it, which this appendix does not model. The modeled gap between the two rates comes from two sources:

Checkpoint overhead (\(\sim\) 3.0 percent): Training pauses during each checkpoint write.
Recovery and rework overhead (\(\sim\) 3.9 percent): Time lost to detection, rescheduling, reloading, and replaying work discarded after each failure.

At 10,000-GPU scale, failures and checkpointing together can consume a substantial fraction of wall time. If they consume a fraction \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\), a fixed amount of useful work takes \(1/(1-\OperationalOverheadFraction)\) times its fault-free duration, not merely that duration plus \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) of it. The fleet orchestration strategies in Fleet Orchestration and ML Operations at Scale focus on narrowing this gap, because every percentage point of overhead recovered saves dollars and shortens training time.

Systems Perspective 1.1: The hidden cost of scaleA common misconception is that doubling cluster size halves training time. In practice, doubling from 5,000 to 10,000 GPUs halves the MTBF and increases failure-related overhead. The effective speedup is less than 2\(\times\), and at extreme scale, adding more GPUs can actually increase wall-clock time if the fault tolerance mechanisms cannot keep pace. The serial overhead of recovery bounds the benefit of parallelism, a reliability analogue of Amdahl’s Law.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Pausing a 10,000-GPU batch training job for several minutes to reload a checkpoint and replay lost steps is an acceptable throughput tax, whereas stalling a live inference service for even a few seconds violates user-facing latency contracts and drops production traffic. Because batch training and online serving tolerate interruption on completely different time scales, fleet architectures choose among checkpoint/restart, active redundancy, and elastic resizing according to the recovery latency, spare capacity, and state-management complexity each workload can afford.


Whether a fault-tolerance mechanism can pause the entire job to replay work, must fail over within milliseconds, or must continue on a shrunk allocation when replacement nodes are unavailable separates the three primary recovery architectures. Checkpoint/restart periodically saves full system state and rolls back to the last checkpoint after failure. It is the workhorse of large-scale training: conceptually simple, well-understood, and effective when MTBF is much larger than checkpoint cost. The weakness is that recovery requires stopping all workers and replaying lost computation.
Redundancy maintains alternate copies of state or computation. A surviving serving replica can take over only when routing, readiness, capacity, and the required request state meet the latency budget. Dedicated duplicate or triplicate execution costs 2–3\(\times\) the compute resources; active-active serving instead shares normal traffic across replicas while reserving failover headroom. The justified overhead depends on the workload and recovery contract.
Elastic training allows a job to resume with fewer workers when the smaller allocation can hold its state and support its parallel decomposition. Membership changes can still require a coordinated restart and checkpoint reload; TorchElastic restarts the worker group. Workers may be added back when capacity becomes available. The recovery path must restore missing shards, preserve data coverage, and either preserve the effective batch size or validate a changed optimization policy. Elasticity can reduce waiting for replacement capacity, but does not guarantee a shorter interruption. The three strategies trade recovery latency against resource overhead and implementation complexity, and each fits a different workload (table 6).



Table 6: Fault Tolerance Strategy Comparison: The latency and overhead ranges are illustrative, not guarantees; elasticity does not by itself require spare capacity. Real-world systems often combine strategies: checkpoint/restart for training with redundancy for the metadata service and checkpoint storage layer.

A single serving replica with 99 percent availability (“two nines”) still accumulates more than 87 hours of downtime per year, far exceeding the outage budget of production inference endpoints that target 99.9 percent (“three nines”) or 99.99 percent (“four nines”) uptime. Redundancy closes that gap by running \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) independent replicas so that surviving instances absorb traffic when one replica fails. Under an idealized model with reliable routing and enough capacity on any surviving replica, the system is unavailable only when all replicas are simultaneously down. Equation 10 captures this, with \(\ReplicaAvailability\) denoting the availability of a single replica and \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) the number of replicas:
\[ \RedundantServiceAvailability= 1 - (1 - \ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount  \tag{10}\]
Evaluating availability stacking with independent replicas (table 7) quantifies the gain from adding serving capacity. Each additional independent replica multiplies the outage probabilities together, cutting expected annual downtime by two orders of magnitude per replica at a 99 percent baseline.

Stacking independent redundant replicas achieves large availability gains. Two replicas that are each available 99 percent of the time yield 99.99 percent availability, reducing annual downtime from 87.6 hours to 52.6 minutes. This is why inference serving systems almost universally deploy multiple replicas behind a load balancer. The cost of an extra replica is small compared to the business value of four-nines availability.
The result, however, depends on the independence assumption. Correlated failures, such as power outages affecting an entire rack, software bugs triggered by a specific input, or network partitions isolating a failure domain, defeat availability stacking. This is why Fault Tolerance emphasizes failure domain isolation: replicas must be placed in different racks, different power zones, and ideally different data centers to reduce shared failure modes. Placement alone does not eliminate common software, control-plane, or regional dependencies.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
When a multi-terabyte checkpoint takes several minutes to flush to shared storage and a 100,000-GPU cluster fails every half hour, the checkpoint write is no longer negligible next to the failure interval. The cluster can then suffer a second crash while still writing the snapshot. Young’s first-order approximation is most accurate when checkpoint time is small relative to the failure interval; Daly’s analysis develops higher-order checkpoint models for regimes where write time is a substantial fraction of MTBF (Daly 2006). The simplified renewal model below shows why finite checkpoint time changes the optimum without claiming to reproduce Daly’s full recovery model.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.


Suppose a worker fails halfway through flushing a 60-second checkpoint snapshot; the job loses both the training steps computed since the previous snapshot and the 30 seconds spent writing the incomplete checkpoint. Let \(\CheckpointInterval\) be useful compute time between completed checkpoints. Assume Poisson failures with rate \(1/\SystemMtbf\), identical failure exposure during computation and writing, and zero detection, restart, or reload delay. A failed attempt loses its partial progress and repeats the interval. The expected elapsed time to complete one uninterrupted compute-plus-checkpoint attempt is:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] = \SystemMtbf \left( e^{\frac{\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime}{\SystemMtbf}} - 1 \right)  \tag{11}\]
Writing \(\CheckpointAttemptDuration= \CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime\) for the attempt duration, the renewal equation is \(\mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] = \mathbb{E}[\min(\NextFailureTime, \CheckpointAttemptDuration)] + \Pr(\NextFailureTime< \CheckpointAttemptDuration) \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime]\), where \(\NextFailureTime\) is an exponential failure time. Since \(\mathbb{E}[\min(\NextFailureTime, \CheckpointAttemptDuration)] = \SystemMtbf (1 - e^{-\CheckpointAttemptDuration/\SystemMtbf})\), solving the equation gives equation 11. Expanding the exponential through its quadratic term then gives the wasted time per completed interval:
\[ \mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime] - \CheckpointInterval \approx \CheckpointWriteTime + \frac{(\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)^2}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf}  \tag{12}\]
When \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf\) is small, dividing equation 12 by \(\CheckpointInterval\) leaves the leading terms \(\CheckpointWriteTime/\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointInterval/(2 \cdot \SystemMtbf)\) of the wasted-time fraction. Minimizing those terms recovers Young’s interval \(\sqrt{2 \cdot \CheckpointWriteTime \cdot \SystemMtbf}\). For finite checkpoint costs, differentiate the unexpanded elapsed time per unit useful work, \(\mathbb{E}[\IntervalCompletionTime]/\CheckpointInterval\), instead. Its stationary point satisfies:
\[ e^{(\OptimalCheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)/\SystemMtbf}\left(1 - \frac{\OptimalCheckpointInterval}{\SystemMtbf}\right) = 1, \qquad 0 < \OptimalCheckpointInterval < \SystemMtbf  \tag{13}\]
For positive checkpoint cost, the equivalent derivative numerator \(e^{(\CheckpointInterval + \CheckpointWriteTime)/\SystemMtbf}(\CheckpointInterval/\SystemMtbf - 1) + 1\) increases from a negative value at zero to a positive value at \(\SystemMtbf\). A one-dimensional root search on equation 13 therefore finds the unique optimum of this simplified model.


The first-order formula is a useful planning estimate when writes are short compared with MTBF. When that condition fails, use a model that includes the deployment’s checkpoint semantics, recovery delays, and failure exposure. The numerical condition in equation 13 covers only the stated zero-restart-delay renewal model; asynchronous writes and correlated failures require different assumptions. All of these checkpoint and redundancy models assume that a hardware fault announces itself by stopping a worker or failing a health check, yet some of the most damaging faults at fleet scale corrupt tensor values silently without halting execution.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Not all hardware faults manifest as explicit system crashes, ECC double-bit errors, or kernel traps. Silent data corruption (SDC) occurs when single-bit errors or arithmetic logic unit (ALU) faults slip past parity checks, corrupting tensor values in SRAM, high-bandwidth memory (HBM), or register files without triggering an exception. In deep learning workloads, SDC is particularly dangerous because single corrupted floating-point values propagate through non-linear operations, destabilizing fleet-wide training (Dixit et al. 2021).

Dixit, H. D., S. Pendharkar, M. Beadon, C. Mason, T. Chakravarthy, B. Muthiah, and S. Sankar. 2021. Silent Data Corruptions at Scale. arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.11245.


Consider an IEEE 754 half-precision floating-point (FP16) tensor element representing a query entry \(\QueryComponent\), activation value, or weight matrix entry. FP16 allocates 16 total bits: 1 sign bit (\(\FloatSignBit\)), 5 exponent bits (\(\FloatExponentField\)), and 10 mantissa bits (\(\FloatMantissaField\)). For a finite normal value, with exponent field \(1 \le \FloatExponentField\le 30\), the scalar \(\FloatEncodedNumber\) represented by the bitstring \((\FloatSignBit, \FloatExponentField, \FloatMantissaField)\) is given by:
\[ \FloatEncodedNumber= (-1)^\FloatSignBit\times 2^{\FloatExponentField- 15} \times \left(1 + \frac{\FloatMantissaField}{1024}\right) \]
Suppose a cosmic ray, voltage drop, or SRAM failure causes a single bit flip in the most significant exponent bit (bit 14). The exponent value changes from \(\FloatExponentField\) to \(\FlippedFloatExponentField = \FloatExponentField\pm 16\):
\[ \BitFlippedFloatNumber= (-1)^\FloatSignBit\times 2^{(\FloatExponentField\pm 16) - 15} \times \left(1 + \frac{\FloatMantissaField}{1024}\right) = \FloatEncodedNumber\times 2^{\pm 16} \]
If both the original and corrupted exponent fields encode finite normal values, the magnitude increases by a factor of \(2^{16}=65{,}536\) or decreases by its reciprocal. Exponent fields of zero or all ones instead invoke the subnormal, zero, infinity, or NaN encodings, so the displayed normal-value formula does not apply.



When a single-bit exponent flip inflates one query entry by a factor of \(65{,}536\), the dot products in that token’s attention row can jump by orders of magnitude and collapse its softmax distribution onto a single key. To trace how that perturbation propagates through one attention head, let \(\AttentionScoreMatrix = \AttentionQueryMatrix\AttentionKeyMatrix^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension} \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength\times \SequenceLength}\) be the pre-softmax score matrix for sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) and head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\). Suppose an SDC event corrupts one element of token row \(\MatrixRowIndex\) of the query matrix \(\AttentionQueryMatrix\), and write the resulting perturbation as \(\FiniteChange\AttentionQueryMatrix\), with only that element nonzero:
\[ \CorruptedAttentionScoreMatrix = \frac{(\AttentionQueryMatrix+ \FiniteChange\AttentionQueryMatrix) \AttentionKeyMatrix^T}{\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}} = \AttentionScoreMatrix + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreMatrix \]
where \(\FiniteChange\AttentionScoreMatrix\) is nonzero only in row \(\MatrixRowIndex\), with entries \(\FiniteChange \AttentionScoreEntry = \FiniteChange\QueryVector_i \cdot \KeyVector_j/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension}\) for the corrupted query row \(\FiniteChange\QueryVector_i\) and key row \(\KeyVector_j\). Passing the perturbed score row through the normalization step shifts the entire row’s attention weights. The attention probability perturbation for token row \(\MatrixRowIndex\) is therefore:
\[ \FiniteChange\AttentionWeightVector_i = \operatorname{softmax}\left( \AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow \right) - \operatorname{softmax}\left( \AttentionScoreRow \right) \]
A large corrupted query component can strongly change several attention logits, with the signs and magnitudes determined by the corresponding key components. If one resulting logit exceeds every other logit by an increasingly large margin, the attention distribution approaches a one-hot vector:
\[ \operatorname{softmax}(\AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow)_j \to 1, \qquad \operatorname{softmax}(\AttentionScoreRow + \FiniteChange\AttentionScoreRow)_{k \neq j} \to 0 \]
This is a conditional saturation limit, not an inevitable consequence of a bit flip. The selected key depends on the corrupted logits; a corrupted query element does not identify one corrupted key. The softmax derivative is \(\partial \SoftmaxOutputProbability_j/\partial \AttentionScoreSummand = \SoftmaxOutputProbability_j(\KroneckerIndicator_{jk}-\SoftmaxOutputProbability_k)\), which tends toward zero under saturation rather than diverging. Other paths through the computation can still produce large or nonfinite activations and gradients. If invalid state enters the optimizer or a collective, it can propagate across ranks. Detection and recovery must therefore verify state before resuming from a clean checkpoint.

title: Reliability Foundations
text:
Failure is a physical constraint of scale. Under independent, constant component failure rates, a single GPU’s mean lifetime is 5.7 years. Yet the modeled 10,000-GPU cluster fails on average every 3.75 hours, because node failure rates sum across components and cluster MTBF divides by node count. The probability that a job is interrupted grows with its duration relative to that interval, so long runs on large clusters must plan for recovery rather than hope to avoid it.
Recovery has four modeled phases (detection, rescheduling, reloading, and replay), and replay is controlled by the checkpoint interval. The Young-Daly formula \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval = \sqrt{2 \CheckpointWriteTime \, \SystemMtbf}\) (principle \(\ref{pri-young-daly}\)) balances write overhead against expected rework when writes are short compared with the MTBF. Section 1.5 examines finite-cost effects under a simplified renewal model. Checkpoint/restart suits batch training, redundancy suits latency-sensitive serving, and elastic training sits between them. Independent replicas reduce unavailability multiplicatively, to \((1-\ReplicaAvailability)^\RedundantReplicaCount\) for \(\RedundantReplicaCount\) replicas, but only to the extent that failure-domain isolation keeps their failures independent.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Every quantitative example in this book, from cluster failure rates to collective-communication costs to carbon footprint estimates, uses a specific set of assumed numbers: canonical cluster sizes, fabric bandwidths, accelerator reliability, power usage effectiveness, regional carbon intensity, and model utilization ranges. This appendix collects those fleet-scale assumptions in one place so the book’s arithmetic can be audited, checked against chapter napkin math, or substituted into worked examples.


Use this appendix to verify a fleet-scale estimate, swap in an alternative assumption (for example, NDR vs. HDR fabric, Quebec vs. Poland carbon intensity, or a different model FLOPs utilization (MFU)), or identify which numerical constants a chapter calculation depends on. Locate the relevant section, read the Value and Unit columns, and substitute those values into target arithmetic:

When auditing or substituting the baseline 175B training job: Use section 1.1 and the Foundational Hardware Recap section.
When scaling a calculation across cluster sizes or network fabrics: Use the Cluster Reference Configurations, Network and Interconnect Specifications, and Communication Model Parameters sections.
When estimating failure frequency or recovery downtime: Use the component lifetime and recovery tables in the Reliability Assumptions section.
When pricing power, water, carbon, or cloud infrastructure: Use the Sustainability Assumptions and Economic Assumptions sections.
When discounting peak FLOP/s to delivered throughput or checking units and sources: Use the Capacity Planning Assumptions and Unit Conventions sections, and trace each constant’s evidence class in section 1.2.

Three worked estimates in napkin math 1.1 combine these constants to calculate cluster failure rate, AllReduce time, and monthly carbon footprint. Hardware and link bandwidths are ceilings unless a chapter states an effective-bandwidth discount; treat the tables as this edition’s shared assumption sheet rather than immutable physical laws.

Napkin Math 1.1: Quick calculations with these assumptionsThese tables support quick distributed-systems napkin math. Three examples show how several assumptions combine.
Problem: How many GPU failures should a large training cluster expect per day?
Variables: Use a cluster of 8,192 GPUs and an individual GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours.
Math: The GPU failure rate is 8,192 GPUs/50,000 hours \(\approx\) 0.16 failures/hour, or roughly 3.9 failures/day.
Result: This estimate excludes network interface card (NIC), PSU, and cable failures. At 100,000 GPUs, the GPU-only rate is approximately 48 failures/day; adding NIC, PSU, and cable failures, whose MTTFs appear in table 6, raises the operational incident stream further.
Systems insight: At fleet scale, failure becomes a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event.
Problem: How long does one AllReduce of the gradients of a 70B model take?
Variables: Use BF16 parameters and InfiniBand NDR with a nominal byte rate of 50 GB/s per port.
Math: The gradient payload is 70 \(\times 10^9 \times\) 2 bytes = 140 GB. The ring AllReduce napkin estimate is 2 \(\times\) 140 GB/50 GB/s \(\approx\) 5.6 s.
Result: The collective can consume a significant fraction of a training step.
Systems insight: Pipeline and tensor parallelism exist partly to shrink the gradient volume each rank must communicate.
Problem: What is the monthly carbon footprint of a 10,000-GPU training run, and how much does the grid change it?
Variables: Each H100 draws 700 W at thermal design power (TDP). Use power usage effectiveness (PUE) 1.12, Quebec grid intensity 20 g/kWh, and Poland grid intensity 820 g/kWh.
Math: A GPU-only facility-power proxy is 10,000 GPUs \(\times\) 700 W \(\times\) 1.12 = 7.84 MW. In Quebec, 7.84 MW \(\times\) 720 h/month \(\times\) 20 g/kWh = 112.9 t CO\(_2\) per month.
Result: The same run in Poland emits 4,628.7 t, a 41× difference.
Systems insight: Grid carbon intensity can dominate the emissions difference for the same hardware, model, and training duration. This proxy excludes host, memory, network, and storage power; total IT power must include those loads before applying PUE for a complete facility estimate.

The relationship between cluster size and system behavior is not linear. A 256-GPU cluster might go days between failures; a 100,000-GPU cluster experiences multiple failures per hour. This nonlinearity is why Fault Tolerance and Fleet Orchestration treat failure as a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event. The network fabric determines whether gradient synchronization across those nodes takes milliseconds or seconds and whether pipeline parallelism is viable across node boundaries.



Distributed training and inference are bottlenecked by data movement between machines as often as by computation within them. The network assumptions fix bandwidth and latency for every interconnect tier, from NVLink/PCIe within a node (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020; Choquette 2023), through InfiniBand, remote direct memory access (RDMA), and Ethernet fabrics (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000; Gangidi et al. 2024; NVIDIA 2026; Ethernet Alliance 2025), to the speed-of-light WAN floor (physics identity).


Splitting a single transformer layer across eight GPUs inside a server requires an all-reduce on every forward and backward pass, which is viable at hundreds of gigabytes per second over NVLink but stalls over a host PCIe bus. Cross-region communication introduces latency floors set by the speed of light in optical fiber. For a 5,000 km link (roughly New York to London), the minimum one-way latency is 5,000 km/200,000 km/s = 25 ms, orders of magnitude higher than intra-data-center latency. This physical constraint is why geo-distributed training uses asynchronous methods or careful placement of pipeline stages, and why federated learning (Edge Intelligence) tolerates stale gradients. Network specifications define how fast data moves across links and regions, but a multi-thousand-node training job can sustain those transfer rates only while every participating accelerator, network card, and switch remains healthy.




At fleet scale, component failures are statistical certainties rather than exceptional events. The reliability assumptions here fix MTTF for each major component class in a data-center GPU node and the time to detect and recover from failures. These values drive analysis in Fault Tolerance and scheduling in Fleet Orchestration. Deeper failure modeling appears in Reliability Foundations.

Compute, network, and reliability constants determine how long a training or serving job runs on the cluster; operating that cluster in a real data center also requires budgeting the electrical power, cooling water, and grid carbon consumed by the surrounding facility.




The environmental impact of fleet-scale ML depends on three factors: how much power the facility draws beyond the IT equipment (PUE), how much water the cooling system consumes (water usage effectiveness (WUE)), and how much carbon the local grid emits per kilowatt-hour. Pricing an accelerator-hour settles what a cluster allocation costs per unit of wall time, but converting that hourly spend into delivered training progress requires discounting datasheet peak FLOP/s by kernel utilization, multi-node scaling efficiency, and operational downtime.



Multiplying a cluster’s GPU count by the H100’s datasheet peak FLOP/s overstates delivered training throughput by more than a factor of three, because single-device kernel inefficiency, multi-node communication stalls, and out-of-step operational downtime each take a cut. The capacity-planning assumptions quantify the fraction of peak hardware performance that real workloads sustain on one device (MFU), how efficiently that performance scales as more machines are added (scaling efficiency), and what share of wall time is lost to operational pauses. Because these factors compound across the fleet, the planning equation is multiplicative:
\[ \EffectiveFleetThroughput = \DeviceCount\PeakRate \times \ModelFlopsUtilization \times \ScalingEfficiency \times (1 - \OperationalOverheadFraction) \]
Here \(\EffectiveFleetThroughput\) is effective fleet throughput, \(\DeviceCount\PeakRate\) is nominal cluster peak throughput. MFU is the single-device baseline measured over productive steps. \(\ScalingEfficiency\) captures the additional in-step losses from distribution, including communication and pipeline bubbles. \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) removes only out-of-step checkpoint, recovery, and maintenance time. These windows must be disjoint: measured fleet-step MFU already includes scaling losses, so it must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again. The three subsections that follow fix those factors in order.


Even on a single accelerator, memory-bandwidth stalls, kernel launch gaps, and non-matmul operations prevent a model from sustaining datasheet peak throughput. MFU measures useful model FLOP/s divided by hardware peak FLOP/s over a stated measurement window, so an MFU of 0.50 means the workload achieves half of peak FLOP/s; synchronization and idle time within that window lower MFU even though they contribute no model FLOPs. Combining hardware peaks, link rates, reliability intervals, facility power, dollar rates, and utilization fractions in a single calculation requires a consistent set of dimensional prefixes and unit aliases.




Combining an accelerator memory capacity in gigabytes, a checkpoint payload in terabytes, and a link rate in gigabits per second produces silent factor-of-eight or base-2-versus-base-10 errors unless every table shares one dimensional system. Every quantitative example in this book therefore follows the unit conventions in table 18, where each row gives the multiplier \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) in 1 alias \(=\) \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) base. Data prefixes use decimal SI (\(\text{KB} = 10^3\) bytes, not 1024). Throughput quantities (FLOP/s, GB/s) combine these aliases with time; adding incompatible dimensions (bytes to FLOP/s) is a category error in napkin math, not a unit conversion.
Hardware capacity labels are the one deliberate exception. Reference tables may retain vendor nameplate numbers and labels; the byte budgets used in calculations follow the device assumptions stored in the book’s hardware registry. For example, the book models an 80 GB accelerator with \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes, so a node of eight such devices holds \(640 \times 2^{30}\) bytes rather than \(640 \times 10^9\). These are modeled capacity assumptions, not universal guarantees inferred from the labels. Every other data quantity, including model footprints, KV-cache sizes, checkpoint volumes, and collective payloads, uses those decimal SI prefixes. Where a worked example subtracts a computed footprint from a device capacity, the stored capacity byte budget is converted to decimal units alongside the footprint so that the arithmetic printed on the page is the arithmetic a reader can reproduce.

Fleet-scale back-of-envelope estimates stay comparable across chapters only when they draw from a single shared assumption sheet. Every napkin-math calculation in this book traces to a row in the reference tables of this appendix, and table 19 records whether that row comes from a datasheet, a fleet study, an MLSysIM model, an illustrative rate, or a book convention. Reliability rows set the failure clock, with failure a steady-state condition at 10,000 or more GPUs (Reliability Foundations models it in depth). Communication rows decide whether synchronous training is viable, and the 33× startup-latency gap between InfiniBand NDR and TCP explains why training clusters favor RDMA fabrics. Sustainability rows expose location as a lever, since grid carbon intensity differs by 82× between Norway and Poland. Capacity rows bridge peak hardware to useful throughput. At 8,192 GPUs, about 56 percent of ideal scaling is realized for the reference job at a fixed batch, and the listed overheads consume about 23 percent of wall time. When a deployment differs in fabric, region, MFU, or cluster size, substitute its values and re-evaluate the corresponding formulas.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Use this appendix to verify a fleet-scale estimate, swap in an alternative assumption (for example, NDR vs. HDR fabric, Quebec vs. Poland carbon intensity, or a different model FLOPs utilization (MFU)), or identify which numerical constants a chapter calculation depends on. Locate the relevant section, read the Value and Unit columns, and substitute those values into target arithmetic:

When auditing or substituting the baseline 175B training job: Use section 1.1 and the Foundational Hardware Recap section.
When scaling a calculation across cluster sizes or network fabrics: Use the Cluster Reference Configurations, Network and Interconnect Specifications, and Communication Model Parameters sections.
When estimating failure frequency or recovery downtime: Use the component lifetime and recovery tables in the Reliability Assumptions section.
When pricing power, water, carbon, or cloud infrastructure: Use the Sustainability Assumptions and Economic Assumptions sections.
When discounting peak FLOP/s to delivered throughput or checking units and sources: Use the Capacity Planning Assumptions and Unit Conventions sections, and trace each constant’s evidence class in section 1.2.

Three worked estimates in napkin math 1.1 combine these constants to calculate cluster failure rate, AllReduce time, and monthly carbon footprint. Hardware and link bandwidths are ceilings unless a chapter states an effective-bandwidth discount; treat the tables as this edition’s shared assumption sheet rather than immutable physical laws.

Napkin Math 1.1: Quick calculations with these assumptionsThese tables support quick distributed-systems napkin math. Three examples show how several assumptions combine.
Problem: How many GPU failures should a large training cluster expect per day?
Variables: Use a cluster of 8,192 GPUs and an individual GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) of 50,000 hours.
Math: The GPU failure rate is 8,192 GPUs/50,000 hours \(\approx\) 0.16 failures/hour, or roughly 3.9 failures/day.
Result: This estimate excludes network interface card (NIC), PSU, and cable failures. At 100,000 GPUs, the GPU-only rate is approximately 48 failures/day; adding NIC, PSU, and cable failures, whose MTTFs appear in table 6, raises the operational incident stream further.
Systems insight: At fleet scale, failure becomes a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event.
Problem: How long does one AllReduce of the gradients of a 70B model take?
Variables: Use BF16 parameters and InfiniBand NDR with a nominal byte rate of 50 GB/s per port.
Math: The gradient payload is 70 \(\times 10^9 \times\) 2 bytes = 140 GB. The ring AllReduce napkin estimate is 2 \(\times\) 140 GB/50 GB/s \(\approx\) 5.6 s.
Result: The collective can consume a significant fraction of a training step.
Systems insight: Pipeline and tensor parallelism exist partly to shrink the gradient volume each rank must communicate.
Problem: What is the monthly carbon footprint of a 10,000-GPU training run, and how much does the grid change it?
Variables: Each H100 draws 700 W at thermal design power (TDP). Use power usage effectiveness (PUE) 1.12, Quebec grid intensity 20 g/kWh, and Poland grid intensity 820 g/kWh.
Math: A GPU-only facility-power proxy is 10,000 GPUs \(\times\) 700 W \(\times\) 1.12 = 7.84 MW. In Quebec, 7.84 MW \(\times\) 720 h/month \(\times\) 20 g/kWh = 112.9 t CO\(_2\) per month.
Result: The same run in Poland emits 4,628.7 t, a 41× difference.
Systems insight: Grid carbon intensity can dominate the emissions difference for the same hardware, model, and training duration. This proxy excludes host, memory, network, and storage power; total IT power must include those loads before applying PUE for a complete facility estimate.

The relationship between cluster size and system behavior is not linear. A 256-GPU cluster might go days between failures; a 100,000-GPU cluster experiences multiple failures per hour. This nonlinearity is why Fault Tolerance and Fleet Orchestration treat failure as a continuous background process rather than an exceptional event. The network fabric determines whether gradient synchronization across those nodes takes milliseconds or seconds and whether pipeline parallelism is viable across node boundaries.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Distributed training and inference are bottlenecked by data movement between machines as often as by computation within them. The network assumptions fix bandwidth and latency for every interconnect tier, from NVLink/PCIe within a node (NVIDIA Corporation 2017, 2020; Choquette 2023), through InfiniBand, remote direct memory access (RDMA), and Ethernet fabrics (InfiniBand Trade Association 2000; Gangidi et al. 2024; NVIDIA 2026; Ethernet Alliance 2025), to the speed-of-light WAN floor (physics identity).


Splitting a single transformer layer across eight GPUs inside a server requires an all-reduce on every forward and backward pass, which is viable at hundreds of gigabytes per second over NVLink but stalls over a host PCIe bus. Cross-region communication introduces latency floors set by the speed of light in optical fiber. For a 5,000 km link (roughly New York to London), the minimum one-way latency is 5,000 km/200,000 km/s = 25 ms, orders of magnitude higher than intra-data-center latency. This physical constraint is why geo-distributed training uses asynchronous methods or careful placement of pipeline stages, and why federated learning (Edge Intelligence) tolerates stale gradients. Network specifications define how fast data moves across links and regions, but a multi-thousand-node training job can sustain those transfer rates only while every participating accelerator, network card, and switch remains healthy.

title: System Assumptions
text:
At fleet scale, component failures are statistical certainties rather than exceptional events. The reliability assumptions here fix MTTF for each major component class in a data-center GPU node and the time to detect and recover from failures. These values drive analysis in Fault Tolerance and scheduling in Fleet Orchestration. Deeper failure modeling appears in Reliability Foundations.


A single data-center GPU runs for tens of thousands of hours on average before failing, yet combining eight GPUs and eight NICs per server across a thousand nodes turns multi-year component lifetimes into a cluster interruption every few hours. The steady-state component MTTFs in table 6 exclude the early “infant mortality” period after deployment and the late “wear-out” period beyond rated lifetime, drawing on large-GPU research-cluster analysis (Kokolis et al. 2025), TPUv4 supercomputer resiliency and operations (Zu et al. 2024), and warehouse-scale machine design (Barroso et al. 2019).

The environmental impact of fleet-scale ML depends on three factors: how much power the facility draws beyond the IT equipment (PUE), how much water the cooling system consumes (water usage effectiveness (WUE)), and how much carbon the local grid emits per kilowatt-hour. title: System Assumptions
text:
Multiplying a cluster’s GPU count by the H100’s datasheet peak FLOP/s overstates delivered training throughput by more than a factor of three, because single-device kernel inefficiency, multi-node communication stalls, and out-of-step operational downtime each take a cut. The capacity-planning assumptions quantify the fraction of peak hardware performance that real workloads sustain on one device (MFU), how efficiently that performance scales as more machines are added (scaling efficiency), and what share of wall time is lost to operational pauses. Because these factors compound across the fleet, the planning equation is multiplicative:
\[ \EffectiveFleetThroughput = \DeviceCount\PeakRate \times \ModelFlopsUtilization \times \ScalingEfficiency \times (1 - \OperationalOverheadFraction) \]
Here \(\EffectiveFleetThroughput\) is effective fleet throughput, \(\DeviceCount\PeakRate\) is nominal cluster peak throughput. MFU is the single-device baseline measured over productive steps. \(\ScalingEfficiency\) captures the additional in-step losses from distribution, including communication and pipeline bubbles. \(\OperationalOverheadFraction\) removes only out-of-step checkpoint, recovery, and maintenance time. These windows must be disjoint: measured fleet-step MFU already includes scaling losses, so it must not be multiplied by scaling efficiency again. The three subsections that follow fix those factors in order.


Even on a single accelerator, memory-bandwidth stalls, kernel launch gaps, and non-matmul operations prevent a model from sustaining datasheet peak throughput. MFU measures useful model FLOP/s divided by hardware peak FLOP/s over a stated measurement window, so an MFU of 0.50 means the workload achieves half of peak FLOP/s; synchronization and idle time within that window lower MFU even though they contribute no model FLOPs. Combining hardware peaks, link rates, reliability intervals, facility power, dollar rates, and utilization fractions in a single calculation requires a consistent set of dimensional prefixes and unit aliases.

title: System Assumptions
text:
Combining an accelerator memory capacity in gigabytes, a checkpoint payload in terabytes, and a link rate in gigabits per second produces silent factor-of-eight or base-2-versus-base-10 errors unless every table shares one dimensional system. Every quantitative example in this book therefore follows the unit conventions in table 18, where each row gives the multiplier \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) in 1 alias \(=\) \(\UnitAliasMultiplier\) base. Data prefixes use decimal SI (\(\text{KB} = 10^3\) bytes, not 1024). Throughput quantities (FLOP/s, GB/s) combine these aliases with time; adding incompatible dimensions (bytes to FLOP/s) is a category error in napkin math, not a unit conversion.
Hardware capacity labels are the one deliberate exception. Reference tables may retain vendor nameplate numbers and labels; the byte budgets used in calculations follow the device assumptions stored in the book’s hardware registry. For example, the book models an 80 GB accelerator with \(80 \times 2^{30}\) bytes, so a node of eight such devices holds \(640 \times 2^{30}\) bytes rather than \(640 \times 10^9\). These are modeled capacity assumptions, not universal guarantees inferred from the labels. Every other data quantity, including model footprints, KV-cache sizes, checkpoint volumes, and collective payloads, uses those decimal SI prefixes. Where a worked example subtracts a computed footprint from a device capacity, the stored capacity byte budget is converted to decimal units alongside the footprint so that the arithmetic printed on the page is the arithmetic a reader can reproduce.

Two fleet-scale conventions deserve emphasis beyond the table because they recur in almost every cross-node or facility calculation:

Network bandwidth appears in both bit-rate (Gbps) and byte-rate (GB/s). Divide by 8 to convert Gbps to GB/s (for example, 400 Gb/s = 50 GB/s for InfiniBand NDR). Chapters use whichever form fits the calculation; byte-rate is usually easier for transfer-time estimates.
Carbon intensity uses gCO\(_2\)/kWh (grams of CO\(_2\) per kilowatt-hour). Multiply total energy (kWh) by regional carbon intensity to get emissions in grams, then divide by \(10^6\) for metric tons.

title: System Assumptions
text:
The reference tables in this appendix mix H100 datasheet ceilings, empirical failure rates from warehouse-scale fleets, modeled MLSysIM scaling curves, and illustrative cloud rental rates, and treating all four as interchangeable measurements would misstate what an estimate proves. Each section therefore carries an explicit source classification and primary bibliography in table 19, separating empirical hardware measurements from modeled scaling profiles and editorial conventions so a reader can see which numbers change with a hardware generation and which reflect a deployment choice.

title: System Assumptions
text: Fleet-scale back-of-envelope estimates stay comparable across chapters only when they draw from a single shared assumption sheet. Every napkin-math calculation in this book traces to a row in the reference tables of this appendix, and table 19 records whether that row comes from a datasheet, a fleet study, an MLSysIM model, an illustrative rate, or a book convention. Reliability rows set the failure clock, with failure a steady-state condition at 10,000 or more GPUs (Reliability Foundations models it in depth). Communication rows decide whether synchronous training is viable, and the 33× startup-latency gap between InfiniBand NDR and TCP explains why training clusters favor RDMA fabrics. Sustainability rows expose location as a lever, since grid carbon intensity differs by 82× between Norway and Poland. Capacity rows bridge peak hardware to useful throughput. At 8,192 GPUs, about 56 percent of ideal scaling is realized for the reference job at a fixed batch, and the listed overheads consume about 23 percent of wall time. When a deployment differs in fabric, region, MFU, or cluster size, substitute its values and re-evaluate the corresponding formulas.
